articles.text: Piedmont’s traditional pancake breakfast on the 4th of July will be held at the Veterans Hall, 401 Highland Avenue, on Monday before the Independence Day parade. Food will be served beginning at 8 a.m. The Pancake Breakfast is operated by the Piedmont Community Service Crew, a youth-led coed Venturing crew under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council, and created in 2004 by Ken Li, its current advisor. The entire event is youth-run, from start to finish. “Thanks to Piedmont Grocery and Village Market, most of the items are going to be donated, with just a few items still to be managed,” Li said. In addition to pancakes, the crew members will be serving sausages, fresh fruit, orange juice and coffee. Before COVID, the group would serve over 400 breakfasts to hungry parade goers. Seating will be different from past years due to COVID concerns, Li explained. An addition this year is ‘al fresco’ seating for the first time. “Per the city guidance, it’s going to be mostly outdoors, but with some limited ‘distanced’ indoor seating and a combination of outdoor tables and chairs on the patio of the Veterans Hall, plus along part of Vista Ave where a portion of the street will be blocked off and reserved for our guests,” he said “Diners can, of course, take their breakfasts ‘to go’ to Piedmont Park, or where they may have staked out their parade viewing spot along Highland Avenue.” The crew will use proceeds Photo courtesy of Ken Li Three PCSC volunteers serve breakfast last year, 2021.

articles.text: Chloe Fineman, a regular cast member of Saturday Night Live and a 2006 graduate of Piedmont High School, will return home next week to appear in Piedmont’s 55th Annual Fourth of July Parade. She recently finished her third season as one of the stars of SNL. Piedmont drama teacher Kim Taylor said, “Chloe is equally brilliant with comedy and drama”. As a sophomore at Piedmont High School she appeared on the Tonight Show with David Letterman as one of the winners of the Piedmont Bird Calling Show. As a junior, Fineman directed Metamorphoses by Mary Zimmerman, and as a senior she directed The Vagina Monologues by Eve Ensler. She also performed lead roles in The Visit by Friedrich Dürrenmatt and Crimes of the Heart by Beth Henley. articles.text: Alameda County ended its mask mandate, the only re-instated mandate in the Bay Area, on Saturday, June 25. County health officials announced the day before the lift that it will align with the state and rescind the local health order. “Conditions have stabilized following the sustained increases in case reports and hospitalizations we saw throughout May,” said Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss. “While we expect continued impacts from COVID-19 in the coming weeks and masks remain strongly recommended, it is appropriate to step down from the Health Office masking order at this time.” The Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD) reported that COVID-19 cases had peaked and continued to decline the week of June 21, and that new hospital admissions of COVID-19 patients had stabilized. The county was moved from the “high” level of community transmission to a “moderate” level last week, according to the Center for Disease Control (CDC) community transmission data tool. articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission will discussion the city’s housing policy update, which includes the draft Housing Element, on July 11. City staff and commissioners will provide a verbal update of the activities of staff leading up and since City Council’s decision to delay sending the draft Housing Element to the state last week. Lisa Wise Consulting is the consulting firm hired by the city to aid it in the drafting process. The meeting will be conducted in the City Council Chambers in City Hall at 5:30 p.m. Public comment can be made in-person, over via Zoom on your computer or smart phone. Visit https://piedmont-ca-gov. zoom.us/j/85368966443 to join the meeting. You can also provide comment by phone by dialing (669) 900-9128 and entering meeting number 853-6896-6443. You can view the 6th Cycle Housing Element prepared by the city and Lisa Wise Consulting by visiting https://www.piedmontishome.org.
articles.title: Planning Commission to discuss Housing Policy Update on July 11

articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost to the person being tested, and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. At this time, appointments are not required but encouraged. More information is available at https://cur.tv/piedmont. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702-9042, or visit their website at curative.com.

articles.text: Applications to City Hall for July 4 block party requests are due to City Hall by 5 p.m. on Wednesday, June 29. Residents may request street closures and barricades from the Public Works Department for Independence Day festivities. The permit is free. Provide your name, address, and phone number, and the name of the street you wish to close, range on the street closure, cross streets, and times of closure. The city also asks applicants to certify that one side of the street be kept open to provide access for emergency vehicles, and that COVID-19 safety protocols will be observed. The city will notify applicants on July 1 if the application for closure is approved. The application is available online at: https://docs.google. com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScTMRWcag2IL99_nUUFMCe- 8CD-wvqtzQVyZfLDGM-Kn3J7m6A/viewform. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. articles.text: The Alameda County Fair, the 7th largest in California, continues through July 10 at the Alameda County Fairgrounds, located at 4501 Pleasanton Avenue in Pleasanton. A plethora of events will transpire over the course of the fair, including the All-Alaskan Racing Pigs, musical events, movies on the lawn, carnival rides and a “drone show.” The fair is open from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily, and carnival hours are Wednesday through Sunday. Every night, a concert will be held at 8 p.m. A list of some of the performers is below. Entertainment at the fair includes a family fun stage, movies on the lawn, live music at the wine garden, and a fireworks display at 9:30 p.m. on July 1 at the Stella Artois Grandstand. The County Fair has live horse racing every Friday through Sunday, with post time beginning 1:45 p.m. For more details, and to purchase tickets, visit www.alamedacountyfair.com. You can also volunteer at the summer fair. About 900 volunteers of all ages help out at the fair each year. Some of the organizations that volunteer include local schools and colleges, youth groups, garden club members, Girl Scout troops, and performing arts groups. pages.text: Wednesday, June 29, 2022 3 Local Items June 29 - July 10 By Jay Russell QUESTION: What is the strangest thing you have eaten at the Piedmont Corporation yard? Asked on June 27 of the goats clearing foliage off the hillside above the Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. ARIES ARNOLD One time I ate my own beard. I enjoyed it so much I ate the beards off my wife and kids. Wednesday-Sunday June 29 – July 10 6 a.m., 7 p.m. June 22 School Board meeting 9 a.m., 4 p.m. Celebrate in Place – a July 4 Retrospective 10 a.m., 10 p.m. June 20 City Council meeting 4 p.m. June 15 Recreation Commission meeting By Jay Russell QUESTION: What is your favorite 4th of July memory? Asked of members of the Piedmont 4th of July Parade Committee on June 24. KATHY KELLEHER, Daughter of Parade Founder It was when I was six years old and on my first float, which was a crepe paper American flag. I waved to people, and felt very proud. We had Betsy Ross and Uncle Sam in a pickup truck leading our float. WINSTON HOOVER We all love license plates, but I am the only goat in this herd to have eaten an Alaskan license plate. EILEEN LICK I once ate a Piedmont Azalea on a dare from a friend. Turns out they are toxic, and boy did I have a stomach ache. For more information on future programming, call KCOM at City Hall at 510-420-3083. READ IT IN THE POST RAM RAMSTEIN Some of my friends call me a picky eater because I’m a strict vegan. The weirdest thing I have eaten is a worm, accidentally. Yuck. BILL SHOCKEY I chewed through the electric fence once when we lost power, so the herd had a night out on the town. ROLAND LAZZAROTTO, Parade Starter I liked the time we had horses and a guy assigned to walk behind the horses to clean up after them. He had a wheelbarrow painted blue with white stars, and he was given a golden shovel. CAROLYN BRUCK, Parade Committee Thinking back through all the years, the creative neighborhood floats were always a highlight for me. The ones from Bellevue Ave. – the Gruber family & neighbors – always showed such imagination and creativity. One year they had the White House, and another the Statue of Liberty. JOHN MORRISON, Parade Car Organizer I had a ‘54 Corvette for several years. My favorite times were driving it in the parade around 20 years ago. I have since sold the car and miss it. CARLA BETTS, Parade Committee Chair Every year for the past 22 years has been a wonderful memory for me. There are a few wonderful repeat entries, and new and exciting ones that come and go, but it is always a beautiful day in the neighborhood. ITCHY RICHIE It’s not weird to us, but I love to eat poison oak. For some reason it doesn’t affect us goats. The Question Kid is able to talk to goats and asks non-prescient questions. MICHAEL BRUCK, Former Mayor That assumes I retain any memories at my age. I would say the annual San Carlos block parties. They are a tradition and a lot of fun and we are back at it this year. articles.text: David Martin’s House Party big band will perform in Piedmont Park on the 4th of July this year immediately following the parade. The concert show will begin at approximately11:30 a.m. on a large stage in the park on Monday, July 4 One of San Francisco’s premier party bands for 25 years, this “interactive” 11-piece allstar group has gained a national reputation for their high energy performances, incredible musical variety, and “anything can happen” hi-jinx. Recent appearances include The Waldorf Astoria in New York City, special Napa Valley performances for Wine Spectator Magazine, concertizing in Maui at the Hyatt Regency Kaanapali and La Costa Resort in Carlsbad; selling out in Reno at the Grand Sierra Resort’s VIP New Years Eve 2010; and entertaining at numerous benefit galas in the greater Bay Area. David Martin is a Bay Area native who began his musical career at the age of six. Known for his powerful vocals and sparkling guitar work, David was a founding member of legendary San Francisco “New Wave” faces The LLoyds and The Buzztones. Martin has assembled a remarkable group of established musician/entertainers including Bobby Strickland (Todd Rundgren, Phil Lesh), Byron Allred (Steve Miller, Todd Rundgren), Gerald Goudeau (Race & Rhythm), Christina Sabatelli (Tubes, Starship), Tim Allen (Silvercreek), Timo Guierrez (Viva Brazil), John Mader (Booker T, Pee Wee Ellis), and Rob Russ (Eddie Money). Rounding out the group’s lineup are the dance artists Sandra Leathley and Stephanie Romano. articles.text: Origins of Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade In 2000, Piedmont lost Dick Johnson, the city’s beloved banjo-playing founder of the 4th of July Parade. As chairman of the Piedmont Recreation Commission in 1965, the man everyone called Pear decided to start a parade. In the early 1960’s under the leadership of neighbors Mary Ellen Sherry, Dorothy Carter and Carolyn Bostrom Renton, a block party was established to keep the children entertained on Independence Day. Events included bike decoration and a parade, a watermelon-eating contest, Professor Arthur Sherry reading the Declaration of Independence, a bar-bque, and swimming at 1504 Oakland Avenue. The concept of creating a citywide parade was pure Pear. “He said it was too quiet in Piedmont in the summer, and something needed to be done”, recalled close friend Ed Bartlett. “Pear came up with the idea of a parade. I told him it would never work – everybody’s at Tahoe. It took off right away. That’s the Dick Johnson plays his banjo with the Yerba Buena Jazz Band in the 1970s. kind of person Pear was.” Johnson was highly regarded for his prodigious musical talent. He wrote, produced, directed and performed in dozens of shows at The Family Club, Claremont Country Club and the Athenian-Niles Club. Every year on the 4th of July, his Yerba Buena Jazz Band rode by on the back of a truck, putting smiles on faces everywhere. The legacy of Dick Johnson is being carried out by his daughter, Kathy Kelleher, who is a member of the July 4th Parade Committee.
articles.title: Piedmont celebrates Dick Johnson’s legacy

articles.text: The July 4 Parade Committee chose a patriotic theme for this year’s event: “Remember Why it’s the Fourth of July.” It’s a theme with intention, explained committee member Roland Lazzarotto. “I think that it is a suggestion that we look back at history and remember why we celebrate July 4 and Independence. We seem to be somewhat divided now as a country with political factions taking extreme views on the constitution and amendments. We may even see a former president convicted of numerous crimes. Yet the country will move on,” Lazzarotto explained. Lazzarotto, who serves as the parade’s official starter at the corner of Highland and Park Way, confirmed that the theme generates more discussion each year than any other item being considered by the 10-member committee. “We review themes from the past 20 years. We try to have a theme that will inspire neighborhood groups to enter a float and have something to build on,” he said. “A theme that has potential to be interpreted in multiple ways is a plus. This theme asks a question and that forces everyone to answer the question in their own mind.” Lazzarotto explained that the committee “tries to avoid the obvious political theme” but wanted to remain topical. “We like a theme that rolls off the tongue when spoken. We narrow it down to 3 or 4 then there is some lobbying on the part of committee members who really like one theme over another. In the end it is a consensus,” he said. The July 4 parade, the largest public event in the city, returns in full-force this Monday starting at 11 a.m. on Highland Avenue.
articles.title: 4th of July Parade theme: “Remember Why it’s the Fourth of July”

articles.text: At the June 22 school board meeting, the board announced the hiring of Dr. Donald Evans as Interim Superintendent for the next year. During the meeting, Board President Cory Smegal outlined the hiring process which led to Evans’ appointment by the board. Dr. Evans, who was in attendance, introduced himself at the meeting in advance of his July 1 start date. – Cory Smegal President, Piedmont School Board “It is so good to be here. After my six years and retiring in Berkeley, I thought I would never be back to do this again. But there is no other place I would want to be than here. So, I thank you for this opportunity, and even though it is just a year, it will be a great year,” said Evans. W h e n R a n d y B o o ke r announced his resignation as Piedmont Superintendent in late Spring, School Board President Cory Smegal and board member Amal Smith spoke with the California School Board Association (CSBA) for advice on the best way to search for a new superintendent. They were advised Dr. Donald Evans, Piedmont School District’s newly named interim Superintendent, was introduced to the School Board on June 22. to issue a Request for Proposal (RFP) and use a search firm. Smegal and Board Vice President Megan Pillsbury spoke with several search firms and the district’s legal advisors and were told they could pursue the following options: 1) Use a search firm starting in late May and into the summer to try and have a Superintendent in place before school starts in August 2) Appoint an internal candidate as Interim Superintendent 3) Appoint an external candidate as Interim Superintendent “The board discussed these options and we agreed that doing a search starting in late May over the summer would not be in the district’s best interest,” said Smegal. “It would not provide enough time or availability for community engagement. Parents, teachers and staff who we would like to be involved in this process deserve a break this summer. It was going to be tricky to pull this off over the summertime,” Smegal added.
articles.title: Hiring process described for Interim Superintendent Evans

Anything more than a sports team is significant. The smallest girls team roster is six, on the girls golf team, so 55 is definitely significant,” said Molly Lloyd, an organizer of the Title IX campaign. articles.text: The artificial turf at Becker Field at Havens Elementary School is in the process of being replaced. The process of pulling up the old turf began on Wednesday June 22 and installation is expected to be completed by the week of July 18. The new turf will cost Piedmont School District approximately $298,000, Director of Facilities Pete Palmer said the new Fieldturf product has a warranty of 7-10 years. Originally installed in 2010, the field was named after Piedmont resident Mark Becker who designed the new Havens School. At the time, Havens was the only elementary school without immediate access to a grass field. The previous turf consisted of artificial turf laid over a coconut husk infill and drainage mat. The composition kept the field easy to maintain, at a moderate temperate and soft for active kids. The expected life span of that turf was 6-8 years, but it has been in use for 12 years. The new surface will have an infill of natural cork and sand, similar to Witter Field. The field is used for many P.E. activities, by Piedmont Soccer Club, and when Witter Field floods, for high school practices. Parents at Havens raised nearly 10% of the cost of the field, and families contributing $1,000 or more, were given the opportunity to have their names “creatively displayed” around the field. “A big thank you must go out to Havens parents club for raising approximately $25,000 in donations to help pay for the new turf,” said Palmer. In the second week of construction, on Monday June 27, the Fieldturf at Becker Playfield at Havens School is removed and replaced by a new surface.
articles.title: Becker Field turf being replaced

articles.text: Sally Ride Club Teen Volunteers “Do you weep when things go wrong on the job?” asked an interviewer before her first space flight, “Will the flight affect your reproductive organs?” Dr. Sally Ride was the youngest American to go to space, the first American woman in space, and the first known LGBTQ+ astronaut. For the Galaxy Explorers, student volunteers at Chabot Space and Science Center, her accomplishments are memorialized in the eponymous LGBTQ+ project team: Sally Ride Club. Her legacy is unmistakable. Yet her whole life, people waited for her to fail. Ride was born in 1951, a time when women’s career options were limited. However, Ride’s tennis prowess gave her access to scholarships for school and even introduced her to her future partner of 27 years, Dr. Tamara O’Shaughnessy. Ultimately, Ride gave up a potential career as a professional tennis player to follow what she loved: science. When NASA opened up their selection to women for the first time in 1978, Ride applied as a doctoral candidate at Stanford. She ultimately became one of the five female candidates selected, and she began her astronaut training the same year she received her PhD in astrophysics. Five years of NASA training and ground crew positions later, she boarded the Challenger and was hailed as the first American woman in space. As the expert with the shuttle’s robotic arm, she helped launch crucial satellites into orbit. Five months after her first mission she returned Sally Ride and Tam O’Shaughnessy with their dog, Gypsy, in 1992. for a second mission to continue her work. However, following the 1986 Challenger disaster, Ride’s third flight was put on hold and she instead served on the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident. Later, she retired from NASA to teach and uplift women in STEM. After she came back to the ground from her second mission, Ride also fell in love with Tamara O’Shaughnessy, a doctor in school psychology. Ride and O’Shaughnessy were strong advocates of science, writing children’s books together and founding Sally Ride Science to encourage girls in STEM. It was only after Ride’s death that it was revealed that they also had a successful and long-lasting relationship together. Ride was able to rise up despite the obstacles of sexism. She was a brave and powerful force that changed the way that women in science were perceived, and she also made history as the first LGBTQ+ astronaut. Most people did not realize Ride was a lesbian until her obituary in 2012 revealed that she had been with O’Shaughnessy for 27 years. Chabot Space and Science Center’s Galaxy Explorers honor her story and keep her name alive with Sally Ride Club, an LGBTQ+ club and project team. Sally Ride Club is dedicated to making STEM more inclusive, in honor of Ride and for all LGBTQ+ trailblazers. She may have been unable to come out in her lifetime, but today Dr. Sally Ride is recognized as a true LGBTQ+ icon. Chabot Space and Science Center, is located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. You can check out the list of Chabot Space and Science Center clubs at the following link: Galaxy Explorers – Chabot Space Times. articles.title: Why we’re called Sally Ride Club

articles.text: Sports, games & crafts offered to middle school students Lucas Scherman, son of Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Scherman, returns for the second year to lead Scherman Summer Camp. Campers will learn new games, get fresh air, practice new skills, make friends and be themselves. Campers will have fun playing kickball, double-dutch, capture the flag, poker, dominos, and more. Lucas, aided by brothers Julian, 19, and Quincy, 15, will teach the art of wood-burning and how to make paracord survival bracelets. Scherman Summer Camp is a screen-free, good old-fashioned camp. The camp is open to students entering grades 6-9, and will be held at Wildwood School lower playground. One-week sessions begin the week of July 11 and continue for nine weeks. pages.text: Wednesday, June 29, 2022 7 SUMMER THOUGHTS Why we’re called Sally Ride Club By Anabel Loucks and Chabot Sally Ride Club Teen Volunteers “Do you weep when things go wrong on the job?” asked an interviewer before her first space flight, “Will the flight affect your reproductive organs?” Dr. Sally Ride was the youngest American to go to space, the first American woman in space, and the first known LGBTQ+ astronaut. For the Galaxy Explorers, student volunteers at Chabot Space and Science Center, her accomplishments are memorialized in the eponymous LGBTQ+ project team: Sally Ride Club. Her legacy is unmistakable. Yet her whole life, people waited for her to fail. Ride was born in 1951, a time when women’s career options were limited. However, Ride’s tennis prowess gave her access to scholarships for school and even introduced her to her future partner of 27 years, Dr. Tamara O’Shaughnessy. Ultimately, Ride gave up a potential career as a professional tennis player to follow what she loved: science. When NASA opened up their selection to women for the first time in 1978, Ride applied as a doctoral candidate at Stanford. She ultimately became one of the five female candidates selected, and she began her astronaut training the same year she received her PhD in astrophysics. Five years of NASA training and ground crew positions later, she boarded the Challenger and was hailed as the first American woman in space. As the expert with the shuttle’s robotic arm, she helped launch crucial satellites into orbit. Five months after her first mission she returned Sally Ride and Tam O’Shaughnessy with their dog, Gypsy, in 1992. for a second mission to continue her work. However, following the 1986 Challenger disaster, Ride’s third flight was put on hold and she instead served on the Presidential Commission on the Space Shuttle Challenger Accident. Later, she retired from NASA to teach and uplift women in STEM. After she came back to the ground from her second mission, Ride also fell in love with Tamara O’Shaughnessy, a doctor in school psychology. Ride and O’Shaughnessy were strong advocates of science, writing children’s books together and founding Sally Ride Science to encourage girls in STEM. It was only after Ride’s death that it was revealed that they also had a successful and long-lasting relationship together. Ride was able to rise up despite the obstacles of sexism. She was a brave and powerful force that changed the way that women in science were perceived, and she also made history as the first LGBTQ+ astronaut. Most people did not realize Ride was a lesbian until her obituary in 2012 revealed that she had been with O’Shaughnessy for 27 years. Chabot Space and Science Center’s Galaxy Explorers honor her story and keep her name alive with Sally Ride Club, an LGBTQ+ club and project team. Sally Ride Club is dedicated to making STEM more inclusive, in honor of Ride and for all LGBTQ+ trailblazers. She may have been unable to come out in her lifetime, but today Dr. Sally Ride is recognized as a true LGBTQ+ icon. Chabot Space and Science Center, is located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. You can check out the list of Chabot Space and Science Center clubs at the following link: Galaxy Explorers – Chabot Space Times. Becker Field turf being replaced By Jay Russell The artificial turf at Becker Field at Havens Elementary School is in the process of being replaced. The process of pulling up the old turf began on Wednesday June 22 and installation is expected to be completed by the week of July 18. The new turf will cost Piedmont School District approximately $298,000, Director of Facilities Pete Palmer said the new Fieldturf product has a warranty of 7-10 years. Originally installed in 2010, the field was named after Piedmont resident Mark Becker who designed the new Havens School. At the time, Havens was the only elementary school without immediate access to a grass field. The previous turf consisted of artificial turf laid over a coconut husk infill and drainage mat. The composition kept the field easy to maintain, at a moderate temperate and soft for active kids. The expected life span of that turf was 6-8 years, but it has been in use for 12 years. The new surface will have an infill of natural cork and sand, similar to Witter Field. The field is used for many P.E. activities, by Piedmont Soccer Club, and when Witter Field floods, for high school practices. Parents at Havens raised nearly 10% of the cost of the field, and families contributing $1,000 or more, were given the opportunity to have their names “creatively displayed” around the field. “A big thank you must go out to Havens parents club for raising approximately $25,000 in donations to help pay for the new turf,” said Palmer. In the second week of construction, on Monday June 27, the Fieldturf at Becker Playfield at Havens School is removed and replaced by a new surface. articles.text: The Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s Ensemble group embarked on its first international tour in two years due to the worldwide pandemic. On June 14, the students boarded a plane in San Francisco and after a 24-hour travel day, arrived in Frankfurt, Germany. The group of 50 students, choral directors and chaperones experienced some travel woes, including airport delays and a long bus ride, but arrived safely in Herning, Denmark on June 16. During their stay in Denmark, the students visited Deep Forest Art Land, owned by Dorte Bille, conductor of the Midtvest Junior Choir. The open-air art center is defined as “Skovsnogen,” a space “that unfolds under the open sky.” On the fourth day of their journey the choir serenaded the Mayor of Ikast, Denmark, Ib Lauristen, as well as the student body of The International School. The Ensemble group prepared for their major concert in Herning at Valgmenighedskirke, a church Singers enjoy a summer day at Deep Forest Art Land, art center in Kibaek, Denmark. This exhibition is “Skovsnogen” – a space not defined by walls or ceiling but that unfolds under the open sky. Artistic Director Eric Tuan (center) speaks to the students before boarding a double-decker bus from Germany to Denmark. Ensemble singers in front of Notburgakirche, the main church in Hochhausen, Germany. Charlotte Rowan, director of Herning Kirkes Drengekor (Boy’s Chorus) with Eric Tuan, Artistic Director of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. with stunning acoustics. On June 20, they bid farewell to their homestay families and traveled to Germany by bus. Upon arrival in Hamburg, the Piedmont choristers met their host choir, Mädchenchor Hamburg, and enjoyed dinner together following a concert in a small church. Choir members, led by their Artistic Director Eric Tuan, spent nearly two weeks traveling to landmark churches and venues in Germany and Denmark, including Mosbach Abbey, a former Benedictine Monastery near Heidelberg, where the Choir’s final tour concert was held. The Choirs returned home yesterday, June 28. Singers in Ensemble greet students from The International School in Ikast, Denmark. Ensemble members on a 3-1/2 hour bus trip from Hamburg, Germany to Herning, Denmark. Piedmont Singers with their “homestays” eating Danish bread on a stick.

articles.text: Piedmont Police Officer Tyler Petit received two pins from the California Highway Patrol for recovering stolen cars. Petit has been a police officer in Piedmont for four years. The awards are known as the Gold Pin. To be eligible an officer, during a 12-month period, must meet one of the following criteria: 1) Make six arrests in separate incidents of rolling stolen vehicles. 2) Recover a total of 12 stolen vehicles 3) Develop information resulting in the identification of a vehicle theft ring, make subsequent arrests of two or more suspects, and recover at least 10 vehicles. Piedmont police are alerted to stolen vehicles from the automatic license plate reader (ALPR) system. Verifying the legitimacy of license plates can also be done on readers located inside patrol cars. “The dispatcher will tell where it was stolen, if it was a carjacking or a strong-arm crime, and whether a gun was involved,” said Petit. Petit said he has gained a lot of knowledge about what is involved Piedmont Police Sergeant Robert Jaime (left) and Captain Chris Monahan with Officer Tyler Petit after he was awarded two pins by the California Highway Patrol. when pulling over a stolen car. “As far as anxiety goes, you just adapt to it because you do it so often. It is something you are mentally prepared for,” said Petit. The weekly log commonly shows as many as 15 ALPR triggers per week, most of which are stolen vehicles. The system can also be triggered by a stolen plate. “It has become the trend. These guys know cities are using the license plate technology so they get around it by switching the license plates [from a car on the street],” explained Petit. Some people believe that cameras are an invasion of privacy, but Petit sees them as less intrusive than tracking devices in every phone or modern vehicle. “Police officers aren’t sitting there all day waiting for [residents] to come home and eat dinner with [their] kids. We are waiting for that felony vehicle to enter a town we try to keep as safe as possible and either prevent them from coming in or try to capture them if we can,” said Petit. Piedmont officers Jason Germano and Jasdeep Singh also received 10851 CHP pins for recovering stolen vehicles. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Provided is a recap of five Piedmont baseball teams that competed in the 32nd Annual Millbrae Baseball Tournament Friday through Sunday, June 24-26. Piedmont Baseball Foundation had one championship win, two other championship appearances, and another semifinals berth. 8 & Under Piedmont Bulldogs The Piedmont Bulldogs Overlay team traveled to Millbrae to compete in the Silver Division. On Friday night, the Bulldogs lost 26-5 to the heavy-hitting Peninsula Pumas, but rallied to win the tournament. The Bulldogs bounced back on Saturday with a 21-7 win over the Pacifica Sea Dogs 21-7. In Sunday’s playoff bracket they defeated the No. 4 Sea Dogs 19-6 in the quarterfinals and won the semifinals with a 10-7 in victory over the South City All Stars. Once in the championship game on Sunday, they rolled past the San Bruno Gold, 7-1. The Bulldogs were led by the infield defense of Nicolas Bivens at short stop, Clive Alanis at third base, Teddy Dietrick at PA, Arian Singh at second base, Max Carver against the Millbrae Blue. Next up for the Wildcats is the Foster City tournament beginning July 5. 10 & Under Piedmont Panthers The Piedmont Panthers played four games and overcame two losses in the pool stage. In the playoffs, they defeated No. 3 seed Millbrae Blue in an exciting 8-7 battle in the first round. They went on to play the Millbrae Gold team in the semi-finals, eventually losing 8-3. 11 & Under Piedmont Tigers The Tigers entered Millbrae looking to become three-peat champions after winning the title at the 8U and 10U levels. Piedmont started off with an 8-3 win over San Bruno Green’s 12 & Under team and followed with a dramatic walk off 9-8 win over South City Fog. Ben McMurtry had multiple hits. The Tigers then topped San Bruno Green 7-4 in the semifinals. The championship game marked a rematch with the Fog, but Piedmont fell short 13-10 in a high-powered offensive game. The Tigers next play in the Alex McLin Courage Classic in Lafayette beginning July 14. The 8 & Under Bulldogs stand proudly with their championship trophies after defeating the San Bruno Gold 7-1. at catcher and Austin Gray at first base. The offense was anchored by Colin Perrin with multiple deep hits to the outfield and Cy Leonard and Cassius Canada helping close out San Bruno with hits in the top of the sixth inning. 8 & Under Piedmont Cobras The Piedmont Cobras playing a separate bracket, opened with a 19-4 win over the Half Moon Bay Pirates and 15-1 over the Millbrae Gold. In the championship game against the San Bruno Green, the Piedmont lost 9-1 and placed second after holding San Bruno scoreless through 3 innings. They will play a tournament in San Carlos beginning July 11. 9 & Under Piedmont Wildcats The Piedmont Wildcats played four games in three days, highlighted by a 7-4 victory in the first round of Sunday’s playoffs with a combined no-hitter by Oliver Hayashi and Elliott Chan to defeat the Peninsula Pumas. Prior to Sunday’s game, the Wildcats lost narrowly 8-7 in the pool stage The 11 & Under Tigers reached the championship game. The 10 & Under Panthers reached the semifinals of the Millbrae Tournament.

articles.text: After defeating Portugal’s Nuno Borges, he faces Richard Gasquet Former Piedmont tennis player Mackie McDonald is set to compete in the second round of the Wimbledon after defeating Portugal’s Nuno Borges in straight sets, 6-4, 6-4, 7-6 (7-3) on Tuesday, June 28. He will now face France’s Richard Gasquet on Thursday, June 30, in the second round. Mackie McDonald lifts his first after defeating Nuno Borges in the first round of the Wimbledon on Tuesday. McDonald was initially scheduled to play the tournament’s No. 14 seeded Marin Čilić, but the Croatian was forced to withdraw after testing positive for COVID-19. This opened the door for McDonald, No. 55 on the ATP ladder, to face the world’s No. 123 ranked Borges. Mackie was solid against Borges, recording 10 aces and was able to land 72 percent of his first serves. He took two of five break points as the receiver, totaling 32 points. He had a very strong two sets, starting both the first and second with a 4-2 advantage after stealing two games as the returner in both sets from the Portuguese. In the third and final set, McDonald and Borges traded points as the server all the way to 6-6, forcing a seven-point tiebreaker. In the breaker, Borges held a 3-1 advantage after earning a break point. However, McDonald took a game as the returner to make it 3-2, then went ahead 4-3 as the server thanks to a ball into the net by Borges followed by a faulty return by the Portuguese on his first attempt to hit Mackie’s serve. From there, McDonald won another game as the returner after a long rally that resulted in Borges angling a shot out of bounds after approaching the net, 5-3. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, June 29, 2022 Sports 5 Piedmont squads compete in Millbrae Baseball Tournament Provided is a recap of five Piedmont baseball teams that competed in the 32nd Annual Millbrae Baseball Tournament Friday through Sunday, June 24-26. Piedmont Baseball Foundation had one championship win, two other championship appearances, and another semifinals berth. 8 & Under Piedmont Bulldogs The Piedmont Bulldogs Overlay team traveled to Millbrae to compete in the Silver Division. On Friday night, the Bulldogs lost 26-5 to the heavy-hitting Peninsula Pumas, but rallied to win the tournament. The Bulldogs bounced back on Saturday with a 21-7 win over the Pacifica Sea Dogs 21-7. In Sunday’s playoff bracket they defeated the No. 4 Sea Dogs 19-6 in the quarterfinals and won the semifinals with a 10-7 in victory over the South City All Stars. Once in the championship game on Sunday, they rolled past the San Bruno Gold, 7-1. The Bulldogs were led by the infield defense of Nicolas Bivens at short stop, Clive Alanis at third base, Teddy Dietrick at PA, Arian Singh at second base, Max Carver against the Millbrae Blue. Next up for the Wildcats is the Foster City tournament beginning July 5. 10 & Under Piedmont Panthers The Piedmont Panthers played four games and overcame two losses in the pool stage. In the playoffs, they defeated No. 3 seed Millbrae Blue in an exciting 8-7 battle in the first round. They went on to play the Millbrae Gold team in the semi-finals, eventually losing 8-3. 11 & Under Piedmont Tigers The Tigers entered Millbrae looking to become three-peat champions after winning the title at the 8U and 10U levels. Piedmont started off with an 8-3 win over San Bruno Green’s 12 & Under team and followed with a dramatic walk off 9-8 win over South City Fog. Ben McMurtry had multiple hits. The Tigers then topped San Bruno Green 7-4 in the semifinals. The championship game marked a rematch with the Fog, but Piedmont fell short 13-10 in a high-powered offensive game. The Tigers next play in the Alex McLin Courage Classic in Lafayette beginning July 14. The 8 & Under Bulldogs stand proudly with their championship trophies after defeating the San Bruno Gold 7-1. at catcher and Austin Gray at first base. The offense was anchored by Colin Perrin with multiple deep hits to the outfield and Cy Leonard and Cassius Canada helping close out San Bruno with hits in the top of the sixth inning. 8 & Under Piedmont Cobras The Piedmont Cobras playing a separate bracket, opened with a 19-4 win over the Half Moon Bay Pirates and 15-1 over the Millbrae Gold. In the championship game against the San Bruno Green, the Piedmont lost 9-1 and placed second after holding San Bruno scoreless through 3 innings. They will play a tournament in San Carlos beginning July 11. 9 & Under Piedmont Wildcats The Piedmont Wildcats played four games in three days, highlighted by a 7-4 victory in the first round of Sunday’s playoffs with a combined no-hitter by Oliver Hayashi and Elliott Chan to defeat the Peninsula Pumas. Prior to Sunday’s game, the Wildcats lost narrowly 8-7 in the pool stage The 11 & Under Tigers reached the championship game. The 10 & Under Panthers reached the semifinals of the Millbrae Tournament. Wednesday, June 29, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. LUKE HARRIS Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2021 Carleton College Class of 2025 Luke Harris just finished his freshman year at Carleton College in Minnesota as an AllMIAC selection after becoming a starter for the Knights. He finished last season with 710 total minutes played, shooting 47 percent from the field and converting 17 of 46 three-point attempts. He finished with 283 points, 72 assists, 21 steals, and five blocks. The Posy named Harris its 2021 Athlete of the Year following his senior campaign at Piedmont High. He finished his high school career with over 1,200 points, concluding the pandemic shortened 2021 season with 383 points, a sparkling 55 percent shooting, 85 free throws made, 46 assists, and 33 steals. A three-year starter at Piedmont, he’s part of three highly successful years. The team posted a 21-11 record in his sophomore season. He was the leading scorer on the North Coast Section championship team that had a school record 24-6 season. What is your workout program this summer? I am doing shooting workouts and open gyms at the high school 3 times a week, then plyometrics and weightlifting on the days in between What are your fitness goals for this summer? My fitness goals for the summer are to get in great cardiovascular shape while still maintaining the muscle that I put on during the school year. How are you measuring your development? I am measuring my development by my ability to run for long periods of time, and trying to increase the duration week by week. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am doing shooting workouts with my dad, and I am working with a basketball trainer other days. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? I received honorable mention all-conference and all first year team at Carleton this past year. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Don’t let anyone else determine the outcome of your athletic career except yourself. Make sure that your work ethic matches your goals. PARKER TERRILL Track and Field Piedmont High Class of 2022 University of California Class of 2026 Parker Terrill was the Post’s Co-Athlete of the Year in 2022 after making PHS history in the pole vault, the 4x400 relay team, and decathlon. He’s set to continue his athletic career as a Golden Bear at the University of California. Terrill broke his own pole vault record three times throughout 2022 after initially setting a high mark of 14-feet, 2- inches on March 5 at the Clayton Valley Relays. He vaulted of 16-feet, 1-inch at the State Meet in Clovis on May 28. Piedmont’s top-five all-time pole vault record is as follows: 1. Parker Terrill, 16 feet, 1 inch (2022) 2. Marshall Wentworth, 14 feet (2011) 3. Irving Moore, 13 feet (1940) 4. Alex Harrison, 12 feet, 7 inches (2016) 5. John Hind, 12 feet, 6 inches (1957) Terrill ran the anchor leg in the 4x400 relay with Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Parker Long. Their time of 3:21.77 broke the school records set 33 years ago by a team led by Piedmont Hall of Fame member Gordon Johnson. Competing in the decathlon at the Del Campo Decathlon on April 16, he won with 5,964 total points, the second-highest score in the United States. He will Staff Photo Parker Terrill was the Post’s 2022 Co-Athlete of the Year. He will continue competing collegiately at the University of California, including the decathlon. focus on pole vault in college, but will also compete in the decathlon. What is your workout program this summer? I’ve recently been given a summer workout plan from my coach at UC Berkeley. It’s a great workout that targets hamstrings, explosiveness when jumping, and reactivity. What are your fitness goals for the summer? To continue training and developing in my events. How are you measuring your development? With my progress through my training. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Currently, I’m training on my own. But in the upcoming weeks I’ll be working with my coaches from Berkeley and Piedmont. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Setting Piedmont’s record in the pole vault. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? I’d say that the biggest thing for aspiring athletes is to find why you’re doing your sport. Whenever something goes poorly, go back to the question and remind yourself why you’re competing. Using those reasons, build up your drive and never give up. helped the Highlanders go 19-9 overall last season on their way to the Shoreline title, earning a firstteam All-League selection in the process. In 2022, Aikawa finished tied for the team-lead in hits with 29 and 25 runs scored, along with four doubles, one triple, one home run, seven RBIs, and a batting average of .363. What is your workout program this summer? My workout program has been mainly to maintain my weight and strength. I am playing in several tournaments that are over a week long, so I try to work out 4-5 times a week after the games. Most of the workouts focus on my entire body instead of specific areas because I can’t afford to be sore on game days. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My primary goal is to increase my arm strength. I’m also working on my mental fitness when reflecting on my play. How are you measuring your development? I’m measuring my development through my play this summer. This is a crucial for my recruitment; I’ve put in a lot of work in order to do my best this summer. I measure my development through the quality of the play I try to achieve in the games. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? It is currently a mix. I work on my own, with my dad, friends, and coaches. I am also working with my trainer to do more workouts when time is available. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? The most recent milestone was being invited to the 2022 Area Code Oakland Athletics tryout because I was recognized as a top player in the upcoming senior class in the Northern California. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Be confident in yourself and put in the work. Once someone believes in themself and they put serious work in, they can reach the goals they want to achieve. MICHAEL AIKAWA Baseball Luke Harris was the Post’s Athlete of the Year in 2021. He recently finished his freshman season at Carleton College with an AllConference selection. Piedmont High Class of 2023 Michael Aikawa was our 2021 Sophomore of the Year and is entering a critical senior campaign as a member of Piedmont High’s Class of 2023. He’s currently in the midst of a busy summer playing baseball on a travel team and competing in some high-level tournaments. articles.text: A preview of this year’s course and favorite riders This year’s Tour de France marks the 109th edition of La Grande Boucle, starting with Friday, July 1’s Grand Départ in Copenhagen, Denmark. The world’s best known cycling race finishes at the Champs-Élysées in Paris on Sunday, July 24, after 3,328 kilometers of racing. This year is the first time the race has begun in Denmark. It is considered a long time coming for the Danes, given that Copenhagen is considered one of the world’s best cycling cities and the country has approximately 12,000 kilometers of bike routes. The city was set to host last year’s Grand Départ, but it moved to France due to COVID related scheduling conflicts. Denmark will host the first three days of the tour, beginning with a 13-kilometer (8.1 miles) time trial through Copenhagen followed by two flat stages, including a 199-kilometer ride from Roskilde to Nyborg in Stage 2 and 182 kilometers in Stage 3 from Vejle to Sønderborg. After a rest day, the Tour turns up the intensity without a flat course for nine consecutive stages. That could be a catalyst toward Tadej Pogačar winning his third consecutive tour. Stages 4-6 provides a collective 327 kilometers of hill riding, including 19.4 kilometers of Stage 5 featuring a cobblestone path that could contribute to crashes. Stage 6 starts in Binche, Belgium. The next stage is the first mountain course from France’s Tomblaine to La Planche des Belles Filles, providing 176 kilometers on the first summit finish of this year’s event. Stage 8 is a medium-mountain stage, 184 kilometers from Dole to Lausanne, Switzerland, the fourth different country in this year’s tour. Stage 9 features a climb into the Alps for 183 kilometers from Aigle, Switzerland to Châtel, France. Stage 10 is a medium-mountain 148-kilometer course that ends with a 19.2-kilometer summit finish at Megève. Stage 11 is a difficult 149-kilometer mountain course from Albertville to Col du Granon, with two steep ascents before a summit finish on the Col du Granon. Stage 12 is on France’s Independence Day, Bastille Day, July 14, providing a 166-kilometer mountain course and an exuberant celebration throughout France. The next four stages fluctuate from flat to medium-mountain runs before the final two mountain stages on 17 and 18. Stage 18’s 143-kilometer course features a final 13.6 kilometers of ascent to Hautacam, it will be the last chance for climbers to gain time. Stage 19 is a 189-kilometer flat course, Stage 20 a 40-kilometer time trial, and Stage 21 is the final day’s 112-kilometer ride into Paris to the ChampsÉlysées. It’s worth mentioning that Mark Cavendish, 37, won’t be in the running after failing to earn a spot on Quick-Step Alpha Vinyl Team. Last year he tied Eddie Merckx’s all-time record of 34 stage victories. Provided are the top five riders to watch. This year’s Tour de France travels 3,328 kilometers from Copenhagen, Denmark to the historic Champs-Élysées in Paris. Slovenia’s Tadej Pogačar enters as this year’s favorite as he looks to capture his third-consecutive yellow jersey. Tadej Pogačar UAE Team Emirates Can Slovenia’s Pogačar be next winner three consecutive times after Chris Froome accomplished the feat from 2015-2017? The nine straight hilly and mountain courses from stages 4-12 certainly play well towards his odds after winning the last two consecutive polka-dot jerseys as the tour’s best mountain rider. At only age 23, Pogačar is putting himself into cycling’s history books. last year’s running. He enters the tour this year after winning the Tour de Suisse earlier this month. Daniel Felipe Martinez Ineos Grenadiers The 26-year old Colombian Daniel Martinez is another ride from the Ineos team. He finished 28th in the 2020 Tour de France and did not compete last year, but has had a strong 2022 season by winning the Tour of the Basque Country in April and was eighth overall in the Tour de Suisse this month. Primož Roglič Team Jumbo–Visma Primož Roglič, 32, also from Slovenia, is Pogačar’s top competition and was leading the 2020 Tour de France entering the second-to-last stage before Pogačar’s breathtaking Stage 20 time trial. Last year, Roglič was in the mix but crashed on Stage 3 and eventually bowed out of the event prior in Stage 9. Jonas Vingegaard Team Jumbo–Visma Danish rider Jonas Vingegaard, a teammate of Roglič, is considered the third favorite entering the race after finishing second last year. Earlier this month, Vingegaard finished second behind Roglič in the Critérium du Dauphiné. Only 25, he is also a rider on the ascent. Geraint Thomas Ineos Grenadiers Geraint Thomas, 36, won the Tour de France four years ago, placed second in 2019, didn’t compete in 2020, and was 41st in Fellow Slovenian Primož Roglič is the highest rated challenger to Pogačar. Denmark’s Jonas Vingegaard is another top-rated challenger.

articles.text: Try the Post’s favorites 4 hikes at Lake Tahoe The Rubicon Trail provides a view of Lake Tahoe’s Fannette Island in Emerald Bay at Lake Tahoe. four trails at Lake Tahoe. Hiking season has arrived with summer and it’s the perfect time to get out and explore nature’s beauties. Lake Tahoe is always a frequent location for Bay Area families to enjoy the great outdoors and the refreshing mountain water. The location provides some of my favorite trails in the entire state, which we’ve been fortunate enough to hike and photograph. Here are the Post’s favorite 1. Horsetail Falls In Twin Bridges, between Strawberry and the Sierra-atTahoe Resort along Highway 50, you can see a magnificent 500- foot waterfall cascading down Pyramid Creek. It’s just 30 minutes from the Stateline area. Horsetail Falls requires just two miles of legwork, four miles round trip with 1,341 feet in elevation gain. While hiking beside the beautiful flowing Pyramid Creek, the trail gets steeper as you ascend toward the falls. The majority of legwork comes in the final half mile over steep boulders and rocks. Sturdy hiking boots are recommended. If hikers opt against making it all the way to the falls, there are countless areas where you can jump into the creek or merely sunbathe on the rocks. Beneath the falls is a popular swimming hole with ample space to jump, swim, or just wade. On a hot summer day, a dip into the cold water was the perfect refresher before the hike back down. The entire trail is largely unmaintained, but keeping your eyes on the main path was simple enough. There are also small blue-spray painted markings to keep hikers on the trail. Punch in “Pyramid Creek Trailhead” to access the parking lot, which is $10 for all day and overnight. 2. Rubicon Trail The Rubicon Trail is 5.9 miles out and back (11.8 round trip, 1,350 feet in elevation. It stretches around Emerald Bay with a view of Fannette Island. Hikers can visit the historic Vikingsholm mansion on the island and nearby quiet Emerald Bay Boat Camp, with countless places to rest beside the crystal blue water on the way to the Rubicon Point Lighthouse. The trail travels beside the white sandy beach along Emerald Bay to the northern portion of the Rubicon Trail. The northern section of the Emerald Bay gives visitors a much more private look of Fannette Island, with spots along the shoreline to cool off on a hot day. One mile from Vikingsholm is the Emerald Bay Boat Camp, a secluded $30 per night boat-in campground. Less than one mile from the Emerald Bay Boat Camp entrance is the secluded Secret Cove, where you will see shallow crystal blue water. Hiking season has arrived with summer and it’s the perfect time to get out and explore nature’s beauties. Lake Tahoe is always a frequent location for Bay Area families to enjoy the great outdoors and the refreshing mountain water. The location provides some of my favorite trails in the entire state, which we’ve been fortunate enough to hike and photograph. Here are the Post’s favorite 1. It’s just 30 minutes from the Stateline area. Horsetail Falls requires just two miles of legwork, four miles round trip with 1,341 feet in elevation gain. While hiking beside the beautiful flowing Pyramid Creek, the trail gets steeper as you ascend toward the falls. The majority of legwork comes in the final half mile over steep boulders and rocks. Sturdy hiking boots are recommended. If hikers opt against making it all the way to the falls, there are countless areas where you can jump into the creek or merely sunbathe on the rocks. Beneath the falls is a popular swimming hole with ample space to jump, swim, or just wade. On a hot summer day, a dip into the cold water was the perfect refresher before the hike back down. The aerial tram to Squaw’s High Camp takes visitors to the viewing platform which has a popular restaurant, outdoor games, a skating rink, and an a museum dedicated to the 1960 Winter Olympic Games. Berkeley Repertory Theatre is currently in production with Dana H., written by Lucas Hnath, with performances through July 10. Dana H. was first presented in New York in 2020 and has been produced in association with Broadway producers Matt Ross, Sally Horchow, and Dori Berinstein. The play has been nominated for three Tony Awards, including Best Direction, by Berkeley’s Les Waters. The play is adapted from interviews with Dana Higginbothan, the playwright’s mother, conducted by Steve Cosson. The titular character of Dana is played by Jordan Baker in the Berkeley Rep production. Photo by Calvin Ngu “I was present for some of the events of the play, so there is a semi-autobiographical aspect to it,” Hnath said. To purchase tickets visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/dana-h/. Dana H, will be shown through July 10 at the Roda Theatre at 2025 Addison Street in Berkeley. Call the box office at 510-647-2949 for details.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s final performance of Mozart’s timeless Don Giovanni is this Saturday, July 2. Don Giovanni, part three of the Mozart-Da Ponte Trilogy, is a dark comedy with a horrific twist ending. The action takes place in Seville and spans 24 hours, following the story of two women set off to confront a notorious libertine. It is an opera in two acts based on the legend of Don Juan, with a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte. The opera is sung in Italian with English supertitles. The San Francisco production casts baritone Etienne Dupuis as the titular role as Don Giovanni Photo by Constanza Hevia San Francisco Opera will perform Mozart’s Don Giovanni next weekend at the War Memorial Opera House. Baritone Etienne Dupuis will sing the title role in Don Giovanni in San Francisco Opera’s production. and soprano Adela Zaharia as Donna Anna. Nicole Car will make her San Francisco Opera debut as Donna Elvira. Car has performed with the Vienna State Opera, Paris Opera, Royal Opera House Covent Garden, Metropolitan Opera, and Deutsche Oper Berlin. She was scheduled to make her first appearance with the company on June 30, but now makes her debut on June 4. Car has performed the role of Donna Elvira on leading stages, including at the Paris Opera in March this year. The opera orchestra will be conducted by Bertrand de Billy, with the opera directed by Michael Cavanagh. To purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfopera.com/on-stage/dongiovanni/. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs

articles.text: The In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform a concert celebrating the music of composer Harry Warren on Sunday, July 10 at Piedmont Center for the Arts. The trio of Bill Jackman (piano), Rich Trevor (bass), and Anthony Pegram (drums) comprise an old-school, classic jazz piano trio. The concert serves as a tribute to one of America’s most successful film composers. Warren wrote music for more than 75 films, starring luminaries like Fred Astaire, Judy Garland, and Bing Crosby. Jackman has been with the trio for the past 27 years; he was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher. He has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Bassist Trevor grew up in Chicago and draws influence from blues and R&B, eventually becoming the bassist for Eli’s Mile High Club in Oakland. Pegram has been a drummer for jazz combo bands and big bands Songwriter Harry Warren in the Bay Area for over 40 years. Most recently, he accompanied singer Marcella Hooks and pianist Rodney Burge as the house trio for the Sunday Jazz Brunch at Scott’s Restaurant in Oakland’s Jack London Square. The concert begins at 3 p.m. Tickets are $20 and are available online or at the door at https://bpt. me/5316993. Seating is limited to 70 guests. The In the Tradition Piano Trio
articles.title: Piano Trio to celebrate music of Harry Warren at PCA July 10

articles.text: Festival Napa Valley, now in its 16th season, opens on July 15 and will conclude on July 24 with a season finale by Festival Orchestra Napa. The 9-day summer arts festival will take place in iconic Napa Valley “We are dedicating the 2022 season to the sounds of America. From Copland and Bernstein to jazz, swing, Broadway, bluegrass and country, this is the music that celebrates our common heritage,” explained Robin Baggett, Chairman of the Festival’s Board of Directors. “The performances at Festival Napa Valley this summer illuminate the importance of the arts in today’s world,” said Festival President & CEO Richard Walker. “Our mission is more vital than ever.” Opening night, July 15, will include Dvorak’s New World Symphony, and Daniel Brewbaker’s Cello Concerto with soloist Sophia Bacelar. The Festival Orchestra Napa will be led by conductor Carlo Ponti. Other noteworthy artists and composers this year include: Trisha Yearwood, Nia Imani Franklin and the Young People’s Chorus of New York City, soprano Mikayla Sager, tenor Mario Chang, baritone Lester Lynch, violinist Tessa Lark, and soprano Alexandra Armantrading. Performances are held outdoors on the Festival Napa Valley Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, the Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at the Culinary Institute of America at Copia in Napa, and at wineries, estates and other venues throughout Napa Valley. For full programming and to order tickets, visit https://festivalnapavalley.org. Festival Napa Valley will return in July as an outdoor 9-day celebration.
articles.title: Festival Napa Valley – 9 days of music opening July 15

The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. articles.text: Music@Menlo, the iconic summer music festival that includes a range of performances and master classes, returns for its 20th season beginning July 14. Tickets are on sale now. Music@Menlo is an internationally acclaimed chamber music festival founded by David Finckel and Wu Han. Inaugurated in 2003 at Menlo School, the festival features concerts, lectures, and a training program for aspiring professional musicians. The festival’s mission is to engage and sustain an audience for chamber music that is programmed, presented, and performed at the highest level of artistic excellence. Concert programs are performed by a collection of the greatest chamber musicians around the world in intimate settings at Menlo School and Spieker Center for the Arts. To view the full program of events, activities and guest artists, and to purchase tickets, visit https://musicatmenlo.org. Spieker Center for the Arts in Menlo Park, home of Music@Menlo summer music festival in July.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré On any given Friday or Saturday night in the early 1960s, it was not unusual to pull into a drive-in filled with cars and kids, some leaning against fenders, others deep in conversation, and hear on more than one car radio Wolfman Jack, rock & roll DJ extraordinaire, a legend in his own time. “Let’s git nakkid” he’d call out as he segued into “It’s All Right (Mama)” by Elvis Presley, one of the first and perhaps greatest rock & roll songs ever. Wolfman Jack. Gravelly voice. Diabolical laugh. No one had ever seen him. He was an enigma. Rumor had it that he was on some ship off the coast of Mexico, staying one record spin ahead of the culture cops. Or possibly he was hold up in a beachside, cinderblock shack with a monster antenna, south of Tijuana. And, as it turned out, that’s exactly where the Wolfman was, slammin’ and jammin’ at station XERB-AM, sending out a powerhouse signal to all places north, up the coast of California, reaching Alaska on a clear night. What was undisputed was that the discs Wolfman played captured the essence of being young during the late 50s and early 60s. Rock & roll was transcendent. It was heart wrenching, spine-tingling, drop to your knees wonderful. And more. There was Big Joe Turner’s “Shake, Rattle & Roll” and Bill Haley and the Comet’s “Rock Around the Clock,” all precursors of some of the most vital, Motown inspired music to ever come out of the 50s, soon morphing into the Stones, Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, Fats Domino, James Brown and the Beach Boys. Rock & roll was the cresting wave, a cultural zeitgeist. Great Britain, in so many ways, mirrored America, creating it’s own unique version of rock & roll, led by groups such as the Who, the Kinks, Cream, Pink Floyd and, of course, the Beatles. And for a time, in the 60s, British kids tuned in late at night to a rogue rock & roll station, beamed from a ship somewhere off the coast. And that is the essence of the film Pirate Radio. An improbable group of disc jockeys kept rock & roll on the radio 24/7, to the absolute delight of the nation’s listeners and to the consternation of the British government and the BBC, which took great umbrage at the airways being filled with such “rot.” Led by Cultural Minister Alistair Dormandy (Kenneth Branagh), a concerted effort is set in motion to sink the renegade ship, so to speak, and shut down the illicit music once and for all. Rock & roll, it was decided, posed a threat to homeland security. Meanwhile, on board, the DJs are running a floating animal house, engaging in pranks and fun and music. The housemother, so to speak, is Quentin (Bill Nighy), the captain and titular head of this ragged crew, with The Count (Philip Seymour Hoffman) and Gavin (Rhys Ifans) filling the prime time radio slots. While the story is thin – there is a subplot, a sort of coming of age saga about young Carl, the nephew of Quentin – the energy and sheer delight conveyed by the film makes for sweet entertainment and the sound track, meaning the platters spun, is, simply, top drawer. Pirate Radio. Directed by Richard Curtis. Starring Philip Seymour Hoffman, Bill Nighy, Rhys Ifans, Talulah Riley and Tom Sturridge. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated R.
articles.title: Pirate Radio – Wolfman Jack and the growth of rock & roll

articles.text: The Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, now in its fifth year with performances the week of July 18 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, is seeking a few families who would like to host one or two guest musicians. The festival in Piedmont is the only residency chamber music festival in the East Bay, and a source of great pride to the community, modeled on the annual Bach Festival in Carmel, where guest musicians and families make lifelong connections and friendships. Host responsibilities are to provide a private room and bath and light breakfast, and if possible, transportation to morning rehearsals at PCA. All other meals and transportation are taken care of. The musicians arrive on Sunday, July 17 and leave Monday July 25. Performance dates are Wednesday, Friday and Sunday, July 20, 22 and 24. For details, call Susan Chamberlain at 510-421-3161, or e-mail susanchacha@gmail.com. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 11am-5:30pm 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org

Pirate Radio – Wolfman Jack and the growth of rock & roll Review by Chris Honoré On any given Friday or Saturday night in the early 1960s, it was not unusual to pull into a drive-in filled with cars and kids, some leaning against fenders, others deep in conversation, and hear on more than one car radio Wolfman Jack, rock & roll DJ extraordinaire, a legend in his own time. “Let’s git nakkid” he’d call out as he segued into “It’s All Right (Mama)” by Elvis Presley, one of the first and perhaps greatest rock & roll songs ever. Wolfman Jack. Gravelly voice. Diabolical laugh. No one had ever seen him. He was an enigma. Rumor had it that he was on some ship off the coast of Mexico, staying one record spin ahead of the culture cops. Or possibly he was hold up in a beachside, cinderblock shack with a monster antenna, south of Tijuana. And, as it turned out, that’s exactly where the Wolfman was, slammin’ and jammin’ at station XERB-AM, sending out a powerhouse signal to all places north, up the coast of California, reaching Alaska on a clear night. What was undisputed was that the discs Wolfman played captured the essence of being young during the late 50s and early 60s. Rock & roll was transcendent. It was heart wrenching, spine-tingling, drop to your knees wonderful. And more. There was Big Joe Turner’s “Shake, Rattle & Roll” and Bill Haley and the Comet’s “Rock Around the Clock,” all precursors of some of the most vital, Motown inspired music to ever come out of the 50s, soon morphing into the Stones, Buddy Holly, Chuck Berry, Fats Domino, James Brown and the Beach Boys. Rock & roll was the cresting wave, a cultural zeitgeist. Great Britain, in so many ways, mirrored America, creating it’s own unique version of rock & roll, led by groups such as the Who, the Kinks, Cream, Pink Floyd and, of course, the Beatles. And for a time, in the 60s, British kids tuned in late at night to a rogue rock & roll station, beamed from a ship somewhere off the coast. And that is the essence of the film Pirate Radio. An improbable group of disc jockeys kept rock & roll on the radio 24/7, to the absolute delight of the nation’s listeners and to the consternation of the British government and the BBC, which took great umbrage at the airways being filled with such “rot.” Led by Cultural Minister Alistair Dormandy (Kenneth Branagh), a concerted effort is set in motion to sink the renegade ship, so to speak, and shut down the illicit music once and for all. Rock & roll, it was decided, posed a threat to homeland security. Meanwhile, on board, the DJs are running a floating animal house, engaging in pranks and fun and music. The housemother, so to speak, is Quentin (Bill Nighy), the captain and titular head of this ragged crew, with The Count (Philip Seymour Hoffman) and Gavin (Rhys Ifans) filling the prime time radio slots. While the story is thin – there is a subplot, a sort of coming of age saga about young Carl, the nephew of Quentin – the energy and sheer delight conveyed by the film makes for sweet entertainment and the sound track, meaning the platters spun, is, simply, top drawer. Pirate Radio. Directed by Richard Curtis. Starring Philip Seymour Hoffman, Bill Nighy, Rhys Ifans, Talulah Riley and Tom Sturridge. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated R. Democracy is not a spectator sport! articles.text: It’s evident going in that Tomb Raider will be a B-movie (pulp cinema). As well, it’s a 2018 reboot of the 2001 Lara Croft: Tomb Raider (starring Angelina Jolie). For good measure, that earlier film was based on a video game, not a comic book. Recall that B-films, when good (and some are really good), represent a special niche in Hollywood. They are the films that that give definition to the term cliffhanger, and prepared the way for contemporary action films, which are derivative of the old Republic Films serials featured in matinees on countless Saturdays. Kids filled the balconies, hands sticky with Milk Duds or JuJubes, sitting stone still when Don Winslow of the Navy careened off a cliff in a black town car (with massive whitewalls). They groaned when the screen was suddenly filled with “To Be Continued.” I don’t think it’s a stretch to point out that the Aquaman in The Shape of Water could be the twin of the man-fish in the 1950s film, The Creature From the Black Lagoon. Ditto the pulpy sci-fi films of the same era, B-movies all. Tomb Raider is remarkable, and as tightly put together as is Alicia Vikander, portraying Lara, who’s completely buff and totally up to what proves to be a fast-paced series of cliffhangers requiring serious physical challenges. It’s pedal to the medal, even in the opening backstory scenes. For seven years, Lara has been grieving for her father, Lord Richard Croft (Dominic West), refusing to believe he is dead. He vanished during an expedition. However he does leave Lara with a clue, discovered as she sits in one of his corporate offices, preparing to sign a document that will do two things: acknowledge he is deceased, thus making her officially the heir to a massive fortune. Clue in hand, Lara abruptly leaves the conference room and returns to the Croft estate, a place she has not visited since his disappearance. She has refused to use his wealth or live in what is actually her home. In his crypt she discovers a secret room, filled with research and a journal that explains where Alicia Vikander stars as Lora Croft in Tomb Raider. he has gone, warning her not to follow; instead she is instructed to burn his papers. Apparently, her father was in the hunt for the tomb of a demonic queen, buried in a mountain on an island in what is known as the Devil’s Triangle, off the coast of Japan. Cut to Hong Kong where Lara is looking for a specific rusty freighter and passage to the Triangle and then to the island shown in his journal. Thus begins the Lara Croft adventure, heading into the unknown, with a drunken captain (David Wu), no crew, and a map. It’s at this point it becomes evident that the story is clearly derivative of The Raiders of the Lost Ark, an iconic adventure film that has inspired not only sequels, but other A/B movies. As an aside, Lara is no Wonder Woman and is never portrayed as a superhero. Nor is she the fragile wife in The Danish Girl (which earned her an Oscar). She is vulnerable while being incredibly courageous and brave and willing to risk all as she searches for her father. Of course, despite treacherous seas and the rusty ship breaking up on the rocks off the found island, she perseveres. What happens is part of the fun of this well-crafted movie – nicely told and gorgeously made. Know that Vikander invests fully in the character. She delivers a fearless performance and is supremely athletic. She is also supported by a talented ensemble of fine actors. The villains are, well, dependably villainous, led by Walter Googins as Mathias Vogel, a man obsessed, even after seven years, with finding a way to break into the forbidden tomb. This is flat-out good B-movie making. And if you’re a fan of this genre, then don’t miss Tomb Raider. Tomb Raider. Directed by Roar Uthaug. Starring Alicia Vikander, Dominic West, Walton Goggins. 2 hrs. Rated PG-13. Released 2018. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

articles.text: A scene from the disaster movie, 2012. Review by Chris Honoré When filmgoers sit down to watch an apocalyptic movie, it’s a given that they suspend their disbelief regarding all that is outlandish. They simply sit back and enjoy the ride. And what a ride it can be. With the ever-growing sophistication of special effects (CGI), films of this ilk grow ever more dramatic and intense. Consider 2012, released in that same year. It’s “end of times” filmmaking on steroids. King Kong of catastrophe. The movie followa a familiar template. Act one: ivory tower scientists, usually reserved in their discourse, discover that a serious problem is approaching, one that could have a devastating impact on the planet and mankind. Act two: how to sell the data to recalcitrant and even hostile government officials. With the help of seismic events – earthquakes, hail showers at the equator, volcanoes erupting, temperatures fluctuating dangerously – the officials are brought around. The question then is, what to do to prepare for the event. Act three: the protagonists find themselves in harm’s way as the crisis escalates and they struggle to survive. All around them, destruction is occurring on a scale never seen before. Act four: the climax and denouement. The sun rises, but on a completely changed world. All of the central characters have survived – bloodied, exhausted, but still standing. Again, not enough can be said regarding the role played by CGI in constructing these films. The technology has taken movies such as this to a totally different realm. The narrative is important, but these movies are rarely about unresolved relationships. Small problems are solved (“Do you really love this guy?”), while trapped in a ship’s compartment with water flooding in, the rising water being far more important than the answer to the question. To create this film, 1,000 people worked at 15 different special effects studios to create the nonstop catastrophes, to include a blue screen that was 600 feet long and 40 feet high. The movie is endlessly gripping and the crises are stacked like Legos with few moments of relief. There will be those who say that John Cusack, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Amanda Peet and Oliver Platt, all exceptional actors, are wasted on this type of movie, given the flat dialogue and skinny plot. But it’s a given that both exist in service of the action – what’s ahead, what’s behind, and how can we save ourselves. As armageddon films go, 2012 is a solid example. One other note: Hollywood has been very successful in creating post-apocalyptic films. An event has occurred, something that has changed the earth dramatically (a worldwide epidemic, a war). How often, in the set-up to such a film, does the central character emerge to find mankind gone, the streets empty, cars abandoned, stores empty. The challenge is, how to survive. Examples would be The Postman, Planet of the Apes, I Am Legend, and The Omega Man. Survival is again the theme. Adapting to a world after a cataclysm is a far different proposition, though no less interesting. 2012. Directed by Roland Emerich, Starring John Cusack, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Amanda Peet, Oliver Platt and Woody Harrelson. 2 hrs., 53 min. Rated PG-13.
