articles.text: There is a lot more to life than the headlines. Everyone knows the name William Randolph Hearst. And why not? He had a very public persona. There is, of course, the castle. And then, there were the sensational parties as well as various and sundry affairs. Need I go on? A chance meeting with the great grandson of William Randolph Hearst resulted in an invitation to a banquet. As I spoke with WR Hearst’s distant relative, I realized that he is about as good a host as was his great grandfather. He explained that there is much more to the Hearst story than the castle itself. WR Hearst always referred to the castle as “the ranch”. And that ranch completely surrounds the imposing castle. He also reminded me that there was much to be appreciated in the largesse of great grandpa. Aside from the gift of the castle itself, there has been a tremendous amount of money given to education and scholarships. The sumptuous banquet I attended featured beef from the Hearst ranchlands that go from the hilltop down to the ocean at San Simeon. The banquet also had two kinds of red wine, also from the Hearst ranch. For some time I have been rather disappointed by the quality of beef available in the stores. It is both tough and tasteless. But, wonder of wonders, the beef from the Hearst cattle ranch was so tender it was easy to cut with a fork. In flavor, it was ideal. The younger Hearst told me that his cattle are grass fed and grass finished. No wonder the Hearst beef is so good and why other beef is so bad. It was the same story with the wines. The Hearst vintner was on hand to describe the virtues of the wine. His 35 years of experience was sufficient proof. There is a limited distribution of the beef and the wine. If you see either, jump at the opportunity. Too much of a good thing Jazz is a “create-as-you-go” art form. It must be made up on the A view of Hearst Ranch above the coastline of San Simeon.

articles.text: Voodoo and Hoodoo cast spells using a mojo charm bag to ward off evil spirts and for healing. A mojo bag may include herbs, minerals, feathers, animal parts, animal and human bones. Hoodoo is an African diaspora folk magic occult tradition created during slavery in the United States. It is unique to black people. The Voodoo spiritual system combines Christianity, Islam and Black Spiritualist religions. Voodoo is a group of religions in the Americas, including Brazilian Vodum, Cuban Vodú and Santeria, Dominican Vudú, Haitian Vodou, Louisiana Voodoo and New Orleans Voodoo. From New Orleans to Chicago especially there is a thread of African America blues songs that embody field hollers, work songs and spirituals in a minor key, usually based on the minor pentatonic scale and on a single chord. They are chant-like, dark and mysterious. They use a musical mojo bag of catchy phrases. Such songs are Howlin’ Wolf’s Spoonful, Smokestack Lightning and Back Door Man; Muddy Waters’ Mannish Boy, and I’m Your Hootchie Kootchie Man. Mojo Voodoo Blues is in this style. Muddy Waters’ 1957 song Got My Mojo Working referred to the magical powers of a mojo bag. Hoodoo Man Blues is the notable debut album by blues vocalist and harmonica player Junior Wells, performing with the Junior Wells Chicago Blues Band, an early collaboration with guitarist Buddy Guy. Screamin’ Jay Hawkins’ I Put a Spell On You is an outrageous supernatural experience, inspired by Hoodoo (with guitarist Mikey Baker who wrote The Complete Course in Jazz Guitar). Popular “mojo” songs by black artists include Mojo Mama by Wilson Pickett, Mojo Handby by Little Buster & the Soul Brothers, Mojo Hannah by the Neville Brothers and Fiesta Mojo by Muddy Waters wrote Got My Mojo Working in 1957. Dizzy Gillespie. Popular “Voodoo” songs include Voodoo Child by Jimi Hendrix, Voodoo by the Neville Brothers, Voodoo by Shay Lia, Under My Voodoo by Sublime, Black Magic Woman by Peter Green and by Santana, and Voodoo Woman by Koko Taylor. Listen to and read my improvised example for this Mojo Voodoo Blues column and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/PostColumns.pdf. The repetitive chord progression to Mojo Voodoo Blues is E-A-G-E, as you can hear repeatedly in the intro. The melodies are largely vocal-oriented melodies in the field holler style. The notes “B” and “D” are frequently used (the last two notes in bar 10), sounding an E7 chord. The mood is darkened with “Bb” the flat five of the key in bars 22-29. Bars 31-35 , 47-50 and 53-57 feature an interplay between the low and high range of pitch, suggesting two instruments. Memorize much or all of the piece and begin using fragments of it in building your own improvisation. Fun! Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. Call (510)923- 9522, text (510)435-3997 or email jim@guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. His course is available for free online at www.guitarimprov.com

articles.text: The Fifth Annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only weeklong residency chamber music festival in the East Bay, celebrates returning to live concerts this summer with three public performances at the Piedmont Center for the Arts opening July 20. Festival musicians will explore the theme “Human. Alone and Together” in works from composers old and new that remind us that life is better together. Led by founders Wayne Lee (violin) a Piedmont native, and his wife Juliana Han (piano), the festival features eight internationally acclaimed musicians from throughout the U.S. Returning musicians Jarmine Lin (violin) and Deborah Pae (cello), will be joined by guest musicians Teng Li (Principal Violinist, Los Angeles Philharmonic), Francisco Fullana (violin), Clancy Newman (cellist & composer), and Paul Laraia (viola). This Week’s Featured Artist: Jasmine Lin, Violin One of four musicians who has performed each year at the festival in Piedmont, Jasmine Line is a member of the Formosa Quartet with Deborah Pae and Festival founder Wayne Lee. “Jasmine Lin is a magnificent player with superb tone and strong interpretive powers” and “a violinist of remarkable intensity”, maintain American Record Guide and the Chicago Tribune. As a member of Formosa Quartet and Trio Voce, faculty member at Roosevelt University and Music Institute of Chicago, Curtis Institute of Music alumna, confidante to a Cremonese violin, arranger of Grappelli tunes, prizewinner in the Naumburg and Paganini competitions, Grammy nominee, Violinist Jasmine Lin returns to Piedmont for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival. and recording artist on Con Brio, EMI, and New World Records, Jasmine likes to solicit magnificence and intensity while leaving raindrops on her nose un-wipedoff. Her biography contains precisely one hundred words. Tickets are $45, with a savings on season passes for all three concerts for $120. To reserve tickets now and for more information, including complete biographies of all musicians and details of the music program, visit the website: www.piedmontcmf.org. All public events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require photo ID and valid proof of full vaccination including booster shot for entry, as well as proper masking while inside. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue in Piedmont.

At The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet the same time, it must be inventive so as to engage the listener. It is more than likely that the jazz greats of the past knew in advance how they would structure a song. But they made it seem freshly invented. The audience was always kept wondering: “What will come next?” A concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, June 19 featured a classic jazz trio. All of the music was well chosen. The pieces were grouped into brief suites in a format that worked brilliantly. Pianist Bill Jackman led from the keyboard, backed by Rich Trevor on bass and Anthony Pegram playing drums. It was really a pleasure watching these three fine musicians create good jazz on the spot for one hour. Art lecture & tour at PCA Artist and art historian Michael Stehr is a frequent presenter in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. All of his presentations are the epitome of perfection. The way he does things should be used as examples of public speaking. On Friday evening, June 24, he led the audience on an illustrated tour of Rome, from the Ponte Umberto to Saint Peter’s, and included the history of famous artists such as Michelangelo, Bernini, and Carlo Maderno. It was a pleasurable experience. First, he speaks without the aid of an amplifier. Doing so engages the audience from the beginning. Second, everything is formatted and so he never uses unnecessary words, like “I mean…so… uh… umm…” Third, his voice projects clearly throughout the main hall of the Center. Finally, his presentation was of a very high quality. This is an example of art appreciation and public speaking at its best. I recommend that every teacher should attend a Michael Stehr art lecture. Mojo Voodoo Blues By Jim Gleason Voodoo and Hoodoo cast spells using a mojo charm bag to ward off evil spirts and for healing. A mojo bag may include herbs, minerals, feathers, animal parts, animal and human bones. Hoodoo is an African diaspora folk magic occult tradition created during slavery in the United States. It is unique to black people. The Voodoo spiritual system combines Christianity, Islam and Black Spiritualist religions. Voodoo is a group of religions in the Americas, including Brazilian Vodum, Cuban Vodú and Santeria, Dominican Vudú, Haitian Vodou, Louisiana Voodoo and New Orleans Voodoo. From New Orleans to Chicago especially there is a thread of African America blues songs that embody field hollers, work songs and spirituals in a minor key, usually based on the minor pentatonic scale and on a single chord. They are chant-like, dark and mysterious. They use a musical mojo bag of catchy phrases. Such songs are Howlin’ Wolf’s Spoonful, Smokestack Lightning and Back Door Man; Muddy Waters’ Mannish Boy, and I’m Your Hootchie Kootchie Man. Mojo Voodoo Blues is in this style. Muddy Waters’ 1957 song Got My Mojo Working referred to the magical powers of a mojo bag. Hoodoo Man Blues is the notable debut album by blues vocalist and harmonica player Junior Wells, performing with the Junior Wells Chicago Blues Band, an early collaboration with guitarist Buddy Guy. Screamin’ Jay Hawkins’ I Put a Spell On You is an outrageous supernatural experience, inspired by Hoodoo (with guitarist Mikey Baker who wrote The Complete Course in Jazz Guitar). Popular “mojo” songs by black artists include Mojo Mama by Wilson Pickett, Mojo Handby by Little Buster & the Soul Brothers, Mojo Hannah by the Neville Brothers and Fiesta Mojo by Muddy Waters wrote Got My Mojo Working in 1957. Dizzy Gillespie. Popular “Voodoo” songs include Voodoo Child by Jimi Hendrix, Voodoo by the Neville Brothers, Voodoo by Shay Lia, Under My Voodoo by Sublime, Black Magic Woman by Peter Green and by Santana, and Voodoo Woman by Koko Taylor. Listen to and read my improvised example for this Mojo Voodoo Blues column and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/PostColumns.pdf. The repetitive chord progression to Mojo Voodoo Blues is E-A-G-E, as you can hear repeatedly in the intro. The melodies are largely vocal-oriented melodies in the field holler style. The notes “B” and “D” are frequently used (the last two notes in bar 10), sounding an E7 chord. The mood is darkened with “Bb” the flat five of the key in bars 22-29. Bars 31-35 , 47-50 and 53-57 feature an interplay between the low and high range of pitch, suggesting two instruments. Memorize much or all of the piece and begin using fragments of it in building your own improvisation. Fun! Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. articles.text: Nº 56 in a biweekly series A deeply polarized America woke up last Saturday, to a new level of division. The day before, June 24, the U.S. Supreme Court handed down a 6-3 ruling in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization overruling its 1973 decision in Roe v. Wade in its entirety. Roe had held by a 7-2 vote that women have a federal constitutional right to abort a pregnancy during its first two trimesters. In Dobbs the court holds that the constitution confers no such right, that Roe was wrongly decided, and the states are therefore free to allow or restrict abortions, as they see fit, as they had done before Roe. The opinion also overrules the Court’s 1992 opinion in Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey which upheld Roe by a 5-4 vote. The Dobbs opinion was authored by Samuel Alito and co-signed by Justices Barrett, Kavanaugh, and Gorsuch. Justice Thomas and Chief Justice Roberts filed separate opinions in concurrence, but for different reasons; and Justices Breyer, Sotomayor, and Kagan filed a joint dissenting opinion. The French Woman’s Reproductive Life French women enjoy undisputed rights safeguarding their privacy and dignity relative to childbearing. Contraceptives have been available since 1967, and birth-control pills are the leading choice, followed closely by the IUD (intrauterine device), le stérilet. For a woman under age 25, getting birth-control pills, an increasingly costly prescription, costs her nothing; and for women over age 25, insurance pays 65%. If a girl or woman finds herself with an unwanted pregnancy, she may obtain an abortion on demand. This women’s health procedure was approved in France in 1975. Statistically, one in three French women have an abortion during their reproductive lives, compared to the U.S. where it’s one in four women. The French seek privacy in matters of childEuropean Union state of Poland has a near total ban on abortion. German gynecologist Kristina Hänel was found guilty of advertising abortions under §219-a bearing, and relative to ending a pregnancy, they do not like to discuss “abortion,” the term is IVG, l’ Interruption Volontaire Grossesse. Clinic protocol does not require a woman to explain or justify her decision, yet aborting an embryo is not taken lightly. She is required to participate in a counseling session where her pregnancy options are fully explored, followed by a period of reflection for at least 48 hours before she may return for a medical procedure. A pregnant female who is a minor under 18 years old retains rights relative to her body, personal health, and choice. In recognition that her home life may be unsafe or unstable, a parent’s consent is not mandatory, though the teenager must be accompanied by an adult who is of her own choosing and remains with her during treatment at the health facility. The pills known as ‘medication abortion’ reliably end a pregnancy and may be prescribed in the first seven weeks of gestation. Alternately, a surgical procedure may be performed up to 12 weeks. Both procedures are covered 100% by French health insurance. Where women choose to carry the pregnancy to birth, they are provided with fullterm maternity healthcare. The mother-to-be will qualify for six months parental leave from work to care for her newborn, and the father is encouraged to apply for six months parental leave as well. France’s official policy is for every person to enjoy responsible, satisfying, and safe sex with the freedom to choose to have children, if, and when they wish. Recent polls show that opinions have grown more divided as to whether 220,000 yearly abortion procedures during the past two decades are an acceptable norm. The French public, like every western society, are swayed by national and foreign news reporting, and the array of infinite clicks leading to both informed and misinformed websites. The panoply of religious and political constructs is head-spinning, vying for your money and amassing more devotees. Pro-abortion and anti-abortion messaging bombards the Millennials (born 1981 to 1996) and Gen-Zees (born 1997 to 2012) to induct them into their orthodoxy. Mon corps, mon choix (my body, my choice) is repackaged as C’est mon corps, pas ton choix (It’s my body, not your choice), noted Antony Bulger, “The Observer” at France-Amérique. Activists, not just in France, but throughout Europe, the Americas, and especially in the United States, demand that embryos be given the same legal status as human beings. Some cite the science of a fetus having unique genome or a heartbeat as early as six weeks gestation. In five U.S. states (Kentucky, Louisiana, Oklahoma, S. Dakota, and Texas) abortion is illegal, perhaps from conception, with exceptions for rape, incest, or saving the woman’s life. Women’s Rights in Europe Across Europe, from Ireland (since 2018) to Spain, abortion is generally available on demand and broadly interpreted to accommodate a wide spectrum of social and economic circumstances, during the first trimester. Women may seek abortion without probing her private life, and universal health insurance covers the cost. But again, Europe isn’t immune from the spiritual battles playing out between people of opposing views. Russia, and former Communist countries offer abortion on demand in the first twelve weeks of gestation. Only two E.U. countries ban abortion entirely, Malta, where recently, a American tourist miscarried and nearly lost her life when no obstetrician stepped forward to terminate an unviable pregnancy; and Poland. Populated with 38 million people, Poland’s highest court tightened access to forbid abortion on grounds of “severe and irreversible fetal defect or incurable illness that threatens the fetus life.” But 90% of abortions result from medical consultation after pre-natal diagnosis. The two exceptions are pregnancy due to rape, or to save a woman’s life; and risk-adverse doctors decline treatment, leaving thousands of women to travel to a different European country; obtain pills; or seek extra-legal abortion. The tightening of abortion laws is tantamount to a total ban. Poland’s near-total abortion ban has sparked the largest political protests in decades, and women are demanding redress. Amnesty International has filed at their behest at the European Court of Human Rights, enjoined by eight other human rights agencies. Under Germany’s Constitution, abortion is technically illegal and punishable by three years in prison with the exception that the pregnancy is a health risk to the woman or the result of a rape. The procedure must be performed prior to 14 weeks from the start of the female’s last menstrual period. Mandatory counseling must occur a minimum of three days prior to an abortion procedure. Under Chancellor Olaf Scholz, Germany is proceeding on the promise to decriminalize abortion. One of the biggest hurdles was the notorious §219-a of the criminal code where a hefty fine or two years in prison was Protests in London The Guardian A grim solidarity protest handed down to medical doctors who could legally disclose that they performed abortions but were under a gag-order to not discuss clinical methods or potential risks with their pregnant patients. Last Friday, the Bundestag parliament struck down the nearly century-old Nazi-era statute, according to Reuters. As recently as last year, clinic websites warned Google searchers that abortion could cause depression, trauma, and infertility, according to gynecologist Kristina Hänel, who was found guilty of “advertising” abortions under §219-a and led to a yearslong protest to effect modernization of Germany’s laws supporting women’s health. Especially in small towns, abortion is a taboo topic, and fearing a reputation as an aborNorth Wales Chronicle tion doctor, they demur. Possibly one in ten doctors provide abortions and considering the many rural areas and heavily Catholic state of Bavaria, medical practices have dwindled over the last two decades, falling by 40%, according to Deutsche Welle (DW) news service. In the documentary Scorned, Concealed, Prohibited, (Deutsche Welle (DW), viewers are introduced to Ordo Iuris, a self-described “very conservative Christian anti-choice think tank” and a European Humanist Federation whose quest is influencing European legislation through their considerable legal expertise. Their social ministries, Citizen Go! and World Congress of Families are strikingly effective in bringing a fresh cultural transFew nations in the world forbid abortion entirely, but that’s a landscape subject to political change.
articles.title: France and Women’s Reproductive Rights in Europe

articles.text: Part 47 in a biweekly series Certainly we have developed great buildings and communities in this age: places that well serve the needs of their inhabitants and even inspire and uplift the users. Unfortunately, these kinds of examples are relatively few. Far too much of the built world in which we live today is mediocre, uninspiring or even sometimes depressing. One-story strip malls line our roadways, old city centers deteriorate as big box retailers drive them to bankruptcy, and parking lots dominate the landscape. Why is this? There are many reasons of course, many causes. But overlaying all of them seems to be a general confusion as to what is desirable – what it is we really want in our communities. The age of specialization has resulted in the design professions concentrating on their small sphere of influence with the big picture; the overall concept is often absent from consideration. I have also found that much of the public is not familiar with many of the concepts, processes and realities connected to the development of our environment. This is obvious just by attending a design review or planning meeting in nearly any municipality. People are very passionate and fight hard against what they don’t want. Unfortunately, they rarely know what they do want. There has also developed a general mistrust of the participants involved with development I like this example, again in Mexico, because it maximizes use of a city park for people in adjacent buildings with access and views. The beautiful use of the second floor of this building in Seattle’s Pike Place Market adds additional area for commercial and civic use. But just as importantly, it enlivens and further animates the entire street. Just imagine the same building without the balcony, umbrellas and flowers. This is pretty nice! ® –from developers to architects, or even homeowners wanting to add a room to their house. How can this confusion and mistrust be remedied? How can we change this current course so that we can more easily and successfully develop our environment in a way that we become proud of our resulting neighborhoods, communities and cities? It is my feeling that only when we are better educated, further informed, and have become thoughtful participants in the development process will this situation change. The “we” I refer to includes the various design professions and the general public. I do see Piedmont as ahead of the curve in this regard, but the effort must be ongoing – a life-long process for all of us. articles.text: Yann Menager has for many years worked as the vineyard manager for the famous Yves Cuilleron winery in the Northern Rhone valley. Using knowledge he gained from that position, he has purchased some superbly sited vineyards to start producing tiny quantities of his own wines from those vineyards. He now produces wine from St. Joseph, Condrieu and Cote Rotie. He tries to keep his winemaking as simple as possible with a minimum of intervention. His production is small with just five to ten barrels of each wine produced each year. Very little of his wine makes it to the U.S. and we are lucky to have Jack Edwards an importer in Napa now bringing in his wines. His tiny winey is located in an old stone barn high above the vineyards of Saint Joseph on his family’s farm in the hamlet of Champailler. The vineyards are tended organically, picking is done by hand, yields are kept low, and he uses native yeast and natural malolactic conversion. The result is a range of wines that shows superb energy and balance, with a freshness and finesse that harks back to a day before super extraction and new oak became popular. These are beautifully fresh terroir-driven wines that speak of the soils in which they were grown. • 2019 Domainie de la Roche Paradis Condrieu Veauvignere Produced from a small 20-year-old Viognier vineyard near the medieval town of Malleval. Ginger, white pepper, and honeysuckle blossom all feature in this medium bodied wine, plus layers of apricots and melon emerging in support of a long, luxurious finish. Drink over the next five years. • 2019 Domaine de la Roche Paradis Saint-Joseph La Bergerie Blanc This is a blend of 50% Marsanne and 50% Roussanne planted on granite soils. Fresh, lively, crisp, and medium-bodied, it has classy notes of citrus blossom, herbs, and light minerality on the nose. Pure, elegant, and crystalline. Drink over the next five years. Perfect with oysters or other shellfish. Yann Menager works the vines. • 2019 Domaine de la Roche Paradis Saint-Joseph Les Vessettes 100% Syrah from 18-year-old vines planted on granite soil, the wine offers sumptuous notes of violets, black pepper, mint, and hints of black fruits. Elegant on the palate, with beautiful length and purity. This is a high-class wine. • 2018 Domaine de la Roche Paradis Cote-Rotie Rozier Made from 100% Syrah from the Rozier vineyard site, this is an elegant old-school style Cote-Rotie. It is loaded with gamy and meaty characteristics, as well as black currants, raspberries, tapenade and loads of peppery spice. Medium-bodied, layered and beautifully ripe, forget the bottles for 4-5 years and enjoy the following decade. pages.text: Wednesday, June 29, 2022 23 The Wine Corner Domaine de la Roche Paradis – A gem of the Rhone By Pierre DuMont Yann Menager has for many years worked as the vineyard manager for the famous Yves Cuilleron winery in the Northern Rhone valley. Using knowledge he gained from that position, he has purchased some superbly sited vineyards to start producing tiny quantities of his own wines from those vineyards. He now produces wine from St. Joseph, Condrieu and Cote Rotie. He tries to keep his winemaking as simple as possible with a minimum of intervention. His production is small with just five to ten barrels of each wine produced each year. Very little of his wine makes it to the U.S. and we are lucky to have Jack Edwards an importer in Napa now bringing in his wines. His tiny winey is located in an old stone barn high above the vineyards of Saint Joseph on his family’s farm in the hamlet of Champailler. The vineyards are tended organically, picking is done by hand, yields are kept low, and he uses native yeast and natural malolactic conversion. The result is a range of wines that shows superb energy and balance, with a freshness and finesse that harks back to a day before super extraction and new oak became popular. These are beautifully fresh terroir-driven wines that speak of the soils in which they were grown. • 2019 Domainie de la Roche Paradis Condrieu Veauvignere Produced from a small 20-year-old Viognier vineyard near the medieval town of Malleval. Ginger, white pepper, and honeysuckle blossom all feature in this medium bodied wine, plus layers of apricots and melon emerging in support of a long, luxurious finish. Drink over the next five years. • 2019 Domaine de la Roche Paradis Saint-Joseph La Bergerie Blanc This is a blend of 50% Marsanne and 50% Roussanne planted on granite soils. Fresh, lively, crisp, and medium-bodied, it has classy notes of citrus blossom, herbs, and light minerality on the nose. Pure, elegant, and crystalline. Drink over the next five years. Perfect with oysters or other shellfish. Yann Menager works the vines. • 2019 Domaine de la Roche Paradis Saint-Joseph Les Vessettes 100% Syrah from 18-year-old vines planted on granite soil, the wine offers sumptuous notes of violets, black pepper, mint, and hints of black fruits. Elegant on the palate, with beautiful length and purity. This is a high-class wine. • 2018 Domaine de la Roche Paradis Cote-Rotie Rozier Made from 100% Syrah from the Rozier vineyard site, this is an elegant old-school style Cote-Rotie. It is loaded with gamy and meaty characteristics, as well as black currants, raspberries, tapenade and loads of peppery spice. Medium-bodied, layered and beautifully ripe, forget the bottles for 4-5 years and enjoy the following decade. For more information: Jack Edwards Collection jackedwardscollection.com 707-246-5401 The Cote Rotie is an exceptional quality. The cellar of the tiny Roche Paradis winery. Born on September 15, 1942 in a small town in Iowa, Ron was an excellent student, a class leader, and played all available sports at his high school in Dike, Iowa. He received his BS and MS degrees in chemical engineering at Iowa State University, where he completed his graduate work in 1964. After college Ron worked at the P&G Technical Center in Cincinnati Ohio, then accepted overseas posts with P&G in both Newcastle, England and Kobe, Japan. In 1977 he began a career with Shaklee Corporation and moved with his family to Piedmont. He continued traveling to Japan for business, became fluent in Japanese, and eventually started his own International consulting business with a focus on Japan. Always involved in his community, Ron attended Piedmont Community Church, where he twice served as president of the Board of Deacons. He was also involved with fundraising for Piedmont schools and was president of the non-profit Bay Area Community Services. In 1992 Ron moved to Ashland, Oregon where he continued his service to the community, including church work, dedication to the food bank, and support for public schools. articles.text: Wednesday Walkers on June 22 included Martin Levy, Sharon Ho, Mary Carter, Jim Kellogg, Adriene Hamlin, Albert Chen, Pat Keller, Harriette Louie, Sherry Jacobs, Kat Lang, Charlene Louie, Pat McMahon, Gloria DaSilva, Alan Goldhammer, Jim Kuo, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Noemi Alvarado, Melba Yee, Laura Goldman, Rob Smith, Judy Wong, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome first-time walker Linda Siegel, and Norene and Dan Stucka from Illinois visiting family. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesday group dodged another weather bullet last Wednesday. The day before had been in the 90s, but on June 22 it was a great morning, and 26 walkers showed up at the Exedra for a weekly walk. It had been almost three years since the group had walked the streets that were on the early 20th Century Key System streetcar lines, and a return to see them was overdue. Charlene Louie, who lives in a home on the former Key System No. 10 line, offered to lead the group on a tour of the area. In the 1890s the area that would become Piedmont was largely dairy farms and open space. As the East Bay population grew in the later years of the 1800’s, land developer Frank C. Havens and his partner Francis Marion “Borax” Smith established “The Realty Syndicate,” which acquired large tracts of undeveloped land throughout the East Bay. Potential buyers needed transportation to get from their new homes to work in the area and in San Francisco. From its beginning, the Key System was conceived by Borax Smith as a way to sell The Realty Syndicate’s land. Borax Smith’s transportation system was a consolidation of several streetcar lines assembled in the late 1890s and early 1900s. After having made a fortune in borax mining in Nevada (hence his nickname) he and Havens turned to real estate and electric traction for streetcars. The Key System was founded as the San Francisco, Oakland, and San Jose Railway (SFOSJR), and incorporated in 1902. Service began in 1903 in Berkeley. In 1904 service started in what was to become the City of Piedmont. The Key System connected the East Bay to San Francisco by a pier on the Bay where passengers boarded a ferry to San Francisco. Later, after the Bay Bridge was completed in 1936, Key System trains ran on the lower deck of the Bay Bridge, with the upper deck reserved for cars going both east and west. The electric streetcars replaced the cable car system in the East Bay, and soon Piedmont had three streetcar lines, the Numbers 10, 11, and 12. The No. 10 line traveled from downtown Oakland along Broadway to the Piedmont Avenue Key Route station at 41st Street, along Pleasant Valley and Grand Avenues through central Piedmont to the Hall Fenway at Crocker and Hampton. These streetcar lines made more neighborhoods in Piedmont desirable. Streetcar lines were routed to serve the real estate properties, thereby enhancing their value by offering convenient, efficient public transportation. In its early years, the Key System was actually a subsidiary of the Realty Syndicate, as was the Oakland-San Francisco ferry. Paths, lanes, walks and stairways were put in place in many of the newly developed neighborhoods, often in the middle of a city block, so that commuters could walk more directly to the new train system. The Key System ultimately provided mass transit in the cities of Oakland, Berkeley, Alameda, Emeryville, Piedmont, San Leandro, Richmond, Albany, and El Cerrito from 1903 until 1960, when it was sold to a newly formed public agency, AC Transit. The local streetcars were discontinued and replaced by buses in 1948, and the commuter trains to San Francisco were discontinued in 1958. Charlene led the walkers on Highland Avenue to explore the lower portion of the former Number 10 route. The group came to Park Way where Highland is reduced from four lanes to two This is because at Park Way the train line turned off Highland and went down the hill, and over to Ramona and Arroyo Avenues. The walkers went down Park recognizing the construction of the older homes on the left side of the street and the newer mid-century homes on the right. The latter infill homes were built after the trains stopped running, and the Key System right of way land was made available for home construction. These homes have streets on both the front and back of the properties, with no backyard neighbors. Some homes have their front doors and addresses on Park Way, while other homes have theirs on Ramona. The walkers took the 107-foot path from Park up to Ramona where they were surprised to hear the clucking of chickens behind a resident’s wall. The group went down Ramona to Monticello
articles.title: Wednedays Walkers explore former Key System line

articles.text: We all want to live long lives. We all expect to live long lives. But are we financially prepared for this longevity? Before we get to the issue of preparation, let’s look at a couple of interesting findings from a 2022 survey by Age Wave and Edward Jones: 1. The surveyed retirees said, on average, they expect to live to 89, and they said the ideal length of retirement is 29 years. 2. When asked if they want to live to 100, nearly 70% of the respondents said “yes.” The main reason for this desire for long life? To spend more years with their family and friends. Of course, none of us can see into the future and know how long we’ll be around. But with advances in medical care and a greater awareness of healthy lifestyles, these aspirations have a real basis in reality. However, if you’re going to enjoy a longer lifespan, and the extra years with your loved ones, you need to ensure your finances are also in good shape. How can you make this happen? Here are some basic steps to follow: • • Save and invest early and often. This may be the oldest piece of financial advice, but it’s still valid. The earlier you start saving and investing for your retirement, the greater your potential accumulation. Consider this: If you began saving just $5,000 per year at age 25, and earned a hypothetical 6.5% annual rate of return, and didn’t take any early withdrawals, you’d end up with $935,000 by the time you reached 65. But if you waited until 35 to start saving and investing, and you earned the same hypothetical 6.5% return – again with no early withdrawals – you’d only end up with $460,000. And if you didn’t start saving until 45, you’d end up with just over $200,000, again given the same 6.5% return. Be mindful of debt. You may not want to be burdened with certain debts when you enter retirement. So, while you’re still working, try to reduce unwanted debts, particularly those that don’t offer the financial benefits of tax-deductible interest payments. The lower your debt load, the more you can save and invest for the future.
articles.title: Prepare yourself for a long retirement

articles.text: Searching for the wizard of OGG. The airline flew us to a mystery Pacific island they designate as OGG, far out to sea, close enough to the Equator that the North Star looks merely like the night firmament’s belly-button, splashed by the sea swell. The airline provided a oncea-lifetime surprise in mid-air, donating a glass of chardonnay on learning of my 90th, celebrated days before. Moral: I recommend that every one work to turn 90, and frequently, to let the airline continue its largesse. OGG, weird name and all, is no recent discovery, to judge by the hundreds of hotels dotting its shores and beaches amongst the big black lava rocks, decorated here and there by U.S. flags. The locals were happily bilingual, speaking both English and US currency. Hard-belching volcanoes had come and gone, spewing lava over thousands of eruptions by grace of the fire-god Pele, enough to produce peaks near 10,000 ft., and land enough that any island circumnavigation by car takes more than an hour. Palms abound, requiring machete-wielding aerialists to shinny up the 40-foot trees to chop off weighty palm fronds before they attack you on windy days. If one broke off, I’d hope to be hit by the soft external fringes in descent. pages.text: Wednesday, June 29, 2022 25 Prepare yourself for a long retirement We all want to live long lives. We all expect to live long lives. But are we financially prepared for this longevity? Before we get to the issue of preparation, let’s look at a couple of interesting findings from a 2022 survey by Age Wave and Edward Jones: 1. The surveyed retirees said, on average, they expect to live to 89, and they said the ideal length of retirement is 29 years. 2. When asked if they want to live to 100, nearly 70% of the respondents said “yes.” The main reason for this desire for long life? To spend more years with their family and friends. Of course, none of us can see into the future and know how long we’ll be around. But with advances in medical care and a greater awareness of healthy lifestyles, these aspirations have a real basis in reality. However, if you’re going to enjoy a longer lifespan, and the extra years with your loved ones, you need to ensure your finances are also in good shape. How can you make this happen? Here are some basic steps to follow: • • Save and invest early and often. This may be the oldest piece of financial advice, but it’s still valid. The earlier you start saving and investing for your retirement, the greater your potential accumulation. Consider this: If you began saving just $5,000 per year at age 25, and earned a hypothetical 6.5% annual rate of return, and didn’t take any early withdrawals, you’d end up with $935,000 by the time you reached 65. But if you waited until 35 to start saving and investing, and you earned the same hypothetical 6.5% return – again with no early withdrawals – you’d only end up with $460,000. And if you didn’t start saving until 45, you’d end up with just over $200,000, again given the same 6.5% return. Be mindful of debt. You may not want to be burdened with certain debts when you enter retirement. So, while you’re still working, try to reduce unwanted debts, particularly those that don’t offer the financial benefits of tax-deductible interest payments. The lower your debt load, the more you can save and invest for the future. • Keep reviewing your progress. It’s important to monitor the progress you need to make toward achieving your goal of a comfortable retirement. Over the short term, your investment balances may fluctuate, especially in volatile financial markets such as we’ve seen in the early part of this year. But you’ll get a clearer picture of your situation if you look at long-term results. For example, have your accounts grown over the past 10 years as much as you had planned? And going forward, do you think you’re in good shape, or will you need to make some changes to your investment strategy? Keep in mind that, if you’re 50 or older, you can make “catch-up” contributions to your IRA and 401(k) that allow you to exceed the regular limits. You may also want to adjust your investment mix as you near retirement to potentially lower your risk exposure. Hopefully, you will enjoy many years of a healthy, happy retirement. And you can help support this vision by carefully considering your financial moves and making the ones that are right for you. articles.text: As an adult son or daughter, spouse, or even grandchild, you want to help a loved one when they become ill, or their abilities change as the result of natural aging. But are there some things that you would prefer a professional caregiver do instead? Let’s get real: not everyone is prepared to bathe their loved one or discuss potentially embarrassing topics. Have you found yourself in one of these predicaments? 1. You notice that a loved one doesn’t smell the same. A change in a person’s odor can be a sign of illness so the first step is to schedule an appointment with their health care provider for a check-up. They may also need to see a dentist, so add that to the checklist. Have they stopped bathing or showering? Are they changing their clothes? Has their diet changed? These are all things to investigate with as much kindness as possible and to get medical professionals involved; for support and so the advice comes from a trusted third-party. 2. Speaking of smells, how does their home smell? As senses dull due to aging or illness, a person’s ability to sniff out food that has gone bad or the need to take out the trash can become an issue. Is the solution to hire someone to help out with weekly housekeeping? Or can a caregiver add light housekeeping to their responsibilities when they come over for medication reminders? Having a clean and fresh-smelling environment might lift their spirits and provide something to look forward to consistently. 3. Back to that lapse in bathing…if you’re an adult daughter, for example, are you comfortable giving your elderly father a bath? There are many reasons why elderly people stop bathing themselves: fear of falling, symptoms of dementia that mean they forget the frequency or steps involved, inability to control water temperature, and more. Hiring a professional caregiver to take on this task is a good option, but then this person needs to be scheduled at a time that is best for your loved one for optimum results. 4. Your loved one won’t go out to eat with you or anyone else, or sit across the table from you to share a meal at home. It’s time for some delicate detective work so that they can once again partake in this pleasant shared activity with others, in part to decrease potential feelings of loneliness. Again, this might be a health problem that needs to be addressed by a dentist or their healthcare provider. If you’re eating with a loved one who is unable to keep their food and drink from spilling or ending up on their clothes, it’s time for some compassionate conversations to help them find a solution to the chewing and swallowing problems they are experiencing. 5. All of the above topics can mean it’s time to have “the talk” with your loved one. Often one of the first signs that someone’s ability to be completely independent shows up is in their driving. Even once you’ve practiced the conversation in front of a mirror, met with their healthcare provider, and done research on local longterm care options, this can be a very challenging talk for families and friends. Be prepared to listen, put yourself in their shoes, show respect, and be patient as they process their options such as home care services and using a caregiver. Becoming a family caregiver can happen gradually with a few errands and evolve into more personal care that requires training to do safely. Caregiving can also happen suddenly after an accident or illness such as a stroke, but the needs for personal and companion care might be the same and prove to be overwhelming for family and friends. Hiring a home care professional can be an act of true kindness in the face of an awkward situation, to preserve the relationship you both know and cherish. articles.text: It’s finally here! I’m talking about summer, my favorite season and it’s great that so many things are happening at Lake Merritt right now. During this season, our residents’ lives are enriched by how close they live to this spectacular body of water, set right in the heart of the city. “It’s like we live right across the street from the lake,” laughs Sam. “Our building at Madison and Lakeshore Avenues is right on the lake and most apartment homes have either a water or city view,” he added. If Lake Merritt itself is getting a lot of attention these days, it’s because of the $198 improvement program for the lake that Oakland’s voters endorsed and was completed a few years ago. The 3.4 miles of sidewalks around the lake are smooth and easy to walk on, and every day the tides move into the lake. Because Lake Merritt is connected to the Bay and Pacific Ocean through the rebuilt Lake Merritt channel, fresh salt water comes into the lake twice a day. If the lake is truly at the heart of the city, then Damon Tighe is the rock star who sings its songs. Tighe, a frequent guest speaker at The Lake Merritt’s free Topics of Merritt program, is gathering quite a following for his frequent talks about what’s going on beneath Lake Merritt. Tighe works on biofuels and single cell genomics in the Bay Area and teaches biotechnology to high school teachers through Bio-Rad Laboratories. He has wonderful Damon Tighe explains exhibits to visitors. presentation skills. In March he made a presentation to The Lake Merritt about “Fish and Friends of Lake Merritt’s Waters.” There was a lot of excitement this spring as Chinook salmon were found in the lake for the first time in over 20 years. The salmon were working their way into the East Bay watershed to spawn. These fish and other creatures have come into the lake through the newly renovated tidal inflow area near the pedestrian bridge on the West side of the lake. Tighe also cited the dark and mysterious bat rays which are now visiting the lake. They can sometimes be spotted from shore, or at the bridge overlook. We also learned about a wide variety of smaller creatures, including some of the mollusk family who are Gloria Frey on Lake Merritt making their homes just under the water near the lake’s shores. Tighe also showed us the microscopic-sized visitors that are an important part of the immense diversity of the revitalized lake. I am a fan of the people who founded and continue to operate the non-profit Lake Merritt Institute. One of their important programs is enlisting volunteers to keep the lake clean. You can see these friendly folks around the lake with nets and poles, the tools that help them scoop out plastic bags and trash that has drifted into the lake. Since 1996, these intrepid volunteers and school groups have pulled out between 1,000 to 9,000 pounds of trash from the lake each month. The group also raised money and partnered with the City of Oakland to ensure that two largescale aerating fountains, situated directly in the lake, splash water high into the air, providing beauty and oxygen to what can sometimes be oxygen-poor water. We are lucky to have such a treasure in our midst. As summer gets going and you find yourself in need of a temperate breeze, or a little extra exercise, or a picnic site, visit Lake Merritt and enjoy one of the very best things about Oakland. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland, For more information, call 510-903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com.

articles.text: What grandparent doesn’t want to indulge their grandchildren? We want to buy them their wished-for birthday present, allow them to eat forbidden sweets, let them watch one more video that they’re begging for. And why shouldn’t we? After all, we’re grandparents! Haven’t we waited long enough for this? Lots of grandparents believe it is their right – no, their duty to spoil their grandchildren. It’s what everyone expects us to do. What possible harm could come from being spoiled by your grandparents? Authors Paul and Diana Miller write in A Guide to Great-Grandparenting (rev. 2021) that for one thing, the practice of spoiling one’s grandchildren contradicts and denigrates the good values, attitudes, and behaviors that parents are trying to instill in their children. Parents have enough difficulty agreeing on rules and expectations for the children they are raising together. It’s even tougher if the child has vastly different sets of rules at home than with their grandparents. The authors go on to describe the adverse long-lasting effects of spoiling: Spoiling is treating people in such a way that they develop a self-image of privilege, lack of self-discipline, lack of accountability for their actions, and are in general obnoxious. We all know people with these traits, and nobody enjoys being around them. It’s unlikely that any grandparent would want to feel that they contributed to the development of their grandchild’s personality and outlook on life in such a negative way. Why do grandparents spoil? Sometimes it’s a way to make up for the things they couldn’t give their own children when they were young. It could be that some grandparents feel a sense of insecurity that without special treats of every kind, children will not enjoy being in the company of the older adults and perhaps won’t love them. Many grandparents simply like to see their grandchild’s happy face. Others spoil children just because they have the means to do so. Alas, each new toy, game, or sweet is soon forgotten. A more meaningful way to indulge your grandchildren is by making sure that they always feel your unconditional love for them. When grandparents communicate to young children that they are loved just for being who they are, they feel secure and confident. Deeply loved children who feel accepted and treasured for themselves, and not for their accomplishments, their good looks, or their perfect behavior, grow into kind, generous, compassionate adults, who can be selfless and responsible. We want to buy them their wished-for birthday present, allow them to eat forbidden sweets, let them watch one more video that they’re begging for. And why shouldn’t we? After all, we’re grandparents! Haven’t we waited long enough for this? Lots of grandparents believe it is their right – no, their duty to spoil their grandchildren. It’s what everyone expects us to do. What possible harm could come from being spoiled by your grandparents? Authors Paul and Diana Miller write in A Guide to Great-GrandWhat’s wrong with spoiling my grandchildren? parenting (rev. 2021) that for one thing, the practice of spoiling one’s grandchildren contradicts and denigrates the good values, attitudes, and behaviors that parents are trying to instill in their children. Parents have enough difficulty agreeing on rules and expectations for the children they are raising together. It’s even tougher if the child has vastly different sets of rules at home than with their grandparents. The authors go on to describe the adverse long-lasting effects of spoiling: Spoiling is treating people in such a way that they develop a self-image of privilege, lack of self-discipline, lack of accountability for their actions, and are in general obnoxious. We all know people with these traits, and nobody enjoys being around them. It’s unlikely that any grandparent would want to feel that they contributed to the development of their grandchild’s personality and outlook on life in such a negative way. Why do grandparents spoil? Sometimes it’s a way to make up for the things they couldn’t give their own children when they were young. It could be that some grandparents feel a sense of insecurity that without special treats of every kind, children will not enjoy being in the company of the older adults and perhaps won’t love them. Many grandparents simply like to see their grandchild’s happy face. Others spoil children just because they have the means to do so. Alas, each new toy, game, or sweet is soon forgotten. A more meaningful way to indulge your grandchildren is by making sure that they always feel your unconditional love for them. When grandparents communicate to young children that they are loved just for being who they are, they feel secure and confident. Deeply loved children who feel accepted and treasured for themselves, and not for their accomplishments, their good looks, or their perfect behavior, grow into kind, generous, compassionate adults, who can be selfless and responsible. These are the kinds of children most grandparents are proud to watch grow up and delight in being around. So, go ahead, shower your grandchildren. With love. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com.

articles.text: On May 14 a hearty band of 14 Piedmont Seniors ventured on a beautiful sunny day to visit the historic Western Railroad Museum in Suisun City. It provided a rare opportunity to ride in an historic streetcar and see the museum’s electric trains from California and other Western States. Visitors learned about the history of the railroads, which played such an important role in the development of California. The idea of a railway museum started in 1946 when individuals learned that an old Oakland streetcar that they had chartered for a day’s outing was to be scrapped within a week. Railroad enthusiasts came up with enough money to buy the car on the spot. Dedicated railroaders wanted to preserve the old streetcars and they selected Solano County as the site. Their daunting task to transform 22 vacant acres into a living history museum, and in 1985 the Western Railway Museum was officially unveiled. The museum’s mission is to continue to preserve the regional heritage of electric railway transportation as a living resource for the benefit of present and future generations. The museum is run by dedicated volunteers and people interested in preserving the golden era of the trains. The Piedmont Seniors first took a one-hour train ride 11 miles from the museum. At the half-way spot, they got off the streetcar so that the seats could be placed in the reverse position for the return trip. Along the way they observed cows, horses, and jackrabbits, along the route, along with some scenic views of Mt. Diablo, and – from a distance – Mt. Tamalpais. The conductor was eager to explain the intricate workings of the train car, and his enthusiasm was contagious. After that the Seniors were in for a special treat. They had a fabulous docent, Bob, who had been giving tours for 40 years. His knowledge of East Bay history was amazing. He showed the group inside the giant barns that A replica hobo hides under a boxcar. The streetcar at the intersection of Highland and Oakland Avenues during World War II in the 1940s. Piedmont Seniors on an outing to Suisun City to see the Western Railroad Museum, Pictured are (front): Larry and Tanya Hu (left), Mona Jamieson, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Irene Westler, Carole Jones, Janet Epstein, Yorkman Lowe, Gregory Jurin; (back) George Epstein, Fred Pemberton, Ann Morales, Cheryl Stanton, and Jim Ayotte. house multiple train cars, with a fleet of trains 80-100 years old. Some were perfectly restored, and others were in their original condition waiting to be restored. One boxcar on display showed how hobos traveled unnoticed underneath the bottom of the train car, something that looked both dangerous and very uncomfortable (see photo). There were many photos of trains in the early 1940’s, including one of a train stopping at St. Mary’s College in Moraga for students, as well as a photo of the former train station in Lafayette. Imagine the Seniors’ surprise when they saw a photograph of the train that stopped at the corner of Highland and Oakland Avenues in Piedmont. The group learned about the history of the various train cars in the “Barn” and were told about the importance of the refrigerated train cars for transporting meat, fruit and vegetables, and the need for large quantities of ice to keep food from spoiling on long journeys from Chicago to Oakland. After observing the exterior of the trains, the group was allowed to go inside a decades old cabin car and a Pullman sleeper. They learned that the men’s bathrooms were much larger than the women’s because they needed room for their daily shaves. The sleeper cars were reminiscent of the berths from the movie Some Like it Hot. These cars catered to gentlemen who would take the trains from San Francisco to Los Angeles on business. The Pullman Company even hired dedicated employees who had to stay awake all night in case someone from the top bunk of a sleeper car needed to be escorted down the ladder to the restroom. The seniors noticed a baseball bat on the wall of the sleeper car, and asked if it was used for unruly passengers. No, they were told. It was used to crush ice to keep the rail cars cool. Lunchtime in the Delta were over, everyone was famished, so they headed to Rio Vista on the Sacramento River, a 15-minute drive, and had lunch at “The Point”, alongside the Delta. The views were very scenic with deck side seating outside. The food was well worth the wait, and it was relaxing to escape to a slower, laid-back town. You don’t have to be a train enthusiast to appreciate the Western Railway Museum. You just need to have appreciation for a slower time in America and an appreciation for a bygone era. Don’t miss the gift shop; it has gifts for children as well as adults and is fairly reasonably priced. The museum has a shaded area for picnics with a snack bar next to the museum. If you are looking for a short day trip, the Western Railway Museum is a wonderful excursion for people of all ages. Become a member of the Piedmont Seniors The Piedmont Seniors, sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, is actively seeking new members to socialize and meet for fun and friendship. The group meets monthly, usually on the fourth Wednesday of the month at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, at 10 a.m. beginning with refreshments and mingling, followed by a short meeting. The group also goes on monthly excursions to interesting destinations in the Bay Area. Seniors of all ages are welcome; you do not have to be a Piedmont resident to join. For further information and to request a quarterly newsletter, contact Janet Epstein at 510-420- 3070, or email her at jepstein@ piedmont.ca.gov.

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, June 29, 2022 By Allyson Aleksey On Saturday morning, June 25, approximately 200 goats were released onto the hillside adjacent to and above Piedmont’s Corporation Yard on Moraga Avenue. They are tasked with carrying out a crucial role in wildfire prevention, but for them, it’s more like five-star dining ‘alfresco.’ The herd was brought to the city to perform weed abatement by grazing on the hills surrounding the Corporation Yard and Coaches Field in Moraga Canyon. Using goats is an alternative to the use of herbicide and mowing, and is a resource that Piedmont has used for years. On Saturday, the goats went to work right away, eliminating dry grasses, weeds, and woody growth - all potential fire hazards. California has entered its third year of severe drought, and many utility companies are imposing mandatory water cutbacks, all of which adds to the value of the fire-prevention goats. “Multiple years of drought conditions in Piedmont mean trees and other woody fuels are more stressed and carry less moisture. These conditions can lead to faster, more intense burning if these heavy fuels catch fire. Annual goat grazing reduces the likelihood of a grass fire climbing ladder fuels into the trees,” said Chief Brannigan. “The goats do the job in large public areas that all of us need to do on our own properties by annually removing hazardous vegetation.” The length of time the goats will be here depends entirely on the herd’s appetite, although they will need to be moved back to the hills before Independence Day, because the sound of fireworks will spook them. articles.text: Event on island’s history open to public this Saturday Treasure Island Museum, a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known Pacific-themed heritage, will host an oral history event on Saturday, June 25. “Treasured Stories” will highlight the work, experience and legacy of those who have made the island a refuge for positive change. “Because the museum is open to the public on weekdays only, this serves as a great opportunity to tell the history of the island,” said Anne Schnoebelen, Vice President of Treasure Island Museum. Schnoebelen is a writer and historian, with expertise in the artistic and architectural legacy of the Golden Gate International Exposition. The 1939 Exposition was held on Treasure Island, in celebration of the city’s two newly built bridges. articles.text: At least 52 total resignations, retirements and leaves of absences in district sets new record The 2021-22 school year in Piedmont led to a high number of faculty and staff turnovers for a second consecutive year in Piedmont School District. After a year of distance learning and limited hybrid instruction in 2021, there were 43 retirements, resignations or extended leaves of absences. This year those numbers grew to at least 52. Most notably, the top three top leadership positions in the district have been vacated. Piedmont High School Principal Adam Littlefield retired, while Superintendent Randy Booker and PMS Principal Ryan Fletcher resigned from their posts. The Classified staff (nonteaching staff), played important roles especially at a time when health, mental illness and hygiene were at the forefront. One year ago, 15 classified staff members left the school district, and this year that number nearly doubled to 29 departures. articles.text: Piedmont School Board is expected to announce at tonight’s board meeting, June 22, that Dr. Donald Evans will become Piedmont’s Interim Superintendent for the 2022-2023 school year. Evans was Superintendent of Berkeley School District from 2013-2019 and is coming out of retirement to lead Piedmont’s School District. Evans has 30 years of experience in education, his first 10 spent as a 5th grade teacher, coach, and Vice Principal in San Diego. He became Principal at in Ravenswood in East Palo Alto, and then took the position of Elementary School Area Superintendent in Oakland before serving as Associate Superintendent in Compton. Prior to Berkeley, he was the Superintendent of Hayward Unified School District. Evans received a Master’s of Education from U.S. International University, and his Bachelor’ degree from University of Delaware. He earned a Doctorate in 2010 from the Graduate School of Education at UC Berkeley, in association with the Leadership resignation. Booker was Superintendent for seven years, and with the school district in several roles for 19 years. Evans’ hiring will be a school board appointment and a streamlined decision made by the five school board members. When Evan announced his retirement from Berkeley, he gave seven months’ notice and worked with their board to create a transition plan to find the next Superintendent. Evans’ resignation letter in 2019 summarized his accomplishments at Berkeley, a school district of approximately 9,700 students and a city population ten times larger than Piedmont. “We’ve worked to create welcoming and inclusive schools. We adopted the Toolbox Curriculum, expanded restorative practices, and changed policies to help keep kids in school. Student leaders successfully challenged us to strengthen our policies and practices to address bullying and sexual harassment. We also successfully transitioned to the Common Core and to the use of new state assessments,” said Evans in 2019. Dr. Donald Evans, the retired Berkeley School District Superintendent, is expected to be hired June 22 by Piedmont School Board as an Interim Superintendent for the 2022-2023 school year. in Educational Equity Program. articles.text: A 2003 Smithsonian Magazine article informs us that Francis Bellamy, the author of the original Pledge of Allegiance, was a Baptist minister’s son from upstate New York. Educated in public schools, he distinguished himself in oratory at the University of Rochester before following his father to the pulpit, preaching at churches in New York and Boston. But he was restive in the ministry (perhaps because he was a socialist?) and in 1891 he accepted a job from one of his Boston congregants, Daniel S. Ford, principal owner and editor of The Youth’s Companion, a family magazine with half a million subscribers. Assigned to the magazine’s promotions department, the 37-year-old Bellamy set to work arranging a patriotic program for schools around the country to coincide with opening ceremonies for the Columbian Exposition in October 1892, the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’ arrival in the New World. The website U.S. History records that the Pledge of Allegiance was written in August 1892 and was originally published in The Youth’s Companion on September 8, 1892. Bellamy had hoped that the pledge would be used by citizens in any country. In its original form it read: “I pledge allegiance to my Flag and the Republic for which it stands, one nation, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.” In 1923, the words, “the Flag of the United States of America” were added. At this time it read: “I pledge allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America and to the Republic for which it stands, one nation, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all.” In 1954, in response to the Communist threat of the times, President Eisenhower encouraged Congress to add the words “under God,” creating the 31-word pledge we say today. Bellamy’s daughter objected to this alteration. articles.text: City Council adopted the proposed budget for 2022-23, as prepared by the Piedmont Finance Department. City Finance Director Michael Szczech facilitated a public hearing on the proposed fiscal 2022- 2023 budget at the most recent city council meeting on June 6. The city is budgeting $33,864,402 in General Fund expenditures, representing an increase of 7% from last year’s projected expenditures. Salary expenses increased 2% from last year’s projections, and is budgeted at $14,862,826. Maintenance and operations costs represent a quarter of general funds; operation costs are budgeted at $8,603,388, amounting to 24% of the fiscal year 2022-23 General Fund budget. This includes employee related expenses including travel and training, supplies, equipment and vehicle maintenance, contract services, technology services, and various public works services. 2020-2021 was a record year for construction and remodeling costs, increasing 28% over the prior year, and continues to remain high. Staff is projecting to exceed the annual budget this fiscal year by $200,000, or 17%. No changes or additions were made to the proposed budget since June 6. City Council unanimously voted to adopt the budget as is.

articles.text: The Alameda County Fair returns this Summer at the Fairgrounds in Pleasanton. The fair is the 7th largest in California. The County Fair continues through July 10 at the Alameda County Fairgrounds, located at 4501 Pleasanton Avenue. A plethora of events will transpire over the course of the fair, including the All-Alaskan Racing Pigs, musical events, movies on the lawn, carnival rides and a “drone show.” The fair is open from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily, and carnival hours are Wednesday through Thursday, and Friday through Sunday. Every night, a concert will be held at 8 p.m. A list of performers is below. July 2 - Blanco Brown July 3 - The B.B King Experience July 6 - Great White July 7 - Blue Oyster Cult July 8 - CoFunkShun July 9 - Bonfire July 10 - Banda Machos Entertainment at the fair includes a family fun stage, movies on the lawn, live music at the wine garden, and a fireworks display at 9:30 p.m. on July 1 at the Stella Artois Grandstand. Horse races take place every Friday through Sunday, with post time beginning 1:45 p.m. For more details, and to purchase tickets, visit www.alamedacountyfair.com. You can also volunteer at the summer fair. About 900 volunteers of all ages help out at the fair each year. Some of the organizations that volunteers include local schools and colleges, youth groups, garden club members, Girl Scout troops, and performing arts groups. The Alameda County Fair is a local, self-sustaining, non-profit organization. Visit https://annual. alamedacountyfair.com/volunteer/ to learn how to volunteer.
articles.title: Alameda County Fair continues through July 10 in Pleasanton

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a Venturing unit with Piedmont Scouts, is expecting to serve pancakes to hundreds of people the morning of Monday, July 4th. Crew Advisor Ken Li confirmed the PCSC members will be in the kitchen at the Veterans Hall cooking and serving breakfast between 8 a.m. and 10:30 a.m. Crew members Maddy Hill and Klara Zietlow serve as co-Vice Presidents of Fundraising and assisted in last year’s pancake breakfast. This year the crew is expecting it will serve over 400 visitors. “We knew we would have a larger event [this year], and Klara and I understood that we would have to dedicate a lot of time to this,” said Hill. “We interact a lot with our [communications department], because we want to get the word out about the event.” “Running a giant fundraising event is nearly impossible if you don’t have the support of a crew or team,” added Zietlow. “PCSC is a great place to gain that experience.” Village Market has donated produce and groceries to PCSC annually for almost a decade, confirmed Li. Piedmont Grocery recently became involved with the fundraiser, and the fundraisMembers of the Piedmont Community Service Crew take over the kitchen in the Veterans’ Hall during the Pancake Breakfast on the 4th of July. ing crew reached out to Starbucks. The crew goes through an application process for donations which vary among the vendors. The crew began the process in late May. “We are on a tight timeframe, but since we have a relationship with Piedmont Grocery and Village Market we can email our [requests] and expedite the process,” Zietlow confirmed. The crew will use proceeds from the Pancake Breakfast to support its philanthropic projects, which includes service work in partnership with Rebuilding Together Oakland to renovate the homes of low-income and elderly Oakland residents. Each year, PCSC raises over $12,000 through fundraisers and parent donations. The annual Pancake Breakfast will be held between 8 a.m. and 10:30 a.m. in the Veterans Hall, 401 Highland Avenue at the corner of Vista Avenue. Advance tickets are available online at: https:// www.piedmontbsa.org/events/ july-4th-pancake-breakfast/. For those who cannot join the breakfast, but would like to donate to the crew’s philanthropic projects, visit https://rtoakland. org/blog/pcsc. For families with teens interested in joining Piedmont Community Service Crew, visit https://www.pcservicecrew.org.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is piloting a self-haul compost program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up every Friday during the summer months, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to self-haul from an unattended pile every Friday starting at 8:00 a.m. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located outside the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. The site is now open every Friday through the summer. The compost is first-come, firstserved, and City staff cannot guarantee or confirm availability of compost. To pick up compost, you should bring your own shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials yourself. Pick-up trucks must tarp their loads. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected in Republic Services communities participating in curbside organics collection services, which includes Piedmont. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials that can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with soil also aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1 this year requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses to be composted. More information can be found at the City’s news and notifications page. If questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont.ca.gov, tel. (510) 420-3058.
articles.title: Free self-haul compost program in Piedmont

articles.text: The Piedmont 4th of July Parade is back after a pandemic-driven hiatus. And so is Piedmont icon Geez, who will be takin’ it to the streets as the leader of the Dynamite Dogs Brigade. Our chief canine correspondent, Willie Oakton, recently caught up with the peripatetic Geez, and had a spirited conversation in advance of the Piedmont parade on Monday, Juyl 4. Q. Welcome back Geez! How long have you led the dog unit in the Piedmont parade? A. My first parade was in 2017. It’s always great, patriotic fun and I was very disappointed when the 2020 and 2021 parades had to be cancelled. Q. What have you been doing since the last parade in 2019? A. Later that year, while life was still normal, I did a road trip through the Great Smokey Mountains, the Carolinas, Tennessee, Georgia and Alabama. Q: The old South! In fact, aren’t you a southern hound? A. Yes. I was born in Bessemer, Alabama and a highlight of the trip was seeing my old pals Lee and Dana who rescued me from life on a chain there. Thanks to them, I’ve now been to all 48 continental U.S. states. I’ve even been to Paris (Texas, that is). Q. When the pandemic hit, how long were you sidelined? A. I was at home for about a case the mobs returned. Q. What’s your all-time favorite place? A: When you’ve been as many places as I have, it’s hard to pick just one. But it’s hard to top the Piedmont 4th of July Parade. I’m looking forward to more patriotic experiences, like this one aboard a ferry bound for Orient, NY. Darn, I wish I had remembered to bring a copy of the Post for a Where In the World Are We picture! Come meet Geez and his handler, the Geezer (Bruce Goddard) at the 2022 Piedmont Parade. The Dynamite Dogs Brigade will assemble at 119 Waldo Avenue at 10:30 a.m. on Monday, July 4th. All well-behaved dogs on leash are welcome to join in the festivities. year and a half. Everything was closed, including the dog parks. It was pretty much just me and a tennis ball. Boring, to say the least! Q. So how did you get back out there? A. With a vengeance in the fall of 2021 on a 9,000 mile, 46 day tour through 29 states. The itinerary included tiny towns like Norfolk, NE, Stonington, ME, Whitehaven, MD, and Borger, TX, along with big cities like Chicago, Boston, New York and Washington, DC. Q. What were some highlights of that trip? A. I especially enjoyed the Johnny Carson Museum in Norfolk, NE, Wrigley Field in Chicago, riding the New York City subway and visiting the U.S. Capitol where a police officer deputized me in Geez aboard a ferry bound for Orient, NY.
