articles.text: After nine years of leading Piedmont Middle School as principal, Ryan Fletcher will be relocating with his family to Denver, Colorado. He will take the position of principal at a small middle school in a suburb outside of Denver. Fletcher earned the unwavering respect of nine years of students to pass through the middle school, his faculty at PMS, and the entire PUSD district. Eighth grade student Sparrow Lieu, a member of Anne Smith’s Yearbook and News Broadcast class, interviewed Fletcher for the PMS Front Page broadcast. A transcript of the interview follows. It was released on the last day of school, June 2. In the interview Fletcher candidly discusses his tenure, his decision to reloPhoto Credit: Brian Killgore Ryan Fletcher with his children Halle and Quinn as they walk down the Witter Field stairs at the 8th grade graduation on June 1. Piedmont Middle School Principal Ryan Fletcher was interviewed by 8th grader Sparrow Lieu in his office. cate, and the lessons learned in the last decade in Piedmont. Lieu: What was your favorite thing about being Principal at PMS? Fletcher: Definitely the relationships that I’ve been able to forge with both students and staff over the years. I feel it’s really important for me to be able to be approachable especially for our students. Lieu: What are you going to miss most about Piedmont Middle School? Fletcher: Definitely all the relationships, it’s been nine years since I’ve been here and this community has been extremely supportive during that time and the folks who I work with each and every day everyone at the school. There’s a lot that I’m going to really miss. It’s all the students that have gone through these doors up through the high school. It’s crazy to think, but my first year here, all of those students are actually graduating college as we speak. I’m going to miss all those connections with folks coming back into the community after graduating and running into them and getting to hear how they’re doing. Moving is sad for me because I’m not going to have the luxury of being able to run into so many folks that I have made relationships with over the years. Lieu: Why are you leaving Piedmont Middle School? Fletcher: Well it’s definitely not because I want to leave Piedmont Middle School. This is bittersweet for me for sure. I think you all know my family, my two kids Quinn and Halle you see them on a daily basis. My wife Laura and I have gotten to a kind of a point where we’re looking to put down some roots in an area where we have a greater network of both friends and family. We have amazing friends here in the Bay Area but not a whole lot of family, and with little kids and young kids that can be hard. So, we have thought about this for quite some time. Because we have a huge network in Denver, we decided to take the plunge and move there. So, it’s bittersweet for sure, because what I’m giving up here in Piedmont is something else. This school, this community, all of that – it’s really hard. Yet, as parents, we believe that this is going to be a good choice for our kids. Lieu: What is something you’ve learned from being principal at Piedmont Middle School? Fletcher: I will say that every day is different. I think that’s true for anybody who works in education and I think that’s one of the most special things about it. I have learned that it’s really important to be a good listener; it’s really important to gain perspectives from others, especially when looking to make any changes within the structure or program. Over the years I feel really fortunate there have been quite a few things that we’ve done here. I walk away from this thinking some great things have happened here and have been added during my time. With all of that there comes the necessity and the need to listen and gather input. Our late start is one example. When I started here, kids went to school early in the morning and research shows that’s not appropriate, especially for growing teens. So, listening and getting feedback from folks around sleep studies and how long our students were sleeping was an important catalyst in why we changed that. Today we have a student versus staff game; the importance of building community, building events on a campus and how that can impact a student’s life is super important. I look back and see what we learned from our students. I see the importance of the students wanting to connect with the adults around them, and so we’ve tried to implement things that have helped with that. Scots Camp was a way for us to make this school a very inclusive environment right away for our sixth grade students. So those are things that I’m going to remember a lot. Lieu: What is the hardest thing about being a principal? Fletcher: Time management – and especially time management as a parent, it doesn’t end with this job. That kind of connects with what I shared with you about every day being different. In my nine years here, I became a brand-new parent and then we had another child. As my kids are getting older, I want to be very involved with what they’re doing. It’s that balance; I do think that’s something this role always will have and it’s true for many roles within education. Lieu: Is there anything else you would like to add? Fletcher: I just want to express a deep appreciation for this community and how I’ve been welcomed here. This has been a very interesting last few

I think that’s true for anybody who works in education and I think that’s one of the most special things about it. I have learned that it’s really important to be a good listener; it’s really important to gain perspectives from others, especially when looking to make any changes within the structure or program. Over the years I feel really fortunate there have been quite a few things that we’ve done here. I walk away from this thinking some great things have happened here and have been added during my time. With all of that there comes the necessity and the need to listen and gather input. Our late start is one example. When I started here, kids went to school early in the morning and research shows that’s not appropriate, especially for growing teens. So, listening and getting feedback from folks around sleep studies and how long our students were sleeping was an important catalyst in why we changed that. Today we have a student versus staff game; the importance of building community, building events on a campus and how that can impact a student’s life is super important. I look back and see what we learned from our students. I see the importance of the students wanting to connect with the adults around them, and so we’ve tried to implement things that have helped with that. Scots Camp was a way for us to make this school a very inclusive environment right away for our sixth grade students. So those are things that I’m going to remember a lot. Lieu: What is the hardest thing about being a principal? Fletcher: Time management – and especially time management as a parent, it doesn’t end with this job. That kind of connects with what I shared with you about every day being different. In my nine years here, I became a brand-new parent and then we had another child. As my kids are getting older, I want to be very involved with what they’re doing. It’s that balance; I do think that’s something this role always will have and it’s true for many roles within education. Lieu: Is there anything else you would like to add? Fletcher: I just want to express a deep appreciation for this community and how I’ve been welcomed here. This has been a very interesting last few See Fletcher Interview on page 30

articles.text: Anne Jumper, an incoming senior at Piedmont High School, was awarded a $2,000 Second Place Award in an international art contest on June 15. The Fort Scott, Kansas based competition, is the 7th annual international ArtEffect Project competition, and is put on by the Lowell Milken Center for Unsung Heroes. Jumper and eight other middle and high school winners were challenged artistically to honor unsung heroes with creativity and skill. A total of $16,750 in cash prizes was given out. Jumper’s piece, titled “The Beauty of Genius – Hedy Lamar,” was on display in the Piedmont AP Art show and was featured in the Piedmont Post in May. Her acrylic on canvas painting honors Austrian inventor and actress Hedy Lamarr, whose communication technology prevented the Nazis from intercepting classified messages during World War II. Her innovations are still utilized in Bluetooth and WiFi technology today. “[Hedy Lamar] is a lot like me in that she has taken a lifetime pursuit of art, along with a STEM career and inventing. To see a woman pursue and have such a multi-faceted life at that time was very inspiring to me,” said Jumper in an awards acceptance speech. “You showed how you could skillfully depict her on that reel in so many different expressions and settings,” said Milken Family Foundation Assistant Director Toni Guglielmo. Lowell Milken Center Executive Director Norm Conard said, “Your work is just marvelous. We were blown away with the design itself and putting all this together.” Piedmont High School artist Anne Jumper holds her winning painting of Austrian inventor and actress Hedy Lamarr. “ArtEffect winners submit works of art that show visionary thinking and creative skills of a superior nature,” explained Conard. “We at the Lowell Milken Center for Unsung Heroes salute excellence and the active imagination of our student champions.” The $6,000 Grand Prize went to Chloe Kim, a 10th grader at The Overlake School in Redmond, Washington. Her art focused on Irena Sendler, a Polish social worker who rescued hundreds of children from the Warsaw Ghetto during the Holocaust. To watch Jumper receive the award and explain her piece visit: Youtube.com/watch?v=HOEkpbKEWps LMC also puts on a 2022 Discovery Award Competition, which awards $14,000 to students entering grades 4-12. The submission deadline for projects is July 1, 2022. View competition guidelines and rules at Lowellmilkencenter.org/competitions/ discovery-award

articles.text: Woodshop has returned to room 125 at Piedmont Middle School, not as a school elective but as a summer class offered by the Recreation Department, with a morning class for kids ages 6-9, and an afternoon section for 8-11 year olds. Instructor Casey Nutt brings his tools to teach kids how to use hand tools and create wooden works of art. Popular projects include boats, bird houses, treasure chests, catapults, trucks and cars, and pinball games. Students use hand tools such as the coping and crosscut saws, hand miter saws, block planes, the shinto rasp, files, hand powered eggbeater drills and brace drills, and also power tools like cordless drills and drivers. “My favorite tool to use was either the plane or the Shinto Rasp Japanese wood shaping tool. There are big teeth on one side and small teeth on the other side. You basically go back and Staff photos Students in a summer Woodshop Class hold up their favorite projects created during the week. Front row Charlie Parker (left), Abigail Droessler, Brendan Edesess, Isaac Milner. Back row Juliette Edesess (left), Charlotte Phung, Owen Milner and Hazel Giacona. Brendan Edesess (left) plays against Isaac Milner on the two-person pinball game, while Charlie Parker (second to left) and Owen Milner play on the solo pinball machines. Ethan Grossberg uses the planer. forth to carve out shapes in the wood,” explained Hazel Giacona, Nutt’s daughter, and assistant for the week. The class is highly popular since Woodshop has been replaced by Makers in the school curriculum. There is a waiting list of 40 kids for some of the sessions. wth a limit of about 10 kids in each week-long session. With eight weeks of both morning and afternoon classes, around 160 kids go through the class each summer. Nutt also teaches an after-school class on Thursdays in Piedmont. “I wouldn’t sell any of my pieces, it’s hard to put a value on Charlotte Phung uses a hand-powered drill to make a hole in a piece of wood. Some of the finished projects include Humvees, ships and catapults. Young carpenters play on the intricate, all analog, wood pinball machines. them. I guess they are priceless,” said student Julia Edesess. “Mr. Nutt basically taught me everything I know about carpentry, I didn’t know anything before. It is pretty helpful because now I can help around the house more. I used to not be able to help my dad hammer nails into the wall, but now I can help hang shelves and picture frames,” said Owen Miller. Nutt went to the Northwest School of Wooden Boatbuilding in 2001 at age 20. After that he worked as a residential and marine carpenter in the East Bay. In 2008 he started teaching parttime, and it eventually turned into his full-time job, with offerings at multiple locations around the Bay Area. “An important point of the class is that it is a physical type of education; kids learn with their hands. They are making important connections between their mind and body. I like to give them the chance to explore those connections in a fun, creative space,” said Nutt. Charlie Parker sends an airplane down the zip line. Charlotte Phung made one of the more ambitious projects this past session, a nesting box for her chicken coop at home. “I am learning how to build big things and how to take measurements,” she said. “At home I have been designing a plan for another big project. My mom is an architect, so it has been nice to work with her,” said Phung. For more information on Nutt’s program, see: Kidscarpentry.com. Instructor Casey Nutt talks shop with some of his student carpenters.

articles.text: Can you remember catching your young child in a lie? For most of us, this experience strikes fear: am I raising a deceitful person? Is this the first step down a dangerous path of dishonesty? Actually, lying is a normal part of cognitive-linguistic development which typically occurs during the preschool years. Studies show that up to 80% of 4-yearolds lie. This milestone indicates that the child has learned that other people have their own and often differing opinions. It signifies that the child has learned that they can use words in a more abstract way than simply to express their needs and wants, namely that words can get someone to think something that is not actually true. The child now understands that what we say does not always correspond with what we are thinking and sometimes we hide what we are really thinking and feeling. To make matters more complicated, this is often the age at which parents may start to encourage lying in certain situations, such as when they receive a present they already have or do not like. Fortunately, many positive traits are associated with this period of language development as well, such as increased communication related to conflict resolution, increased social competence and relationship building. The concomitant emergence of these skills will help parents when attempting to discuss this complicated topic with their little language learners. So, if we view the early Photo Caption: There are positive ways to talk to your toddler about lying. appearance of lying as an important developmental milestone, rather than a morality issue, how can we best react to it? First, it is important to determine the function of the lie. Common functions include: to get something the child wants, to avoid embarrassment, to gain approval or attention, to remove the spotlight from themselves, to spare someone’s feelings, to avoid a consequence or conflict, or poor impulse control. Keeping the truth hidden or creating a “story” often makes the child feel better. Once we have determined the function of the lie, we can discuss it. Resist the impulse to ask “why did you do that?” It is the first question parents go to, and unfortunately it does nothing to increase awareness or insight and adds the negative element of shame. Instead, stick to “what” and “how” questions to review what happened in a supportive and positive way. For example, you can ask what happened first, second, last. You can ask the child how they worked it out. You can discuss what the options were. You can talk about what the child can do differently next time. You can model what you would or would not have done in the situation. And lastly, postponing this kind of a discussion to a later time can allow for a more effective exchange and successful learning opportunity. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of Speech Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com. S P E E C H , I N C .

articles.text: On a sunny Friday afternoon on May 20, members of Cub Scout Pack 5 Webelos started showing up at Boundary campground in Mt. Diablo State Park. When we started to set things up, there were pretty much no completely flat spots for good tent ground, so we took what we could get. When everyone was done setting up, we all played around and talked while the coals warmed up so we could cook our food. Everybody brought a unique foil packet dinner, and everybody enjoyed their foil packet dinner. Once everybody got their share of food, we all played and talked Felix Kansal and Anu Kansal setting up their tent. Nico Wolff helps haul gear to set up for the overnighter on Mt. Diablo. Families enjoy dinner cooked by Cub Scouts. Ben Cole keeps an eye on the foil packet dinners while they’re cooking. Madison Jung enjoys her dinner. Madison Jung, Anna Benson, and Nico Wolff checking out the views from the summit of Mt. Diablo. some more until we got to, the amazing, s’more time! The kids definitely raided the marshmallows like hungry cattle, but it was all in good fun. I’d say everybody got their fair share of s’mores. After all the sticky and gooey s’mores, I decided to tell a spooky but funny story. Once the story was finished, the whole den got together and did a couple of spooky but still funny skits. After skits, s’mores, and a little mischief, it was time to head to bed. Everyone went into their nice and cozy sleeping bags and slept. And then morning came. Everyone went sleepily to the breakfast bench for a nice breakfast of eggs, hash browns, and glorious bacon. The Jungs graciously gave everyone two tictacs and an icebreaker, and we all decided how we were going to spend the last few hours. First, we went to the summit, which is 3,849 feet above sea level. That’s high! There was a tower at the summit, with a beacon attached to it. Nobody wanted to leave, but we had to go to the campsite, pack up all our stuff, and then head to our final destination: Rock City. We got to the campsite, packed up our stuff, and headed out.

articles.text: With the 2022 school year over, high schools throughout the country say goodbye to former student athletes. With that, Piedmont Class of 2023 looks past the summer break to what could be a defining year of their careers as seniors. In this article, the Post takes a look at three seniors who could have big seasons waiting for them. MORGAN HUNT Soccer & Softball Morgan Hunt is a key member of both the soccer and softball teams. She will be a four-year starter on both teams, a goalkeeper in soccer and outfielder and first baseman in softball. In the recent softball season, Hunt was a power hitter for coach Gene Denard, with six home runs, 18 RBIs on 17 hits with 17 runs scored, and a .279 batting average. She helped the team posy an 18-7 record and win the Shoreline league title with a perfect 10-0 record. She earned a first-team All-League selection and had two in a 4-0 win over Mt. Eden on April 27. On the soccer pitch, Hunt earned another first-team AllLeague selection after helping the team to a 7-5-6 rec record and 5-4-3 against Foothill Division teams. Staff Photos Morgan Hunt is a four-year starter on the softball and soccer teams, earning first-team AllLeague selections in both sports. EMILY FITZGERALD Soccer & Swimming DARIUSH KASHANI Water Polo Emily Fitzgerald was the leading scorer on the soccer team on the winter and also was a member of the swimming team’s 400 freestyle relay and 200 medley relay teams. She will be a four-year starter on Dan Chubbock’s soccer team as a striker, and also as a central attacking midfielder. She helped Piedmont earn the No. 6 seed in the Division 4 NCS playoffs and scored all four goals in the Highlanders’ 4-0 win over No. 11 College Prep on February 26. In the spring she was part of the swim team’s winning 200-medley relay race against Arroyo, and the 400 freestyle relay race versus Encinal and Mt. Eden in April. Dariush Kashani is a four-year starter on the water polo team and earned first-team All-League honors last fall. He was the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2020 and 2021 honorable mention for Sophomore of the Year. Kashani was a major factor in the water polo team’s 19-6 overall season and its first-ever WACC Championship title with a 12-8 win over Berkeley on October 30, a game in which he recorded nine saves and one steal. The Highlanders reached the NCS Semifinals as the No. 3 seeded team in November but lost 7-4 to No. 2 Marin Academy in a heated defensive game. To get there, they earned a first-round bye and defeated No. 6 Terra Linda 7-4 in the quarterfinals. Emily Fitzgerald was the leading scorer on the soccer team. She scored all four goals in Piedmont’s 4-0 North Coast Section win against neighboring College Prep. Dariush Kashani was a major part of the water polo team’s league championship, their first in at least 15 years.
articles.title: A look ahead at the Class of 2023

Wednesday, June 22, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. LUKE BARRETT Basketball Piedmont High Class of 2020 St. Mary’s College Class of 2024 Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, finished up his sophomore year at St. Mary’s College as a member of the basketball team. He played in 15 games last season, including an appearance in the Gaels’ 82-53 win over Indiana in the first round of the NCAA Tournament, where he recorded two rebounds in three minutes of action. Barrett averaged 3.9 minutes per game and scored his first career point against Southern Utah in November. He scored a high of five points against Stanislaus State on December 14, where he also recorded two steals and an assist. He also finished with two points, three rebounds, and three assists in just seven minutes of action on February 10 against San Diego. Barrett finished 2022 shooting 47 percent, converted one 3-point shot, and had 14 total rebounds, six assists, and three steals. He’s a member of Piedmont’s 2020 North Coast championship team and was named as Athlete of the Year by the Post. What is your workout program this summer? I am working out with my team for most of the summer, which includes strength and conditioning, skill workouts, and open gyms. What are your fitness goals for this summer? My main goals are to get more flexible and mobile, as well as increasing my lateral quickness. I also want to add 10 pounds of muscle to my lower body. How are you measuring your development? Our trainers do a great job of assessing our development in specific movements and telling us where we need to improve. I am monitoring my weight and overall strength to make sure I am doing the right things. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Currently, I am working with my coaches and trainers, but I’ll continue doing similar training sessions on my own when our summer workout program ends. pages.text: Wednesday, June 22, 2022 15 HIKING WITH JON Walking Angel Island State Park’s perimeter trail By Jonathan Comeaux It’s hard to think of a better location to take in the beauty of the Bay Area and acknowledge its history. Angel Island State Park is a true gem resting next to the Marin County shore, where hikers, campers, bikers, and families can take in its gorgeous surroundings and learn about some important Bay Area history. The perimeter loop of Angel Island is approximately 6.2 miles with 495 feet of elevation gain, but added detours to the Immigration Station, Fort McDowell, Quarry Point and Beach, or other beaches will equate to a hike of roughly eight miles with 1,000 feet of elevation gain. Starting your hike walking past the Angel Island Visitor Center, turn left once you hit the paved Perimeter Road, you’ll walk slightly under two miles to the Immigration Station. The station was constructed in 1905 and controlled the entry of approximately one million Chinese citizens into the U.S. The area provides a reminder of the culture of America when the Chinese Exclusion Act was created, and the harsh A view of the abandoned soldier barracks at Fort McDowell. The Post Exchange at Fort McDowell, with the Golden Gate Bridge in the distance. The lush captain’s quarters on Angel Island. The view from Quarry Beach, a great place to rest for a snack. The view of the Angel Island Immigration Station. reality for Asian immigrants. Outside the Detention Center reads phrases reflecting the reality for the Chinese immigrants: “Bravery, Loneliness, Frustration, Anger, Segregation, Confinement, Courage, Sacrifice.” There is a $5 admittance cost to enter. The hospital is free to the public and shows the process used to admit Asian immigrants into the country. Along the shore is “The Wharf,” where immigrants took their first steps into the country. You can picture how it might have looked while gazing out to the Bay. Although it’s a beautiful place to rest, it’s a harsh reminder of what immigrants endured upon arrival in the United States. A half mile past the Immigration Station are the abandoned buildings of Fort McDowell, a former soldiers’ barracks, the plush captain’s quarters, and a decrepit building that was once the mess hall. Nearby is the former officer’s building, which is now a museum. Although it is currently closed, a park ranger allowed me inside to take photos. Inside are old relics from World War I and World War Staff Photos There is a great view of the Bay from the Wharf, but a harsh reminder of the experience for Asian Immigrants entering the country in the early 1900s. II, old cannon balls, and a section of jail cells. The area is typically open in the busy season around the 4th of July, so be sure to visit. Continuing for nearly three miles along the western side of the Island, you’ll have a constant view of San Francisco, Alcatraz, and the Golden Gate Bridge until reaching the Camp Reynolds Hospital. If you continue off trail past the hospital, a short walk takes you to Point Stuart, which provides a secluded view of the Golden Gate, Sausalito, and Belvedere Island of Marin County. From Point Stuart, it’s just a mile hike back to the starting point where you can wait for the ferry. Enjoy a bite to eat and a drink at the Angel Island Café, which often has live music on the weekends. If you want to save your legs, you can also rent a bike for $26 per hour or $99 for the day. The western side of the island offers a great view of San Francisco and Alcatraz Island. Point Stuart provides a secluded view of the Golden Gate.

articles.text: Festival Opera will perform Vincenzo Bellini’s two-act opera, Norma, at the Lesher Center for the Arts in Walnut Creek on July 8 and 10. Shana Blake Hill will sing the title role, directed by Mark Foehringe. The Festival Opera Orchestra and Chorus will be conducted by Bryan Nies. Hill has sung important roles in a number of noteworthy operas, including Rosalba in Daniel Catan’s Florencia en el Amazonas with Los Angeles Opera and Cincinnati Opera, Mimi in La Bohéme with Los Angeles Opera, Violetta in La Traviata with Dayton Opera, and the title role in Aida with Opera Southwest and Baltimore Concert Opera. The cast also includes Ashley Dixon, Dane Suarez, Kevin Thompson, Marcus Paige, and Lily Bogas. Festival Opera, now in its 31st season, is based out of Walnut Creek that strives to advance the operatic art form and to build community by producing culturally rich and diverse programming. The opera will be performed on Friday, July 8 at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday, July 10 at 2 p.m., both at the Hoffman Theatre at the Lesher Center for the Arts. Tickets now on sale at www. festivalopera.org or by calling (925) 943-7469. articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California was one of six recipients of the 2022 National Medal for Museum and Library Service, the nation’s highest honor given to museums and library institutions. The medal was awarded by the Institute of Museum and Library Services on June 7. “We are pleased to recognize the outstanding performance and meritorious community and professional service of our six National Medal recipients,” said Institute Director Crosby Kemper. “We look forward to celebrating them and calling attention to their great work not only in their widespread locales but across the land.” Oakland Museum was nominated for the honor by Congresswoman Barbara Lee, explained Oakland Museum CEO Lori Fogarty. “We are deeply honored to receive this award from the Institute of Museum and Library Services and are grateful to our Congresswoman, Barbara Lee, for the nomination,” said Fogarty. “While The Oakland Museum of California this recognition pays tribute to the work and service by the OMCA staff, Board, volunteers and community partners over more than five decades, it is also a call to action for our continued efforts. Museums are more necessary than ever before as places to build connection, trust, and belonging – to foster understanding of our history so we can imagine a more just and healthy future – and this award reminds us of this opportunity and obligation.” Congresswoman Lee described OMCA as a “Museum of the People,” that celebrates the diversity and character of California. “The Oakland Museum of California plays an important role for all of us in learning about the many stories of our State, particularly those stories that are untold and underrepresented,” said Congresswoman Lee. “It is a museum that reflects and uplifts voices from our communities and from our history while also inspiring our future artists, scientists, and history-makers.”
articles.title: Oakland Museum wins national award for Museum and Library Services

articles.text: Stern Grove Festival’s 85th season is underway, with a range of free concerts now through August 14. This Sunday, June 26, vocalist Liz Phair will headline the evening. Phair is a Grammy-nominated singer whose 1993 debut studio album Exile in Guyville was released to international acclaim; it has been ranked by Rolling Stone as one of the 500 Greatest Albums of All Time. Reservations for the show are required. Entry is on a first come, first served basis. Entrances open at noon and the concert begins at 2 p.m. To reserve entry, visit https://www.sterngrove. org/85th-concert-season/lizphair. For a full lineup of artists at this year’s festival visit https:// www.sterngrove.org/. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the free concert series, “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts – including opera, theatre, and music – completely free. Reservations are required to attend. Liz Phair performs this Sunday at Stern Grove Festival.
articles.title: Liz Phair performs this Sunday at Stern Grove Festival

articles.text: In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform a concert on Sunday, July 10 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts celebrating the music of composer Harry Warren. The Trio consists of Bill Jackman (Piano), Rich Trevor (Bass), and Anthony Pegram (Drums), who collectively make up an oldschool, classic jazz piano trio. The concert serves as a tribute to one of the most successful film composers; Warren has composed music for more than 75 films, starring luminaries like Fred Astaire, Judy Garland, and Bing Crosby. Jackman has been with the trio for the past 27 years; he was a student of the late Oakland jazz pianist Art Fletcher. He has recorded six CDs in the piano trio format. Bassist Trevor grew up in Chicago and draws influence from blues and R&B, eventually becoming the bassist for Eli’s Mile High Club in Oakland. Pegram has been a drummer for jazz combo bands and big bands in the Bay Area for over 40 years. Most recently, he accompanied singer Marcella Hooks and pianist Rodney Burge as the house trio for the Sunday Jazz Brunch at Scott’s Restaurant in Oakland’s Jack London Square. The concert begins at 3 p.m. Tickets are $20 and are available online at https://bpt.me/5316993 or at the door. In the Tradition Piano Trio will perform a concert in Piedmont on July 10. 196 Moraga Way • Orinda • (625) 254-3714 Open Wednesday – Sunday ®

articles.text: The final chamber music concert of the season by Berkeley Symphony musicians will be held this Sunday, June 26, at 3 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. A sextet of musicians will perform a program of music that includes Heinrich Biber’s Passacaglia in G Minor for solo violin, Caroline Shaw’s Limestone and Felt for viola & cello, and Brian Raphael Nabors’ Caged for string quintet. The concert will conclude with Ravel’s timeless String Quartet in F Major. Brian Raphael Nabors is a New Music USA Amplifying Voices Composer in Residence. The musicians include Emanuela Nikiforova and Gabrielle Wunsch, violin; Alexandra Simpson and Christina Simpson, viola; and Chloé Mendola and Saul Richmond Rakerd, cello. Berkeley Symphony violinist Emanuela Nikiforova will perform in a chamber music concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday, June 26 at 3 p.m. For tickets, call Berkeley symphony at 831-8200, ext. 1, or click on its website at berkeleysymphony.org. articles.text: The battleground for artistic philosophy is as old as time. They say youth must be served, but I ask: is change for the sake of change obligatory? Jaume Torrent, the noted concert guitarist and composer, observes the following. I found it most apropos, as you will see. An artist’s philosophy of life is one that consists of an unconditional commitment to music. This commitment derives from a vocation that is above economic enrichment and fame. These two objectives, unfortunately, are not in the forefront of all musicians, but they must permeate the spirit that moves our artistic society. Without them we will experience many of the tragedies that humanity continues to experience. Last Sunday Berkeley Symphony presented its final concert of the season. They played up to their usual high standard. Before the actual concert began, the audience was subjected to the usual spoken inanities that have become all too common at concerts these days. The written program notes were excellent. Common sense tells us that we, the audience, can read the program notes for our own intellectual enlightenment, or we can listen to the music and take it at face value. Any more is gratuitous. The concert began with a new piece by Jimmy Lopez Bellido entitled “Rise.” It is a brilliant piece enhanced by an almost Tchaikovsky-inspired orchestration. Exciting and colorful melodies entered and exited making for a most enjoyable listening experience. As the music progressed, I was surprised by the extreme difficulties. It is a fun piece, but the difficulties are daunting. I began to watch individual players in the orchestra. I couldn’t believe my eyes. After the concert was over I talked with some of them whom I know. These are Composer Jimmy Lopez Bellido’s fiendishly difficult work, “Rise”, was performed by Berkeley Symphony at Zellerbach Hall on Sunday as part of the final concert of the season. extraordinary players, and they told me they have never played a piece so difficult in all of their lives. I remember one time in Gregor Piatigorsky’s master class he said to a composer, “You are a very mean man. Why do you write music that is so immensely difficult?” The concert continued with a lofty interpretation of Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony. The Berkeley Symphony is a very well-balanced ensemble. The woodwind playing was outstanding. I was especially impressed by the timpani playing of Kevin Neuhoff. In general the strings play exceptionally well, except for some weakness in the first violins. All these things were to the good. The four vocal soloists were in good voice. articles.text: Artist and art historian Michael Stehr returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, June 24, for an illustrated lecture entitled “A Stroll in Rome: The Ponte Umberto to San Pietro.” Doors open at 6:30 p.m., and lecture begins at 7 p.m. Tickets are $20 at the door cash only. Stehr will take the audience on one of his favorite strolls in Rome, the walk from the Ponte Umberto to Saint Peter’s Basilica. Along the way audience members will see some of the world’s greatest urban vistas, while experiencing encounters with Michelangelo, Bernini, and Carlo Maderno, among others. “The city of Rome boasts some of the more noteworthy destinations in the Western World. The Pantheon, the Sistine Chapel, and Saint Peter’s Basilica are just a few of the landmarks that attract visitors from around the world,” said Stehr. “But with so much history around every corner, sometimes the short journey to arrive at a destination is as thrilling as the encounter with that destination itself.” For more information on the artist, visit http://www.mstehr. com/about. An illustrated lecture celebrating one of the great walks in Rome Doors open at 6:30 pm Proof of vaccination required for entry and, in accordance with Alameda County mandate, masks will be required indoors. $20 per person at the door (Cash only) For more information, contact Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com

articles.text: The annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only weeklong residency chamber music festival in the East Bay, celebrates its fifth festival at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in a series of intimate concerts opening July 20. This season festival musicians will explore the theme “Human. Alone and Together” in works from composers old and new that remind us that life is better together. Led by founders Wayne Lee (violin) a Piedmont native, and his wife Juliana Han (piano), the festival features eight internationally acclaimed musicians from throughout the U.S. Returning musicians Jarmine Lin (violin) and Deborah Pae (cello), will be joined by guest musicians Teng Li (Principal Violinist, Los Angeles Philharmonic), Francisco Fullana (violin), Clancy Newman (cellist & composer), and Paul Laraia (viola). This Week’s Featured Artist: Cellist Clancy Newman Cellist Clancy Newman enjoys an extraordinarily wide-ranging career, not only as a cellist, but Photo by Lisa-Marie Mazzucco Cellist and composer Clancy Newman makes his second appearance in the annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival this summer. also as a composer, producer, writer, and guest lecturer. First prize winner of the Naumburg International Competition and recipient of an Avery Fisher Career Grant, he has performed as soloist throughout the United States, as well as in Europe, Asia, Canada, and Australia. As a composer, he has been featured on series by the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center and the Chicago Chamber Musicians, and his “Pop-Unpopped” project has expanded cello technique in ways heretofore unimagined. In 2021 he was commissioned by the Kingston Chamber Music Festival to produce four educational videos to assist school teachers as they navigate the COVID-19 pandemic. Mr. Newman is a graduate of the five-year exchange program between Columbia University and The Juilliard School. Tickets are $45, with a savings on season passes for all three concerts for $120. To reserve tickets now and for more information, including complete biographies of all musicians and details of the music program, visit the website: www.piedmontcmf.org. All public events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require photo ID and valid proof of full vaccination including booster shot for entry, as well as proper masking while inside. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue in Piedmont.

articles.text: Tom Cruise in a scene from Top Gun: Maverick. Top Gun: Maverick, an update of the original film, is now playing in theaters nationwide. It carries the hope that after more than two years of COVID-19 audiences will return to movie houses and to the larger- than-life big screen. Its opening weekends were encouraging; however, I wonder if the box office response to this sequel has more to do with the nostalgic buzz that still prevails 36 years after the original high octane Top Gun was released. The movie wowed audiences and turned Tom Cruise from a well-received actor (Risky Business) into a movie star. But a few words about sequels: When the first movie is as compellingly good as was Tony Scott’s Top Gun, to create a solid, fresh legacy sequel represents a huge, sometimes impossible challenge. The writers have to find a story that feels new, yet has the same intensity as the original. Of course, there has to be an enemy, one that shall not be named, and a hair-on-fire mission crisis involving the swaggering best of the best naval aviators from Miramar Top Gun school flying F-18s and F-35s barely above the hard deck at Mach whatever. Top Gun: Maverick clearly has a bevy of harrowing flight photography moments that makes this film a big screen must. It rips. But to make a complete movie, one that complements the harrowing action, there has to be a narrative that captures the audience. The new cast of characters must have their feet on the ground and not just on the pedals or hands on the stick. In other words, the writers have to find that Top Gun sweet spot. Of course, Maverick is still a captain, still a rebel (it’s pointed out that after almost four decades he should be an admiral), and still a gifted flyer (now a test pilot for the Navy). But in my view the story is thin, the characters vague and not fully developed. The dramatic conflict between Maverick and Goose’s son (Miles Teller), known as Rooster, now a Top Gun aviator, is unconvincing. There is also a love interest, Penny Benjamin (Jennifer Connely). Her underused presence is absent any backstory other than she runs a popular bar filled with doppelganger Navy flyers. Following a familiar playbook, Top Gun: Maverick may be viewed as a start-of-summer blockbuster preceded with endless hype. The film even begins with a sit-down monologue by Cruise, thanking the audience for showing up. We’ll see how it goes and whether this sequel will also become a phenom and a pop culture touchstone. Top Gun: Maverick. Directed by Joseph Kosinski. Starring Tom Cruise, Miles Teller, and Jennifer Connelly. 2 hrs., 11 min. Rated PG-13. Showing in theaters. Streaming on VUDU. Tom Cruise reprises his role as Pete ‘Maverick’ Mitchell.
articles.title: New Top Gun: Maverick now playing in theaters

articles.text: Samuel L. Jackson, Jennifer Jason Leigh and Kurt Russell star in The Hateful Eight. Movie review by Chris Honoré Writer/director Quentin Tarantino occupies an interesting niche in Hollywood’s filmmaking panoply. He’s quirky, over-the-top, and does most of his own writing. In the opening shot of The Hateful Eight he includes the fact that this is his eighth feature film. Clearly he can be a master of story and of mayhem and when he is at the top of his game, as he was in Inglorious Basterds. He can offer up a stylized and hard-edged film. Even Pulp Fiction had its moments. The Hateful Eight is not one of those films. It’s as if Tarantino decided to do an Agatha Christie tale set in the post-Civil War west of Wyoming with wide shots of snow-covered mountains and a stagecoach making its way across breathtaking vistas. There’s a hellishly brutal blizzard on the way and the cold is palpable. But most of the story takes place in the hermetic confines of a stagecoach outpost called Minnie’s Haberdashery, a stopover on the way to a town called Red Rock. Two stagecoaches have stopped for shelter and the cast of characters find themselves waiting out the storm in one very large room. They are quite a crew – mostly bounty hunters and rogues with an overlay of suspicion that some may not be who they say they are. What the film quickly devolves into is endless dialogue filled with racial epithets, punctuated eventually by moments of violence, gore and mayhem. Much of what takes place seems gratuitous, misogynistic and sadistic. There’s a sense that Tarantino wanted to make an interesting film but had a failure of imagination, and so resurrected his standard trope of tight-shot gore and violence, falling back on themes developed in previous films such as Django Unchained. Tarantino has brought together a fine ensemble of actors who each give their characters a solid credibility. They are all rough trade, and they’re all treading water in what is an overly long, indulgent exercise. I was tempted to add a bit of summary of this film (who is who and what brings them to this outpost) as part of the review. But it would be pointless. The plot meanders endlessly while Tarantino attempts to construct a tension that uses a wobbly scaffolding of curiosity). What is really going on? It quickly begins to feel tedious. As an aside: there is one woman among all the men in Minnie’s Haberdashery, a woman named Daisy Domergue played by Jennifer Jason Leigh. She’s quite a piece of work and Leigh’s performance, outrageous and convincing, has earned her a Best Supporting Actress nomination. The Hateful Eight. Starring Kurt Russell, Jennifer Jason Lee and Samuel L. Jackson. Directed by Quentin Tarantino. 2 hrs., 47 min. Rated R. Of course, there has to be an enemy, one that shall not be named, and a hair-on-fire mission crisis involving the swaggering best of the best naval aviators from Miramar Top Gun school flying F-18s and F-35s barely above the hard deck at Mach whatever. Top Gun: Maverick clearly has a bevy of harrowing flight photography moments that makes this film a big screen must. It rips. But to make a complete movie, one that complements the harrowing action, there has to be a narrative that captures the audience. The new cast of characters must have their feet on the ground and not just on the pedals or hands on the stick. In other words, the writers have to find that Top Gun sweet spot. Of course, Maverick is still a captain, still a rebel (it’s pointed out that after almost four decades he should be an admiral), and still a gifted flyer (now a test pilot for the Navy). But in my view the story is thin, the characters vague and not fully developed. The dramatic conflict between Maverick and Goose’s son (Miles Teller), known as Rooster, now a Top Gun aviator, is unconvincing. There is also a love interest, Penny Benjamin (Jennifer Connely). Her underused presence is absent any backstory other than she runs a popular bar filled with doppelganger Navy flyers. Following a familiar playbook, Top Gun: Maverick may be viewed as a start-of-summer blockbuster preceded with endless hype. The film even begins with a sit-down monologue by Cruise, thanking the audience for showing up. We’ll see how it goes and whether this sequel will also become a phenom and a pop culture touchstone. Top Gun: Maverick. Directed by Joseph Kosinski. Starring Tom Cruise, Miles Teller, and Jennifer Connelly. 2 hrs., 11 min. Rated PG-13. Showing in theaters. Streaming on VUDU. articles.text: A scene from Maya the Bee Movie. Released in 2015, Maya the Bee Movie is ideally suited for preschoolers. This animated film features a young apian moppet named Maya (Coco Jack Gillies) and is based on the 1922 children’s book titled The Adventures of Maya the Bee. Maya, raised by a Miss Cassandra (Justine Clark), is by nature curious and adventurous. Against the stern advice of her teacher, Miss C., Maya leaves the hive most mornings to explore the nearby gardens. Ever friendly, Maya engages with a bevy of interesting residents of the flora and fauna. such as dung beetles, ants, spiders and even hornets (considered to be the enemy of the bees). However, given her spunky, motor-mouth personality, and her refusal not to stay put in the hive and do her homework, so to speak, she is soon expelled from the hive by the nasty Buzzlina von Beena (Jacki Weaver). Buzzlina, we learn, is scheming to do away with the Queen of the hive (Miriam Margoyles), and thereby take over the throne, with the help of her dodgy wingman Crawley (Noah Taylor). Maya gets wind of Buzzlina’s nefarious plan to steal the royal jelly and with the help of her friends Flip the violin-playing grasshopper (Richard Roxburgh), and nerdy bee Willy (Kodi Smith-McPhee) tries to upset the plan. The cohort even recruits Sting (Joel Franco), a young hornet, who is, surprisingly, the son of the boss hornet, Hank (Andy McPhee). And with the unexpected help of the hornets, Maya manages to save the hive from Buzzlina. The tension in the story is between the plucky little Maya and friends and the hive’s higher ups, who insist that bees don’t dream and shouldn’t have any fun. They should just keep their noses to the grindstone, work hard, and do as the are told. Maya is a rebel, but still manages to become the heroine of this adventure, preventing a confrontation with the hornets. Maya the Bee Movie will capture the attention of preschoolers who will enjoy this family animated tale. Maya The Bee Movie. Directed by Alex Stadermann. Animation. With voices of Coco Jack Gillies, Jacki Weaver, and Joel Franco. 1 hr., 19 min. Rated G. Released in 2015 and now Streaming on VUDU/Prime/peacock.

Taron Egerton and Jamie Foxx star in the 2018 Robin Hood. By Chris Honoré The tale of Robin Hood, a film released in 2018, is iconic, having endured for centuries, dating back to the Crusades. It tells the story of a singular rebel who takes umbrage with the personal and governmental corruption exacted by the Sheriff of Nottingham, a remorseless predator who takes from the poor in order to make himself and his enablers rich. As the story goes, Robin, having just returned from the Crusades where he fought alongside King Richard the Lionhearted, discovers the repression under which his people are living. He, and a cohort of disaffected denizens of Nottingham, takes shelter in Sherwood Forest, forming a band of outlaws who plot to take back the silver and gold coin – referred to as taxes – and return it to the locals. Robin, of course, is Robin the righteous and his mission is not only to enrich the poor but to bring down the evil sheriff while waiting for King Richard to return from the Crusades. The first Robin Hood appeared in film almost a century ago. It seems that each generation must have its own iteration. The 2018 Robin Hood version is meant to satisfy a hip audience that craves a stylized take, given their schooled sophistication with social media and pop culture while feeling most at home in an urban setting. Hence, this film is slick, with hand-held stuttering camera work, plus a rapid fire series of smash cuts. The story is told at a pace that barely makes room for exposition, and rarely pauses to explore the relationship between Robin (Taron Egerton), Maid Marian (Eve Hewson) and Little John, the Syrian (Jamie Foxx). Visually, Robin Hood is a tour de force, with action scenes depicting Robin’s athleticism and his gravity-defying, lethal accuracy with a long bow. But the film soon loses its core story (if it ever existed) and starts to feel like a 12th century take on The Hunger Games, strangely futuristic with the Sheriff’s (Ben Mendelsohn) haute couture, tailored coats and Robin’s de rigueur midnight hoodie). The heroes and the villains are blemish free, with superior dental care and bright whites that require lots of flossing and enamel bleaching. I acknowledge that the filmmakers are confronted with a dilemma: include a bevy of tight shots of the actors – Robin and Marian are indeed beautiful people, but the shots take on a patina of 2018 and not 1118. Furthermore, there’s a punkish, edgy feel to the narrative. And thee is no forest in sight. Perhaps Sherwood Forest will indeed appear in the second installment. There likely will be a sequel, for the last images of Robin and Marian were of them and the merry band walking into said woods. One last comment: the dialogue is peppered with verbiage lifted from the gnarly streets of Santa Monica. Characters, such as Friar Tuck (Tim Minchin), say stuff like, “What else you got?” or “I wanna go big.” “This is not going to end well.” Plus I still recall the first voice over line spoken at the beginning of the film: “Forget what you think you know” (about the mythic Robin Hood). Fine. But now what? Robin Hood. Directed by Otto Bathurst. With Taron Egerton, Jamie Foxx, Ben Mendelsohn, Eve Hewson, and Jamie Dornan. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated PG-13. Released in theaters in 2018. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, June 22, 2022 Features By Edward Kaplan I have been in practice for over 35 years in the East Bay, San Francisco, and the greater Bay Area, and have seen many trends come and go in residential architectural design. My interest has always been to search for and create architectural spaces that have a timeless characteristic. What I mean by this is to develop design solutions that are functional at the core but have a visual expression that does not tie it to a particular fashion of the moment. A true test of this idea is to look at our projects that were completed 25 years ago and ask if they hold up today. Do they still look and function well in the context of current times? articles.text: As readers of my wine column know, Pierre is always in search of a bargain. It’s from the maternal Scottish side of my family. I like nothing better than finding a great French Cote du Rhone or Spanish Garnacha or a Provencal rose at Grocery Outlet for $5.99, but as we all know the term “bargain” is relative. The way a $35 wine can be a bargain is if it tastes as good or better than wines that cost much more. That’s why I am featuring Domain Clavel’s Copa Santa this week. My first experience with this wine was several years ago when I brought it to a blind tasting of my Piedmont wine group. At the end of the evening when the votes were tabulated, the Copa Santa was voted number one wine. When all the wines were revealed we realized it had prevailed over a Cote Rotie, a Hermitage and several Chateauneufs du Pape that were two to four times more expensive than the Copa Santa. That’s why I call it a great bargain. Domaine Clavel is in the Pic St. Loup AVA in the Languedoc region of France. Because it does not have the cache of French regions like Bordeaux, Burgundy or the Rhone Valley, the Languedoc is home to lots of France’s greatest wine bargains. The first vintage of Cope Santa was 1992 and it has become an iconic Languedoc wine since then. It is made of 70% Syrah grapes and 30% Grenache. I was able to obtain a bottle of Domain Clavel’s 2018 Copa Santa. the current release, the 2018 Copa Santa, to see if it was as good as the earlier vintages. The nose of blackberries, cassis and chocolate jumps out of the glass to begin the enchantment. On the palate it is full bodied, hugely rich and packed with plum and dark fruit flavors with a touch of earth. It is layered and complex with good tannin and structure. The finish is long and lingering. The wine is enjoyable now and has the potential to age for two decades. This wine would make a great partner to a cassoulet or a classic French beef daube. Clavel Copa Santa is imported by Pierreclos Imports in Alameda and can be ordered from their website pierreclosimports.com. Check out their other interesting French wine finds while you are there. They offer free shipping with six bottles.

articles.text: Pictured in Davie Tennis Stadium are Wednesday Walkers Mary Carter, Nancy Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Mike Henn, Laura Goldman, Priscilla Wanerus, Claudia Lopez, Stella Houston, Sherry Jacobs, Bob Wong, Jim Kellogg, Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Alan Goldhammer, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Sarah Johnson, Nadine Guffanti, Harriette Louie, Aaron Katzel, Charles Katzel, Elizabeth Richter, John Lenahan, Charlene Louie, Quincy Dong, Helen Dong, Abe Edelson, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Kat Lang, Edith Lee, Tamar Stein Edelson, Dave DeRoche, Noemi Alvarado, Martin Levy, Dena Belinkoff, Gloria DaSilva, and Dick Carter. It was another warm summer day on Wednesday, June 15, when 35 walkers and rwo K-9 best friends showed up for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesday outing. The walkers hadn’t been to the south side of Piedmont for a few weeks, and it had been over a year since they visited the Davie Tennis Stadium. It’s a unique facility with some history in a beautiful setting. It has been described as a place where time stands still. Visitors always enjoy the stadium with its historic clubhouse. The walkers went to the stadium via Requa Road. They started off going through the top of Piedmont Park past the Community Hall where youth summer camp participants were having fun. Frequent walker Christine Calliste joined the group with eight year old Charles Katzel, so the group’s average age got immediately reduced. The walkers made their way up to Guilford Road, and found the almost hidden, 153-foot path and steps down to Hazel Lane. At Hazel and Requa the walkers saw a large redwood tree that marks the entrance to the Hazel Lane loop. It was noted that this tree also marked the entrance to the first school in Piedmont. Amy Long hired Julia Morgan to design a school building with classroom and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane, and opened the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls in 1913. Going down Requa Road they saw that an elaborate gazebo which had been damaged in a storm last winter, has been repaired. The group emerged on Wildwood Avenue, went down Prospect Road, onto Oakmont Avenue and then Oak Road to the entrance of the Davie Tennis Stadium. As they walked through its gates the strong smell of eucalyptus trees that surround the stadium welcomed them. It was noted that Frank C. Havens brought eucalyptus to the area from Australia with the idea that the wood would be a fast growing building material replacement for all the redwoods that were cut down during the late 19th and early 20th Century. Unfortunately, the wood proved generally not suitable for lumber as it is quite heavy and shrinks when dry, causong splitting and cracking. Once inside the stadium, more interesting information was shared. Stone quarries were an important part of Oakland’s growth and development. In Oakland’s earliest days, construction materials like stone blocks or paving stones were often used as sailing-ship ballast around Cape Horn. Since much of Oakland’s period of rapid growth occurred prior to the adoption of asphalt in the 1920s, macadam was used extensively in road building. This led to the creation of quarries throughout the area as the city grew. A quarry was opened in 1878 by the Alameda Macadamizing Company, and reopened as the Piedmont Paving Company in about 1892 ta the current site of Davie Tennis Stadium. The land was given to the City of Oakland in 1931 by former Oakland mayor John L. Davie and his family. Mayor Davie announced this sta-

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Walt Ruxton, 92, loving husband, father, brother, grandfather, and great grandfather, passed away peacefully on April 24, 2022 with family members at his side. Born Walter Alexander Ruxton on April 22, 1930 at Fabiola Hospital in Oakland, he was the son of Muriel Cozens Ruxton of England and Alexander Ruxton of Scotland. A resident of Piedmont for over 75 year, he attended Piedmont High School where he excelled at football and track and field and was an outstanding high jumper. It was at PHS that he met his future wife, Barbara Healy. Walt was an Alumnus of the University of California, Berkeley, where he was a member of Zeta Psi fraternity. He served in the U.S. Air Force during the Korean War and loved his country. As the son of immigrants who worked hard to achieve the America dream, he was a true believer in the promise of America. Growing up in Oakland and Piedmont, Walt spent many summers sailing on San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean and cruising the San Joaquin Delta on his family’s historic sail and power boats. He helped construct some of the beautiful facilities at the St. Francis Yacht Club’s Tinsley Island in the delta. Walt was an executive in the Ruxton family business, Pacific Pumping Co., which at the time was one of the largest pump manufacturers in the country. PACO pumps were used in the construction of both the Golden Gate and Bay Bridges, the Kaiser Center, the Transbay Tube and Marine World (as well as the original Piedmont Swim in Carmel. Walt was always very handy with electrical, carpentry and plumbing projects. “Papa’s big toolbox” provided hours of learning opportunities for his grandchildren over the years, as well as help to the rest of the family. He was a member of Piedmont Community Church and Claremont Country Club, where he especially enjoyed going for meals with friends and relatives. He remained an avid sports fan, and went to countless football, track, volleyball, and lacrosse events at Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School to watch his grandchildren. He also frequently traveled to Salinas and Modesto to cheer for more of his grandchildren in their games and events. He will be remembered as a loving family man, loyal friend, and true gentleman. Family was the center of his life. He was preceded in death by his loving wife of 56 years, Barbara Healy Ruxton. Walt is survived by his three daughters, Karen Ruxton Barbieri (Dean), Linda Ruxton Taylor (Bruce), and Dana Ruxton Rotticci (John), as well as his sisters Shirley Ruxton Soper and Patricia Ruxton Hobson (Doug), and sister-in-law Ann Healy. articles.text: Judith Rowe Tulloch passed away on June 15, 2022. A beloved Nana, mom, sister, aunt, and friend, she was a woman who lived life on her own terms. Growing up in Piedmont, she loved spending many a summer at her family’s cabin on the north shore of Lake Tahoe. She worked for Bechtel Corporation for many years and retired in 2000. While she was a longtime Bay Area resident, her work life took her to New York, Alaska, Boston, San Diego, Moscow, and Virginia, among many locations. She was an avid traveler and enjoyed exploring new places and cultures. She was an avid reader and loved attending theatre performances. Affectionately known as “Nana,” one of her greatest joys was spending time with her grandchildren and watching them grow. She loved the art of home decorating and spent a great deal of time creating a warm and inviting space, taking special pride in decorating her home for holidays throughout the year. Her generous nature and huge heart will be remembered by all who knew her. She is survived by her son, daughter-in-law, grandchildren, brother, sisters-in-law, nieces, and many friends. A private memorial will be held. Donations in her memory may be made to UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland (https:// give.ucsf benioffchildrens.org/ honormemorial), or to UCSF Judith Tulloch passes away on June 15 Benioff Children’s Hospital Foundation, P.O. Box 45339, San Francisco, CA 94145-0339).

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, June 22, 2022 Obituary Longtime Piedmont resident Walt Ruxton dies at age 92 Walt Ruxton, 92, loving husband, father, brother, grandfather, and great grandfather, passed away peacefully on April 24, 2022 with family members at his side. Born Walter Alexander Ruxton on April 22, 1930 at Fabiola Hospital in Oakland, he was the son of Muriel Cozens Ruxton of England and Alexander Ruxton of Scotland. A resident of Piedmont for over 75 year, he attended Piedmont High School where he excelled at football and track and field and was an outstanding high jumper. It was at PHS that he met his future wife, Barbara Healy. Walt was an Alumnus of the University of California, Berkeley, where he was a member of Zeta Psi fraternity. He served in the U.S. Air Force during the Korean War and loved his country. As the son of immigrants who worked hard to achieve the America dream, he was a true believer in the promise of America. Growing up in Oakland and Piedmont, Walt spent many summers sailing on San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean and cruising the San Joaquin Delta on his family’s historic sail and power boats. He helped construct some of the beautiful facilities at the St. Francis Yacht Club’s Tinsley Island in the delta. Walt was an executive in the Ruxton family business, Pacific Pumping Co., which at the time was one of the largest pump manufacturers in the country. PACO pumps were used in the construction of both the Golden Gate and Bay Bridges, the Kaiser Center, the Transbay Tube and Marine World (as well as the original Piedmont Swim in Carmel. Walt was always very handy with electrical, carpentry and plumbing projects. “Papa’s big toolbox” provided hours of learning opportunities for his grandchildren over the years, as well as help to the rest of the family. He was a member of Piedmont Community Church and Claremont Country Club, where he especially enjoyed going for meals with friends and relatives. He remained an avid sports fan, and went to countless football, track, volleyball, and lacrosse events at Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School to watch his grandchildren. He also frequently traveled to Salinas and Modesto to cheer for more of his grandchildren in their games and events. He will be remembered as a loving family man, loyal friend, and true gentleman. Family was the center of his life. He was preceded in death by his loving wife of 56 years, Barbara Healy Ruxton. Walt is survived by his three daughters, Karen Ruxton Barbieri (Dean), Linda Ruxton Taylor (Bruce), and Dana Ruxton Rotticci (John), as well as his sisters Shirley Ruxton Soper and Patricia Ruxton Hobson (Doug), and sister-in-law Ann Healy. Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. articles.text: Former Piedmont Scout Council president one of only 32 in the U.S. Former Piedmont Scout Council president Anne-Marie Lamarche was named a recipient of the Silver Antelope Award. The award recognizes adult Scouters whose work affects the movement at the territory level. Piedmont is part of Territory 3, covering all of the California and Hawaii. Only two volunteers are recognized from the territory annually. Lamarche has helped guide the territory from a collection of areas into a more cohesive whole, better serving youth and councils who face unique challenges and opportunities here. She served as Territory President and invested countless hours connecting with and guiding leaders throughout this service area. “This recognition is a tribute to Anne-Marie’s tremendous organizational and relationship skills,” said Rob James, a former Piedmont Council president and current territory volunteer. “She has skillfully navigated Scouting through transformations that will strengthen opportunities for youth development.” Lamarche, Piedmont Council’s first female president, has been involved with Scouting for more than 20 years. “Anne-Marie’s leadership and potential was recognized early and she rose through the ranks to successfully lead the territory.” said Wes Smith, a former Piedmont council president and recipient of the Silver Antelope Award. “We are incredibly fortunate with the caliber of volunteer Scouting leadership here in Piedmont,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “Our local youth benefit from the wisdom and expertise of 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03 Anne-Marie Lamarche recently was presented with Scouting’s prestigious Silver Antelope Award. Anne-Marie and hundreds of others who join her in stepping up.” Lamarche joins Smith, Bob Coleman, and Dale Radcliff as Piedmont Scouters who have been recognized at the Territory level.
articles.title: Anne-Marie Lamarche earns Scouting’s Silver Antelope Award

They tend to be the largest sites that could meet the state’s requirements for large [developments] that would accommodate moderate and low-income housing,” Bergman said. Comment was heard from over 30 residents at Monday night’s meeting. Dozens were received by the city in writing prior to the meeting. Many responses received by the city were related to the draft housing element site inventory. According to the report prepared by LWC, the site inventory was expanded to include city-owned sites to meet the HCD’s eligibility and feasibility requirements. “Many questions we’ve received have dealt with the identification of sites,” confirmed council member Jennifer Long. “Many of us [and city staff] have expressed a commitment to build housing, but I’m concerned about tying ourselves down [to these sites],” said Vice Mayor Jen Cavenaugh. “It feels like a reach too far. If we commit our intention [to build there], we might be locked in.” City Attorney Michele Kenyon reminded City Council that these sites would be “considered an alternative use for any non-vacant sites, that could be implemented in the planning period.” She added that, at this point in the process, cities don’t usually go into a financial feasibility analysis because it is difficult to determine financial feasibility years in advance. “The intent here is good, to add housing. The block we’re sitting in now, needs an overhaul, it needs a master plan,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand, referring to the city’s Civic Center. “We need to understand the benefits and risks to keeping [these sites] in the housing element, when considering improving our civic structure. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, June 22, 2022 Treasure Island Continued from page 1 of the island, those who created the World’s Fair or were involved in [the Exposition’s] architecture and art,” Schnoebelen said. “Considering the limitations of the history of our island - only 85 years or so - I’m always impressed by the speakers we attract.” The event on Saturday will be held in partnership with One Treasure Island, and formally documents the experiences of those who have lived and worked on the island over the last 24 years. A panel of speakers will discuss the documentary process, and will include Sherry Williams, Rheanna Binkley, Bryce Albright, Joanna Black, and Anna Morel. Schnoebelen became involved with the museum in 1989, when the Naval Station was still housed on the island. “At the time it was the 50th anniversary of the Fair, and there were quite a few people still around who had gone to the fair, including artists and architects. A friend and I created a symposium for the anniversary, and included speakers, a slide show, and presentations,” she said. “The museum took special notice of that and invited me to be on the board.” Schnoebelen noted that almost all signs of the World Fair are gone, but that since the museum’s creation in 1975, the City of San Francisco has made earnest efforts to preserve the island’s history. Pied mont resident and museum board member Rebecca Schnier has a special connection to the island. Her father Jacques Schnier created large sculptures for the 1939 World’s Fair which still stand on the island today, preserved by the museum. “What grabbed me was not only the history of my father’s sculptures being there since the late 30s – the historical connection of these beautiful sculptures that I adore, but the history of the island itself. I’m also interested in historical preservation, and as a fifth generation San Franciscan, I was captivated by Treasure Island and all the remarkable things that happened there, starting with the fact that the island itself was actually constructed in the middle of the Bay for the 1939 World’s Fair,” said Schnier, an architect. Her father’s sculptures are on display in front of Building One at the museum. Schnoebelen explained that Building One, where the museum is located, is one of few buildings that will remain among the slew of new developments on the island. Speaker series events held at the museum like “Treasured Stories” help preserve the oral history of Treasure Island, she said. The museum is open 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. articles.text: Staff photo Piedmont resident Jeff Bleich, the former U.S. Ambassador to Australia. The following is an abridged version of the commencement address given by former Ambassador Jeff Bleich at Piedmont High School’s graduation ceremony on June 2 at Witter Field. My great grandparents faced persecution and poverty in Eastern Europe for years. At some point, they decided that even if their life elsewhere would be no better, they owed it to their children and grandchildren to at least try. They left behind everything they had, everyone they knew and loved, to come to America. Their family members who remained, our ancestors in Europe, perished in the Holocaust. I do not have heirlooms, or pictures, or distant cousins I can find on 23andMe. The only place our family exists is in America. It was the one nation that let my great-grandparents in and gave them a chance. So I owe a debt to my great grandparents and to the people who welcomed them. Know this: I would not be alive today were it not for the courage of my ancestors, and the courage of people from this country who were willing to take them in. Each day is the gift that others’ courage gave me. We don’t stand on the shoulders of giants. We stand on the shoulders of people just like us – people who struggle with these decisions and who are uncertain. But in the end, they had a choice, and they chose to take risks and sacrifice for a greater good. And all they expected from us is to do the same. articles.text: Report finds $500,000 will be cost of full electrification Piedmont Connect, a community organization that supports city efforts on sustainability, released a newsletter on June 6 praising the city for moving forward with an all-electric aquatic facility. “We are proud that our Council unanimously voted for an all-electric facility, powered by an on-site solar PV-thermal array, electric heat pumps, and supplemental clean electricity from East Bay Community Energy (EBCE), our county’s Electrical Energy Aggregator,” said Piedmont Connect Board Member Hope Salzer. “Our new aquatics facility will produce no greenhouse gas pollution directly, a significant step towards the City’s goal of municipal facilities and activities emitting no fossil pollution by 2050.” The organization anticipated that city council’s commitment to electrifying the aquatic facility will also inspire community members to electrify their homes. City Council unanimously approved the plan to proceed with full electrification of the pool at an April 4 meeting. However, City Administrator Sara Lillevand noted at the time that upfront construction costs for the project could reach $500,000, according to an updated energy use report. These costs include eighteen heat pump chillers, four heat exchangers, and HVAC related items, including seismic work, hauling and other building-related HVAC scope. Lillevand proposed proceeding with the project, and seeking additional funding from outside sources. City Council adopted a policy entitled “acceptance of donations and naming of city owned facilities” at a meeting on May 2. The purpose of the policy is to encourage public-private partnerships that provide donations to support and enhance city services and facilities, which will help fund the all-electric facility. Photo courtesy of ELS Architecture and Urban Design An early design schematic of the proposed aquatic facility.

articles.text: Teacher wages, girls’ athletics a low priority for Piedmont School Board Editor: Piedmont School District has a priorities problem. On May 11th, scores of teachers testified to the school board that inadequate teacher pay is the key factor in the frequent teacher turnover at PUSD. They seek a reasonable cost of living adjustment. On May 25th, Piedmont’s female athletes and coaches presented the board with details of PUSD’s deficient Title IX funding and disparate treatment of female athletes. These were very moving presentations on high priority matters, and yet our school board obsessively focuses attention and funding on Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging (DEIB) initiatives. The latest of many examples of the school district’s misplaced priorities is last week’s creation and funding of a high school class to teach BIPOC (Black Indigenous People of Color) students how to “mentor” other BIPOC students in our elementary and middle schools. Many of us agree that including some DEI-B content into the curriculum is appropriate, but clearly, using PUSD’s limited funds to teach “mentoring” solely for BIPOC students is not a current priority compared to funding adequate teacher pay or fulfilling Title IX legal obligations. And let’s not forget that the high school still doesn’t have AP courses for physics, chemistry, or robotics, raising the question once again of misplaced priorities. I believe our school board needs to adjust its priorities toward academic excellence, recruitment and retention of excellent teachers, and meeting its Title IX legal obligations. If you agree, email the PUSD board at: schoolboard@ piedmont.k12.ca.us.
