articles.text: Before entering the ministry, I spent nearly 20 years owning and operating a construction business in Boston, Massachusetts. Some of my contracts were for new construction but a fair amount of my business involved renovation. As a result, I have always seen demolition as part of the process of creating something better. For me, the dust, the piles of debris and the disruption of life don’t bother me because I know it can lead to a better future. As the pandemic rages on with yet another wave of destruction, there are also dangerous riptides of division tearing at the fabric of our country. Being so divided as we are, it seems almost impossible to imagine a future where we, as a society, actually live up to our name, The United States of America. These were very moving presentations on high priority matters, and yet our school board obsessively focuses attention and funding on Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging (DEIB) initiatives. The latest of many examples of the school district’s misplaced priorities is last week’s creation and funding of a high school class to teach BIPOC (Black Indigenous People of Color) students how to “mentor” other BIPOC students in our elementary and middle schools. Many of us agree that including some DEI-B content into the curriculum is appropriate, but clearly, using PUSD’s limited funds to teach “mentoring” solely for BIPOC students is not a current priority compared to funding adequate teacher pay or fulfilling Title IX legal obligations. And let’s not forget that the high school still doesn’t have AP courses for physics, chemistry, or robotics, raising the question once again of misplaced priorities. I believe our school board needs to adjust its priorities toward academic excellence, recruitment and retention of excellent teachers, and meeting its Title IX legal obligations. articles.text: Oakland resident Sara Paul and a team of volunteers developed and operate a smart phone application that delivers information on high-risk vegetation fires and wildfires that have the potential to become high-risk. Watch Duty launched in August 2021 in Sonoma, Napa, and Lake counties. Two weeks ago, the app expanded to include all 58 counties in California. An interactive map shows where wildfires are burning across the state in real-time with information gathered from a variety of channels and agencies. “Watch Duty fills important gap – a source of reliable fire information provided in a timely manner,” said Paul. “Everyone who is involved in the fire reporting side of our app – about 15 of us – have been sharing and reporting information about fires on other [social media] platforms like Facebook and Twitter. But let’s face it, social media is a horrible place to have to troll through to get information that might save your life.” The app was created by John Clarke Mills. Paul explained that Mills created the platform after his own experience searching for information on his ranch in Sonoma County - which has been in the radius of wildfire danger multiple times over the past three years. Mills recruited developers from his professional background and soon an original team of fire reporters joined. “We are all volunteer,” Paul said. “We coordinate on a very active internal communications platform during every incident. Some people are gathering information, others are fact checking or preparing the post. We have a very scrappy and very collaborative start-up mentality. The app is constantly improving based on user feedback.” fires burned more than 4.3 million acres of land. One of the strongest of that season, the SCU Lighting Complex, included Alameda County in its radius. “Our target audience is anyone living in fire country in California. In 2022, that’s all of us,” Paul said. “While the Oakland Hills fire of 1991 is a distant memory for some, it showed how quickly a vegetation fire could spread through an urban area. That fire was my first evacuation.” According to CAL FIRE, current climates could cause another devastating wildfire season. Extended dryness originating from late winter continued into spring, with little perception. “Drought conditions have once again taken ahold of California and are already contributing to another year of early fire activity,” said Joe Tyler, CAL FIRE Director and Fire Chief. Paul said she hopes that users gain a sense of security using the app, and that they are able to make decisions in a timely manner. “Lack of information fuels anxiety,” she said. “Information can still be a bit of a challenge to track down, but that’s what our reporters were doing independently and continue to do. And now we’re doing it together, with true strength in numbers.” To learn more, and to download the app on your smart phone or tablet, visit https://www.watchduty.org. – Sara Paul, App Developer and Oakland Resident The team monitors a network of sources to bring information directly to the user. articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew members prepare pancakes for the 4th of July Parade. Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade will be anchored once again by the community pancake breakfast served by the Piedmont Community Service Crew in the Veterans Hall from 8:00 to 10:30 a.m. Guests will be serenaded with the music of the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band playing music at the front of the building. The Pancake Breakfast is organized completely by the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a youth-led coed Venturing Crew, part of the Piedmont Scouts, founded in 2004 and still led by Ken Li. The entire event is youth-run from start to finish. Crew members Klara Zietlow and Madelyn Hill, who serve as co-Vice Presidents of Fundraising, have the task of soliciting donations from Village Market and Piedmont Grocery which have long supported the event. “There’s a lot of work that goes into it. Right after the girls were elected in spring, they had to work quickly. Planning for the pancake breakfast, typically begins months in advance,” Li said. In addition to flipping flapjacks and serving them to a large crowd, crew members will be serving sausages, fresh fruit, orange juice and coffee. All food is freshly prepared. Prior to COVID, the group would serve over 400 plates of breakfast before the parade. The crew uses proceeds from the pancake breakfast to support their philanthropic projects, which includes service work in partnership with Rebuilding Together Oakland to renovate the homes of low-income and elderly Oakland residents. Each year, PCSC raises over $12,000 with the help of fundraisers like this and parent donations. “It’s nice that PCSC has this very positive standing and respect [in the community]. And the teams feel really proud of that, which spurs them to do a great job,” Li said. “On a typical project, we’ll spend a few thousand dollars on materials. We plan, execute and fund the projects.” Advance tickets to the breakfast are available on the Piedmont BSA website at: https://www. piedmontbsa.org/events/july-4thpancake-breakfast/. For those who cannot join the breakfast, but would like to donate to the Community Service Crew, visit https://rtoakland.org/ blog/pcsc.
articles.title: Pancake breakfast returns to July 4th Parade

articles.text: The Alameda County Fair returns this summer at the Fairgrounds in Pleasanton. It is the seventh largest in California and will take place June 17 through July 10 at the Alameda County Fairgrounds, located at 4501 Pleasanton Avenue. A plethora of events will transpire over the course of three weeks, including the Alaskan Racing Pigs, musical events, movies on the lawn, carnival rides and a “drone show.” The fair will be open 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily, and carnival hours are Wednesday through Sunday. Concerts are scheduled every night at 8 p.m. The fair kicks off on Friday, June 17, and admission is free that day until 3 p.m. On Saturday, June 18 at 3:30 p.m., Nathan’s Famous Hot Dog Eating Contest will host its only West Coast event. For more details, and to purchase tickets, visit www.alamedacountyfair.com. Consider signing up as a volunteer. Nearly 900 volunteers of all ages help out at the fair each year. Organizations that volunteer include local schools and colleges, youth groups, garden clubs, Girl Scout troops, and performing arts groups. The Alameda County Fair is a local, self-sustaining, non-profit organization. Visit https://annual.alamedacountyfair.com/volunteer/ to learn how to volunteer. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: A bike path in Piedmont. The city will move forward with a bike lane on Moraga Avenue as recommended by the Piedmont Pedestrian and Bicycle Committee last year, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed. Recommendations made by the committee considered survey responses and suggestions from the community, which culminated in the Safer Streets plan. The Safer Streets plan was adopted by city council on December 6, 2021. The plan was launched in November 2014 to identify sites and make recommendations to make the city more pedestrian- and bike-friendly. The proposed bike lane, a high priority item in the Plan, will complete the bike lane improvements on Moraga Avenue. A current bike lane on Moraga Avenue exists between Ramona and Bonita Avenues, and between Bonita and the City limit to the east. The new project will be a Class 2 bike lane, generally five-feet wide, established along streets and defined by pavement striping and signage. The new bike lane would be on the uphill direction from Red Rock Road to the city limits. Plans for the project will be reviewed by Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. It is estimated to go out to bid in late July and awarded in August, Gonzales confirmed, with construction anticipated to begin in September.
articles.title: Bike lane coming to Moraga Avenue

articles.text: For the 19th year, the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band will take a lead position in Piedmont’s 4th of July Parade, with its parasol-toting, shuffle-stepping Grand Marshal leading the way. Zenith, a Berkeley-based group, lays claim to being the most authentic brass band playing the music of old New Orleans from the formative years of 100 years ago to the present. Parade bands in New Orleans are still part of the musical tradition in the Crescent City, playing for funerals, parades, picnics and dances. All members of the Zenith band have been playing in similar jazz bands in the Bay Area for many years. Its Grand Marshal leads the way, proudly holding a fringed parasol, wearing a colorful sash, and doing a shuffle step down the length of Highland Avenue. People dancing behind the band, sometimes swirling parasols, are known as the second line. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band has been a major attraction for many years at the New Orleans By the Bay production at Shoreline Amphitheater. It has been part of the Traditional Jazz portion of the Concord Jazz Festival for 17 years, and for the past seven years it has appeared at the Bodega Bay Fisherman’s Festival. The band plays each year at the Sacramento Jazz Jubilee in Old Town during June. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band to open Piedmont’s 55th annual 4th of July Parade on Highland Avenue.
articles.title: Piedmont’s New Orleans tradition

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Band is the city’s only musical organization that can claim only needing a single rehearsal during the year. The band was winner of the Highland Cup – the highest award – in 2006 as best entry in the Piedmont Parade. The band is comprised of amateur and professional musicians – all volunteers – who live in town and who can’t resist the challenge of playing music while marching in formation. Dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief, they are led by Ken Kawaichi, who, dressed as Emperor Norton, has the distinction of walking the length of the parade route backwards. All members of the Zenith band have been playing in similar jazz bands in the Bay Area for many years. Its Grand Marshal leads the way, proudly holding a fringed parasol, wearing a colorful sash, and doing a shuffle step down the length of Highland Avenue. People dancing behind the band, sometimes swirling parasols, are known as the second line. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band has been a major attraction for many years at the New Orleans By the Bay production at Shoreline Amphitheater. It has been part of the Traditional Jazz portion of the Concord Jazz Festival for 17 years, and for the past seven years it has appeared at the Bodega Bay Fisherman’s Festival. The band plays each year at the Sacramento Jazz Jubilee in Old Town during June. The Zenith New Orleans Parade Band to open Piedmont’s 55th annual 4th of July Parade on Highland Avenue. articles.text: Four years ago, near the start of freshman year of high school, I read a sentence that stood out. One sentence that I couldn’t get out of my head; a sentence that I think is relevant now and will be relevant for as long as I live. Now, before I say what I read, I want everyone to think back, let’s say four years ago, 2018, when you started freshman year. Think about who you were, what you believed, what you did, and what you said. Think about how others perceived you and, more importantly, how you perceived yourself. Now I want you to reflect on everything that has changed since then. I am willing to bet that there are a great number of things that you think now that you would not have thought before and things you said back then that you would not say now. In the past four years I have truly become much more grateful for my parents and friends for always being there to help and support me. The ability to change is one of the most beauPiedmont High School’s Class of 2022 Valedictorian Aaron Drumm tiful parts of life. So, why does it sometimes feel like your brain is sitting there fighting you saying, “Nope! You are not going to change that because we have been doing it this way our whole life.” And why is it that after making the decision to change, you can be called a hypocrite for doing something differently or believing something new? Why is it that changing is often so hard? Overcoming this opposite pull to change, this change inertia, is crucial to moving forward. The sentence I read, in Brandon Sanderson’s book, Oathbringer, that helped me realize this was, “Sometimes a hypocrite is nothing more than a man in the process of changing.” Among us, everyone here has been a hypocrite at some point. But you cannot let the label of being a hypocrite or being an imposter pull you down. Like Jacob and Wesley said, don’t be afraid to put yourself out there to make a change in the world – and within yourself. Don’t be held down by anything or anyone saying you can’t. Change is a journey that should never end, and as we overcome our own change inertia in order to move forward today, I want to leave everyone with one last quote. Coming from the same book, Sanderson writes, “The most important step a person can take is always the next one.” So today, when you get your diploma, take that next step, and stay in motion!

articles.text: year, or the next year, or the next 25 years. That’s right, there hasn’t been a mass shooting in Australia since that legislation passed 25 years ago. I visited with a couple of the officials who had lost their seats in Parliament, to ask them about their decision. One of them said to me: “I knew I’d lose my seat. The proudest thing I ever did in Parliament was cast that vote that cost me my re-election. I didn’t run for office so that I could stay in office. I ran for office so that I could make a positive difference in people’s lives. There are hundreds of people alive today who would have lost their lives to gun violence. I would not trade that for anything. Not anything.” Courage is measured not by how much people are willing to do to win. It is measured by how much they would be willing to lose. Which brings me to my last story; it’s both personal and political. And it’s about what happens without courage. In 1999, I received a call from the White House. Thirteen high school students, people your age or younger, had been senselessly killed with assault weapons by two students in their class. It shocked our Country. Then-President Clinton had been reading everything he could find about gun violence. Somehow he’d read an article I’d written with one of my professors years earlier. The people at the White House said that President Clinton liked my article. He wanted to talk to me about heading up a youth violence commission to help prevent more school shootings. My wife, Becky, and I had three young kids then. I had just made partner at a law firm, we had no savings (because, of course, we’d just bought a house in Piedmont), and I didn’t want to move to DC. So I told the White House I wasn’t really qualified and that there were real experts out there who would be better than I was. A few days later, I got another call from the White House. They said the President wanted to see me. I flew to DC and met with President Clinton. It was the first time I’d ever met a President. And he asked me a very simple question. What would it mean to me, if someone else were willing to give up their job and do something difficult, simply because it might save the life of one of my children. I said it would mean everything to me. He said “If you do this job, it will mean everything to every other parent in America. Are you willing to give up your job if it might save some of their children’s lives?” There was only one answer to this. “Yes.” So I left my job as a law firm partner. And I took the job. For the next two years I worked all over America. I visited the shell-shocked communities where these shootings occurred. I sat with parents and saw the empty chair at their table – their daily reminder of the child who was never coming back. I visited parents like that in towns you have never heard of – in Jonesboro, and Springfield, and Paducah – and towns shattered and haunted by these shootings. It changed me forever. I can still see the pain and bewilderment on their faces. Those images will not go away. The question that haunted them all was “why?” There were answers. And there were things we could do, just as they did in Australia. Americans weren’t genetically more violent than other people. We were just governed differently. There were things we could do that had worked in other countries. In fact, every other developed nation in the world has stopped these sorts of mass shootings. So we provided that information to Congress -- about the mental health and counseling programs that could help, public information campaigns about warning signs, about ways other nations restricted access to assault weapons, and required background checks for all gun owners, and kept guns away from people who were dangerous to themselves or others. The only challenge we faced was that the NRA opposed background checks and the assault weapons ban. Some members in close elections might lose their seats over these measures. It would take courage. And some members of Congress would need to risk sacrificing their own job to potentially save the lives of someone else’s child. They had the same question that I had, and that those leaders in Australia had. “Would you be willing to give up your own job, to save a child’s life?” But this time, their answer was “no.” Instead, they voted to make assault weapons more easily available. The number of young people killed in our schools by gun violence after that year has kept growing. By 2012, it had tripled. Even in the face of 20 second graders and their teachers being gunned down at Sandy Hook Elementary School, they did nothing. Members of Congress who could have made a difference did nothing ... except keep their jobs. In the 10 years since, there have been 900 more shootings on school grounds in America. Firearms are now the leading cause of death for Americans under the age of 24. We have lost thousands of young people to senseless gun violence for one reason – because of the absence of courage. And then this week it happened again. At Robb Elementary School. And Senators who you’d think would finally tell us “enough is enough, take my job.” Instead tell us to take their thoughts and prayers. Jesus. But I haven’t lost hope. I haven’t lost hope because a nation that had the courage to welcome my great-grandparents and give sanctuary to millions of others is a courageous nation. I haven’t lost hope, I have seen political leaders in every other modern nation risk the highest offices in their land to do the right thing. I have not lost hope because I know courage exists in all of us, and calls out to all of us. So when the day comes when you are asked “would you give up your job to save a child’s life?” listen to that voice in your head. Courage is everywhere and it is in all people. Courage is what challenges us. Courage is what defines us. Courage is what sustains us. That courage is within you, the resilient class of 2022. Go forward and let it inspire others.

articles.text: Hello Piedmont Class of 2022, Wesley here. Today I am honored to join a long line of quiet, socially awkward nerds forced by tradition to speak in front of you. Hmm… This is gonna go great. So this may come as a shock to some, but we nerds don’t really give speeches much. So, thinking about doing this one was pretty scary. I imagined looking into the crowd and all of you staring back at me like some kind of hideous multi-eyed blob. And I would mutter, and my knees would shake, and I would forget my script. Thinking about it all brought up a memory, my first day at Piedmont nine years ago, August 2013. Back then the metal doors of Wildwood stretched upwards and the hallways were filled to the brim with strangers. With my little blue backpack, I tentatively walked to Ms. Holt’s 4th grade classroom. There I found kids talking amongst themselves; since they were returning to school, they were greeted by old friends. Being new, I was greeted with a little name tag marking my spot on a wooden desk - “Wesley”. strangers no more. Now when I look into the crowd, I see accomplished musicians. I see unyielding activists. I see talented athletes, scientists, journalists, rappers, dancers, leaders and everything in between. Now when I look into the crowd I see friends. I look into the crowd and my knees shake no more. I look into the crowd and I am fearless. Take a look around you. See the amazing individuals you’ve come to know. And while this momentous day marks our final union, this community we’ve built will always remain. Separated by distance but forever bound in our common Piedmont memory. Embarking on your new adventures ahead, you may find that your knees begin to shake or that your words become muddled… and to this I give one final word of Wes-dom. Class of 2022, as we walk onto this stage and into the world, we have been given a chance to change it. So be bold and be brave, knowing you’re in a world of peers. Keep up the good work class. Go Highlanders! Wesley Jeng, Piedmont High School Salutatorian for the Class of 2022. As the class settled, Ms. Holt began the day and the new school year. Everything was going as planned, but then the worst happened. Ms. Holt asked me… to introduce myself in front of the entire class. Terrified, I slowly rose from my seat. articles.text: On June 8, the Piedmont School Board voted to levy the maximum 2% increase of the Parcel Tax as recommended by the School Support Tax Advisory Subcommittee. The subcommittee, consisting of Ruchi Shrivastava Medhekar, Claire Arno and Robert Phillips, expect this to result in a $219,674 increase in revenue to the General Fund for the 2022- 2023 school year. The increase is based on an assumed base School Support Tax amount for the current year of $10,982,759. The increase amounts to $56.37 which when added to the current per parcel levy of $2,818.26 equates to an annual $2,874.63 tax per parcel for 2022-23. “Even with these sources of additional revenue [from the state] PUSD continues to face significant revenue challenges primarily resulting from declining enrollment in the last six years,” said Medhekar. The Parcel Tax, also known as the Measure G School Support Tax, has the responsibility of “maintain[ing] the quality of Piedmont’s schools.” Measure G was approved by Piedmont voters in 2013. The subcommittee also recommend to keep the Measure H School Support Tax at the same level of $0.25 per square foot of building improvements. For the smallest Piedmont parcel amounts to $139, an amount approved in 2013. The goal of Measure H is to provide funding to attract and retain high quality teachers and educational support staff. For more information on Measures G and H visit: Piedmont. k12.ca.us/district-info/budget/ measure-g-and-h-parcel-taxes.
articles.title: School Parcel Tax increase of 2% approved

I visited parents like that in towns you have never heard of – in Jonesboro, and Springfield, and Paducah – and towns shattered and haunted by these shootings. It changed me forever. I can still see the pain and bewilderment on their faces. Those images will not go away. The question that haunted them all was “why?” There were answers. And there were things we could do, just as they did in Australia. Americans weren’t genetically more violent than other people. We were just governed differently. There were things we could do that had worked in other countries. In fact, every other developed nation in the world has stopped these sorts of mass shootings. So we provided that information to Congress -- about the mental health and counseling programs that could help, public information campaigns about warning signs, about ways other nations restricted access to assault weapons, and required background checks for all gun owners, and kept guns away from people who were dangerous to themselves or others. The only challenge we faced was that the NRA opposed background checks and the assault weapons ban. Some members in close elections might lose their seats over these measures. It would take courage. And some members of Congress would need to risk sacrificing their own job to potentially save the lives of someone else’s child. They had the same question that I had, and that those leaders in Australia had. “Would you be willing to give up your own job, to save a child’s life?” But this time, their answer was “no.” Instead, they voted to make assault weapons more easily available. The number of young people killed in our schools by gun violence after that year has kept growing. By 2012, it had tripled. Even in the face of 20 second graders and their teachers being gunned down at Sandy Hook Elementary School, they did nothing. Members of Congress who could have made a difference did nothing ... except keep their jobs. In the 10 years since, there have been 900 more shootings on school grounds in America. Firearms are now the leading cause of death for Americans under the age of 24. We have lost thousands of young people to senseless gun violence for one reason – because of the absence of courage. And then this week it happened again. At Robb Elementary School. And Senators who you’d think would finally tell us “enough is enough, take my job.” Instead tell us to take their thoughts and prayers. Jesus. But I haven’t lost hope. I haven’t lost hope because a nation that had the courage to welcome my great-grandparents and give sanctuary to millions of others is a courageous nation. I haven’t lost hope, I have seen political leaders in every other modern nation risk the highest offices in their land to do the right thing. I have not lost hope because I know courage exists in all of us, and calls out to all of us. So when the day comes when you are asked “would you give up your job to save a child’s life?” listen to that voice in your head. Courage is everywhere and it is in all people. Courage is what challenges us. Courage is what defines us. Courage is what sustains us. That courage is within you, the resilient class of 2022. Go forward and let it inspire others.

articles.text: Heat, Insulation, and reactions. Making s’mores is a great way to highlight heat transfer and heat reactions, When a s’more waffle cone is placed into a fire, heat (or energy) is transferred from the fire to the waffle cone. The additional heat raises the temperature, which can cause the ingredients inside to react and transform. As the temperature rises above a certain threshold, ingredients inside reach their melting point. Those that begun as solid ingredients begin to break down into less-than-solid states. This is why the ingredients begin to melt, mix, and become gooey! Adding foil around the waffle cones helps with the heating and melting process. Aluminum foil contains metal and therefore, acts as an insulator. This means it helps trap heat closer around the waffle cone, distributing the heat more evenly. Even though s’mores may seem like a simple, summer activity, they involve a lot of science that goes unseen. In this activity, learners will make s’mores using waffle cones and ingredients of their choosing. They will predict and observe how the heat and insulation of the cooking process transforms their cone into a melty, gooey, snack. Then, they will enjoy the results! This activity is fit for learners of all ages. Background information can be found at the end of this guide. PROCEDURE 1. Start by gathering around the campfire (or oven) and observing what happens when you place a single marshmallow into the heat. a. What do you notice happening to the marshmallow? b. Why do you think it is reacting that way? c. What do you think a marshmallow is made of that causes it to look/move/ react like that? 2. After making observations, pass out waffle cones and fill them with ingredients of your choice. 3. Make a few different cones. Fill one with classic ingredients, then experiment with different flavors, textures, and layers in the rest. 4. Once assembled, wrap it with foil. 5. Place them in the coals of a campfire and let it cook for about 5 to 7 minutes. a. If using the oven, bake them for 5 to 7 minutes at 400 degrees Fahrenheit. 6. While they’re cooking, make some predictions about your cones: a. What do you think the texture of each will be like? b. Which kinds of flavors do you think we will taste? c. What do you think is happening on the inside of the waffle cones? d How might the fire change them? Do you think it’s similar or different to the

articles.text: A delicious experiment. marshmallow earlier? 7. Once they’re done cooking, remove them from the heat and let cool for about a minute. 8. Carefully remove from the foil and make some observations of your results: a. Does it look the same or different from how it was before? b. What do you notice about it now? c. Where else have you seen something melt like this in the kitchen? What other ingredients melt and become gooey like marshmallows do? 9. Finally, enjoy the results of your experiment! articles.text: Kayla Wong, who graduated from Piedmont High School in 2021, just completed her first year at the University of Southern California as a Film & Television Production student. In 2016 Wong first attended Camp Reel Stories, that focuses on increasing gender representation in the media industry. This summer she returns to Reel Stories in Oakland as a Producer. In 2014, Wong’s affinity for film began in Anne Smith’s film course at Piedmont Middle School. There she learned cinema history, igniting her passion for the art form. One of Wong’s first films was a spy film made from an amalgamation of scenic b-roll she shot on a summer vacation and scenes done with friends. Smith, seeing Wong’s enthusiasm, introduced her to the non-profit Camp Reel Stories, of which Smith is a board member. Wong attended her first session of Camp Reel Stories in 2016 where she learned more about the importance of sharing her voice and perspective with the world, as well as making her directorial debut on her short film 13. Since then, Wong has become a vital member of the Reel Stories community. She served on the student board for three years, attended the very first Reel Stories Professional Institute, and helped Reel Stories navigate hybrid programming during the summer of 2021. Wong’s films include Blue, a utopian-turned-dystopian sci-fi about a world where everyone Ideas, Coven, the Girls Make Movies by Hawai’i Women In Filmmaking, Drunken Film Festival, and the American High School Film Festival. “Reel Stories provided me with foundational filmmaking skills and helped me find the confidence to share my voice with the world through film. My experience as a Reel Stories student allowed me to build a portfolio of work that I am proud to share. articles.text: Sports, games & crafts offered to middle school students Lucas Scherman, son of Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Scherman, returns for the second year to lead Scherman Summer Camp. Campers will learn new games, get fresh air, practice new skills, make friends and be themselves. Campers will have fun playing kickball, double-dutch, capture the flag, poker, dominos, and more. Lucas, aided by brothers Julian, 19, and Quincy, 15, will teach the art of wood-burning and how to make paracord survival bracelets. Scherman Summer Camp is a screen-free, good old-fashioned camp. The camp is open to students entering grades 6-9, and will be held at Wildwood School lower playground. One-week sessions begin the week of July 11 and continue for nine weeks. Morning classes run from 10:00 a.m.-1:00 p.m., and afternoon sessions are from 2:00-5:00 p.m. To register and for more information, call the Piedmont Recreation Department at 420-3070 or visit: Register. capturepoint.com/reg/cat_program_class_detail.cfm?s=&t=&- season_id=24069&program_ id=1420272&family_mbr_str=. The azure-blue coastline has been the playground of the rich since the Brits believed the sea air cured consumption (tuberculosis). It was previously a coastline of impoverished villagers who fished and farmed for a living, but when the Nice-Paris train route opened in the 1860s, English aristocrats infused wealth and built luxury villas. Celebrities and royalty followed, including Queen Victoria who made repeat visits. The region of ProvenceAlpes-Côte d’Azur was known to ancient mariners as Land’s End. Proof of ancient tribes is derived from artifacts and excavation, Voyagers dazzled by the blue sea date to the pre-historic era. Ancient paths became roads cut from the great walls of rock from the southern flank of the Alps, which abruptly rises from the eastern shoreline. The lower Rhône River drains into the Mediterranean, and following westward, the sea is pinched through the Straits of Gibraltar, then empties into the North Atlantic. The Greeks, already settled at Marseilles, moved eastward to found Nicaia, or Nice, around 350 BCE. The Greeks were swept out by the Romans around 150 BCE, and when Rome fell in 476 A.D., the Goths defended the coastline. Many historical peoples fought to control the mystically calm Mediterranean Sea. During the Middle Ages, Nice was part of Italy under the control of citystate Genoese, From the Renaissance and for the next five centuries, Nice was ruled by the Duchy of Savoy. France’s Emperor Louis Napoléon III courted Nice to join France. By1860, the port of Genoa had gained immense importance over Nice’s seaport, and Italy let go without a fight. Nice and La Côte d’Azur Visitors to Nice may detect the strong Italian influence, noticed by native French speakers. The café americano is annoyingly served as an espresso, among other useful facts. articles.text: When it comes to growing soccer talent, there’s no better place to be than Europe. For Russell Tan, who completed his junior year on Piedmont High’s NCS Championship winning program, he is set to take his talents across the globe in August to Spain on one of the world’s most legendary franchise’s development academy, Atletico Madrid. “I am really excited for that, it’s a really big opportunity,” said Tan. Atlético Madrid, known simply as Atleti, plays in Spain’s La Liga and finished third in last season’s standings behind Barcelona and Real Madrid. Their development academy routinely pumps out some of the highest valued were other major clubs in Europe that I trained with as well, and that was a major turning point,” said Tan. Tan featured in Piedmont’s starting lineup last season as a major piece in Todd Sullivan’s attack and often found himself isolated against defenders to turn them inside-out with technical footwork. Those factors impressed the coaches at Atleti. “They said that I have good technique on the ball and saw that I have good 1-on-1 ability as well. They saw that I could send in crosses, those were some things that they said was good. But they also gave constructive criticism as well. They said I need to work on my decision-making and positioning, that is something I’m Staff Photo eager to work on,” said Tan. Per the Academy’s public roster lists, Russell is set to be the only American prospect in its ranks. He’s been practicing the Spanish since elementary school and stepping into a totally new environment to put his studies to use. Moreover, he will be traveling completely on his own and residing in Ateltico Madrid’s residency program. “It does make me a little bit nervous because the whole team is Spanish. But, as long as I keep practicing my Spanish, I’ll be fine. It can be a little bit daunting going into a new team, but I’ll get used to the atmosphere and it’ll be an incredible experience. pages.text: Wednesday, June 15, 2022 13 Summer Workout Series Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 15th year in the Post. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmontpost.org. IZZY EPSTEIN Softball Piedmont High Class of 2022 Chapman University Class of 2026 Izzy Epstein heads to Chapman University after earning The Post’s Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year. She was the WACC Shoreline’s Pitcher of the Year this spring after posting an impressive 12-1 record, with a 1.36 ERA, 123 innings pitched, and 187 strikeouts. She finished the season with 15 complete games, threw a perfect game on May 6 against Hayward, and recorded an astonishing 19 strikeouts in Piedmont’s 10-1 win over Arcata in the first round of the North Coast Section playoffs. She led the team to an 18-7 overall record and a perfect 10-0 against Shoreline teams on their way to a league title when they defeated Encinal 8-5 on May 12. On offense, she batted .368 with 25 hits and four home runs. Epstein was also named Honorable Mention by the Post as Freshman of the Year and Sophomore of the Year in 2020. What is your workout program this summer? Weight training and endurance conditioning three days a week with a trainer. I’ll also be doing hitting and throwing drills two days a week, practicing with a pitching coach once a week, and spot appearances on tournament softball teams throughout the summer. What are your fitness goals for this summer? Increase my strength and athletic coordination. I want to be prepared to step up to competitive college athletic fitness levels. How are you measuring your development? Weight levels on exercises like leg press, hip thrusts, kettle balls. In addition, I’ll measure my fastball velocity via radar gun and feedback from my pitching coach, Rich Balswick. Are you working out on your own? With a coach? A trainer? All of the above. What is a recent milestone that you’ve achieved? Increasing my pitch velocity by about 5 percent into the high 50s. Also, after having no homeruns through my first three years on varsity, I had four this year. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring athletes? Dedicating yourself to training is a mindset. If you can stay dedicated for about the first 45 days, it gets a lot easier to train, workout, and practice since it becomes part of the fabric of your weeks. The only bad workout is no workout. Piedmont High Class of 2022 Chico State Class of 2026 JoJo Murphy heads to Chico State this fall after finishing his illustrious PHS basketball career with 1,488 points and be named the WACC’s Foothill Player of the Year honors. Last winter, the Highlanders finished 17-11 and narrowly lost 57-55 in the D3 semifinals against Branson after answering a 10-point deficit late in the third quarter. Murphy finished his senior campaign by averaging 22 points per game. He was a key member of Piedmont’s North Coast Section Championship team in 2020 as a sophomore. He was named Honorable Mention by the Post for Freshman of the Year and Sophomore of the Year in 2020. What is your workout program this summer? I am starting my workouts this summer with high altitude training and will continue to work with some of the best trainers around the Bay Area, including coach Bryan Gardere, who I’ve been working with my whole career at Piedmont. I’ll also train with Evolve Performance on Piedmont Avenue on my strength and conditioning. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I hope to gain 10-15 pounds in muscle along with increasing my cardio cap. I plan on doing this by spending all of my time in the weight room and kitchen. How are you measuring your development? I’ll be tracking each workout by increments. Whether it is shooting or running, each day I’ll be able to see my progress on a board that will tally each category. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’ll be working out with coaches and trainers. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? Winning WACC Player of the Year and being ranked a top-five prospect by WestCoastPreps. com. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Always keep working and weathering the storm. If being CHIARA LUNDIN Softball Piedmont High Class of 2022 Wellesley College Class of 2026 Chiara Lundin is another senior who graduated this year. She’ll continue her softball career at Wellesley College in Massachusetts. She was a four-year starter on the softball team as catcher, calling the games for all-league pitcher Izzy Epstein. She earned first-team All-League honors after compiling a stellar .581 batting average, with 43 hits, nine doubles, three triples, and two home runs this spring. Lundin was a major fixture in the lineup for coach Gene Denard for all four years. In the shortened 10-game 2021 season, she hit .483 with 14 hits, 16 runs scored, 11 RBIs, three doubles, one triple, and three home runs. In 2020, with just four appearances prior to the pandemic causing cancellation of the season, she hit .308 with four hits, two doubles, a homer, and seven RBIs. She was named Freshman of the Year by the Post in 2019 after stepping into the starting lineup as the No. 2 hitter; What is your workout program this summer? I get workout plans from my college during the weekdays, which generally switch between weight training and running/ other conditioning. I also do JoJo Murphy ended a stellar Piedmont career with 1,488 total points, and was named WACC Player of the Year. great were easy, than everybody would do it. It requires perseverance, and the largest thing for me was learning to be comfortable when situations are uncomfortable. weights with a personal trainer twice a week, practice two to three times a week with a travel team, and have catching lessons once a week. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I want to lower my time in the mile, and generally just get better at my position. I really want to prove myself when I get to college. How are you measuring your development? I time my miles, so that’s pretty easy. But specifically for softball, I try to get a quicker transition and release when throwing, as well as faster blocks and transfers when catching. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? Most of the stuff I listed is with a coach or trainer, but I do the workouts my school sends me, as well as batting practice and catching exercises on my own. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I feel very proud to have deadlifted 225 pounds for eight reps, which is pretty good in my book! What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Don’t focus only on your workouts or your training. Although getting good at your game is important, it doesn’t mean you can stop thinking about school or improving yourself mentally. A lot that goes into sports is the mental aspect, so practice working on mental fortitude as well as physical strength in order to be a better athlete in general. articles.text: Eight Piedmont teenagers participated in the 27th annual U.S. Rowing Youth National Championship Regatta from June 9-12 in Sarasota, Florida. The prestigious event attracted over 3,500 student-athletes from hundreds of teams across the U.S. to compete in 34 different boating events. To qualify for the Junior Nationals, three Piedmont athletes with Oakland Strokes, two from Artemis Rowing, and another three from the OARS organization, had successful topfour performances weeks earlier at the Southwest Regional Championships at Lake Natoma near Sacramento. PHS graduating senior and soon-to-be St. Lawrence University rower Max Cole, a member of the Strokes, was part of the coxless quad boat with a winning time of 6:19.244. They edged out the second place boat from Marina Aquatic Center of Los Angeles by just 0.6 of a second. Cole will row for St. Lawrence University next fall. Jackson Violich, who just finished his sophomore year at PHS, was a member of the Strokes’ U-17 eight boat, which placed 8th and was second of six boats in the B Final. They clocked a 6:24.434 in Saturday’s final, less than a boat length behind Row New Jersey of Mount Arlington. Ali Gallacher, an incoming Piedmont junior, was a member of the Strokes’ coxed four boat, which finished 11th overall. It was fifth in the B Final on Sunday with a time of 7:29.7. Representing the OARS, organization PHS students Chris Fung and Aaron Feldhammer made the podium at the Nationals with a third-place finish in quad scull with a time of 6:31.2, 1.2 seconds Piedmont High senior Max Cole celebrates the Oakland Strokes victory in the coxed quad scull event at the U.S. Rowing Youth National Championship Regatta in Sarasota, Florida. Piedmont High School freshman Anna Lavin (top right) and Corpus Christi senior Isabella Warner (2nd from top right), members of Artemis Rowing. qualified for Junior Nationals in their coxed quad scull. Two Piedmont High students, Aaron Feldhammer (left) and Chris Fung (second from left), members of the OARS rowing organization. earned third-place finishes on quad scull. behind 2nd place Nereid Boat Club of Rutherford, New Jersey. The race was won by Maritime Rowing Club of Norwalk, Connecticut. PHS sophomore Zachary Feldstein, a member of OARS, placed 15th in single sculls. He was third in the C Final with a time of 7:52.632, a boat length back of second-place Eban Tracy of Washington’s Vashon Island Rowing Club and two boat lengths ahead of fourth-place Nikola Antich of Bergen County Rowing Academy of New Jersey. Artemis Rowing of Oakland also had two Piedmont teens at the Junior Nationals. PHS incoming sophomore Anna Lavin, and Isabella Warner, a recent graduate at Corpus Christi School, finished 14th in the coxed quad, and second of eight boats in the C Final with a time of 8:03.31, two seconds back of Atomic Rowing of Tennessee. Lavin and Warner’s boat narrowly missed out on the semifinals after finishing 13th in Thursday’s time trial in 7:55.5, just 1.1 second back of the 12th-place qualification. articles.text: “Old Survivor” is estimated to be 500 years old Towering 250 feet high in Leona Heights Park in the Oakland hills is the last remaining old growth redwood tree in the East Bay. “Old Survivor” sits on a steep hill side, inaccessible by public trails, but peeks over the tree-line with visible points from the York Trail on the park’s floor and on the McDonell trail near the canopy. Old Survivor was designated as a City of Oakland Historic Landmark on June 24, 1980. There is a plaque in the parking lot of Carl B. Munck Elementary school from where you can see the crown of the tree. Perhaps the tree being situated on a steep and rocky terrain prevented loggers in the 1850s from cutting it down during the lumber-wave of the early Bay Area. Save The Redwoods League created a video in 2019 about Old Survivor, where they describe the rarity of the tree left behind during the Gold Rush era. “I think “Old Survivor,” the name says it all. That sense of an entity that has survived the devastation of the forest around it, that now serves as the anchor from which the rest of the forest recovery will germinate. Old Survivor is a gnarly old tree and because it was so difficult to get to, it was left behind,” said Save the Redwoods League CEO Sam Hodder. And now for the hike Starting your day from Leona Height’s entrance on Mountain Boulevard, you won’t require much walking on the York Trail to gain sight of Old Survivor. Less than one-third of a mile in, the mammoth tree begins to creep into sight behind your right shoulder. Leona Heights is among the best small treasures of Oakland, where you can find sprawling trees and a thriving babbling brook of Horseshoe Creek along the York Trail. Up the McDonell trail provides more unique sights, there is foundation of an old factory building that is littered with artThe view of Old Survivor from the McDonell Trail. Another sight of Old Survivor (middle) peeking through the trees from the Leona Heights’ York Trail. The canopy of Old Survivor stands high above the rest of the tree line. work from muralists and graffiti artists. Continuing towards the end of the McDonell trail is the remnants of the Leona Heights Sulfur Mine, which was active in the 1890s until 1934. In 2003, the area was fenced off after several young explorers needed rescuing after being overcome by toxic fumes. If you turn left when the McDonell Trail intersects with the York Trail, the path will continue up Leona Heights to an open area that conjoins with the former Merritt College parking lot. It’s an area that provides this writer’s favorite lesser-known view of the Oakland hills, where you have an intimate sight of the Mormon Temple overlooking Oakland, Emeryville, and San Francisco. To locate Leona Heights, simply search “Leona Heights Park” in your GPS device.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 15, 2022 17 Bouquets to Art Continued from page 16 chose Martin Johnson Heade’s Singing Beach, Manchester, MA (1863), based on its palette. This is her 23rd year as a participant. “I’ve been lucky enough to get [my] first choice of artwork,” she said. “The calmness and serenity of Singing Beach at dusk is mesmerizing. The gentle arc of peach and apricot hues symbolizes true hope of peaceful days in our future.” For her display, Lee chose smokebush, phalaenopsis orchids, pincushion protea, hypericum berries, boxwood, succulents, parakeet proteas and Japanese maple - a vibrant interpretation of the landscape artwork and eventide hues. Her team included Robin Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers, and Jacqueline and Robby Ow. The display would likely fetch a pretty penny at the floral shop due to the labor involved and sheer size of flora. “These Bouquets to Art exhibits take a considerable amount of time and floral materials - from scouting the market to see what is available this season, to the design concept, actual design, and installation,” Lee said. “I like to think of the displays as priceless.” Over 100 experienced floral designers participated this year, all hailing from the Bay Area. Display created by Joy Somersett of Miss Scarlett’s Flowers in Portola Valley, based on Franklin Simmons’ Penelope (1896). Two attendees view a display. articles.text: Photo by Calvin Ngu Jordan Baker plays Dana in Berkeley Rep’s Dana H. Berkeley Repertory Theatre is currently performing Dana H., written by Lucas Hnath, through July 10. First presented in New York in 2020, Dana H. has been produced in association with Broadway producers Matt Ross, Sally Horchow, and Dori Berinstein. The play has been nominated for three Tony Awards, including Best Direction by Berkeley’s Les Waters. The play is adapted from interviews with Dana Higginbothan, the playwright’s mother. The title character Dana is played by Jordan Baker. “I was present for some of the events of the play, so there is a semi-autobiographical aspect to it,” Hnath said. The production will be shown now through July 10 at the Roda Theatre, 2025 Addison Street in Berkeley, phone 510-647-2949. To purchase tickets, visit https:// www.berkeleyrep.org/shows/ dana-h/. articles.text: San Francisco Symphony has released a concert film of Igor Stravinsky’s The Soldier’s Tale as part of its free video streaming service, SFSymphony+. The film is Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen’s signature digital project released for the 2021-22 season. “The Soldier’s Tale has a very interesting place in history because it represents a complete change of paradigm,” said Salonen. “The opulent post-Romantic, late-Romantic era has come to a very violent and abrupt end: the world has experienced the first World War, the world has experienced a pandemic, and the new art looks very different, and sounds very different. It deals with contemporary issues, sometimes in an allegorical way, and there’s a sort of an ironic and distant approach to things. The Soldier’s Tale is thoroughly modern, and it represents the new era.” The Soldier’s Tale features actor Bruce Davison as the narPhoto by Kristen Loken Behind the scenes during filming of Stravinsky’s “The Soldier’s Tale.” rator, soldier, and devil; Alonzo King ballet dancer Adji Cissoko; and seven San Francisco Symphony musicians: Concertmaster Alexander Barantschik, Principal Bass Scott Pingel, Principal Clarinet Carey Bell, Principal Bassoon Stephen Paulson, Associate Principal Trumpet Aaron Schuman, Principal Trombone Timothy Higgins, and Principal Percussion Jacob Nissly. “I’ve always wanted to do a proper studio production of Soldier’s Tale, because it’s one of my favorite pieces and deserves a very well-thought-out, detailed production,” said Salonen. “Between the fact that it represents a new era in composition – and in the arts more generally – coupled with the Influenza pandemic, which was a big factor in driving all these changes, you cannot help but to draw parallels between that and our time. A hundred years earlier, Stravinsky was going through the same experiences in his life as we are now in our lives, and that’s almost spooky.” Visit https://www.sfsymphonyplus.org to access the film. Streaming is available on multiple devices.
articles.title: SF Symphony’s The Soldier’s Tale now streaming

articles.text: Festival Napa Valley, now in its 16th season, opens on July 15 with a wide range of concerts, concluding on July 24 with a finale concert by Festival Orchestra Napa. The 9-day summer arts festival takes place in iconic Napa Valley locations. “The performances at Festival Napa Valley this summer illuminate the importance of the arts in today’s world,” said Festival President & CEO Richard Walker. “We are dedicating the 2022 season to the sounds of America. From Copland and Bernstein to jazz, swing, Broadway, bluegrass and country, this is the music that celebrates our common heritage,” added Robin Baggett, Chairman of the Festival’s Board of Directors. The opening night concert on July 15 will be led by conductor Carlo Ponti and the Festival Orchestra Napa in Dvorak’s New World Symphony, and Daniel Brewbaker’s Cello Concerto with soloist Sophia Bacelar. Other noteworthy artists performing this summer are Trisha Yearwood, Nia Imani Franklin and the Young People’s Chorus of New York City, soprano Mikayla Sager, tenor Mario Chang, baritone Lester Lynch, violinist Tessa Lark, and soprano Alexandra Armantrading. Concerts will be outdoors at several locations – the Festival Napa Valley Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, the Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at the Culinary Institute of America at Copia in Napa, and at wineries, estates and other venues throughout Napa Valley. To order tickets and for the full program, visit https://festivalnapavalley.org. Photo courtesy of Festival Napa Valley Festival Napa Valley will return in July as an all-outdoor, 9-day celebration. articles.text: Mendocino Music Festival returns live this summer, beginning July 9 at Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg. Established in 1986 by Allan Pollack, Susan Waterfall and former principal bassoonist of the San Francisco Symphony, Walter Green, the festival features a blend of genres. Evenings include orchestra concerts, Big Band, chamber music ensembles, dance, blues, jazz, folk, and bluegrass. Daytime events include lectures and recitals at the Piano Series, a performance by participants in the Emerging Artists Program, and small concerts in intimate venues throughout the historic town of Mendocino on the North Coast. Featured artists and bands this year include Steel Wheels, Spencer Myer, Gloria Cheng, and Kim Nalley. Concerts will be limited to one hour with no intermission. Steel Wheels will perform at the Mendocino Music Festival this summer. Proof of vaccination is required, and masks must be worn while on event premises. The festival will follow official recommendations of local and state public health agencies
articles.title: Mendocino Music Festival opens July 9

articles.text: Well-known pianist Mary Lou Williams convinced record producer John Hammond to audition Charlie, and Hammond recommended Charlie to Benny Goodman. Goodman was reluctant to hire a young musician on an obscure electric instrument, so Hammond snuck Charlie on stage during a Goodman performance. Angered, Goodman called out the difficult song Rose Room, thinking it would stump Charlie, not knowing that Ralph Hamilton had shown that to Charlie years earlier. Charlie was a sensation and Goodman hired him with the band from 1939 until 1941 when Charlie got tuberculosis and died in March 1942. Charlie was one of the founders of bebop while playing with Charlie Parker, Thelonius Monk, Dizzy Gillespie and Kenny Clarke at Minton’s Playhouse in Harlem. From 1939 through 1941, Charlie was rated Best Guitarist in DownBeat magazine. My improvised example of Charlie Christian is a 12-bar jazz blues featuring diminished chords and the diminished scale with a “Sears and Roebuck” bridge like I Got Rhythm. Many Goodman-Christian tunes use diminished sounds. Listen to and read my improvised example for this Charlie Christian column and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/PostColumns.pdf. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. Call (510) 923-9522, text (510) 435-3997 or email jim@guitarencyclopdeia.com for videoconference or in-person lessons. His course is available for free online at www. guitarimprov.com Charlie Christian was an American jazz musician who was an early master of the electric guitar.
articles.title: Charlie Christian

articles.text: Violinist (and actress) Jayne Mansfield. Sex and violence. That’s what’s in the news. The news mongers assure us that’s what sells. Since the public demands it, I must concur. But look at the title of the column again. This article is about sex and VIOLINS. Let’s look back at some Hollywood history. Does anyone remember one of the greatest sex symbols of all time… Jayne Mansfield? There is a lot more to her than meets the eye (so to speak). Much that follows will surprise you. When I told my sister-in-law, Susan Hirshfield, that I intended to write an article about Jayne Mansfield, she related the following story. “I was 15 and in my first job at the famed May Company at the corner of Fairfax and Wilshire Boulevard in Los Angeles. The store received a call from Jayne Mansfield’s agent that she was coming to the store to shop. Everybody was told to show up. This was Hollywood, after all. I remember standing on the mezzanine of that amazing department store waiting for the show. Jane and her entourage finally swept in a good half hour later than she was supposed to arrive. All the photographers and other attendees were trailing behind her, including her little boy, who was about 10. The child was dressed in a Little Lord Fauntleroy costume… lace collar and all. The child looked positively humiliated. Jayne, wearing a remarkably tight dress, moved around conspicuously; the cameras flashing all the while. She went to the perfume counter and sampled a few while waving at people, and then she turned around and left just as quickly. The staff went back to work, feeling a bit downhearted about that poor little boy.” This vivid account is just a small part of a very big story that was Jayne Mansfield. But she was much more than just a publicity agent’s dream. The next part might surprise you very much. Another friend, who knew her, remarked on her disarming intelligence. In reality, Mansfield’s IQ was 163. She was a linguist and spoke five languages fluently. In addition to English she spoke French, Spanish, German, and Italian. I knew that she played the violin rather well. With a little bit of research, I found examples of her violin solos on YouTube. She played quite well. Jack Benny is remembered as being a very serious violinist, which he was. Jayne Mansfield was a much better player than Jack Benny. And she also played the piano. The Academy Awards ceremony has deteriorated in recent years. Back in 1958 an orchestra was formed to perform at the Academy Awards. Some of the musicians in the orchestra were some of the most famous Hollywood personalities. Dick Powell, who was a very fine singer, was the trumpet player. Hollywood tough guy Robert Mitchum played woodwinds. Elegant Fred Astaire was the drummer. Comedian Jerry Lewis conducted the band. Two famous Hollywood personalities who were notable for their absence were conductor Danny Kaye and singer extraordinaire Gloria Swanson. And yes, in that orchestra, Jayne Mansfield was the featured violinist. That was some orchestra! You will surprise yourselves by doing your own research on the musical talent named above. Even in death, Jayne Mansfield was a publicity agent’s dream. She was killed in an automobile accident on June 29, 1967. The headlines were exaggerated, but the tragedy was real. There are certain constants that we must remember in art. Look beneath the glitz. You might be surprised by genuine talent.
articles.title: How about sex and violins?

By Jim Gleason It’s hard to make a living as a musician, especially a black musician. Imagine trying to do so during the Great Depression. Charlie Christian was 13 when the Depression started and he died in 1942, three years after it ended. He was only 26. Under the direction of their blind father, Clarence Henry Christian, Charlie and his elder brothers Edward and Clarence would play in wealthier neighborhoods of their Oklahoma City hometown for cash or supplies. Charlie first entertained by dancing. Later, he learned trumpet, piano, then guitar. Electric guitar pioneer Eddie Durham said of Charlie: “We met in an Oklahoma City pool hall… Charlie was only playing a little piano then. He wasn’t playing guitar yet. He asked me to give him some pointers, like what to do if you want to play with class and get through life with the instrument. He wanted to know technical things, like how to pick a certain way. So I showed him the way to sound like I did. I said, ‘Don’t ever use an upstroke, which makes a taga-tag-a-tag sound; use a downstroke. It takes an awful fast wrist to play a downstroke— it gives a staccato sound, with no legato, and you sound like a horn.’ ” Eddie Durham also inspired Charlie to use a guitar amplifier. Brother Edward led a band as a pianist in Oklahoma City. Edward’s guitarist, Ralph Hamilton, taught Charlie how to play Sweet Georgia Brown, Rose Room, and Tea for Two. He played them at a jam session and was well-received. He jammed with notable performers including legendary jazz pianists Teddy Wilson and Art Tatum. articles.text: Michael Stehr, an artist and art historian, returns to Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, June 24 with an illustrated lecture entitled “A Stroll in Rome: The Ponte Umberto to San Pietro.” Doors open at 6:30 p.m., and the lecture begins at 7 p.m. Tickets are $20 at the door, cash only. Stehr brings audience members on one of his favorite strolls in Rome, the walk from the Ponte Umberto to Saint Peter’s Basilica. His talk will include illustrations of some of the world’s greatest urban vistas, with details of the work of famed artists Michelangelo, Bernini, and Carlo Maderno, among others. “The city of Rome boasts some of the more noteworthy destinations in the Western World,” explained Stehr, a Piedmont native. “The Pantheon, the Sistine Chapel, and Saint Peter’s Basilica are just a few of the landmarks that attract visitors from around the world. But with so much history around every corner, sometimes the short journey to arrive at a destination is as thrilling as the encounter with that destination itself.” For more information, visit http://www.mstehr. com/about. Michael Stehr

I am collectively calling these master plans, but they include community plans, area plans, neighborhood plans, and specific plans. The names are sometimes used interchangeably and can often be confused one with the other. What they all have in common is a more detailed design of a limited specified geographical area following the overall policies of a city’s General Plan. For all, the ultimate goal is to end up with good development that is feasible and an enhancement to the built environment. The mention of “Specific Plan” has come up during Piedmont’s current process of updating our General Plans’ housing element. So…what exactly is a specific plan? In a word, it is the most detailed planning/design document of the area plans described above. Unlike some of the other types, Specific Plans come with statuary requirements set by the state and among other things include land use within the area covered, public and private transportation, standards and criteria by which development will proceed, as well as implementation and financial measures. This area covered by a Specific Plan can be huge with thousands of acres, or. as is the case in Piedmont, as small as one or two acres. Specific Plans are the most comprehensive of the master plan family and for this reason cities normally need to work with consultants to design and implement them. They can assume a number of different forms but the main component is most often a large inclusive site plan, as illustrated on the adjacent examples. I believe that this master plan drawing, in one form of plan or another, should in fact be the starting point for any good building, landscape or street design as it always includes a somewhat larger area around the immediate project concern. It also illustrates the design concept in a less abstract and more familiar way than the typical general planning document. With this the context into which the project fits can be clarified and appropriately responded to. It is my experience that the These two conceptual master plans illustrate how developments respond to their surroundings, including existing street patterns, building shapes and sizes, playfields, mature trees and water features. These considerations are for current proposals as well as future phases of new development. necessity and value of these types of enlarged plans cannot be overstated. This is because they reach beyond one or two buildings and necessarily involves the relationships, connections, and synergy – the context, of an entire area. They consider and deal with the imperative of Urban Design, the critical (but often neglected) design field frequently referenced in this column Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who have lived in Piedmont for 30 years. articles.text: It was another beautiful, warm day for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group when they met on June 6 outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. Participating were Laura Goldman, Martin Levy, Jerry Gragg, Darby Gragg, Sarah Johnson, Adrienne Hamlin, Pat McMahon, Phil Witte, Dick Carter, Melba Yee, Ken Young, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. The readers had selected The Body, a non-fiction book by British-American author Bill Bryson, who takes readers on a head-totoe, comprehensive tour of the human body, how it functions, its remarkable ability to heal itself, the ways it can fail, and ultimately how its passenger dies. The story is filled with extraordinary facts, such as your body made a million red blood cells since you started reading this. The book provides the reader with a deeper understanding of the miracle that is life in general, and you in particular. Bryson says that each of us is a walking, talking catalogue of wonders. “And how do we celebrate the glory of our existence?” Bryson asks. “Well, for most of us by exercising minimally and eating maximally.” After all Bryson’s collection of amazing facts, the ultimate conclusion of his book is a simple prescription for better life: eat a little bit less, move a little bit more. To the mild surprise of the group, the discussion was lively one that not only covered the book, but also took off on related topics. Martin Levy got the discussion started by sharing that long ago he read a 1968 book also titled The Body, this one by Anthony Smith. Priscilla Wanerus said that book sparked an interest that led to her having a career in the medical industry. Martin said he found the differences between what society found medically important then and now to be interesting. What people died from 50 years ago, compared to today is different and interesting. Most of the readers found that Bryson made the science of our personal, physical worlds both understandable and entertaining. He moved the readers through the book’s 464 pages with jokes, factoids, and biographical information that made reading a book about science enjoyable. Bryson is a good storyteller. Each chapter deals with a different part of our bodies. It was noted that at the end of them, Bryson wrote about what we still don’t know about how and why this or that part of us works the way it does. The readers then turned to future book selections. They had previously picked Cloud Cuckoo Land by Pulitzer-prize-winning fiction author Anthony Doerr for July, and The Chancellor, a biography of contemporary German chancellor Angela Merkel by Kati Marton for August. The group then selected Magpie Murders, a 2016 mystery novel by British author Anthony Horowitz, for September. Since the first Monday in July is July 4th, the next discussion will be Monday, July 11 at 1:30 p.m. outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, Registration is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Cloud Cuckoo Land by Anthony Doerr is the July pick.
articles.title: First Mondays Reading Group discusses The Body

articles.text: Jaxon Keyes is one of the wineries that is bringing Mendocino County to the forefront as a major quality wine-growing region. The property the winery sits on in the town of Hopland dates back to a Mexican land grant from 1844 given to Fernando Feliz. The property was bought by Scottish immigrant John McGlashen who built the beautiful wooden farmhouse that houses the winery tasting room today. The winery is now owned by the Wilson family whose portfolio of wineries includes Mazzoco, Wilson, Pezzi King, DeLorimer, Matrix, St. Anne’s Crossing and others. I was delighted to have a chance to taste the current Jaxon Keyes releases with the winemaker Antoine Favero. Antoine, who also produces the exquisite wines of Mazzocco winery, is a very interesting guy. Born in France, he spent his boyhood in Peru then moved to California at age 10. He ended up studying enology at UC Davis and afterwards worked for Sebastiani Winery and Gundlach-Bundschu Winery. For the past 20 years he has worked for Wilson Family Wines and is responsible for winemaking at multiple wineries. The following wines are a partial showcase of the Jaxon Keyes portfolio. • 2020 Jaxon Keys Rose Made from Carignane grapes, the JK rose is flush with ripe strawberry aromas. It is fresh and bracing on the palate with a good balance between fruit and acid. Clean and refreshing finish. Winemaker Antoine Favero.at Jaxon Keyes winery. Jaxon Keyes winery in Hopland in Mendocino County.
articles.title: Jaxon Keyes – Mendocino Rising

articles.text: When the Wilson family bought the winery they had in place a distillery and a tradition of making brandy. They have kept up the tradition today and produce three brandies: Jaxon Keys Rare ($80) which is aged for 5 years in cask, Jaxon Keys Old Stock ($150) aged for 7 to 10 years, and Jaxon Keys Signature Reserve ($395) aged 10 to 15 years. While they were all fine brandies that can compare to Cognacs, to me the smart purchase is the Rare. While the two more expensive ones were slightly more complex, it was incremental, and does not justify the much higher price. Jaxon Keys Winery 10400 US 101, Hopland, CA 95449 www.jaxonkeys.com

Winemaker Antoine Favero.at Jaxon Keyes winery. 2020 Petite Sirah from Alie Keys Vineyard, part of the Jaxon Keyes family of wines. • 2021 Jaxon Keys Viognier The wine is loaded with notions of ripe peach, tangerine, flowers, and spice; it’s rich, medium-bodied and crystalline on the palate with good purity and focus. Drink over the next two to three years. • 2019 Jaxon Keys Grenache Ravazzi Vineyard The JK Grenache explodes from the glass with layers of expressive fruit. Most of the wine’s charms are in its up-front, juicy personality. On the palate it has lovely cherry fruit and a touch of spice. This would be a great partner to a big grilled hamburger. • 2020 Jaxon Keys Syrah Anna Mac Vineyard This Syrah is scented with black plum, blackcurrant, chocolate, and cured meats. The palate is full-bodied and driven by ripe black fruits, framed by chewy tannins and just enough freshness finishing on a savory note. • 2019 Jaxon Keys GPS This is a blend of Grenache, Petite Sirah and Syrah. It is a huge inky dark brooding wine. It has plenty of minerals as well as a hint of violets, huge tannins, but also massive fruit concentration. It is a wine to forget for 5 years and drink over the next two decades. • 2019 Jaxon Keys Burnee Hill Blend This is a Bordeaux style blend of 60% Cabernet Sauvignon and 40% Merlot. It’s shy to open, but with coaxing, it gives up kirsch, blackberries and currants on the nose with nuances of cedar and tobacco. The palate is medium to full-bodied with a firm frame and juicy freshness on the long finish. Jaxon Keyes winery in Hopland in Mendocino County.
