The group then selected Magpie Murders, a 2016 mystery novel by British author Anthony Horowitz, for September. Since the first Monday in July is July 4th, the next discussion will be Monday, July 11 at 1:30 p.m. outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, Registration is required at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Cloud Cuckoo Land by Anthony Doerr is the July pick. Jaxon Keys Distillery When the Wilson family bought the winery they had in place a distillery and a tradition of making brandy. They have kept up the tradition today and produce three brandies: Jaxon Keys Rare ($80) which is aged for 5 years in cask, Jaxon Keys Old Stock ($150) aged for 7 to 10 years, and Jaxon Keys Signature Reserve ($395) aged 10 to 15 years. While they were all fine brandies that can compare to Cognacs, to me the smart purchase is the Rare. While the two more expensive ones were slightly more complex, it was incremental, and does not justify the much higher price. Jaxon Keys Winery 10400 US 101, Hopland, CA 95449 www.jaxonkeys.com

articles.text: John Igo, a 52-year resident of Piedmont, passed away on May 28, 2002. He met his wife, Mittie, in the Emergency Room at Kaiser Hospital in Oakland many years ago. Perhaps it was fitting, she said, that they “celebrated” their 59th wedding anniversay on May 19th in his hospital room at Kaiser. When Mittie smuggled in a bit of wine, John did his clasic eye roll. TRIBUTES FROM THE IGO GRANDCHILDREN “Mama and Baba would pick me up from day care and I would take a nap on Baba’s lap… and sometimes he would sleep, too!” – Claire (age 17) “My favorite thing about Grandpa was his laugh. The only way I could describe it is as a chortle. It was soft, but deep and resonant at the same time. And always jolly.” – Scott (age 16) “My favorite memory of Grandpa was when I was freaking out because I thought my heart was beating too fast and he came all the way from Piedmont to Orinda with his stethoscope to listen to my heart. This showed me how kind and caring he was.” – Charlotte (age 16) “I remember sitting to the left of Grandpa around the breakfast table, playing Five Crowns, and him asking me which of his cards I wanted him to discard; he always wanted to help us, even in a competitive card game!” – Eleanor (age 15) “I loved watching football with Baba and reading with him in his leather chair.” – Alix (age 14) “I love that I have Grandpa’s middle name as my middle name. My favorite memory was going to Hawaii with our whole family to celebrate Grandma and Grandpa’s 50th anniversary.” – Benjamin (age 13) “Grandpa dressed up like Santa Claus and cheerfully sat through a four-hour virtual Christmas murder mystery game with the whole family when we couldn’t gather in person for the holidays. We could always count on him to take part in activities and games when we were all together in California.” – Greta (age 12) “One of my memories of Grandpa is of his generosity. The cousins and I would mix ingredients into bottles and sell them as potions to cure something, and Grandpa would always buy them, no matter how silly they were. For example, last Thanksgiving he bought a ‘Digestion Potion’ I made using ginger, brown sugar, and water. Believe me, it did not look appetizing, but Grandpa always supported us.” – Ian (age 12) “One of my favorite things about Grandpa was his big heart. I remember him sitting in his leather chair in the T.V. room and opting to move so one of us could sit there.” – Hattie (age 10)
articles.title: Memories of Dr. John Igo

articles.text: A tiger-hybrid was rescued by Oakland Zoo from a roadside attraction in Oklahoma on Friday, June 10. Four big cats will now live safe, dignified lives after a cross-country rescue facilitated on June 10 by Oakland Zoo and two other animal organizations. The Zoo and globally accredited big cat sanctuaries Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge from Eureka Springs, Arkansas, and Lions, Tigers, and Bears in Alpine, California, teamed up to rescue a lion, a tiger hybrid and two tigers from a defunct, abandoned drive-thru roadside zoo offering cub petting and photo opportunities in northeast Oklahoma. The roadside attraction was cited and shut down by the USDA in 2008 for multiple animal safety and welfare violations. Its owner was reported to have ties to “Joe Exotic” from the Netflix series “Tiger King.” The rescue operation was initiated by Oakland Zoo, which was first contacted for help by a concerned Oklahoma resident last month. The concerned individual knew the defunct roadside zoo had four big cats that had been abandoned and were in poor condition. Colleen Kinzley, VP of Animal Care, Conservation and Research for Oakland Zoo, contacted two animal sanctuaries to team together in the effort. Oakland Zoo and Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge traveled to the defunct roadside zoo and conducted the onsite animal evaluations earlier this month. Funded by Oakland Zoo, the critical cross-country journey for the three tigers began with the help of a state-of-the-art animal rescue hauler owned by Lions, Tigers, and Bears. One tiger and the tiger-hybrid, now named “Lola” and “Mia” by the animal care team, arrived in Oakland on Sunday morning, June 12, and were transferred to the Zoo’s veterinary hospital for evaluation. “For the past 30 years, we’ve fully committed Oakland Zoo’s tiger habitat as a sanctuary for tigers victimized by the circus, roadside zoo, private ownership, and cub-petting industries. Those tigers need help, and we can provide that help while educating the public about the dangers of animal exploitation practiced in those industries,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. The rescued big cats, all female and some declawed, a standard practice in the cub-petting industry, include: • An elderly, arthritic lioness subjected to solitude for seven years. She required immediate medical attention and care. She is now at Turpentine Creek Wildlife Refuge. • A tiger-hybrid in poor condition with bowed legs and a badly infected tooth that has caused facial deformity, is now at Oakland Zoo. • Two tigers in separate enclosures, both energetic, but lean. One is now at Oakland Zoo and one is at Lions, Tigers & Bears. “Most likely, these cats were bred to be photo props, and once they grew too big and couldn’t be profitable, they were abandoned. We’re the animals’ voices, and we need to work toward education and legislation, because each animal rescued makes a difference,” said Bobbi Brink, founder and director of Lions, Tigers & Bears. Oakland Zoo’s tiger habitat features climbing platforms, two pools for swimming, trees, and a grass-covered ground. The tigers will receive four weeks of medical attention and care at the Zoo’s veterinary hospital before moving to the Zoo’s tiger habitat.
articles.title: Oakland Zoo helps rescue four big cats

articles.text: Suma Landscaping again swept the landscaping awards of the East Bay Chapter of the California Landscape Contractors Association on Friday, June 6. It won six awards for landscape maintenance and installation for a second consecutive year. Suma has won multiple awards for the past nine years it has entered the competition. It won the highest award, the Judge’s Award for best overall of entries in all 22 categories, for its work maintaining a gorgeous residential yard belonging to Piedmont resident Lois De Domenico. “In these tumultuous times, this garden provides peace and tranquility in my life,” she said. Pam Delgado, the Maintenance Account Manager for the yard and two other award-winning gardens, said that the secret to their success is “a team effort with clear lines of communication and everyone working towards a common goal”. This star team includes Suma’s professional gardening team, pruning specialist Yoshi Kuraishi, account manager Pam, and also Lois herself, a homeowner with great interest in and vision for her space. About Suma Landscaping Suma Landscaping, Inc. is an award-winning full-service, professional landscaping business that offers all aspects of garden design, installation, and maintenance. Suma is a certified Women-Owned Small Business, a member of the California Landscape Contractors Association, certified Bay-Friendly, and is fully bonded, licensed, and insured. The company is dedicated to providing the highest quality of service at a reasonable cost and is always striving to exceed expectations.
articles.title: Suma Landscaping wins Award for lush garden in Piedmont

articles.text: Nancy DeRoche wanted to take the Walking on Wednesdays group to the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) reservoir on Scenic and Blair Avenues at the top of Piedmont. Though it involved a lot of climbing, there was a good turnout of 32 walkers. The group started out going across Highland Avenue to Piedmont Court to take the shortcut path to Mountain Avenue. However they were struck by a house covered in Golden State Warriors signs, flags, banners, t-shirts, and other memorabilia. The team was playing that night in the NBA Finals, so there was a reason for the excitement. Homeowner Debbie Lee came out and joined the group for a photo in front of her house. On the climb up Mountain, they passed the home of the late Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis, and on Sea View, the stately home that was used in the 2006 Will Smith movie The Pursuit of Happyness. The walkers turned up Dudley Avenue and stopped at the top of Littlewood Drive for a short talk about Piedmont’s first manufacturing industry. A past Piedmont Post article by Gail Lombardi of the Piedmont Historical Society told the surprising history of Piedmont’s Silk Farm. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land and planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are silk worms’ food. They built a twostory, eight-room cocoonery, but the Silk Farm didn’t prosper, and it closed in 1895. The walkers continued up Dudley, including the Dudley Court cul-de-sac, and then on to Blair Avenue and EBMUD’s Reservoir Number 2. The reservoir is just above Blair Park, and occupies nine acres straddling the Oakland-Piedmont border with 8.3 acres in Piedmont. A 22.8 million gallon water storage tank provided water for Piedmont from 1905 to 2003. The facility was decommissioned and drained in 2003 as part of EBMUD’s facility modernization program, and Piedmont’s water now comes from other large tanks in the Oakland Hills. The group continued up Blair past Scenic Avenue, then began their descent on Mountain and Hager Avenue, with spectacular views of the Bay as they returned to the Community Hall. Everyone agreed it had been a great walk with the Warriors, worms, water, and wonderful Bay views. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Walking on Wednesday members got caught up in the excitement of the Warriors in the NBA finals, and took a photo with Debbie Lee in front of her well-decorated house. Pictured are: Mary Carter, Charlene Louie, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Harriette Louie, Priscila Wanerus, Evelina Bowen, Helen Dong, Elizabeth Richter, Martin Levy, Laura Goldman, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Kat Lang, Tami DeSellier, Erni Ng, Celeste Woo, Quincy Dong, Jim Kuo, Elane Rehr, Nadine Guffanti, Pat Keller, Brenda Ferrero, Jim Kellogg, Tamar Stein Edelson, Dick Carter, Sarah Johnson, Dena Belinkoff, Abel Edelson, Judy Wang, and Brandon Keller. pages.text: Wednesday, June 15, 2022 29 Camp Dracena Continued from page 1 added the title of sheriff to their already busy identities of Scout and camper. The theme meant plenty of horseshoe games were played through a week in which they also made pinhole cameras and leather neckerchief slides. A favorite activity among the campers turned them into scientists, as they recorded the fantastic results of inserting mentos into a 2-liter bottle of Coca-Cola. Friendly sporting matches on the lawn and “banana tag” kept the kids running around all afternoon. There were three age-divided dens this year, each making a flag and a den cheer. After practicing all week, the campers recited their cheers in front of the entire camp. The youngest group of campers named themselves the “Avocado Ninjas”, while other dens took on the names “Turtles” moniker and “Bob is a Buffalo.” By the end of camp, the cub scouts were nearly professional in raising the flag, reciting the pledge of Allegiance, and Scouts Oath and the Scout Law. On the final day of camp, June Families took advantage of the shade on the blistering hot Friday, June 10, before watching the Cub Scout Day Camp’s Egg Drop. Piedmont Firefighter Paramedic Brian Protheroe descends from the 75-foot ladder during the Cub Scout Egg Drop on June 10 the egg drop. Kindergarten graduate, Barrett Williamson, holds up his egg capsule which easily floated back to earth like a feather. On a windless day, this egg gently floated down to the Dracena Park grass to the roar of the crowd. 10, the Scouts were presented with a special visit by the Piedmont Fire Department. Each Scout created a landing capsule (crash container) to hopefully allow their raw eggs to survive the 75-foot drop from the top of the fire engine ladder to the lawn of Dracena Park. Families gathered for a picnic dinner to watch on the lawn of the panhandle portion of Dracena Park. After all 16 egg capsules were dropped, the Scouts could hardly contain their excitement to see the results. One by one the fate of each egg was revealed by the Scout leaders. Grand cheers went up for every surviving egg and applause reigned down for every successful Scout as they collected their rewards, a Mulberry’s coupon for a free ICEE. 2nd grader Sam Malione proudly holds the flag made by the Turtles Den. A camp favorite, Banana tag, involves freeze tag, and rock, paper, scissors. After Scout leaders secured the halyard and presented the colors, the flag was raised at the start of each day of the Cub Scout camp at Dracena Park. Campers eagerly awaited the opening of their egg drop containers after the drop.

articles.text: that there still remains a time for everything under the sun, even a time to tear down, but also a time to build up. In the Christian Scriptures the Apostle Paul refers to believers as “co-creators with God.” The troubles we face should not be signs of failure alone, but also as opportunities for growth. If a structure excludes others from the advantages we have enjoyed, perhaps it’s time to rip out a wall or two and expand our vision to include all. Perhaps it’s another time in our history to see opportunity in the chaos and blessing in the struggle. As we approach Thanksgiving, let us be cautious about what we are thankful for. I suppose it’s only human practice what I call “comparative gratitude”, that is, being thankful for things we have that others do not. But Jesus actually defined blessings as challenges. In his most famous sermon on the mount, he said, “Blessed are the hungry, blessed are those who mourn, and blessed are those who are persecuted...” One could argue that it is a very un-Christian thing to define a blessing as something we have that others do not. Jesus understood blessings as challenges that open us up to more profoundly rely on each other and inspire us to rebuild together. Perhaps we should allow our “comparative gratitude” to disturb us in a way that leads to action, rather than lull us into complacency. So if a blessing is something

articles.text: Youth singers leave today for Denmark and Germany The Notburga Church, 1000 years old, towers over the village of The tour will conclude in the beautiful village of Hochhausen, Germany, where we will be hosted by John and Sue Malick of Piedmont and members of the local community (including a Count). On June 29th we will return to the States. Despite all the obstacles that we’ve faced over these last three years, it’s finally happening. – and I couldn’t be more excited to go. I have been in the Choir for 10 years, and have been lucky to tour with PEBCC before as part of the Concert Choir. The first, in 2018 was to Tampa and Orlando, Florida. The concerts were great and the trip to Disneyland was a blast. There were some challenges, such as flickering lights at the hotel and some doors that didn’t close; sandwiches with an unnecessary amount of jalapenos; and 100° temperatures with 100 percent humidity the entire time. Still, we made the best of it. Some of my closest choir friendships originated there. Then there was the 2019 tour to Seattle with great food, great views, and great people. We were split into groups and stayed with members of the choir that hosted us. I will never forget the visits we made to MOD Pizza, a place where you make your own pizza; our performance of the Ukrainian Christmas carol (I got to help teach the words in Ukrainian to everyone); going to the Space Needle, the famed tower in Seattle; and singing in the Chihuly Gardens surrounded by stunning glass sculptures and plants. And now we are going out of the country for the first time in three years. Traveling has always been a passion of mine, from visiting the grand Tower Bridge in London, to the proud Eiffel Tower in Paris, and to the golden beaches of Cancun. Traveling to Denmark and Germany with my friends after two years of Zoom choir rehearsals and other COVID-19 shenanigans is like a dream come true. I can’t wait to walk the cobblestone streets of Herning and Hochhousen, where I hope I meet the Count. I’m also excited to try all the delicious food that the countries have to offer. In Germany, the Currywurst (Fried sausage, usually pork, typically cut into bite-sized chunks and seasoned with curry ketchup, with a side of fries), Berliner Pfannkuchen (A doughnut that has some jelly filling), and of course, authentic German Bratwurst. And in Denmark, Smørrebrød (Buttered rye bread with pickled herring and salad or with ham and aspic jelly topped with red onions), Hindbærsnitter (A short bread with a raspberry filling and a sugar glaze), and finally Kanelstang (the Danish version of a cinnamon roll). I am not the only one who’s excited about the upcoming trip. My friend Eliza Van de Water said: “So hyped for tour again, I love traveling the world with my friends and learning about different choral traditions.” For some singers, like Mirella Piccoloboni, this will be the first tour ever. It reminds me of the time when I was going on my first tour, how nervous I was and how in the end I knew I would go back and do it all over again because of the adventures we had. Our repertoire this year includes a Danish song, “Morgesang af Elverskud,” a German song, “Guten Abend Gut Nacht,” an American spiritual, “Every Time I Feel the Spirit When I Sing,” and “Song of Peace.” Our Photos by Susan Malick Hochhausen residents are preparing to host the vocalists with Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir this summer. rehearsals are spent going through each song to make sure they will be perfect. Each day this week we have had three-hour rehearsals. The part of the tour that I don’t find so glamorous is that we have to wear uniforms the whole time, and no phones are allowed. I understand the uniforms, after all we are an international touring choir and we have an image to maintain. However, when we all decide to go out on the town, we’ll be wearing stuffy polos and shorts that don’t do anyone much justice, but when we go out with our homestay families, we can wear casual clothes. This year, two of its three touring choirs are going: Ensemble to Germany and Denmark, and Concert Choir to Seattle. My friend Eliza Van de Water said: “So hyped for tour again, I love traveling the world with my friends and learning about different choral traditions.” For some singers, like Mirella Piccoloboni, this will be the first tour ever. It reminds me of the time when I was going on my first tour, how nervous I was and how in the end I knew I would go back and do it all over again because of the adventures we had. Our repertoire this year includes a Danish song, “Morgesang af Elverskud,” a German song, “Guten Abend Gut Nacht,” an American spiritual, “Every Time I Feel the Spirit When I Sing,” and “Song of Peace.” Our Photos by Susan Malick Hochhausen residents are preparing to host the vocalists with Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir this summer. rehearsals are spent going through each song to make sure they will be perfect. Each day this week we have had three-hour rehearsals. The part of the tour that I don’t find so glamorous is that we have to wear uniforms the whole time, and no phones are allowed. I understand the uniforms, after all we are an international touring choir and we have an image to maintain. However, when we all decide to go out on the town, we’ll be wearing stuffy polos and shorts that don’t do anyone much justice, but when we go out with our homestay families, we can wear casual clothes. Now for the cell phone rule, I disagree. Yes, if we have unrestricted access to our phones, it won’t be much of a tour. But why not have our chaperones take our phones and keep them in a designated place until a certain time when we can use them to contact our families and friends and keep up with what’s going on in the world? Alas, that’s not the route we’re going. Our parents will have to keep up with us by reading the daily tour blog. So ladies and gents, if you’ll excuse me, I have rehearsals to get back to, a suitcase to pack, a camera to get, and of course a COVID test to take. Bon Voyage from your favorite writer. See you in two weeks with a story all about the Summer of 2022 Choir Tour. articles.text: Pied mont High School seniors, the Class of 2022, celebrated their graduation with a grand commencement ceremony on Thursday, June 2 at Witter Field. The weather was idyllic, and the grandstands were packed with tittering family and friends to honor Piedmont’s 101st graduating class. Seniors walked down the steps of the grandstand past their loved ones to join their seated classmates on the field, as the Piedmont High School Band played “True Blue.” Principal Adam Littlefield, looking dapper with a white fedora and a purple and white tie, called the Class of 2022 the most actively engaged in his 38-year career. This year, his fifth as principal at Piedmont, will also be his last as he heads into retirement. The first speaker was Salutatorian Wesley Jeng whose playful speech honored the event which “marked their final union.” Co-Salutatorian Jacob Hsia acknowledged the difficulty the class endured, and did not shy away from the tough topics of racism, the pandemic and gun violence. The class Valedictorian Aaron Drumm followed with a thoughtful speech about character and perseverance. Quoting novelist Brandon Sanderson from his book Oathbringer, he said, “Sometimes a hypocrite is nothing more than a man in the process of changing. articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council directed the Park Commission to form a subcommittee to memorialize the Sidney Dearing family. At a May 16 meeting, the council discussed the possibility of the naming of the triangle park at the intersection of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues as “Dearing Family Memorial Park,” in memorial of Sidney Dearing. Sidney and Irene Dearing were Piedmont’s first black homeowners. The couple purchased a home in the city in 1924 and were driven out by a mob of white Piedmont residents. The Piedmont Police Department did little to help the family as a 500-person mob demanded the family’s removal. Instead of taking action on the agenda item on May 16, City Administrator Sara Lillevand advised City Council to “slow down on the name itself, and provide more opportunity for public engagement on this important effort.” Lillevand explained that there have been numerous calls from residents asking the city to address the treatment of the Dearing family and to publicly acknowledge the behavior of past public officials. The triangle park being considered is located across the street from the former Dearing home. Several residents called in asking if City Council had discussed the proposal with residents in the area of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenue, as well as Dearing’s descendants. On Wednesday, June 1, Park Commissioners considered establishing a subcommittee to make recommendations on an appropriate way to memorialize the family. Lillevand introduced commissioners to Cornelia Sylvester, a Certified Professional Coach, who has been working with the city staff as a consultant since September 2020 facilitating antibias training and discussions. “We looked at the Dearing story not as a unique case, but as a case that is common in most suburbs across the United States. We wanted to think about what each person’s role was in getting this family out of Piedmont,” Sylvester said. “There were several governmental bodies that played a large part.” Sylvester presented questions for commissioners to consider: how many people and facets of the government did it take to accomplish the goal of removing the family? What was preserved by moving the Dearings out of town? What was lost? And at what critical junctures could this incident have been prevented? “In order to have homogenous communities, it takes a considerable amount of effort and exclusion,” she explained. Lillevand explained that city staff was “new” to the Sidney Dearing story in 2020, when Sylvester first began working with the city on bias training. City staff role played as members of the community in 1924, acting out the removal of the Dearing family. “It was powerful, impactful, and memorable,” Lillevand said. The subcommittee will consist of members of the Park Commission and will gather opinions and comments from the community in making their decision, Lillevand explained. The subcommittee

articles.text: St. Francis is known for that famous saying “preach the gospel, and if you have to, use words.” God is probably less concerned about what we believe and more concerned about the way we act. When we get right down to it, there are simply too many words flying around and not enough meaningful action. And as Christians approach Easter, the celebration of Jesus’ resurrection, it is easy for us to get sidetracked by words in the form of creeds, liturgies and theologies. These provide enough words to suffocate the real story that was all about meaningful action. It’s in that context that I share what I consider to be an Easter Story. A few years ago, Elizabeth Gilbert, author of “Eat, Pray, Love”, wrote about an incident that changed her life. She was riding the midtown bus in New York City in evening rush hour traffic. The weather was the worst January had to offer, complete with sleet and gusting wind. To quote her, “It sucked”. The bus was moving at a crawl, tempting her to get out and walk, but the cold icy world she was staring at through the window paralyzed her. The depression in that mobile metal tomb was palpable. articles.text: Dave Martin’s House Party big band will perform in Piedmont on the 4th of July. David Martin’s House Party big band will perform in Piedmont Park on the 4th of July this year immediately following the parade. The concert show will begin at approximately 11:30 a.m. on a large stage in the park on Monday, July 4. One of San Francisco’s premier party bands for 25 years, this interactive 11-piece all-star group has gained a national reputation for their high energy performances, incredible musical variety, and “anything-can-happen” hi-jinx. Recent appearances include The Waldorf Astoria in New York City, special Napa Valley performances for Wine Spectator Magazine, concertizing in Maui at the Hyatt Regency Kaanapali and La Costa Resort in Carlsbad; selling out in Reno at the Grand Sierra Resort’s VIP New Years Eve 2010; and entertaining at numerous benefit galas in the greater Bay Area. David Martin is a Bay Area native who began his musical career at the age of six. Known for his powerful vocals and sparkling guitar work, David was a founding member of legendary San Francisco “New Wave” faces The Lloyds and The Buzztones. Martin has assembled a remarkable group of established musician/entertainers including Bobby Strickland (Todd Rundgren, Phil Lesh), Byron Allred (Steve Miller, Todd Rundgren), Gerald Goudeau (Race & Rhythm), Christina Sabatelli (Tubes, Starship), Tim Allen (Silvercreek), Timo Guierrez (Viva Brazil), John Mader (Booker T, Pee Wee Ellis), and Rob Russ (Eddie Money). Rounding out the group’s lineup are the dance artists Sandra Leathley and Stephanie Romano. Contacts: David Martin dm_24@earthlink.net 510- 351-6492 davidmartinshouseparty.com Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is planning a program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up every Friday during the summer months, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to pick up from an unattended pile every Friday starting at 8:00 a.m. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located outside the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. The site is now open every Friday and will close for the season in the fall. The compost is firstcome, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee availability of compost. To pick up compost, residents should bring a shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials. Pickup trucks must have a tarp on their loads. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected by Republic Services in communities participating in curbside organics collection services. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with soil aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1, 2022, requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses and that it be composted. More information can be found on the City’s news and notifications page. If questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager, Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont.ca.gov or (510) 420-3058.

articles.text: Cit y Financial Plan ner Michael Szczech facilitated a public hearing on the proposed fiscal year (FY) 2022-2023 budget at the most recent city council meeting on June 6. This was the first public hearing on the proposed budget, as well as a proposed levy of the municipal Services Special Tax. Piedmont’s Finance Department is budgeting $33,864,402 in General Fund expenditures, an increase of 7% from last year’s [FY 2021-22] projected expenditures. Property-related tax revenue decreases The report prepared by Szczech found that property-related taxes, the city’s primary revenue source, saw a decrease of $739,280 based on the city’s projection one year ago, over the 2021-22 projected actual. The proposed budget this year consists of property tax revenues budgeted at $16,875,000, a 5.5% increase. “The increase is [due to] a high volume of home sales at record high prices, which increased the assessed valuation of those homes at 120%,” explained Szczech. The Parcel Tax revenue, based on the measure approved by a majority of voters in March 2020, is estimated at $2,522,000, a 4% increase over the 2021-22 projection. “The housing market continues to be strong and is a key factor in maintaining the stability of City revenues,” Szczech said. “There is no assurance this trend will continue, as the overall economy faces serious headwinds with rising interest rates and inflation. Real Property Transfer Tax receipts have been higher than [budgeted] through the first nine months of the fiscal year and are trending to surpass the budget by approximately $2.2 million.” Recreation revenue Revenue generated by the city Recreation Department is now back at pre-pandemic levels, the report showed. The proposed budget accounts for an increase of $276,00 in revenue from the prior year. The new budget assumes that programs will no longer be impacted by COVID-19-related revenue loss. “Recreation program revenue has returned to a normal [pre-pandemic] state after being severely impacted by cancelled programs and reduced capacity in varying degrees between March 2020 and June 2021 due to COVID-19. Recreation staff did an outstanding job in navigating the fluctuating rules and guidelines issued by County and State Health officials,” said Szczech. Pre-school revenue is budgeted at a slightly smaller increase of $165,000 over 2021-22 projections. Programming was increased from 4-day to 5-day programs, but revenue suffered due to reduced class sizes. Preschool programs next year are at pre-pandemic, full class-size levels. Facility rentals for use at 801 Magnolia Avenue is budgeted at $45,000 for FY 2022-23. Construction market exceeds budget expectations FY 2020-2021 was a record year for construction and remodeling costs, increasing 28% over the prior year, and continues to remain high. Staff is projecting to exceed the annual budget this fiscal year by $200,000, or 17%. Administrative costs related to this market include building permits, planning fees, plan check fees, general plan maintenance fees, and records management fees. “This category continues to surprise us. Consistent with the City’s overall budget philosophy, staff is budgeting for declines in revenue in all areas of this category as staff does not expect the high level of activity to continue as the city faces mounting economic uncertainty,” said Szczech.

articles.text: Piedmont Girl Scouts in Troop 33943 preparing kits for Children’s Hospital. Pictured are: (front) Zayda Weber (left), Emma Syhabout, Calder Hondorp, Eliza Hupp, Elizabeth Ackerman, Sicheng Wu, Olivia Chan, Troup Leader Amera Rizk; (back) Halston Pinsky, Makeena Small, Violet Shrieve, Hazel Schaeffer, Evie Luskin, Paige Rampton, Phoebe Hess, Penelope Hopper, Zara Ashraf, and Sai Ahuja. Not pictured: Rae Barker, Kayleigh Anderson, and Havia Leonard. Members of Piedmont Girl Scout Troop 33943 spent time at their last meeting of the school year putting together comfort kits for kids and parents at Children’s Hospital in Oakland. Donations for the kits from the community and cookie sale funds were used to purchase all the items. The 20 Girl Scouts began collecting donations in late April and used the money to purchase socks, stress balls, nut-free snacks, journals, lotions, chapsticks, and gum. They also made friendship bracelet kits. Troop member Emma Shyabout made her own word search puzzles and coloring pages. “The girls also donated their own [items] from home, giving unused journals, coloring books, stickers, beads, washi tape and embroidery thread,” said Troop parent Amy Vallerie. “They will still have $500 to donate to the hospital in addition to the kits they made.” Piedmont Girl Scouts creating “comfort kits” for patients and parents at children’s Hospital.

articles.text: Piedmont residents have a wealth of opportunities to volunteer within their community and the East Bay this summer. Thanks to suggestions from residents, Piedmont Post has compiled a list of organizations that are currently seeking volunteers. Wardrobe for Opportunity Oakland Wardrobe for Opportunity Oakland provides access to transformational career support services for low-income individuals seeking employment. The organization was founded in 1995 to help low-income women look professional in workplace settings and has since evolved to provide a complete suite of career development services to men, women, and youth. There are various ways you can volunteer with the organization, which is seeking volunteers to conduct mock interviewers, style clients, facilitate workshops, and process donations. Wardrobe for Opportunity also accepts gently-used and new clothing donations. Visit https://www.wardrobe.org/donate to learn more. e-Buddies E-Buddies promotes social inclusion online for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities such as autism and Down syndrome. Like a modern version of a letter writing program, the organization pairs your child and a child with developmental disabilities as e-mail pen pals. It is a great opportunity for students who would like to volunteer remotely and helps encourage technology literacy and communication skills. Participants are matched based on age, gender, and similar interests; anyone over the age of 10 and with parents’ permission can participate in e-Buddies. To sign up, visit https://www.bestbuddies. org/what-we-do/ebuddies/. Lake Merritt Institute Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland Unified School District students to help keep Lake Merritt’s shoreline and creeks clean on a weekly basis. Volunteers meet at the Institute office on the 2nd floor of the Boating Center, 568 Bellevue Avenue next to the parking lot, in Lakeside Park. The office entrance is up the stairs behind the Boathouse office at the end of the building. Volunteers usually work 2-3 hours during a shift. Gloves are provided. Individuals who have been trained may also work alone using one of the four “U-Clean-It” boxes around the Lake where you will find gloves, trash bags, barrels, nets, directions and a sign-in sheet. Visit https://lakemerrittinstitute.org/how-you-can-help/ to sign up. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes over 1 million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors in their Oakland neighborhoods were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping at distribution sites, and translating written materials. Visit https:// mercybrownbag.org/volunteer/ to sign up. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? Email suggestions to Allyson Aleksey at Allysonaaleksey@gmail.com. Lake Merritt Institute volunteers help keep the lake clean and free of debris. Free Delivery to Piedmont

articles.text: I am here today with some advice to my classmates as we transition into high school: show up. Be present. If you ask a question such as “how are you?” actually listen to them. Don’t just ask out of habit and keep walking. One thing COVID taught me is that we need each other. By being present and taking the time to listen to the answer, you are engaging in the conversation. You’re showing up. Right now you might be thinking, “When will this ceremony be over?” That is a perfect example of how not to be present in the moment. Instead of wondering what you are going to do with your friends on the last day of school, try being grateful in this moment. Just remember, we could still be doing school in our bed. I learned this lesson about the importance of showing up during COVID. I’m not going to lie, middle school was not always easy for me, especially distance learning. But whenever I would get down on myself about missing assignments, or something that wasn’t going well, my mom and dad would tell me not to feel sorry for myself because everyone in the world was living through this. My parents showed up for me with this advice, our teachers showed up for us online, and we should do the same for each other. Nothing in this world is given to you; you’re going to have to work for it. This transition to high school will be challenging, but every student experiences it. Was middle school hard? Sometimes, yes. But here we all are today. Was distance learning hard? Yes, but we found ways to connect Were TED Talks nerve-wracking? Yes. But we all survived. Will 9th grade be hard? Sometimes. But together we will get through it as long as we continue to show up. So, stop to actually listen to “How are you?” Put down your phone when you’re with your friends. Go to practice even when you don’t feel like it. Think positively about the future and yourself. Show up, Piedmont Middle School, today, tomorrow, and in the future. We all need each other. Mom- there’s a box of tissue in your purse. I put it there this morning. I tried to show up for you. Patrick Brayer spoke at the 8th grade commencement celebration on Wednesday, June 1. the students which made the class so well rounded. Students stood as classmates received their certificate of completion, one by one, from Fletcher. After shaking hands with Fletcher one final time, they retook their seats in advance of becoming high school students in the fall.

articles.text: Sometimes when we think about bringing creativity into our family life, it can feel overwhelming. There are so many competing needs and objectives in our busy lives, how can we possibly make room for one more thing? As I reflect on this question, I am thinking about a science experiment that I did with my son when he was about 5 years old. We took a mason jar and filled it with rocks and asked the question, “Is it full?” To which, he dutifully answered, “Yes!” And then we poured smaller rocks in and around the larger rocks. Again, we asked, “Is it full?” This time he answered “Yes” with a little more hesitation. Then we poured sand in, which filled the space around the smaller and larger rocks. This time he knew it wasn’t full, even though the jar looked completely full. For the last step, we added water and filled it to the brim. The point is, there is always more room if we are willing to fill some of the cracks and crevices. The key is how do we fill those things in a way that feels easy and meaningful, but without exhausting ourselves even more? If you are looking to bring more creativity into your family, maybe it’s not about big projects with epic outcomes. Maybe it’s about tiny micro-moments that are tucked in between soccer camp and family vacations. Here are just a few ideas for fitting creativity into the summer space that already exists, but maybe we aren’t paying attention to it: • Airplane Coloring Challenge Doing some traveling this summer? While we are all grateful for the invention of the ipad, when you want your kids to take a screen break in the middle of a flight, try a simple coloring game. Are the jars full? Take out your box of markers or crayons. Give your child some blank paper. Have them close their eyes and hand them one color. When they open their eyes, they look at the color and they have to draw the first thing that pops into their heads that might be that color. Red? Maybe they draw a cherry. Purple? A funny elf from a dream the night before. • Morning Music Getting my kids up in the morning during the school year has a very different energy than summer wake ups. The school year tends to be tense and rushed. But, for summer wake ups, I like to blast a different genre of music every morning. One day they might be awakened by Beethoven’s 9th Symphony and then the next, some early 2000s Avril Lavigne. Have fun and choose music that gives YOU energy! • Once Upon a Time in the Grocery Store Starting with whatever the very first thing you put in your grocery cart, tell a story with your child while shopping. articles.text: Children’s Fairyland is bringing back its annual Book Festival after a two-year pandemic-driven pause. The festival, now in its fifth year, will feature 25 Bay Area children’s authors and illustrators for a full day of story-time. A mix of well-established and emerging authors will be present. Six authors and illustrators will give 25-minute book presentations and live art demonstrations at Fairyland’s Emerald City Stage. Headliners include award-winning authors Mac Barnett, JaNay Brown-Wood, Johanna Ho, C.V Monterrubio, Wednesday Kirwan and Nina LaCour. Attendees will have a chance to purchase books which can be signed by featured authors during scheduled meet-and-greet times, which will be broken up into five-minute time slots. Student writers age 8 through 12 from Fairyland’s Youth Writer’s Workshop will then share a joint reading at the Youth Author Table in the afternoon. Other featured authors and illustrators this year are John Casselberry, Madeline Connor, Angela Dalton, Cindy Derby (2021 Caldecott Honor for Outside In), Hayley Diep, Meg Fleming, Alia Gabres, Michael Genhart (2022 Pura Belpre Award for May Your Life Be Deliciosa), Jill Guerra, Felicia Hoshino, Illustoria, Nancy Johnson James, Dawood Marion, Constance Moore, Christina Newhard, Jane Park (2015-2016 Asian Pacific American Librarians Association’s Asian Pacific American Award for Juna’s Jar), Keely Parrack, Lea Redmond, Nadia Salomon, Victoria Sanchez, Simone Shin, Emma Bland Smith, Meera Sriram (2021 South Asia Book Award for A Gift for Amma), Meredith Steiner, and Justine Villanueva. Also participating is Maggie Tokuda Hall, a Piedmont High School graduate whose work of fiction for young adults. Squad, won the Poppy Award in 2021. Festival attendance is free with park admission. The festival takes place on Saturday, June 1, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Learn more at www.fairyland. org or visit the park at 699 Bellevue Avenue in Oakland.

articles.text: FireCracker Math offers small group and private instruction on extra-curriculum math topics. It aims to spark children’s interest in math, deepen their knowledge, and further develop their aptitude and talent in math. The company’s curriculum focuses on the exploration and understanding of mathematical concepts and on teaching kids the skills of problem-solving and logical reasoning. Enrollment for summer camps and in the fall is now open. Oneweek in-person summer math camps will be offered in Piedmont starting on June 13, June 27, and July 11. The camp is designed for curious and challenge-loving kids ages 6 to 16. Morning classes cover selected topics from number theory, algebra, geometry, combinatorics, graph theory, logic, and the basics of computer science. Instruction employs math games, math-based magic tricks, curious paradoxes, and contests to spark kids’ interest and boost their skills and confidence in math and other STEM subjects. After lunch, full-day students will participate in various fun afternoon activities. This year’s activities include chess, art, and fun science. Create your own Summer Camp with our Learning Pods and private lessons. Sign up for in-person or online learning pods of 3-5 students. The curriculum will be customized to help kids with school topics or homework. pages.text: Wednesday, June 8, 2022 9 Once Upon a Time at Fairyland Fairyland’s annual Book Festival is Saturday, June 18 By Allyson Aleksey Children’s Fairyland is bringing back its annual Book Festival after a two-year pandemic-driven pause. The festival, now in its fifth year, will feature 25 Bay Area children’s authors and illustrators for a full day of story-time. A mix of well-established and emerging authors will be present. Six authors and illustrators will give 25-minute book presentations and live art demonstrations at Fairyland’s Emerald City Stage. Headliners include award-winning authors Mac Barnett, JaNay Brown-Wood, Johanna Ho, C.V Monterrubio, Wednesday Kirwan and Nina LaCour. Attendees will have a chance to purchase books which can be signed by featured authors during scheduled meet-and-greet times, which will be broken up into five-minute time slots. Student writers age 8 through 12 from Fairyland’s Youth Writer’s Workshop will then share a joint reading at the Youth Author Table in the afternoon. Other featured authors and illustrators this year are John Casselberry, Madeline Connor, Angela Dalton, Cindy Derby (2021 Caldecott Honor for Outside In), Hayley Diep, Meg Fleming, Alia Gabres, Michael Genhart (2022 Pura Belpre Award for May Your Life Be Deliciosa), Jill Guerra, Felicia Hoshino, Illustoria, Nancy Johnson James, Dawood Marion, Constance Moore, Christina Newhard, Jane Park (2015-2016 Asian Pacific American Librarians Association’s Asian Pacific American Award for Juna’s Jar), Keely Parrack, Lea Redmond, Nadia Salomon, Victoria Sanchez, Simone Shin, Emma Bland Smith, Meera Sriram (2021 South Asia Book Award for A Gift for Amma), Meredith Steiner, and Justine Villanueva. Also participating is Maggie Tokuda Hall, a Piedmont High School graduate whose work of fiction for young adults. Squad, won the Poppy Award in 2021. Festival attendance is free with park admission. The festival takes place on Saturday, June 1, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Learn more at www.fairyland. org or visit the park at 699 Bellevue Avenue in Oakland. articles.text: Good evening, everyone. I’d first like to begin by thanking all of you, parents, students, teachers, and administrators, for fostering my growth both intellectually and as an individual throughout my four years in high school. So, Piedmont High School class of 2022, we finally get a break. We’re finally done thinking about anything intellectual for the next couple of weeks. Oh wait, nope! You have to listen to one of Jacob’s speeches, which you best bet will have some sort of intellectual reference. Now I promise you that I’ll only make one such reference this time, and that’s going to be “Frankenstein” by Mary Shelley, so for those of you that haven’t read it, you have about 30 seconds to scour SparkNotes before I start making my references. Don’t worry, I know many of you all have experience doing this. But really, I am genuinely honored to speak in front of you today, to represent the successes of this amazing class. It’s safe to say that our class has been through a lot together. We’ve endured a year and a half of distance learning during what many would consider the heart of our high school experience. We’ve gone through the horror of processing mass shootings, both school and racially motivated shootings, that have really become too many to count. We’ve experienced first-hand a worsening political climate. Every day, we expect to wake up to some shocking headline about the future of our country or our planet. The examples go on. Oh, yeah, and I almost forgot. About a week ago today our senior prank was…well, let’s not talk about that. But it is because of these difficult times we’ve shared together that we’ve become more united. We can collectively bond over many of these struggles, which drives us to create change in response to those struggles. And change we’ve seen. Everywhere you look, you’re bound to see an activist of some sort, whether someone who directly helped the community demonstrate a commitment to social justice, or simply someone who you can have insightful, introspective conversations with, conversations that are the basis for change. I feel as if I could go up to any one of you right now and have one of these insightful conversations. That is the unique unity and passion of our class at work. You see, society is like Dr. Frankenstein: a flawed society creates flawed but passionate individuals, and we are those passionate individuals. Frankenstein’s creature was powerful, and much of that power may be attributed to his flaws, but also his drive to come to terms with Dr. Frankenstein. He was distanced by society solely due to his appearance, as I’m sure many of you may feel detached from a society controlled by older generations that hold different values. But let’s not let the flaws of society destroy us and fall to the same fate as Frankenstein’s creature. Let’s use our drive and persistence; let’s come to terms with our Dr. Frankenstein. Let’s carry forward in our lives with this unity and passion that we’ve developed here at Piedmont High School. Let’s not be that apathetic, meme-obsessed, social-media generation that those in Washington and Wall Street think we are. We aren’t new to creating change. We’ve done it before, and looking out at you guys right now, I’m optimistic that we can do it again. PHS co-Salutatorian Jacob Hsia, who will be attending Washington University in St. Louis in the fall, delivered an impassioned speech at graduation. Bill Jeng, the father of Salutatorian Wesley Jeng, proudly holds a bigger-than-life poster in the Witter Field stands.

He spoke of taking a job to fight gun violence at the behest of President Clinton, sacrificing career aspirations and family time for a greater good. The speech garnered the largest applause and cheers of the afternoon and a standing ovation lasting minutes. As diplomas were handed to the graduates, with audience members cheering for each and every graduaate, students took their final steps as a high schooler, grabbed their diploma, shook Littlefield’s hand and walked into a new chapter in their lives. The dash is on as the class of 2022 ditch their high heels to run after the graduation ceremony. Leaving years of frustration and isolation from the pandemic, distance learning and four years of high school in their wake, the graduates leapt for joy, and hugged one another as their caps flew through the air. The grandstand emptied as family members flooded the field and Piedmont’s newest class of graduates, the 101st class, moved on to their next great adventures. articles.text: JACK STEIN Cross Country & Track Jack Stein did what no other PHS athlete has done in nearly 20 years, breaking two well established school records in track. He is now the school’s all-time record holder in the 1600 and 3200 meters. He won the Double Crown this spring at the WACC Track Championship on May 5, setting new records of 9:24.12 in the 3200 meters, and 4:21.01 in the 1600 meters. Last fall he was named WACC Cross Country Runner of the Year award by winning the league championship on November 6 with a time of 18:38.6. He set a new school record in the 3200 on April 9 at the Arcadia Invitational with a time of 9:12.62, five seconds faster than Steve Brown’s time in 1994. Piedmont’s top five times in the 3200: Jack Stein, 9:12.62 (2022) Steve Brown, 9:17.71 (1994) Tom Phelps, 9:35.72 (2000) Carl Moren, 9:38.60 (1998) Crosby Freeman, 9:39.8 (2001) His record time in the 1600 came one week earlier at the prestigious Stanford Invitational on April 2, clocking a 4:14.77, eclipsing Tom Phelps’ 2001 time in 2001 by a mere .15 of a second. Top-five times in the 1600 Jack Stein, 4:14.77 (2022) Tom Phelps, 4:14.92 (2001) Mark Ceraldi, 4:17.40 (2005) Cooper Downing, 4:17.85 (2022) Will Sanford, 4:23.65 (2001) In the fall, Stein led the cross-country team on November 6 to the League title with a winning time of 15:34.76, 21 seconds ahead of second-place David Song of Alameda. He went on to the NCS Championship at Hayward on November 20, where he was 2nd to place second of 144 runners with a time of 15:29.4, which eclipsed Reece Proctor’s 2016 course record at Hayward High by three seconds. The boys’ cross-country team placed third of 19 schools to qualify for the CIF State Championship at Woodward Park. At the State meet on November 27, Stein placed 12th of 209 runners in 15:43.4. He will continue his running career at Pomona College in the fall. Staff Photo PARKER TERRILL Track and Field Parker Terrill burst onto the scene this spring to make school history in multiple events and multiple times as a pole vaulter, sprinter, and decathlete. He’s the school’s all-time record holder in the pole vault, ran the anchor leg on the record-setting 4x400 relay team, and was the school’s first athlete to compete in the decathlon in more than 30 years. Terrill broke the pole vault record three times during the season after initially setting a new record of 14-feet, 2-inches on March 5 at the Clayton Valley Relays. He cleared 15-feet, 5-inches at the Castro Valley Ellie Black earns our 2022 Athlete of the Year after a historic cross country and track season. Invitational on March 26, vaulted 15-7 at a league meet on April 21, and shattered all previous school records on May 28 by clearing 16- feet, 1-inch at the State Championships in Clovis. Piedmont’s top-five all-time pole vault records Parker Terrill, 16 feet, 1 inch (2022) Marshall Wentworth, 14 feet (2011) Irving Moore, 13 feet (1940) Alex Harrison, 12 feet, 7 inches (2016) John Hind, 12 feet, 6 inches (1957) In the 4x400 relay, Terrill made more history by helping teammates Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Parker Long set a school record in the 4x400 meters of 3:21.77, breaking a record set 33 years ago by a team led by Piedmont Hall of Fame runner Gordon Johnson. Competing at the Del Campo Decathlon on April 16, Terrill posted the second-highest decathlon score in the U.S. with 5,964 points. He recorded a winning pole vault of 13-feet, 6-inches and notched personal best performances in five other events, the 400, 1500, shot put, high jump, and long jump. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco presents its newest exhibition, Still Lives in Contemporary Art, now through August 12. The exhibition brings together an international group of artists who have unique takes on contemporary art and still life. Each artist has created a work within a framework of Black diasporic identities and histories. The featured artists include Sadie Barnette, LaKela Brown, Elizabeth Colomba, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, David Antonio Cruz, Awol Erizku, Leslie Hewitt, Yashua Klos, Deana Lawson, Azikiwe Mohammed, Rashaad Newsome, Toyin Ojih Odutola, Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Devan Shimoyama, William Villalongo, and Brittney Leeanne Williams. articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present Mozart’s Don Giovanni now through July 2. Don Giovanni, part three of the Mozart-Da Ponte Trilogy, is a dark comedy with a horrific twist ending. The action takes place in Seville and spans 24 hours, following the story of two women set off to confront a notorious libertine. It is an opera in two acts based on the legend of Don Juan; libretto is by Lorenzo Da Ponte. The opera is sung in Italian with English supertitles. Etienne Dupuis sings the title role, and Adela Zaharia is Donna Anna. Soprano Nicole Car will make her San Francisco operatic debut as Donna Elvira, replacing Carmen Giannattasio, who is recovering from surgery. “We are deeply saddened that Carmen is having to withdraw from the role of Donna Elvira this summer, and we wish her all good health as she continues her recovery,” said San Francisco Opera General Director Don Giovanni set design by Erhard Rom. Matthew Shilvock. “Carmen is a great friend of San Francisco Opera, having made such an incredible impact on our stage as Tosca in 2018. We and our audiences are eager for her return this summer.” “We are deeply grateful to Nicole Car for joining this new production, making her house debut a few weeks earlier than planned.” Car has performed on the stages of the Vienna State Opera, Paris Opera, Royal Opera House Covent Garden, Metropolitan Opera and Deutsche Oper Berlin. She was scheduled to make her first appearance with the company in San Francisco on June 30. She has performed the role of Donna Elvira on leading stages, including Paris Opera earlier this year in March. The opera is conducted by Bertrand de Billy and directed by Michael Cavanagh. To purchase tickets, visit h t t p s: // w w w. sfo p e r a .c o m / on-stage/don-giovanni/.
articles.title: SF Opera’s Don Giovanni in performance through July 2

articles.text: Music@Menlo returns this year with a special 20th anniversary, beginning July 14. Tickets Music@Menlo is an internationally acclaimed chamber music festival founded by David Finckel and Wu Han. Inaugurated in 2003 at Menlo School, the festival features concerts, lectures, and a training program for aspiring professional musicians. The festival’s mission is to engage and sustain an audience for chamber music that is programmed, presented, and performed at the highest level of artistic excellence. Concert programs are performed by a collection of the greatest chamber musicians around the world, provided in intimate settings at Menlo School and Spieker Center for the Arts. Visit https://musicatmenlo.org to purchase tickets and to view a list of announced artists and programs.

articles.text: The cast of a fully staged Oedipus Rex. San Francisco Symphony will perform fully staged performances of Stravinsky’s Oedipus Rex this weekend, June 10 through 12 at Davies Symphony Hall. Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen said, “ritual is at the very heart of Stravinsky’s craft.” Salonen and the Orchestra are joined by a cast of vocalists for the production, as well as the San Francisco Symphony Chorus, and legendary director Peter Sellars for this staged event. Oedipus Rex casts Sean Panikkar in the titular role; J’Nai Bridge as Jocasta, and Willard White as Creon. The production also casts tenor Jose Romero and actor Breezy Leigh. Tickets are available for Friday and Saturday, June 10-11, both at 7:30 p.m., and a performance on Sunday, June 12, at 2 p.m. Tickets are limited and can be purchased at https://www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2021-22/ S T R AV I N S K Y- S - O E D I - PUS-REX. ®

articles.text: The past 2-1/2 years have presented monumental problems artistically. For many, it was the kiss of death, but for others they saw it as an opportunity knocking at the door. In reality, the musical state of affairs remains unchanged. The target remains the pursuit of excellence, but the path has been changed. Logic tells us that we can quantify excellence. We do it in sports. Why not in music? I have made this analogy many times before. It is because musical art is a labyrinth of intangibles. In baseball, the home run is immutable. In art, nothing is immutable. Money, influence, and luck are helpful, but nothing replaces diligence and determination – combined with a large pinch of artistic intelligence. The pandemic has had a major impact on music worldwide, and some have benefited greatly. Let’s first examine their pursuit of excellence. I frequently turn to Ambrose Bierce’s magnum opus “The Devil’s Dictionary” for insight. There is a similar book, purportedly by Bierce, on music, in which he defines practice as “an unpleasant hour devoted to repeating your mistakes ad nauseam.” Bierce then defines a concert as “practicing in public.” Cynical as he may sound, his observations are not far from the mark. Those who equate excellence in music with excellence in sports should take heart. I appreciate both, but appreciate the tremendous differences. Playing all the notes that a composer writes doesn’t really impress me very much. Two musical friends come to mind. One is Jaume Torrent, who is well known to Piedmont audiences as an outstanding guitarist and composer. The other is Hungarian violinist Antal Zalai. Both of these musicians have a fantastic work ethic. Their philosophy of practice is exactly what Jascha Heifetz told me when I interviewed him. It goes something like this: “When I go into my practice room, the outside world ceases to exist.” During this very difficult time, Torrent has composed numerous original pieces and has recorded them. Zalai probably has more videos on the Internet than any other violinist anywhere. However, it is not just the industry of the musicians which is impressive, it is their artistic attainment. articles.text: It was a quiet afternoon in 2018 when Susan Freeman paused mid-sentence and asked, “Would you like to host some musicians for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival?” The question wasn’t entirely from left field. We had recently hosted eight members of the Afghan Girls Robotics Team in our home. Susan had been a part of that, taking the girls one day to explore San Francisco. Knowing how much we had enjoyed that experience, Susan suggested our family might also want to host musicians for the weeklong music festival, especially since our son was a budding cellist. We had not known of the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival (PCMF), which was founded in 2016 by Wayne Lee, a Piedmont native, and his wife, Juliana Han. Susan had been involved from the beginning as the indefatigable box office manager. Her passion for the festival was contagious. Just hearing her talk about it, one would think that the PCMF was one of Piedmont’s best kept secrets. And she was right. So began our ties with the festival. The honor of hosting worldclass musicians in our home was an unforgettable experience. Not only did we get to enjoy their music, but we got to know the personalities and lives behind their music-making. And what could beat the privilege of attending concerts in the intimacy of Piedmont Center for the Arts without driving across the bridge to the festival’s early success. Friends of Susan would like to raise funds to sponsor Friday’s concert, July 22, in her memory. The program for this concert features A Sanguine Clockwork, composed by Paul Wiancko, a celebrated composer and cellist. He is also a past featured performer at the festival during the years that Susan was an active volunteer. In reference to A Sanguine Clockwork, Wiancko states, “The title of this work refers to the intricate inner workings of the human body as well as the joyful interconnectedness of human beings on a much larger scale. A Sanguine Clockwork explores the relationship between the molecular and the cultural – that inexplicable science which links the sentiment of a well-loved folk song to the blood in our veins.” On July 22, we hope to celebrate the “joyful interconnectedness” that Susan brought to all of us. If you would like to join us in sponsoring the concert in Susan’s honor, please visit piedmontcmf. org and click on Support. You may specify that your donation be applied to the concert honoring Susan Freeman. To volunteer for the festival or to host musicians, contact Susan Chamberlain at susanchacha@ gmail.com. Tickets for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival are available at piedmontcmf.org. Concerts will be held July 20, 22, and 24. Following each concert is a reception and an opportunity to meet the musicians. Susan Freeman to Davies Symphony Hall? Parking, gas, and bridge toll combined were equivalent to the price of a PCMF ticket. Sadly, just two and a half years after introducing us to the festival, Susan passed away following a long but heroic battle with cancer. Susan’s mark can be found in so many facets of Piedmont. In fact, last year’s Turkey Trot was held in her memory, commemorating her 18 years of support. But perhaps Susan’s greatest legacy lies in the generations of youth who have benefited from her guidance in the college application process. For some students, she was as much life coach as counselor, helping them achieve not only success but, more importantly, happiness. For our family, she became a dear friend. From July 20-24 this summer the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival returns for its fifth season with the theme, “Human, Alone and Together.” It seems fitting to honor Susan’s contribution
articles.title: Piedmont Chamber Music Festival to honor Susan Freeman

articles.text: The annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only weeklong residency chamber music Festival in the East Bay, celebrates its fifth festival at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in a series of intimate concerts opening July 20. This season festival musicians will explore the theme “Human. Alone and Together” in works from composers old and new that remind us that life is better together. Led by founders Wayne Lee (violin) a Piedmont native, and his wife Juliana Han (piano), the festival features eight internationally acclaimed musicians from throughout the U.S. Returning musicians Jarmine Lin (violin) and Deborah Pae (cello), will be joined by guest musicians Teng Li (Principal Violinist, Los Angeles Philharmonic), Francisco Fullana (violin), Clancy Newman (cellist & composer), and Paul Laraia (viola). This Week’s Featured Artist First Prize winner of the 13th Lionel Tertis International Viola Competition and the 14th Sphinx Competition, violist Paul Laraia is enjoying the early stages of a multifaceted career as soloist, chamber musician, and new music advocate. Acclaimed for offering “long lines with lyricism and poise,” Paul has been soloist with the Pittsburgh Symphony, Atlanta Symphony, Filharmonica de Bogata, New Jersey SymPaul Laraia phony, Nashville Symphony, New Haven Symphony, San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, and St. Paul Chamber Orchestra. As a principal member of the internationally acclaimed Sejong Soloists and as the violist of the Grammy Award winning Catalyst Quartet, Paul has given hundreds of performances globally in venues such as Carnegie Hall’s Stern Auditorium, the Kennedy Center in DC, Seoul Arts Center, Moscow’s Tchaikovsky Hall, and Lincoln Center’s Great Performers Series. Tickets are $45, with a savings on season passes for all three concerts for $120. To reserve tickets now and for more information, including complete biographies of all musicians and details of the music program, visit the website: www.piedmontcmf.org. All public events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require photo ID and valid proof of full vaccination including booster shot for entry, as well as proper masking while inside. Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue in Piedmont.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 8, 2022 19 Piedmont Chamber Music Festival to honor Susan Freeman By Eliza and Doug Chin It was a quiet afternoon in 2018 when Susan Freeman paused mid-sentence and asked, “Would you like to host some musicians for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival?” The question wasn’t entirely from left field. We had recently hosted eight members of the Afghan Girls Robotics Team in our home. Susan had been a part of that, taking the girls one day to explore San Francisco. Knowing how much we had enjoyed that experience, Susan suggested our family might also want to host musicians for the weeklong music festival, especially since our son was a budding cellist. We had not known of the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival (PCMF), which was founded in 2016 by Wayne Lee, a Piedmont native, and his wife, Juliana Han. Susan had been involved from the beginning as the indefatigable box office manager. Her passion for the festival was contagious. Just hearing her talk about it, one would think that the PCMF was one of Piedmont’s best kept secrets. And she was right. So began our ties with the festival. The honor of hosting worldclass musicians in our home was an unforgettable experience. Not only did we get to enjoy their music, but we got to know the personalities and lives behind their music-making. And what could beat the privilege of attending concerts in the intimacy of Piedmont Center for the Arts without driving across the bridge to the festival’s early success. Friends of Susan would like to raise funds to sponsor Friday’s concert, July 22, in her memory. The program for this concert features A Sanguine Clockwork, composed by Paul Wiancko, a celebrated composer and cellist. He is also a past featured performer at the festival during the years that Susan was an active volunteer. In reference to A Sanguine Clockwork, Wiancko states, “The title of this work refers to the intricate inner workings of the human body as well as the joyful interconnectedness of human beings on a much larger scale. A Sanguine Clockwork explores the relationship between the molecular and the cultural – that inexplicable science which links the sentiment of a well-loved folk song to the blood in our veins.” On July 22, we hope to celebrate the “joyful interconnectedness” that Susan brought to all of us. If you would like to join us in sponsoring the concert in Susan’s honor, please visit piedmontcmf. org and click on Support. You may specify that your donation be applied to the concert honoring Susan Freeman. To volunteer for the festival or to host musicians, contact Susan Chamberlain at susanchacha@ gmail.com. Tickets for the Piedmont Chamber Music Festival are available at piedmontcmf.org. Concerts will be held July 20, 22, and 24. Following each concert is a reception and an opportunity to meet the musicians. articles.text: A scene from Sofia Coppola’s film, The Beguiled. The Beguiled, released in 2017, opens with a young girl Amy (Oona Laurence), walking among the moss-covered trees of an aging southern estate. It’s 1864, one year before the end of the Civil War. The place is rural Virginia. She is humming to herself and in the distance is the hollow sound of cannon fire. Abruptly she comes upon a wounded union solder lying against a tree. His leg is bloodied and he can’t move. She agrees to help him back to the mansion of her all-girls’ school for southern belles, a place where they are waiting out the war, trying to carry on, though they know that the Union soldiers are slowly advancing. Amy, helping the soldier, corporal John McBurney (Colin Farrell), stops to ring a bell near a tall iron gate and then waits for help from head mistress, Martha Farnsworth (Nicole Kidman), and her charges, to include teacher Edwina Dabney (Kirsten Dunst). The presence of the corporal presents a dilemma. They can turn him over to the Confederate soldiers that often pass the school, or, as Mistress Farnsworth opines, they can do the Christian thing and clean and stitch his wound, give him time to heal, before turning him over to the Confederate army. They all agree that they should do the latter and it is that decision that changes in all ways, both subtle and obvious, the delicate balance of the school and its students. At first all is rigid decorum, the females in their high neck dresses, sitting down to their dinners served on fine china, candlelight giving a soft glow, their manners polite. During the day they labor in the garden. But gradually, like moths to a flame, the young women are pulled to McBurney’s room where he lies waiting to mend. As he meets each one, he is struck by his good fortune, his lyrical Irish brogue complementing each with a deft touch of kind words and seemingly sincere interest. Gradually the school environment, at first cool and suspicious of this enemy soldier, turns into a Southern hothouse of obsession and irresistible lust, expressed initially as a disguised formality but ultimately as something else entirely. What McBurney doesn’t realize is that it is not he who is spinning a web to ensnare the inhabitants of this seemingly benign school, but it is he who is the butterfly, pulled into their insulated, lonely world and caught, absent his awareness. While there is a war being fought over slavery just beyond the compound, and all of the slaves that once resided on the Farnsworth plantation have left, this film is not about the issues that perpetuated the war. Rather it is a study of characters, each one of them interpreting McBurney’s presence in her own way. That is the essence of what co-writer and director Sofia Coppola chose to make, one she manages very nicely with a superb ensemble. The Beguiled, Starring Colin Farrell, Nicole Kidman and Kirsten Dunst. Directed by Sofia Coppola. 1 hr., 53 min. Rated R. Released in 2017. articles.text: Kate Maberly, Andrew Knott and Heydon Prowse in The Secret Garden. The Secret Garden, released in 1993, is a family-friendly film. Adapted from the classic book of the same name, and written by Frances Hodgson Burnett in 1911. For more than a century it has been embraced by generations of young readers. As a movie, it is a visual delight, created by the same filmmakers responsible for the equally extraordinary Black Stallion. The story focuses on 10-yearold Mary Lennox (Kate Maberly), an unsmiling British girl, orphaned while living in India. Tragically, her parents died in an earthquake, and she is sent to live with her uncle, Lord Craven (John Lynch), at his bleak manor called Misselthwaite. A widower, heartbroken, he has spent a decade reclusively mourning the death of his wife. Upon her arrival, Mary realizes that she will be looked after by the manor’s strict and unsympathetic housekeeper, Mrs. Medlock (Maggie Smith). Mary is taken to her room and admonished not to wander about. Of course, curious, she discovers countless narrow passageways and musty rooms, the sparse furniture covered with dusty sheets. To her surprise, she discovers a musty, dark room with its curtains closed inhabited by her 10-year-old cousin, Colin Craven (Heydon Prowse). The boy is Lord Craven’s bedridden son who is treated like a fragile invalid. He is short-tempered, indulged by the house staff, and ever demanding. He never leaves his room and believes that the world outside is filled with dangerous “spores.” Continuing her exploration of the manor and then its grounds, Mary discovers a long-neglected walled-in garden. Using a large key that she found in one of the rooms, she opens an ivy-covered door, only to find the trees and plants brittle and brown. By chance she also meets another boy, Dickon Sowerby (Andrew Knott), similar in age, who is the younger brother of one the housemaids, Martha (Laura Crossley). He is a free spirit and believes he can talk to animals. Together, they begin to restore the secret garden. At the same time Mary begins the process of convincing the recalcitrant Colin that he can indeed venture outside and be unharmed. Soon, along with Dickon, she takes him to see the hidden sanctuary where Colin, along with the garden, begins the magical journey of restoration. He is soon standing on unsteady legs and taking tentative steps. Of course, the garden is a metaphor. At the outset it is a symbol of sadness and loss. But as it changes – flowers bloom, the trees turn green, birds return – the stark sadness of the manor lifts. The three children, and Lord Craven as well, are transformed, which eventually leads to a heartwarming conclusion. The Secret Garden. Directed by Agnieszka Holland. Starring Kate Maberly, Heydon Prowse, and Maggie Smith. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated G. Released in 1993. Now streaming on HBO/VUDU/Apple TV.
