articles.text: Kelly Reno stars in The Black Stallion. The Black Stallion, released in 1979, and adapted from the classic 1941 children’s book written by Walter Farley, is a breathtakingly beautiful film, timeless and filled with innocent wonder. The story begins somewhere off the coast of Africa. Pre-teen Alec Ramsey (Kelly Reno) and his father (Hoyt Axon) are travelling north on a steamer. It is the summer of 1946. As Alec boards the ship, he pauses to watch a group of men trying to subdue a magnificent black Arabian stallion and get it into a stable. Later that night, Alec, sound asleep, is thrown out of his bunk by an explosion, caused by a fire in the engine room. The ship is sinking. Alec’s first thought is of the horse and he runs topside and frees the stallion, which jumps over the railing into the ocean. Alec is swept overboard by a crashing wave. Later, in the early morning, he finds himself lying on a sandy beach. Uncertain where he is, still dressed in his pajamas, he begins to explore what proves to be a deserted island. To his surprise, he encounters the black horse, its harness snagged in the rocks. Using a pocketknife given to him by his father the evening before the fire, he manages to cut the horse free and the stallion races off. Using the knife, Alec learns to fish and finds that seaweed is edible. He often spots the stallion, which he names “The Black,” running along the beach. Gathering some seaweed in a large frond, he places it at the water’s edge and waits. Curious and hungry, the horse tentatively approaches the seaweed. Before long The Black is eating from Alec’s hand, and so the two fashion a bond. Soon Alec is riding the stallion across the stretching sand, creating a kind of poetry as the boy and horse become one. Weeks pass, and unexpectedly a fishing boat anchors just off shore and Alec and the horse are both rescued. Together they return to America and to the boy’s mother (Teri Garr), now widowed. The Black is kept in their fenced-in back yard; however, it soon escapes through an open gate and gallops through town. Alec, desperate to find the horse, finally finds him in an old barn owned by Henry Dailey (Mickey Rooney). And so act three begins. Alec discovers that Henry was once a jockey and trainer. Henry soon comes to realize how extraordinary The Black is, having remarkable speed. The idea comes to Henry to enter the stallion in a much publicized match race, and so they begin to prepare, Henry teaching Alec to ride like a jockey while exercising The Black on an oval racetrack. Of course, the story is familiar, reminding us of the classic film National Velvet, also starring Mickey Rooney. Naturally, The Black Stallion will have an exciting conclusion, and kids of all ages will be captivated by what proves to be wonderful fable. The Black Stallion. Directed by Carroll Ballard. Starring Kelly Reno, Mickey Rooney, and Teri Garr. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated G. Released in 1979. Now screening on VUDU/Netflix/Prime.

pages.text: Wednesday, June 8, 2022 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS The Secret Garden a timeless treasure The Black Stallion – timeless, breathtaking Kate Maberly, Andrew Knott and Heydon Prowse in The Secret Garden. By Chris Honoré The Secret Garden, released in 1993, is a family-friendly film. Adapted from the classic book of the same name, and written by Frances Hodgson Burnett in 1911. For more than a century it has been embraced by generations of young readers. As a movie, it is a visual delight, created by the same filmmakers responsible for the equally extraordinary Black Stallion. The story focuses on 10-yearold Mary Lennox (Kate Maberly), an unsmiling British girl, orphaned while living in India. Tragically, her parents died in an earthquake, and she is sent to live with her uncle, Lord Craven (John Lynch), at his bleak manor called Misselthwaite. A widower, heartbroken, he has spent a decade reclusively mourning the death of his wife. Upon her arrival, Mary realizes that she will be looked after by the manor’s strict and unsympathetic housekeeper, Mrs. Medlock (Maggie Smith). Mary is taken to her room and admonished not to wander about. Of course, curious, she discovers countless narrow passageways and musty rooms, the sparse furniture covered with dusty sheets. To her surprise, she discovers a musty, dark room with its curtains closed inhabited by her 10-year-old cousin, Colin Craven (Heydon Prowse). The boy is Lord Craven’s bedridden son who is treated like a fragile invalid. He is short-tempered, indulged by the house staff, and ever demanding. He never leaves his room and believes that the world outside is filled with dangerous “spores.” Continuing her exploration of the manor and then its grounds, Mary discovers a long-neglected walled-in garden. Using a large key that she found in one of the rooms, she opens an ivy-covered door, only to find the trees and plants brittle and brown. By chance she also meets another boy, Dickon Sowerby (Andrew Knott), similar in age, who is the younger brother of one the housemaids, Martha (Laura Crossley). He is a free spirit and believes he can talk to animals. Together, they begin to restore the secret garden. At the same time Mary begins the process of convincing the recalcitrant Colin that he can indeed venture outside and be unharmed. Soon, along with Dickon, she takes him to see the hidden sanctuary where Colin, along with the garden, begins the magical journey of restoration. He is soon standing on unsteady legs and taking tentative steps. Of course, the garden is a metaphor. At the outset it is a symbol of sadness and loss. But as it changes – flowers bloom, the trees turn green, birds return – the stark sadness of the manor lifts. The three children, and Lord Craven as well, are transformed, which eventually leads to a heartwarming conclusion. The Secret Garden. Directed by Agnieszka Holland. Starring Kate Maberly, Heydon Prowse, and Maggie Smith. 1 hr., 41 min. Rated G. Released in 1993. Now streaming on HBO/VUDU/Apple TV. Kelly Reno stars in The Black Stallion. By Chris Honoré The Black Stallion, released in 1979, and adapted from the classic 1941 children’s book written by Walter Farley, is a breathtakingly beautiful film, timeless and filled with innocent wonder. The story begins somewhere off the coast of Africa. Pre-teen Alec Ramsey (Kelly Reno) and his father (Hoyt Axon) are travelling north on a steamer. It is the summer of 1946. As Alec boards the ship, he pauses to watch a group of men trying to subdue a magnificent black Arabian stallion and get it into a stable. Later that night, Alec, sound asleep, is thrown out of his bunk by an explosion, caused by a fire in the engine room. The ship is sinking. Alec’s first thought is of the horse and he runs topside and frees the stallion, which jumps over the railing into the ocean. Alec is swept overboard by a crashing wave. Later, in the early morning, he finds himself lying on a sandy beach. To his surprise, he encounters the black horse, its harness snagged in the rocks. Using a pocketknife given to him by his father the evening before the fire, he manages to cut the horse free and the stallion races off. Using the knife, Alec learns to fish and finds that seaweed is edible. He often spots the stallion, which he names “The Black,” running along the beach. Gathering some seaweed in a large frond, he places it at the water’s edge and waits. Curious and hungry, the horse tentatively approaches the seaweed. Before long The Black is eating from Alec’s hand, and so the two fashion a bond. Soon Alec is riding the stallion across the stretching sand, creating a kind of poetry as the boy and horse become one. Weeks pass, and unexpectedly a fishing boat anchors just off shore and Alec and the horse are both rescued. Together they return to America and to the boy’s mother (Teri Garr), now widowed. The Black is kept in their fenced-in back yard; however, it soon escapes through an open gate and gallops through town. Alec, desperate to find the horse, finally finds him in an old barn owned by Henry Dailey (Mickey Rooney). And so act three begins. Alec discovers that Henry was once a jockey and trainer. Henry soon comes to realize how extraordinary The Black is, having remarkable speed. The idea comes to Henry to enter the stallion in a much publicized match race, and so they begin to prepare, Henry teaching Alec to ride like a jockey while exercising The Black on an oval racetrack. Of course, the story is familiar, reminding us of the classic film National Velvet, also starring Mickey Rooney. Naturally, The Black Stallion will have an exciting conclusion, and kids of all ages will be captivated by what proves to be wonderful fable. The Black Stallion. Directed by Carroll Ballard. Starring Kelly Reno, Mickey Rooney, and Teri Garr. 1 hr., 58 min. Rated G. Released in 1979. Now screening on VUDU/Netflix/Prime.

articles.text: We have a joke at the LMB Interiors studio that I would wallpaper the world if I could. This passion is born out of a childhood experience. Often, the wounds of our past transform into gifts. Whether it’s a broken heart, selfharm through narrow-minded thinking, family contention, or trauma done unto us either purposely or unwittingly, we can recognize how these ultimately enhance our own growth and purpose if we are willing to inquire within. Such was the case when my beloved mother decorated our childhood home, and applied a wallpaper in her bedroom that was wrong in every way. Since starting my business 20 years ago, I’ve been on a mission to beautify interiors and apply gorgeous wallcoverings – the right way – to every powder room, bookcase, wall, or ceiling I can get my hands on. It’s not just my mom who made design mistakes. I’ve certainly looked back on some of the choices I made in my early years as a professional designer and thought, “I’ll never do that again.” My mom didn’t have the luxury of do-overs, though. As a professional, I get to fix my mistakes (at my own expense). She didn’t have the resources for that. If she did, she might have reconsidered her wallpaper choice. I was 11 years old and already noticing details in my interior environment. My parents were building a home on a property my dad inherited from his mom in a woodsy neighborhood near Lake Sawyer in Black Diamond, Washington. I was enthusiastic Photo by Sen Creative The boldness of this powder room was made possible with elegant wallcovering by Phillip Jeffries. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, June 8, 2022 Features Not your mother’s wallpaper By Laura Martin Bovard We have a joke at the LMB Interiors studio that I would wallpaper the world if I could. This passion is born out of a childhood experience. Often, the wounds of our past transform into gifts. Whether it’s a broken heart, selfharm through narrow-minded thinking, family contention, or trauma done unto us either purposely or unwittingly, we can recognize how these ultimately enhance our own growth and purpose if we are willing to inquire within. Such was the case when my beloved mother decorated our childhood home, and applied a wallpaper in her bedroom that was wrong in every way. Since starting my business 20 years ago, I’ve been on a mission to beautify interiors and apply gorgeous wallcoverings – the right way – to every powder room, bookcase, wall, or ceiling I can get my hands on. It’s not just my mom who made design mistakes. I’ve certainly looked back on some of the choices I made in my early years as a professional designer and thought, “I’ll never do that again.” My mom didn’t have the luxury of do-overs, though. As a professional, I get to fix my mistakes (at my own expense). She didn’t have the resources for that. If she did, she might have reconsidered her wallpaper choice. I was 11 years old and already noticing details in my interior environment. My parents were building a home on a property my dad inherited from his mom in a woodsy neighborhood near Lake Sawyer in Black Diamond, Washington. I was enthusiastic Photo by Sen Creative The boldness of this powder room was made possible with elegant wallcovering by Phillip Jeffries. Photo by Mo Saito This patterned wallpaper from Cowtan and Tout felt like a risk to the client at first. Now she will tell you it turned out to be one of her favorite elements of the room. and eager to help choose the finishes. The closest design center was a JC Penny in Kent, so we drove there one day to make some selections for our new home. This included deciding on the wallpaper for my parents’ bedroom. I recall vividly flipping through the giant book of designs and being mesmerized by all the options. I flipped through the oversized pages one after another, envisioning how beautiful each one could be. Behind me, I heard my mother take in an excited breath. “That’s the one!” she said. Beauty is in the eye of the beholder, and in her eye, it was a silver, reflective landscape that appeared to me like a plantation home painted by a color-blind novice. I couldn’t see what she saw, but she loved it, and so off we went with our sample. It was bad enough that the wallpaper was atrocious. To make matters worse, she applied it incorrectly so the pattern lined up horizontally rather than staggered as it was designed to be. I learned early on the importance of hiring trades people who are skilled in their craft. For the rest of my childhood, I bore witness to that decision. (Side note: this is further evidence for why it is so important to have a reliable sounding board via your friend with excellent taste or an interior designer). As I previously mentioned, within every wound is a gift to be discovered. This experience was no exception. I swore if I ever got to choose wallpaper in my life, I would do so exquisitely and thoughtfully. So thank you, Mom. I am so grateful that you exposed me to appreciating the fine art of making home so I could grow up and do it for others. Here are a few of our projects where we installed wallpaper to beautify spaces. To all the skeptics who complain it’s hard to remove, I offer you this. Two days of scraping 10 years from now is well worth the enjoyment you’ll experience until you find a wallpaper you love even more, or new homeowners decide to replace it. Plus, modern wallpapers are easier to remove, and the amount of options these days is beyond belief. Life is short – let’s make it beautiful! Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. The firm has garnered numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s most sought after interior design agencies. articles.text: Photos by Reenie Raschke Delicious food is central to the Montclair Beer, Wine & Music Festival. The Montclair Village Association has announced that the 8th annual Montclair Beer, Wine & Music Festival returns to Montclair Village on Saturday, June 18 from 12-6 p.m. This beloved outdoor celebration, the largest of the year in the village, will be live this summer after an absence of two years due to Covid-19. No surprise: the community is buzzing with anticipation. Featured will be live performances by local bands: • Andre Thierry and his Accordion Soul Music (12 p.m.) • Citizens Jazz (1:45 p.m.) • Wolf Jett (3:15 p.m.) • Mio Flores and his Latin Jazz All-tars (4:45 p.m.) Other free family-friendly features include: • Innovative pedal-powered sound system provided by Rock the Bike • Play Palooza Fun Zone with Oakland Fire Department’s parade rig. Includes bubbles, face painting, crafting, chalk drawing, hula hoops, giant puppets, the Montera School Cheer Squad, and festival food favorites. • The event also marks the launch of the Montclair Cares Club (MCC) to ensure more outdoor events occur in Montclair Village year-round. For wine and beer lovers, an Unlimited Tasting Package ($35 in advance / $40 at the door) includes a commemorative glass and more than 40 craft beers and artisan wines. One free tasting package is offered upon enrollment in the Montclair Cares Club ($120 for 12 months). Proceeds from the Festival will benefit the non-profit Montclair Village Association, which has served the Montclair Village business district and surrounding community for almost 75 years. Ample parking will be available in the Montclair Parking Garage at 6235 La Salle Ave. Sponsors include Bay Alarm, Crown Wines & Spirits, CRUfit, F & M Bank. Farmstead Cheeses & Wines, Meet Your Core Pilates, Mister Beever’s Paws & Claws, Montclair Sports Tennis, Orange Theory Fitness, Red Oak Realty, Village Chiropractic & Wellness Center and Winter Williams Presents. For full event details and to purchase tasting packages, become Vendor and/or Volunteer, visit MontclairVillage.com. A Zydeco band peerforms for a crowd in 2019.

articles.text: One of my favorite things to do when on vacation in France is to visit the local charcuterie shop. I am always amazed by the wonderful variety of products available, many of which are unknown in the U.S. There will often be 10 types of pate, goose, duck and pork rilliettes, tons of different types of salami, confit of goose and duck, foie gras of various sorts – an amazing panoply of meaty goodness. Over the years of travel to France, I realized you do not even have to find a charcuterie shop to locate these products. Any good French Supermarche, like Leclerc, Casino, Intermarche, or Carrefour, will have a long charcuterie counter where you can purchase the same quality of products that you find in the small shops. After years of smuggling home pate and rillettes in my suitcase, I was amazed and delighted to discover the wonderful Fabrique Delices here in he East Bay. It was a dream come true – a company started by French entrepreneurs to create French-style charcuterie in America. On top of that it was nearby in Hayward. The company began in 1920 in Meaux, France and was called SAPAR. It became the leading producer of pates in Europe, with its products carried by Fauchon in Paris as well as gourmet stores all over Europe. In 1985 Jean Claude Auge decided to establish Fabrique Delices and bring French charcuterie to the American market. The idea was to produce products of outstanding and consistent quality with unique and eye-catching presentations. In 1996 Marc Poinsignon and Antonio Pinheiro were brought from France to oversee the U.S. subsidiary. In 2002 Fabrique Delices moved into a newly built plant in Hayward, and today it is the largest producer of French charcuterie in America. I reached out to Fabrique Delices president Sebastien EspiDuck Rilletes nasse about the idea of throwing a dinner party to highlight some of their products. He loved the idea, so I recruited my Kensington Road neighbors Mike, Drennen, Jennifer, Jason, Megan, Ittai, and Margaret to be my guinea pigs. We started with the duck and pork rillettes. Most Americans know about pate, but not many know rillettes which are very popular in France. Every charcuterie place has big bowls of duck, goose and pork rillettes which they scoop out for you. It is basically moist meat mixed with extra fat which gives it an incredibly rich taste. You spread it on crusty French bread and finish with a tart cornichon pickle to cut the fat. Both types of rillettes were good, but the nod went to the duck. There was something almost decadent about spreading this essence of duck on bread. We progressed to the salumi course, which featured Dry Coppa, Wild Boar Salami and Black Truffle Salami. The Coppa was a large 6-inch diameter log of fat marbled meat similar to what you might find in an Italian deli. It was tasty and well received but I found its girth made it difficult to slice thin enough with just a knife. The Wild Boar salami was very intense and dark. The label said it was made from feral pigs (where do you get those?) and it did have a sort of “wild” taste. It was really great, especially with a piece of Conte cheese and some bread, but by far the favorite salami was the Black truffle. Considering how expensive they are, I did not expect it to really have that much truffle flavor. But was I wrong. This salami Fabrique Delices in Hayward offers 10 types of pate, goose, duck and pork rilliettes, different types of salami, confit of goose and duck, and foie gras of various sorts.
articles.title: Fabrique Delices – the taste of France in Hayward

pages.text: Wednesday, June 8, 2022 23 The Wine Corner Fabrique Delices – the taste of France in Hayward By Pierre DuMont One of my favorite things to do when on vacation in France is to visit the local charcuterie shop. I am always amazed by the wonderful variety of products available, many of which are unknown in the U.S. There will often be 10 types of pate, goose, duck and pork rilliettes, tons of different types of salami, confit of goose and duck, foie gras of various sorts – an amazing panoply of meaty goodness. Over the years of travel to France, I realized you do not even have to find a charcuterie shop to locate these products. Any good French Supermarche, like Leclerc, Casino, Intermarche, or Carrefour, will have a long charcuterie counter where you can purchase the same quality of products that you find in the small shops. After years of smuggling home pate and rillettes in my suitcase, I was amazed and delighted to discover the wonderful Fabrique Delices here in he East Bay. It was a dream come true – a company started by French entrepreneurs to create French-style charcuterie in America. On top of that it was nearby in Hayward. The company began in 1920 in Meaux, France and was called SAPAR. It became the leading producer of pates in Europe, with its products carried by Fauchon in Paris as well as gourmet stores all over Europe. In 1985 Jean Claude Auge decided to establish Fabrique Delices and bring French charcuterie to the American market. The idea was to produce products of outstanding and consistent quality with unique and eye-catching presentations. In 1996 Marc Poinsignon and Antonio Pinheiro were brought from France to oversee the U.S. subsidiary. In 2002 Fabrique Delices moved into a newly built plant in Hayward, and today it is the largest producer of French charcuterie in America. I reached out to Fabrique Delices president Sebastien EspiDuck Rilletes nasse about the idea of throwing a dinner party to highlight some of their products. He loved the idea, so I recruited my Kensington Road neighbors Mike, Drennen, Jennifer, Jason, Megan, Ittai, and Margaret to be my guinea pigs. We started with the duck and pork rillettes. Most Americans know about pate, but not many know rillettes which are very popular in France. Every charcuterie place has big bowls of duck, goose and pork rillettes which they scoop out for you. It is basically moist meat mixed with extra fat which gives it an incredibly rich taste. You spread it on crusty French bread and finish with a tart cornichon pickle to cut the fat. Both types of rillettes were good, but the nod went to the duck. There was something almost decadent about spreading this essence of duck on bread. We progressed to the salumi course, which featured Dry Coppa, Wild Boar Salami and Black Truffle Salami. The Coppa was a large 6-inch diameter log of fat marbled meat similar to what you might find in an Italian deli. It was tasty and well received but I found its girth made it difficult to slice thin enough with just a knife. The Wild Boar salami was very intense and dark. The label said it was made from feral pigs (where do you get those?) and it did have a sort of “wild” taste. It was really great, especially with a piece of Conte cheese and some bread, but by far the favorite salami was the Black truffle. Considering how expensive they are, I did not expect it to really have that much truffle flavor. But was I wrong. This salami was heavily flecked with black truffles which gave a distinctive, enchanting, almost indescribable nose that makes truffles so highly coveted. This stuff was addictive, and the slices flew off the platter. We took a break from the meats with our pasta course. Fabrique Delices makes both black truffle butter and white truffle butter. There is something magical to me about the aroma of truffles. Buying a real truffle costs an arm and a leg, so for most of us mere mortals the easiest way to access truffle magic is with truffle butter. We cooked up a box of penne and basted it in the tub of truffle butter, which was more than enough for that amount of pasta. Adding a ton of coarse ground Tellicherry black pepper and you have a simple, delicious hit on your hands. Back to duck land with the smoked duck breast and the duck sausage with figs. The smoked duck was unctuously good with the deep flavor and richness of a fine jambon Iberico. The duck sausage with figs was a wonderful contrast of savory and sweet and a truly interesting combination. The evening’s coup de gras was the duck leg confit. FD sells these in packages of 1, 3 and 6 legs. Confit is the leg of a duck or goose cooked and then preserved in its own fat. In rural France this was a way of ensuring the family had meat during the lean months of winter. Today, it is a way of serving duck with absolutely no hassle. Because it’s already been cooked, all you do is heat up the legs under the broiler in the oven. After about 20 minutes the skin becomes crisp while the meat stays tender. You can use the duck legs in cassoulet, tear the meat off for use in pasta, or a salad, or do what we did – eat it plain. The Kensington gang agreed that there is something especially delicious about the meat of a duck that you just don’t get from chicken. And yes, we also had a salad and some cheese to balance out the meats. The wines of the evening were magnums of Morgon Beaujolais and Paul Jabuolet Parallel 45 Cotes du Rhone, both simple basic wines they drink in France with this kind of food. It was a wonderful evening of good food, good wine, and good friends. Congratulations to Fabrique Delice for replicating the French gastronomic experience here in America. For information, see Fabriquedelices.com. articles.text: Jim Wulfsberg, a longtime former Piedmont resident with a larger-than-life personality and a wide circle of friends, passed away on May 28, 2022 from metastatic ocular melanoma. He died peacefully in his home in Reno, Nevada surrounded by his dear wife and loving family. He was 78. Born Harold James Wulfsberg on May 24, 1944 in Long Beach, California, he was the son of Rudolf Einer Wulfsberg and Margaret Grace Adams Wulfsberg. He graduated from Woodrow Wilson High School as a football star and thespian, often commanding shared lead roles with his twin brother, Richard. Jim graduated from high school with highest honors and went on to graduate Summa Cum Laude from the University of Southern California. He completed his law degree at the University of California Berkeley at Boalt Hall School of Law in 1969. He was chairman at Wulfsberg, Reese & Colvig, where he practiced construction law representing a diverse clientele worldwide. Jim was known as a powerhouse litigator, often being referred to as a force of nature in the courtroom. Among his many talents, Jim was an outstanding athlete, competing in multiple marathons and triathlons over his illustrious career. At age 55, he won the Vine Man Ironman in his age group. Jim continued with his passion for running and cycling in beautiful locations around the world from Lake Tahoe to Tuscany. Spending quality time with his beautiful wife, Janet, his loving family, and dear friends was paramount to Jim. He squeezed every ounce of joy out of life and was a shining example of living Jim Wulfsberg life to the fullest. Jim is survived by his wife Janet, daughter Analisa, oldest son, Tyler and his wife Brittany, and his youngest son Todd and his wife Dianne. He is also survived by his brothers Richard and David Wulfsberg, sister Elaine Hutchinson, and by grandchildren Schuyler, Safira, Isabella, Addisyn, Ellison, Hannah, Lindyn and Alannah. Jim touched so many people all over the world but he made the greatest impact on the family that he leaves behind. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests making a memorial donation to any of the following charitable organizations: • The Navy SEAL Foundation: https://www.navysealfoundation.org • Tunnel to Towers Foundation: https://www.t2t.org • The Wounded Warrior Project: https://www.woundedwarriorproject.org The family will announce a memorial service at a later date.
articles.title: Piedmont’s Jim Wulfsberg dies at 78

articles.text: According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), an individual’s carbon footprint is the aggregate of activities — such as using electricity, driving a car, or disposing of waste — that cause greenhouse gas emissions. The EPA’s Carbon Footprint Calculator (https://www3.epa.gov/ carbon-footprint-calculator/) estimates your footprint in three areas: home energy, transportation, and waste, according to your location, habits, and personal choices. The calculator estimates greenhouse gas emissions, including carbon dioxide – the gas most commonly emitted by humans – and methane, nitrous oxide, and fluorinated gases. These gases are known to trap heat in the atmosphere and cause climate change, or what is also known as global warming. Much of our individual carbon footprint is the result of our consumption, commonly defined as the items which we purchase with the largest contributors including food, clothing, and other household items. In relation to food, summer means that many tasty fruits and vegetables are in season and available locally. Shopping for food that has been produced and grown within a closer geographic region can reduce “food miles” and as a result its carbon footprint. Another piece to consider is food waste, both at the grocery store and in your own home. When disposing of your food waste, you can reduce methane emissions by diverting food waste to a composting facility rather than a landfill. Finally, it’s important to stay hydrated this summer! Think twice about buying plastic water bottles and use a reusable water bottle instead. Another significant portion of an individual carbon footprint is emissions from both day-to-day and holiday travel. Opting for a stay-at-home vacation, or one that doesn’t require flying, can significantly reduce your personal or family carbon footprint. Emissions from domestic aviation alone have increased 17% since 1990, to account for 9% of greenhouse gas emissions from the U.S. transportation sector. Flights departing from airports in the United States and its territories are responsible for almost one-quarter of global passenger transport-related carbon emissions. Using shared or active transportation, like busses, trains, and bikes, can reduce the emitted greenhouse gas emissions from personal travel by more than one half. Plus, active transportation like biking and walking can be a fun summer activity to help you and your family get out of the house! Finally, energy and natural gas used within your home on a daily basis consist of one of the largest factors in calculating your individual carbon footprint. Replacing your HVAC and water heating systems with heat pump technology can result in at least three to four times more energy savings than gas appliances. While some local incentives, such as the TECH Clean California program, are currently exhausted of funding, other local programs can help electrify your home and reduce the amount of energy your home is using. Through the Bay Area Regional Energy Network (BayREN) Home+ Program, single-family homeowners are eligible for a wide range of incentives, from Heat Pump Water Heaters to Heat Pump HVAC systems, in addition to insulation, duct sealing or replacement, and more. articles.text: When I tell people the tale that as a Piedmont boy at age 12 in 1966, I possessed a young lad’s summer dream car in a stripped down shell of a red 1960 Vespa 400-they do not believe me. When I relive the events related to this magic car, they bring smiles and laughter 56 years later. Without this Polaroid photo, no one would ever believe the trouble we got into and the havoc caused when riding around Piedmont in this bare motorless mini, micro car. How does a young boy acquire such a rare vehicle and become envied by all the other young dreamers? Simple, you wander over to Nace Avenue, where you bump into your 18-year-old family friend who had blown the engine on his Vespa 400. He had just finished stripping the Vespa down to 4 wheels, brakes, emergency brake and steering. No doors, hoods, transmission, engine, glass, etc. With all of the parts removed, it weighed only about 350 pounds. So I asked Lowell if I could have the car, and he said yes. I just drove off on a cloud. The light weight of the car meant that three or four young 12-year-olds could easily push it all over town, in exchange for riding in it if you were lucky, – or maybe even driving it. We drove it over to Linda Beach playground and would take turns driving it down the asphalt pathway to the lower playground with several of us on it. We left with only minor mishaps. The next stop would be Piedmont Park and at the stores, now Wells Fargo Bank. Then it was onto Magnolia Avenue, where all of us took turns driving down the hill. What did the Police think about all of this? We talked with them, and since the car had no motor it fell into a gray area regarding possible citations. They requested only that we keep it on the sidewalk. We had the whole summer on our hands and could be seen in Mountain View Cemetery, and down by Lake Merritt. We would get up early in the morning with everyone waiting outside for the day’s adventure. Everywhere we went, other young groups pleaded for a ride or to drive it. People wanted to trade for it or buy it from us. We all have very fond memories of our Summer of 1966 and the one-of-a-kind Vespa 400. For a few short weeks we had magic on four wheels. For any doubters, just look at the photo and imagine. Piedmont resident Neil Teixeira at age 12 in front of the family home on Fairview Avenue.

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, June 8, 2022 Obituary Piedmont’s Jim Wulfsberg dies at 78 Jim Wulfsberg, a longtime former Piedmont resident with a larger-than-life personality and a wide circle of friends, passed away on May 28, 2022 from metastatic ocular melanoma. He died peacefully in his home in Reno, Nevada surrounded by his dear wife and loving family. He was 78. Born Harold James Wulfsberg on May 24, 1944 in Long Beach, California, he was the son of Rudolf Einer Wulfsberg and Margaret Grace Adams Wulfsberg. He graduated from Woodrow Wilson High School as a football star and thespian, often commanding shared lead roles with his twin brother, Richard. Jim graduated from high school with highest honors and went on to graduate Summa Cum Laude from the University of Southern California. He completed his law degree at the University of California Berkeley at Boalt Hall School of Law in 1969. He was chairman at Wulfsberg, Reese & Colvig, where he practiced construction law representing a diverse clientele worldwide. Jim was known as a powerhouse litigator, often being referred to as a force of nature in the courtroom. Among his many talents, Jim was an outstanding athlete, competing in multiple marathons and triathlons over his illustrious career. At age 55, he won the Vine Man Ironman in his age group. Jim continued with his passion for running and cycling in beautiful locations around the world from Lake Tahoe to Tuscany. Spending quality time with his beautiful wife, Janet, his loving family, and dear friends was paramount to Jim. He squeezed every ounce of joy out of life and was a shining example of living Jim Wulfsberg life to the fullest. Jim is survived by his wife Janet, daughter Analisa, oldest son, Tyler and his wife Brittany, and his youngest son Todd and his wife Dianne. He is also survived by his brothers Richard and David Wulfsberg, sister Elaine Hutchinson, and by grandchildren Schuyler, Safira, Isabella, Addisyn, Ellison, Hannah, Lindyn and Alannah. Jim touched so many people all over the world but he made the greatest impact on the family that he leaves behind. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests making a memorial donation to any of the following charitable organizations: • The Navy SEAL Foundation: https://www.navysealfoundation.org • Tunnel to Towers Foundation: https://www.t2t.org • The Wounded Warrior Project: https://www.woundedwarriorproject.org The family will announce a memorial service at a later date. READ IT IN THE POST By Annie Wensley According to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), an individual’s carbon footprint is the aggregate of activities — such as using electricity, driving a car, or disposing of waste — that cause greenhouse gas emissions. The EPA’s Carbon Footprint Calculator (https://www3.epa.gov/ carbon-footprint-calculator/) estimates your footprint in three areas: home energy, transportation, and waste, according to your location, habits, and personal choices. The calculator estimates greenhouse gas emissions, including carbon dioxide – the gas most commonly emitted by humans – and methane, nitrous oxide, and fluorinated gases. These gases are known to trap heat in the atmosphere and cause climate change, or what is also known as global warming. Much of our individual carbon footprint is the result of our consumption, commonly defined as the items which we purchase with the largest contributors including food, clothing, and other household items. In relation to food, summer means that many tasty fruits and vegetables are in season and available locally. Shopping for food that has been produced and grown within a closer geographic region can reduce “food miles” and as a result its carbon footprint. Another piece to consider is food waste, both at the grocery How to reduce your carbon footprint this summer store and in your own home. When disposing of your food waste, you can reduce methane emissions by diverting food waste to a composting facility rather than a landfill. Finally, it’s important to stay hydrated this summer! Think twice about buying plastic water bottles and use a reusable water bottle instead. Another significant portion of an individual carbon footprint is emissions from both day-to-day and holiday travel. Opting for a stay-at-home vacation, or one that doesn’t require flying, can significantly reduce your personal or family carbon footprint. Emissions from domestic aviation alone have increased 17% since 1990, to account for 9% of greenhouse gas emissions from the U.S. transportation sector. Flights departing from airports in the United States and its territories are responsible for almost one-quarter of global passenger transport-related carbon emissions. Using shared or active transportation, like busses, trains, and bikes, can reduce the emitted greenhouse gas emissions from personal travel by more than one half. Plus, active transportation like biking and walking can be a fun summer activity to help you and your family get out of the house! Finally, energy and natural gas used within your home on a daily basis consist of one of the largest factors in calculating your individual carbon footprint. Replacing your HVAC and water heating systems with heat pump technology can result in at least three to four times more energy savings than gas appliances. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Abe and Tamar Stein Edelson from Santa Fe, and Bev Mann from New Jersey. During the previous Wednesday walk, the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group took their second of Will Adams’ tour of Albert Farr-designed Piedmont homes, ending at the home of Dave and Nancy DeRoche where Farr once lived. The DeRoches welcomed the walkers for a visit and refreshments. Nancy also offered to take the group on a later tour of their upper Oakland Avenue neighborhood, which continues up to Blair and Scenic Avenues. The group happily accepted Nancy’s offer for their next walk, but they didn’t know what an additional treat it would be. The weather on June 1 was more than cooperating – a beautiful, warm Piedmont morning. There was a strong turnout of 35 walkers and one K-9. Before the tour It was announced that Phil Witte, a regular walker and a cartoonist with the Post, is having an exhibit of his cartoons at Dominican University in San Rafael opening June 18. Nancy announced that her tour would take the group past the Sutro mansion on Blair Avenue, She also announced that there is a tour of the gardens at the Shartsis home on Sunday, June 12. (More information is available at https://www.gardenconservancy.org/open-days/garden-directory/the-shartsis-gardens.) The area above Oakland Avenue was a bit of Bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters including Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there in some unique homes. Before them, Frank C. Havens and his nephew George Sterling were also important residents. Nancy led the walkers a house that might have been an early office for Havens, a real estate developer in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He partnered with Francis “Borax” Smith, a businessman who made his fortune in borax mining but also invested in real estate. He and Havens created the Realty Syndicate in 1895, which developed many of Oakland and Piedmont’s neighborhoods. The group continued uphill on on Blair Avenue where Nancy pointed out the top of a home hidden by other homes. She said it is the Sutro mansion (the Shartsis residence). The Sutro mansion with five gardens is behind it further up the hill, but is barely visible. Earler a much smaller, craftsman-style home was built there in 1876-77 by Joseph Worcester. This house has a special claim to fame. It was there that Jack London lived and wrote his classic novel, The Call of the Wild in 1902-03. The house has a cedar shake shingle exterior, and was enlarged after it was moved by adding a new first floor. London was a prominent part of the artist colony that occupied this part of Piedmont in the early 1900s. He was a free-spirited man who sailed to the Orient, drank freely, and had at least three important women in his life. The success of The Call of the Wild provided him with considerable wealth, and he built a separate home for first wife, Bessie, and two daughters, Joan and Becky, further up the hill on Scenic Avenue. He was building his own grand home in Glen Ellen, but it burned to the ground shortly before it was completed. Sadly, London died at age 40 from the continuing effects of a tropical disease that he contracted during his travels and his drinking. The group made their way down this narrow part of Scenic, and made their way home on Piedmont’s longest pedestrian pathway, the 281 stairs that connect Blair and Scenic. The group thanked Nancy for providing a wonderful tour of her historic neighborhood. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.n. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. articles.text: McCutcheon Construction The past couple of years have found most of us spending more time at home. For many this has been a way to reorient how we work and live. For others, being home has only highlighted what we don’t like about our property. If you’re looking to improve your living spaces, increase the value of your home to sell in the future at a higher value, here are some ideas to help you do just that with minimal effort. Utilizing spaces that are otherwise not used is a great place to start. Do you have a closet in your home collecting junk? Take that footage and connect it to an adjacent room to increase the living space. If the layout of your home isn’t serving your needs, combine two underutilized rooms into a grand larger room with more appeal. A qualified contractor can determine which walls are load-bearing and help you explore your options to create a more open living space. If you aren’t prepared to do a major remodel, minor changes can have a big impact on the aesthetics of your home. Using wallpaper or fresh, updated colors on walls, replacing countertops or tile, and refinishing rather than replacing cabinetry make big changes to your home without the expense of a major remodel. Wallpaper and matching wall switches creates glamour in a powder room. Recessed lighting and fresh paint update a classic room. Updating your lighting, by replacing ceiling and wall fixtures or installing recessed lighting, will have a powerful impact on your environment. Today’s lighting is more energy efficient, so you’ll also see the benefit on your monthly utility bill. Don’t forget the exterior of your home. Replacing your garage door with a more modern design can greatly increase the curb appeal of your home. Decking or a new patio will add extra living space as well as an interesting look and design to your property. Repairing cracks in your driveway, adding gravel to pathways and updating your landscaping complete the look. Many home buyers shop for move-in ready houses, so they don’t have to begin with major projects. If you decide to carry out remodeling to increase home value, bathroom remodeling, kitchen remodeling, and installation of decks and patios should be at the top of the list. Whether you are looking to do extensive or modest remodeling, a qualified contractor can help you prioritize to spend your dollars wisely. “Relying On Experience” is a new feature by McCutcheon Construction, Inc., an employee-owned company, highlighting the latest innovations and best practices of home remodeling. Founded by Michael McCutcheon in 1980 and proudly serving Piedmont and surrounding communities. articles.text: Notice is hereby given that the City Council of the City of Piedmont will conduct a public hearing on Monday, June 20, 2022, in Council Chambers, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA, to consider that the City Council direct staff to provide the Draft Housing Element for the 6th Cycle to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (“HCD”) for its 90-day review. State law requires cities to update their General Plan Housing Element. The City of Piedmont Draft Housing Element for the 6th Cycle (2023 - 2031) (“Draft Housing Element”) is part of the City’s General Plan and applies City-wide. The Draft Housing Element provides a plan for addressing housing needs over the next 8 years. The proposed Draft Housing Element has been developed to meet the State of California’s legal requirements, including the requirement to plan for the City’s share of the regional housing needs allocation (“RHNA”). The City of Piedmont is in the process of developing a programmatic and comprehensive Environmental Impact Report (“EIR”) in accordance with the California Environmental Quality Act for the Draft Housing Element. The EIR will be considered for certification in conjunction with the City’s final certification of the Housing Element. The Draft Housing Element is available for public review on the City’s web page at https://piedmont.ca.gov as well as https://piedmontishome.org. It is also available at City Hall, located at 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611, between the hours of 8:30 a.m. and 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday. On May 12, 2022, the Planning Commission recommended that the City Council direct staff to send the Draft Housing Element to HCD for its 90-day review. articles.text: On the last day of school, Thursday, June 2, Park View Avenue was closed off for a block party for kids in the neighborhood. A fifteen foot inflatable waterslide inhabited the street and kids quickly embraced the summer spirit. The block that runs below the PHS baseball Field and Wildwood’s lower playground epitomizes the Piedmont spirit. Even in the thick of the pandemic, in July of 2020, the block came together for the house decorating Fourth of July competition and won the Highland Spoon for “Best Quaranteam.” On Thursday, tables were set out in the street for food, and the Yeh family provided a slushie machine operated by daughter Coral Yeh and her friend MacKenzie Seto-Nguyen. With the street blocked off and reserved for fun, kids rode their bikes, scooters and big wheels. Even Piedmont Police Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz stopped by to say hello and hand out water balloons. Within hours of school letting out, students traded their backpacks and pencils for swim trunks and water guns. The special occasion was a welcome sight after 2-1/2 years of restrictions due to COVID-19. Kids celebrated making it through another year and the anticipation of what everyone hopes will be life back to normal this summer. A giant inflatable water slide pumped up the start of summer spirit on Park View Avenue. Coral Yeh (left) and MacKenzie Seto-Nguyen served slushies to the revelers at the block party. Park View Avenue hosted a day of fun for kids on the block Thursday, June 2 in the afternoon prior to high school graduation at nearby Witter Field. Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz stopped by to offer some water balloons. He is pictured with Annabelle Malione enjoying a slushie. Deer spotted in yard on lower piedmont.
articles.title: Last day of school block party celebrates arrival of summer

articles.text: Hundreds of Piedmont High School students participated in a walkout on Thursday, May 26 in response to the elementary school shooting in Uvalde, Texas two days earlier that left 19 school children and two adults dead. PHS juniors Eleanor Lavin, Odessa Dando and Aryana Fisher organized the protest event in coordination with Piedmont Students Demand Action, one of many chapters across the country. The walkout occurred at 9:00 a.m. as students gathered on the high school quad and made their way to Piedmont Park one block away. The 20-minute gathering began with a moment of silence, as students joined hands in solidarity, followed by Lavin and Dando giving brief speeches to the large crowd. “We are looking for recognition from the media and from lawmakers because nothing is PHS students held hands during a moment of solidarity with the victims of the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas on May 24. happening to protect us. As students we don’t have a voice, we can’t vote, we are not involved in the political process or having our voice heard diplomatically,” said Odessa Dando. Student leaders used social media to get the word out to the student body, and teacher Aaron Barlin sent an email to the entire school. Flyers were created and posted around the school within 24 hours of the mass shooting.
articles.title: Piedmont students stage walkout over gun violence

articles.text: On May 25, Piedmont School District Superintendent Randy Booker informed the community that anti-Semitic messages were drawn in chalk in the area behind the high school gymnasium. “Late [May 25] afternoon, Piedmont High School Administration was alerted to the discovery of a swastika and ‘Hitler’ written in chalk on the ground,” Booker said. “As a community, we denounce this act of anti-Semitism and any messages of hate that targets a group of people based on their culture, religion, race, ethnicity, ability, gender or gender expression, or sexual orientation. These actions have no place in our schools, district, or community and stand in direct opposition to the values we share as a society.” Although the investigation is ongoing and no more information has been made public, the event occurred nine days after the City proclaimed May as Jewish American Heritage month. “In recent years, Jewish Americans have increasingly experienced anti-Semitism, including but not limited to physical attacks, vandalism, verbal and physical harassment, and hateful comments posted on social media,” said Mayor Teddy Gray King at the proclamation signing on May 16. “Piedmonters share an obligation to condemn and combat anti-Semitism wherever it exists.” The city did not respond to request for comment. articles.text: On May 25, the Piedmont Police Depar tment (PPD) announced via social media that it will increase police presence in and around all Piedmont schools. The Instagram post referenced the mass shooting of 19 children and two adults at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas on May 24 - and stated, “we cannot be too cautious.” “We have asked staff to be in the area and on campus at random times. Normally, we only enter the school campuses when called for assistance. In discussions with PUSD staff, until the end of school, you will see more [police] on campus,” PPD Capt. Chris Monahan said. The police department will discuss summer school and police presence after graduation on June 2. The effort will be conducted principally by PPD Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz. On April 16, PPD posted on Instagram that a resident had advised officers of a student who made threatening comments about bringing a gun to campus and shooting people. At the time, police officers contacted the student and parents to investigate the threat and determine the accessibility of firearms to the alleged student. On May 27, Capt. Monahan explained that the infor mation was “unfounded.” The department “determined that the student did not have the means to carry out the threats at that time,” he said. The department declined to discuss the matter further, stating that “it is a juvenile medical issue.” Statement from school district Piedmont School District Superintendent Randy Booker sent an email to the community on May 24 regarding the mass shooting. “The safety and well-being of our students and staff remain our top priority. We are fortunate to partner with the Piedmont Police Department to provide training in our schools to educate staff and students in responding to an active shooter or other internal threat,” Booker said. “I would also ask your help in reminding students of the importance that if they ‘see something,’ to ‘say something.’”
articles.title: PPD increases officer presence on school campuses

articles.text: Editor: The following letter was presented to the Piedmont School Board recently. Dear School Board: I’ll be brief because we all have a lot of emails... and some of us have kids. Piedmont teachers need to be given a raise for two primary reasons. First, teachers are humans doing incredibly valuable work who deserve to be paid a decent wage. Secondly, the Piedmont schools and School District are suffering because it is difficult to attract and retain talented, dedicated teachers because (frankly) we don’t pay wages comparable to other communities like Piedmont, such as Palo Alto, or other communities full of highly educated, well-off folks (Communities that are not particularly diverse either ethnically or economically). Looking at salaries, Piedmont School District Salaries go from around $59,480 to $107,315, according to [published salary schedules], Palo Alto teacher salaries range from $71,484 to $146,979. I love Piedmont, but if I were a new teacher, I’d go to Palo Alto given the chance, wouldn’t you? As we’re focusing on wages, looking at the numbers Palo Alto teachers make between 20% and 37% more than Piedmont teachers with comparable experience. Given this lens, a COLA of 7.5% seems inadequate and indicates we should try to do better and thereby support our kids, our community, and the high property values that depend on our excellent school system. Many thanks for your work. Christina Paul is a Wildwood School parent.
articles.title: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR School Board needs to pay teachers more

articles.text: On Tuesday May 24, 2022 at Robb Elementary school in Udalve, Texas, an 18-year-old gunman opened fire, killing 19 students and two adults as well as injuring 17 others. The shooter was killed by responding officers. This “massacre” is unacceptable. What happened was wrong and it needs to change. “Stronger gun laws” some may say. No, I say. “Walk out protests” others declare. No, I say. Ninety percent of shooters will not be affected if stronger gun laws are passed. If some sick person wants to blow up a school, some laws aren’t going to stop them. As my dad says, ”A locked door keeps honest people out”. If things are going to change we need to change as a society. On Wednesday my teacher gathered us to talk about it. Choked up, he said. “We should never start thinking something like this is normal.” We are starting to think that things like this happen and we are starting to think that it’s going to happen again and we can’t do anything. We can, but we need to do the right things. As a society we think charity is shameful and we sell lucky charms marshmallows separate from cereal (why?). The world is crazy. Let me introduce you to Salvador Rolando Ramos. He was an 18-year-old boy who was bullied and teased for his lisp. He was a loner with few friends and had a substance abusive mother. He was plagued by family dysfunction and mental health struggles. He was a high school dropout with mental health issues fascinated with guns. And then, eight days after he turned eighteen he entered a Robb elementary school with more rounds of ammo than a soldier going into battle would carry. He murdered 21 people, 19 of whom were elementary school students, injuring 17 others. This kid was messed up. He needed help – and love – all while his life literally crumbled apart. He would have been shamed for asking for help. So, let’s start with education and mental health awareness. Salvador Rolando Ramos dropped out of high school after the pandemic.
articles.title: Texas school shooting an American disgrace

articles.text: The following letter was sent recently to members of the Piedmont School Board. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, June 1, 2022 Opinion LETTERS TO THE EDITOR School Board needs to pay teachers more Editor: The following letter was presented to the Piedmont School Board recently. Dear School Board: I’ll be brief because we all have a lot of emails... and some of us have kids. Piedmont teachers need to be given a raise for two primary reasons. First, teachers are humans doing incredibly valuable work who deserve to be paid a decent wage. Secondly, the Piedmont schools and School District are suffering because it is difficult to attract and retain talented, dedicated teachers because (frankly) we don’t pay wages comparable to other communities like Piedmont, such as Palo Alto, or other communities full of highly educated, well-off folks (Communities that are not particularly diverse either ethnically or economically). Looking at salaries, Piedmont School District Salaries go from around $59,480 to $107,315, according to [published salary schedules], Palo Alto teacher salaries range from $71,484 to $146,979. I love Piedmont, but if I were a new teacher, I’d go to Palo Alto given the chance, wouldn’t you? As we’re focusing on wages, looking at the numbers Palo Alto teachers make between 20% and 37% more than Piedmont teachers with comparable experience. Given this lens, a COLA of 7.5% seems inadequate and indicates we should try to do better and thereby support our kids, our community, and the high property values that depend on our excellent school system. Many thanks for your work. Christina Paul is a Wildwood School parent. Parent group wants active role in selection of new Supt. Seymour On Tuesday May 24, 2022 at Robb Elementary school in Udalve, Texas, an 18-year-old gunman opened fire, killing 19 students and two adults as well as injuring 17 others. The shooter was killed by responding officers. This “massacre” is unacceptable. What happened was wrong and it needs to change. “Stronger gun laws” some may say. No, I say. “Walk out protests” others declare. No, I say. Ninety percent of shooters will not be affected if stronger gun laws are passed. If some sick person wants to blow up a school, some laws aren’t going to stop them. As my dad says, ”A locked door keeps honest people out”. If things are going to change we need to change as a society. On Wednesday my teacher gathered us to talk about it. Choked up, he said. “We should never start thinking something like this is normal.” We are starting to think that things like this happen and we are starting to think that it’s going to happen again and we can’t do anything. We can, but we need to do the right things. As a society we think charity is shameful and we sell lucky charms marshmallows separate from cereal (why?). The world is crazy. Let me introduce you to Salvador Rolando Ramos. He was an 18-year-old boy who was bullied and teased for his lisp. He was a loner with few friends and had a substance abusive mother. He was plagued by family dysfunction and mental health struggles. He was a high school dropout with mental health issues fascinated with guns. And then, eight days after he turned eighteen he entered a Robb elementary school with more rounds of ammo than a soldier going into battle would carry. He murdered 21 people, 19 of whom were elementary school students, injuring 17 others. This kid was messed up. He needed help – and love – all while his life literally crumbled apart. He would have been shamed for asking for help. So, let’s start with education and mental health awareness. articles.text: Increase of at-home tests mean underreporting of cases New data released by the state public health agency found that new COVID reported cases per day and COVID patient-occupied beds have doubled in a month. However, the surge is far lower than what we experienced with the Delta variant spike last year. “This is nothing like the Delta spike. It is far lower and is resulting in far fewer severe cases,” explained UCSF Epidemiologist and Infectious Diseases expert Dr. George Rutherford. As we enter year three of the COVID pandemic, far more individuals are vaccinated and boosted, which may also account for cases being less severe than months prior. “Fortunately, cases remain far below what we observed during [past] surges, and hospitalizations have shown only modest increases so far,” said Alameda County Health Officer Dr. Nicholas Moss. “A little caution can help keep it that way. If you’ve chosen not to wear a mask indoors recently, now is a good time to start masking again. Even with new variants, masks and vaccines continue to be effective in preventing the worst impacts of COVID.” The testing positivity rate, or average rate over seven days, is 7% the week of May 27 according to the California Department of Public Health (CDPH). This is a slight uptick from the week prior, where test positivity rate was reported as 6.6%. During the week of May 15 to May 21, the average time California patients waited for test results was 0.8 days. The Curative clinic at Piedmont Community Hall usually processes results for PCR tests within 24 hours. At-home COVID tests have become increasingly popular. They can be purchased at CVS Pharmacy for $20 or less, are FSA eligible, and free with most insurance plans. However, the increase in at-home testing has led to undercounting, and thereby underreporting of cases, confirmed Dr. Rutherford. “We estimate that there are probably twice as many cases occurring than are being reported through regular channels. We do, however, feel that this percentage is relatively constant over time, at least since January, so we’re fairly confident following trends in reported cases to know what’s going on,” he said.

articles.text: The Piedmont Community Pool Project has advanced to the construction documents phase. City Council approved modifications to conceptual design on May 2 along with a unanimous approval to proceed with the project. City Administrator Sara Lillevand presented a pool design package to city council members on May 2 and proposed expansions to the shallow-water activity pool. She added that the design modifications were the result of March 21 and April 4 meetings, which included a reduction in size of the recreation pool and the elimination of the majority of the second story of aquatics facility. The city council also moved forward with the proposal of an all-electric pool heating on April 4, increasing the cost of the project. (See the attached construction costs estimates, with comparison cost estimates for March 21 and March 31.) Project Architect and ELS Architecture and Urban Design CEO Clarence Mamuyac shared design development drawings and Operational Analysis Consultant Stuart Isaac discussed the implications of recommended designs made by City Council. Public testimony was received from six residents at the May 2 meeting, mostly expressing excitement for the project as well as recommendations that city council consider water polo standards when considering pool depth. City council received and considered correspondence from 15 residents before advancing the project. Some public testimony asked city council to reconsider the pool depth to serve the entire community appropriately. “I would love to have a few shallow lanes that transition into the 7-foot deep end,” said resident Heather Chan. “It is too big a leap to go from the smaller shallow pool directly into an all 7-foot deep large pool. How will new swimmers feel comfortable learning to swim? Even old swimmers don’t like to tread water every second they are in the pool. Please consider the Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. Appointments are not required but encouraged. More information is available at https://book.curative.com/ sites/34538. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702-9042, or visit their website at curative.com.

articles.text: Piedmont homeowners should be reminded that a City ordinance that dates to 1990 prohibits the use of gas-powered leaf blowers. Piedmont was one of the first cities in California and the first in the East Bay to issue an outright ban based upon the damage to air quality, in addition to the noise pollution created. As complaints are received by the Police Department about the use of gas-powered leaf blowers, the police make an effort to contact the homeowner, not the gardener, and remind them of the city ordinance. Homeowners continuing to allow such leaf blowers are subject to a citation and fine. Electric-powered leaf blowers are now common, and fully comply with city laws. If questions, contact the Piedmont Police Department at 420- 3010.
articles.title: Gas leaf blowers prohibited in Piedmont

articles.text: More than 50 years ago, KNBR disc jockeys Mike Cleary of Piedmont and Frank Dill challenged their Bay Area listeners to put on a parade, and Pleasanton was selected. It became the KNBR Good Times Parade, and anyone with a little red wagon could enter. A Mariners group at the Pleasanton Presbyterian Church entered with a Viking ship the first year, then came up with the idea of the tubby sailors carrying mops. The group quickly became a comic marching group. articles.text: The Barrelhouse Jazz Band has been playing traditional (Dixieland) jazz in the Bay Area since 1972. Like the earliest traditions of jazz music, the Barrelhouse boys sprang from a church. More than 48 years ago a small group of musicians at the Montclair Presbyterian Church formed a traditional jazz band. The band’s focus remains the West Coast brand of New Orleans-style jazz developed by San Francisco musician Lu Watters using a two-trumpet sound. The band loves to see people dancing to its music, something that brings out the best in the Barrelhouse musicians. The band often plays for church services in several denominations in the Bay Area, providing joy among the parishioners. In addition to playing swing music and fox-trots for dance music, the band plays struts, stomps, blues and rags. Band members are director Al Flood (clarinet & sax), Chuck McLain (trombone & vocals), pianist Margaret McElwain, Jim Lockie-Brown on banjo, Viki Jacobsen (bass sax), and Art Wood and Joel Jacobsen on trumpet. articles.text: Here comes the summer, a time when adults and children alike want to have outdoor fun. Engaging in play is an important part of early childhood and contributes to healthy brain development - the benefits are cognitive, physical, social, and emotional. Honestly, it’s good for people of all ages. For children, it helps with language, communication, and emotion control. For adults, play reduces stress, and improves brain functionality. And playing together – a departure from the structured segmentation of the pandemic home/office/gym/classroom/playground space where we do separate things next to one another – enhances learning and creativity benefits for both. According to Richard Louv, author of The Last Child in the Woods, playing outside, due to its relatively unstructured nature, also has the added benefit of feeding creativity and imagination. When children spend time playing outside the opportunities to invent, discover, pretend, and problem-solve are bountiful. Dragon fun at Children’s Fairyland This kind of break allows children (and adults) to attend to structured participation and formal zoom-room in a much more effective way. Working at Children’s Fairyland, I have had the benefit of looking out my magical window to see children become swashbuckling mates on a pirate ship, play peekaboo with a donkey, climb on the back of the happy dragon, or catch bubbles blown by an elf. I also see their adults running behind them full of glee, smiles, relief, and with a cup of coffee. Ever yone deser ves this moment to explore, imagine, create, play, scream, and run. Invest in restorative self-care for the whole family – get outside and play! Kymberly Miller is Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, America’s first storybook theme park, located on the shores of Lake Merritt in the heart of Oakland since 1950.

articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation’s Board of Directors approved a $3,350,000 grant to Piedmont schools for the next school year, 2022-23, based upon its fundraising this past year through the Giving Campaign. The grant focuses primarily on teacher retention with 72% of grant funds supporting teacher salaries, inclusive of librarians and other specialists. Another 20% invests in student support staff, such as paraeducators, classroom aides, and counselors, and 8% for classroom support, curriculum development, diversity, equity and inclusion work, and professional development. After salary support, professional development opportunities for teachers and staff are a key recruitment and retention tool, leading to a significant increase in funds for this line item. Based on input from surveys, the grants committee recommended that the additional funding be used to continue two newer programs whose government funding was ending. PEF funds will maintain the expanded tutoring program and extended mental health counseling in the district. PEF will fund two elementary school priorities: aides to re-open school libraries at lunchtime for student use, and the continued use of paraeducators to supervise lunchtime at each school. The middle and high school representatives prioritized a secondary reading specialist, who will provide ongoing support for older readers. “This year’s process was really special since the Giving Campaign raised far more money than expected,” says PEF Executive Director Heather Frank. “We were able to satisfy PUSD budget needs and save some programming.” Piedmont parent clubs sent out surveys which generated nearly 500 people offering views on the current distribution of funds, and their priorities for additional fund expenditures. Survey results are available at: Piedmontedfoundation.org/ o u r-i m p a c t / 2 0 2 2 -f u n d i n gsurvey/. The grants were recommended by the year’s PEF Grants Committee, which included the presidents of each parent club, several parent support groups, and PEF board members.
articles.title: Ed. Foundation gives $3,350,000 to school district for 2022-23

articles.text: Sports, games & crafts offered to middle school students Lucas Scherman, son of Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Scherman, returns for the second year to lead Scherman Summer Camp. Campers will learn new games, get fresh air, practice new skills, make friends and be themselves. Campers will have fun playing kickball, double-dutch, capture the flag, poker, dominos, and more. Lucas, aided by brothers Julian, 19, and Quincy, 15, will teach the art of wood-burning and how to make paracord survival bracelets. Scherman Summer Camp is a screen-free, good old-fashioned camp. The camp is open to students entering grades 6-9, and will be held at Wildwood School lower playground. One-week sessions begin the week of July 11 and continue for nine weeks. Morning classes run from 10:00 a.m.-1:00 p.m., and afternoon sessions are from 2:00-5:00 p.m. To register and for more information, call the Piedmont Recreation Department at 420-3070 or visit: Register. capturepoint.com/reg/cat_program_class_detail.cfm?s=&t=&- season_id=24069&program_ id=1420272&family_mbr_str=.
articles.title: Scherman Summer Camp returns for 2nd year

articles.text: Little learners can unleash their curiosity and imagination in the newly created OMCA Kids: Nature Playspace at Oakland Museum of California. The area is designed for the unique needs of children ages 2 to 5, along with their families and caregivers. The Playspace, located within the Gallery of California Natural Sciences, opens June 4 to the public, with a preview of OMCA members on June 3. Play is critical to every child’s healthy development and the Nature Playspace offers something for everyone – from building materials and nature-themed puzzles to hands-on activities that spark creativity, wonder, and joy. The youngest museum visitors can discover the animals that reside in Oakland’s streams, hills, and backyards. The Playspace gives families a fun, safe place to play, and to build community with other families. The Oakland Museum of California is located at 1000 Oak Street, Oakland. Call 318-8427 or go to Museumca.org for advance ticketing. Museum hours: Wednesday – Sunday – 11:00 a.m.–5:00 p.m. Friday – 11:00 a.m.–9:00 p.m. The new “Kids: Nature Playspace” at OMCA opens on June 4.
articles.title: Oakland Museum Kids Nature Playspace unveiled June 4

articles.text: On Monday, May 23, at 10:39 a.m. Piedmont Police Department dispatch advised all units that an Automatic License Plate Reader was activated on Trestle Glen Road by a black 2005 Chevrolet Silverado truck stolen from Oakland. A Piedmont Police Officer located the Silverado on Rand Avenue in Oakland. When the suspect saw the patrol car he got out of the truck and immediately entered a white 2000 GMC Sierra. The Sierra was also reported stolen out of Oakland. The suspect fled at a high rate of speed with “wanton disregard for the safety of pedestrians and property,” according to the police department. The driver reversed down the wrong way of a one-way street. No pursuit was initiated. The driver then crashed on MacArthur Blvd. He got out of the truck and started to run towards Excelsior Court. While running, he dropped a black backpack containing a stolen Makita Bandsaw. The suspect was caught on foot and was detained. Witnesses stated the suspect threw something under a parked vehicle. A Piedmont officer checked under the vehicle and found a fully loaded Glock 33 handgun. A records check revealed the suspect, Rhyon Griffin, 36, from San Leandro, had multiple outstanding felony warrants for his arrest and was on parole for assault with a deadly weapon. Piedmont paramedics transported him to Summit Hospital due to Fentanyl use. He was then transported to Santa Rita Jail where he was charged with Parole Hold, Possession of the handgun, Possession of the stolen vehicles, Evading Police, Hit & Run and four outstanding warrants. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School teacher Anne Smith invited the Post into her Period 4 Yearbook class on May 13 to view their work as writers, editors and creators of a news broadcast called The PMS Front Page. Now in their second year, the news team produces two, eight-minute videos per week on Wednesdays and Fridays, with the help of the middle school IT guru Adam Saville. The broadcast looks like a regular nightly news show, using a green screen for the news anchors appearing to be at a real TV news desk. Samantha Huy n h, who worked on the yearbook last year, explained the genesis of the project. “This year, coming back to school we wanted to make sure that we all get to see what happens at school and the benefits of it, so we started this broadcast idea,” she said. Quincy Antaya films the anchors of the middle school front page, Ava Rivera (left) and Sadie Shoop. The class takes place in room 125, the former woodshop class that now serves as a home base for ceramics, yearbook, a computer class, a fabrication lab, and for the video broadcast.
