articles.text: Piedmont Makers awarded husband and wife Helen Potter & John Lambert the 2022 Maker of the Year award at a year-end barbecue celebration on Monday, May 30. Helen and John have been on a six-year journey with Robotics in Piedmont with their sons Charlie and Henry. They were part of the founding team for the FIRST Tech Challenge (FTC) Piedmont Pioneers in 2016, the second Piedmont robotics team after Scotbotics. They created a great experience for that founding team, and with that energy created incredible momentum behind robotics in Piedmont. That soon expanded to FIRST LEGO League and FIRST Robotics Competition. Three years ago, Helen and John decided to take on their next challenge and formed the Highlander FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) team. They contributed their energy, knowledge and inspiration to make it happen. They contributed their garage and turned it into Piedmont’s unofficial Fab Lab with high-end digital equipment like a CNC router and laser cutter. They basically operated the team out of their home for the first 2-1/2 years, but they knew the team needed a permanent home. They catalyzed a fundraising campaign with Piedmont Makers that ultimately resulted in raising $420,000 for the high school’s Engineering Lab, now John Lambert and Helen Potter were named winners of the 2022 Maker of the Year Award by the Piedmont Makers. the permanent home for the Highlanders in the STEAM Building. This FRC season was a culmination of that energy as the team advanced to the semifinals of the Sacramento Regional, the quarterfinals of the Silicon Valley Regional, and ultimately the semifinals at the World Championship. They also welcomed a “third child,” the Highlander robot Selkie. Both of their sons took many lessons from their robotics team and have chosen to study engineering in college - Henry at Worcester Polytechnic Institute in Worcester, Massachusetts, and Charlie at Harvey Mudd College in Claremont, California in the fall. Seven years after founding the Pioneers, the community of Piedmont now has more than 50 robotics teams with 400 students in grades K-12. Not incidentally, John Lambert is now working for the school district as Manager of the Engineering Lab. “Because of all of this, the Piedmont Makers board could not be more pleased to award Helen Potter and John Lambert our 2022 Makers of the Year award,” announced David Ragones, president of Piedmont Makers.
articles.title: Helen Potter, John Lambert receive Maker of the Year Award

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School 6th graders renewed a decades-long tradition on Friday, May 27 by participating in the popular Greek Olympic games at Witter Field. The event serves as an end-of-school year celebration, coupled with a culmination of their studies of Ancient Greece. Students were divided up into four city-states – Athens, Sparta, Olympia, and Rhodes – and competed for top awards for the winning city-state. Rhodes was declared the overall winner with the most overall wins. The events included tug-ofwar, jump rope. long jump, a 3-legged race, shot put (softball), discus (frisbee), javelin (toilet plunger), and relay races. Citystates also competed against each other musically by reciting their city-state’s anthem and designing individualized jerseys. “I definitely loved how hard all the teachers and parent volunteers worked to make it all come together,” said 6th grader Samantha Pell. Student Olympians rotated through each event with faculty members and parents helping record the athletic feats. “All in all, the kids have been doing great and having fun, and Students competed for their city-states of Athens, Sparta, Olympia, and Rhodes. that’s the whole point. There have been some rough landings in the long jump sand pit, so I expect some of their spinal columns to be feeling that tomorrow morning,” said parent Xenia Meyer who was recording the long jump results. The students’ athletic prowess may only be rivaled by their historical knowledge. This reporter did not have to go too far to find students eager to share their observations of their favorite Greek gods and goddesses. “I really like Hades, the brother of Zeus and the god of the underworld,” explained Avi Tug-of-war is a student favorite event every year at the Greek Olympics. Colt Hitchcock sticks a long jump landing. The relay races garnered stiff competition and unorthodox rules as students were asked to skip, hop and strafe as well as sprint. Boguslavsky. “Zeus’s daughter Persephony ate a single pomegranate seed from the underworld and could not come back, so she became Hades’ wife and has to remain in the underworld for onethird of the year.” While Rhodes tallied the most victories, the Greek Olympics of 2022 will be fondly remembered by all participants as a grand return to tradition after a twoyear absence, with friendly competition and teamwork, things that have been hard to come by in the last couple of years. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s star distance runners Jack Stein and Ellie Black were named as the school’s 2022 Outstanding Senior Athletes, noting their academic success, student leadership, and prowess in their sports. Both were key members of the cross-country and track teams, and qualified to compete at the State Meet in each sport. It is one of the few times the awards have gone to students in the same sport, a testament to the success of Jeanine Holmlund’s running program this year. Piedmont’s all-time top-five times in the 1600 are: Jack Stein, 4:14.77 (2022) Tom Phelps, 4:14.92 (2001) Mark Ceraldi, 4:17.40 (2005) Cooper Downing, 4:17.85 (2022) Will Sanford, 4:23.65 (2001) Distance runner Ellie Black was named Outstanding Senior Female Athlete Award after being named League Runner of the Year in both cross country and track. School record holder in the 1600 meters and 3200 meters Jack Stein earned Piedmont’s Outstanding Senior Male Athlete award.

articles.text: A unique opportunity is available for budding soccer stars in Piedmont and the Bay Area. Erin Greening, a 2015 graduate of Piedmont High School and the leading scorer on the soccer team, played four years for the University of Colorado before turning pro. She was drafted by the Orlando Pride in the National Women’s Soccer League and also signed with Klepp IL of Norway’s top-tier Toppserien league. Greening is currently back in town and is offering private training sessions to players of all ages. “I’ll be hosting private training and lessons for individuals, groups, and some teams,” she explained. “I was playing overseas, and I ended my rehab in April. Now that I’m back at home and done with rehab, I’m getting back into the training. I’m just looking for different groups and helping anyone who is interested,” said Greening. Greening graduated from Piedmont High in 2015 as its alltime leading goal scorer at the time. She played in 74 matches with Colorado before being drafted by the Orlando Pride in the third round of the 2019 NWSL College Draft. Greening made 17 appearances with the Pride, scoring once, and played alongside some U.S. Women’s National Team greats like Alex Morgan, Ali Krieger, and Marta Vieira da Silva. “I loved Orlando. It’s definitely a totally different game than the college level, but I learned a lot. I loved playing alongside people I looked up to since I was a little girl, especially Alex Morgan, Ali Krieger, and Marta. When you play with people like that, they Erin Greening is now hosting private soccer lessons. articles.text: Last fall Black qualified for the State Cross Country Championship as an individual runner, and clocking a 18:44 to finish 17th of 207 runners. Her time made her the second-best on Piedmont’s all-time behind Sophia Zalewski’s time of 17:50.64 in 2020. She won her second consecutive cross country WACC Runner of the Year by winning the league championship in 18:38.6 at Hayward High, 48 seconds faster than her previous top time. To reach state, she clocked a time of 18:10.7 to place 4th of 105 runners at the North Coast Section Championship at Hayward. articles.text: Stein’s monumental year began last fall in cross-country when he helped lead his team to the CIF State Championship in Fresno for the first time at State since 2017. To reach the state meet, Stein helped the team to a 3rd place finish of 19 schools at the North Coast Section Championship at Hayward High on November 20. He set a course record with a time of 15:29.4, and finished 2nd out of 144 runners. It eclipsed Reece Proctor’s record time in 2016 by three seconds. Stein was named WACC’s Runner of the Year after winning the League Championship. Competing in the State meet, at Woodward Park in Fresno, Stein placed 12th of 209 runners with a time of 15:43.4. This spring, Stein etched his name into the PHS history books with record runs, breaking school records in both the 1600 and 3200 meters. He clocked a time of 9:12.62 in the 3200 at the Arcadia Invitational on April 9, and ran a 4:14.77 in the 1600 at the Stanford Invitational on April 2, He was named the WACC’s Runner of the Year award in track. Piedmont’s all-time top-five times in the 3200 are: Jack Stein, 9:12.62 (2022) Steve Brown, 9:17.71 (1994) Tom Phelps, 9:35.72 (2000) Carl Moren, 9:38.60 (1998) Crosby Freeman, 9:39.8 (2001)
articles.title: Jack Stein

articles.text: Piedmont native Mackie McDonald competed in another Grand Slam last week, advancing to the third round of the prestigious French Open before losing to No. 11 Jannik Sinner of Italy in three sets on Saturday, May 28. To get there, McDonald upset No. 22 seed Nikoloz Basilashvii of Georgia in three sets on Thursday, May 26 and defeated Italy’s Franco Agamenone in four sets in the opening round on Monday, May 23. Following the tournament, McDonald’s ATP Tour world ranking jumped nine positions to No. 51, two spots shy of matching his career high ranking of No. 49. In the opening round, Mackie defeated Adamenone after dropping the first set, 1-6, 6-2, 6-3, 7-6 (7-3). McDonald was great on the return, claiming seven of eight break points and 45 points as the receiver, while also winning 74 points when serving despite having just one ace on the day. McDonald’s second-round win came against Basilashvii, the No. 26 player in the world in three sets in dominant fashion by scores of 6-3, 6-1, 6-4. McDonald gained seven break points out of 25 opportunities, which showed his prowess in challenging as the returner. Basilashvii struggled while serving with six double faults compared to Mackie’s one. McDonald’s third-round loss in three sets (6-3, 7-6 (8-6), 6-3) was against Sinner, an Italian player ranked No. 12 in the world. Sinner won with help of four aces and won 75 percent of the time on his first serves. McDonald also competed in the doubles ladder in the French Open with Tommy Paul. They defeated Aisam-ul-Haq Qureshi and Aleksandr Nedovyesov in the first round on May 25, 3-6, 6-2, 6-3. In the second round the American duo defeated No. 10 seeded Bruno Soares of Brazil and England’s Jamie Murray, 7-6 (9-7), 4-6, 6-3. McDonald and Paul lost in the third round to No. 6 seed Neal Skupski of England and Dutchman Wesley Koolhof in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2. McDonald will now prepare for his next Grand Slam tournament later this month at the Wimbledon June 27-July 10 in London. Stay tuned for more coverage of McDonald’s matches this summer. Photos courtesy of Sportskeeda.com Mackie McDonald’s world ranking improved to No. 51 following his success at the French Open.
articles.title: Mackie McDonald makes third round of French Open

The game is a bit more physical than other leagues See Erin Greening on page 30 Mackie McDonald makes third round of French Open By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont native Mackie McDonald competed in another Grand Slam last week, advancing to the third round of the prestigious French Open before losing to No. 11 Jannik Sinner of Italy in three sets on Saturday, May 28. To get there, McDonald upset No. 22 seed Nikoloz Basilashvii of Georgia in three sets on Thursday, May 26 and defeated Italy’s Franco Agamenone in four sets in the opening round on Monday, May 23. Following the tournament, McDonald’s ATP Tour world ranking jumped nine positions to No. 51, two spots shy of matching his career high ranking of No. 49. In the opening round, Mackie defeated Adamenone after dropping the first set, 1-6, 6-2, 6-3, 7-6 (7-3). McDonald was great on the return, claiming seven of eight break points and 45 points as the receiver, while also winning 74 points when serving despite having just one ace on the day. McDonald’s second-round win came against Basilashvii, the No. 26 player in the world in three sets in dominant fashion by scores of 6-3, 6-1, 6-4. McDonald gained seven break points out of 25 opportunities, which showed his prowess in challenging as the returner. Basilashvii struggled while serving with six double faults compared to Mackie’s one. McDonald’s third-round loss in three sets (6-3, 7-6 (8-6), 6-3) was against Sinner, an Italian player ranked No. 12 in the world. Sinner won with help of four aces and won 75 percent of the time on his first serves. McDonald also competed in the doubles ladder in the French Open with Tommy Paul. They defeated Aisam-ul-Haq Qureshi and Aleksandr Nedovyesov in the first round on May 25, 3-6, 6-2, 6-3. In the second round the American duo defeated No. 10 seeded Bruno Soares of Brazil and England’s Jamie Murray, 7-6 (9-7), 4-6, 6-3. McDonald and Paul lost in the third round to No. 6 seed Neal Skupski of England and Dutchman Wesley Koolhof in straight sets, 6-3, 6-2. McDonald will now prepare for his next Grand Slam tournament later this month at the Wimbledon June 27-July 10 in London. Stay tuned for more coverage of McDonald’s matches this summer. articles.text: Parker Terrill places fourth in pole vault in 16-feet, 1-inch Parker Terrill placed fourth in the State in pole vault with a personal record of 16 feet, 1 inch. Piedmont’s record setting track and field team finished its season at the 102nd California State Championships at Buchannan High School in Clovis last weekend, May 27-28. Parker Terrill adding six inches to his pole vault personal record with a height of 16-feet, 1-inch to place Photo by Steve Zirkelbach Cooper Downing (#1) narrowly missed the finals in the 800 meters, placing 13th in the trials with a time of 1:53.40, a personal record. fourth among 12 vaulters on Saturday. Six Piedmont athletes qualified for State, the largest number in recent history. It matches the combined total of PHS athletes sent over the last 20 years. This year’s team featured four school record holders: Parker Terrill in the pole vault, Jack Stein in the 1600 and 3200, and the 4x400 relay team. “This is the first time Piedmont scored points as a team at the state meet in at least 20 years,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. “We’re all super proud of seeing our athlete wearing a Piedmont jersey on the podium. Throw in four all-time school records for our 2022 season. It’s been so fun!” Terrill, a soon-to-be California Golden Bear, broke his own school record a total of three times this year after clearing 14-feet, 2-inches on March 5 at the Clayton Valley Relays. His breakout season as a senior began last year. He was a two-sport athlete with basketball in 2021 during the pandemic-shortened school year. “I put a lot of dedication into the pole vault. Now it’s a good benchmark leading into my collegiate career. It really started at the beginning of last summer around June. I’m just focused on heights. Seeing that I’ve been up to par or even surpassing some (other vaulters) is a really good feeling, knowing that the work I’m putting in is going somewhere,” said Terrill. Although Terrill’s strength is a pole vaulter, he intends to compete in the decathlon. As a high school senior, he has the second-highest score in the United States on April 16 when winning the Del Campo Decathlon with 5,964 total points. “My main event is the pole vault, but I plan on competing in the decathlon when some competitions come around. I haven’t found my secondary, tertiary events that I’ve truly been focusing on, so I really want to identify those and progress in those as well,” said Terrill. Ellie Black competed ta State in the 3200, finishing with a time of 10:49.25, 15th of 23 runners. She concludes her high school career with the second-best time in the 3200 meters behind legendary Sally Wood’s 10:42.45 with a 10:46.09 set on April 9 at the prestigious Arcadia Invitational. Similar to Terrill, Black will be attending UC Berkeley in the fall. Black is also Piedmont’s third all-time fastest runner in the 1600 with a time of 5:07.23. a few seconds back of twins Jehan Sparks (5:04.56 in 2003) and Naomi Sparks (5:02.51 in 2004). Stein ran the 1600 in 4:23.75, placing 24th in the trials at State. He holds the school record in 1600 meters (4:14.77 at the Stanford Invitational on April 2), and the 4200 meters (9:12.62 at the Arcadia Invitational on April 9). Cooper Downing narrowly missed out qualifying for the State finals in the 800 after clocking a time of 1:53.40 to finish 13th. The top-12 runners moved on to the finals. Downing’s time was the third best time in Piedmont history, just 1.2 seconds behind Reece Proctor (1:52.64 in 2018) and 2.2 seconds behind Gordon Johnson’s 34-year old record of 1:51.69 in 1988. The 4x400 relay team of Luke Alban, Parker Long, Downing, and Terrill finished with a time of 3:26.79 to place 20th. Their relay team holds the School record with a time of 3:21.77 set at the NCS Meet of Champions on May 21. They broke a records that was set 33 years ago, in 1989, by Johnson and three teammates Ellie Black (#4) finished 15th in the 3200 meters at State with a time of 10:49.25. articles.text: The Piedmont Cobras are off to a sizzling start. Piedmont Baseball-Softball Foundation’s 8 & Under All-Star team was undefeated in six games last weekend to win the Foster City Memorial Day Tournament. This was the first-ever tournament for the Cobras, helmed by PHS varsity baseball coach Eric Olson. The Foster City tournament mostly featured teams from the Peninsula, as well as two from Orinda. The 8U division was packed with 14 teams, only seven of which would make it to Monday’s single--elimination playoff bracket. The Cobras got off to an exhilarating start, topping the Pacifica Cages in extra innings on a walkoff single by Jonah Emanuelson. Solid defense and power hitting across the board catapulted the Cobras into Monday’s playoff round. The win-or-go-home day began with a 12-11 nail-biting win over the Orinda Americans. Nolan White’s sacrifice fly provided the go-ahead run for Piedmont. The Cobras then beat the Peninsula Rays 14-7 in the semifinals. Stone Cameron, Sylas Blanco, and Theo Delventhal all had three hits, and nothing got by Lucas Olson at shortstop. The championship game pitted Piedmont against the Hillsborough Hawks, a team that beat Piedmont’s 8U squad last year. The Cobras jumped out to a 7-2 lead thanks to hot bats and stellar defense. Nate Stein made a number of plays at third base. The Hawks started chipping away at the Cobras’ lead, cutting the lead to 7-5 with one out in the bottom of the 6th inning with the tying run at the plate. The game ended when second baseman Delventhal ranged to snag a hard hit grounder in the hole and fired to Emanuelson at first base who made a great stretch to secure the final out for the championship. The Cobras now head to Burlingame to compete in the BYBA Tournament from June 8-12. Piedmont will host the annual 8U-9U Caldecott Cup at Hampton Field beginning the weekend of July 23. The Piedmont Cobras 8 & Under baseball team won the Foster City Memorial Day Tournament, beating the Hillsborough Hawks 7-5 for the title. articles.title: Piedmont All-Stars win Foster City Tournament

articles.text: More than 50 tennis players and friends gathered at Piedmont’s Corey Reich Tennis Center on Friday, May 20, to participate in the 2022 Spring Fling Tennis Social. Lead sponsors Michelle Heafey and Sarah Meyjes from The Grubb Co. welcomed participants on the beautiful spring morning. Trainers from StretchLab in Albany led the group in a warm-up, followed by instructors Andrew Wendel, Sydney Williams, Ali Stein, and Michael Hieu offering drills and tennis games with fun prizes. After the tennis matches, everyone walked to the home of Grace and Taylor Harris to enjoy brunch and a game of tough tennis trivia. More than $5,000 was raised at the event to support Piedmont elementary schools through the Piedmont Education Foundation, the event organizer. Co-hosts for the event included Cortney Allen, Tonya Antonucci, Courtney Azad, Sasha Bainer, Katherine Bini, Susie Burden, Chrissy Droessler, Penny Graham, Grace and Taylor Harris, Emily Harrold, Amelie Kappes, Cori Kau, Molly Kennedy, Srikant and Laurie Misra, Dre and Ashley Stevanovic, Alissa Welch, and the Piedmont Recreation Department. articles.text: Filoli Pride celebration is June 4 & 5 Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside any Thursday evening starting June 2 for its popular “Summer Nights” festivities. Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli. They serve as a time to gather with family and friends, who enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance-style garden. Also, this weekend, June 4-5, Filoli will celebrate the LGBTQ+ community with Pride-themed Filoli Gardens in Woodside will transform Estate Trail into a “Rainbow Walk” this weekend to celebrate the first weekend of Pride Month. drinks at the Bluebird Bar and hikes along the Rainbow Walk. Live performances throughout the weekend include Mexican folk dancing by Folcorico Colibri, Drag Queen Storytime, and Japanese taiko drumming by Queer Taiko. Filoli is located at 86 Canada Road in Woodside. Phone number is (650) 364-8300. Visit https:// filoli.org/visit#seasonal to purchase tickets and to learn more about summer at Filoli.
articles.title: Filoli “Summer Nights” begin tomorrow, June 2 at 5 p.m.

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California has created a series of free events entitled “Friday Nights at OMCA,” which offer food truck options, music, and art activities inspired by the museum’s current exhibitions. Every Friday beginning at 5 p.m., an assortment of food trucks parked on 10th Street between Oakland and Fallon Streets will be parked, with beer and wine available. The food variety changes weekly. Activities and music will be available on OMCA’s new outdoor lawn space. Oakland-based landscape architect and MacArthur Genius award-winner Walter Hood, with architecture firm Mark Cavagnero Associates, led the lawn project design. Renovations were funded by the “All In! The Campaign for OMCA,” which was undertaken to expand OMCA’s role in the community as a public gathering place. On the lawn you will find outdoor games like “Giant Jenga” and “Connect-Four.” For more information, visit https://museumca. org/2022/friday-nights-omca-grid. An outdoor stage at Oakland Museum of California opens up to the lawn, renovated in summer 2021. The area is used for programs and performances as the museum rolls out events this summer. articles.text: Bouquets to Art, the de Young Museum’s premiere fundraiser and annual display of artwork-inspired floral installations, will begin on June 7. Now in its 38th year, the event is back to full-capacity following a virtual event in 2020 and a hybrid, limited-capacity event last year. For one week, more than 100 experienced floral designers will converge at the de Young to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s vast array of paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Bouquets to Art is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events every year. It is presented by the volunteer members of the Fine Arts Museums, and has generated $7 million since its inception. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. Visitors will be greeted with a large-scale aerial artwork piece by Bay Area artist Windy Chien. Entitled The Three Dragons, the hand-knotted artwork hangs in the museum’s Wilsey Court. Those who visit during the week of Bouquets to Art will have a chance to view Hung Liu’s large piece Resident Alien, first exhibited at the Capp Street Project in 1988 and exhibited by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco last year. The painting, arguably Liu’s most famous, depicts her own “Green Card” on a larger-than-life scale. It is now in the collection of the San Jose Museum of Art. “Hung Liu is uniquely positioned to tell the stories of immigrants to the United States. In 2020, she celebrated the milestone of having lived an equal number of years in China and the United States. As one of the foremost painters in the United States, Liu is a testament to the fact that our brightest citizens are often born under foreign skies,” said Janna Keegan, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art and Programming at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Bouquets to Art is a weeklong event that officially begins on Monday evening, June 6, with the traditional opening-night party. Between June 7 and June 12, a series of book launches, speaker events, and raffles will take place. For a full list of programming, visit https://www.famsf.org/ press-room/bouquets-art. Tickets sold out weeks prior to the event in 2021. Reserve yours now by visiting https://deyoung. famsf.org/bouquets-to-art. Bouquets to Art begins next week. Fresh new look, no guesswork! pages.text: 16 Wednesday, June 1, 2022 Arts & Entertainment Oakland Museum begins Friday Nights with food, music and art By Allyson Aleksey Oakland Museum of California has created a series of free events entitled “Friday Nights at OMCA,” which offer food truck options, music, and art activities inspired by the museum’s current exhibitions. Every Friday beginning at 5 p.m., an assortment of food trucks parked on 10th Street between Oakland and Fallon Streets will be parked, with beer and wine available. The food variety changes weekly. Activities and music will be available on OMCA’s new outdoor lawn space. Oakland-based landscape architect and MacArthur Genius award-winner Walter Hood, with architecture firm Mark Cavagnero Associates, led the lawn project design. Renovations were funded by the “All In! The Campaign for OMCA,” which was undertaken to expand OMCA’s role in the community as a public gathering place. On the lawn you will find outdoor games like “Giant Jenga” and “Connect-Four.” For more information, visit https://museumca. org/2022/friday-nights-omca-grid. Sculpt your own mini dinnerware at the ‘EARTH-enware Table’, inspired by the current exhibition on Edith Heath. The collective has been hosting “Oakland’s favorite daytime dance party” since 2011. Filoli “Summer Nights” begin tomorrow, June 2 at 5 p.m. Filoli Pride celebration is June 4 & 5 By Allyson Aleksey Visit Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside any Thursday evening starting June 2 for its popular “Summer Nights” festivities. Summer Nights are a tradition at Filoli. They serve as a time to gather with family and friends, who enjoy the sunset and summer blooms. Every Thursday night throughout the summer the Grove Bar is serving wine and beer in the garden, nestled under the shade of the Olive Grove. The Georgian-style terraces around the historic house offer sweeping views of the Santa Cruz Mountains, a contrast to the 16-acre formal English Renaissance-style garden. articles.text: The SF Jazz Broadcast Gala and Fundraiser is this Friday, June 3, at 8:30 p.m., with an encore broadcast on Saturday at 11 a.m. and Sunday at 5 p.m. The Gala serves as a fundraiser for SF Jazz’s artistic and education programs, headlined by trumpeter Wynton Marsalis. A multi-Grammy award winner and composer and teacher, his work was the first jazz composition to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Marsalis, the artistic director of Jazz at Lincoln Center, comes from a lineage of jazz greats, including brothers Branford, Jason and Delfeayo. Marsalis will perform alongside trumpeter Terence Blanchard and vocalist Catherine Russell. Trumpeter Wynton Marsalis will headline a fundraiser by SF Jazz this Friday night, June 3. The Gala is hosted by Wendell Pierce. Visit https://www.sfjazz. org/watchgala/ to donate and to learn how to watch the Gala this weekend.

articles.text: This is the last weekend to see “Memento: Jayashree Chakravarty and Lam Tung Pang” at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. The exhibition, part of an ongoing series of singular exhibitions at the museum entitled Today’s Asian Voices, ends on Monday, June 6. The exhibition marks the inaugural Hambrecht Contemporary Gallery installation, Memento, which includes two contemporary works that speak to global issues of urbanization and political uncertainty. The Hambrecht Contemporary Gallery is formerly used for special exhibitions and has recently been transformed into a dedicated space for a rotating selection of both modern and contemporary works. Viewers will see Personal Space by Chakravarty (2001), an 8-foot-tall, 30-foot-wide work built from painted strips of paper. An immersive video by Hong Kong-based mixed media artist Pang entitled A day of two Suns (2019), combines unsynchronized images from four projectors that combine with the shadows of museum visitors and moving objects. “This work is prophetic and nostalgic,” said Head of Contemporary Art Abby Chen about the newly acquired work. “It documents a city, and a system, in the process of fading and awakening.” For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/memento-jayashreechakravarty-and-lam-tung-pang/. Asian Art Museum is located at 200 Larkin Street in San Francisco. (415) 581-3500.
articles.title: Chakravarty, Pang exhibit in final week at Asian Art Museum

articles.text: Chuck Berry followed Booker T. Washington’s philosophy, advocating African American advancement through education and entrepreneurship. He ventured to Chicago at the suggestion of Muddy Waters to look for a record label and began a long, successful business relationship with producer Leonard Chess, who ran jazz clubs on the South Side of Chicago. Chuck Berry borrowed heavily from white people’s genres. Maybellene, his first hit, was a remake of the 1938 Bob Wills’ country hit Ida Red. Maybellene was named after a bottle of mascara by Leonard Chess in the studio. Contrary to the usual swing rhythm used in electric guitar roots genres like blues, R&B and swing in the forties, Chuck Berry used straight rhythm in all his hits: Maybellene, Roll Over Beethoven, Rock and Roll Music and Johnny B. Goode. Many Chuck Berry songs like Maybellene and Sweet Little Sixteen also use root to fifth in the bass, like hillbilly music. Johnny B. Goode was autobiographical. Chuck Berry’s first home was at 2520 Goode Avenue in the Ville district of northeast St. Louis. The lyrics speak to the African American migration from New Orleans to Missouri, ending with “someday your name Rock & Roll pioneer, guitarist and songwriter Chuck Berry. will be in lights, saying ‘Johnny B. Goode tonight’ ”. Chuck Berry used syncopation to keep the rhythm interesting without swing, playing and singing notes on the offbeats. He used repeated themes with durations less that whole numbers of beats. Bars five through eight of the Johnny B. Goode intro guitar solo use a repeated one-anda-half beat theme that alternates starting on the first half and last half of the beat (“anti-metric” rhythm). “Improv Level 3: Pentatonics and Modes”/Rock a Berry at this link: https://drive.google.com/ file/d/1pzPUbilJvRS5H7ufbTr_ DGbchFszQdG2/view?usp=sharing John Lennon once said, “If you tried to give Rock ’n’ Roll another name, you might try ‘Chuck Berry’.” Keith Richards, Eric Clapton, George Harrison, Eddie Van Halen and most mainstream rock guitar players included Chuck Berry’s licks in their bag of tricks. Beach Boys’ Fun, Fun, Fun and Surfin’ U.S.A. use Berry’s guitar style. Chuck Berry borrowed guitarist Carl Hogan’s intro and solo on Louis Jordan’s Ain’t That Just Like a Woman (1946) for Johnny B. Goode. Berry said: “The first time I heard [the riff] was Carl Hogan in Louis Jordan’s band. We have T-Bone Walker; I love [his] slurs he’s bluesy. So I put a little Carl Hogan, a little T-Bone, a little Charlie Christian together, and look what a span of people you will please! Ain’t nothing new under the sun.” Listen to and read my improvised example for this Chuck Berry column and my previous columns at: http://www.guitarimprov.com/PostColumns.pdf Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. articles.title: The legacy of Chuck Berry

articles.text: There were two big programs at the Piedmont Center for the Arts last weekend. The first was a piano program by Eric Tran. The second was a return engagement of the San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra. Eric Tran grew up in Piedmont, and I don’t think we’ve had a greater treasure. His artistry was acknowledged at an early age. The muses and Apollo have been with him ever since. I think he is pursuing his PhD at the University of Wisconsin, but PhD or not, he deserves the title Maestro. His recital in Piedmont on Saturday gave ample proof of his accomplishments. Owing to a previous engagement, I missed the first half of the program. I arrived in time to hear him take us on a picturesque trip to the Austrian concert side. One of Beethoven’s most original compositions is his Sixth Symphony which is known as the “Pastoral”. Most of us know it in the original version for orchestra. But Franz Liszt arranged it for solo piano. In this version it loses absolutely nothing. It is a work of genius in itself. Eric plays with a composer’s understanding of music. The multihued pastoral symphony proved a perfect vehicle for his broad talent. All of us know the original version… And a work of genius it is! But Liszt appropriates that very genius and transforms it into a grand symphony for the piano. When Tran plays it, no one will miss the orchestra. How impressive is that?! Everything that he does is done with a casual charm. The sonorities rise from the piano in an effortless fashion. Because of this, the listeners can appreciate the music all the more. Mandolins in Piedmont The concert on Sunday afternoon was a completely different sensibility. The San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra returned to the Piedmont Center for the Arts after the hiatus due to the pandemic. A brief word of explanation is due. The mandolin is a userfriendly version of the violin. It has the same tuning as the violin but uses a guitar-like pic instead of the bow to make the tone. Mandolins can play all the music that the violin plays, but with less effort…and the results are very good. The conductor/music Director of SF Mandolin Orchestra is the Achille Bocus, founder and leader of San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra. Italian born Achille Bocus. He is both an inspiration and a man of many parts. While the Mandolin is his main instrument, he is also a professional bass player, a composer and arranger as well as an outstanding conductor. Bocus arranged all of the compositions that the orchestra performs. His conducting is crystal clear. You could watch him conduct with the sound turned off and know exactly how to play. That’s the way conducting should be. Because of this, the mandolin orchestra plays above their abilities. They also take their time, and in doing so, they make an expressive presence simply because there is no haste. All of these things result in a performance of uncommon sensitivity. Especially notable is to understand that these are not professional musicians. An occasional clinker here or there was compensated for by lofty music making. Of special mention was Bocus’ performance of Schubert’s magnificent “Arpeggione Sonata.” The brief program notes offered a good insight into what we heard: “Music can bring us to an enchanted world. All you need to do is open your imagination and fly to joyful meditation.“ The caveat… Anyone who has attended performances at the Piedmont Center of the Arts or attended an art show knows what marvelous things are going on. When things are going well, it is a good idea to let them alone. Advice like this has stood humanity in good stead for a long time. Unfortunately, some of the folks in City Hall have other ideas. The PCA has been successful Piedmont native, pianist and composer Eric Tran.
articles.title: Dynamic duo…and a caveat

articles.text: The annual Piedmont Chamber Music Festival, the only weeklong residency chamber music Festival in the East Bay, celebrates its fifth festival at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in a series of intimate concerts opening July 20. This season festival musicians will explore the theme “Human. Alone and Together” in works from composers old and new that remind us that life is better together. Led by founders Wayne Lee (violin) a Piedmont native, and his wife Juliana Han (piano), the festival features eight internationally acclaimed musicians from throughout the U.S. Returning musicians Jarmine Lin (violin) and Deborah Pae (cello), will be joined by guest musicians Teng Li (Principal Violinist, Los Angeles Philharmonic), Francisco Fullana (violin), Clancy Newman (cellist & composer), and Paul Laraia (viola). This Week’s Featured Artist Spanish-born violinist Francisco Fullana, winner of a 2018 Avery Fisher Career Grant, the 2015 Pro Musicis International Award, and the 2014 Johannes Brahms International Violin Competition, has been hailed as a “rising star” (BBC Music Magazine), an “amazing talent” (conductor Gustavo Dudamel), and “a paragon of delicacy” (San Francisco Classical Voice). The subtext of the film that is never explored is the question as to whether people, in mental and physical extremis, who are so lost can ever truly be salvaged, no matter the sincerity and commitment of the salvager. The film offers a stark glimpse of the more than 11,000 homeless people living in L.A., confined mainly to 50 blocks referred to as Skid Row. It’s as if every lost, broken soul has been carried there by a tide of poverty, mental illness, drug abuse, many tormented by a panoply of demons, now wandering the Darwinian streets trying only to survive another day. What Lopez does offer Ayers is the hand of friendship, discovering that there are moments when that is enough. But there are also moments, lots of them, when it isn’t. Because there is only the most fragile bond connecting Lopez and Ayers, the film seems strangely remote. Ultimately for Ayers, there is no redemptive moment. For Lopez there is no breakthrough, when the two men face one another in a flash of lucidity and understanding. In truth, Ayers has fled into a world apart and chooses to remain there. His only consistent bridge to others and to himself is music, his lifeline – except when it isn’t. The Soloist. Directed by Joe Wright. Starring Jamie Foxx, Robert Downey, Catherine Keener and Tom Hollander. 1 hr., 57 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2009. Now Streaming on Prime/ VUDU. Lights Out, released in 2016, is an effective, compact horror-thriller that uses a minimalist conceit – fear of the dark – to its full advantage. I would judge that there is not a horror film made today that can avoid the criticism that it is derivative; and so the challenge becomes how to make the familiar sufficiently original to be downright creepy. Lights Out manages to do that in spades. Just the title signals that when the light on the nightstand or the one in the ceiling begins to flicker, bad things are going to happen. Here’s the set up for this tidy little chiller: A specter – called Diana – has returned to inhabit a spooky old house and torment an emotionally fragile single mom, Sophie (Maria Bello), and her increasingly terrified, sleep-deprived 10-year-old son, Martin (Gabriel Bateman). Martin wakes and hears his mother having late night conversations with someone/something in the dark of her bedroom. Finally, desperately, he turns to his estranged sister, Rebecca (Teresa Palmer), for help. She has long ago left the family and lives a kind of Goth, hip life over a tattoo parlor. Her boyfriend is perpetually kept at arm’s length, implying some attachment or childhood abandonment issues that are tangentially explored. Diana, who vanishes when the lights go on and appears when the lights go off, is a long-limbed, snake silhouette whose mission is the elimination of all all who are close to Sophie. They were childhood friends, stemming from a time when the two were committed to a mental institution for depression. It was there Diana died during treatment. Now this malevolent apparition has returned to take possession of Sophie’s life. Sophie is the catalyst, and Bello perfectly balances the sincere jeopardy she feels for herself and her family and her wacko delusions, foremost being that she and Diana are “friends.” Ultimately it’s her family that is in harm’s way, not Sophie. And it’s Rebecca and Martin who are subjected to the murderous machinations of Diana. They quickly discover that light is essential if they are to Gabriel Bateman and Teresa Palmer star in Lights Out. survive. What first seems a delusion (mom is off her meds?) soon becomes a pure, supernatural, physical presence representing evil. Of course, the film is filled with moments that scream, “Don’t leave Martin alone in his room!” or “Don’t walk down that long dark basement passageway carrying only a light!” “Don’t sleep downstairs while Martin is sleeping in his room upstairs with his door closed!” Really? His door closed? “Do not open that one particular door, yes that one!, behind which is a very dark room.” Admittedly, Lights Out possesses all the familiar tropes. But still, the essence of the film plays to that core of insecurity that seems almost universal: all of us believe in some deep or hidden way that there is something beyond the evidence. It is that reality that has made films of this genre – jeepers-creepers-poltergeists – so durable and effective after decades of iterations. So, if you appreciate the genre you will like this film. It has its goosebumps moments. Lights Out. Directed by David F. Sandberg. Starring Teresa Palmer, Maria Bello, Gabriel Bateman. 1 hr., 17 min. Rated PG-13. Released in theaters in 2016. Review the same year in the Post. Now streaming on hulu/ VUDU/Prime. A scene from Lights Out. articles.text: A scene from Disney’s Lilo and Stitch. Lilo and Stitch is a Disney animated feature, released in 2002, and nominated for an Oscar at the 75th Awards ceremony. It was hand-drawn with a rich palette of lush, vivid colors. It’s family friendly, poignant, and at times even beguiling and will bring to mind the extraordinary film E.T., long overdue to be discovered by a new generation of kids. At the center of the story, set on the Hawaiian island of Kauai, are Lilo (Daveigh Chase), a 7-year-old Hawaiian girl, and her older teen sister Nani (Tia Carrera). They recently lost their parents in a car accident, and are now orphaned. Lilo, always rambunctious, is now struggling to cope with her loss. She is lonely, ostracized from her hula class, and troubled at school. Nani, feeling a bit desperate, takes her to an animal shelter where they pick out a “dog,” which is a small blue koala-like critter that she names Stitch. In reality Stitch is an escaped E.T. from a world faraway. He’s actually an experiment called 620, and created to cause a world of chaos. Though Lilo and Nani have a strong sister bond despite their arguments, their social worker, Cobra Bubbles (Ving Rhanes), doubts that Nani can care for Lilo alone. He thinks Lilo is too quirky, feeds peanut butter to the fish and takes strange pictures of beachgoers, and has strange-looking dolls. Meanwhile, since Stitch has escaped from his home planet, two representatives, mad scientist Dr. Jumba Jookiba (David Ogden Stiers), 620’s creator, and agent Wendell Pleakley (Kevin McDonald) of the Galactic Federation, are sent to earth to look for him. Though Stitch was created to cause chaos and bedevilment, Lilo and the diminutive E.T fashion a strong bond, and with Nani form a small nuclear family, referred to in Hawaiian as O’hana. Gradually the idea of O’hana comes to be the center of the story. Lilo introduces Stitch to Elvis albums, hula dancing, and surfing with Nani. Meanwhile the two Federation E.T.s are in the hunt for Stitch. Lilo and Stich is filled with gags and energy and intergalactic conflict. Kids will enjoy the characters in a story that ends with an action-packed aerial chase. Lilo and Stitch. Directed by Dean DeBlois & Christopher Sanders, Walt Disney animation. With voices of Daveigh Chase, Tia Carrera, Christopher Sanders. 1 hr., 25 min, Rated PG. Released in 2002, Now streaming on Disney+/ VUDU/Prime.
articles.title: Lilo and Stitch

articles.text: What is a swashbuckler movie, really? The definition may not quickly come to mind, but we know one when we see it, and Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time is a genuine 6th century pull-out-all-the-stops swashbuckIs there lots of swordplay? You bet. Is there a stunning princess whose subjects live behind the massive walls of a sacred city? Yep. And is there a hero, a commoner-prince no less, chiseled, athletic, agile and a really, really lucky swashbuckler? Indeed. Is there a bright spark between the princess and the swashbuckler? Of course, though unrequited, but with lots of chemistry with a closing, almost chaste kiss. Is there an antagonist, a traitorous, duplicitous villain? You bet. Is there a nifty story? Well, kind of. It’s a bit thin, a bit chaotic, dealing with a magical dagger that possesses the ability to bend time. But is there a nice twist at the end? Definitely. Jake Gyllenhaal stars as Dastan, the street-wise, adopted son of King Sharaman; Gemma Arterton is the spunky, lovely Princess Tamina; and Ben Kingsley portrays the dastardly villain who covets power and gold and his brother’s throne. Of course, the movie defines action. In fact, one element that A scene from Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time. makes Prince of Persia exciting is the introduction of parkour to countless chase scenes. Parkour was introduced in France as an urban form of free running, filled with controlled, acrobatic movements involving jumping, climbing and vaulting. Free runners, also called Traceurs, move with speed and agility from building to building, over walls, across concrete barriers, all if which are found in any city setting. Actually, the long, very intense opening of the James Bond movie, Casino Royale, began with a long chase involving breathtaking parkour. In Prince of Persia, Dastan practices hair-raising parkour as he runs through back city streets and across rooftops, all to great effect. But then, he’s a swashbuckler. It would be easy to get snarky and pick on the Prince of Persia. But the bottom line is that kids will love this movie. For them, it’s pure entertainment. Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time. Directed by Mike Newell. Starring Jake Gyllenhaal, Gemma Arterton and Ben Kingsley. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Now streaming on Disney+/VUDU/Prime.

The definition may not quickly come to mind, but we know one when we see it, and Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time is a genuine 6th century pull-out-all-the-stops swashbuckler. Is there lots of swordplay? You bet. Is there a stunning princess whose subjects live behind the massive walls of a sacred city? Yep. And is there a hero, a commoner-prince no less, chiseled, athletic, agile and a really, really lucky swashbuckler? Indeed. Is there a bright spark between the princess and the swashbuckler? Of course, though unrequited, but with lots of chemistry with a closing, almost chaste kiss. Is there an antagonist, a traitorous, duplicitous villain? You bet. Is there a nifty story? Well, kind of. It’s a bit thin, a bit chaotic, dealing with a magical dagger that possesses the ability to bend time. But is there a nice twist at the end? Definitely. Jake Gyllenhaal stars as Dastan, the street-wise, adopted son of King Sharaman; Gemma Arterton is the spunky, lovely Princess Tamina; and Ben Kingsley portrays the dastardly villain who covets power and gold and his brother’s throne. Of course, the movie defines action. In fact, one element that A scene from Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time. makes Prince of Persia exciting is the introduction of parkour to countless chase scenes. Parkour was introduced in France as an urban form of free running, filled with controlled, acrobatic movements involving jumping, climbing and vaulting. Free runners, also called Traceurs, move with speed and agility from building to building, over walls, across concrete barriers, all if which are found in any city setting. Actually, the long, very intense opening of the James Bond movie, Casino Royale, began with a long chase involving breathtaking parkour. In Prince of Persia, Dastan practices hair-raising parkour as he runs through back city streets and across rooftops, all to great effect. But then, he’s a swashbuckler. It would be easy to get snarky and pick on the Prince of Persia. But the bottom line is that kids will love this movie. For them, it’s pure entertainment. Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time. By Chris Honoré Lilo and Stitch is a Disney animated feature, released in 2002, and nominated for an Oscar at the 75th Awards ceremony. It was hand-drawn with a rich palette of lush, vivid colors. It’s family friendly, poignant, and at times even beguiling and will bring to mind the extraordinary film E.T., long overdue to be discovered by a new generation of kids. At the center of the story, set on the Hawaiian island of Kauai, are Lilo (Daveigh Chase), a 7-year-old Hawaiian girl, and her older teen sister Nani (Tia Carrera). They recently lost their parents in a car accident, and are now orphaned. Lilo, always rambunctious, is now struggling to cope with her loss. She is lonely, ostracized from her hula class, and troubled at school. Nani, feeling a bit desperate, takes her to an animal shelter where they pick out a “dog,” which is a small blue koala-like critter that she names Stitch. In reality Stitch is an escaped E.T. from a world faraway. He’s actually an experiment called 620, and created to cause a world of chaos. Though Lilo and Nani have a strong sister bond despite their arguments, their social worker, Cobra Bubbles (Ving Rhanes), doubts that Nani can care for Lilo alone. He thinks Lilo is too quirky, feeds peanut butter to the fish and takes strange pictures of beachgoers, and has strange-looking dolls. Meanwhile, since Stitch has escaped from his home planet, two representatives, mad scientist Dr. Jumba Jookiba (David Ogden Stiers), 620’s creator, and agent Wendell Pleakley (Kevin McDonald) of the Galactic Federation, are sent to earth to look for him. Though Stitch was created to cause chaos and bedevilment, Lilo and the diminutive E.T fashion a strong bond, and with Nani form a small nuclear family, referred to in Hawaiian as O’hana. Gradually the idea of O’hana comes to be the center of the story. Lilo introduces Stitch to Elvis albums, hula dancing, and surfing with Nani. Meanwhile the two Federation E.T.s are in the hunt for Stitch. Lilo and Stich is filled with gags and energy and intergalactic conflict. Kids will enjoy the characters in a story that ends with an action-packed aerial chase. Lilo and Stitch. Directed by Dean DeBlois & Christopher Sanders, Walt Disney animation. articles.text: Part 45 of an ongoing biweekly series. Just before the pandemic in 2019, I spent a month walking the Camino de Santiago in northern Spain. This is the most wonderful place I have seen anywhere for walkers. For those unfamiliar with the Camino, it is a popular pilgrimage started in the middle ages. People from all over the world walk this route for spiritual reflection, to admire the cultural heritage and beauty of the country, or simply for the exercise and pleasure of walking. There are actually numerous routes of the Camino de Santiago (The Way of St. James, as example) starting in different countries in Europe, all winding hundreds of kilometers, and all ending up at the main cathedral in the city of Santiago de Compostela in northwest Spain. Like most people who make this trek, after arriving at the Camino, I didn’t get onto a train or bus or into a car for a month, but covered 267 kilometers, The pedestrian trails take many forms over the length of the Camino, from dirt paths in the country, to paved paths in the villages, to passages over historical Roman bridges. walking from place to place along a marked route that passes through countryside, along various roads, through wonderful small villages and some larger cities. Walkers stay in different types of numerous accommodations, have their meals, and drink coffee in the many locally owned establishments along the way. I found it an incredible journey, both introspective and fun. The only reservations I made were for my first and last nights in Spain. Considered a prime example of the more recently named “slow tourism” movement, it represents a choice of experience and meaningful reflection, instead of trying to squeeze in too much in as little time as possible—a perfect fit for the walking experience. What I think is especially relevant about this place for us in Piedmont, is the remarkable accommodation of the pedestrian in virtually all the small towns, villages and larger cities that walkers encounter along the way. There are many places to stop and rest along streets where pedestrians clearly have the right of way. And in the medium sized, and (somewhat) larger sized cities through which this Camino passes, you experience carefully thought out pedestrian car-free zones that have become natural municipal plazas and gathering places used by both visitors and locals. The final destination of all the Camino routes is the Praza Obradoiro in front of the Catedral in Santiago de Compostela. Not a very large city, with around 96,000 population, its urban design is highly influenced by accommodation of the incredible number of pedestrians who arrive here on foot and experience the place strictly as pedestrians.
articles.title: El Camino de Santiago

articles.text: Piedmont to try self-haul program this summer The City of Piedmont is planning a program that offers free compost for Piedmont residents to pick up every Friday during the summer months, as weather and availability allow. This pilot program is different than recent free compost giveaway events, in that the compost will be available to residents to pick up from an unattended pile every Friday starting at 8:00 a.m. The compost will be available in a dumpster box located outside the entrance to the City’s Corporation Yard located at 898 Red Rock Road. The site is now open every Friday and will close for the season in the fall. The compost is firstcome, first-served, and City staff cannot guarantee availability of compost. To pick up compost, residents should bring a shovel, container, and gloves to load the materials. Pickup trucks must have a tarp on their loads. The compost originally comes from the green waste (yard trimmings and food waste) that is collected by Republic Services in communities participating in curbside organics collection services. The green waste is brought to a processing plant in Richmond where it is converted into a highly aerobic, microbial compost. The compost making process involves the careful mixing of the waste and monitoring of the carbon to nitrogen ratio, CO2, temperature, and moisture. As the compost is locally based and free, it models the concept of a circular economy, where a resource is used and reused in a cycle that turns “waste” back into new products or materials than can reenter the supply chain. This process helps to keep organic materials from emitting greenhouse gasses in the landfill and creates opportunities to use these nutrient-rich resources to regenerate our soils. Mixing compost with soil aids in water retention and pest control and helps plants thrive. Senate Bill 1383, a state law that went into effect January 1, 2022, requires all municipalities to collect organic waste from residents and businesses and that it be composted. More information can be found on the City’s news and notifications page. If questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager, Alyssa Dykman at adykman@piedmont.ca.gov or (510) 420-3058.
articles.title: Free compost program for residents

articles.text: The Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover (VIPER) will be on board NASA’s Artemis 1, the 2023 trip to the moon, NASA’s first since 1972. The public got its first look at a full-scale replica of NASA’s water-hunting Moon rover last weekend at Chabot Space & Science Center in the Oakland hills. VIPER (Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover) will be launched in 2023 on a journey to the Moon’s South Pole in search of ice and other potential resources. The lunar rover is part of NASA’s Artemis missions, which will return astronauts to the Moon and land the first woman and first person of color on the lunar surface. VIPER will scout the lunar South Pole of the moon to look for ice and other resources to help enable long-term human exploration of the Moon and other parts of deep space. The model’s debut was a part of the NASA Artemis preview weekend hosted by NASA’s Ames Research Center. The event featured exhibits, hands-on activities, and Ames employees who have contributed to the Artemis lunar missions. In Artemis I, the most powerful rocket in the world takes f light, leading the way for humanity’s return to the Moon for the first time since Apollo 17 in December 1972. The 100-day mission will answer big questions about lunar water and how it can be used for future human space exploration.

articles.text: The Salvation Army serving Alameda County will celebrate its fifth Certified Nurse Assistant (CNA) Training Program class on Thursday, June 2 at 11 a.m. at Oakland Garden Street Center, 2794 Garden Street in Oakland. The graduation ceremony will recognize 14 graduates for their successful completion of the program. The Salvation Army’s Certified Nurse Assistant Training Program is conducted in partnership with the Quest Nursing Education Center. Over 90 percent of past graduates have secured jobs in the healthcare industry. The program also helps some students who have been unhoused and struggled with addiction get their lives back on track. The Training Program lasts five-weeks, consisting of soft skills training, online lessons, and a practical lesson at Quest School of Nursing. The program costs $1,500 per student, but full scholarships are available. Students receive new shoes, scrubs, stethoscopes, and other supplies upon graduation. Participants in the CNA Training Program are individuals who are currently or have recently been involved in local homeless or recovery-based programs. The Salvation Army believes in a wholistic approach to social services. The nonprofit provides essentials to families and individuals in need but also provides tools to lead them on a path to self-sufficiency, including Workforce Development Training In Alameda County, The Salvation Army not only provides the CNA Training Program, but also a Construction Training Program. To learn more, e-mail privilege. chadwick@usw.salvationarmy. org or call 510.383.9300 x1209.

The returning group – four mothers, seven two-year-olds, and two one-year-old calves – are all descendants of the iconic ‘Pablo Allard’ herd. These are the first calves born since the addition of two Yellowstone males back in 2019. The introduction of these males marked the second step in the conservation program, intended to diversify the genetics of future offspring of Oakland Zoo’s herd. The calves, along with their mothers, have lived for the past Two adult American Bisons and their calf seen at Oakland Zoo’s California Trail in May. Four mothers, seven two-yearolds, and two one-year-old calves were transpoorted on May 26 from Oakland Zoo to their anscestral home on Blackfeet Nation land near Yellowstone National Park in Montana. two years in the 13-acre habitat at the zoo’s California Trail. They are now old enough to make the trip to Montana. Since the program’s start in 2018, 30 calves have been born at Oakland Zoo. With the latest trip, 24 bison have been returned to Montana. The Zoo welcomed four new calves earlier this month, and the Zoo expects more to come during this year’s mating season. The multi-pronged effort for genetic diversity ensures the health and longevity of future American bison generations; the species reached near-extinction in the early 1900s when millions were killed during the westward expansion for grasslands needed to feed livestock. Though their numbers have increased tremendously, herds in the wild, and in private and public reserves, are quite inbred. Bison have provided food and other crucial materials needed for survival on the prairie for millenia, but the loss of this iconic animal also severed the spiritual connection to wildlife and the land. This conservation effort is not only significant in strengthening wild herds, but also has a vital cultural significance to the Blackfeet Nation. articles.text: A generous offer from Nancy and Dave DeRoche provided the opportunity for the Walking on Wednesdays group to have a second tour of the legacy of architect Albert Farr in Piedmont. Nancy and Dave shared that Farr was the owner of their Oakland Avenue house for 25 years in the early 20th Century. He didn’t design it, but made major modifications. One week earlier, Will Adams, a planner, urban designer, architect, and Post feature writer, led a tour of some of Farr’s most famous buildings in Piedmont, including City Hall, and Piedmont Community Church. Dave DeRoche has collected ancient artwork from Africa, Oceania, and the Americas for decades, so the group knew his house would be special. Will Adams was available to come back, so this also provided the opportunity to see more Farr-designed homes before visiting the DeRoche house. A large turnout of 37 people and two K-9 best friends showed up at the Exedra on a lovely Wednesday morning, May 25. As the group assembled, another offer from Dave and Nancy was shared with the group. Their upper Oakland Avenue portion of Piedmont, which continues up to Blair and Scenic Avenues, was a bit of bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters including Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there in some unique homes. Will Adams writes the biweekly “Walking Piedmont” feature in the Post in which he observes “the built environment of a beautiful city.” In his remarks at the start of the day’s walk, Will complimented the Wednesday Walking group as being a model for community walking. It was now time to two Albert Far-designed homes, one on Crocker Avenue and another nearby on Lincoln Avenue that Farr designed for the same owner. On the way, the walkers were able to revisit the recently sold mansion at Wildwood and Sheridan Avenue, one of Farr’s masterpieces. The group continued to Crocker to a house just off to the right at wildwood and Crocker, referring to research done by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi, Farr designed this house for Henry Drew Nichols. He was born in 1874 in New York and moved to Oakland in 1890. In June 1900, he married Ethel Kellogg, the granddaughter of Hiram Tubbs who founded the Tubbs Cordage Company in San Francisco, a business that started during the Gold Rush and was the first to manufacture rope west of New England. In 1905, Nichols contracted Farr and builder Charles Stockholm to build the two-story frame house on the east side of Crocker Avenue. The cost of construction was $11,370, and Henry and Ethel moved in just two months before the San Francisco earthquake in April 1906. Will Adams explained that Farr designed this Craftsman house high on the lot to provide views of San Francisco Bay from the West-facing rooms. It is a six bedroom, four and a half bath, and 7,818 square foot home. Large curved bays in the living room and dining room provided expansive views of the Bay in 1905. Nichols lived in the house until 1922 when he again hired Farr to build a second home around the corner on Lincoln. The walkers continued up to the second Farr house on Lincoln. It wraps around to Crocker, where there is a driveway leading to a gate with a garage, and the back of the house. The front of the house is on Lincoln, and the entrance is less visible with an ivy-covered wall and columns providing privacy. It is the childhood home of Saturday Night Live cast member Chloe Fineman, a 2006 graduate of Piedmont High School. It was now time to visit the DeRoche house, where Nancy said the house was built in 1897 for a member of Frank C. Havens’ family. She and Dave led the group past Pre-Columbian Aztec and Mayan art objects into the house. A set of stairs with a 19th Century feel to them took the walkers to the living area where there are countless museum-quality pieces of Tribal Art, some 2,000 years old, and one estimated at 3.000 years old. Many of them were burial pieces from Africa, as well as Central and South America. At the back of the house, Nancy had beverages, cakes, and other refreshments ready for the group to enjoy, The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Walking on Wednesday members gathered on the front steps at the home of Nancy and Dave DeRoche on May 25. Pictured are Judy Wang, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Pricilla Wanerus, Melba Yee, Judith Lee, Charlene Louie, Lois Price, Jim Kuo, Sarah Johnson, Elane Rehr, Winston Lee, Siow Fang Tan, Martin Levy, Quincy Dong, Dave DeRoche, Nancy DeRoche, Pat Keller, Phil Witte, Sherry Jacobs, Sharon Ho, Pat McMahon, Stella Houston, Helen Dong, Laura Goldman, Kat Lang, Cheryl Stanton, Bob Wong, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Alicia Rivera, Elizabeth Richter, Adrienne Hamlin, Harriette Louie, Eric Behrens, Christine Calliste, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, and Will Adams.

articles.text: The first time I made these “foolproof” biscuits, I followed the original recipe for Strawberry Drop Biscuits from New York Times Cooking. They were a winner and I’ve kept the recipe for repeat versions. Jerrelle Guy’s recipe encourages switching up the fruit, using other berries or diced stone fruits. Now that we’re edging toward summer fruits, this is a perfect time to get this easy baking project into your rotation. These biscuits are just a hint sweet and perfect for breakfast, brunch, or afternoon tea. You could split them crosswise for a very fruity berry shortcake too. Blueberry Drop Biscuits Adapted from Jerrelle Guy, New York Times Cooking Makes 6 biscuits, each about 4” round INGREDIENTS • 1-1/2 cups all-purpose flour • 1/4 cup granulated sugar • 4 teaspoons baking powder • 1/8 teaspoon sea salt • 1/2 teaspoon finely grated lemon zest, just the outermost yellow part, optional • 6 tablespoons cold butter, cut into 1/2-inch cubes • 2/3 cup whole blueberries • 1/2 cup icy cold water • 1/4 cup heavy cream plus additional 1 tablespoon to brush on top • Turbinado sugar, or other coarse grind sugar to sprinkle on top INSTRUCTIONS 1. Place an oven rack in the center of the oven. Preheat oven to 425° F. Line a large baking sheet pan with parchment. Set aside 2. Whisk the flour, granulated sugar, baking powder, salt, and lemon zest in a large mixing bowl. Toss the pieces of butter into the flour mixture to coat. Using your fingers or a pastry cutter, work the butter into the flour until the mixture is mealy and small pieces of pea-size butter remain. (I prefer using my fingers for more control and tactile satisfaction. But if your fingers are warm, you may have to use a tool to prevent the butter getting too soft.) 3. Add the blueberries and toss with a fork to combine. Make a well in the center of the mixture and add the 1/2 cup ice cold water and 1/4 cup heavy cream. Continue tossing with the fork until the dough is just evenly damp and shaggy. Be careful to not overwork the dough too much. Add more water if needed, 1 teaspoon at a time, if the dough is too dry to work with. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, June 1, 2022 Photo by Deborah Quok Homemade Blueberry Drop Biscuits are delicious and easy to make. Blueberry Drop Biscuits…. Mmm good By Deborah Quok The first time I made these “foolproof” biscuits, I followed the original recipe for Strawberry Drop Biscuits from New York Times Cooking. They were a winner and I’ve kept the recipe for repeat versions. Jerrelle Guy’s recipe encourages switching up the fruit, using other berries or diced stone fruits. Now that we’re edging toward summer fruits, this is a perfect time to get this easy baking project into your rotation. These biscuits are just a hint sweet and perfect for breakfast, brunch, or afternoon tea. You could split them crosswise for a very fruity berry shortcake too. Blueberry Drop Biscuits Adapted from Jerrelle Guy, New York Times Cooking Makes 6 biscuits, each about 4” round INGREDIENTS • 1-1/2 cups all-purpose flour • 1/4 cup granulated sugar • 4 teaspoons baking powder • 1/8 teaspoon sea salt • 1/2 teaspoon finely grated lemon zest, just the outermost yellow part, optional • 6 tablespoons cold butter, cut into 1/2-inch cubes • 2/3 cup whole blueberries • 1/2 cup icy cold water • 1/4 cup heavy cream plus additional 1 tablespoon to brush on top • Turbinado sugar, or other coarse grind sugar to sprinkle on top INSTRUCTIONS 1. Place an oven rack in the center of the oven. Preheat oven to 425° F. Line a large baking sheet pan with parchment. Set aside 2. Whisk the flour, granulated sugar, baking powder, salt, and lemon zest in a large mixing bowl. Toss the pieces of butter into the flour mixture to coat. Using your fingers or a pastry cutter, work the butter into the flour until the mixture is mealy and small pieces of pea-size butter remain. (I prefer using my fingers for more control and tactile satisfaction. But if your fingers are warm, you may have to use a tool to prevent the butter getting too soft.) 3. Add the blueberries and toss with a fork to combine. Make a well in the center of the mixture and add the 1/2 cup ice cold water and 1/4 cup heavy cream. Continue tossing with the fork until the dough is just evenly damp and shaggy. Be careful to not overwork the dough too much. Add more water if needed, 1 teaspoon at a time, if the dough is too dry to work with. (It will be shaggy, with some dry bits, but needs to hold together enough to retain its shape when forming the dough into biscuits.) 4. Drop six mounds of dough onto the baking sheet, spacing at least 1-1/2 inches apart. This will be about 1/2 cup each of dough. Pat and shape the dough into as round a shape as the dough allows, firmly patting any stray bits of dough into place. 5. Lightly brush the tops with 1 tablespoon of heavy cream and sprinkle with turbinado sugar, or any other coarse sugar crystals. 6. Bake until deep golden brown and cooked through – about 15 minutes. Remove from the oven and transfer the biscuits to a wire rack to cool for about 5 minutes. 7. Serve warm or at room temperature. NOTE: The baked biscuits will freeze well. To serve, thaw and reheat in a 350°F oven for about 5 minutes. Take care to not overdo the reheating to avoid over-dry biscuits. Post your ad in the Call (510) 626-2468 nancy@cmc-ads.com Walking on Wednesday Taking a tour of architect Albert Farr’s former Piedmont home By Dick Carter A generous offer from Nancy and Dave DeRoche provided the opportunity for the Walking on Wednesdays group to have a second tour of the legacy of architect Albert Farr in Piedmont. Nancy and Dave shared that Farr was the owner of their Oakland Avenue house for 25 years in the early 20th Century. He didn’t design it, but made major modifications. One week earlier, Will Adams, a planner, urban designer, architect, and Post feature writer, led a tour of some of Farr’s most famous buildings in Piedmont, including City Hall, and Piedmont Community Church. Dave DeRoche has collected ancient artwork from Africa, Oceania, and the Americas for decades, so the group knew his house would be special. Will Adams was available to come back, so this also provided the opportunity to see more Farr-designed homes before visiting the DeRoche house. A large turnout of 37 people and two K-9 best friends showed up at the Exedra on a lovely Wednesday morning, May 25. As the group assembled, another offer from Dave and Nancy was shared with the group. Their upper Oakland Avenue portion of Piedmont, which continues up to Blair and Scenic Avenues, was a bit of bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Writers and painters including Jack London and Xavier Martinez lived there in some unique homes. Will Adams writes the biweekly “Walking Piedmont” feature in the Post in which he observes “the built environment of a beautiful city.” In his remarks at the start of the day’s walk, Will complimented the Wednesday Walking group as being a model for community walking. It was now time to two Albert Far-designed homes, one on Crocker Avenue and another nearby on Lincoln Avenue that Farr designed for the same owner. On the way, the walkers were able to revisit the recently sold mansion at Wildwood and Sheridan Avenue, one of Farr’s masterpieces. The group continued to Crocker to a house just off to the right at wildwood and Crocker, referring to research done by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi, Farr designed this house for Henry Drew Nichols. He was born in 1874 in New York and moved to Oakland in 1890. In June 1900, he married Ethel Kellogg, the granddaughter of Hiram Tubbs who founded the Tubbs Cordage Company in San Francisco, a business that started during the Gold Rush and was the first to manufacture rope west of New England. In 1905, Nichols contracted Farr and builder Charles Stockholm to build the two-story frame house on the east side of Crocker Avenue. The cost of construction was $11,370, and Henry and Ethel moved in just two months before the San Francisco earthquake in April 1906. Will Adams explained that Farr designed this Craftsman house high on the lot to provide views of San Francisco Bay from the West-facing rooms. It is a six bedroom, four and a half bath, and 7,818 square foot home. Large curved bays in the living room and dining room provided expansive views of the Bay in 1905. Nichols lived in the house until 1922 when he again hired Farr to build a second home around the corner on Lincoln. The walkers continued up to the second Farr house on Lincoln. It wraps around to Crocker, where there is a driveway leading to a gate with a garage, and the back of the house. The front of the house is on Lincoln, and the entrance is less visible with an ivy-covered wall and columns providing privacy. It is the childhood home of Saturday Night Live cast member Chloe Fineman, a 2006 graduate of Piedmont High School. It was now time to visit the DeRoche house, where Nancy said the house was built in 1897 for a member of Frank C. Havens’ family. She and Dave led the group past Pre-Columbian Aztec and Mayan art objects into the house. A set of stairs with a 19th Century feel to them took the walkers to the living area where there are countless museum-quality pieces of Tribal Art, some 2,000 years old, and one estimated at 3.000 years old. Many of them were burial pieces from Africa, as well as Central and South America. At the back of the house, Nancy had beverages, cakes, and other refreshments ready for the group to enjoy, The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Walking on Wednesday members gathered on the front steps at the home of Nancy and Dave DeRoche on May 25. Pictured are Judy Wang, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Pricilla Wanerus, Melba Yee, Judith Lee, Charlene Louie, Lois Price, Jim Kuo, Sarah Johnson, Elane Rehr, Winston Lee, Siow Fang Tan, Martin Levy, Quincy Dong, Dave DeRoche, Nancy DeRoche, Pat Keller, Phil Witte, Sherry Jacobs, Sharon Ho, Pat McMahon, Stella Houston, Helen Dong, Laura Goldman, Kat Lang, Cheryl Stanton, Bob Wong, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Alicia Rivera, Elizabeth Richter, Adrienne Hamlin, Harriette Louie, Eric Behrens, Christine Calliste, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, and Will Adams.
