articles.text: Judith Swope Clark, 49-year resident of Piedmont, died May 27, 2022 of Lewy Body dementia complications at her home in Piedmont. She was 76. Born on July 26, 1945 in Howard Memorial Hospital in Willits, California, she was the daughter of Glenn Swope and Anita Hoffman. Her parents divorced in the early 1950s, a very difficult event for Judie, and they both continued to live most of the rest of their lives in Willits. Her father, a CHP officer, died in 1995, and her mother died in 2010. Except for a brief detour with her mother and sister to Oakland during her parents’ breakup, Judie grew up in Willits alongside Tom Clark in the same class. The precocious Judie skipped 8th grade and stepped ahead to high school. Judie and Tom began dating in 1962 when they were 15. They married in 1968 in Berkeley. In 1973, shortly after Tom began practicing law, Judie and Tom purchased a house in Piedmont, where they have lived ever since. Judie was noteworthy for her fast mind, sharp wit, reading abilities, artistic sensibilities, organization skills, gentleness, love for animals and children, compassion for the disadvantaged, and completing daily New York Times crossword puzzles in ink. She graduated from Willits High School in 1962 and in 1966 received a B.S. degree in Anthropology from the University of California, Berkeley. For a brief period she taught school in Oakland. After helping put Tom through law school by working at UC Berkeley in various administrative capacities, Judie graduated from Golden Gate Law School in 1977 and began practicing law at the Oakland law firm where she clerked while attending law school. He legal career ended their daughter Olivia was born in 1978. Judie devoted much of her adult life to caring for her daughter and helping her overcome serious medical problems, including seizures resulting from removal of a brain tumor in 1984. Judie was a very active quilter, designing and making quilts, often in her house, with two separate groups of other Piedmont mothers. She was also active for many years in Junior Alliance that supported Lincoln Child Center in Oakland and Piedmany hours and overnight visits with Tom and Judie until his mother, Melanie, suddenly died at age 40 In 2012 Judie was diagnosed with Lewy Body dementia and gradually lost her ability to speak, stand or walk. Eventually, Tom hired caregivers to help Judie in their home. In 2018 Tom added to their house a new downstairs bedroom, bathroom and kitchen extension, and installed a chairlift from the sidewalk up the 52 steps to their house. Tom’s goal always was to keep Judie at home with him and a team of caregivers, no matter how her condition might worsen, and to ensure that Judie’s life would be as good as he could make it. Judie picked out their Piedmont house, loved it dearly and took the lead responsibility for a major renovation to the house in 1988. During their 61 years together, Judie was a faithful, honest and loving friend, as well as wife to Tom for 54 years. Tom has lost the best friend in his life. He will be eternally grateful that Judie civilized him, treated him so well despite his shortcomings and devoted her life to caring for their daughter Olivia. During her final years, Judie received excellent care from her several caregivers, Tina Smith, Ovetta and Shaniesa Gill, Nikki Howell, Nanettee Cansceco and Eden Wildemichael. Oakland Kaiser Permanente staff, especially nurse Dee Dee Bellong, provided wonderful in-home hospice care during the final weeks of her life. Judie was beloved by Tom’s entire family. She was close to Dave Sinclair, her brother-in-law, and Warren Jorgensen, both Willits classmates. She was particularly grateful for her enduring lifelong friendship with LeAnna Spence, a classmate from Willits. In addition Judie cherished her close friendship with Tom’s cousin James Curtiss and her sister-in-law Joan’s friend Peggy Cash. Judie is survived by her husband Tom; her daughter Olivia of Pleasant Hill; her niece Sandhya Clark Singh (Steven) of Teaneck, New Jersey; her sister Jayne of Los Angeles; Jayne’s children Troy Brown (Mary) of San Pablo and Shari Brown of Santa Rosa. She is additionally survived by many friends and an extended family. Judie Clarke, a Piedmont resident for nearly 50 years, passed away on May 27. She was 76. mont’s Dress Best for Less that supported the Piedmont Education Foundation Additionally, Judie was also very involved with her mother’s family winery in Napa Valley. Her maternal grandmother Rose was one of 12 children of late- 1800s Swiss emigrants Anton and Caterina Nichelini who homesteaded and founded the still-operating Nichelini winery in Chiles Valley in the eastern hills of Napa Valley. Judie was instrumental in the formation of the Nichelini Family Corporation that gathered the fractional interests of Anton and Caterina’s far-flung progeny. For many years Judie served as Secretary of the Nichelini Family Corporation, and was always partial to her great uncle Fred Nichelini, the founding President of the corporation. Tom was a self-taught winemaker. Judie and Tom, together with Tom’s sister Joan and her husband Dave Sinclair, and Tom’s brother Hugh, purchased property in 1982 in Sonoma County near Calistoga. Over the next 33 years, operating under the name Petrified Forest Vineyards, they maintained rental property, planted a vineyard from which they made 22 annual vintages of wine, and constructed a cabin retreat. Judie did not drink wine, but happily tolerated the family vineyard and wine making. Judie and Tom especially enjoyed providing a second home to Micah Stamps, the grandson of their Willits classmates Sherry and Aubrey Stamps. articles.text: On a beautiful Sunday afternoon, Sunday, May 29, neighbors and friends were invited by Lisa Chan Carnazzo, a realtor at the Grubb Company, to meet her client and one of Piedmont’s newest residents. Joanne Larson had just moved into Piedmont and was excited to meet her new neighbors. Carnazzo also invited Piedmont police officers Thomas Krolczyk and Jorge Faucher to come and meet Larson. articles.text: PHS and MHS students danced the night away in the Rotunda at Chabot Space and Science Center. Piedmont High School’s Class of 2022 was treated to a Senior Prom on Saturday, April 30 at the Chabot Space and Science Center in the Oakland hills. Students enjoyed casino games, a live band, a bounty of food and beverages, and a planetarium show leading up to the night’s dance party. Two years ago, 2020, the school had no Prom due to the COVID pandemic, and last year the graduating class had a modified Prom in the school gym. Students from 2021 will forever be reminded of the gym locale when they see their photos of prom dresses paired with gym sneakers, as only soft soled shoes were allowed on the gym floor. The class of 2022, has largely been able to experience most school traditions, and the smiles on everyone’s faces showed the relief and enjoyment. The grand evening was also a send off for Principal Adam Littlefield who Photos by Jonathan Payne, Katie Goldberg and Kevin Lee will be retiring at year’s end. For Piedmont’s Class of 2022, it was a night to remember, and held special importance given the interruptions of tradition of the last two years. Members of the 2022 Piedmont High class all dolled and cleaned up for prom. articles.text: Editor: It is astonishing to see the number of Piedmont Unified School District administration and teacher resignations and retirements this school year. With this, a heightened level of animosity is brewing within a growing contingency of Piedmont families towards PUSD. Piedmont parents continue to struggle to ensure their child’s academic needs are met while simultaneously protecting their mental health. During the past two years, the leadership of Randall Booker and Cheryl Wozniak turned their backs on the students and allowed the erosion of PUSD. Students were not the focus of their concerns. Their main concern was the goal of fulfilling DEI initiatives. It is unsettling that PUSD leadership instructed teachers to devote energy to social initiatives rather than utilize the time to help children academically; while failing to earmark additional funds to the Wellness Center to help struggling students. Although DEI is a needed element, it is essential that the PUSD leadership realign its current focus on the needs of the students: academics and mental health. Along with many PUSD families, I maintain hope that the school board will retain a new Superintendent whose sole focus is the educational and mental welfare of students rather than politicized agendas. Ask yourself: “how many more Piedmont families must send their children to local private schools before PUSD leadership wakes up and realizes that there is a major problem within the district?”
articles.title: PUSD needs to get back to educating our kids

articles.text: Scouting. Almost all will develop hobbies that will add interest throughout the rest of their lives. At least one will use it to save another person’s life and many will credit it with saving their own. Of the one hundred, 17 will later become Scout leaders and will provide leadership to thousands of additional Scouts. Only two of the one hundred will reach the rank of Eagle, the highest honor for uniformed Scouts. On May 22, five members of Piedmont’s Troop 1 were celebrated at a National Court of Honor. With paper plates made just for the event, you know it’s a pretty big deal. The ceremony started with the Troop 1 Committee chair, the legendary John Stewart, a longtime former Troop 1 Scoutmaster, convening the event. Senior patrol leader Liam Campbell, the master of ceremony, introduced the Four Winds, a Troop 1 tradition. The winds are two of four Scouts who discuss the importance of the Scout Law. The winds were followed by the Path to Eagle, where Scouts explained the significance of each rank leading up to Eagle. Rank requirements were discussed along with other rank qualifications. Next up was one of my personal favorite parts: the remarks by Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill. I loved hearing him talk about the Eagle Scouts. After the “main event” of the ceremonial presentation of the Eagle medals came a very special Troop 1 tradition. All the patches and merit badges New Eagle Scouts Aaron Drumm (left) Fisher Gibbs, Nicholas Kho, Haik Kibarian, and Theodore Markopoulos. earned by the Eagle Scouts are framed and presented to the honorees as a keepsake. The Eagle Scouts then delivered their own “Eagle remarks,” an opportunity for them to thank everyone who helped on their journey as well as share some stories from their trail to Eagle. The Eagle remarks are among the highlights of the Court of Honor. Their stories and experiences of becoming Eagle really touched me and inspired me to work towards the goal of Eagle. Lastly, an enormous congratulations to the new Eagle Scouts: Aaron Drumm, Fisher Gibbs, Haik Kibarian. Nicholas Koh, Theodore Markopoulos, and their families. Smantha Pell is a member of Piedmont Scouts Troop 1. Troop One Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill (right) talks about new Eagle Aaron Drumm. Scoutmaster Brian Cantrill (right) talks about new Eagle Nicholas Koh. Eagle Scout Haik Kibarian provides comments at the Eagle ceremony.

articles.text: Former Piedmont City Administrator steps in to help his hometown Former Piedmont City Administrator Paul Benoit is stepping in as interim City Manager of Astoria, Oregon, his hometown. Benoit retired from Piedmont in 2019 and moved back to Oregon. He has worked in various interim and ad-hoc capacities for Piedmont’s city government throughout the pandemic. Piedmont’s City Council named Benoit as a Special Assistant in the Measure UU implementation project (Community Pool) at its January 19, 2021 meeting. In that role, Benoit acted as an assistant to City Administrator Sara Lillevand throughout the project’s timeline, as needed. Benoit also acted in an interim City Administrator in June 2021 when Lillevand took time to care for a family member. During his tenure in Piedmont, Benoit was credited with modernizing City Hall technology, transforming Piedmont’s Recreation Department, and assembling a competent team of city staff. He succeeded Geoff Grote who served as Piedmont City Administrator for 25 years. Benoit was City Administrator from 2014 to 2019 after serving as Astoria’s City Manager for seven years. He also served as community development director in Astoria, and as assistant city manager of Alameda. Benoit will take over Astoria City Manager Brett Estes’ role beginning July 4. articles.text: Piedmont Planning Commission approved the draft 6th cycle housing element with modifications at a May 12 meeting. Now the document will be up to City Council for consideration before it is submitted to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for review. The draft housing element, published by the city on April 8, considers new land uses, housing types, code changes, and other initiatives that aim to accommodate nearly 600 new housing units in Piedmont by 2031. Piedmont’s Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA), or how many new and affordable units the city must identify space for, is exactly 587. Piedmont declined to appeal its RHNA, making it an outlier in small-population municipalities across the state. articles.text: Drop boxes for mail ballots on Highland Way The California Primary Election is Tuesday, June 7. The entirely vote-by-mail election includes selections for candidates for U.S. Senate and House of Representatives, as well as statewide elected officials, including Governor, and Alameda County officials. The general election will occur on Tuesday, November 8, 2022. Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, this year’s election will be entirely vote-by-mail; all registered voters should have received a vote-by-mail ballot by this date. Who’s on the ballot Current U.S. Senator Alex Padilla will face nine challengers. Re p. Ba rba r a Lee, a long-standing member of Congress representing District 13 (Piedmont, Oakland, Berkeley), is running for District 12 office against four candidates. Gov. Gavin Newsom is on the ballot with 25 others and is running for a second term after withstanding a recall election in 2021. Buffy Wickes, Piedmont elected representative in the State Assembly, is on the ballot, and Tony Thurmond the State School Superintendent is up for re-election. For a full list of candidates, visit https://www.acgov.org/rov_ app/candidatelist?electionid=247. Vote by Mail drop-boxes Drop-boxes are located on Highland Way and Highland Avenue outside Wells Fargo Bank. The boxes will be open until 8 p.m. on Election Day, June 7. The Veterans’ Memorial Hall serves as an Accessible Voting Location. Any resident of Alameda County may visit the Veterans’ Hall and cast their ballot or drop off their vote-by-mail ballot, which will be open June 4 through June 7. A drop box on Highland Way is now open for mailed ballots for the June 7 California Primary Election.

articles.text: Editor: Piedmont has a history of using city resources to exclude non-white families from the community. But we have an opportunity to redress those wrongs because state law requires California cities to find sites for low-income housing. To avoid again using city power to exclude, segregate, and stigmatize residents, current City of Piedmont policy is to “Support equitable distribution of affordable units across the City.” City staff has unveiled a draft list of sites that mostly complies with the policy of equitable distribution although nearly half of the 211 required low-income units appear in the city corporation yard in Moraga Canyon. City Council reaction to the draft list will, in large part, determine how far Piedmont has come from our exclusionary past. The Council’s most telling choice will be whether to comply with the city’s stated policy of “equitable distribution of affordable units across the city.” Equitable distribution has become an issue because public comment includes the recommendation that the Council reassign low-income units from elsewhere in Piedmont to Blair Park across Moraga Avenue from the 100 units assigned to the corporation yard. Blair Park is an isolated former landfill where pedestrians and bicyclists regularly encounter speeding vehicles with drivers whose sight corridors are limited by the curves of Moraga Avenue. Editor: Piedmont has a history of using city resources to exclude non-white families from the community. But we have an opportunity to redress those wrongs because state law requires California cities to find sites for low-income housing. To avoid again using city power to exclude, segregate, and stigmatize residents, current City of Piedmont policy is to “Support equitable distribution of affordable units across the City.” City staff has unveiled a draft list of sites that mostly complies with the policy of equitable distribution although nearly half of the 211 required low-income units appear in the city corporation yard in Moraga Canyon. City Council reaction to the draft list will, in large part, determine how far Piedmont has come from our exclusionary past. The Council’s most telling choice will be whether to comply with the city’s stated policy of “equitable distribution of affordable units across the city.” Equitable distribution has become an issue because public comment includes the recommendation that the Council reassign low-income units from elsewhere in Piedmont to Blair Park across Moraga Avenue from the 100 units assigned to the corporation yard. Blair Park is an isolated former landfill where pedestrians and bicyclists regularly encounter speeding vehicles with drivers whose sight corridors are limited by the curves of Moraga Avenue. Indeed, pedestrian use of Moraga Avenue proved so dangerous that a plan to locate soccer fields in Blair Park a decade ago had to be abandoned. The Safer Streets Plan recently adopted by OPINIONthe Council states, moreover, that “The Moraga Avenue/Red Rock Road location has been removed from the 2014 list (i.e., of pedestrian safety improvements) because of feasibility issues in providing adequate pedestrian access in Blair Park…” An observer aware of Piedmont’s history and of the suggestion to locate nearly all the 210 State-required low-income units in Blair Park, could reasonably conclude that we had reverted to our exclusionary past. Stigmatizing low-income families by isolating them in Blair Park would reek of a history most Piedmonters regret. I endorse use of the corporation yard for low-income housing. But as a Piedmonter who believes that our shameful history compels us to honor our inclusionary policies, I object to leaving open the possibility of reassigning housing units now shown elsewhere to Blair Park. Such a reassignment would signal a cynical reversion to the despicable exclusionary policies of the last century. The Council should honor current policy and explicitly reject such reassignment. –Ralph Catalano 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Allyson Aleksey PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Piedmont Police Department (PPD) partnered with University of Texas, San Antonio (UTSA) researchers on July 19, 2021 to conduct an analysis of calls for service. The city released the results of the analysis and its key findings on May 20. The city contracted the services of Dr. Michael Smith and Dr. Rob Tillyer from UTSA to analyze five years of data from the PPD. The purpose of the study was to analyze calls for service for frequency of bias-related calls from the public, and use information gathered as a basis for police intervention. The University focused its research on the type of calls for service which officers respond to. The city stated that the work is “part of the effort to understand bias and the historical role racism has played in Piedmont and the community-at-large, in order to better lead a city which is a safe, welcoming, and equitable place for all people committed to by the City Council in Resolution 60-2020.” “A key question that many communities are asking themselves, is whether there are alternatives to police response for certain types of calls,” Dr. Smith said. “What we’re interested in helping the city understand is the impact of calls that come into the department, how [that] drives [the department’s] responses, and whether or not there are potential racial or ethnic disparities in those calls.” The scope of the data covers July 2016 to July 2021, or a fiveyear range of data. The data report states that “[Piedmont] and Police Chief Jeremy Bowers were interested in an analysis that would examine the potential problem of bias by proxy in the city.” Key findings The majority of calls to the department over the five-year period involved ‘checking for evidence of a theft/burglary’ (14.9%), report of a ‘burglar alarm’ (12.7%), responding to ‘suspicious circumstances’ (9.1%), ‘ambulance emergency’ (7.4%), and ‘parking complaints’ (5.5%). The average time it took for an officer to respond to a call was four minutes, and 30% of calls resulted in officer arrival in under one minute. According to the UTSA report, some [focus group] participants expressed concerns about young people from outside the community coming into Piedmont to commit property crimes and were appreciative that PPD is responsive to concerns about suspicious persons when called. Other respondents were “clearly sensitive to being perceived as racially biased,” and expressed that PPD should not respond to calls about suspicious-looking individuals unless callers can specifically describe behaviors or mannerisms that suggest the potential for criminal activity. There was a consensus among the focus group participants about “the need for community engagement and education by the PPD on when residents should call the police about suspicious persons in their neighborhoods, what behaviors to watch out for, and questions to expect from PPD call- takers when residents call to report suspicious behavior.” To view the report in full, visit https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/city_news___notifications/ police_call_data_analysis_town_ hall_meeting_5_23. The published report includes questions asked to focus group participants and more key findings.
articles.title: Police Dept. studies key findings of Univ. of Texas study

articles.text: Piedmont Planning Department is now allowing residents to schedule building permit inspections online rather than come to City Hall. The city rolled out the new feature on May 9 – previously, building inspections had to be made by calling the department directly to book. To schedule a building inspection, visit https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning___building/building_ inspections. Select the date of your desired inspection. Appointments can be made 48 hours in advance of the date selected. To schedule an inspection online, you will need the property address, building permit number, your name, phone and email address, and the type of inspection. Daily inspection schedules will be posted on the city’s website by 9 a.m. every day. The city noted that this is an interim improvement that will likely last until the end of 2022, when the city expects to roll our a new public portal designed that residents may use to schedule inspections. articles.text: Piedmont Community Church through its Refugee Task Force will host a fundraising dinner on Saturday, June 4 at 6 p.m. to benefit the Putrenkov family, who recently escaped from the wartorn Donbas region of Ukraine. Alex Putrenkov, his wife Maryna and son Vlad are now safe and living with a family in Piedmont but are in need of financial aid to help them settle, become employed and to obtain reliable transportation. The evening will begin with a cocktail reception in the church courtyard before moving into the Guild Hall for a dinner at 7 p.m. The event will be capped off by a live auction at 8 p.m. A limited number of 100 tickets will be sold at $150. Tickets may be purchased online at piedmontchurch.org/RTF. Piedmont Community Church is located at 400 Highland Avenue.

articles.text: Groups across Piedmont have already begun celebrating and raising awareness for the 50th anniversary of the passage of Title IX legislation on June 23. Title IX is considered by many to be the most important law for equal rights for women after the 1918 right to vote. In 1971-72, only 7% of U.S. high school athletes were girls. Now, girls comprise 43% of high school athletes. Title IX of The Education Amendments Act of 1972 states: “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” A Piedmont Title IX Audit Task Force will present its findings and recommendations to the School Board on May 25, The meeting starts at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. Title IX T-shirts and hoodies can be purchased at the Piedmontstore.org to support Title IX activities. Donations are also accepted on the website and Title IX stickers are available at various locations at PHS.
articles.title: Piedmont celebrates 50-year anniversary of Title IX

articles.text: City Council approved the appropriation of an additional $30,000 from the facilities maintenance fund to pay for four electric vehicle (EV) charging stations on Magnolia Avenue by the Exedra. The city entered into a 10-year agreement with East Bay Community Energy (EBCE) for the project which initially was promoted as free. “The request for additional funds is related to the inclusion of an American with Disabilities Act (ADA) compliant parking space, and the sidewalk and curb ramp improvements that will be included as a result,” said Gonzales. “This additional component of the project will increase accessibility to Piedmont Park and the EV chargers for all our residents and park users. Unfortunately, EBCE doesn’t have the budget for these ADA improvements and as a result the city will be funding them.” The chargers on Magnolia are designed to provide EV charging service to four parking spaces, including one space to account for Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) requirements. EBCE sets pricing and performs maintenance at no cost to the city, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The city council approved a 90-minute parking limit for cars being charged. Construction is expected to occur this winter.
articles.title: City Council spends $30,000 on EV charging stations

articles.text: Alessandra Lanzara, a Piedmont resident and Physics Professor at the University of California in Berkeley is among the 261 members nominated this year to the American Academy of Art and Science (AAAS). The Academy is widely acknowledged as one of the most prestigious in the world. With this election Lanzara joins the company of illustrious AAAS members spanning multiple fields and professions starting with the founders of the Academy: John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Alexander Hamilton, and George Washington. Celebrated leaders, artists and scientists that profoundly shaped society have been members since, such as John F. Kennedy, Martin Luther King, Jr., Nelson Mandela, Georgia O’Keeffe, Gabriel Garcia Márquez, Alexander Graham Bell, Charles Darwin and Albert Einstein, in addition to more than 250 Nobel and Pulitzer Prize winners. “We are celebrating a depth of achievements in a breadth of areas,” said David Oxtoby, President of the American Academy. “These individuals excel in ways that excite us and inspire us at a time when recognizing excellence, commending expertise, and working toward the common good is absolutely essential to Alessandra Lanzara (left), children Daniel and Raffaello Banin, and huband Yoav Banin. Alessandra Lanzara in her laboratory at UC Berkeley, where she is an Endowed Professor and the Charles Kittel Chair in Physics. realizing a better future.” The new members will work together with the Academy to set the direction of research and analysis in science and technology policy, global security and international affairs, social policy, education, and the arts and humanities. “It is an incredible honor for me to join a circle of thinkers and visionaries who have inspired the history of humanity. As an immigrant to this country, this recognition means even more to me. Leaving my country and my family has required many sacrifices and to overcome a lot of challenges. Today, being awarded with this incredible recognition makes it all worthwhile,” said Lanzara. Lanzara arrived in the U.S. from Rome, Italy in 1999 to conduct post-doctoral research at Stanford University. “I thought I was going to be here for only six months,” Lanzara said, “but life often has a different plan for us, so here I am 20 years later.” Lanzara joined UC Berkeley’s physics faculty in 2002 and is the founder and director of the Center for Sustainable Materials and Innovation. She works in the area of quantum materials, materials where quantum phenomena dictate exceptional new properties. “If we are able to understand the fundamental physics that drives these properties, then we will be able to harvest these materials to drive revolutionary advances in electronics, quantum computing, energy and medical imaging,” said Lanzara. Lanzara has also been an active advocate for women in science and a promoter of kids engaging with science from a young age. She has served on the Scientific Board of the Lawrence Hall of Science, presented at the Scienza Palooza Fair, spoken at Nano High, and has been on the board of Piedmont Makers. Lanzara resides in Piedmont with her husband, Yoav Banin, an entrepreneur and Chief Product Officer at Nauto, and her two sons, Daniel Banin, a sophomore at Piedmont High School and Raffaello Banin, an 8th grader at Piedmont Middle School. “Piedmont is an incredible community; I have found many friends here and it has been great to see my kids thrive over the years through the Piedmont school system, inspired by incredible and dedicated teachers. I hope I can help to set a strong science program in the high school and continue being an inspiration for young women and young kids who want to pursue a scientific career,” said Lanzara. This article was written by staff members of The Piedmont Highlander, the student newspaper at Piedmont High School. TJ Stevko, CFP® Financial Advisor 370 Highland Avenue Suite 201 Piedmont, CA 94611 510-547-4589 edwardjones.com Member SIPC

Lanzara resides in Piedmont with her husband, Yoav Banin, an entrepreneur and Chief Product Officer at Nauto, and her two sons, Daniel Banin, a sophomore at Piedmont High School and Raffaello Banin, an 8th grader at Piedmont Middle School. “Piedmont is an incredible community; I have found many friends here and it has been great to see my kids thrive over the years through the Piedmont school system, inspired by incredible and dedicated teachers. I hope I can help to set a strong science program in the high school and continue being an inspiration for young women and young kids who want to pursue a scientific career,” said Lanzara. This article was written by staff members of The Piedmont Highlander, the student newspaper at Piedmont High School. articles.text: Piedmont High School’s first ever Guitar Engineering Showcase, held Thursday, May 19, was a monumental success with over 20 guitars on display along with end-of-the-year student projects. Parents, relatives, friends and community members perused the exhibits inside the engineering lab while sampling desserts and listening to the sounds of a student band formed from the class. Students Will Davies, Oliver Cheng, Hannah Govert, Jackson Thornborrow and Nathan Sturdivant developed the showcase as a fundraising event. It was their community service project to help with the continuation of the guitar engineering course for future years. They proposed building new guitars and auctioning them off to raise funds for purchasing next year’s materials. The primary focus of Guitar Engineering class is for students to learn the skills necessary to construct their own electric guitars. Students used many varieties of hand and power tools for Photos by Will Becker Marna Chamberlain’s Guitar Engineering students held a showcase on May 19, with a gallery of newly produced guitars, a fundraising auction for next year’s class, and a live band performance. Charlie Lambert (left) explains the circuitry in the Farris Saffouri’s guitar was on display at he first electric guitar he created this year. Guitar Engineering Showcase. body shaping. They also learned how to solder and make circuits for the electronic systems. After the guitars were completed, students were given the opportunity to participate individually or in groups on a community service project that incorporates skills learned throughout the year. As they worked on the guitars, the groups decided nothing would be better than a rock show for entertainment to drive attendance for the event and auction participation. The event started at 7:00 p.m. and by 7:30 there were close to 100 people happily chatting, eating and talking with the students about their experience in the class. At 7:45 there were over 150 people on the engineering lab and patio when the band, consisting of Davies, Govert, Thornborrow and Sturdivant, started to play. Once they started with the first few notes of “Basket Case,” by Green Day, the crowd joined in singing along and dancing just a bit. After the band’s fourth song the crowd demanded an encore. The student group had only played together once, but they were game for another song. All the musicians showed off their talents to the extreme and Sturdivant entertained the crowd all evening with his humor and showmanship. The evening ended with the closing of the auction and three guitars going to various community members as high bidders. Patrons all requested reassurance this will be an annual event. With the support of this community, that will likely happen. articles.text: There is a common misconception that summer vacation is a relic of the agrarian past when kids would be let out of school in the summer to help with the farming duties. While there is some truth to the notion that kids in rural communities took time off from school to help, this happened in the spring and fall when planting and harvesting occurred. Winter and summer were when many schools in agrarian societies met since that is when the kids had more free time. So where did the summer break come from? Escaping the heat. Before the school calendars were nationally synchronized, many schools were open yearround and students showed up whenever they could or chose to. The extreme heat of the East Coast summers caused many urban residents to escape to cooler environments and attendance at school was lowest in the summer. So that became the time for the big vacation. Summer Slide Is Real As any teacher will tell you, the “summer slide” – the loss of academic knowledge and functioning that occurs over summer break – is real, especially in low-income communities. Some research has found that the loss can be as much as one month. The questions then are: is the slide a problem and if so, how do we fight it? Should We Worry? Our first response as educators and parents is…Yes! But let’s examine this more carefully. Sports have off-seasons. Enjoy the summer and fight the “Summer Slide.” We all sleep. Performers don’t go year-round. Rest is an important part of healthy growth since it is where we can recover and solidify our gains. While the summer slide leads to a loss of learning, the information is not permanently lost. It just shifts away from the most readily available part of the brain. It often takes only a week to regain what we have “lost” over the summer. The flip side is that losing our scholastic gains can be a problem. Students work very hard to learn, score and achieve. To watch all of that wither away as our students play video games and sleep until 3:30 pm is difficult and scary. Plus, we have to wonder if our students would do even better if they gained instead of lost during the summer. How to Fight the Slide There are a myriad of ways to fight the summer slide, and there is no best way to do it. There is a consensus to keep their minds working. This can involve science-based camps, strategy games, summer school, yearround school, an hour of flashcards a day, etc… The point is not necessarily finding the optimal way to fight the slide, but finding any way to fight the slide and make sure it happens. It’s probably much more important that the fight happens than how you choose to fight it. Paul the Tutor (aka Paul Osborne) runs Paul the Tutor’s Education Services online and on Piedmont Avenue. They specialize in tutoring and test prep for non-traditional learners and traditional students. Paul is dyslexic, holds a Masters from the Harvard Graduate School of Education and authored of the LD SAT Study Guide. For more information, go to www.paulthetutors.com, email info@paulthetutors.com or call (510) 730-0390.

articles.text: Want to get a jump on the 6th-grade school year? Join Ted Scherman, a veteran teacher at Piedmont Middle School, for the popular boot camp just for sixth graders. The two-day camp helps students acclimate to a new school, make new acquaintances, and feel confident and ready when classes start. Sixth grade in Piedmont is the first time students from the three elementary schools will be in the same school. The camp includes indoor and outdoor activities. Scherman and his staff will prepare incoming 6th graders by teaching organizational strategies, engaging in math and writing activities, and participating in team-building activities that promote friendship and cooperative learning. Students will make new friends, become familiar with the campus and procedures of PMS, and feel ready to begin their 6th-grade year. Lunch and snacks are provided daily including picnics and a barbeque lunch together. ($50 food and materials fee is included).

articles.text: On Thursday and Friday, May 6-7, Beach School’s 52-year tradition of presenting a fully staged and costumed musical revue returned live. A total of 187 Beach elementary students in grades kindergarten through 5th performed outdoors at the high school amphitheater for the first time. The beloved Beach Revue celebration of music, dance and sketch comedy came back after a two-year hiatus due to COVID. The kids performed a range of songs, representing their “Comeback” spirit including “Feeling Good” by Nina Simone, “Won’t Back Down” by Tom Petty and “Rise Up” by Andra Day. The 5th graders carried the show throughout, with clever entr’actes, written by the parent Martina Heppner’s 1st graders performed the song “Can’t Stop the Feeling” by Justin Timberlake. Jessica Sprague’s 5th grade students performed the song “Roar” by Katy Perry. Holding the tiger are Luca Ceccarelli and Violet Shreve. Maggie Butler and Alaleh Ford’s 3rd graders performing to the song “Break My Stride” by Matthew Wilder.

Pickup games of football, volleyball and frisbee ensued, and it felt more like lunch recess at Beach than a high school activity. No one seemed to mind the long lines at the food trucks. pages.text: Wednesday, May 25, 2022 11 8th graders celebrate with traditional Boat Dance By Jay Russell After a two-year hiatus Piedmont Middle School was able to send its 8th grade graduates out on the Bay to enjoy the traditional year-end Boat Dance. The fun-filled evening took place on the Hornblower Empress from Event organizers Barbara Dickason (left), Michelle Heafey, and Jenny Osman Middle School administrators THE BEST CARE FOR YOUR BEST FRIEND Berkeley Marina. The kids were treated to casino games, a bountiful buffet of food, a photo booth, a DJ, and dancing. The weather was perfect for a tour of the Bay, including McCovey Cove, views of Alcatraz, and a trip under the Golden Gate Bridge. Students enjoyed the evening in style, on the majestic three-story modern replica of a turn-of-the-century river steamboat. The “Rock the Boat” theme was a fitting goodbye to their pandemic- impacted tenure at PMS, and a grand sendoff to their swelling futures at Piedmont High. articles.text: Highlanders beat Arcata 10-1 in first round Piedmont’s softball team, seeded No. 5 in the North Coast Section post-season playoffs, walloped No. 12 Arcata in the opening round at Witter Field on May 16, but was shut out 9-0 by No. 4 Cardinal Newman in the NCS quarterfinals on Saturday, May 21 in Santa Rosa. The Highlanders finished with an 18-7 record, a perfect 10-0, in League on the way to an 8-5 victory over Encinal for the league title. It concludes pitcher Izzy Epstein’s illustrious career at PHS. She finishes her season with a 12-1 overall record with 187 strikeouts, a 1.36 earned run average over 123 innings pitched, and concludes her high school career with 285 strikeouts despite having last season shortened due to the pandemic and the spring of 2020 canceled. She had 19 strikeouts in the 10-1 victory over Arcata. “I love my pitcher,” gushed coach Gene Denard of the fouryear starter. “We’re going to miss Izzy; she will be extremely difficult to replace. We’ve been extremely lucky to have her as a leader these last four years,” 10-1 win over Arcata Playing on their home field, the Highlanders trailed 1-0 entering the bottom of the fourth inning, but scored five runs to take a comfortable lead, and added five more in the next inning to put the game away. In the five-run fourth inning, Chiara Lundin got the rally started with a one-out double to score Leah Bell. Lundin then scored on a ground ball fielder’s choice, 2-1, beating the throw home. With two outs, Epstein stole home to make it 3-1, followed by Miya Fujimoto singling in Gretchen Gerhardy and Hailey Ronen. In the bottom of the sixth, PHS got started with two straight singles by Ronen and Fujimoto. Ronen scored on an error by the catcher, and Annabell Castronovo brought in Fujimoto on a groundout, 7-1. Bell then cracked a double to the left field wall, while Lundin singled in Ball. Epstein then stepped to the plate and cracked her fourth home run of the year over the Staff Photos Pitcher Izzy Epstein struck out 19 batters in Piedmont’s 10-1 win over No. 12 Arcata.

articles.text: Six PHS athletes in five events qualified for the 102nd CIF State Track and Field Championships at Buchanan High School in Clovis after placing in the top 3 at the North Coast Section Meet of Champions on Saturday, May 21, at Dublin High School. This year’s track team etched its name into the history books in yet another event when the 4x400 Ellie Black qualified for the State Meet in the 3200 meters, She placed third at the Meet of Champions with a time of 10:57.65. Cooper Downing (right) placed second in the 800 meters with a time of 1:57.47. Photos by Steve Zirkelbach Parker Terrill (right) sprints toward the finish line in the 4x400 relay. The relay team broke a 33-year old PHS record with a time of 3:21.77. relay team of Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, Parker Long, and Parker Terrill clocked 3:21.77 to finish third of eight teams. It beat the school record set in 1989 by 1.2 seconds. “The day before in the prelims we came .09 away from it, so we knew it was something we could go for. I gave my leg everything and I’m keeping one eye on Parker anchor leg) and another eye on the clock. I remember looking at the record in past years thinking, ‘That’s never going to get broken; there’s no way.’ To break it makes me so proud of my teammates,” said Downing. The 4x400 is now this year’s track team’s fourth All-Time record. Jack Stein holds the new school records in both the 1600 and 3200 meters, and Terrill shattered the pole vault record several times. Ellie Black, meanwhile, is narrowly behind Sally Wood in the 3200, and third behind Naomi and Jehan Sparks in the 1600. “As a team, we keep setting records, and that helps push each other. Jack (Stein) was super fast during cross-country, and that helped push me. As a team we have the mentality that we’re all capable of running fast. It creates a sense of unity,” said Downing. Downing,, who has had a breakout year, placed second of 13 in the 800 meter run at the Meet of Champs with a time of 1:57.47, just .21 of a second behind first place Timothy Keller of Berkeley. Downing and Keller have had quite the rivalry; the Piedmonter defeated the Yellowacket at the Bayshore Championship, while Keller was the victory at the WACC Championship on May 6.

articles.text: Highlanders defeat St. Patrick 4-3 in opening round Piedmont’s baseball season came to an end on Saturday, May 21, at the College of Alameda. On the verge of an upset victory over no. 4 seeded St. Joseph, Piedmont, the No. 5 seed, gave up three runs in the bottom of the last inning to lose 6-5 in the North Coast Section quarterfinals Three days earlier, May 18, the Highlanders defeated No. 12 St. Patrick in a comeback of its own, 4-3, at Humphries Diamond in Piedmont. PHS finishes its season with a 19-9 overall record, 9-1 in the Shoreline Division of WACC. It went on to win the league title, beating Encinal 6-5. Freshman Markos Lagios had a big post-season performance, batting Staff Photos Outfielder Markos Lagios, a freshman, had 7 RBIs in the last three games of the season. Nico DeFazio had two RBIs against St. Joseph and scored once against St. Patrick. Ryan McConathy celebrates after grabbing the final out in Piedmont’s 4-3 comeback victory over No. 12 St. Patrick. in 7 runs in three games. “I’ve been working in the batting cage a lot. I’ve been trying to hit the ball to the opposite field and just making contact to get the runner over,” said Lagios. Against St. Patrick, the Highlanders answered a 3-0 deficit after the top of the first inning by scoring one in the bottom of the second, one more in the fourth, and two runs in a critical bottom of the sixth. As for the devastating loss to the Pilots, the Highlanders similarly scored three in the top of the first and led 5-2 after the bottom of the fourth. However, St. Joseph scored once in the bottom of the sixth and put up three runs in the final inning of the game to win. 4-3 win over St. Patrick Trailing 3-0 entering the bottom of the second inning, Piedmont began its comeback with a leadoff double by Davis Alazraqui, who advanced to third after a sacrifice fly by Ryan McConathy. Lagios sent a ground the ball to short, but Alazraqui raced home for the first run. In the bottom of the fourth, Lagios got his second RBI with a sacrifice fly to bring in Alazraqui, who led off with a single. In the sixth inning, Peter Krumins led off with a single followed by DeFazio getting him over to third base on a single. Alazraqui, smacked a double off the right field wall, bringing in Krumins for a 3-3 tie. McConathy then hit another sacrifice fly

articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team sent 11 riders to the Northern California Championships at Six Sigma Ranch in Clear Lake on Saturday May 21. It marked a return to the annual championship race for the first time in three years due to the global pandemic. The Norcal League includes 1500 high school riders in 85 teams. More than half of Piedmont;s riders qualified for the Championship meet, including Artun Duransoy (varsity), Heather Stoneman (JV girls), Andres Roberts, Kurt Wilson, Griffin Stein and Aleksi Valkonen (JV Boys), Schuyler Sawicki, Matteo Scanu, Max Rivera, and Mark Hsia (Sophomore boys), and Cary Ward (Freshmen boys). The Championship course was six miles on a windy single track with a lot of elevation changes, including a few water crossings In the Sophomore boys category, Schuyler Sawicki finished seventh out of 60 riders with a time of 1:04:02 in two laps. Matteo Scanu was two seconds back in 9th place. Schuyler and Matteo jointly won the team award for the greatest achievement in the season. Max Rivera finished 22nd and was named the team’s most improved rider for the season. Mark Hsia finished 29tth. “Congratulations to Schuyler and Matteo for finishing in the top 10 riders in D1 in Northern California in the Sophomore Boys category at the 2022 Championships,” said coach Sally Aldridge. “They both have worked very hard all season.” In the JV Boys category, Junior Andres Roberts was 14th out of 73 with a time of 1:38:23 over three laps. In Kurt Wilson’s final race as a senior, he finished 32nd after starting at the back of the field and passing 40 riders. Juniors Griffin Stein finished 40th and Aleksi Valkonen was 43rd In the Varsity boys field, Duransoy had to retire after two laps due to a knee injury. After a rest, he returned to the course in a valiant effort to finish. In JV Girls, junior Heather Stoneman was 50th out of 53 over two laps. Training for next season starts in the Fall. For more information go to www.piedmontmtb.com or email piedmontbiking@gmail. com. Schuyler Sawicki finished seventh out of 60 riders with a time of 1:04:02 in the two-lap Sophomore Boys category. Sophomore Matteo Scanu was ninth in 1:06:09. Andres Roberts was 14th of 73 in the JV Boys race with a time of 1:38:23 on three laps.

articles.text: Piedmont High School hosted a college recognition ceremony on Thursday, May 19 in the high school amphitheater to honor 16 Piedmont seniors who will be playing sports in college after graduation. Players were introduced by athletic director Bradley Smet and coaches of the respective teams, with classmates and family members present. Five athletes from Piedmont’s record-setting track and field team were honored: Ellie Black and Parker Terrill who will be attending the University of California in Berkeley; Jack Stein (Pomona ColTrack and c ross-country coach Jeanine Holmlund (left) with distance runner Ellie Black, who is set to become a Cal Golden Bear. Staff Photos Piedmont honored 16 student-athletes set to play in college. Pictured are (front row]: Claire Bogart left), Izzy Epstein, Claire Dean, Hannah Govert, Ellie Black, Corinn Richards, Chiara Lundin, Kate Aubrecht; (back row): Parker Terrill, Jack Stein, JoJo Murphy, Tobin Cantrill, Nico DeFazio, Luke Alban, Max Cole, and Anna Romanczuk. lege), Luke Alban (Connecticut College), and Anna Romanczuk (Chapman University). Black and Stein were named WACC League Runners of the Year in both cross country and track, and Terrill as WACC’s Field Athlete of the Year. Terrill is Piedmont’s all-time record holder in pole vault, and Stein holds the school record in both the 1600 and 3200 meters in track. Jeanine Holmlund introduces School record pole vaulter and decathlete Parker Terrill, also headed to Berkeley. Softball pitcher Izzy Epstein (left) will be attending Chapman University. and teammate Chiara Lundin will head East to Wellesley College. Baseball coach Eric Olson honored Tobin Cantrill (left) and Nico DeFazio. Cantrill will play for Chabot College and DeFazio heads to the University of the Pacific in Stockton. articles.text: Piedmont artist and lecturer Michael Stehr returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts on May 27 for a lecture entitled “A Stroll in Rome: The Ponte Umberto to San Pietro.” Doors open at 6:30 p.m., and the illustrated talk begins at 7 p.m. Tickets are $20 at the door; cash only. Join art historian Michael Stehr as he brings club members along for one of his favorite strolls in Rome- the walk from the Ponte Umberto to Saint Peter’s Basilica. Guests will view some of the world’s greatest urban vistas, while experiencing learning about the art of Michelangelo, Bernini, and Carlo Maderno, among others. “The city of Rome boasts some of the more noteworthy destinations in the Western World. The Pantheon, the Sistine Chapel, and Saint Peter’s Basilica are just a few of the landmarks that attract visitors from around the world,” said Stehr. “But with so much history around every corner, sometimes the short journey to arrive at a destination is as thrilling as the encounter with that destination itself.” For more information on the artist, visit http://www.mstehr. com/about. The Castel St. Angeloin in Rome as seen through the trees along the Tevere. Free Delivery to Piedmont Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
articles.title: Michael Stehr art lecture on Rome at PCA May 27

articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco is showing Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy now through September 5. The fashion exhibit features the extraordinary designs of Chinese couture designer Guo Pei, who is widely considered China’s first couturier. More than 80 works over the past two decades will be on display, many of them were shown on Beijing and Paris runways. Pei is known for her craftsmanship, embroidery, and unconventional dressmaking techniques. “As a creator and artist, there is no greater honor than to share my creativity with a wider audience,” the artist said. “I hope that, through the artistry of couture and universal language of art, that it will foster cross-cultural appreciation, connections, and ideas.” To obtain tickets visit: https:// legionofhonor.famsf.org/guo-pei. The Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy exhibit is now on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco.
articles.title: Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy on view now at Legion of Honor

articles.text: Filoli Historic House and Garden is hosting a series of events in June called “Flora Parties.” Guests will join a resident horticulturist who will guide them through gardening basics. A new theme each month will be introduced, starting with trendy succulents. Horticulturalists will teach participants how to layer soil, assort the plants, a use decorative gravel in unique containers. They will also offer tips on how to care for your succulents so they continue to thrive and bloom for years through repotting and propagating. The Flora Parties will be held outdoors in Filoli’s garden Tuesday through Thursday, June 14-16 from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. Registration includes: • A table for four • All materials needed to create four succulent containers • Instruction from Filoli’s Horticulture team • Sparkling wine, rosé, and light snacks To register and learn more, visit: https://filoli.org/events/flora-party/. The grounds at Filoli Historic House & Garden in Woodside abound with color this spring.
articles.title: Filoli “Flora Parties” to take place June 14-16

articles.text: Eric Tran, a 2009 graduate of Piedmont High School, returns to the city to perform a solo piano recital at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, May 28 at 7 p.m. He will perform a solo piano recital centered on the theme of “Joy!” Tran will perform three transcriptions of Bach, a raucous, virtuoso piece of Messiaen Regard de l’esprit de joie, and the complete Beethoven Symphony No.6 (Pastoral) transcribed for solo piano by Franz Liszt. He has performed in Italy, Korea, Canada, China, and 20 states in the US, and was named a 2022 Gilmore Fellow. A graduate of Stanford University, the San Francisco Conservatory of Music, and the University of Wisconsin, Eric won the concerto prizes at all three institutions. He won awards at the Siena Music Festival, Wideman Piano Competition, and the MTNA-Stecher and Horowitz Two Piano Competition. Tran is also a proud graduate of Havens Elementary and Piedmont Middle School, For more information, visit erictranmusic.com. Advance tickets are $25 general and $10 for students at https://www.brownpapertickets. com/event/5425449. Tickets at the Eric Tran, a Piedmont graduate in 2009, will perform a solo piano concert on May 29 at Piedmont Center for the Arts. door are $30 general/ and $15 for students. A light reception will follow. The Piedmont Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera will present Don Giovanni beginning June 4 and running through July 2. Don Giovanni, composed by Wolfgang Mozart, and part 3 of SF Opera’s Mozart-Da Ponte Trilogy, is a dark comedy with a horrific twist ending. The action takes place in Seville, Spain, and spans 24 hours as two women set off to confront a notorious libertine. It is an opera in two acts based on the legend of Don Juan with a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte. The opera is sung in Italian with English supertitles. The cast includes Etienne Dupuis as Don Giovanni, Adela Zaharia as Donna Anna, and Carmen Giannattasio as Donna Elvira. The opera orchestra is conducted by Bertrand de Billy with Etienne Dupuis will sing the lead role in San Francisco Opera’s production of Don Giovanni, opening June 4. direction by Michael Cavanagh. To purchase tickets visit: h t t p s: // w w w. sfo p e r a .c o m / on-stage/don-giovanni/.

articles.text: Mendocino Music Festival returns live this summer, beginning July 9 at Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg. Tickets are on sale now. Founded in 1986 by Allan Pollack, Susan Waterfall and Walter Green, principal bassoonist of San Francisco Symphony, the festival features a blend of genres. Evening events include orchestral concerts, Big Band, chamber music ensembles, dance, blues, jazz, world, folk, bluegrass and more. Daytime events include lectures and recitals at the Piano Series, including a performance by participants in the Emerging Artists Program, and small concerts in intimate venues throughout the historic North Coast town of Mendocino. To view the full program of events, see: https://mendocinomusic.org/events/2022-07/. Featured artists and bands this year include Steel Wheels, Spencer Photo by Ruth Kaiser American singer Kim Nalley is slated to perform this year. Myer, Gloria Cheng, vocalist Kim Nalley, and many more. Proof of vaccination is required, and masks are to be worn. Concerts will be one hour with no intermission. The festival will follow official recommendations of local and state public health agencies as July approaches.
articles.title: Mendocino Music Festival opens on July 9

Someone noticed that the infant was breathing so they didn’t bury him. That was the morbid beginning. Paganini’s father was a brute and beat his little son mercilessly. Father Paganini wanted to have a musical genius and he thought that brutality was the way. But the little Niccolo not only survived, he prospered. Through his lie he was noted for his famous love affairs, gambling addictions, avarice, and suffering from Marfan syndrome. The Catholic Church had a vendetta against him and refused him holy burial. As if that was not enough, his coffin was exhumed and his corpse examined some 58 years after he died. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet While in Portland, Oregon Most tourists see the usual tourist sites, and tourists are advised to remember that many cities offer restaurant tours. This The difference between sensationalism and genius is a most pleasant way to get to know any city. My wife and I took a restaurant tour and were absolutely delighted. We ate in six restaurants and along the way we learned about the city of PortBy Joseph Gold land. The historical district is like going back to Victorian times. We all know the sensational entertainers of recent years. Take Elvis for example. For all of his gyrations, Elvis never sold his soul to the devil. They say that Paganini did. How about Jimi Hendrix? He smashed his guitar on stage. But he never murdered his wife and used her intestines on his guitars. They said that Paganini did. We know that Johnny Cash served a term in prison… But not for murdering his wife. And he didn’t practice 12 hours a day while in prison… On one string. They said that Paganini did all of these things. Women cried at Frank Sinatra’s concerts. But that was the scene at Paganini’s concerts 130 years before. And none of these famous entertainers had a chorus line of witches dancing to his music. And that’s only the tip of the iceberg. As Al Jolson famously said, “you ain’t heard nothing yet.” May 27 is the anniversary of the death of Niccolo Paganini. This year is also another anniversary year. The greatest virtuoso and showman of all time, Niccolo Paganini, was born in 1782, exactly 240 years ago. He revolutionized violin playing and was the prototype for every sensational performer who came after him. So, move over Elvis, Sinatra, Al Jolson and all of the others. Hats off to Paganini in this, his anniversary year. It is amazing that Paganini accomplished as much as he did and, lived to be 57 years old. You name the disease, and Paganini had Portland has preserved these areas rather than tear down the historical buildings. They make every accommodation they can to preserve them. Likewise with the food. We ate well and had a fantastic time. The tour we took was “Portland by Mouth” and our guide was the owner Sherri Brown. I would give it highest recommendations. We finished our trip with a concert by the Oregon Symphony on Sunday afternoon. Because of the pandemic, the orchestra had to make some changes in the program, but they were up to the challenge. A modern composition for percussion and string orchestra by Gabriella Smith opened the program. The percussion soloist was Michael Roberts, the new leader of the percussion section of the Oregon Symphony. The soloist on the orchestra played beautifully, but I fail to find much value in music like this. Nonetheless the performance was impressive. Robert Schuman’s rarely heard violin concerto was played by Stefan Jackiw, who is being pushed toward an international career. The concerto was one of Schumann’s last works and has had difficulty making it as a standard work. It is dramatic and hot blooded from the outset - and then the patented Schumann tenderness is applied to offset the drama. It is a worthy piece despite some misgivings. But it needs a gifted interpreter. Sadly, that was not the case with Jackiw. He plays well, but only if you don’t look at him. His constant gyrations and body twistings are a distraction. Everything he does is pro forma. Many patrons around me loved his music-making. I did not. All of the notes were in place. The rhythm was correct etc. etc. but there was no artistic insight. Correctness does not an artist make. The Oregon Symphony really shone in the second half of the concert. It is a tonally resplendent ensemble. As I watched the orchestra play, I noted sensitive leadership from the concertmaster Peter Frajola, who encouraged idiomatic and sensitive playing from the string section. The result was a unity of purpose and richness of tone. articles.text: The San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra will perform its first concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts in two years on Sunday, May 29 at 5:00 p.m. The orchestra will perform pieces that inspire relaxation, concentration, and joy, including music from: • The Arpeggione Sonata by Franz Schubert (featuring soloist Achille Bocus) • The Faery Queen by Henry Purcell. • Fidelio by Ludwig van Beethoven • Chaconne by Gustav Holst • Meditation (from Thais) by Jules Massenet Achille Bocus, mandolin virtuoso and musical director of the SF Mandolin Orchestra, will be the featured soloist in Schubert’s Arpeggione Sonata. Raised in Milan, Italy, Achille Bocus studied mandolin, double bass, electric bass, composition and conducting. Following his studies, he went on to play double bass with some of the finest symphonic, operatic and chamber music orchestras in Italy, performing throughout Europe. From 2005-2008 he was conductor of the Orchestra a Plettro Città di Milano. In 2009 Achille moved to San Francisco where he began teaching mandolin to students throughout the Bay Area with his “Il Tremolo” method and took up the baton for the SF Mandolin Orchestra. He also performs as a soloist and arranges music for the orchestra. Admission is $20 general, $15 student/senior, and free for children 12 and under. Tickets may be purchased at the door or at the orchestra’s website: https://sfmandolin.square.site. The original San Francisco Mandolin Orchestra in 1920.

The festival has brought more than eight decades of performing arts - including opera, theatre, and music - completely free. articles.text: World-renowned are Stanford University’s technology expertise and her women’s sports teams. But across town, there’s a little miracle called West Bay Opera, which despite a postagestamp-sized auditorium to play in, brings off productions that are both presentable and downright moving. Cheers should ring out with WBO resuming performances after the two-year Covid padlock, now hitting its stride in its 66th season. Imagine a theater incapable of scene changes. Half the musicians are sitting in the wings like caged birds, barely able to see the baton of conductor Juan Luis Moscovich, who must also double as the company’s general director. In Tchaikovsky’s Queen of Spades, you have armies of performers, including some unpaid choruses, walk-ons, children, and a trio of Commedia dell’Arte dancer-singers who nearly stole the show in their cameo (at least, when not hopscotching over footlights). The performance on May 20 – the phoenix rising from the viral ashes. a fateful drama about gambling, gamboling, and the supernatural – came off powerfully at the heart of the matter, at least if you didn’t examine the edges too much. The cast sang in Russian. And if your vocabulary never went beyond “Tri karti” (3 cards) and “Ya vas lyublyu” (I love you), you had the projected text translations to help out. It has weaknesses common to the genre, like pieces stopping the drama dead in its tracks with irrelevant choral scenes – once proclaiming a sunny day, later judging it a stormy day. To their credit Verdi operas eliminated those fillers with choruses propelling the action or juicy subplots to replace fillers. But the racy central story, with assignations and secret rendezvous, is engrossing. A man, Hermann, caught between a love interest in Liza and an obsession for gambling at cards in scenes of the elegant Czarist aristocracy. He loves the gaming table more, literally forcing an old clairvoyant Countess to divulge future outcomes and enable him to make his fortune. In the end the ghost of the victimized Countess thwarts his greed with a flawed prediction. The turning up of the queen of spades in the casino leads to his merited end. WBO made the seven-scene opera work through dazzling architectural projections. The masterful touch was a lovers’ quarrel at the walls of the canal where, as if in a video, the image slowly shifts to the canal waters, showing the demise in a watery suicide – a great touch by projection designer Peter Compton. The heavyweight voices of Michael Boley (Hermann) and Rhoslyn Jones (Liza) rang through the hall and rafters with power and authority. They cautiously tended to the sharp side vocally to skirt tending flat. Jones’ surprising mobility added plausibility to the doomed pair. In the scene-stealing secondary role of the Countess, mezzo Laure de Marcellus proved to be the night’s best actress. In strong supporting low voices of nobles came Kiril Havezov (Tomsky) and Jonathan Beyer (Yelensky). Audience sympathies had to be with WBO, playing a 19th-century Russian opera at a time of great public antipathy toward Russia, a factor definitely cutting into attendance at the opener. But given the many months of contracted operatic preparation, WBO was in a position to substitute Otello, Mme. Butterfly or Porgy and Bess. Stage Director Ragnar Conde did some of his best work staging the song-and-dance trio of Commedia dell’arte performers Sarah Benzinger, Maria Kaganskaya and Kiril Havezov in the Masked Ball scene. For the audience, Vaccination ID was required and masks strongly recommended. OPERA NOTES Tchaikovsky’s opera Pique Dame (Queen of Spades), by West Bay Opera, Lucie Stern Theatre, Palo Alto, through May 29. In Russian with supertitles. 3.5 hours, 3 acts, two intermissions. For tickets, call (650) 424-9999, or go online. www.wbopera.org Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, writes regularly online on classical music via the arts journal artsSF.com

articles.text: Youth Musical Theater Company will perform Shrek the Musical the weekend of May 27-May 30. Shrek is the world’s most beloved fractured fairy tale set to a score by Jeanine Tesori, It is an outrageously funny story of a swamp-dwelling ogre’s quest to rescue Princess Fiona with the help of a talkative donkey. The adventure is filled with exciting dance numbers, evil men of little character, and fairy tale creatures who learn to let their freak flag fly. Piedmont High School freshman Dahlia Saffouri will make her debut with YMTC in the ensemble in the role of Dragon. She has previously appeared in A Christmas Story (Berkeley Playhouse), Seussical (Piedmont Middle School), and Junie B. Jones (Bay Area Children’s Theatre Advanced Performers). YMTC is a stellar company which produces captivating PHS freshman Dahlia Saffouri musicals with a live orchestra and performing arts students from local high schools, as well as colleges and universities. YMTC has come to be known as the East Bay’s preeminent company whose sole mission is to train young artists in all the disciplines of musical theater, while also producing excellent productions in a year-long season in multiple venues in the East Bay. It brings together the Bay Area’s most talented and dedicated young performers, musicians and students of technical theater (ages 12-21) with professional directors, designers, choreographers, and musicians. The show will be performed at its beautiful outdoor Bolivar Stage, with a total of six shows. To purchase tickets, visit ymtcbayarea.org.

articles.text: Bouquets to Art, the de Young Museum’s premiere fundraiser and annual display of artwork-inspired floral installations, will begin on June 7. Bouquets to Art, now in its 38th year, is back to full-capacity following a virtual event in 2020 and a hybrid, limited-capacity event last year. For one week, more than 100 experienced floral designers will converge at the de Young to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s vast array of paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Bouquets to Art is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events every year. The event is presented by the volunteer members of the fine arts museums - and draws nearly 800,000 visitors a year, with net proceeds of more than $7 million. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. Bouquets to Art in a photo from 2015 Photo by Thomas Henthorne Guests will be greeted with a large-scale aerial artwork piece by Bay Area artist Windy Chien. Entitled The Three Dragons, the hand-knotted artwork hangs in the museum’s Wilsey Court. Those who visit during the week of Bouquets to Art will have a chance to view Hung Liu’s large piece Resident Alien, first exhibited at the Capp Street Project in 1988 and exhibited by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco last year. The painting, arguably Liu’s most famous, depicts her own “Green Card” on a larger-than-life scale. It is now in the collection of the San Jose Museum of Art. “Hung Liu is uniquely positioned to tell the stories of immigrants to the United States. In 2020, she celebrated the milestone of having lived an equal number of years in China and the United States. As one of the foremost painters in the United States, Liu is a testament to the fact that our brightest citizens are often born under foreign skies,” said Janna Keegan, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art and Programming at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Bouquets to Art is a weeklong event that begins on Monday evening, June 6, with an opening-night reception. Between June 7 and June 12, a series of book launches, speaker events, and raffles will take place. For a full list of programming, visit https://www.famsf.org/pressroom/bouquets-art. Tickets sold out weeks prior to the event in 2021 - reserve yours now by visiting https://deyoung. famsf.org/bouquets-to-art.
articles.title: Bouquets to Art returns to de Young Museum June 7-12

In strong supporting low voices of nobles came Kiril Havezov (Tomsky) and Jonathan Beyer (Yelensky). Audience sympathies had to be with WBO, playing a 19th-century Russian opera at a time of great public antipathy toward Russia, a factor definitely cutting into attendance at the opener. But given the many months of contracted operatic preparation, WBO was in a position to substitute Otello, Mme. Butterfly or Porgy and Bess. Stage Director Ragnar Conde did some of his best work staging the song-and-dance trio of Commedia dell’arte performers Sarah Benzinger, Maria Kaganskaya and Kiril Havezov in the Masked Ball scene. For one week, more than 100 experienced floral designers will converge at the de Young to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s vast array of paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Bouquets to Art is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events every year. The event is presented by the volunteer members of the fine arts museums - and draws nearly 800,000 visitors a year, with net proceeds of more than $7 million. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. Entitled The Three Dragons, the hand-knotted artwork hangs in the museum’s Wilsey Court. Those who visit during the week of Bouquets to Art will have a chance to view Hung Liu’s large piece Resident Alien, first exhibited at the Capp Street Project in 1988 and exhibited by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco last year. It is now in the collection of the San Jose Museum of Art. “Hung Liu is uniquely positioned to tell the stories of immigrants to the United States. The 9-day summer arts festival will take place in iconic Napa Valley locations. “The performances at Festival Napa Valley this summer illuminate the importance of the arts in today’s world,” said Festival President & CEO Richard Walker. “Our mission is more vital than ever.” “We are dedicating the 2022 season to the sounds of America. Opening night on July 15 will include conductor Carlo Ponti leading Festival Orchestra Napa in Dvorak’s New World Symphony, and Daniel Brewbaker’s Cello Concerto with soloist Sophia Bacelar. articles.text: The film Crazy Heart, released in 2010 and published in The Post the same year, is one of those rare films that examines a character with insight and, in its own way, affection. That isn’t to say that country western singer Bad Blake (Jeff Bridges) is by any stretch attractive. Charming to be sure, in a dissipated, chain-smoking, alcoholic, resolutely self-destructive way. After decades on the road, he’s beyond the nadir of his career as a performer and song writer, now solidly middle-aged, broke and playing bowling alleys in adjunct lounges named “The Spare Room,” or small, smoky bars frequented by those who remember when and still resonate to lyrics like, “I use to be somebody, but now I’m somebody else.” His nights are spent in seedy motels, sometimes in the company of a woman who looks at Blake and sees only a memory, that once deeply talented musician/singer and not the staggering wreck of a man who rushes off the stage and vomits in a back alley. Clearly that sounds grim, but it’s not. Bridges’ portrayal of Blake is compelling – a fascinating study of a man circling the drain who can still muster the will to live, singing music that remains embedded in his heart. Maggie Gyllenhaal portrays Jean Craddock, a young journalist in Santa Fe, who shows up at one of Blake’s gigs asking for an interview for the local paper. She’s lovely, a single mom, and attracted to Blake for reasons that are never really clear. She acknowledges that she isn’t looking for another man to break her heart, or a man whose life is dominated by alcohol (“It’s like living with a rattlesnake”). Yet Maggie Gyllenhaal and Jeff Bridges star in Crazy Heart. here comes Bad Blake, wrinkled and sweaty and paunchy, smelling like a gym sock left in a P.E. locker over the summer. And yet there she is, all but courting him. What is never becomes convincing is why she would ever allow anyone remotely like Blake into her life. He’s an emotional wreck, a man poised on a precipice. And still she allows him to babysit her 4-year-old son, an act of startling trust that almost requires a suspension of disbelief. Actually, the best thing about Crazy Heart is not the story, which is a variation on a theme that is all too familiar. Instead, what makes the film compelling are the fine performances of Bridges and Gyllenhaal who both were nominated for Oscars. They transform themselves, each delivering nuanced portrayals of interesting people. Not attractive people or people who have all their rough edges sanded down, but flawed and fallible. Crazy Heart, Starring Jeff Bridges, Colin Farrell, Maggie Gyllenhaal and Robert Duval. Written and directed by Scott Cooper. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated R.
