articles.text: Initially the title Paper Towns seems enigmatic, puzzling. Paper towns, apparently, are fake destinations, used by cartographers as a way of copyrighting their work. It’s a metaphor soon explained. The film is a coming-of-age story set in Orlando, Florida, involving seniors in high school on the cusp of graduating. At the movie’s center is Quentin Jacobsen (Nat Wolff), a quintessential nerd, and his two best friends, Ben (Austin Abrams) and Radar (Justice Smith). In the opening set up, Q explains in voice over that from the first day that he saw Margo Roth Spiegelman (Cara Delevingne), moving in across the street, he has been in love with her (they were both 10). Even during high school, when Margo becomes popular and Q, Ben and Radar are on the fringe of the school’s social hierarchy, he’s still crazy about her. They pass each other in the halls like strangers and it breaks his heart. Late one night Margo appears at his window. She talks him into taking his family car and driving her to the houses of some kids. The first is Margo’s best friend, with whom her boyfriend has been cheating. Margo is wild and reckless. Q is conservative and has had his nose to the academic grindstone for the last four years. He’s going to Duke U. and wants to be a doctor. Take his mom’s van? No way. But then this is Margo Roth Spiegelman, the girl of his dreams, excessively cool and Halston Sage and Nat Wolff in a scene from Paper Towns. alluring and mysterious. On second thought. At the end of the evening, after breaking into several houses, Saran wrapping a car of another girlfriend, Margo tells Q, “The way you felt tonight is the way you should feel your whole life.” There’s some truth in her admonition, however, there’s also a lot of youthful naiveté. Q, being Q, is not so sure he’s ready to follow Margo. But he never gets a chance to spend more time with her to explore their experience or to discuss an encore. The next morning she disappears, though she leaves behind some clues, which sets up a road trip. Q has decided that he must find her. He can’t let go of his memories, not only those from the night before but those of the last decade when he has worshipped her from afar. And so the three buddies and two girls – Radar’s girlfriend, Angela (Jaz Sinclair), and Margo’s best friend, Lacey (Halston Sage) – hit the road, bound for upstate New York and a Paper Town. Q is convinced that he knows exactly where Margo has gone. The movie is more than a shallow rite of passage film about the vagaries of adolescence and its potential bleakness. If you appreciate the genre, know that the story is based on a young adult novel written by John Green, also the author of The Fault in Our Stars. It has a ring of truth, a fine ensemble of young actors, and is a solid portrayal of high school life, without any mean kid drama. Paper Towns. Starring Nat Wolff, Cara Delevvingne and Halston Sage. Directed by Jake Schreier. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2015. Now streaming on VUVU/Prime/Apple TV. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs

articles.text: Joey Cramer stars in Flight of the Navigator. The Flight of the Navigator, released in 1986 by Disney, will definitely appeal to a new generation of tweens and teens. Using what was then groundbreaking CGI, this time-travel adventure stars Joey Cramer portraying a 12-year-old boy named David Freeman. The setting is Ft. Lauderdale, the year is 1978, the day is July 4, and David is walking through the woods on his way to pick up his 8-year-old brother, Jeff (Matt Adler). Lost in thought, not watching where he is going, David tumbles into a ravine and is knocked unconscious. When he comes to, he runs home and finds that strangers are living in his house. When he is finally reunited with his parents, Helen and Bill (Veronica Cartwright and Cliff DeYoung), to his surprise he finds them and brother Jeff now eight years older. We learn that David was abducted by aliens, placed on a spaceship, and transported to the distant planet Phaelon, some 560 light years away. Exceeding the speed of light, time is distorted and while David remains the same age, eight years pass by on earth while only some two hours have gone by for David. The spaceship, we learn, is commanded by a robotic computer named Max (Paul Reubens), and during the journey David is studied by the aliens. When returning David to the ravine, the ship crashes and is captured by NASA. A group of scientists, headed by Dr. Louis Faraday (Howard Hesseman), convince David to come to NASA, where they examine him. They discover that his brain is filled with star charts and techie information that far exceeds anything known to researchers on earth, thus they treat him like a research subject. Realizing that the manipulative Faraday is actually holding David and Max captive, the two manage to escape and using telepathy signal the ship. Max tells David that the navigational charts he has in his head are needed if Max and crew are ever to return to Phaelon. For David it proves to be quite an adventure. And, of course, as narratives of this ilk go, David does wonder if his experience was only a dream. He soon discovers that nothing has changed. Time has passed – yet it hasn’t. It’s still the 4th of July and of course there are fireworks launched to celebrate that much-anticipated day. Kids will enjoy what proves to be a compelling, and underrated sci-fi tale filled with twists and turns. Flight of the Navigator. Directed by Randall Kleiser. Starring Joey Cramer, Veronica Cartwright, Cliff DeYoung. 1 hr., 29 min. Rated PG. Released in 1986 by Disney. articles.text: Will Adams Talking with Group A walking tour led by Will Adams drew a big crowd on May 18 for Walking on Wednesdays. Pictured are: Priscilla Wanerus, Jo Normington with K-9 best friend Penny Lane, Alicia Rivera, Lois Price, Edith Lee, Stella Houston, Noemi Alvarado, Siow Fang Tan, Brenda Ferrero, Judy Wang, Dave DeRoche, Helen Dong, Swee Ling Chen, Phil Witte, Tami DeSellier, Jim Kuo, Albert Chen, Kat Lang, Harriette Louie, Sherry Jacobs, Eric Behrens, Adrienne Hamlin, Joyce Hicks, Pat Sheehan, Pat Keller, Dena Belinkoff, Melba Yee, Laura Goldman, Aaron Katzel, Sarah Johnson, Ellen Manolis, Nadine Guffanti, Martin Levy, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Cheryl Stanton, Christine Calliste, Nancy DeRoche, John Lenahan, Elizabeth Richter, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Quincy Dong, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome first time walkers Christina Miller, Kirk Miller, Corky Roberts, Molly Roberts, Raymond Ritter, and others. John Malick, a local architect and friend of Will, was there to join in the fun too. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group came close to needing a parade permit last Wednesday, May 18. There were a total of 55 walkers and three K-9 best friends who met at the Exedra Plaza on a beautiful morning. However, they didn’t attend just for the weather. Piedmont planner, urban designer, and architect Will Adams was there to lead a special walking tour of historical Piedmont buildings designed by famed architect Albert Farr. Nancy and Dave DeRoche invited everyone to their home the following Wednesdasy for a follow up to the tour with Will. Nancy and Dave reported that Albert Farr lived in their house on Oakland Avenue for 25 years in the early 20th Century. Will Adams provided an introduction to and overview of Albert L. Farr. He was an American architect, who during the first decades of Piedmont’s development, designed many homes and some of Piedmont’s most prominent buildings, including the City Hall, Piedmont Community Church and the Piedmont Community Center. Farr was born in Omaha, Nebraska, but grew up in Yokohama, Japan. The Farr family returned to the United States in 1891, and settled in the San Francisco Bay Area. Farr lived at various times in San Francisco, Berkeley, Oakland, and Piedmont where he died in 1945 at age 76. Farr earned his architecture license in 1901, one of the first in California, and was designing grand mansions for his clients while still in his 20s. His clients were primarily in the San Francisco in the neighborhoods of Russian Hill, Pacific Heights, Seacliff, and St. Francis Wood. Farr also designed prominent estate homes and commercial and public buildings in Belvedere, Woodside, and Piedmont and had a strong interest in planning and urban design. He the Exedra, as well as the layout of “downtown” Piedmont. Will asked the walkers to evaluate the urban design of the town center and how well connected the various key buildings are. Will talked about Farr’s architectural training and how architects will study and apply different styles to their work. Farr’s use of the Spanish Revival styles in the Piedmont public buildings has defined to a large degree the character of Piedmont. Will took the group to City Hall to illustrate both the symmetrical (more formal) and asymmetrical (less formal) design approaches Farr employed on his different buildings. Will noted the “outdoor room” to the right of the City Hall’s entrance now with replica concrete benches that provide a well-used informal meeting place. Will said there is a relief hidden behind climbing vines on the front of the City Hall that he wished was visible. Will then led the group through Piedmont Park, past the Farr-designed Community Hall on Highland Avenue to Wildwood Avenue and an historic mansion at the corner of Sheridan. The estate was just sold. Behind its wrought iron gate, Will talked about Farr’s classical training that allowed him to add architectural details, like interesting rain downspouts, to enhance the house’s beautiful design. He also noted how Farr mitigated what an Asian audience would consider the negative feng shui of a straight-on axial street at the house’s front gate with a lovely water fountain in front of the house’s entrance. Next was a walk to the foot of Lincoln Avenue to see how Farr had integrated the features of different European architectural styles in a home. Visible through the front door was an outdoor water fountain. It was then on to a home on Mountain Avenue that Will’s architect friend, John Malick, had remodeled. John, who was on the tour, shared some ideas architects use to satisfy the desires and budgets of clients. The final stop was the Piedmont Community Church. The group went up its front steps to the church’s lovely courtyard with roses in full bloom. Will noted that it was Mission Revival style, with its simplified execution that limited the construction expense, while keeping its design compatible with other important buildings in Piedmont’s center. In the church’s sanctuary Will pointed out the impressive ceiling trellises and confessed he had once copied this Farr design concept for one of his projects. The slope from the back of the church to its front was also noted, and the better visibility of the service that it provides worshipers was appreciated. At the conclusion of the tour, the group expressed their appreciation for Will and the informative tour he led. They were also pleased that they would have another opportunity to talk with Will next Wednesday when they all visit the DeRoches. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: As an investor, you can easily feel frustrated to see short-term drops in your investment statements. But while you cannot control the market, you may find it helpful to review the factors you can control. Many forces affect the financial markets, including geopolitical events, corporate profits and interest rate movements – forces beyond the control of most individual investors. In any case, it’s important to focus on the things you can control, such as these: • Your ability to define your goals – One area in which you have total control is your ability to define your goals. Like most people, you probably have short-term goals – such as saving for a new car or a dream vacation – and long-term ones, such as a comfortable retirement. Once you identify your goals and estimate how much they will cost, you can create an investment strategy to help achieve them. Over time, some of your personal circumstances will likely change, so you’ll want to review your time horizon and risk tolerance on a regular basis, adjusting your strategy when appropriate. And the same is true for your goals – they may evolve over time, requiring new responses from you in how you invest. • Your response to market downturns – When the market drops and the value of your investments declines, you might be tempted to take immediate action in an effort to stop the losses. This is understandable – after all, your investment results can have a big impact on your future. However, acting hastily could work against you – for example, you could sell investments that still have solid fundamentals and are still appropriate for your needs. If you can avoid decisions based on short-term events, you may help yourself in the long run. • Your commitment to investing – The financial markets are almost always in flux, and their movements are hard to predict. If you can continue investing in all markets – good, bad or sideways – you will likely make much better progress toward your goals than if you periodically were to take a “time out.” Many people head to the investment sidelines when the market tumbles, only to miss out on the beginnings of the next rally. And by steadily investing, you will increase the number of shares you own in your investments – and the larger your ownership stake, the greater your opportunities for building wealth. • Your portfolio’s level of diversification – While diversification itself can’t guarantee profits or protect against all losses, it can help greatly reduce the impact of market volatility on your portfolio. Just how you diversify your investments depends on several factors, but the general principle of maintaining a diversified portfolio should govern your approach to investing. It’s a good idea to periodically review your portfolio to ensure it’s still properly diversified. The world will always be filled with unpredictable, uncontrollable events, and many of them will affect the financial markets to one degree or another. But within your own investment world, you always have a great deal of control – and with it, you have the power to keep moving toward all your important financial objectives. For a refresher course, the main ones are for red wines – Syrah, Grenache, Mourvedre and Petite Sirah, and the white wines are Viognier, Grenache Blanc, Roussanne and Marsanne. Amazing progress has been made in the past 30 years. The vast majority of these wines are now much better than they were years ago. It took a while to find the right growing areas and to develop the right vineyard management techniques, but many of these wines can now rival their French cousins. One of the most exciting developments on the American Rhone scene is the emergence of Southeast Washington state as a Rhone grape powerhouse. The area around the town of Walla Walla is the home to wineries making some of America’s finest Syrah wines. The Paso Robles area of California also continues to be a capital of great Rhone wine making. The following wines are my nominations for this year’s best Rhone wines. • 2019 The Walls “Mahana” Washington’s Walla Walla Valley is the homeland for this blend of 61% Syrah, 38% Grenache and 1% Viognier. A deep plum/ruby color is accompanied by aromas of smoked meats, vanilla, blueberries and currants. Medium to full-bodied, this sexy, delicious Rhone blend possesses good purity and length as well as a broad, expansive, velvety-textured mouthfeel. Enjoy it over the next decade. • 2018 Onx “Reckoning” This Paso Robles wine is 67% Syrah, 31% Petite Sirah and 2% Zinfandel. It has a nose of plums, crème de cassis and blackberry pie with touches of spice box, earth, and anise plus a hint of violets. Very full bodied with firm powerful tannins and a lively line of freshness supporting the muscular black fruit, it finishes long and spicy. • 2020 The Pundit Syrah This wine is a collaboration between Washington State’s Chateau Ste. Michelle and the Rhone’s Michel Gassier. It is a big, fleshy Syrah that exhibits a deep purple color as well as plenty of blackberry and cassis • 2019 Sixteen 600 Rossi Hommage Blanc A blend of Roussanne, Marsanne and Grenache Blanc is the creation of Phil Coturri one of Sonoma’s finest winegrowers and vineyard managers. It is forward, dense, and structured, revealing peach, citrus, honeysuckle, and a hint of cloves. It is round and full in the mouth with a clean, savory finish. The wine would make a delicious aperitif or partner to roast chicken. • 2019 Booker “Ripper” Grenache This Paso Robles winery was new to me. The Ripper Grenache is pale ruby-colored and wafts sensuously from the glass with fragrant notions of raspberries, roses, and kirsch with a touch of spice box. The festival, now in its fifth year, will feature 25 Bay Area children’s authors and illustrators for a full day of story-time. A mix of well-established and emerging authors will be present. Six authors and illustrators will give 25-minute book presentations and live art demonstrations at Fairyland’s Emerald City Stage. Headliners include award-winning authors Mac Barnett, JaNay Brown-Wood, Johanna Ho, C.V Monterrubio, and Nina LaCour. Piedmont High School alum Maggie Tokuda Hall, winner of the 2021 Poppy Award for Young Adult Fiction for Squad, will be among the guest authors. Attendees will have a chance to purchase books signed by the authors during scheduled meetand-greet times. Student writers from Fairyland’s Youth Writers’ Workshop will share a joint reading at the Youth Author Table in the afternoon. Other featured authors and illustrators this year are John Casselberry, Madeline Connor, Angela Dalton, Cindy Derby (2021 Caldecott Honor for Outside In), Hayley Diep, Meg Flemchez, Simone Shin, Emma Bland Smith, Meera Sriram (2021 South Asia Book Award for A Gift for Amma), Meredith Steiner, and Justine Villanueva. Festival attendance is free with park admission. The festival takes place on Saturday, June 18, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. To learn more, see www.fairyland.org or visit the park at 699 Bellevue Avenue at Lake Merritt in Oakland.

articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.
articles.title: Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online

pages.text: Wednesday, May 25, 2022 25 Fairyland’s annual Book Festival is Saturday, June 18 ing, Alia Gabres, Michael Genhart (2022 Pura Belpre Award for May Your Life Be Deliciosa), Jill Guerra, Felicia Hoshino, Nancy Johnson James, Dawood Marion, Constance Moore, Christina Newhard, Jane Park (2015-2016 Asian Pacific American Librarians Association’s Asian Pacific American Award for Juna’s Jar), Keely Parrack, Lea Redmond, Nadia Salomon, Victoria SanBy Allyson Aleksey Children’s Fairyland is bringing back its annual Book Festival after a two-year pandemic-driven pause. The festival, now in its fifth year, will feature 25 Bay Area children’s authors and illustrators for a full day of story-time. A mix of well-established and emerging authors will be present. Six authors and illustrators will give 25-minute book presentations and live art demonstrations at Fairyland’s Emerald City Stage. Headliners include award-winning authors Mac Barnett, JaNay Brown-Wood, Johanna Ho, C.V Monterrubio, and Nina LaCour. Piedmont High School alum Maggie Tokuda Hall, winner of the 2021 Poppy Award for Young Adult Fiction for Squad, will be among the guest authors. Attendees will have a chance to purchase books signed by the authors during scheduled meetand-greet times. Student writers from Fairyland’s Youth Writers’ Workshop will share a joint reading at the Youth Author Table in the afternoon. Other featured authors and illustrators this year are John Casselberry, Madeline Connor, Angela Dalton, Cindy Derby (2021 Caldecott Honor for Outside In), Hayley Diep, Meg Flemchez, Simone Shin, Emma Bland Smith, Meera Sriram (2021 South Asia Book Award for A Gift for Amma), Meredith Steiner, and Justine Villanueva. Festival attendance is free with park admission. The festival takes place on Saturday, June 18, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. To learn more, see www.fairyland.org or visit the park at 699 Bellevue Avenue at Lake Merritt in Oakland. Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. articles.text: Albert Farr designed the elegant Mediterranean home at 395 Hampton Road in Piedmont in 1927 in his iconic style with a grand arched entry surrounded by quoins and a cartouche and finials above. Tall windows, a Spanish tile roof, shutters and a symmetrical façade complete his design. The house sits behind a circular driveway which retains the original light poles. New lights at the entry match the original lights. Marble steps lead to metal double doors with original nailhead detail and windows with spindles. In the foyer, architect Farr placed French doors leading to the living room, game room, dining room, and rear terrace and gardens for excellent flow from room to room. To the left, double doors open to the impressive 30-foot living room filled with southern light from tall windows. The ceilings throughout the house are high and were designed to accommodate the original owner’s large artwork and furniture. Wood beams enrich the living room, dining room and library ceilings. Beyond, the sunroom provides an intimate, well-lit room to relax. Farr reportedly returned two years after the house was built to convert the former terrace to a sunroom with the resulting room above in the master suite. The original library, now used as a game room, provides a casual spot for gathering with family and friends by the fireplace. Two sets of tall French doors open to the rear garden and terrace. The mirrored bar off the foyer opens to the rear terrace, and conveniently provides a sink, refrigerator, and dishwasher for entertaining indoors and out. The spacious dining room across the entry foyer continues Farr’s high ceiling design. More tall windows bring in light and provide garden views for diners. The high ceilings extend to the handsome, modern kitchen beyond with a large center island, range, second sink and seating for six. The freezer and refrigerators are faced to match the cabinets. Dishwashers, a steam oven with warming drawer and a roomy pantry with a ladder to reach the top shelves add to the conveniences of this up-to-date kitchen. The banquette provides more eat-in dining, and the adjacent sunny patio offers outdoor dining. The kitchen area extends to a coffee bar beyond, laundry room, former maid’s room, and a full bath. The reconfigured mud room provides convenient access to the driveway, parking pad and garages. From the foyer, the graceful, curving stairway with slender wrought-iron balustrade leads to five generously-sized bedrooms with ensuite baths and several bonus rooms on the second floor. The stained-glass skylight above this circular staircase dates to the original 1927 design. The grand master suite has a gas fireplace to warm the room, sunny windows that overlook the front garden, and an adjacent sunroom offering views of the redwood trees. A large balcony overlooks the rear gardens. Two dressing rooms with ample walk-in closets and two full bathrooms complete the suite. The upstairs hallway opens to a comfortable sitting room with a balustrade and views to the lawns. A television, fireplace, The mansion at 395 Hampton and an adjacent study make this a room of many uses. Two large closets in the hall offer lots of space for linens and storage. Four additional bedrooms overlook the front or rear gardens, each with an ensuite bath. A second sitting room is large and provides two additional desks, a window seat, and several bookcases. Back stairs descend to the kitchen from this sitting room. Back in the main foyer, a second curving staircase descends to the lower level with a theater room, a second laundry room, wine cellar, and full bath. Beyond, the former ballroom with its high ceiling is now a spacious gym which opens to a covered terrace and patio. The sixth bedroom is off the gym. The seventh bedroom is the former maid’s room off the kitchen, now used as an office. French doors from the foyer open to a very private terrace for outdoor dining, relaxing and enjoying the fire pit. The terraced lawns extend to an arched fountain-like planter within an exedra, a curved outdoor bench. To the east, the tennis court has a batting cage and basketball hoop. Above the garage, a legal ADU (accessory dwelling unit) studio provides more living space. Two 2-car garages provide covered parking for four cars. The parking pad for the garages and circular drive provide additional offstreet parking. This grand estate was designed by Albert Farr for William St. Cyr Cavalier and his wife Camille in 1926. Cavalier was an investment broker in stocks and bonds and president of his own business, William Cavalier & Company. He and Camille had three children when they built their new home, Dixie (8), Camille (6), William, Jr. (3), and a nurse and servant to help with duties. William St. Cyr Cavalier was a prominent Oakland and San Francisco financier and civic leader. articles.text: This light-filled home was so well-loved by its 1926 owners that they took it with them when they moved from Grand Avenue! The living room with a cozy fireplace and large picture window flows seamlessly into the formal dining room and on to the sunny, updated kitchen. Off of the kitchen are a large and wonderful patio and side yard. Downstairs provides yet another level for work or gathering in the rumpus room and other great flex spaces. The detached 2-car garage is great for cars, crafts, or storage galore. A special home with a truly unique history! William Cavalier died in 1945, and Mrs. Cavalier continued to live in the house on Hampton Road until her death in 1966. In 1968, it was part of the Decorators’ Showcase to benefit the Oakland Symphony. At that time, it was called “Hampton House” and was completely covered in vines. The house was a Decorator Showcase again in 1983. Several owners have remodeled this home, but it continues to maintain Albert Farr’s grand design. The terrace off the living room was enclosed to create today’s sunroom, with another sunroom above in the master suite. The former dark wood beams in the living room, dining room, and library have been painted out to lighten the rooms. The library was originally paneled in oak with tall bookshelves on each wall. The house retains evidence of the former radiant heat, now hidden behind grates in the living room, dining room and library. The radiators have since been replaced by a modern HVAC system. Over the years, the kitchen has been expanded to one large room, eliminating the breakfast room, butler’s pantry, and other utility rooms. When built, the basement rooms were unfinished. The ballroom was finished in 1934 for daughter Dixie Cavalier’s wedding in 1938. Later, the Cavalier family used it as a recreation room. Albert Farr was a well-respected architect in the Bay Area and practiced from 1905 to 1937. He has been called one of the most artistic architects on the West Coast. He is known for his Period Revival designs of large homes with monumental entries and generous public rooms with high ceilings, often trimmed with elegant woodwork. Farr designed more than 40 homes in Piedmont, and six Farr-designed houses have been on Decorator Showcase tours. Farr’s brother, Harry St. Sure Farr, was on the Piedmont Board of Trustees, and early in his career he designed the Bonita Avenue School in 1909, the predecessor of Havens School, Piedmont’s City Hall (1910), and the Oakland Avenue Bridge (1910). He returned to design the city’s Exedra and Community Hall in 1925. Gail G. Lombardi is President of the Piedmont Historical Society and an architectural historian. The city is able to use 140 units to meet its Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) because it has a track record of producing up to 17 ADUs a year over the last three years, explained Piedmont Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell. “The 140 new ADUs are based on the average building permit activity from the last three years [17.5 ADUs], extrapolated out 8 years [17.5 x 8 years = 140 ADUs.],” she said. “We may see more ADUs constructed in the future, but State HCD limits each city to the prior averaged rate of construction.” Last chance for public input The City Council meeting will be a last-chance opportunity to provide public comment on the draft housing element before it heads to HCD for review. However, it will not be the last time for public comment on the 6th housing element before it is officially adopted in Spring 2023. Once Piedmont receives review findings from HCD, it can then revise the housing element to comply with the statute and adopt it, or adopt the draft without revising it. Assembly Bill 215, approved by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2021, requires that prior to submittal of the first draft to the HCD, all local governments must make the draft available for public comment for at least 30 days, and if any comments were received, take at least 10 business days to consider and incorporate public comments in the draft. Since the publication of the draft housing element, the city has discussed the document during its most recent public Park Commission, Planning Commission, and Recreation Commission meetings, as well as during Housing Advisory Committee Meetings. articles.text: Piedmont City Council considered the naming of the triangle park at the intersection of Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues as “Dearing Family Memorial Park,” as a memorial to Sidney Dearing, Piedmont’s first black resident in 1924. City Administrator Sara Lillevand said more public input should be sought as the city seeks to address what is widely considered a blight on Piedmont’s past. Sidney and Irene Dearing were Piedmont’s first black homeowners. They purchased a home in 1924 and were driven out by a mob of white Piedmont residents. The Piedmont Police Department did little to help as a mob estimated at 500 people demanded the family’s removal. The City Council offered to purchase the home from the Dearing family but offered less than the family had originally paid, claiming that the property purchase was needed to construct a road between Wildwood and Fairview Avenues, a road that was never constructed. “I would suggest that we slow down on the name itself, and provide more opportunity for public engagement on this important effort,” Lillevand said. “I do believe the triangle park (at Wildwood and Magnolia) is an appropriate place to acknowledge and remember the Dearing family.” Rather than recommending to City Council that they approve the naming of the city park, Lillevand revised the agenda item to direct Park Commission to explore “and make recommendations to city council on opportunities to memorialize the Sidney Dearing family history.” The triangle park is across the street from the former Dearing home. Councilmember Jennifer Long, echoing Lillevand’s introduction, said that the renaming is meant to recognize this specific story and that the city would engage in other actions not specifically related to Dearing but to the goal of creating an inclusive community. Shelia Leuning, President of Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC), urged City Council to seek input directly from the Dearing family and descendants. Lois Corrin, a member of PADC, League of Woman Voters, and a Piedmont resident for over 30 years, offered comments on the next step. “I know we have the resources, the political will, and the social will to actually do something about this and perhaps lead by example for other communities,” she said. “I’m looking forward to this being a first step.” “This is a meaningful step on, not an end to, the journey to achieving the vision laid out by City Council in its anti-racism resolution,” Lillevand said.
articles.title: City to consider naming triangle park for Dearing family

articles.text: The Principals of PHS and PMS and Superintendent Booker are leaving PUSD. The principal replacements were found quickly. There is talk of hurriedly hiring an external Interim Superintendent to allow a new school board to hire the permanent replacement. This could cheat our children and schools. An Interim Superintendent passively holding steady to current momentum could become the default permanent choice. Since champion fundraisers of PEF win almost every school board seat, causing board groupthink, the new school board is unlikely to think any differently. Is there an heir apparent? Will a yearlong search merely yield another insider Superintendent? These risks were apparent in the 2011 rapid promotion of Booker to Assistant Superintendent and quick 2015 appointment to Superintendent. PUSD’s job description specified a Superintendent to “work effectively with a highly capable and dedicated [School] Board.’’ But Booker rubber stamped all wishes of the largest donors to the Ed Foundation even while calling out this “pay to play” system. Some shenanigans included refinancing school bonds to defer property taxes, backing an overpriced theater renovation designed by a large donor with no prior theater design experience (that voters struck down), expanding his roster of highly paid administrators at the expense of paying teachers a living wage, and taking curriculum decisions away from Department Chairs. Multiple scandals erupted in the local and national press from 2015 to 2022. Meanwhile, it became harder for graduates to get into their colleges of choice and visits to the Wellness Center by high school students skyrocketed. Early in Booker’s tenure, school board meetings were not well attended. Few knew that the school board was not leading or researching the issues or that Booker’s research was lacking
articles.title: Time for school board to start making sense

Time for school board to start making sense By Margaret Moneypenny The Principals of PHS and PMS and Superintendent Booker are leaving PUSD. The principal replacements were found quickly. There is talk of hurriedly hiring an external Interim Superintendent to allow a new school board to hire the permanent replacement. This could cheat our children and schools. An Interim Superintendent passively holding steady to current momentum could become the default permanent choice. Since champion fundraisers of PEF win almost every school board seat, causing board groupthink, the new school board is unlikely to think any differently. Is there an heir apparent? Will a yearlong search merely yield another insider Superintendent? These risks were apparent in the 2011 rapid promotion of Booker to Assistant Superintendent and quick 2015 appointment to Superintendent. PUSD’s job description specified a Superintendent to “work effectively with a highly capable and dedicated [School] Board.’’ But Booker rubber stamped all wishes of the largest donors to the Ed Foundation even while calling out this “pay to play” system. Some shenanigans included refinancing school bonds to defer property taxes, backing an overpriced theater renovation designed by a large donor with no prior theater design experience (that voters struck down), expanding his roster of highly paid administrators at the expense of paying teachers a living wage, and taking curriculum decisions away from Department Chairs. Multiple scandals erupted in the local and national press from 2015 to 2022. Meanwhile, it became harder for graduates to get into their colleges of choice and visits to the Wellness Center by high school students skyrocketed. Early in Booker’s tenure, school board meetings were not well attended. Few knew that the school board was not leading or researching the issues or that Booker’s research was lacking or biased. These shortcomings became widely apparent during the pandemic with hundreds of parents attending school board meetings. The school’s response to the pandemic was Booker’s chance to shine. But instead, he burned bridges with parents, often refusing or failing to answer questions about his policies or overlooking the alternatives. District-wide enrollment declined from 2,708 in the 2015- 16 school year to 2,348 students in the 2022-22 school year. Of the 360-student decline, 219 left during the 2020-22 pandemic. Voters in 2020 ushered in school board members who took a back seat to Superintendent Booker, giving him a CEO title and apparently deferring to him. They also told him that DEI-B would be the primary lens through which he will govern the school district. Will any new Superintendent share the community’s views and expectations on Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging (DEI-B), educational excellence, and transparency in decision-making? Let’s not shortchange our kids and schools with a hastily chosen Interim Superintendent being the default choice for the permanent position. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Allyson Aleksey PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. The singular Bike to Work event has been one of the largest bicycle commute celebrations in the United States for over 20 years. articles.text: The New Wheel, an entrepreneurial Bay Area business focused on providing e-bikes to consumers, will open its first Oakland store with a Grand Opening this Sunday, May 22, at 1446 Leimert Boulevard near Rocky’s Market. It’s the third Bay Area e-bike shop opened by married couple Brett Thurber and Karen Wiener, whose vision for The New Wheel began more than a decade ago. “We began to realize the transformational nature of e-bikes for experiencing the richness of local life,” said Weiner. “At the same time, we understood it would take a lot of time and effort to proliferate this vision to the public. We are very pleased to open a new shop in Oakland and serve the community.” The couple find it inspiring to help bring positive change to so many individuals and families throughout the Bay Area, including an improved quality of life. It’s also gratifying for them to know that they are helping to better the environment and spur public policy decisions that support e-bikes as a highly beneficial means of transportation. Brett and Karen started their journey together at UC Berkeley. They opened their first e-bike shop in 2012 in the Bernal Heights neighborhood of San Francisco and a second location in Larkspur four years later. According to University of Tennessee Professor Chris Cherry, whose research focuses on e-bikes and other sustainable modes of transportation, the average cost of ownership, maintenance, and fuel for a car is about $8,000 per year. The average e-bike owner may spend $400 a year on those same expenses. An e-bike is a great way to reduce travel expenses and still have a lot of mobility. For the environment, cars - even EVs - emit 10-30 times more greenhouse gas emissions than e-bikes. “The electric bike has become a crowd-pleaser among cyclists and mobility and urban planning advocates who see it as a catalyst for building more bike infrastructure and addressing issues like traffic congestion,” said Professor Cherry. “It’s taking bicycling out of this very niche group of riders that are either Sunday riders or hard-core commuters and expanding it across the board.” The New Wheel’s mission is a labor of love that started with a fledgling idea more than a decade ago, followed by a tremendous amount of fortitude in the intervening years. In addition to supporting The New Wheel’s customers, Brett and Karen are proud to have created a positive, family-oriented work environment for bike professionals in service, sales and administration. The new store is located at 1446 Leimert Boulevard in the Oakmore neighborhood near Rocky’s Market. The public is invited to the Grand Opening this Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. The event includes live music, food treats by Two Local Girls Catering and food trucks by Rocky’s Market. Jeremy Medina is store manager of The New Wheel in Oakland. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: In February 2021, the Piedmont City Council adopted reach codes that require energy efficiency measures to be included in new construction and existing building renovations. Reach codes are local amendments that go above and beyond existing California building codes (Title 24) to improve the energy efficiency of buildings and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The primary goal of the reach codes is to help Piedmont meet its Climate Action Plan 2.0 emission reduction goals by reducing natural gas use and increasing energy efficiency in buildings. Title 24 receives updates every three years to incorporate the latest changes in construction and technology. The latest update (2019 Energy Code) went into effect on January 1, 2020. Starting January 1, 2023, the 2022 Energy Code will go into effect. When the Energy Code is updated, the City will also need to adopt any local amendments to the Code, including re-adoption of the reach codes. To help inform the development of the next iteration of reach codes, City staff request all those who live and work in Piedmont to participate in an online survey to provide feedback about the current reach codes and suggestions for the next round. The survey is live and will be open until May 20, 2022. All those who complete the online survey will be entered into a raffle to receive a sustainability prize. Take the Community Survey here (https://tinyurl. com/reachcodesurvey). For more information about the reach codes and additional community engagement opportunities, visit the City’s Reach Code Information webpage housed under the Planning & Building Department. Alyssa Dykman is Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be reached at adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Reach Code survey deadline is Friday

articles.text: As of May 9, Piedmont Planning Department is now allowing residents to schedule building permit inspections online. Previously, building inspections had to be made by calling the department or going into City Hall. To schedule a building inspection, visit https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning___building/building_ inspections. Select the date of your desired inspection. Appointments can be made 48 hours in advance of the date selected. To schedule an inspection online, the following information is needed: property address, building permit number, name, phone and email address, and the type of inspection requested. Daily inspection schedules will be posted on the city’s website by 9 a.m. every day. The city noted that this is an interim improvement that will likely last until the end of the year, when the city expects to have a new public portal to schedule inspections.
articles.title: How to schedule building permit inspections online

articles.text: Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King had an accessory dwelling unit (ADU) delivered by Abodu and installed by crane in her backyard on Friday morning, May 4. It will be the new home of her father, Kenneth Gray. “He didn’t want to move to Rossmoor and he wasn’t interested in a senior apartment somewhere. So, we moved forward with the Abodu,” she said. Mayor King added that it has taken almost a year for the installation to be finalized, with the finishing touches of painting and technology hookups completed last week. Abodu is a full-service ADU company that oversees the entire process from backyard assessment, building permits, and installation. The entire process Mayor King speaks with an Abodu crew member on installation day, May 4. Pictured inside a new ADU in the backyard of Mayor Teddy Gray King are Kenneth Gray (left), Teddy King and dog Murphy, John Whitehurst, and Nicholas King, a high school freshman. Kenneth Gray, is welcomed to his new home in the backyard of his daughter, Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King. can take anywhere from six months to a year - construction of the ADU happens off-site, and once completed, the entire unit is crane-lifted onto the homeowner’s property which takes less than a day. The service is available through Northern and Southern California as well as the Pacific Northwest. The structure is a 500-square foot, one-bedroom unit with a base price of $242,000. It has a bedroom, built-in wardrobe, a full bathroom with shower, a full kitchen with dishwasher and sink, and a living room with a window bench. “It’s a big expenditure but a nice product,” noted King. “It can be a good option for people who need to develop more housing, as was my case.” In addition to installing the ADU, Abodu staff were on-site serving coffee and pastries to neighbors who came to see the unit being fitted by crane over the house and onto the backyard. This is the second Abodu ADU delivery in town, In July 2021, resident Jason Villaluz had a 340-square foot studio-style ADU installed in his backyard on Oakland Avenue for his mother to live in. “It was inconceivable that four or five [crew members] set the foundation up so quickly. They moved at light-speed,” said Villaluz at the time. Piedmont City Code allows properties with a single-family residence to have an ADU subject to provisions of City Code division 17.38. A detached one-bedroom ADU may be installed up to 850 square feet, must have independent exterior access, and cannot be taller than 16 feet. Accessory Dwelling Units have become popular in Piedmont as the city moves to meet its Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) goal of 587 units. An ADU is lifted by crane onto Mayor King’s backyard.
articles.title: Mayor King has ADU delivered to her backyard

articles.text: Urban Compassion Project is hosting a bake sale in Oakland this Saturday, May 21 between 11 a.m. and 6 p.m. Urban Compassion Project volunteers will be selling various baked goods to raise funds for the organization’s operating costs. The Project, founded by Vincent Ray Williams, hosts cleanups every Saturday morning at various locations in Oakland. Piedmont residents have joined Williams in this humble mission since the group’s inception. The organization seeks to build communities between the unhoused and housed community through these simple acts of kindness. The volunteer-led grassroots effort started under the name Urban Park Cleanup and has since expanded to provide a variety of resources for the unhoused community of Oakland. If interested in baking something to donate for volunteers to sell, visit https://urbancompassion project.org/events/april2nd-5plgf- 3jzjf-ey38f-wyx89-ama77-lblbxx3nwc-k6bzb-9tnt4-8xenz-6pt25- hly7x-p6bpf-nb3w8-l2yb2 to sign up. You can also sign up to volunteer if you are not bringing baked goods to donate. The bake sale will be held on Grand Avenue near Children’s Fairyland in Oakland, beginning at 11 a.m. Visit the above link for more information.

articles.text: Piedmont Community Church through its Refugee Task Force will host a fundraising dinner on Saturday, June 4 at 6 p.m. to benefit the Putrenkov family, who recently escaped from the wartorn Donbas region of Ukraine. Alex Putrenkov, his wife Maryna and son Vlad are now safe and living with a family in Piedmont but are in need of financial aid to help them settle, become employed and to obtain reliable transportation. The evening will begin with a cocktail reception in the church courtyard before moving into the Guild Hall for a dinner at 7 p.m. The event will be capped off by a live auction at 8 p.m. A limited number of 100 tickets will be sold at $150. articles.text: Mollie King, a senior at Bishop O’Dowd High School, and a youth leader in Piedmont Scout Council’s Troop 4, was honored at a National Court of Honor ceremony on Sunday, May 15 at Lake Temescal in Oakland. She is the first female Scout in Piedmont to become an Eagle Scout, Scouting’s highest rank. “We are proud of the effort and determination that Mollie put forth to earn the rank of Eagle Scout,” said Piedmont Scout Executive Kate Benson. The lessons she learned will have lifelong benefits. We are also thankful that Scouting in Piedmont is now open to everyone. The values instilled through the Scouting program – service, integrity, and respect – are more important now than ever.” Mollie was Camp Crew president last year and responsible for leading the planning of Cub Scout Day Camp. Her leadership with Camp Crew last year and the previous summer as a virtual camp was the basis of earning the Council’s annual William Peterson Youth Leadership Award. Reflecting on her journey to Newly honored Eagle Scout Mollie King wearing a hat of the late, legendary Scout leader Bill Peterson. Mollie was winner of the annual Bill Peterson Award this year. articles.text: Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) will hold a meeting tonight, May 18, at 6 p.m. to discuss the book The Three Mothers by Anna Malaika Tubbs, a local Bay Area author. Piedmont Middle School teacher and PADC Board Member Karen Bloom will facilitate the discussion. The book is a New York Times Bestseller, originally published in February 2021. Tubbs is a multidisciplinary expert on current and historical understandings of race, gender, and equity. After graduating Phi Beta Kappa from Stanford University with a BA in anthropology, she earned her MA in gender studies and a Ph.D. in sociology from the University of Cambridge as a Bill and Melinda Gates Cambridge Scholar. articles.text: Various groups in Piedmont have already begun celebrating and raising awareness for the 50th anniversary of the passage of Title IX legislation, which will occur on June 23. At the May 25 school board meeting the Piedmont Title IX Audit Task Force will present its finding which shows that high school girls’ sports have 55 fewer athletes than the boys. 91% of high school students play a sport and 78% of females play a sport. For those numbers to be equal, 55 more spots need to be made available for and filled by female high school students. Boys Girls PHS Athletes 406 332 Total PHS Students 446 425 % of Participants 91% 78% Title IX is considered by many to be the most important law for equal rights for women after the 1918 right to vote. In 1971-72, only 7% of U.S. high school athletes were girls. Now, girls comprise 43% of high school athletes. Title IX of The Education Amendments Act of 1972 states: “No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” The Task Force will also present the following research. Overall, girls who play sports have higher grades and score higher on standardized tests than non-athletes. Girls who participate in regular exercise experience lower rates of depression. A 2013 study by Ernst & Young of 821 senior managers and executives found that 94% of female executives played organized sports after primary school. The activity drew over 400 participants. • Smet and Boosters President Chris Hart will recognize seniors planning on playing a sport in college next year. May 25: School Board Presentation, 7:00 p.m. at City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. Piedmont Title IX Audit Task Force will present its findings and recommendations. Title IX T-shirts and hoodies can be purchased at the Piedmontstore.org to support Title IX activities. Donations are also accepted on the website and Title IX stickers are available at various locations at PHS.

articles.text: What makes a Rover? How do scientists use them to discover far-away places? Use this activity guide to explore rovers that humans have built, then design one of your own to explore a location in the solar system. Viper rover rolls into Chabot Starting on May 28, see a scale model of NASA’s Artemis lunar rover, the Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover, or VIPER. Launching in 2023, this rover is heading to the Moon’s South Pole in search of ice and other potential resources. Its 100- day mission will answer big questions about lunar water and how it can be used for future human space exploration. Learn more: https://chabot s p a c e.o r g /c a le n d a r / n a s a s - artemis-takeover/2022-05-28/. What is a rover? When humans want to learn about other planets or objects in the solar system, they can use tools like telescopes, satellites, and rovers. A rover is a small, mobile robot that scientists send to moons and planets to land on their surfaces and explore. Rovers can take pictures and collect information about the planet by taking temperature readings, rock, and soil samples. The rovers then send this information back to scientists on earth through radio signals. Rovers can help scientists learn about faraway places without having to send people to space, which can be tricky. Rover research NASA uses rovers to explore other places in our solar system. Research some of NASA’s past missions to learn about what rovers have in common, and how they can be different. Is NASA planning to send any rovers to space in the future? A rendering of NASA’s Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover, or VIPER sheet, sketch what you’d like your rover to look like. Optional Extension: Build a Prototype 1. Build the body of your rover. a) You can use a variety of materials for the body, but it should be something sturdy that you can attach other materials too. 2 Decorate the base. You can paint, color, or wrap your body however you’d like. 3. Build the wheels and legs of your rover. For help making a rover that rolls, follow steps (4-9) below. a) Materials that are round and can roll make great wheels. b) Straws are a helpful material if you’d like to build a rover that rolls. 4. Tape a straw, or cylinder of paper horizontally across the bottom of your rover. 5. Repeat with one, two, or three more straws/paper cylinders. Try to make them equally spaced out on your rover. 6. Identify the materials you will be using as wheels, and as axles. The axel will hold your two wheels together. a) You will need the same number of axles as paper cylinders or straws, and twice the number of wheels. 7. Thread the axle material through the straws or paper cylinders underneath your rover. 8. Use tape or glue to attach the center of your wheel to one end of an axle. Make sure the axel is still threaded through the straws on your rover. 9. Repeat so that each axle has two wheels attached to it, and is suspending on the bottom of your rover. 10. Add the arms, neck, and head to your rover. Use glue, tape, or poke them through the body of your rover to hold them in place. a) Strong, skinny materials that can stand up make good arms or necks. b) You can add different tools to the ends of your rover arms. 11. Add a brain, and an energy source to your rover. You can make them out of paper, cardboard, whatever material you think works best. 12. Decorate with logos, a flag, even passengers 13. France has a prestigious tradition for breeding and riding, and its center at Le Pen two hours west of Paris was a national center until taken private in 2013. We hiked the country roads around Lessard-et-la-Chêne to see the horses grazing at pasture, not skittish or distracted as we walked by. French Trotters are a popular breed, crossed more than a century ago with the English thoroughbred to make a more muscular horse suitable for riding and racing. These noble domestic creatures and mares with their foals have been in service to humankind for tens of thousands of years. We climbed a ridge and at the overlook and marveled at the stunning geometry of green fields brilliant in the sunlight. We spotted the Hippodrome de la Bergerie. Horse riding is popular in France, and much of the countryside is unspoiled with rights-ofway kept open and riding trails that usually avoid paved roads. Walled towns, ancient churches and châteaux are everywhere. Les Plus Beaux Villages de France lists 156 notable small towns with heritage landmarks. From June to September the Federation of haras receives the public with spectator sports of racing and showjumping. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team was crowned once again as the Shoreline Division’s Western Alameda County champions on Friday, May 13 at the College of Alameda after beating Encinal 6-5 on Davis Alazraqui’s hard ground ball that caused an error, allowing Peter Krumins to score from second. The Highlanders rushed the field in celebration. It was Piedmont’s second WACC title in three attempts after last losing to Encinal 3-1 in the 2019 finals. It was coach Eric Olson’s third league championship victory. Friday’s meeting marked the third consecutive time the Highlanders and Jets faced one another for the league title. In 2018 Piedmont defeated Encinal 4-2 in the eighth inning. “This was the rubber match,” said Olson. “We played Encinal twice last week and knew that beating a team three times in a row is extremely difficult, it proved to be that way,” said Olson. Piedmont finished its regular season with an 18-8 overall record and 9-1 against league opponents. The Highlanders were 8-0 in 2021 but weren’t awarded a league banner due to the Covid-abbreviated season “I was just super happy that our kids got to experience success in the playoffs which they missed out on the last two seasons,” said Olson, a Piedmont native. Freshman center fielder Markos Lagios had a monster game, going 3-for-3 with a double, four RBIs, and a stolen base. “I always look forward to Markos’ at bats. He’s super competitive and has all the tools. Like any freshman on varsity, sometimes they try and do a little too much. We’ve wanted him to slow down in games, and we’re starting to see that. He’s had some big hits in the last few games,” said Olson. After the game, Piedmont shortstop Nico Defazio was awarded the Shoreline’s Most Valuable Player award alongside seven other All-League recipients: Alazraqui, Mike Aikawa, Tobin Cantrill, Will Sprague, Peter Krumins, and Alex Tafapolsky. The Highlanders, the no. 5 seed in the North Coast Section playoffs will square off with No. 12 St. Patrick today, May 18 at 5:00 p.m. Piedmont defeated the Bruins 3-2 on March 2. Game Recap Encinal led 3-1 following the top of the third inning and Piedmont narrowed the gap to 3-2 in the bottom of the fourth before Photo by Mike McConathy Piedmont players race onto the field to celebrate winning the league championship against Encinal. jumping ahead 5-3 in the bottom of the fifth. The Jets tied the game with one-run innings in the top of the sixth and seventh. The Highlanders and Alazraqui brought in the game-winner in the bottom of the seventh after a leadoff single by Krumins and five-pitch walk by Defazio. articles.text: Piedmont High star swimmer Simon Lins is back from the CIF State Championship meet at Clovis West in Fresno on Friday and Saturday, May 13-14, where he competed in the 50 freestyle and 100 backstroke. He finished seventh of 18 in the freestyle by clocking a time of 20.44 in the finals, and was timed in 20.20 in the preliminaries, 2nd among 43 swimmers. Ethan Harrington of Palo Alto won with a State record in 19.85 seconds. “I knew going in that it would be really tight. I’m usually ahead on my dive and first breakout, but Ethan beat me in the underwater. It was a pleasure racing him and I’m looking forward to racing him again,” said Lins. Lins’ times qualified him for All-American honors. He entered the State meet after winning NCS’ 50 free with a time of 20.20 and was fifth in the 100 backstroke in 49.64. Lins also won the WACC Championship’s 50 free in 20.49 and had a time of 50.91 in the 100 Back. “I felt like I choked in the finals after being seeded second in the state for the 50. That morning I just felt [I wasn’t] in the right zone. I was looking to break 19 seconds and just wasn’t able to execute,” Lins said. He finished 12th of 16 in the finals of the backstroke with a time of 49.42. In the preliminaries, Lins was 12th of 39 with a slightly better time of 49.40. “In March, I got really sick and was unable to train for twoand-a-half weeks. I could barely eat or sleep, and couldn’t race. Come April, I was able to train and got back in racing ability. In January, I got COVID after winter break and was out for a few weeks; it put me in a bad place. And then right when I was starting to get back into racing shape, Simon Lins will compete over the summer with Piedmont Swim Team and has eyes on the Junior National in July. Lins now moves into the summer swim season, where he will be competing with Piedmont Swim Team and coach Stefan Bill. He’ll be swimming in multiple events aiming for the Junior Nationals on July 28-31 in the Irvine Aquatics Center. “I’m going to work super hard this summer with my coach. I plan on attending Junior Nationals to get some high-quality racing in,” said Lins.

pages.text: 12 Wednesday, May 18, 2022 Sports Piedmont wins WACC Championship in walk-off fashion By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s baseball team was crowned once again as the Shoreline Division’s Western Alameda County champions on Friday, May 13 at the College of Alameda after beating Encinal 6-5 on Davis Alazraqui’s hard ground ball that caused an error, allowing Peter Krumins to score from second. The Highlanders rushed the field in celebration. It was Piedmont’s second WACC title in three attempts after last losing to Encinal 3-1 in the 2019 finals. It was coach Eric Olson’s third league championship victory. Friday’s meeting marked the third consecutive time the Highlanders and Jets faced one another for the league title. In 2018 Piedmont defeated Encinal 4-2 in the eighth inning. “This was the rubber match,” said Olson. “We played Encinal twice last week and knew that beating a team three times in a row is extremely difficult, it proved to be that way,” said Olson. Piedmont finished its regular season with an 18-8 overall record and 9-1 against league opponents. The Highlanders were 8-0 in 2021 but weren’t awarded a league banner due to the Covid-abbreviated season “I was just super happy that our kids got to experience success in the playoffs which they missed out on the last two seasons,” said Olson, a Piedmont native. Freshman center fielder Markos Lagios had a monster game, going 3-for-3 with a double, four RBIs, and a stolen base. “I always look forward to Markos’ at bats. He’s super competitive and has all the tools. Like any freshman on varsity, sometimes they try and do a little too much. We’ve wanted him to slow down in games, and we’re starting to see that. He’s had some big hits in the last few games,” said Olson. After the game, Piedmont shortstop Nico Defazio was awarded the Shoreline’s Most Valuable Player award alongside seven other All-League recipients: Alazraqui, Mike Aikawa, Tobin Cantrill, Will Sprague, Peter Krumins, and Alex Tafapolsky. The Highlanders, the no. 5 seed in the North Coast Section playoffs will square off with No. 12 St. Patrick today, May 18 at 5:00 p.m. Piedmont defeated the Bruins 3-2 on March 2. The Jets tied the game with one-run innings in the top of the sixth and seventh. articles.text: Piedmont’s softball team got the job. It won the league championship, defeating Encinal 8-5 on Thursday, May 12 at Arroyo High in San Lorenzo. It finished the regular season with a 17-6 overall record, and a perfect 10-0 against league teams. It marks their first league title with coach Gene Denard. “Everything was possible this year because of the young ladies buying into what we were trying to do,” Denard said with a big smile. “We had some new coaches, which required an adjustment, but the ladies bought in with the path we set forward this year.” Piedmont’s victory was never in doubt. It led 8-2 by the fourth inning. With another complete game by senior pitcher Izzy Epstein, who struck out seven batters. Epstein was awarded the Shoreline’s Pitcher of the Year award after the win, currently recording 112 innings pitched, an 11-1 overall record, an ERA of 1.375 with 165 strikeouts. Notably, she pitched a one-hitter in Piedmont’s 12-0 semifinals win over Hayward on Tuesday, May 10, and also pitched a perfect game in another 12-0 win over the Farmers on May 6. “Everybody on the team was aware that Izzy was going to get a lot of work. I let her and [catcher] Chiara Lundin take charge, and it really worked out for us. I love my pitcher and my catcher, said Denard. The win gives Piedmont its first league title since 2018, when it had an identical record. PHS will lose stalwarts Epstein and Chiara Lundin to graduation but returns the bulk of its batting order next year to give itself a good shot at back-toback titles. Denard shifted the batting order to feature Leah Bell in the three spot, Morgan Hunt at cleanup, Chiara Lundin in the five, and Epstein behind her. It loaded the middle of the lineup with potent firepower. Lundin and Gretchen Gerhardy were instrumental in the victory, both going 3-for-3 at the plate with two doubles and two runs scored, while Gerhardy also had two RBIs. After the game, it was announced that Piedmont earned eight All-League recipients, including Epstein, Lundin, Bell, Hunt, Gerhardy, Miya Fujimoto, Angelina Wu, and Hailey Ronen. Staff Photo Gretchen Gerhardy had a big game in the title game, going 3-for-3 with two doubles, two RBIs, and two runs scored. Izzy Epstein was named Shoreline Pitcher of the Year award. She had a complete game against Encinal with seven strikeouts. Piedmont players hold the 2022 WACC Shoreline banners after defeating Encinal 8-5. Big win vs. Arcata The Highlanders opened the post-season playoffs by beating Arcata 10-1 in the first round of the North Coast Section playoffs yesterday at Witter Field. Encinal narrowed the gap with three runs in the top of the fifth, but Epstein and the Highlanders retired the next six of the next eight batters for the victory. Lundin smacked a leadoff double and Epstein reaching first after getting hit by a pitch in the second inning. Gerhardy hit an RBI double, followed by Ginger Gardner hitting a sac-fly to score Epstein. With two outs, Fujimoto brought in Gerhardy after a groundball went through the first baseman’s legs for a 3-2 lead. In the bottom of the fourth, Lundin hit a double to left field and Gerhardy brought her in from second with another double to left. With two outs, Ronen got on base by getting hit by a pitch, and advanced to second on a wild pitch. Fujimoto forced an error on the third baseman to bring in Gerhardy and Ronen. Wu then followed with a single to center and Bell cracked a double past the center fielder through Arroyo’s lengthy outfield without a fence, 8-2. Bell was 2-for-3 with a double and two RBIs. Epstein pitched all seven innings with seven strikeouts and allowed two earned runs. articles.text: The Highlander track team had a highly successful meet at the North Coast Section Bayshore sectional on Saturday, May 14 at Hayward High, with 11 PHS athletes in eight events earning topsix results. All qualified for the NCS Meet of Champions at Dublin High this Friday and Saturday, May 20-21. Jack Stein, Christian Taylor, Jamie Schwarz and Ellie Black qualified for the 1600 meters, and Black also qualified in the 3200 and plans to focus only on the 2-mile event. Cooper Downing and Schwarz qualified in the 800. The boys’ 4x100 relay team of Luke Alban, Quincy Munyan, Parker Terrill, and Matthew Riordan qualified for the MOC, in addition to the 4x400 team of Alban, Parker Long, Downing, and Terrill. Terrill will principally compete in the pole vault and 110-meter hurdles, and Brie Sotelo will compete in the shot. It’s the largest number of Piedmont athletes to qualify for the NCS Meet of Champions in five years. “It’s a great feeling. This team has really had a great season and had a lot of fun. I feel like this team is closer than other teams in all the disciplines, from the throws group, sprinters, and distance. It’s a really close group,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. Saturday was a memorable day for Downing, who won the 800 with a blazing time of 1:55.20 in a field of 21 runPhotos by Steve Zirkelbach Coach Jeanine Holmlund and Cooper Downing at the finish of the 4x400 relay. Downing won the 800 and helped the relay team finish second. Ellie Black qualified for the 3200 meters at the Meet of Champions. Parker Terrill qualified for the Meet of Champions in four events: pole vault, 110-meter hurdles, and 4x100 relay. ners. After finishing second to Berkeley’s Timothy Keller in the WACC Championship the previous week, Downing beat his opponent by .49 of a second. Downing also ran the anchor leg of the 4x400 relay which was second among 17 schools with a time of 3:27.915. Berkeley won in a photo finish by a razor-thin margin of .003 of a second. “Cooper is looking really good, and I still think he can run faster. His photo-finish in the relay was exhilarating to watch,” said Holmlund. Multi-event athlete Terrill qualified in three events. He won the pole vault with a height of 14 feet, 6 inches in a field of 14, finished fourth of 21 in the 110- meter hurdles in 16.99, and was on the 4x100 relay team. The 4x100 team of Terrill, Alban, Munyan, and Riordan was fourth of 15 teams with a time of 43.63. Holmlund credits Terrill’s presence as a decathlete as a key catalyst in the success of the team this season. Black finished second in both the 1600 and 3200, clocking 5:07.23 in the 1600 against 21 other runners, and posting a time of 11:14.08 in the 3200 in a field of 19. Schwarz, a sophomore, finished fifth in the 1600 in 5:23.63, and placed sixth of 22 in the 800 in 2:28.56. Sotelo was sixth in the shot with a distance of 27 feet, 10 inches. Stein finished second of 23 runners in the 1600 with a time of 4:17.93. He lost by .21 of a second to Alameda’s David Song after holding the lead over the Hornets’ runner until the last lap. Stein also competed in the 3200, and finished 10th in 10:02.34. It’s worth mentioning that Stein recently won the 1600 and 3200 at the WACC Championship ahead of Song, but Piedmont’s senior runner was dealing with an illness one week earlier, making his result in the 1600 an impressive accomplishment given his condition. Stein considers the 3200 his main event and holds the Piedmont school record in both the 1600 and 3200 meters. NEXT UP Piedmont heads to the NCS Meet of Champions in Dublin on Friday and Saturday, May 20-21. Events start 1:30 pm on Friday and 12:00 pm on Saturday. The top three finishers in each event qualify for the California State Meet at Buchanan High School in Clovis on Friday and Saturday, May 27-28.
articles.title: 11 PHS athletes qualify for NCS Meet of Champions

articles.text: Piedmont’s tennis season came to an end on Saturday, May 14, with a tough 6-1 loss to No. 1 ranked Head-Royce in the Division 2 North Coast Section Team Tournament. The Highlanders entered as the No. 5 seed and upset No. 4 Lick Wilmerding 5-2 in the quarterfinals on Thursday, May 12 in San Francisco. Piedmont won its first-round match over No. 12 Sonoma Academy by forfeit due to a COVID-19 outbreak on the opposing team. The No. 1 Jayhawks went onto win the team title with a 5-2 win over No. 2 University of San Francisco. It marks the first NCS banner in Head-Royce school history. “Head-Royce is a very strong team. Although the score was lopsided, we put up a good fight.” said Piedmont coach Jim Landes. Piedmont was able to avenge a 4-3 loss to Lick Wilmerding on April 20 while playing in windy Golden Gate Park. This time, Piedmont controlled the day despite having three matches go to a third-set. “We beat Lick in the quarterfinals 5-2,” Landes said. “We played very well, winning three of four singles and two of three at doubles. There was a lot of tension when we were leading 3-1 with the three remaining matches going to a third set, but we took two of them.” Piedmont ended its season at 15-5 and earned this year’s Western Alameda County Conference banner after going a perfect 10-0 against league opponents. The Highlanders earned five All-League recipients, including Charlie Lambert, Ben Breber, and Lennie Burchardt at singles, and Kai Baudendistel and Charlie Olcott at doubles. 5-2 win over Lick Wilmerding Piedmont’s 5-2 victory started with two quick doubles wins, the No. 2 pairing of Monte Imburg and Charlie Sullivan winning 6-1, Staff Photos Monte Imburg won 6-1, 6-2 with Charlie Sullivan against Lick Wilmerding and 6-1, 6-4 over Head-Royce with Oliver Maxwell. 6-2, and No. 3 Brady Colbert and Oliver Maxwell winning 6-4, 6-4. In singles, Burchardt lost 6-4, 6-4 at No. 2, but Ethan Pham at No. 3 won 6-0, 7-5 to put Piedmont ahead 3-1. Charlie Lambert at No. 1 singles reeled in a three-set win to clinch the afternoon, 6-4, 4-6, 6-2. Also winning was Breber at No. 3 in three sets, 7-5, 4-6, 6-2. The No. 1 doubles team of Baudendistel and Olcott lost 5-7, 6-0, 6-2. 6-1 loss to Head-Royce Piedmont lost 6-1 to the eventual NCS champions in the semifinals on May 14 while playing at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. It was their second loss to HeadRoyce and by the same score this season. At doubles, Imburg and Oliver Maxwell claimed Piedmont’s only win of the day in straight sets at No. 2 by scores of 6-1, 6-4. At No. 1, Baudendistel and Olcott lost in three sets, 6-3, 3-6, 10-7. Sullivan and Jacob Hsia lost 6-4, 6-0 at No. 3. In singles, PHS lost all four matches in straight sets. Lambert lost 6-1, 6-3 at No. 1, Burchardt fell 6-2, 6-1 at No. 2, Breber lost 7-5, 6-3 at No. 3, and Pham lost 6-1, 6-2. Charlie Sullivan helped win at No. 2 doubles with Monte Imburg against Lick Wilmerding. At No. 1 singles, Charlie Lambert won in three sets against Lick Wilmerding.
articles.title: Piedmont falls to No.1 Head- Royce in NCS Semifinals

Black finished second in both the 1600 and 3200, clocking 5:07.23 in the 1600 against 21 other runners, and posting a time of 11:14.08 in the 3200 in a field of 19. READ IT IN THE POST Piedmont falls to No.1 HeadRoyce in NCS Semifinals By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s tennis season came to an end on Saturday, May 14, with a tough 6-1 loss to No. 1 ranked Head-Royce in the Division 2 North Coast Section Team Tournament. The Highlanders entered as the No. 5 seed and upset No. 4 Lick Wilmerding 5-2 in the quarterfinals on Thursday, May 12 in San Francisco. Piedmont won its first-round match over No. 12 Sonoma Academy by forfeit due to a COVID-19 outbreak on the opposing team. The No. 1 Jayhawks went onto win the team title with a 5-2 win over No. 2 University of San Francisco. It marks the first NCS banner in Head-Royce school history. “Head-Royce is a very strong team. Although the score was lopsided, we put up a good fight.” said Piedmont coach Jim Landes. Piedmont was able to avenge a 4-3 loss to Lick Wilmerding on April 20 while playing in windy Golden Gate Park. This time, Piedmont controlled the day despite having three matches go to a third-set. “We beat Lick in the quarterfinals 5-2,” Landes said. “We played very well, winning three of four singles and two of three at doubles. There was a lot of tension when we were leading 3-1 with the three remaining matches going to a third set, but we took two of them.” Piedmont ended its season at 15-5 and earned this year’s Western Alameda County Conference banner after going a perfect 10-0 against league opponents. The Highlanders earned five All-League recipients, including Charlie Lambert, Ben Breber, and Lennie Burchardt at singles, and Kai Baudendistel and Charlie Olcott at doubles. 5-2 win over Lick Wilmerding Piedmont’s 5-2 victory started with two quick doubles wins, the No. 2 pairing of Monte Imburg and Charlie Sullivan winning 6-1, Staff Photos Monte Imburg won 6-1, 6-2 with Charlie Sullivan against Lick Wilmerding and 6-1, 6-4 over Head-Royce with Oliver Maxwell. 6-2, and No. 3 Brady Colbert and Oliver Maxwell winning 6-4, 6-4. In singles, Burchardt lost 6-4, 6-4 at No. 2, but Ethan Pham at No. 3 won 6-0, 7-5 to put Piedmont ahead 3-1. Charlie Lambert at No. 1 singles reeled in a three-set win to clinch the afternoon, 6-4, 4-6, 6-2. Also winning was Breber at No. 3 in three sets, 7-5, 4-6, 6-2. The No. 1 doubles team of Baudendistel and Olcott lost 5-7, 6-0, 6-2. 6-1 loss to Head-Royce Piedmont lost 6-1 to the eventual NCS champions in the semifinals on May 14 while playing at St. Mary’s College in Moraga. It was their second loss to HeadRoyce and by the same score this season. At doubles, Imburg and Oliver Maxwell claimed Piedmont’s only win of the day in straight sets at No. 2 by scores of 6-1, 6-4. At No. 1, Baudendistel and Olcott lost in three sets, 6-3, 3-6, 10-7. Sullivan and Jacob Hsia lost 6-4, 6-0 at No. 3. In singles, PHS lost all four matches in straight sets. Lambert lost 6-1, 6-3 at No. 1, Burchardt fell 6-2, 6-1 at No. 2, Breber lost 7-5, 6-3 at No. 3, and Pham lost 6-1, 6-2. Charlie Sullivan helped win at No. 2 doubles with Monte Imburg against Lick Wilmerding. At No. 1 singles, Charlie Lambert won in three sets against Lick Wilmerding.
