articles.text: The Piedmont High badminton team wrapped up its season in the Division 2 North Coast Section Tournament at Washington High in Fremont on Saturday, May 14, with impressive results. Isa Griffis and Jerry Liu won the mixed doubles gold medal in a three-set victory over Mary Kelly and Sam Brainard of University by scores of 21-12, 19-21, 21-8. Griffis was officially named the WACC’s Co-Player of the Year along with San Lorenzo’s Edison Manzanilla. The Highlanders earned four All-League recipients including Griffis, Liu, Ivan Munn, and Naprine Xiong. The Highlanders also competed in the League Championship Tournament on May 7 at Mt. Eden, where Griffis and Liu won mixed doubles with a 21-8, 21-4 straight set win over Piedmont teammates Ivan Munn and Dylan Ong. Ethan Tran (left) and Gary Zhou (right, ducking) won the league title in doubles. Isa Griffis (left) and Jerry Liu won the mixed doubles at NCS and WACC. In addition, Gary Zhou and Ethan Tran won the boys’ doubles championship with a 21-13, 21-10 victory over PHS teammates Edwin Tang and Justin Phmah. Nasreen Schulze advanced to the girls’ finals but lost to San Lorenzo’s Patricia Quinzon by scores of 21-8, 21-19. To get there, she defeated Reenoa Manzanilla of San Lorenzo, 21-11, 21-17. Maddie Xiong finishing fourth after losing a third-place match to Manzanilla in three-sets, 13-21, 21-14, 17-21. In girls’ doubles, Sophie Hess and Emma Eisemon earned third-place with a three-set win over PHS teammates Angie Foo and Anna Jansson, 18-21, 21-11, 21-12. The Highlanders finished their regular season with a 6-4 overall record and placed third in the Shoreline Division, back of Berkeley (6-3-1) and San Lorenzo (7-3).

articles.text: Montclair Village will host an Art Walk on Saturday and Sunday, May 22-23. This sidewalk art show will have 40 artists from the Bay Area displaying their handcrafted works. Presented by the Montclair Village Association, this open-air art gallery will take place from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. For more information, contact the Montclair Village Association at (510) 339-1000 or Pacific Fine Arts Festivals at (209) 267-4394. Featured artists include: Alice Glass of Alice Reva Designs of Albany, uses flora and fauna to dye eco-friendly fashions. Alice’s creations of mulberry silk pillowcases and raw silk eye pillows offer rest and relaxation. She also creates silk bandanas, scrunchies and headbands. George Ehrenhaft discovered his watercolor painting talent after years of teaching high school English in New York. A resident of Moraga, he enjoys plein air painting depicting old barns and celebrating nature’s landscapes, mountains, trees, lakes and rivers. Susan Berger of Strong Heart Glass in Berkeley, creates fused glass pieces that are both functional and artistic. She creates a mosaic by placing bits of glass next to each other using foil and paints for detailing. Kelly Morgen of Kelly Morgen Jewelry in Mountain View creates necklaces created with precious metals, natural cabochons, gemstones, ivory from recycled piano keys. Steven Andersen of Spring Garden Cedar uses Western red cedar to handcraft lovely, durable outdoor furniture. Choose from Adirondack and rocking chairs, glider benches, dining tables, chairs and end tables. Artist Susan Berger display her glasswork.
articles.title: Montclair Village Art Walk this weekend

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco currently is showing the “Memento: Jayashree Chakravarty and Lam Tung Pang” exhibit through June 6. The exhibition is part of an ongoing series of singular exhibitions at the museum entitled Today’s Asian Voices. The exhibition marks the inaugural Hambrecht Contemporary Gallery installation, which includes two contemporary works that speak to global issues of urbanization and political uncertainty. The Hambrecht Contemporary Gallery was formerly used for special exhibitions and has recently been transformed into a dedicated space for a rotating selection of both modern and contemporary works. Viewers will see Personal Space by Chakravarty (2001), an 8-foot-tall, 30-foot-wide work built from painted strips of paper. An immersive video by Hong Kong-based mixed media artist Pang entitled A Day of Two Suns (2019), combines unsynchronized images from four projectors that combine with the shadows of museum visitors and moving objects. “This work is prophetic and nostalgic,” said Abby Chen, Head of Contemporary Art about the newly acquired work. “It documents a city, and a system, in the process of fading and awakening.” For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/memento-jayashreechakravarty-and-lam-tung-pang/. Asian Art Museum is located at 200 Larkin Street in San Francisco; phone (415) 581-3500. Personal Space, 2001, by Jayashree Chakravarty, currently on view at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco.
articles.title: Chakravarty and Pang exhibit at Asian Art Museum through June 6

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California’s exhibition celebrating Edith Heath, designer and founder of Heath Ceramics, is on display now through October 30. Edith Heath: A Life in Clay showcases the legacy of the artist with over 50 pieces of ceramics, clay samples, photographs, and personal memorabilia on display. A documentary video is shown inside the museum as well. The new exhibition introduces visitors to the artist’s career, which was deeply expressive of California’s land and lifestyle. Heath, who died in 2005, focused on creating dependable and long-lasting products for the home, with a focus on sustainability. A Life in Clay was organized by Oakland Museum’s Curator of Photography Drew Johnson, and guest curator Jennifer Volland. “Edith Heath transformed our notion of ‘good design,’ pioneering a new aesthetic of natural, stylish yet functional products made from local materials and designed to endure,” said Johnson. “As an icon of quintessential California design who lived and worked in Sausalito and San Francisco, OMCA is excited to share the extraordinary story of Heath’s life and legacy.” (510) 652-1662 Office (510) 652-1690 Fax info@woodwindowswarehouse.com woodwindowswarehouse.com 1301 66th Street Emeryville, CA 94608 Wood Windows Warehouse Residential & Commercial Custom & Standard CA Contractors License No. 823258 Edith Heath, founder of Heath Ceramics A Life in Clay examines Heath’s technical experimentations with native California clays and glaze formulas. Her love of natural landscapes shaped the quality of her design and inspired her to seek clays from California rather than what was traditionally used for dinnerware. “What began as a rebellion against imported white clay more than fifty years ago is now a modern-day classic,” said Volland, who has researched the artist since 2014 and served as an essayist for the book Edith Heath: Philosophies. To learn more about the exhibition, and to purchase tickets, visit www.museumca.org.
articles.title: Edith Heath’s Life in Clay exhibit at Oakland Museum through Oct. 30

articles.text: Mountain Theatre’s production of Hello Dolly opens this Sunday, May 22 on Mt. Tamalpais above Mill Valley. Hello, Dolly!, the blockbuster Broadway hit, bursts with humor, romance, high-energy dancing, and some of the greatest songs in musical theater history. The romantic and comic exploits of Dolly Gallaher-Levi, turn-of-the-century matchmaker and “woman who arranges things,” are certain to entertain audiences of all ages. Starring Dyan McBride as Mrs. Dolly Gallagher Levi and Randy Nazarian, as Horace Vandergelder, the production includes Miranda Long, a sophomore at Piedmont High School, in the ensemble. Long is the only cast member under 17 years old and is thrilled to make her Mountain Play debut. Jerry Herman’s feel-good score includes such memorable songs as “Put on Your Sunday Clothes,” “Ribbons Down My Back,” “Before the Parade Passes By,” “Elegance,” “It Only Takes a Moment,” and the title song “Hello, Dolly.” This one-of a kind mountaintop event takes place at Cushing Memorial Amphitheatre, better known as the Mountain Theatre, an open-air venue in Mount Tamalpais State Park with 3750 seats. It has redwood groves and oak woodlands with a spectacular view from its 2,571-foot peak. On a clear day, visitors can see the Farallon Islands 25 miles out to sea, the Marin County hills, San Francisco and the bay, hills, and cities of the East Bay, and Mount Diablo. The musical will be performed at 2 p.m. on May 22 and 29, and June 5, 11, 12 and 19. For tickets, visit mountainplay.org.
articles.title: Miranda Long in cast of Hello, Dolly at Mountain Theatre

articles.text: Opera and theater, from Greek tragedy to those 18th Century rock stars the Castrati, have historically told stories through a broad spectrum of voices, personalities, and gender expressions. Performed and curated by mezzo-soprano Lily Bogas and countertenor Matheus Coura, They Sing! will be performed at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, May 22 at 5 p.m. Explore feelings from sublime to irreverent to comedic: recognizing that voices of the same range have validity in roles across the gender spectrum. This program will feature arias, songs, and duets by Monteverdi, Handel, Mozart, Bizet, Strauss, Kurt Weill, and Ricky Ian Gordon. They Sing! will take you on a journey through the past, present and into the future of how music has shaped and reflected the multifaceted human experience. Mezzo soprano Lily Bogas is a student at the Eastman School of Music, Her recent credits include Taller Daughter in Missy Mazzoli’s Proving Up, Dido in Dido and Aeneas, and Cinderella in Into the Woods. A finalist in the National CS Vocal Competition, and third place winner in the Schmidt Vocal Competition, Bogas was also a finalist in the American Songbook Academy, performing jazz standards alongside Michael Feinstein. Bogas will be making her mainstage debut with Festival Opera as Clotilde in Norma this season. Praised for his “sonorous voice” and “delightful spontaneity”, Brazilian-American countertenor Matheus Coura’s recent performances include Giuliano in Eliogabalo with West Edge Opera, and Narcissus in Two united in a single soul with San Francisco Ballet. Coura is a recipient of the SF Artist Grant, was a finalist in the Bethlehem Bach Competition, and was a prize winner at the St. Petersburg Opera Guild and Cooper-Bing Competitions. Coura is also an international portrait photographer, and resident artist at The Convent Arts Collective where he co-founded the drag revue Bad Habits. Poster for They Sing!
articles.title: Festival Opera presents They Sing at PCA on May 22

articles.text: Conductor Jessica Bejarano Ham radio enthusiasts open the airwaves by saying CQ. This column wants to open the airwaves and will use the words “seeking quality” (Quality Control). My question to you is: “are the most famous musicians on the international concert circuit really the best?“ It is an ongoing question, and open to constant review. It was a busy weekend of four concerts in three days. On Friday evening the San Francisco Philharmonic played a gala concert in Herbst Theater. They are one of the newer ensembles and are trying to establish a niche. These days, many musical organizations send out “subliminal messages“ in order to secure a fan base. Philharmonic seems to be in alliance with this philosophy. My interest is purely musical. I need to state this unequivocally. In my opinion, Philharmonic is a high level musical ensemble. They play well, despite some shortcomings in membership. Their conductor, Jessica Bejarano, is an inspiration and encourages the players to play above their ability. That is what matters to me and, to be honest with you, that is what matters to the music. Philharmonic‘s assets are: 1) a conductor who inspires the best effort in the players and the music. And 2) A supportive and enthusiastic audience. The evening’s concert had an added bonus…a cello soloist who is worthy of a worldwide solo career.
articles.title: Seeking quality…CQ, CQ

articles.text: Alex Gibson as Henry (center), Margo Seibert (Jessica), Justin Gregory Lopez (Toby), and Isabel Santiago (Paula) star in the West Coast premiere of Dave Malloy’s Octet at Berkeley Rep. Tony Award nominee playwright Dave Malloy makes his debut at Berkeley Repertory Theatre with Octet, with performances now through May 29. articles.text: Local artist and Piedmont native Michael Stehr will host an illustrated art lecture at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, May 27 at 7 p.m. Titled “A Stroll in Rome: The Ponte Umberto to Saint Peter’s”, his lecture will describe a recent guided tour he led in Rome. The city of Rome boasts some of the more noteworthy destinations in the Western World. The Pantheon, the Sistine Chapel, and Saint Peter’s Basilica are just a few of the landmarks that attract visitors from around the world. But with so much history around every corner, sometimes the short journey to arrive at a destination is as thrilling as the encounter with that destination itself. Join art historian and lecturer Michael Stehr as he discusses one of his favorite strolls in Rome, the walk from the Ponte Umberto to Saint Peter’s Basilica. Viewers will see some of the world’s greatest urban vistas and experience encounters with artists Michelangelo, Bernini, and Carlo Maderno, among others. Artist Michael Stehr on the Ponte Umberto in Rome.

articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Michael Friedes, an artist and interior designer, is having his debut art exhibition at Piedmont Center for the Arts. The show, titled “A Time of Place”, marks Friedes’ 20th anniversary living in California, and this new collection is a love story of his years living in the East Bay, San Francisco, and Sonoma. The collection features an array of abstract landscape paintings that reflect the diversified beauty of the Bay Area, evoking Friedes’ visual joy and memories that he has experienced while living in California. The images range from the majestic sunsets to the sparkling views of the coastline to the glistening hills of the wine country. Friedes’ point of view and love of surrealism is echoed in a reflective, meditative manner throughout the collection. The next gallery dates are Saturday and Sunday, May 28-29 from 11 a.m to 2 p.m. The Center for the Arts is located at 801 Magnolia Avenue.
articles.title: Friedes art exhibit continues at PCA on May 28

articles.text: An art exhibit honoring the life and work of local artist Diane Levy will be held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from June 11 to June 26. Founder of the San Francisco Children’s Art Center at Fort Mason, she taught art in West Oakland in a storefront studio where children came to paint and use art materials free of charge. The exhibit is an homage to her artwork and honors her lifelong dedication to bringing art to children. All proceeds will go to Arts for Oakland Kids, which provides grants to artists and arts organizations for hands-on programs in Oakland’s most under-resourced public schools. The gallery hours are Saturday and Sunday 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. the weekends of June 11-12. 18-19, and 25-26. Background Diane Levy, also known as Andy, created a close community of friends, family and artists in Berkeley. In her youth, she studied art at UC Berkeley with Margaret O’Hagan, who had been a student of Hans Hofmann, Vaclav Vytacil and André Lhote. Margaret O’Hagan’s style was further informed by Picasso and the indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest. Andy’s early work reflects her teacher’s influences. In her later years and after a long hiatus from painting, she developed a more whimsical style filled with images and figures inspired by quick sketches of people in cafes, friends who were willing models, newspaper clippings, fantasy, and dreams. unformed thoughts and feelings in a language of images. She felt this approach provides an affirming experience for every child. As a project of the San Francisco Children’s Art Center, with sponsorship from The Junior League of San Francisco, Andy developed and brought an art therapy program to both UCSF and SF General hospitals. She and her staff enriched the lives of injured and sick children by bringing to their bedsides a variety of expressive media, and an atmosphere in which self-expression was encouraged and supported. Prior to founding the San Francisco Children’s Art Center, Andy established in conjunction with the Peter Maurin House a storefront child art studio in West Oakland, where children came to paint and to use other art materials free of charge. In her later years she offered art lessons to individual children in her own studio. This current exhibition celebrating Andy’s art and spirit offers an opportunity for friends and the larger community to purchase her work to display in homes, businesses, or other venues where it can be seen and enjoyed. To honor Andy’s lifelong dedication to teaching art to children, Arts for Oakland Kids, which provides grants to artists and arts organizations for hands-on programs in Oakland’s most under-resourced public schools, will be the recipient of all proceeds from the sale of the paintings in this exhibit. A young Diane Levy. In her middle years, Andy founded the San Francisco Children’s Art Center at Fort Mason. Her instruction involved a carefully structured environment in which children learned to respect an orderly use of materials but were given the opportunity to express themselves freely without prescribed methods of representation. Her philosophy of teaching art was derived in part from Rhoda Kellogg, an educator and collector of children’s art who, based on extensive research, found that children’s art unimpeded by adult interference develops along a universal continuum from simple scribbles to rudimentary shapes to more complex pictorial representations. Andy believed that engaging children in the creative process in this way enhances their self-confidence, allowing them to gain insight into themselves and crystallizing their previously

articles.text: On Thursday, May 12, Piedmont High School art students showcased their masterpieces from throughout the year at the All-School Art Show. The exhibit was on view from 6:00-8:00 p.m. in the new theater building foyer, the second such event in the building. More than 200 students from Art 1-4, Ceramics 1-4, Digital Design and Digital Photography entered pieces. The exhibit included 300 pieces. Sophomore Taylor Rolefson’s piece contrasts the world of color with that of black and white. The May 12 Art show gave every Piedmont High School art student the opportunity to display 1-3 pieces. “It was a wonderful celebration of their work. So many artists were there and received support from friends, family, and community members,” said PHS Art teacher Gillian Bailey. All art students at PHS and MHS were represented in the show, except for AP students, who had their own show two weeks earlier. Junior Henry Brayer explained the lessons he learned from Ceramics teacher Hannah Bjork to create his teapot. “I’m usually pressing the clay down really hard and trying to muscle it, but clay is much more delicate. Ms. Bjork showed me a lot of ways to maneuver your way around the clay. She says don’t fight the clay, use the clay to your advantage and don’t try to force anything to it.” The Introduction class, Art 1, created pieces which focused on a color background and moved from the back to front, by trying to develop form with a small object. Hot sauce labels and food Hailey Ronin’s newspaper ship literally sails off the page. Art teacher Department Chair Gillian Bailey stands by a taco truck project constructed from photopaper. trucks were made by the Digital Design students, requiring not only the design, but production of the label for sauce bottles and miniature trucks folded from photo paper. A 3D-Art class focused pieces on textures of underwater landscapes. Another favorite project of Art 2 was the shoe project, producing fine representations of student’s prized Converse, Nike and high heel footwear. In one of Bjork’s ceramics classes, her students were challenged to produced 2-D aerial views of their homes and a ceramic 3-D piece accompanying. This was their first gallery showing in high school for many students. The last one was in 2019. “During the pandemic some kids really flourished in art, but some kids really felt locked down. If you don’t have emotional energy trying to do creative things and break out if that is not a natural outlet for you, it can be very tough,” said Bailey. Sophomore Bauer Peterson used acrylic paint to produce the largest piece in the show measuring 3 x 5 feet.

articles.text: In honor of Asian American Pacific Islander Heritage Month, join a special screening of Far East Deep South followed by a discussion with the producer/ director. The event will be virtual. • May 21-24 Film Screening (on demand) • May 23, 7 p.m. A discussion with producer Baldwin Chiu and director Larissa Lam, moderated by Bryant Lin. The screening is sponsored by Stanford Center for Asian Health Research and Education, and the Vincent V. C. Woo Memorial Foundation, in partnership with the American Medical Women’s Association and Piedmont Asian American Club. About the film Far East Deep South follows Charles Chiu and his family as they travel from California to Mississippi to find the grave of Charles’ father, K.C. Lou. Their search leads to stunning revelations about their family and they get a crash course on the history of Chinese immigrants in the segregated South. Through encounters with local residents and historians, this Chinese American family not only discovers their family’s important role in the Mississippi Delta, but they also learn about the symbiotic relationship between the Black and Chinese communities during the Jim Crow era. The film provides a window into the struggles of Chinese immigrants in the American South during the late 1800s to mid-1900s and the discrimination they faced. The Chiu family’s history demonstrates how exclusionary immigration laws like the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 separated their family for generations. This deeply moving and unforgettable story offers a poignant and important perspective on race relations, immigration and American identity. For more information visit www.fareastdeepsouth.com.
articles.title: AAPI celebrates heritage Month with film & discussion May 23

articles.text: It’s an interesting experience to approach a film with one set of expectations and realize, as the story evolves, that it is entirely something else. That’s the case of Mr. Holmes. Going in I assumed that the setting would be London, during those nascent years of the 20th century, not long after the end of World War I. Mr. Holmes is at the top of his deductive game and often takes intricate cases with subtle clues to be cleverly unraveled. Buttressing my assumption is the fact that Ian McKellen, a gifted character actor, is portraying Holmes, sans deerstalker cap and oversized Meerschaum pipe (something Watson added), but in all ways a perfectly cast Holmes. But Mr. Holmes is a different movie. Based on the novel A Slight Trick of the Mind, by Mitch Cullin, the narrative is set in 1947. Sherlock Holmes, now in his 90s, is living on his bucolic Sussex farm. He has been retired for some 30 years and has used this time to raise bees and study botany. He lives a solitary life, with the exception of his housekeeper, Mrs. Munro (Laura Linney), and her precocious 10-yearold son, Roger (Milo Parker). As is soon made evident, Mr. Holmes is a penetrating character study of a man once renowned, thanks to the embellished writings of his friend and case collaborator, Dr. John H. Watson, who wrote what Holmes refers to as “penny dreadfuls” about their exploits. He has retreated from his former life and is now confronted with the harsh realities of aging – his once keen mind going sideways, his powers of observation, always the fulcrum of his detection, growing increasingly elusive. Holmes is gradually becoming a man who has outlived the person he once cherished: his former self. His daily frustration with his decline, compounded by regret for certain choices from his past, has made him taciturn and even a bit desperate. At one point, his face folding in emotional pain, he acknowledges, “I have been alone all of my life.” There is one seemingly minor case offered up through flashbacks, relevant because it causes Holmes such pain that its conclusion results in his retirement. He remembers only that the year was 1919 and it involved a recently married woman (Hattie Morahan) who was enamored with learning to play the glass harmonica. Against her husband’s wishes. Holmes is hired to follow her and discover how she is paying for her lessons. What he can’t sort out is what occurred that caused him to leave his flourishing practice and move to Sussex 30 years ago from London. With the encouragement of Roger, who has clandestinely read the initial pages, Holmes tries to write down the details of the case, hoping to puzzle out its denouement. Meanwhile, he is also in search of a restorative herb that will revitalize his mind as well as his body. He makes a journey to Hiroshima, Japan, but to no avail. What makes Mr. Holmes worthwhile is the exceptional performance of Ian McKellen. He is, in every respect, Sherlock Holmes. In the backstory we see a face that is a study in incisive intelligence and vitality, his style incomparable. It’s only later that he falls into a kind of helpless sadness and longs for what once was. McKellen is, in a word, remarkable in both roles. Mr. Holmes. articles.text: Bouquets to Art, the de Young Museum’s premiere fundraiser and annual display of artwork-inspired floral installations, will begin on June 7. Bouquets to Art, now in its 38th year, is back to full-capacity following a virtual event in 2020 and a hybrid, limited-capacity event last year. For one week, more than 100 experienced floral designers will converge at the de Young to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s vast array of paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Bouquets to Art is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events every year. The event is presented by the volunteer members of the fine arts museums - and draws nearly 800,000 visitors a year, with net proceeds of more than $7 million. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. Guests will be greeted with a large-scale aerial artwork piece by Bay Area artist Windy Chien. Entitled The Three Dragons, the hand-knotted artwork hangs in the museum’s Wilsey Court. Those who visit during the week of Bouquets to Art will have a chance to view Hung Liu’s large piece Resident Alien, first exhibited at the Capp Street Project in 1988 and exhibited by the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco last year. The painting, arguably Liu’s most famous, depicts her own “Green Card” on a larger-than-life scale. It is now in the collection of the San Jose Museum of Art. “Hung Liu is uniquely positioned to tell the stories of immigrants to the United States. In 2020, she celebrated the milestone of having lived an equal number of years in China and the United States. As one of the foremost painters in the United States, Liu is a testament to the fact that our brightest citizens are often born under foreign skies,” said Janna Keegan, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art and Programming at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. Bouquets to Art is a weeklong event that officially kicks off on the evening of June 6 with an opening-night party. Between June 7 and June 12, a series of lectures, book launches, and raffles will take place. For a full list of programming, visit https:// www.famsf.org/press-room/bouquets-art. Tickets sold out weeks prior to the event in 2021. Reserve your tickets now by visiting https:// deyoung.famsf.org/bouquets-toart. Bouquets to Art in 2010. Photo by Yuri Krasov

pages.text: Wednesday, May 18, 2022 21 AAPI celebrates heritage Month with film & discussion May 23 In honor of Asian American Pacific Islander Heritage Month, join a special screening of Far East Deep South followed by a discussion with the producer/ director. The event will be virtual. • May 21-24 Film Screening (on demand) • May 23, 7 p.m. A discussion with producer Baldwin Chiu and director Larissa Lam, moderated by Bryant Lin. The screening is sponsored by Stanford Center for Asian Health Research and Education, and the Vincent V. C. Woo Memorial Foundation, in partnership with the American Medical Women’s Association and Piedmont Asian American Club. About the film Far East Deep South follows Charles Chiu and his family as they travel from California to Mississippi to find the grave of Charles’ father, K.C. Lou. Their search leads to stunning revelations about their family and they get a crash course on the history of Chinese immigrants in the segregated South. Through encounters with local residents and historians, this Chinese American family not only discovers their family’s important role in the Mississippi Delta, but they also learn about the symbiotic relationship between the Black and Chinese communities during the Jim Crow era. The film provides a window into the struggles of Chinese immigrants in the American South during the late 1800s to mid-1900s and the discrimination they faced. The Chiu family’s history demonstrates how exclusionary immigration laws like the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 separated their family for generations. This deeply moving and unforgettable story offers a poignant and important perspective on race relations, immigration and American identity. For more information visit www.fareastdeepsouth.com. Bravura performance by Ian McKellen in Mr. Holmes By Chris Honoré It’s an interesting experience to approach a film with one set of expectations and realize, as the story evolves, that it is entirely something else. That’s the case of Mr. Holmes. Going in I assumed that the setting would be London, during those nascent years of the 20th century, not long after the end of World War I. Mr. Holmes is at the top of his deductive game and often takes intricate cases with subtle clues to be cleverly unraveled. Buttressing my assumption is the fact that Ian McKellen, a gifted character actor, is portraying Holmes, sans deerstalker cap and oversized Meerschaum pipe (something Watson added), but in all ways a perfectly cast Holmes. But Mr. Holmes is a different movie. Based on the novel A Slight Trick of the Mind, by Mitch Cullin, the narrative is set in 1947. Sherlock Holmes, now in his 90s, is living on his bucolic Sussex farm. He has been retired for some 30 years and has used this time to raise bees and study botany. He lives a solitary life, with the exception of his housekeeper, Mrs. Munro (Laura Linney), and her precocious 10-yearold son, Roger (Milo Parker). As is soon made evident, Mr. Holmes is a penetrating character study of a man once renowned, thanks to the embellished writings of his friend and case collaborator, Dr. John H. Watson, who wrote what Holmes refers to as “penny dreadfuls” about their exploits. He has retreated from his former life and is now confronted with the harsh realities of aging – his once keen mind going sideways, his powers of observation, always the fulcrum of his detection, growing increasingly elusive. Holmes is gradually becoming a man who has outlived the person he once cherished: his former self. His daily frustration with his decline, compounded by regret for certain choices from his past, has made him taciturn and even a bit desperate. At one point, his face folding in emotional pain, he acknowledges, “I have been alone all of my life.” There is one seemingly minor case offered up through flashbacks, relevant because it causes Holmes such pain that its conclusion results in his retirement. He remembers only that the year was 1919 and it involved a recently married woman (Hattie Morahan) who was enamored with learning to play the glass harmonica. Against her husband’s wishes. Holmes is hired to follow her and discover how she is paying for her lessons. What he can’t sort out is what occurred that caused him to leave his flourishing practice and move to Sussex 30 years ago from London. With the encouragement of Roger, who has clandestinely read the initial pages, Holmes tries to write down the details of the case, hoping to puzzle out its denouement. Meanwhile, he is also in search of a restorative herb that will revitalize his mind as well as his body. He makes a journey to Hiroshima, Japan, but to no avail. What makes Mr. Holmes worthwhile is the exceptional performance of Ian McKellen. He is, in every respect, Sherlock Holmes. In the backstory we see a face that is a study in incisive intelligence and vitality, his style incomparable. It’s only later that he falls into a kind of helpless sadness and longs for what once was. McKellen is, in a word, remarkable in both roles. Mr. Holmes. Architects and Landscape Architects call this important passage the “entry sequence” or “entry experience” and it includes all movement and impressions from the curb all the way up and through the front The front landscaping clearly plays a major role in this area of design, especially the associated The function of walls and gates as well as their associated symbolism in one form or another has fascinated humans and kept architects and landscape architects busy for centuries. There is something that seems to resonate with us relative to nicely designed gates and their associated walls, leading to their continued popularity at all scales. Starting with the original concept of what was certainly just an opening in a defensive barrier, the idea has evolved in many cultures to be much more. In the ancient Egyptian culture as well as the Hindu tradition the gates of a temple came to represent the separation between the secular and the sacred – a passage between worlds. Gates also became centers for public life, symbols of wisdom or power and ultimately famous architectural and landscape architectural landmarks such as the Arc de Triomphe or the St. Louis Gateway Arch. This has all filtered down to the residential scale, examples of which are plentiful in Piedmont today. Still used for privacy and security, walls and gates in their various forms are also designed to enhance the transition from public spaces into the private. Often the challenge is to maintain a welcoming feeling through decoration and good design when employing these kinds of entries – part of what realtors refer to as “curb appeal”. This has all filtered down to the residential scale, examples of which are plentiful in Piedmont today. Often the challenge is to maintain a welcoming feeling through decoration and good design when employing these kinds of entries – part of what realtors refer to as “curb appeal”. I can’t help but leave this suggestion to the next generation of designers based on what I have observed as lacking in many areas of the world: many gates are primarily decorative This great “wall” of redwood trees on Lake View Ave in Piedmont is a special example of a number of urban design concepts we have been considering in this column: the sense of enclosure it provides for the public street and sidewalks; the “borrowed open space” it provides for the whole neighborhood; and the first demarcation of individual properties further defined by more traditional fences and gates beyond. articles.text: After an incredible two years of triumph and transition during the pandemic, Stagebridge, the East Bay’s longest running and most renowned performing arts organization for older adults, welcomes the return to in-person classes with its popular Performing Arts Camp this June. “I’m excited to see the students return to Stagebridge, to see how much they enjoy the classes, and to see what they can accomplish with the performances they create,” said Outreach Coordinator Barbara Johnson. T he su m mer ca mp is designed to introduce Stagebridge’s lifelong learning programs to students 50 years and older. The two-week session will showcase some of the talented teaching artists, many of whom joined Stagebridge as a part of distance learning programming. The camp will feature local and national phenoms, such as poet Tony Aldarondo, global dance and movement leader April Axé Charmaine, theatre performer Andy Alabran, and Heidi Carlsen of American Conservatory Theater. “At the start of the pandemic, Stagebridge was forced to embrace online learning, which was particularly challenging given the population we serve,” explained Elissa Glickman, Stagebridge’s new Managing Director. “For a community in complete isolation, Stagebridge was a connective lifeline, a hub of creative expression.” “When I arrived two months ago, everyone asked when we’d return to in-person learning. I’m proud to say that time is now,” Glickman added. During the pandemic Stagebridge students have showcased incredible Bay Area artists such as Margo Hall, Jennifer Le Blanc, and Ely Sonny Orquiza. Building upon the past, Stagebridge will re-introduce the company’s flagship community service program, Seniors Reaching Out, in addition to showcasing full-length productions created by students. In 2021, instructors Scrumbly Koldewyn and Joanne Grimm led students in creating The Dell, following fictional and fairytale characters fighting against a developer threatening to tear down their home. This year, they return with A Full and Complete Stop, a new, original musical featuring a group of seniors finding their deepest desires fulfilled. “After two long years and a few false starts, I’m excited to be able to plan for in-person learning again.” Performing Arts Institute Director Lily Nguyen said. “Our students inspire and encourage each other; that’s all part of the creative process. It’s exciting to see that energy, as students transform into fully-realized artists.” For more information and to register for classes, visit www. stagebridge.org/pai-register. pages.text: Wednesday, May 18, 2022 23 By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. My Dear Readers: One of my clients, Linda, called me and described how she was taken for several hundred dollars by one of the many tech-support scams that are going around. This is what happened to her. She woke up and turned her computer on, and started checking her email, checking the news websites that she usually does, and all of a sudden, a screen appeared, with a very loud alarm noise and message indicating that she had a virus. The alert sound was loud and continuous. The pop-up window said, “COMPUTER SCAN - ALERT! Suspicious activity detected on your computer. Contact a live agent at APPLE immediately. Call this number now, toll free 1-800-xxx-xxxx” WARNING! DO NOT SHUT DOWN YOUR COMPUTER!” Since the pop-up window indicated that the number that she was going to call would be Apple support, but pf course it wasn’t, she called it right away. They sent her a small application so they could log onto her computer and showed her some very scary looking files. They said that they were malware and that she would have to act immediately so that they could clean her system of any viruses. They said that because they had a security protocol in place, she could pay them with a credit card, but she would have to authenticate that with a bank account, and her Social Security number. She gave them the credit card number, she also gave them her checking account routing number and account number, she was about to give them her Social Security number when her roommate came into the room and said to her, “What are you doing!?” She realized that she was being By Benjamin and Leah Bloom May is Older Americans Month, a recognition promoted by the Administration for Community Living. The theme changes from year to year and this time it is a focus on aging in place titled, “Age My Way.” It is described as a way to show how older adults can plan to stay in their homes and live independently in their communities for as long as possible. The Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) defines aging in place as, “the ability to live in one’s own home and community safely, independently, and comfortably, regardless of age, income, or ability level.” Under any definition of aging in place, there is a mention of support, Seniors scammed, and told Linda to shut off her computer and hang up immediately. When the scammer heard the roommate telling her to shut the computer off, yelled at her and said, “No! If you shut your computer down, all of the virus files will reload when you start it up again!” Linda was obviously frightened and froze. Her roommate ran over to the computer and turned it off. At this point, the scammer on the phone called them both some colorful names and hung up. But not before Linda was out about $700. She called me after this happened, and I told her to call her bank and credit card immediately and try to block the charges. She was able to recover all but about $250. This was a very expensive lesson, and Linda was incredibly shaken by the experience. She was worried about losing the contents of her computer, as she is finishing a PhD and she felt that all her work was at stake. Linda is a very smart woman, but the cunning of this scammer took advantage of her fear of losing her precious data. There are so many of these types of scams going around, sometimes by email, sometimes by phone calls, and sometimes like this with a pop up on your computer. In many cases they convince their targets to pay by gift cards and of course credit cards. How to avoid scams There are two things you should know about how to avoid these scams: 1. Microsoft, Apple, or any legitimate tech company will not contact you by phone, email, text or pop up that there is something wrong with your computer. 2. And not all security pop-ups are scams, but no legitimate one will ever give you a phone number to call. What to do if you think you have been scammed 1. Call your bank immediately, call your credit card immediately and if you have been the victim of a gift card scam, where the scammers asked you to pay by Amazon gift card, call Amazon customer support and let them know you have been a victim of fraud. They may be able to invalidate the card and refund your money 2. You can report the scammer to ReportFraud.ftc.gov. 3. Change your password at your bank if you have a password to access your credit card. If you are the victim of a gift card fraud, change your password with that company. 4. Be very careful about clicking on links in email messages, or in text messages. Tell your friends not to send you links to newspaper articles, etc. If you want to look something up, go to the newspaper website and look up the subject or the article in question. 5. Make sure your operating system is up to date. If you feel it’s necessary, install security software on your computer. If you’re a MacUser, I recommend Malwarebytes. Of course, security software will not prevent scammers from sending you phishing emails. 6. If your computer is too old to receive security updates, consider purchasing a new machine. You can block the pop-up windows on the browser you were using and only enable them if you are filling out a form that requires a pop-up to complete. It’s obvious that these types of scams are not going away, so, it’s important that you remain vigilant, and informed. As more and more people put precious data on computers, on the Internet, and in the cloud, we are all vulnerable to being hacked. Computers have made our lives easier in some ways, but we must always be careful not to fall prey to these ruthless scammers. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com 7. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Wednesday, April 20 was another day of exploration by the Piedmont Seniors group, as 19 members ventured halfway to San Francisco to learn more of the city’s history. Their first stop was a visit to Treasure Island, which is currently undergoing extensive construction. Huge boulders from the original construction of the Caldecott Tunnel are strategically placed on the side of the main road. Treasure Island. Located on Yerba Buena Island in the middle of San Francisco Bay, offers a breathtaking view of the San Francisco skyline. On their visit, the Seniors also witnessed a new ferry terminal, which recently opened. The terminal will be particularly valuable when the residential housing and redevelopment is completed. The first stop was the Treasure Island Museum, founded by the U.S. Navy in 1975. The museum occupies the lobby of one of the original airport buildings constructed in 1937. and is protected on the National Register of Historic Places. Its claim to fame is that it served as the administrative center for the Golden Gate International Exposition (the World Fair in 1939, and also for Pan American Airways, and headquarters for the Twelfth Naval District. The museum originally was an Allied Navy, Marine, and Coast Guard Museum. It has an outElene Manolis in front of the Islands of the Pacific statue created for the Golden Gate International Exposition on Yerba Buena Island in 1938. standing mural on the museum’s back wall measuring 251 feet long and 26 feet high, representing scenes in the history of the Navy and Marine Corps in the Pacific since 1813. The Golden Gate International Exposition of 1939-1940, also known as the “Pageant of the Pacific” was a glowing Art Deco island of towers, gardens, goddesses, and dazzling lighting effects to celebrate California and San Francisco as an economic, political, and cultural force in the Pacific region. At that time San Francisco was also celebrating the engineering achievements of the completion of both the Golden Gate and Bay Bridges. There was even the controversial Sally Rand Nude Ranch on the island featuring the well publicized stripper, and creating quite a stir. In addition, visitors could see the first “incubator babies” and even Botticelli’s “Birth of Venus” on display. These exhibits were in addition to the carnival rides and traditional booths one might see at an international fair. However, as America prepared for World War II, the island became a major training, supply, and embarkation station for American military efforts throughout the Pacific and Asia. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, May 18, 2022 Wednesday Evening Meditation Group is online The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000. articles.text: As a small boy I remember my grandmother’s talent for arts and crafts. I would sit while she attempted to teach me how to do whatever project she was working on. Whether it was making beautiful beaded ornaments for a Christmas tree, hand-made lace doilies or embroidering napkins, I was mesmerized. Over the years I’ve heard people say, “I think I’ll take up watercolors when I retire” or “Learning how to make pottery in my later years has been exhilarating.” I can’t help but wonder if there is a correlation between finally having the time to create and the benefits that could affect our well-being. Studies show that engaging in creative art pursuits provide older adults with multiple benefits, not the least of which is enhanced cognitive function. Scientists examining the engagement of older adults with art therapy and music therapy confirm that art can affect them in very positive ways. Exercising our creative selves can often induce psychological and physiological healing, while nurturing overall well-being. And it’s fun. Gene Cohen, MD, PhD, director of the Center on Aging at George Washington University, was the first researcher to conduct a national study on art and the quality of life. He found that engagement with the arts has a positive effect on health and illness as we age. The benefits are there for both the creator and viewer. Some of these benefits include helping individuals relax, assisting in socialization, encouraging playfulness and a sense of Oakland painter and poet Charles Blackwell humor. The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living boasts a large group of residents who are artists. Pat K. (pictured) has been painting all her life. She told me she chose her apartment in our community because the kitchen has a lake view and she set it up as an art studio. Jon C. has been drawing for over sixty years. He currently has a collection of his sketches on exhibit at The Lake Merritt from the present day dating back to 1946. Jon said he looks forward to our weekly open art studio where he can draw in the company of others and share creative ideas with fellow artists. Another resident, Pat R. has dabbled with different art forms throughout her life. She said, “Now that I am retired, I have so much more time for art, and I believe it’s good for my soul.” Many of our residents share a love of art and that’s what drives some of the programs at The Lake Merritt. We visit Bay Area arts and crafts exhibits, open art studios, take art history courses and make regular trips to museums and galleries. As for me, I am inspired by the many talented artists at The Lake Merritt, and though I won’t equal their caliber, when I retire I think I’ll take up watercolors. How about you? On this theme, we are particularly excited to offer a FREE Zoom presentation by Oakland painter and poet Charles Blackwell entitled, “Painting Beyond Vision” on May 26 at 3:30 p.m.. An artist since a young age, Blackwell suffered an accident that damaged his eyes and is now legally blind. When he lost most of his eyesight, his doctor told him, “Take your defect and make it an asset.” Blackwell has grown to embody this phrase. He creates art using acrylic paints, ink and canvas by leaning in very close to see the canvas through his limited peripheral vision. Blackwell has been the subject of a documentary film The God Given Talent and was featured recently in a profile by the San Francisco Chronicle. We’re thrilled to host this talented and uplifting artist in our Topics of Merritt series. The public is invited to join us by registering at https://tinyurl.com/ beyondvision or you may call 510-903-3600 for more information. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living, 1800 Madison Street, Oakland. Tel. (510) 903-3600. Pat K., a resident at The Lake Merritt, has been painting her entire life. Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03 3820 Broadway, Oakland

articles.text: Gloria (Gabriel) Lawler, a Piedmont resident for 55 years, passed away on May 1 after a year-long battle with uterine cancer. She was 85 years old. Gloria grew up in a tight-knit Italian family outside of Philadelphia. She was an exceptional student in the Lower Merion school system and won a full scholarship to Rosemont College. While at Rosemont, she met Kaz Lawler, an ensign in the U.S. Navy, who attended nearby Villanova University. Shortly after her graduation from Rosemont with honors in Chemistry, Gloria and Kaz married. She and Kaz then made the first of many moves in the U.S. with the Navy, and along the way, they started their family. The couple and their five children eventually landed in Piedmont, California, where they have lived for 55 years. At a time when women were scarce in the Sciences, Gloria was a STEM pioneer and advocate for women in technology. After some time as a chemist for the FDA, Gloria became a technical writing innovator for chemical informatics start-ups, as well as a valued contributor to the scientific missions of Lawrence Berkeley Lab, Stanford Research Institute, and Lawrence Livermore Lab. In addition to raising her five children and working full-time, Gloria was active in the community, holding board positions and working to advance early childhood education. Following retirement, Gloria became the volunteer publicist for the Youth Musical Theater Company in Berkeley, writing theater reviews for the Piedmont Post. After their last child graduated from college, Gloria and Kaz hit the road and traveled around the Gloria Lawler died on May 1 after a year-long battle with cancer. She was 85. globe. Gloria loved traveling and visited 25 countries. France was a favorite, particularly Paris. Over the years, she and Kaz joyfully introduced each of their eight grandchildren to this magical city. Gloria is survived by her husband of almost 64 years, Kaz; her children Ann (Steve), MaryJo, Kaz Jr (Anne), Bob (Shannon), and Dave (Saroja). She is also survived by grandchildren Mike, Katherine, Andy (Rocky), Gates (Ben), Glynnis (Andy), Finn, Shayla, and Karina. Additionally she is survived by brother Michael Gabriel and sister Veronica Gabriel; nieces Sandy Mayson and Sarah Jo Mayson, and nephew Joe Gabriel. A memorial service will be held on June 3 at 11 a.m. in the Tower Chapel at Mountain View Cemetery, 5000 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. The family suggests that memorial donations may be made to The American Cancer Society at www.cancer.org.
articles.title: Longtime Piedmont resident Gloria Lawler dies on May 1

articles.text: Customers to see 8% drought surcharge on July 1 East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) announced on April 26 a district-wide “Stage 2 Drought Emergency”, following the driest January to March period on record. A “Stage 2” drought is triggered when EDMUD reservoirs fall below 75%; currently, reservoirs are 71% full. “Despite a strong rainy start in October and December, the dry winter has compelled us to move into our next phase of action to ensure we have adequate supplies in case the drought continues next year,” EBMUD Board President Douglas Linney said. “We’ve spent decades planning and preparing for these events and are confident our efforts, combined with customer water savings, will get us through this drought.” The EBMUD Board voted 6-1 to mandate a 10 percent district-wide water use reduction target, which affects Piedmont residents. EBMUD serves 1.4 million customers. Declaring a Stage 2 drought ensures the water utility meets the needs of its customers if the dry weather continues, explained Linney. Board members also voted to impose an 8% surcharge for all customers beginning July 1, in an attempt to offset costs due to the drought. “We are making the best use of all our tools to handle the drought, including purchasing water from partner agencies, increasing conservation from customers, and discouraging waste among high-volume users,” Linney said. “These emergency actions are outside our normal scope of work, and this drought surcharge will help us cover a portion of these costs.” The Board reinstated an excessive use penalty ordinance charged to households that use more than 1,600 gallons per day. The agency will issue one warning, then charge $2 for every 748 gallons used above the penalty threshold if not amended. The agency also updated restrictions on outdoor water use - outdoor watering is now limited to three times per week. is about the entire World War II, as is the Bayeux Museum. Another two museums were founded by individuals whose extensive collections of WWII memorabilia are displayed. The Normandy Victory Museum covers the battles in the hedgerows (les bocages). The Falaise Memorial follows the path of what it was like for the civilian population in wartime. Le Grand Bunker features the plight of the Sword Beach invasion along a section of the dangerous Atlantic Wall, heavily booby-trapped by the Germans. pages.text: 30 Wednesday, May 18, 2022 EBMUD declares “Stage 2 drought emergency” Customers to see 8% drought surcharge on July 1 By Allyson Aleksey East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) announced on April 26 a district-wide “Stage 2 Drought Emergency”, following the driest January to March period on record. A “Stage 2” drought is triggered when EDMUD reservoirs fall below 75%; currently, reservoirs are 71% full. “Despite a strong rainy start in October and December, the dry winter has compelled us to move into our next phase of action to ensure we have adequate supplies in case the drought continues next year,” EBMUD Board President Douglas Linney said. “We’ve spent decades planning and preparing for these events and are confident our efforts, combined with customer water savings, will get us through this drought.” The EBMUD Board voted 6-1 to mandate a 10 percent district-wide water use reduction target, which affects Piedmont residents. EBMUD serves 1.4 million customers. Declaring a Stage 2 drought ensures the water utility meets the needs of its customers if the dry weather continues, explained Linney. Board members also voted to impose an 8% surcharge for all customers beginning July 1, in an attempt to offset costs due to the drought. “We are making the best use of all our tools to handle the drought, Americans in Paris Continued from page 11 including purchasing water from partner agencies, increasing conservation from customers, and discouraging waste among high-volume users,” Linney said. “These emergency actions are outside our normal scope of work, and this drought surcharge will help us cover a portion of these costs.” The Board reinstated an excessive use penalty ordinance charged to households that use more than 1,600 gallons per day. The agency will issue one warning, then charge $2 for every 748 gallons used above the penalty threshold if not amended. The agency also updated restrictions on outdoor water use - outdoor watering is now limited to three times per week. is about the entire World War II, as is the Bayeux Museum. articles.text: Piedmont’s third annual Art Walk, conceptualized by residents Jon Schleuning and Larraine Seiden in 2020, took place last Saturday, May 7. The openair art studio format showcased the talents of 40 Piedmont artists in a myriad of art mediums, which was expanded to include digital art this year. The event followed the success of an art walk “born out of necessity,” in June 2020 when shelterin-place guidelines had obliterated live events and decimated the arts industry in the process. The Art Walk has since expanded into a full-blown annual event. articles.text: Girl Scout Troop 33521 built a piece of art from trash they collected at Piedmont Middle School and from their homes. The Troop wanted to reuse trash to show reasons to salvage trash; to save money on materials and reduce littering. They came up with the idea to collect trash on the grounds of Piedmont Middle School, where they are students, and to show how much littering occurs. They observed students leaving food wrappers behind or not picking up their trash when it falls on the ground. They said some reasons people are littering could be because trash bins are not accessible nearby, or awareness of littering has not been brought to their attention. After spending days collecting trash left on the ground and seating areas, the troop decided to use the trash for an art project. They collected additional trash at their homes to complete the artwork. One challenging part of the construction process was getting the trash, including plastic containers, plastic food bags, and aluminum cans, to adhere to a large plastic trash bag used for the head with bendable wires, Gorilla Glue, and tape. In the end, the Girl Scouts seemed pleased with their creation, titled “A Work of Trash.” Troop 33521 hopes to inspire others to create art using trash for summer projects. For inspiration, search “how to prevent littering with art” or “trash art” for amazing creations. Members of Girl Scout Troop 33521 collect trash from the middle school campus to convert into art. Girl Scout Troop 33521 creates “A Work of Trash.”
articles.title: Piedmont Girl Scouts creates art from trash

articles.text: PADC welcomes Sukanya Goswami as new PHS principal Editor: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) is thrilled to welcome Sukanya Goswami as the new principal of Piedmont High School, an experienced teacher and school leader with more than 20 years of experience. Goswami will be the first woman of color to lead Piedmont High School. Her appointment represents an opportunity for our community to learn from a new perspective, to prioritize academic excellence, diversity, equity, and inclusion, and to usher in a new era at Piedmont High School. PADC supports Piedmont Unified School District’s goal to develop, maintain and support a high school experience that meets and exceeds the standards of academic excellence in every area. Academic excellence is defined by the demonstrated ability to perform, achieve, and excel in scholastic studies, which is best accomplished in an environment that is inclusive, equitable and welcoming for all. Goswami’s experience and commitment to excellence positions her well to provide leadership in all of these necessary areas. Being inclusive means cultivating a culture of respect and care. It requires trust and intention. We are excited to collaborate with Goswami to continue supporting PUSD’s goal of academic excellence, centering the need for equity and belonging for all, and building an inclusive community at Piedmont High School. –Sheila Leunig President, Piedmont Anti-Racism & Diversity Committee (PADC) PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS B. articles.text: The City of Piedmont recently released its draft Housing Element–a state-required plan for how to enable 587 units of housing in the next eight years. The Housing Element provides a great opportunity to implement policy changes that can help ensure that diverse current and future members of our community, including teachers, city employees, seniors, and children and grandchildren, will be able to live in Piedmont. The City’s draft plan includes a number of excellent ideas for housing: encouraging homeowners to build backyard cottages or ADUs, increasing the allowable density in the commercial and multifamily zones, and exploring the viability of building affordable housing on several publicly owned parcels. articles.text: My colleague Lauren Lisa Ng is a poet, a preacher and a mother. Her poem, The New, is a reflection on an ordinary day in her life. The poem concludes, “I’ll build the border of a puzzle, stand from my desk before the sun starts is setting, remove backpacks from tired shoulders, plant kisses on cold cheeks and call it a day lived.” Lauren is telling us that much of her experience is outside the public eye. That experience is not unimportant but it is private. It is neither to be celebrated nor critiqued. In our history, we humans have not done well in extending to women the right to privacy. Instead, we have made a habit of holding them, their feelings, their experience, their decisions up for public scrutiny. We have subjected them to frequent critique and justified that critique with an occasional compliment or celebration. articles.text: Conservation-based nonprofit Sierra Watch successfully halted a luxury development in the Lake Tahoe Basin in February 2022. The legal win will provide more oversight of Environmental Impact Report (EIR) compliance, explained the organization’s executive director and Piedmont native Tom Mooers, a 1987 graduate of Piedmont High School. California’s Third Court of Appeals ruled in favor of Sierra Watch in a long-running legal battle against developers of the Martis Valley West proposal, an area near Truckee on a corridor to Lake Tahoe. The project’s developer, Sierra Pacific Industries, proposed the construction of a gated development with new roads, commercial malls, and 760 vacation homes that would lie in a high-fire hazard zone on an undeveloped Ridgeline of the Tahoe Basin. The Placer County Board of Supervisors approved the project 4-to-1. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that all California counties research and provide an EIR that fully assesses and discloses the negative impacts of new developments. Sierra Watch, and co-petitioners Save Lake Tahoe and Mountain Area Preservation, asserted that developer Sierra Pacific Industries failed to meet state law and CEQA standards by downplaying impacts on the clarity of Lake Tahoe, greenhouse gas emissions, traffic, and fire safety. “California’s most basic planning law, known as CEQA, is designed to ensure that the public can be involved in big, landuse decision-making questions,” explained Mooers. “The decision makers, in this case the Placer County Board of Supervisors, need to adequately assess what the proposed development would do. In the case of these developments that were proposed and approved in the Tahoe area, we wanted to know what it would do to Lake Tahoe, and the clarity of the Lake.” Petitioners pointed to a legal win in 2021 that set precedent for such protocol in the Tahoe Basin. In November 2016, the Placer Piedmont High grad Tom Mooers is Executive Director of Sierra Watch, which recently won a major court decision to prevent the housing sprawl in Martis Valley near Lake Tahoe. County Board of Supervisors voted to approve plans by Alterra for a luxury development, “The Village at Squaw Valley,” (now Olympic Valley) in a 4-to-1 vote. Jennifer Montgomery, who represented District 5 in Tahoe, was the single naysayer, and was the only Supervisor to represent a part of the county in Tahoe. Sierra Watch appealed the decision immediately. Alterra proposed a 90,000- square-foot “adventure park,” equipped with a 96-foot indoor water park, and 1,493 rooms. Mooers said that it became apparent in both wins through public hearings and court proceedings that “decision-makers consistently down-played impacts of development, and did not share critical information with the public.” “It’s a key part of our work, to make sure that decision makers are indeed held to the letter of the law,” he said. In its appeal, Sierra Watch targeted the validity of both projects’ EIR in response to the county’s decision. The five-year legal battle against Alterra ended with a successful appeal in California’s Third District Court of Appeals in August 2021. In the case of Martis Valley, the appellate court agreed that Sierra Watch v. Placer County (2021) set precedent that a developer cannot abuse its discretion by not describing Lake Tahoe’s existing water quality. “The developers’ interest is to make as much money as possible and get a return on their investment. Sometimes the decision-makers don’t think of longterm values of their constituents, and these great mountain places,” said Mooers. “We’ve been fighting these [developments] in both Martis Valley and Olympic Valley in the interest of protecting these places. But of course it’s all related to the Sierra Nevada (Mountain range), so it was affirming that our success in protecting Olympic Valley had created a precedent to allow us to protect Martis Valley.” Mooers said he has always been interested in conservation. About 40 years ago, he wrote an article in the Piedmont Highlander, the school newspaper, describing Tahoe’s clarity. After graduating from Piedmont, Mooers attended UCLA and then became an organizer with Green Corps. Mooers described his time with the nonprofit as a “launch pad” for the work he does today. The Green Corps one-year, full-time Field School for Environmental Organizing includes intensive classroom training and hands-on field experience running environmental campaigns. He became Executive Director of Sierra Watch in 2001 and has worked as an advocate for land conservation throughout California for over 25 years. “Sometimes the work I do now, I feel like I’m writing that article over and over again. I really appreciate the opportunity to do something that I’ve been interested in my whole life, since I grew up in Piedmont,” he said. hours.
articles.title: PHS alum Tom Mooers leads Sierra Watch in preventing Lake Tahoe housing sprawl

pages.text: Wednesday, May 11, 2022 3 PHS alum Tom Mooers leads Sierra Watch in preventing Lake Tahoe housing sprawl By Allyson Aleksey Conservation-based nonprofit Sierra Watch successfully halted a luxury development in the Lake Tahoe Basin in February 2022. The legal win will provide more oversight of Environmental Impact Report (EIR) compliance, explained the organization’s executive director and Piedmont native Tom Mooers, a 1987 graduate of Piedmont High School. California’s Third Court of Appeals ruled in favor of Sierra Watch in a long-running legal battle against developers of the Martis Valley West proposal, an area near Truckee on a corridor to Lake Tahoe. The project’s developer, Sierra Pacific Industries, proposed the construction of a gated development with new roads, commercial malls, and 760 vacation homes that would lie in a high-fire hazard zone on an undeveloped Ridgeline of the Tahoe Basin. The Placer County Board of Supervisors approved the project 4-to-1. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that all California counties research and provide an EIR that fully assesses and discloses the negative impacts of new developments. Sierra Watch, and co-petitioners Save Lake Tahoe and Mountain Area Preservation, asserted that developer Sierra Pacific Industries failed to meet state law and CEQA standards by downplaying impacts on the clarity of Lake Tahoe, greenhouse gas emissions, traffic, and fire safety. “California’s most basic planning law, known as CEQA, is designed to ensure that the public can be involved in big, landuse decision-making questions,” explained Mooers. “The decision makers, in this case the Placer County Board of Supervisors, need to adequately assess what the proposed development would do. In the case of these developments that were proposed and approved in the Tahoe area, we wanted to know what it would do to Lake Tahoe, and the clarity of the Lake.” Petitioners pointed to a legal win in 2021 that set precedent for such protocol in the Tahoe Basin. In November 2016, the Placer Piedmont High grad Tom Mooers is Executive Director of Sierra Watch, which recently won a major court decision to prevent the housing sprawl in Martis Valley near Lake Tahoe. County Board of Supervisors voted to approve plans by Alterra for a luxury development, “The Village at Squaw Valley,” (now Olympic Valley) in a 4-to-1 vote. Jennifer Montgomery, who represented District 5 in Tahoe, was the single naysayer, and was the only Supervisor to represent a part of the county in Tahoe. Sierra Watch appealed the decision immediately. Alterra proposed a 90,000- square-foot “adventure park,” equipped with a 96-foot indoor water park, and 1,493 rooms. Mooers said that it became apparent in both wins through public hearings and court proceedings that “decision-makers consistently down-played impacts of development, and did not share critical information with the public.” “It’s a key part of our work, to make sure that decision makers are indeed held to the letter of the law,” he said. In its appeal, Sierra Watch targeted the validity of both projects’ EIR in response to the county’s decision. The five-year legal battle against Alterra ended with a successful appeal in California’s Third District Court of Appeals in August 2021. In the case of Martis Valley, the appellate court agreed that Sierra Watch v. Placer County (2021) set precedent that a developer cannot abuse its discretion by not describing Lake Tahoe’s existing water quality. “The developers’ interest is to make as much money as possible and get a return on their investment. Sometimes the decision-makers don’t think of longterm values of their constituents, and these great mountain places,” said Mooers. “We’ve been fighting these [developments] in both Martis Valley and Olympic Valley in the interest of protecting these places. But of course it’s all related to the Sierra Nevada (Mountain range), so it was affirming that our success in protecting Olympic Valley had created a precedent to allow us to protect Martis Valley.” Mooers said he has always been interested in conservation. About 40 years ago, he wrote an article in the Piedmont Highlander, the school newspaper, describing Tahoe’s clarity. After graduating from Piedmont, Mooers attended UCLA and then became an organizer with Green Corps. Mooers described his time with the nonprofit as a “launch pad” for the work he does today. The Green Corps one-year, full-time Field School for Environmental Organizing includes intensive classroom training and hands-on field experience running environmental campaigns. He became Executive Director of Sierra Watch in 2001 and has worked as an advocate for land conservation throughout California for over 25 years. “Sometimes the work I do now, I feel like I’m writing that article over and over again. I really appreciate the opportunity to do something that I’ve been interested in my whole life, since I grew up in Piedmont,” he said. articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. Appointments are not required by encouraged. More information is available at https://cur.tv/piedmont. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702-9042, or visit their website at curative.com.

articles.text: Volunteer some time or donate fresh-baked goods Urban Compassion Project is hosting a fundraising bake sale near Children’s Fairyland on Saturday, May 21 between 11 a.m. and 6 p.m. Urban Compassion Project volunteers will be selling various baked goods to raise funds for the organization’s operating costs. The Project, founded by Vincent Ray Williams, hosts cleanups every Saturday morning at various locations in Oakland. Piedmont residents have joined Williams in this humble mission since the group’s inception. The organization seeks to build community between the unhoused and housed community through these simple acts of kindness. The volunteer-led grassroots effort started under the name Urban Park Cleanup and has since expanded to provide a variety of resources for the unhoused community of Oakland.
