articles.text: Valerie Ow Lee of J. Miller Flowers in show for 23rd year Bouquets to Art, de Young Museum’s premiere fundraiser and annual display of art-inspired floral installations, will begin on June 7. For one week, more than 100 experienced floral designers will converge at the de Young to showcase arrangements inspired by the museum’s vast array of paintings, sculptures, and architecture. Bouquets to Art is one of the Fine Arts Museum of San Francisco’s most popular and well-attended events every year. The event is presented by the volunteer members of the fine arts museums - and draws nearly 800,000 visitors a year, with net proceeds of more than $7 million. Funds from the event help underwrite special exhibitions, conservation projects, and educational programming. Valerie Ow Lee, co-owner of J. Miller Flowers on Piedmont Avenue, will be one of the featured floral artists at this year’s event. She has shown at Bouquets to Art for 23 years, and acknowledged, “I’ve been lucky enough to get my first choice of artwork A floral arrangement by J. Miller Flowers for the 2016 Bouquets to Art exhibit at the DeYoung Museum in San Francisco. for years.” Her floral design this year will be based upon a tranquil landscape entitled “Singing Beach, Manchester, Massachusetts” by Martin Johnson Heade. Floral artists will be given five hours to set up their designs on Monday morning, June 6. Florists are mindful of how much water is needed, and typically return each day to refresh their flowers. “There is a lot of room for creativity, but you have to consider the flowers you’re using,” she said. “The temperature inside the museum can cause some flowers to wilt. Hydrangeas, for example, are harder to use in displays. We will be choosing our batch at the flower market [in San Francisco] carefully.” Tickets sold out weeks prior to the event in 2021, so visitors are encouraged to reserve tickets now at: https://deyoung.famsf. org/bouquets-to-art.
articles.title: Bouquets to Art begins June 7 at de Young Museum

articles.text: In February 2021, the City Council adopted reach codes that require energy efficiency measures to be included in new construction and existing building renovations. Reach codes are local amendments that go above and beyond existing California building codes (Title 24) to improve the energy efficiency of buildings and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The primary goal of the reach codes is to help Piedmont meet its Climate Action Plan 2.0 emission reduction goals by reducing natural gas use and increasing energy efficiency in buildings. Title 24 receives updates every three years to incorporate the latest changes in construction and technology. The latest update (2019 Energy Code) went into effect on January 1, 2020. Starting on January 1 next year, the 2022 Energy Code will go into effect. When the Energy Code is updated, the City will also need to adopt any local amendments to the Code, including re-adoption of the reach codes. To help inform the development of the next iteration of reach codes, the City staff is asking all those who live and work in Piedmont to participate in an online survey to provide feedback about the current reach codes and suggestions for the next round. The survey is live and will be open until May 20. All those who complete the online survey will be entered into a raffle to receive a sustainability prize. Take the Community Survey here (https:// tinyurl.com/reachcodesurvey). For more information about the reach codes, visit the City’s Reach Code Information webpage housed under the Planning & Building Department. Alyssa Dykman is Piedmont’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be reached at adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Reach Code survey deadline is May 20

articles.text: Piedmont Fire Department welcomes two new firefighter-paramedics, Matt Ziebarth and Josh Brockett, to its staff. They completed their two-week orientation periods in late March and have begun their 18-month probation periods with the department. Ziebarth comes from El Dorado County where he spent 16 years as a firefighter-paramedic. Brockett spent six and half years as a paramedic at American Ambulance and four years as a firefighter-paramedic for the Sanger Fire Department in Fresno County. Both reside outside the Bay Area, Brockett in Fresno and Ziebarth near Placerville. The 37-year-old Brockett heard about Piedmont in an unconventional manner – from a coffee mug, not a job posting. “About three years ago a colleague left a Piedmont Fire Department coffee mug at my previous firehouse. I started drinking coffee out of it frequently, then I started thinking, ‘Where’s Piedmont?’ So, I looked it up, started researching the department and I was blown away. I thought, wow, this is a place I want to work,” said Brockett. With fire season now a household term in California, the job of firefighters is much more demanding and not for the faint of heart. For Brockett and Ziebarth, their commitments to their careers resulted from formative events in their lives as young adults. Ziebarth’s story began around 25 years ago when he and two friends were hiking and building a fort in the rain. ”My friend went to put his pick down, slipped, and it went through his foot into the ground. I didn’t know what to do, but I knew a neighbor was a firefighter so I ran and got him. He knew exactly what to do. I looked up to that firefighter and was inspired by him. It was then that I knew I wanted to be a firefighter myself,” he said. Brockett’s gravitation to the profession resulted from his dad, who was a firefighter, paramedic and a police officer in a small community. “About a week before he passed away in 2008, he told me that he wanted me to pursue a career as a firefighter. At the time I wanted to be a police officer, but after he passed away that’s when I turned it all around. I haven’t looked back. He was right – being a firefighter is way better than being a police officer,” added Brockett. The two are quickly learning the ins and outs of their new department and will be tested at three, six, nine and 12 months before the final test of their probationary period in the fall of 2023. Josh Brockett (left) and Matt Ziebarth are Piedmont Fire Department’s newest firefighters and paramedics.
articles.title: Fire Dept. adds 2 new firefighter-paramedics

articles.text: Students raising money for endangered animals The SEAL Club (Saving Endangered Animals Lovingly) will host a bake sale this Friday, May 13, at the Exedra after school at 3:15 p.m. Funds raised will support the World Wildlife Foundation. SEAL is a Piedmont Middle School club with about 20 6th graders. We meet weekly to learn about endangered animals, pick one to sponsor, and organize a bake sale to raise money for conservation. We have had three bake sales in front of the Piedmont Exedra. The first one was on November 6, when we raised money for the Vaquitas, of which there are fewer than 10 left. The second bake sale was on December 17 when we raised money for the Javan Rhinos, of which there are only 60 left. The most recent bake sale was on January 13. We raised money for the Irrawaddy dolphins, of which there are 92 left. The group has raised about $1,000 by selling treats at the bake sales. The bake sale this Friday will raise money for the Amur Leopard of which there are about 90 left. The money raised will be donated to the World Wildlife Foundation. Photo courtesy of the World Wildlife Foundation Money raised will help aid conservation efforts for the critically endangered Amur Leopard.
articles.title: Bake sale at Exedra this Friday

articles.text: Holden Temple’s essay “Money Talks: Limits on Individual Political Donations,” was named winner of the third annual Piedmont League of Women Voters Essay Contest. Piedmont High School senior Holden Temple was named the winner of the Piedmont League of Women Voters’ Essay Contest. The winning essay, titled “Money Talks: Limits on Individual Political Donations,” earned him a $500 cash award. “It was a pleasure to read my essay at the LWV annual board meeting, and to share my thoughts. Free speech is an integral part of real democracy, and campaign donations are one area where America can expand people’s speech further still,” said Temple. Now in its 3rd year, the contest was open to juniors and seniors who are Piedmont residents regardless of where they attend school. This year’s essay prompt was: “Should monetary political contributions be treated as ‘speech’ that deserves First Amendment protection? What actions should the League of Women Voters take with respect to this issue?” Temple’s thesis stated, “Monetary contributions to political campaigns should be treated as speech, and as such, contributions by individuals should be less limited, though corporations and unions should have much harsher regulation.” For more information on joining the League of Women Voters, and the League’s education and advocacy contributions at each level of government, visit www. lwvpiedmont.org.
articles.title: Holden Temple wins LWV essay contest

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, May 11, 2022 SchOOLs Bake sale at Exedra this Friday Students raising money for endangered animals By Sophia Puckett The SEAL Club (Saving Endangered Animals Lovingly) will host a bake sale this Friday, May 13, at the Exedra after school at 3:15 p.m. Funds raised will support the World Wildlife Foundation. SEAL is a Piedmont Middle School club with about 20 6th graders. We meet weekly to learn about endangered animals, pick one to sponsor, and organize a bake sale to raise money for conservation. We have had three bake sales in front of the Piedmont Exedra. The first one was on November 6, when we raised money for the Vaquitas, of which there are fewer than 10 left. The second bake sale was on December 17 when we raised money for the Javan Rhinos, of which there are only 60 left. The most recent bake sale was on January 13. We raised money for the Irrawaddy dolphins, of which there are 92 left. The group has raised about $1,000 by selling treats at the bake sales. The bake sale this Friday will raise money for the Amur Leopard of which there are about 90 left. The money raised will be donated to the World Wildlife Foundation. Holden Temple wins LWV essay contest Photo courtesy of the World Wildlife Foundation Money raised will help aid conservation efforts for the critically endangered Amur Leopard. Holden Temple’s essay “Money Talks: Limits on Individual Political Donations,” was named winner of the third annual Piedmont League of Women Voters Essay Contest. Piedmont High School senior Holden Temple was named the winner of the Piedmont League of Women Voters’ Essay Contest. The winning essay, titled “Money Talks: Limits on Individual Political Donations,” earned him a $500 cash award. “It was a pleasure to read my essay at the LWV annual board meeting, and to share my thoughts. Free speech is an integral part of real democracy, and campaign donations are one area where America can expand people’s speech further still,” said Temple. Now in its 3rd year, the contest was open to juniors and seniors who are Piedmont residents regardless of where they attend school. This year’s essay prompt was: “Should monetary political contributions be treated as ‘speech’ that deserves First Amendment protection? What actions should the League of Women Voters take with respect to this issue?” Temple’s thesis stated, “Monetary contributions to political campaigns should be treated as speech, and as such, contributions by individuals should be less limited, though corporations and unions should have much harsher regulation.” For more information on joining the League of Women Voters, and the League’s education and advocacy contributions at each level of government, visit www. lwvpiedmont.org. articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Commissioners announced the winners of the annual Betty C. Howard Award. At a March 16 meeting, they announced that Don Eidam was the Volunteer of the Year, and the Recreation Department’s Preschool teaching staff would be honored as Employees of the year. The awards are for 2021. A celebration to honor recipients will be on May 26 this year. The Award was created in 1979 by Recreation Director Mark Delventhal upon the retirement of secretary Betty C. Howard, who held the position from 1950 to 1979. The award honors volunteers and members of the staff for outstanding service and dedication to the community. Volunteer of the Year Don Eidam is being honored for his work in educating the community about bees and other pollinators. Eidam has presented live bee demonstrations to Piedmont youth and Scouts groups. “He has volunteered for many years, now educating the community on the importance of bees in our city,” said Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. “He has been instrumental in assisting the city with swarm removal, and educating youth and adults on the ecological importance of bees as pollinators. Every year, groups of Scouts visit Don at his home, where he provides an educational experience that Scouts remember for years. He has a whole program of bees’ life cycles and beekeeper equipment, and lets kids explore his bee hives safely.” The Recreation Department hosted “The Bee Movie” in the park on September 17, 2021 that also served as an important lesson on honeybees. Eidam’s live bee demonstration hive shown prior to the film in Piedmont Park was a highlight with youth. “He has never asked for payment for these visits [and demonstrations]. He enjoys sharing his knowledge with the children of Frances MacMichael and Noe Schroeder get a lesson in Mondrian art from their teacher and Hillside Playschool Director, Kara Grover. She and the Preschool teachers were recognized as the Recreation Department’s employees of the year in 2021. our community,” Putzer added. Staff of the Year All teachers at the department’s Preschool program received the Betty C. Howard Award as Employees of the Year for 2021. “No one could have predicted the world coming to a halt in 2020. Knowing the importance of early childhood education for children’s social and emotional development, our preschool directors began to brainstorm innovative methods to pivot and stay connected with the children in their programs,” said PRD Preschool Director Katrina Morris. At the onset of the pandemic, preschool programs were offered virtually. Teachers prepared at-home play kits for kids when COVID made live activities impossible. When surges waned throughout the health crisis, preschool directors and staff made the wise call to offer more outdoor programs - which became so popular amongst young kids that it became a permanent feature last year. Don Eidam was named as winner of the Recreation Department’s annual Betty C. Howard Award as its volunteer of the year in 2021. He is shown describing to a group of young Piedmonters a live bee demonstration hive.

articles.text: A two-minute email from you can help save math education in Piedmont and California. This Monday is the deadline to let the California State Board of Education know that you don’t want them experimenting on our children using mathematics. Hundreds of respected educators agree that the changes are highly inferior and detrimental. It’s important to a functioning society that all children have a solid foundation in math. And any changes in curriculum should have their efficacy verified in advance. These changes have no conclusive testing for effectiveness. So, the proposed changes represent a reprehensible social experiment on children. At www.SaveMath.net you can send an email to the State Board of Education and read more about the proposed radical changes to mathematics. Thank you in advance for everyone who gives their two minutes. Michael Malione is a private tutor, advocate for high quality STEM education, and Co-President of Piedmont ALPS the proposed and radical math curriculum known as the California Math Framework (CMF). articles.text: Piedmont Girl Scout troop 3943 is supporting the children and parents at Children’s Hospital in Oakland by selling cookies. It has already donated $700, and has set up an online meeting with Gilmarys Rivera, the outreach coordinator at the hospital. Children’s Hospital gives special kits to new patients and are helping by collecting items to complete the kits. The troop is asking for donations from families who want to help the Hospital. Welcome Kits The items needed to complete the Welcome Kit are: • Coloring books/ pages • Playdoh • Crayons/ markers/ colored pencils • Stickers • Word searches/ mazes • Stress ball Parent Comfort Kits Items needed to complete the Parent Comfort Kits are: • Socks • Tissues • Mints/ gum • Lip balm • Sleep mask • Individually wrapped, nut-free snacks • Hand lotion (unscented preferred) • Colorful pens and pencils • Journal/ puzzle books/ adult coloring book Donations may be dropped off at 1382 Oakland Avenue in Piedmont. articles.text: Highlander Robotics, an FRC team in the FIRST Robotics league, will host an Open House at the High School Engineering Lab in the STEAM Building on Monday, May 16 from 7:00 to 8:00 p.m. High school students and their parents are encouraged to attend to learn more about the team and this season’s robot “Selkie,” who just returned from the Houston World Championships. The event will include a presentation of the program as well as a demo of the robot. “The open house will provide a great feel for what it’s like to be a part of Robotics,” said sophomore programmer Vale Prieto Black. “Robotics fosters an environment that encourages creativity and problem solving skills, and sets its members up for future professional success” added Ambassador Lead Chloe Kessinger. Working under the mentorship of eight experienced industry professionals, members are guided through the build process with full support. Team members gain real-world engineering experience and get to work in a constructive learning environment amongst 30 other like-minded and passionate team members. When prompted with a fieldgame challenge at the start of each build season, student members get an opportunity to learn and apply the fabrication, design, prototyping and coding skills learned during the off season training that takes place each fall. Highlander Robotics welcomes all students regardless of experience. “Our program expects to train students from scratch and we believe that anyone can become a leader on the team if they have the interest and dedicate the time” said Lead Mentor Kevin Clark. The Highlanders provide training in programming, CAD (computer aided design), and general building. Outside of the more traditional robotics work, the Highlanders also seek members with other diverse interests including community outreach, visual and industrial design, marketing, branding, video production and other roles needed to flush out a well-functioning robotics team ecosystem. “With college admissions getting more competitive, joining a robotics team is a dynamic way to apply any of your interests into a well established organization” said Team Manager Helen Potter. To learn more, please join the team next week, May 16 in the Engineering lab, visit frc8033. com, or contact Kevin Clark at kevin.clark@gmail.com.
articles.title: Highlander Robotics to host Open House on May 16

articles.text: Plan creative summer activities the family can do together. Summer is just around the corner. Time for camps, backyard BBQs, vacations and, hopefully, some much needed downtime for your family. The school year is fun and hectic and there is a ton of learning, but let’s face it, sometimes we can all get way too busy for our own good. So, this summer, why not slow down a little? ACK…did you just have a freak out at the idea of “nothing to do” with your kids for extended amounts of time? Flashbacks to COVID shut downs? Visions of battles with screen time? Yeah. Me too. And yet, we know from the studies that downtime for kids and for you is absolutely critical for a healthy mind and body. So, how do we reconcile these needs? We don’t want to go back to the worst of the worst of 2020 AND we want quality time with very little scheduled. Enter Creativity Goal Setting. I know that might sound like an oxymoron, but in fact, the more that we make our downtime and creativity time intentional, the more we can guarantee that it will actually happen. Creativity Goal Setting is a way to prioritize how you and your family will engage in creative play. The kind of play that we are doing just for fun, not for mastery or perfection. How to Set Creativity Goals: 1. Call a Family Meeting. Ask each person in your family, to rank order the following types of activities: • Playing or Listening to Music • Building Something • Baking or Cooking • Dancing or Fun Movement Games (like Wacky Hopscotch or Limbo) • Drawing or Painting • Reading Stories and Making Up Stories 2. Use all of the categories that came out as the number one picks and brainstorm activities that you could do as a family in that category. For instance, if “Building Something” came out on top, your brainstorm list might look like this: • Make a space shuttle out of the cardboard boxes in the garage • Build a boat out of straws and marshmallows, and see if it floats • Create the world’s largest LEGO forest The list will depend on the ages of your kids, or course. 3. Now that you have your list of possible activities, the entire family votes on one for each category 4. Have your kids create a big poster that can hang in the kitchen that lists the 3 or 4 creative activities that you have voted on to do this summer. Now, whenever there is that precious moment of “nothing to do” time, you have already prepared a list of ideas that everyone has agreed on. Voila! Creative play for the summer is ready to go! Nina Meehan is the CEO and Founder of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. This summer find some creative time with your family by going to see their upcoming production of Llama, Llama, Red Pajama, the Musical. www.bactheatre.org
articles.title: Creativity Goal Setting for Your Family

articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group met on April 4 at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park to discuss Amor Towles’ latest book, The Lincoln Highway, published in October last year. The group had enjoyed one of Towles’ two previous novels, A Gentleman in Moscow, and Rules of Civility, so they couldn’t resist selecting another of his novels. The Lincoln Highway is set in June 1954, with 18-year-old Emmett Watson being driven home to Nebraska by the warden of the work farm where he has just served a year for involuntary manslaughter. His mother is long gone, his father recently deceased, and the family farm foreclosed upon by the bank. It is Emmett’s intention is to pick up his brainy, eight-year-old brother, and head west where they can restart their lives in pursuit of a better future. Their mother had abandoned them when Billy was a baby and Emmett was eight. Billy is determined to follow the Lincoln Highway west to San Francisco and find their mother. But when the warden drives away, Emmett discovers two friends from the work farm have hidden in the trunk of the warden’s car. They are the trouble-maker Duchess and the hapless, but sweet, Woolly. They have an altogether different plan for Emmett’s future. The story is told from multiple points of view with many different settings, characters, and themes; all packed into just 10 days. The readers generally liked The Lincoln Highway. They considered it to have a tight structure from beginning to end, but with flexibility. Towles’ love of writing is evident. He knows the beginning and end of his story, and he allows his rich imagination to take over in between. pages.text: Wednesday, May 11, 2022 9 FIRST MONDAY READING GROUP First Monday Reading Group discusses The Lincoln Highway By Dick Carter The First Mondays Reading Group met on April 4 at the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park to discuss Amor Towles’ latest book, The Lincoln Highway, published in October last year. The group had enjoyed one of Towles’ two previous novels, A Gentleman in Moscow, and Rules of Civility, so they couldn’t resist selecting another of his novels. The Lincoln Highway is set in June 1954, with 18-year-old Emmett Watson being driven home to Nebraska by the warden of the work farm where he has just served a year for involuntary manslaughter. His mother is long gone, his father recently deceased, and the family farm foreclosed upon by the bank. It is Emmett’s intention is to pick up his brainy, eight-year-old brother, and head west where they can restart their lives in pursuit of a better future. Their mother had abandoned them when Billy was a baby and Emmett was eight. Billy is determined to follow the Lincoln Highway west to San Francisco and find their mother. But when the warden drives away, Emmett discovers two friends from the work farm have hidden in the trunk of the warden’s car. They are the trouble-maker Duchess and the hapless, but sweet, Woolly. They have an altogether different plan for Emmett’s future. The story is told from multiple points of view with many different settings, characters, and themes; all packed into just 10 days. The readers generally liked The Lincoln Highway. They considered it to have a tight structure from beginning to end, but with flexibility. Towles’ love of writing is evident. He knows the beginning and end of his story, and he allows his rich imagination to take over in between. The group found Towles’ characters to be interesting and well developed, but the lack of a single, central, lead character kept some of them from developing a strong empathy for the different people. Some readers also found the cliffhanger endings of most chapters a little too dramatic. Some readers wanted a reunion of the boys and their mother. Other readers found the story to drag a little in the middle of the book’s nearly 600 pages, but most enjoyed the many twists and turns, and found the book to be another excellent work by Towles. The book’s surprising and dramatic ending was an example of ambiguity and Towles’ masterful, creative writing, often evoking ancient Greek tragedy comparisons, provided for thoughtful discussions that made the session all the more enjoyable. articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Council hosted its annual Camporee the weekend of April 29 with more than 200 Scouts and adult leaders. The Camporee is a council-wide event where Piedmont’s five troops (Troop 1, Troop 4, Troop 6, Troop 11, and Troop 15) compete against each other in Scout related events. The Camporee by led by Senior Patrol Leader Jack Gross-Whitaker, and adult leaders Robert Barbosa, and Maria Topete. The staff included Elles Krieckhaus, Annika Hattan-Kutter, Lauren Ashton, Ethan Alering, Aiden Haines, Jonah Dupree, Alex Cantrill, Brendan Devine, Trenton Downing, Mollie King, Trenton Downing (right) and Evan Friedman (left) judge an entry for the Iron Chef competition. Saturday’s opening flag ceremony led by Camporee SPL Jack Gross-Whitaker. Simon March-Cunningham, Evan Friedman, and Oscar Robertson. Planning began in January, involving everything from designing shirts to filing permission slips. This year we decided on a “Heist” theme, creating special events including a game of cops and robbers, and “Find the Gem” (an orienteering course). Scouts spent Saturday morning and early afternoon competing as patrols at stations operated by the staff. The first station was the Lizzigator, a popular activity at Camporee for at least 20 years. Scouts take four barrels and roll them on their side, standing on a large piece of plywood placed on top of the barrels and pushing with a pole. The goal is to get to the other side of a small field. To do this, Scouts must take the barrel in the back and place it in front of them and move the plywood over and repeat. “Lizzigator was super fun; probably my favorite,” said Maddox Ma of Troop 15. But the Lizzigator wasn’t the only fan favorite. At the chariot races, patrols were given three wooden poles and some rope. They use their knowledge of lashings to tie the poles into a triangle in which one of their patrol Lauren Ashton, Annika Hattan-Kutter and Elles Krieckhaus help out at check-in. Rangemaster Walter Stokes coaches a scout on how to use a bow and arrow. Scouts from Troops 1, 6, 11, and 15 enjoyed a 2 mile hike to see a historic B17 bomber engine. Troop 15 Scouts conquer the Lizzigator. Troop 4 Scouts watch the competing Troop 15 patrol at the Fire Building station. members will sit while the rest of the patrol carries them down the hill. The first to make it to the end wins. “The chariot races were pretty fun, definitely my favorite,” noted Scout Zach Dupree od Troop 15. Another popular activity was the pool noodle sword fighting, where two patrols would get in line, take pool noodles, and two at a time stand on two poles facing each other. After that, the first person to fall off loses. As it went on there would be challenges, such as having to stand on one foot or hopping up and down. Not all the stations were a total hit. The fire building station was a bit difficult for some kids, but it was a great way for the Scouts to learn a little about building fires.

articles.text: Photo by Sara Kimball Piedmont volleyball players are pictured after beating West County 3-2 in the first round of the North Coast Section playoffs. Pictured are PHS Principal Adam Littlefield (left), Danny Allen, Wilson Wong, James MaNguyen, Shunji Higashi, Felix Broach, John Champion, Brayden Day, Mason Kimball, Kai Lambert, Eric Olaru-Hagen, Owen Kelly, Adel Sahuc, and coach Mariah Cardenas. Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team made its first North Coast Section appearance since 1999 on Tuesday, May 3. Seeded No. 11, the Highlanders upset No. 6 West County 3-2 in a first-round match in Sebastopol. Piedmont lost 3-1 in the second round on May 5 at No. 3 Archie Williams in San Anselmo (formerly Drake HS). This was the first time Piedmont made the playoffs in 23 years and we were just thrilled to get in, and we were so excited to get to the second round. You can tell they love this game and that they love each other. Some of these kids never played volleyball before. I’m proud of them,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. It was the school’s first effort at qualifying for the post-season playoffs. “No one expected us to get here, I’m not sure if we expected to get here given our division was so difficult,” said team captain Wilson Wong, a junior. “Our progress is crazy. A couple of years ago, we barely even knew what volleyball was. To be able to win a game in NCS says a lot about how far we’ve come,” said classmate John Champion. When looking ahead to next year’s team, the team will have to fill two big holes in the middle with Mason Kimball and Felix Broach graduating. But returning will be the bulk of the lineup: Wong, Champion, Kai Lambert, Owen Kelly, Brayden Day, Eric Olaru-Hagen, James MaNguyen, and Shunji Higashi. “Last season, we only had three different plays. This time we had eight different plays to choose from in the middle, outsides, and back row attack. Next year, we want to come back stronger,” said Champion. Coach Cardenas served in an interim role after coming from the JV team. “I’m excited about next year. We have a lot of time for a lot more growth. We’re going to go further in playoffs. I love this group so much that I will probably be back,” said Cardenas. pion had three, Day had two, and Higashi had one. 3-2 win over West County The Highlanders upset No. 11 West County in five sets, of 25-21, 21-25, 20-25, 25-20, and 15-13. Kimball was instrumental with a team-leading 11 kills, Champion finished with nine kills, Kelly had six kills, while Wong had five. As for services, Wong led with six aces, Cham- 3-1 loss to Archie Williams Against No. 3 Archie Williams, Piedmont fell by scores of 25-17, 24-26, 25-10, 25-19. Piedmont’s winning second set featured five lead changes down to the final two points. The Highlanders trailed 24-23 but finished with three straight points to win 26-24 when Archie Williams had a serve go into net, had a net violation, and then had a shot attempt sail out of bounds. John Champion had nine kills against West County. Staff Photo Shunji Higashi goes up for a block. Staff Photo

articles.text: Staff Photos Parker Terrill won the pole vault with a leap of 15 feet, 6 inches. The Piedmont High track team proved its dominance last weekend, May 6-7, at the West Alameda County Conference Championship at Hayward High with six winners and several top-six finishers to qualify for the North Coast Section Bayshore Championship next weekend at the same location. Piedmont’s all-time record holder in the pole vault, Parker Terrill, won Saturday’s pole vault with a height of 15 feet, 6 inches, defeating the second-place vaulter by 4 feet, 6 inches in a field of 10. He broke the league’s all-time record by two feet set by Bishop O’Dowd’s Ryan Gervin in 2002. Terrill nearly cracked the 16 foot mark on his final attempt. Terrill also won the 110-meter hurdles on Friday with a time of 16.48 seconds in a field of 15 hurdlers. He also second of 16 in the high jump with a height of 5 feet, 8 inches, and will be competing in all three events at the North Coast Section Bayshore meet this weekend. “I didn’t even know about the record. I wanted to set a PR, and I got really close, but the wind conditions set me off a tiny bit with the headwind. I think it’s still possible to hit the 5-meter mark. Getting in a more competitive environment will help a lot,” said Terrill. Ellie Black won gold in the 1600 and 3200 on Saturday. In the 3200, Black clocked a Her winning time in the 3200 was 10:58.6 in a field of 15, and she nearly lapped the entire field. Black overtook third-place Asha Torok of Berkeley as she finished the race and defeated second-place Sophia Carpenter of Alameda by 41 seconds. Her time in the 3200 broke the former League record by 11 seconds, set by Castro Valley’s Kesley Santisteban in 2011. In the 1600, Black won with a time of 5:09.74 in a field of 34, beating the second-place finisher by nine seconds. “This is my first full track season. Last season was combined with cross country. My first track race ever was sophomore year. It feels amazing just being able to run here at Hayward as a senior; just running with all these girls who I’ve known for so long, I’ve been friends with the Alameda girls since I was a freshman, it makes it all that more special,” said Black. Jack Stein, Piedmont’s alltime record holder in the 1600 and 3200, also got the job done in both events at the WACC Championship. He won Friday’s 1600 with a time of 4:21.01, beating Alameda’s David Song by five seconds. Stein also beat Song in the 3200, this time by 13 seconds by clocking a 9:24.12. Song remained in Stein’s shadow for the first two-and-a-half laps, but the Piedmont senior progressively lost his competitor with every stride. Also qualifying for the NCS Bayshore was senior runner Cooper Downing in the 800 with a second-place finish in 1:56.03, Ellie Black leads the field in the 3200 meters. She won the 1600 and 3200 at the WACC Championship.

articles.text: Staff Photos The Highlanders concluded their season after a 21-7 loss to No. 4. Vista del Lago of Folsom in the first round of NCS. Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team was defeated 21-7 by Vista Del Lago of Folsom in the opening round of the Division 1 North Coast Section playoffs on Tuesday, May 3 at Witter Field. The No. 13 Highlanders hosted the game because they were the league champions after beating Bishop O’Dowd 10-9. The Eagles came out hot with eight goals in the first quarter and allowed none. The Highlanders scored twice in the second quarter with Nate Fredericks and Soren Dixon, and five second-half goals by Spencer Settlemier, two by Fredericks for his hat trick, once by Jack Nelson, and another by Dixon. Piedmont ended its season with a 9-8 record and its sixth consecutive league title. Most of the players will be returning next season with just two seniors graduating, Settlemier and Ben Heske. Next year, the Highlanders will be poised to repeat as WACC Champions and could be formidable. The Highlanders were promoted to D1 in the North Coast Section in 2019 after winning the Division 2 section title over Novato, which defeated Piedmont this season 10-6 on April 22. Looking ahead to next year’s roster, all four captains will return: Fredericks, Dixon, Henry Brayer and Jack Nelson. They will be joined by a potential roster of 28 returners. “We have a junior and sophomore heavy roster. This is a team that can compete over the next few years,” said coach Al Yu. Seniors will include leading scorers Fredericks, Dixon, and Jack Nelson, while Brayer, Bailey Cain, Keita Clear, Noah Lindenbaum, Matteo and Bautista Costa make a strong cast. Meanwhile, Rylan Nelson, Oliver Shafroth, Emmett Maxwell, Andrew McLaughlin, George Stein, Logan Huh, Curtis Hohener, Axel Saldanha, and Cole Nash will be juniors. Getting time as freshmen included Miles Silver, Bede Levin, Ethan Alering, and starting goalie Gus von Metzsch, who had a career night against O’Dowd in the league championship game, and was sterling in goal throughout the season. “Gus had his best performance against Bishop O’Dowd. He has a bright future, you see how much he progressed throughout the season,” said Yu of the freshman keeper. Piedmont looks ahead to having leading scorer Nate Fredericks back in the fold for 2023. Starting goalie Gus von Metzsch will be a sophomore next season.

articles.text: Simon Lins wins 2 events; qualifies for CIF State meet in 50 freestyle & 100 backstroke The PHS swimming program was well represented at the North Coast Section Championships on Friday and Saturday, May 6-7 at the Concord Community Pool with 10 swimmers in Friday’s trials and junior Simon Lins making the finals on Saturday. Lins qualified for the CIF State Meet on May 12-14 at Clovis West High School with two eligible times in the 50 freestyle and 100 backstroke. “This year was very special as we were able to build a 50-athlete team after having two years of no swim seasons. The kids and parents came back with full excitement and a readiness to compete and helped create one of our most successful teams,” said coach Colby Price, whose team has not had a home pool for more than a year. Lins, a junior who is committed to the University of Virginia, won the 50 Free with a time of 20.2 in a field of 16 swimmers. He also finished fifth of 16 in the 100 Back with a time of 49.64, 1.1 second back of first-place swimmer Tommy Roder of De La Salle. Lins will compete in a field of 43 swimmers 50 free at the Piedmont High swimmers wrap up a successful season at the NCS Championship. Pictured are: PHS principal Adam Littlefield (left), Sonja ten Grotenhuis, Maddie Payne, Taylor Rolefson, Josie Oesterer, Kate Aubrecht, Ryan Stokes, Farris Saffouri, Tom Rolefson, Chuck White, Frank Udovch, Simon Lins, and coach Colby Price. State meet this Friday, May 13. He enters with the third-fastest qualifying time. His time of 20.2 is .04 ahead of the Buchanan’s Colby Hatton and .12 behind Harvard-Westlake’s Ronald Dalmacio and a half-second behind Palo Alto’s Ethan Harrington. In the 100 back, Lins’ time of 49.64 is the 13th fastest time in the state. He will compete in a field of 40. Lins swam the first leg of the 400 freestyle relay team with Thomas Rolefson, Farris Saffouri, and Ryan Stokes. The team finished 21st of 39 with a time of 3:21.87. The boys’ 200 free relay team finished 33rd with a time of 1:35.51. The team included Rolefson, Chuck White, Saffouri, and Stokes. Senior Kate Aubrecht clocked a time of 24.76 in the 50 Free to place 24th of 40 athletes. Sophomore Taylor Rolefson competed in the 200 Free, placing 21st with a time of 1:58.90. Sophomore Josie Oesterer was 33rd in the 100 Back in 1:02.36. The girls’ team also competed in the 200 medley and 400 freestyle relay. Their 200 medley relay featured Oesterer, Taylor Rolefson, Aubrecht, and Sonja ten Grotenhuis placed 21st in 1:54.47. The 200 freestyle relay squad of Rolefson, Aubrecht, ten Grotenhuis, and Maddie Payne was 20th of 40 in 1:42.97. The 400 freestyle relay team of Rolefson, ten Grotenhuis, Oesterer, and Payne clocked a time of 3:49.11 to finish 21st. articles.text: Dear Piedmont and the PUSD community: We are a group of Piedmont High School students who play on many sports teams at PHS: volleyball, lacrosse, baseball, swim, soccer, football, and track and field. We represent just a tiny slice of the students at PHS, MHS and PMS who answered a Student Interest Sports Survey a couple of months ago that was sent out as part of Piedmont High School’s Title IX sports audit. The student survey asked what sport PHS could offer that it currently doesn’t have. The top student vote was beach volleyball. We’re aware of possible sand court locations being considered between the high school and middle school campuses, with a possibility at the Linda Beach re-design. Some of us have called into City Council and Recreation Commission public meetings to ask for outdoor sand courts, letting them know that high school and middle school teens need another outdoor, fun space to hang-out within Piedmont. These courts would be a shared use space for everyone in the community. Without outdoor courts in Piedmont, there is nowhere to play nearby. Having courts would allow the Piedmont Recreation Department to offer camps to younger kids. The Piedmont High volleyball teams would love to run camps. Most of our parents love to play, too! Fun fact: did you know that 84% of PHS students this school year play on Piedmont High sports teams? This community loves sports, and supports its students, so please take the survey either by turning on your cell phone camera and hovering over the black and white QR code. Piedmont residents can email their thoughts to the Recreation Commission’s Sub-committee on Volleyball: piedmont.bvb@ gmail.com. For more information or to join in support, email: KimLovesTahoe@gmail.com. Thank you! Signed, Bree DeYoung, Eden Lorin, Wilson Wong, Shelby Cavenaugh, Tara Kothari, John Champion, Sadie Town, Shunji Higashi, Bauer Peterson, Ryan McConathy, Brayden Day, Lila Town, Brie Sotelo, Bosco Lorin, Juliana DeYoung, Izzy Grimmer, Klara Zietlow, Beck Peterson, Andrew Szerdy, Macy Puckett, Annika Hattan-Kutter, Maddy Hill, Ella Puckett, Nathan Fredricks and Kai Lambert. Several PHS students have submitted their interest in installing beach volleyball courts after a Title IX audit.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 11, 2022 17 Art Walk Continued from page 16 designated stops on the Art Walk map. “I was really impressed with how well it was run,” Friedes said. “They were very communicative with us from the get-go and gave us great tools to help promote the event. The graphic presentation of materials was concise and beautifully executed.” Rob Duncan, Creative Director at Mucho Design, is the mastermind behind the red and white Art Walk logo that has now become synonymous with the event. The logo has been featured in the Creative Review Annual, has won two Type Directors Club Awards in New York, and a Gold Art Directors Club award. “At Mucho, as designers, we always try to raise a smile - whether that’s rebranding a global corporation like Visa or designing the visual identity for the Piedmont Art Walk,” he said. “Art is often seen as elitist. The Piedmont Art Walk is the complete opposite of this - great artists, living in a great neighborhood, creating great work that can benefit local schools. How can we create an identity that speaks to everybody in a fun way? We took the word ‘Art’ and made it walk,” Duncan said. Twenty percent of funds raised from purchased art goes to benefit the Art Fund, which is used exclusively to benefit visual and performing arts programs at Piedmont schools. Last year, the event raised $17,000 to support art in Piedmont schools. “This school year we especially focused on instrumental music programming, such as supporting clinicians in the band and orchestra, as there was a real learning loss through the pandemic with the shift to online classes,” said Rebecca Posamentier, Co-chair of the Piedmont Arts Fund. Posamentier was at the information booth this year, ensuring that attendees had a central location to stop by for information, maps, and sweet treats for young art-walkers. articles.text: Alexander String Quartet to appear Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players will present the fourth in a series of five concerts entitled Cultural Crossroads this Saturday, May 14, at 7:30 p.m. at the Don Tatzin Community Hall at the Lafayette Library, 3491 Mt. Diablo Boulevard in Lafayette. Cultural Crossroads explores the Black and Indigenous influences on Dvorak and will feature Native American flutist R. Carlos Nakai, the Alexander String Quartet, soprano Michele Kennedy, and violist Pamela Freund-Striplen, founder of Gold Coast. T he prog ram i ncludes Dvořák’s String Quintet, op. 97 and the Lento from his String Quartet, op. 96. Also on the program are original works by R. Carlos Nakai, Clan of the Mists, Butterflies Dancing, and Honoring Song, written for the Gold Coast Chamber Players, as well as Nakai’s arrangement of Amazing Grace. Guests will hear two songs by African American composer Florence Price, Sunset and Night, as well as African American Spirituals that influenced Dvořák, Swing Low Sweet Chariot, By an’ By, and My Lord What a Morning. The program’s finale is an arrangement of Goin’ Home, taken from Dvořák’s New World Symphony. Tickets can be purchased online at https://app.arts-people. com/index.php?show=123574 &rd=1&rd=1, or by phone at (925) 283-3728.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera presents Don Giovanni, part three of the Mozart-Da Ponte Trilogy. San Francisco Opera will present Mozart’s Don Giovanni beginning June 4 and running through July 2. Tickets are on sale now. Don Giovanni, part three of the Mozart-Da Ponte Trilogy, is a dark comedy with a horrific twist ending. The action takes place in Seville and spans 24 hours as two women set off to confront a notorious libertine. It is based on the legend of Don Juan, with a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte. The opera is sung in Italian with English supertitles. Etienne Dupuis sings the title role of Don Giovanni, Adela Zaharia is Donna Anna, and Carmen Giannattasio is Donna Elvira. The opera is conducted by Bertrand de Billy and directed by Michael Cavanagh. Visit https://www.sfopera. com/on-stage/don-giovanni/ to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Opera to perform Don Giovanni June 4 through July 2

articles.text: Opera and theater, from Greek tragedy to those 18th Century rock stars the Castrati, have historically told stories through a broad spectrum of voices, personalities, and gender expressions. Performed and curated by mezzo-soprano Lily Bogas and countertenor Matheus Coura, They Sing! will be performed at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, May 22 at 5 p.m. Explore feelings from sublime to irreverent to comedic: recognizing that voices of the same range have validity in roles across the gender spectrum. This program will feature arias, songs, and duets by Monteverdi, Handel, Mozart, Bizet, Strauss, Kurt Weill, and Ricky Ian Gordon. They Sing! will take you on a journey through the past, present and into the future of how music has shaped and reflected the multifaceted human experience. Mezzo soprano Lily Bogas is a student at the Eastman School of Music. Their recent credits include Taller Daughter in Missy Mazzoli’s Proving Up, Dido in Dido and Aeneas, and Cinderella in Into the Woods. A finalist in the National CS Vocal Competition, and third place winner in the Schmidt Vocal Competition, Bogas was also a finalist in the American Songbook Academy, performing jazz standards alongside Michael Feinstein. Bogas will be making their mainstage debut with Festival Opera as Clotilde in Norma this season. Praised for their “sonorous voice” and “delightful spontaneity”, Brazilian-American countertenor Matheus Coura’s recent performances include Giuliano in Eliogabalo with West Edge Opera, and Narcissus in Two united in a single soul with San Francisco Ballet. Coura is a recipient of the SF Artist Grant, was a finalist in the Bethlehem Bach Competition, and was a prize winner at the St. Petersburg Opera Guild and Cooper-Bing Competitions. Coura is also an international portrait photographer, and resident artist at The Convent Arts Collective where they co-founded the drag revue Bad Habits.
articles.title: Festival Opera presents They Sing at PCA on May 22

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony welcomes soprano Julia Bullock at Davies Symphony Hall on May 17 for an original program entitled History’s Persistent Voice. Bullock is an American soprano originally from St. Louis, who will team with guest conductor Christian Reif in this original and ever-developing program that highlights the work and experiences of Black American artists. This mixed media concert includes voices that span across generations, from the 1860s to modern day. The program features newly commissioned works performed by talented women of color, including Jessie Montgomery, Carolyn Yarnell, Allison Loggins-Hull, Pamela Z, and Tania León. Hana S. Kim will serve as a visual artist for the performance. For tickets, visit: https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2021-22/Julia-Bullock-Historys-Persistent-Voice, or call the box office at (415) 864-6000. Davies Symphony Hall is located at 201 Van Ness Avenue in San Francisco. Soprano Julia Bullock
articles.title: Julia Bullock to perform with SF Symphony on May 17

articles.text: Annual chamber music festival begins on July 14 Music@Menlo, the iconic chamber music festival based in Menlo Park, returns this year with a special 20th anniversary, beginning July 14. Tickets are on sale now. Music@Menlo is an internationally acclaimed chamber music festival founded by David Finckel and Wu Han. Inaugurated in 2003 at Menlo School, the festival features concerts, lectures, and a training program for aspiring professional musicians. The festival’s mission is to engage and sustain an audience for chamber music that is programmed, presented, and performed at the highest level of artistic excellence. Concert programs are performed by a collection of the greatest chamber musicians around the world, provided in intimate settings at Menlo School and Spieker Center for the Arts, as well as on-line. Visit https://musicatmenlo.org to purchase tickets and to view a list of announced artists and programs. Music@Menlo founders David Finckel and Wu Han, seen performing at the 2021 Music@Menlo Chamber Music Festival.
articles.title: Music@Menlo 2022 tickets on sale now

A finalist in the National CS Vocal Competition, and third place winner in the Schmidt Vocal Competition, Bogas was also a finalist in the American Songbook Academy, performing jazz standards alongside Michael Feinstein. Bogas will be making their mainstage debut with Festival Opera as Clotilde in Norma this season. Praised for their “sonorous voice” and “delightful spontaneity”, Brazilian-American countertenor Matheus Coura’s recent performances include Giuliano in Eliogabalo with West Edge Opera, and Narcissus in Two united in a single soul with San Francisco Ballet. Coura is a recipient of the SF Artist Grant, was a finalist in the Bethlehem Bach Competition, and was a prize winner at the St. Petersburg Opera Guild and Cooper-Bing Competitions. Coura is also an international portrait photographer, and resident artist at The Convent Arts Collective where they co-founded the drag revue Bad Habits.

articles.text: Mia Wasikowska protrays the title character Jane Eyre. Mia Waskowska, who portrayed Alice in Tim Burton’s Alice in Wonderland, is a remarkable actress and perfectly cast in the 2011 film Jane Eyre. Told in flashbacks, the story is of an orphaned child, sent to Lowood, a boarding school, by a spiteful aunt who was charged with her care. At Lowood she is subjected to a rigorous curriculum, to include sadistic, unprovoked punishments delivered for what seems to be the sheer pleasure of torturing the innocent and the defenseless. Despite a childhood that would have damaged most children beyond repair, Jane grows into a young woman of remarkable intelligence and courage, demonstrated when she finds a position as the governess to a young French child. She comes to reside at Thornfield Hall owned by Edward Rochester (Michael Fassbender), striking in its size and grandeur, stark and isolated, and surrounded by the damp and blustery Yorkshire moors. There is a sense about the house that the servants, to include Mrs. Fairfax (Judi Dench), go for days without saying a word. That is until Mr. Rochester returns. The story, though familiar, is wonderfully adapted for the screen by Moira Buffini, and stunningly photographed by Ariano Goldman. Goldman captures, in wide shots, not only the isolation of the stretching North England countryside, sepia and windswept, but conveys a sense of melancholy that has gripped the mansion’s interiors for years. This is a house that holds a terrible secret. And this is a house that improbably nurtures a relationship between Jane, ever plain, bound by the severe conventions of Victorian formality, a formality reflected in the restrained and stilted language of the time, and Mr. Rochester, as she calls him. The story is a character study of a young woman who refuses to be defined by her past nor the rigidity of her times or station. She was never encouraged to define for herself the meaning of freedom and independence. After all, what Victorian woman was? And yet she does. When asked, she speaks her mind. Behind her unvarnished exterior, her dark dresses, her hair wound tightly in a bun, her face free of even the hint of blush, is a keen intelligence – factors that make her all the more alluring to Edward Rochester. Like most English women of the 19th century, she was regarded as property. If a woman like Jane was to survive, it was through the good graces of a man. Women of no means led lives of sustained uncertainty. Charlotte Bronte, like Jane Austen, wrote captivatingly about such women, and though they might be called romance novels today, they possess a startling subtext of feminism and equality that was decidedly not then the norm, a subtext that might have encouraged future suffragettes and feminists. Director Cary Joji Fukunaga (Sin Nombre) does a marvelous job of capturing the period as well as creating an engaging if brooding film with a superb ensemble of actors. Jane Eyre, Directed by Cary Joji Fukunaga. Starring Mia Wasikowska, Michael Fassbender, Judi Dench, and Jamie Bell. 1 hr. 58 min. Released 2011. Published in the Post in 2011. Now streaming on VuDu. articles.text: Sunday was Mothers Day. Curiously, there are not many classical pieces which celebrate motherhood. Pop music has far more. French composer Claude Debussy had little regard for women. He even treated his mistress miserably. Is it any wonder that he composed La Mer (The sea) rather than “La Mere” (The mother)? At the other end of the spectrum was Debussy’s competitor, Maurice Ravel, who composed the Mother Goose Suite and was noted to be extremely reverent of his mother. The short list of memorable maternal songs must include Dvorak’s hauntingly beautiful “Songs My Mother Taught Me.” For recommended listening, check out Marian Anderson’s vocal version and also the violin version as played by Fritz Kreisler. For pure sentiment, nothing can be better than “Mother Machree” as sung by the immortal Irish tenor, John McCormack. Musical shortcomings are somewhat counterbalanced when it comes to famous names and their connection to famous foods. A quick psychological association of foods and their famous personages proves the case. For beverages you can get a Shirley Temple or an Arnold Palmer. For appetizers there are Oysters Rockefeller. Famous salads include the Caesar salad, which was not named for Julius Caesar, and the Cobb salad which was not named for Baseball Hall of Fame player Ty Cobb. The sandwich, however was named for Sandwich, as in, the Earl of. Next come some pasta courses named for opera stars Enrico Caruso and Louisa Tetrazzini. Caruso’s recipe combines spaghetti and chicken livers, and Tetrazzini’s combines chicken or turkey with pasta. The main courses have equally famous names. We note the very difficult-to-make Beef Wellington and the Tornadoes of beef a la Rossini. There are equally famous sauces made for the Russian nobleman Stroganoff, and Bechamel sauce especially for King Louis XIV. For dessert you might enjoy Peach melba, which was created for opera star Nelly Melba, or a Napoleon, named for you know who. And let’s include a Baby Ruth candy bar, with a great story about it. If I remember correctly, the candy was developed in 1921. So Claude Debussy, composer of Mother Goose Suite. the connection with the candy bar and Babe Ruth, the baseball player, is logical. But the candy manufacturers denied any connection. Babe Ruth sued for the obvious reasons, but lost the case. The manufacturers were elated. The publicity made them wealthy. Some time later they admitted that Babe Ruth was actually the inspiration for their candy bar. The walk off home run is saved for last. It was my pleasure to host seven people for dinner on Mother’s Day this past weekend. The main course was my version of Chicken Clemenceau. named for French President Georges Clemenceau. This spectacular dish was developed for Clemenceau by Galatoire’s restaurant in New Orleans, and there are only three main ingredients: equal amounts of cubed-sautéed potatoes and peas. The original recipe calls for canned peas but fresh or frozen are much better. The vegetables are then topped with shrimp, chicken, or turkey. If you have any meat leftovers use them in this dish. To make “Clemenceau” even more special, I made Potatoes Brabant. If you want to do this, cut your favorite potato into half-inch cubes. Boil the potatoes in salted water. Drain well. Then sauté the potatoes in olive oil or butter until they are lightly browned. Put the potatoes into a 375° oven for one hour. Then combine the potatoes with an equal amount of peas and top with your favorite meat. Spectacular! Start the meal with a citrus salad. I forgot one thing. The “Sloppy Joe” was not named for me.

articles.text: Storks, a charming, kidfriendly animation released by Warner Bros. in 2016, answers the question, “Where do babies come from?” as only Hollywood can –with a delivery service, provided by long beaked and long-legged storks. Prospective parents need only send in their request, and voila!, the little one arrives, wrapped in a diaper. But that was then, and this is now. Apparently, due to a disastrous mixup the storks are now out of the baby delivery business. Instead they’re in the employment of Cornerstone. com, an online outfit that delivers packages. What happened, long ago, was that a stork grew so attached to an infant that it failed to make the delivery, which created quite a brouhaha. That youngster, named Tulip (Katie Crown), grew up among the storks, and now works for Cornerstone. She’s a ditzy firecracker, full of energy, often accident- prone, and sports a mop of red hair. But the head of Cornerstone, Hunter (Kelsey Grammar), is not happy with Tulip’s clumsiness. He calls in Junior (Adam Sandberg), one of the worker storks, and assigns him the task of firing Tulip. But kind-hearted Junior is reluctant to carry out his assignment and doesn’t let Tulip go. But his hesitation has one major unintended consequence: Tulip accidentally activates the unused baby-making machine, which produces an adorable infant. As it turns out, the baby is slated to be the sister of a kid named Nate (Anton Starkman). He has been pleading with his workaholic parents (Jennifer Aniston and Ty Burrell) for a sibling to no avail. Nate even goes as far as writing a letter to the storks at Stone Mountain, asking for a sister. When Junior and Tulip read his intercepted letter, well, they’re confronted with the problem of how to get the little one delivered to the family. Of course the duo confront a number of obstacles, one being a pigeon named Toadie (Stephen Glickman), and an ominous pack of baby-stealing wolves, led by Alpha and Beta (Keegan-Michael Key and Jordan Peele) that have the ability to shape shift (they even turn themselves into a bridge). Storks is a frenetic story, fastpaced and guaranteed to make the kids laugh. Simply put, it’s a romp that focuses on the many challenges of parenthood and all the accompanying responsibilities. It’s fun from start to finish, all while skirting the question of where do babies come from? Storks. Directed by Nicholas Stoller & Doug Sweetland. Warner Bros. animation. With voices of Andy Sandberg, Katie Crown, & Kelsey Grammar. 1 hr,, 23 min. Rated PG. Released in 2016. Now streaming on Prime/Vudu.

articles.text: The Angry Birds Movie, a Sony animated feature, is based on a hugely popular video game. This origin story is filled with frenetic antics, puns and jokes targeted for grade school youngsters. It will entertain kids familiar with the game... or send those who haven’t played the game in search of same. The story takes place on Bird Island where all the businesses have avian names. It is home to flightless birds who are constantly cheerful. Well, not all of them. Take Red, for example. His feathers are scarlet, he has a permanent scowl, and thick black eyebrows that express his cranky demeanor. He hangs out with fellow discontents Chuck (Josh Glad), Bomb (Danny McBride), and Terrence (Sean Penn) All four are so grumpy that they are told to attend an anger management class led by the very patient Matilda (Maya Rudolph). One day a mysterious pirate ship, arrives at the island, its crew made up of green pigs, so many in number that they invade the island. Their leader and captain is Green Pig Leonard (Bill Hader). The pigs are on a clandestine mission, and to accomplish their objective they have to distract the birds. So they ply them with gifts A scene from The Angry Bird Movie. and parties. Meanwhile they set out to steal as many bird eggs as they can find. Red and cohort are suspicious (especially Red) and agree to keep an eye on the pigs. Red even consults with his idol, the mythical Mighty Eagle (Peter Dinklage). When Red finally convinces the island birds of what has happened to their pre-chick eggs, well, let the games begin. A battle against the pigs ensues. They plant TNT on the pirate ship, and slingshot volunteers at the pigs, managing to knock over a lot of stuff. It’s all a bit crazy with lots of frantic action. The objective is to get the eggs back before the pigs can make an omelet. Parents should know that The Angry Birds Movie is aimed at the little guys – the equivalent of a Saturday morning cartoon. It’s cute and childish and filled with bird and pig puns. The filmmakers have done their best to give Red and company distinctive personalities: Red is sarcastic and prone to tantrums. Bomb is slow to anger; Chuck is frenetic; and Terrence only growls. The youngsters will be entertained and will find the film to be a hoot. Their parents, if they are tempted to join them, will risk head shaking migraines. The Angry Birds Movie. Directed by Clay Kaytis/Fergal Reilly. Animation by Sony. With voices of Jason Sudekis, Josh Gad, & Danny McBride. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated PG. Released in 2016. Now Streaming on VUDU/Prime.
articles.title: The Angry Birds Movie will keep the youngest kids howling

articles.text: Those of you who have tracked these columns or follow me on Instagram have likely noticed a theme that revolves around my passion for quality handmade, objects and furniture, preferably locally procured. Often our projects involve a mashup of handmade pieces with more accessible, easily-obtained items mixed in. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth Bancroft when it was her private, personal garden, but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. articles.text: You might enjoy owning your home – but the mortgage? Not so much. In fact, you might want to do everything you can to pay it off as quickly as possible. But is that always the best strategy? In one sense, your mortgage can be considered a “good” debt because it’s backed by a tangible asset – your home – that has real value and may even gain further value. Furthermore, by historical standards, you’re probably paying a pretty low interest rate on your mortgage, so you’re getting a lot of benefit – a place to live and a potentially appreciating asset. And if you itemize on your taxes, you can possibly deduct some, or maybe all, of your mortgage interest. Nonetheless, despite these benefits, a mortgage is still something you have to pay, month after month and year after year. And for some people, it may feel good to pay it off. After all, there may well be a psychological benefit to being free this long-term debt. But is it really in your best financial interest to make extra payments? Suppose, for example, that you need a large sum of money quickly for a new car, a new furnace or some other unexpected, significant expense. Or, in an even more serious scenario, what if your job ends and you need money to tide you over until you get a new one? In these situations, you need liquidity – ready access to available cash. And your house may not be the best place to get it. You could apply for a home equity loan or line of credit, but these typically require approvals (which might be difficult if you aren’t employed), and you’ll be using your home as collateral. A home equity loan or credit line isn’t always bad – under the right circumstances, it can be a valuable financial tool. But that doesn’t change the basic fact that your home is essentially a non-liquid asset. So, instead of making extra house payments, make sure you have built an emergency fund containing several months’ worth of living expenses, with the money kept in a low-risk, accessible account. articles.text: Lifelong Piedmont resident a bagpiper, historian, lecturer Fred Rutledge passed away on March 26 at his Orinda home with his wife Jane by his side. A beloved husband, father and brother, Fred was a historian, educator, bagpiper, military veteran, and humanitarian. Born Frederick Stuart Rutledge in Piedmont in 1956, Fred was a fourth generation native Californian. After receiving a B.A. in History from U.C. Berkeley, and a Master of Arts in Education Administration from Saint Mary’s College, he enrolled in history classes at Oxford University in London. During his long and successful career in higher education he was appointed Vice Principal of Piedmont Adult School and of the Pleasanton Unified School District’s Adult and Career Education program. He later was named Principal of Adult and Correctional Education for the Tri-Valley Regional Occupational Center. In his free time, Fred was a popular guest lecturer on the Civil War and World War I, appearing in Bay Area schools, community organizations and museums. For these appearances he often wore Center for Military History and achieved the rank of Colonel. His other volunteer duties included counseling soldiers on balancing military service with civilian life. He also played a lead role in organizing the annual Wheelchair Regatta and Remembrance Day Service. Fred’s many civic activities included serving as president of Encinal Yacht Club, Royal Canadian Legion Post 25, Pleasanton-Blairgowrie-Fergus Sister Cities Organization, St. Andrews Society of San Francisco, the Order of St. John and Commodore of the Pacific Inter-Club Yacht Association. Colleagues often credited his special sense of humor for bringing levity to board meetings. Fred is survived by his wife, Jane, two daughters Jean (Jack) Stein, Kirsten (Josh) Gooley, and two brothers, Bill and Steve. The family suggests that memorial donations may be made to the Marine’s Memorial Foundation, (www.MarinesMemorial. org), and the U.C. articles.text: Piedmont resident Suzanne Evans quietly passed away surrounded by her family on May 2, 2022. She was 82. Born Suzanne Elizabeth Warrington on September 29, 1939, Suzanne was the daughter of Doris Elizabeth Warrington and Richard Hudson Warrington. She attended John Muir High School in Pasadena and proudly graduated from the University of California, Berkeley in 1961. At Cal, she joined the Alpha Omega Pi Sorority where she made lifelong friends. She hosted a Cal/Stanford Big Game party every year for more than 50 years. After graduating from Cal, Suzanne taught students in third, fourth, and fifth grades in Berkeley and Daly City. She was a member of the Junior League of Oakland - East Bay and Junior Alliance. She was married to James Daniel Evans, Jr. in 1966, and was the loving mother to her two children, James Daniel Evans III and Anne Evans Wheeler, and treasured “Mayme” to her five grandchildren. Suzanne was a longtime member of Piedmont Community Church, taking seniors out to lunch for many years with the “Lunch Bunch.” She was a lover of books, bridge, good food and music. For years, she attended the San Francisco Symphony Suzanne Evans dies at age 82. rehearsals with friends. Suzanne also started a book club called the “Second Tuesday Bookies,” which has met monthly for more than 30 years. She often played the role of librarian, suggesting the perfect book for family and friends. Suzanne is preceded in death by her husband. She is survived by children Jim (Karen) Evans, Anne (Greg) Wheeler, and her grandchildren Jacqueline, James, Isabelle, Beatrice and Camille. She is remembered with great love and affection by her family and many friends. She was an inspiration to many for her resilience and will be dearly missed. A memorial service will be held on Friday, May 20 at 2 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA. Please join us to help celebrate Suzanne.
articles.title: Longtime Piedmont resident Suzanne Evans passed away on May 2. She was 82.

At Cal, she joined the Alpha Omega Pi Sorority where she made lifelong friends. She hosted a Cal/Stanford Big Game party every year for more than 50 years. After graduating from Cal, Suzanne taught students in third, fourth, and fifth grades in Berkeley and Daly City. She was a member of the Junior League of Oakland - East Bay and Junior Alliance. She was married to James Daniel Evans, Jr. in 1966, and was the loving mother to her two children, James Daniel Evans III and Anne Evans Wheeler, and treasured “Mayme” to her five grandchildren. Suzanne was a longtime member of Piedmont Community Church, taking seniors out to lunch for many years with the “Lunch Bunch.” She was a lover of books, bridge, good food and music. For years, she attended the San Francisco Symphony Suzanne Evans dies at age 82. rehearsals with friends. Suzanne also started a book club called the “Second Tuesday Bookies,” which has met monthly for more than 30 years. She often played the role of librarian, suggesting the perfect book for family and friends. Suzanne is preceded in death by her husband. She is survived by children Jim (Karen) Evans, Anne (Greg) Wheeler, and her grandchildren Jacqueline, James, Isabelle, Beatrice and Camille. She is remembered with great love and affection by her family and many friends. She was an inspiration to many for her resilience and will be dearly missed. A memorial service will be held on Friday, May 20 at 2 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA. Please join us to help celebrate Suzanne. articles.text: A large turnout of 45 walkers was on hand last Wednesday for a tour of Tyson Lake by former Mayor Bob McBain, whose house is located at the lake. He took the group on a walk around the lake two years ago just before the pandemic, and generously invited the walkers to return. Many had never seen the small lake which lies between Sotelo Avenue and LaSalle Avenue. The walkers headed out on Highland, through the Hall Fenway to Crocker Park and Hampton Road. As they passed the park, Annis Kukulan spotted her friend, Veronique Sumnicht, and invited her to join the group. When the long line of walkers reached the Sotelo-Glen Alpine loop, the history of this section of Piedmont was shared based upon Gail Lombardi’s research. This entire neighborhood was once intended to be the grand estate of Louis Titus, a successful Berkeley real estate developer. In 1911 he purchased 50 acres of land and was going to build a magnificent mansion. When the new City of Piedmont changed its property tax basis after incorporating in 1907, it increased his taxes to a reported $200,000. Titus dropped his plans and moved on. The group continued up Sotelo and Bob McBain with his K-9 best friend, Mac, were in front of his house. There Lombardi’s history of Tyson Lake was also told. In 1914 James Tyson, a successful lumber and shipping businessman, bought 30 acres of Titus’ land to build his own mansion. Tyson had three sons and he built a dam on the small creek that ran through his property to create a reservoir that became a swimming hole for his sons and neighborhood kids. Tyson was also a supporter of the new Piedmont Boy Scout Council, and he made a portion of his land available for a Boy Scout camp. It later became Hampton Park. However, in the 1930s Tyson’s health began to fail and he moved to Alameda. He transferred the title of the Scout camp to Piedmont High School and his lake to a homeowners association. During this time and later Tyson Lake became an attraction for teenage boys. In 1949 four of them were caught swimming nude in it, and each fined $25. Tragically, in 1951 a 17-year old boy drowned in the lake, and another 19 year-old also drowned there in 1952. After some failed negotiations with the City, the homeowners spent $6,000 on improvements, and the lake and its dam were declared safe by 1959. Bob McBain led the walkers down to the lake on a new set of concrete stairs, which made getting to the path around the lake much easier than it was two years earlier. There was lots of vegetation and many large, purple thistles along the way that seemed appropriate for Piedmont. The lake is about 25 feet deep, and there are some fish in it. There is a fountain in the middle of the lake that acts to keep the lake clean. articles.title: Mayor Bob and a tour of Tyson Lake

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, May 11, 2022 Walking on Wednesday Mayor Bob and a tour of Tyson Lake A large turnout of 45 walkers was on hand last Wednesday for a tour of Tyson Lake by former Mayor Bob McBain, whose house is located at the lake. He took the group on a walk around the lake two years ago just before the pandemic, and generously invited the walkers to return. Many had never seen the small lake which lies between Sotelo Avenue and LaSalle Avenue. The walkers headed out on Highland, through the Hall Fenway to Crocker Park and Hampton Road. As they passed the park, Annis Kukulan spotted her friend, Veronique Sumnicht, and invited her to join the group. When the long line of walkers reached the Sotelo-Glen Alpine loop, the history of this section of Piedmont was shared based upon Gail Lombardi’s research. This entire neighborhood was once intended to be the grand estate of Louis Titus, a successful Berkeley real estate developer. In 1911 he purchased 50 acres of land and was going to build a magnificent mansion. When the new City of Piedmont changed its property tax basis after incorporating in 1907, it increased his taxes to a reported $200,000. Titus dropped his plans and moved on. The group continued up Sotelo and Bob McBain with his K-9 best friend, Mac, were in front of his house. There Lombardi’s history of Tyson Lake was also told. In 1914 James Tyson, a successful lumber and shipping businessman, bought 30 acres of Titus’ land to build his own mansion. Tyson had three sons and he built a dam on the small creek that ran through his property to create a reservoir that became a swimming hole for his sons and neighborhood kids. Tyson was also a supporter of the new Piedmont Boy Scout Council, and he made a portion of his land available for a Boy Scout camp. It later became Hampton Park. However, in the 1930s Tyson’s health began to fail and he moved to Alameda. He transferred the title of the Scout camp to Piedmont High School and his lake to a homeowners association. During this time and later Tyson Lake became an attraction for teenage boys. In 1949 four of them were caught swimming nude in it, and each fined $25. Tragically, in 1951 a 17-year old boy drowned in the lake, and another 19 year-old also drowned there in 1952. After some failed negotiations with the City, the homeowners spent $6,000 on improvements, and the lake and its dam were declared safe by 1959. Bob McBain led the walkers down to the lake on a new set of concrete stairs, which made getting to the path around the lake much easier than it was two years earlier. There was lots of vegetation and many large, purple thistles along the way that seemed appropriate for Piedmont. The lake is about 25 feet deep, and there are some fish in it. There is a fountain in the middle of the lake that acts to keep the lake clean. A canoe and a rowboat were along the bank waiting to be put to use, but two Canadian geese were already in the middle of the lake. The path around the lake had a few narrow and elevated spots, and some slippery places, but all the walkers safely circled the lake and enjoyed its beauty. The walkers enjoyed Gail Lombardi’s history of the area, and especially appreciated the personal tour of the lake by former Mayor McBain. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
