January 1 marked the launch of Oakland Zoo’s centennial year. Since June 6, 1922, the Zoo has evolved from a single building in Snow Park near downtown Oakland, to Joaquin Miller Park in 1926, to its current location in 1939, the hills of Knowland Park. Today, the Oakland Zoo has evolved greatly with the changing times and attracts almost 900,000 guests per year. At 100 acres, it is one of the four largest zoos in California. elephants, are now practiced by zoos worldwide. The Zoo is a leader in animal rescue by providing animal care, rehabilitation, and sanctuary for animals rescued from human-wildlife conflict, the exotic pet trade, or natural disasters. Oakland Zoo is also dedicated to youth education and partners with over 25 conservation organizations globally, equally committed to preserving species and their habitats in the wild. “It’s with enormous pride to serve as CEO during this incredible milestone,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. “There has been so much accomplished over these many years in making the Zoo what it is today, and I’m honored to lead Oakland Zoo into the next 100 years. So much has evolved in the past century in the world – and in the role of zoos and their purpose – Oakland Zoo is fully committed in doing our part and leading the next generation of conservationists to blaze the trail ahead.” In the early years, from 1922 to 1950, Oakland Zoo was founded by and under the management of naturalists Henry A. Snow and his son Sidney Snow. Although no longer privately owned, and managed by the Conservation Society of California, the Snow family legacy remains actively present today, through the great granddaughter of Henry Snow and the granddaughter of Sidney Snow, Nancy Clark: “As great granddaughter and granddaughter of the Zoo’s founders, Henry and Sidney Snow, and as current Co-Chair of the Board of Trustees, I am thrilled personally and profesNik Dehejia, Oakland Zoo’s current CEO. Oakland Zoo’s Main Entrance in 1990 vs. the Zoo’s Main Entrance in Present Day. sionally at how much the Oakland Zoo has accomplished and grown in 100 years,” said Nancy Clark. “Our family is certain that Henry and Sidney would be beyond proud at what the Oakland Zoo has become.” While Oakland Zoo takes pride in its accomplishments, milestones, and animal-focused efforts, much was undertaken in recent decades to evolve and improve the zoo’s facilities, programs, and public reputation. Virtually bankrupt and branded by media and the Humane Society as one of the ten worst zoos in the U.S. in 1984, Dr. Joel Parrott began his tenure as CEO and President that same year and began turning things around. Significant changes were made to improve animal care and welfare, habitats and infrastructure. Conservation work and education programs were created. In 1988, Oakland Zoo received accreditation from the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA). With Dr. Parrott’s vision, the Zoo grew from 25 acres to 100 acres, 15 employees to 240, and is the nationally accredited, award-winning, progressive, conservation and education-focused Zoo it is today. One of the most significant Oakland Zoo projects in the past decade is the opening of the California Trail, a 45-acre, transformational project which furthered the Zoo’s commitments to animal care, education, and conservation. The California Trail expansion spotlights the significance of the state’s unique environmental history and what we can all do to ensure the future of California’s wildlife and the nature that surrounds us. The next 100 years will lead a purpose-driven future focused on the pursuit of excellence in animal care and welfare, the rescue and rehabilitation of animals in the wild, and the conservation of threatened species everywhere. Education programs will expand, Photos Credit Oakland Zoo and work to inspire youth in natural sciences to find solutions to the growing climate challenge, the preservation of nature and the importance of wildlife. To celebrate with the community and Zoo guests throughout the year, new and exclusive events are planned, including a birthday celebration festival on June 5 at the Zoo’s original birthplace, Snow Park in downtown Oakland. The special day will be filled with festivities for all ages to enjoy and free to the community. The Zoo has brought back and enhanced many favorite events as well, such as Brunch for the Wild Bunch, Earth Day, Walk in the Wild, and Boo at the Zoo. As the Zoo reflects on its history, it invites the community to share their Oakland Zoo memories, and Zoo visits this year by tagging them on social media using #OZ100. For more information on the Zoo’s Centennial Celebration and festivities, visit: oaklandzoo.org/centennial. Dr. Joel Parrott CEO of Oakland Zoo from 1987 to 2021. We believe the City should create policies to enable affordable housing throughout Piedmont, in all the zones, rather than planning for it in just one or two areas. Second, to achieve the goal of distributing more housing everywhere, we believe the City should amend the zoning for Zones A and E (the Single Family and Estate zones) to allow duplexes, triplexes, and small multifamily buildings. These types of housing already exist in the middle of Piedmont’s single-family zones and fit in well: We should allow more of them to be built. Lastly, we think the City should move forward more expeditiously with building affordable housing on publicly owned land. To facilitate this, the City should expand the number of publicly owned sites under consideration and do feasibility studies of all to determine which are most viable. Building on public land is the City’s most realistic path to creating real affordable housing and we should make sure the Housing Element will enable thoughtful and sustainable change in our community. We are grateful that Piedmont, unlike many other cities in California, has taken a positive, proactive approach to the Housing Element, and we look forward to supporting the City in its efforts to build more housing, for everyone, everywhere. Irene Cheng is co-chair of Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign Housing Committee

The reputation of the religious leader is defended while the desperation of a woman caught in an untenable situation is ridiculed. There is no right to privacy for Hannah. There is no respect for her desperation. Instead, she is made the object of a sermon. One ought not think they can bargain with God. As the story unfolds, Hannah gives birth to Samuel and, after he is weaned, dedicates him to the service of the LORD. We are not told the LORD was moved by Hannah’s offer of her son or by her desperation. I like to think it was the latter. Regardless, as it was in the time of Hannah, we have a long way to go in appreciating, understanding and respecting the desperation woman can feel. articles.text: By: Daisy R. Seymour The Arbor Day celebration in Piedmont Park on Thursday, April 28, followed by a screening of the documentary, “Intelligent Trees”, proved to be very enjoyable, though with only a modest turnout. But wait, what is Arbor day anyway? According to Wikipedia Arbor Day is a secular day of observance in which individuals and groups are encouraged to plant trees. And that’s what we did. Upon arriving at the Community Hall, guests chatted and were served popcorn by Havens Cub Scouts. As a side note, the popcorn was delicious. People entered their raffle tickets to win two trees. Although I feel the cubs did more eating than distributing, everyone got their fair share. A crash course on trees being honored as this year’s Heritage Trees followed. The ceremony recognizes and celebrates Piedmont residents who nominated the trees with the presentation of a pin. The raffle tickets were then drawn by the Cubs and read by the den chief. The standard gift certificates were replaced by glow-in-the-dark custom tokens made with stumps from the tree lot. The winners wanted to donate the trees, saving them from digging up their back yard. Samantha Pell (left) Jonathan Pell, Aiden Patel, Blake Mellers, Ayyan Agarwal, and Roya Agarwal help pass out popcorn to guests on Arbor Day.

articles.text: Piedmont City Council received an informational update on Reach code implementation from city Sustainability Manager Alyssa Dykman and Climate Action fellow Annie Wensley at a meeting on Tuesday, May 2. Reach codes (Ordinance 750 N.S.) went into effect on June 1, 2021. The amendment was adopted by Piedmont’s City Council on February 1, 2021 and affects the sales and transfers of real estate and the construction of new and existing residential buildings. Reach codes require certain home renovation projects to include energy efficiency measures or photovoltaic systems. Additionally, Ordinance 751 N.S., or the home energy assessment policy, went into effect on March 3, 2021 and affects homeowners and real estate agents. When selling a property or transferring the title, the seller must provide potential buyers with a Home Energy Score or Home Energy Audit prepared in the past five years, in addition to the normal disclosure information. In preparation for the adoption of a 2022 Energy Code, city staff have conducted ongoing evaluations of the reach codes enacted in 2021, heralded by the city’s Sustainability Department. articles.text: Piedmont resident Eric Havian gave a presentation at the April 27 school board meeting on preventing gun violence. Havian, who has been involved with Brady United, the national gun control organization, for nearly 40 years, proposed to the board steps that can be taken to raise awareness of parents and students. The Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, commonly known as the Brady Bill, was passed by Congress in 1993 after James Brady, the White House Press Secretary was permanently disabled from a gunshot wound during the attempted assassination of President Ronald Reagan in 1991. The law requires federal background checks for all gun purchases and a five-day waiting period on purchases. Havian made proposals of actions the school district can take which focus on the safety of children by communicating with parents the importance of gun safety. “I’m guilty of this myself. Many times [we] think Piedmont is immune to a lot of the problems of violence, that are in the other communities in the Bay Area. But we are not,” said Havian. Havian’s advice would give the school district a leading opportunity to implement what may soon be a state requirement. Assembly Bill 452, passed 60-1 in the State Assembly and waiting for approval by the State SenStaff photo A slide show by Piedmont resident Eric Havian showed statistics revealing that the U.S. far and away has the largest number of gun violence incidents in the world. There are 71 times more firearm homicides per capita in the U.S. than in England and the UK.
articles.title: Presentation on gun violence delivered to School Board

articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. The test offered is a self-collected nasal PCR test, with results available within 48 hours from receipt of the sample at the lab. There is no cost and insurance is not required. PCR testing is accepted as required testing before air travel in the United States according to the Center for Disease Control. Appointments are not required by encouraged. More information is available at https://cur.tv/piedmont. For further information, contact Curative directly at 888-702-9042, or visit their website at curative.com. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmontpost.org, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.
articles.title: COVID testing at Community Hall available 5 days a week

articles.text: Barber Alex Putrenkov, his wife Maryna and their seven-year-old son, Vlad, recently set out on an unimaginable journey. On April 1, they gathered a few personal belongings, stuffed them into a couple of suitcases and left their war-torn home in the Donbass region of Ukraine to make a new life in America. “The military operations (in Ukraine) were drawing out all the resources.” Alex said. “As long as the country is at war, it cannot be prosperous and does not offer a good future. It is simply too dangerous to live there.” The family drove from Crimea to Moscow, then to Lithuania and on to Warsaw, Poland before flying to Paris, Madrid and Mexico City. They arrived in Tijuana on April 11 at the same time the Piedmont Community Church Mexico house-building mission was taking place. Church member Scott Willis was onsite in Tijuana helping Piedmont students and adult leaders tackle the task of building 12 homes for families in need. Willis is also the chair of the church’s Refugee Task Force, a group that has helped settle families from Afghanistan, Pakistan and Syria. Willis made contact with the family through a former Mexico mission participant, Jenny Miller-Feinberg, who works for Bayer, Inc. Alex’s brother, who also works for Bayer, had posted on the company’s intranet bulletin board the need for housing for his brother and family who were already on their way to the U.S. Piedmont Community Church members Bob and Judy Wright obtained plane tickets for the family to fly to Oakland, and Kirk and Christina Miller, Jenny’s parents, met them at the airport on April 13 and offered to host the family on an ongoing basis. “Of course, we calmed down when we got to Piedmont,” Alex said. “We are finally in a safe place where we can feel comfortable, but at the same time, we are worried about our parents and loved ones who stayed in our city. We have feelings of anxiety.” While they are now physically secure, Maryna finds the current situation emotionally difficult. “I have relatives still in Photo by Michael Barber Alex Putrenkov, his wife Maryna and their seven-year-old son, Vlad pose for a family photo taken in the courtyard of Piedmont Community Church after attending services on April 24. Ukraine who I miss,” Maryna said. “I understand that there is no future in my country, but my heart is there, and I ache for those places, and for the people left there.” Vlad, the couple’s son, has already begun attending Wildwood School and is adapting nicely. “I thought that it would be much more difficult for Vlad to be in this school since he does not understand English,” Maryna said. “Surprisingly, he feels good and goes to school in a good mood. He likes his new teacher, who he says is kinder than the teacher he had in Ukraine.” In addition to sharpening their English-speaking skills and learning the rules of the Bay Area roads, Alex and Maryna are seeking employment. They will require the services of an immigration attorney to file the necessary paperwork to obtain jobs. Alex was trained as a mechanical engineer and worked in agriculture, while Maryna worked in accounting. Piedmont Church is asking for donations through their website, PiedmontChurch.org, to help with legal fees and transitioning. “We are infinitely grateful to people and the church that helps us at the moment,” Alex said. Last week, Vlad told his parents that the children in his new class treat him well. “He brought home a postcard from a classmate who expressed his feelings,” Maryna said. “He wants to be friends with him.” To donate to the Piedmont Community Church Refugee Task Force, visit PiedmontChurch.org and click ‘Giving.’ hours.

articles.text: The Diversity Film series continues with a screening of Power to Heal tomorrow, Thursday, May 5. The screening is being co-hosted by the City of Piedmont, Adult Education Program, the Piedmont League of Women Voters, and the Piedmont Anti-racism Diversity Committee (PADC). A Zoom webinar will feature The Power to Heal: Medicare and the Civil Rights Revolution, a film by Charles Burnett. The documentary highlights the genesis of Medicare, when it was signed into law, as well as its relation to the Civil Rights Revolution. The hour-long documentary movie describes the history of segregated hospitals and a brief summary of civil rights activism to the internal workings of the federal government that led to integrated hospitals and African American access to health care. It narrates the early days of health inequity, powerfully demonstrating how race and poverty denied African Americans equal access to healthcare. Included are interviews that reveal personal experiences of African Americans’ struggles with illness and death without adequate healthcare. The film transitions from these individual stories to a broader review of disparities in hospital care throughout the United States. Physicians, civil rights leaders, and historians recount the dangerous tasks of documenting egregious incidents, tracking down patients, and the risks of blacks and whites workDr. Neil Powe will be the speaker following the screening. ing together to put desegregated structures in place. Following the screening, viewers will hear from Dr. Neil Powe, a leader in Public Health and the ongoing effort to correct healthcare disparities. Dr. Powe is a Harvard-trained physician, a professor of medicine at UCSF, and Chief of Medicine at San Francisco General Hospital. Viewers will hear from him about the history and current-day status of healthcare and will be able to ask him questions after the screening. To stream The Power to Heal, and for the conversation on zoom with Dr. Neil Powe from 6 p.m. to 7 p.m. on Thursday, May 5, click on diversityfilmseries.org. articles.text: Piedmont City Council approved at its May 2 meeting a contract for Arborworks, the low bidder, to do pruning of city trees in the amount of $145,370. Based on an annual assessment by the city’s certified arborist, Nick Millosovich, as well as input from residents, city staff recommended the pruning of 811 street trees and the removal of three trees. An Oak tree in Piedmont Park near Guilford Road will be removed, and two Liquidambar trees on Bellevue Avenue will be removed. Bids were due on April 20 and were received by Arborworks and three other companies. The tree pruning and removal will be completed within 50 days from the city’s Notice to Proceed. a detailed, actionable plan for transitioning Piedmont towards a fossil fuel-free future,” the report explained. “Additionally, as identified through stakeholder engagement prior to and following Reach Code adoption, the costs of electrification upgrades is a main concern from residents. articles.text: City Council members and City Administrator Sara Lillevand agreed that the city has engaged in many successful public-private partnerships in the past. “These projects have included the construction of the playschool building at Hampton Field, the renovation of Hampton Field, and the Corey Reich Tennis Center among others. Though the City has undertaken these partnerships through the years, best practices for doing so have changed and it would be wise to adopt an updated policy to guide the process of accepting of donations,” said Lillevand. The adopted policy sets procedures and criteria for the acceptance of donations and sets required record keeping standards. It authorizes the City Administrator to accept donations valued at up to $75,000. All public requests for donation or sponsorship must be submitted to the City Administrator; once a proposed donation is accepted, it becomes city property and can be used at the city’s discretion. The city cannot guarantee tax deductions for donations. All facility naming requests must be approved by City Council. Piedmont City Council adopted a policy entitled “acceptance of donations and naming of city owned facilities” at a meeting on Tuesday, May 2. The purpose of the policy is to encourage public-private partnerships that provide donations to support and enhance city services and facilities. At a meeting on April 4, City Council directed staff to develop a policy that would facilitate the acceptance of donations, namely for the Piedmont Community Pool to offset rising costs related to electrification of the facility. rounding trees and stay alive without any leaves to photosynthesize. We are one big community but individuals too. Like a tapestry, we need all the threads to shine, but each one is unique in its own way. To me, that’s what Arbor Day is – not just a day to plant trees, but a day to connect, to make the environment and our community a better place. Asked what she thought Arbor Day was, third grader Roya Agarwal summed it up perfectly, “I think it’s about seeing everyone and the community just having fun.” This community is many things: we support each other in everything, but most importantly is the word that best defines Arbor Day: Grow. No action was able to be taken by the board, but the presentation was well received. Board member Veronica Thigpen said, “The recommendations you outlined seemed very doable and very sensible. Giving people language and tips for how to address something that may be uncomfortable, like asking if there is a gun in the home, can be really useful.” The discussion turned to practical applications, for example Brady’s “Asking Saves Kids” program. In the situation of a kid staying at a friend’s house, the program “Ask Saves kids,” encourages parents to ask other parents if there is a gun in the house, and if so, where is it stored and is it stored safely? Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, the father of three school-age children, took the microphone to give an anecdote of a parent who asked him that question. Piedmont Police Department offers free gun cable locks to residents. Bowers also informed the board about gun restraining orders, which can remove guns temporarily (or permanently) from homes. “If you can’t keep your gun safely stored, come turn them into the police department. pages.text: Wednesday, May 4, 2022 5 City Council adopts policy for donations, naming of city facilities City Council members and City Administrator Sara Lillevand agreed that the city has engaged in many successful public-private partnerships in the past. “These projects have included the construction of the playschool building at Hampton Field, the renovation of Hampton Field, and the Corey Reich Tennis Center among others. Though the City has undertaken these partnerships through the years, best practices for doing so have changed and it would be wise to adopt an updated policy to guide the process of accepting of donations,” said Lillevand. The adopted policy sets procedures and criteria for the acceptance of donations and sets required record keeping standards. It authorizes the City Administrator to accept donations valued at up to $75,000. All public requests for donation or sponsorship must be submitted to the City Administrator; once a proposed donation is accepted, it becomes city property and can be used at the city’s discretion. The city cannot guarantee tax deductions for donations. All facility naming requests must be approved by City Council. By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont City Council adopted a policy entitled “acceptance of donations and naming of city owned facilities” at a meeting on Tuesday, May 2. The purpose of the policy is to encourage public-private partnerships that provide donations to support and enhance city services and facilities. At a meeting on April 4, City Council directed staff to develop a policy that would facilitate the acceptance of donations, namely for the Piedmont Community Pool to offset rising costs related to electrification of the facility. Arbor Day Continued from page 1 The screening of the film “Intelligent Trees” followed soon after, along with more popcorn. The film was about how trees communicate with each other, and support each other. I think that this shows how our community supports each other. Like trees, if one member of the community suffers, the entire community feels it. However, if one tree has more to share, the whole community benefits. Old trees that have been blown down receive support from surrounding trees and stay alive without any leaves to photosynthesize. Piedmont is like that. We are a tight, close-knit community, and we support each other, and feel each other’s failures and successes. We share, we laugh, we cry, we connect. We are one big community but individuals too. Like a tapestry, we need all the threads to shine, but each one is unique in its own way. To me, that’s what Arbor Day is – not just a day to plant trees, but a day to connect, to make the environment and our community a better place. Asked what she thought Arbor Day was, third grader Roya Agarwal summed it up perfectly, “I think it’s about seeing everyone and the community just having fun.” This community is many things: we support each other in everything, but most importantly is the word that best defines Arbor Day: Grow. It turned out not to be a realistic threat, but nevertheless, it shows that some kids in our district are just as troubled as the ones we read about in other school districts,” said Havian. The statistics and data Havian shared were powerful. Every year approximately 150,000 people are shot in the U.S. and guns are used in 60% of suicides. In 2017 there were almost 40,000 gun homicides in the U.S. A Wall Street Journal study of mass school shootings by teens revealed that 85% of the time the guns came from the shooter’s home. Havian made clear proposals to the board, by first asking the district to send a one-page email to all parents on gun safety and how to help if someone is in a crisis. A sample letter authored by the San Francisco School District was forwarded by Brady United to the Piedmont School Board. Further actions suggested by Havian included the addition of a paragraph on gun safety in existing school newsletters and inserting gun safety information in back-to-school family resource guides. No action was able to be taken by the board, but the presentation was well received. Board member Veronica Thigpen said, “The recommendations you outlined seemed very doable and very sensible. Giving people language and tips for how to address something that may be uncomfortable, like asking if there is a gun in the home, can be really useful.” The discussion turned to practical applications, for example Brady’s “Asking Saves Kids” program. In the situation of a kid staying at a friend’s house, the program “Ask Saves kids,” encourages parents to ask other parents if there is a gun in the house, and if so, where is it stored and is it stored safely? Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, the father of three school-age children, took the microphone to give an anecdote of a parent who asked him that question. Piedmont Police Department offers free gun cable locks to residents. Bowers also informed the board about gun restraining orders, which can remove guns temporarily (or permanently) from homes. “If you can’t keep your gun safely stored, come turn them into the police department. We will gladly take them and will destroy them. It’s really a life and death situation,” he added. For more information visit Bradyunited.org. City Council awards tree pruning contract to Arborworks for $145,000 By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont City Council approved at its May 2 meeting a contract for Arborworks, the low bidder, to do pruning of city trees in the amount of $145,370. Based on an annual assessment by the city’s certified arborist, Nick Millosovich, as well as input from residents, city staff recommended the pruning of 811 street trees and the removal of three trees. An Oak tree in Piedmont Park near Guilford Road will be removed, and two Liquidambar trees on Bellevue Avenue will be removed. Bids were due on April 20 and were received by Arborworks and three other companies. The tree pruning and removal will be completed within 50 days from the city’s Notice to Proceed. articles.text: The Piedmont Advanced Learners Program Support (ALPS) parent group held a forum last Thursday night, April 28, in the high school library to better define what “Academic Excellence” means to Piedmont residents. More than 40 parents were in attendance for the event led by ALPS President Michael Malione and Vice President Ella Grossberg. ALPS is a longstanding group of parents with the goal of pursuing high academic standards and providing resources to accelerate opportunities and joy in learning. In the two-hour meeting, parents broke into groups for English Language Arts (ELA), Math, and Science for a chance for everyone to speak and be heard. Participants identified gaps they’ve encountered between expectations and recent experiences with the strength of academics in the school district. Concerns included both the elementary and middle school foundations in reading and mathematics, as well as more specific programs and courses at the high school level. Parents espoused the virtues of a path for rigorous education that solidifies foundational skills and growing subject depth over time. This reporter joined the English and Language Arts group, at which Beach parent Esti Iturralde explained the benefits of building a knowledge base and excitement on topics through reading before focusing on analysis. Many attendees said they believe the school district should look beyond the California State educational standards, which address statewide declines in student proficiency not being seen in Piedmont. Attendees included two high school teachers, Science Chair Andy Willats and Math Department Head Kate Waldron, and a school district administrator. Some parents of high school students requested that the school district have a curriculum consistent with and in support of how the College Board defines its AP curricula. Parents also expressed the need for Piedmont High School to offer more AP courses like AP Physics. The argument for a return to more of a quantitative focus in the high school science curriculum was commonly voiced. A general sentiment expressed from the participants was that the academic strength of Piedmont’s education has been declining for a number of years. According to US News and World Education in 2022, Piedmont High ranked #237 nationally and #30 in California. In 2008, Piedmont was ranked #64 nationally. Rankings come from performance on state-required tests, graduation rates and preparation for college. For details go to: Usnews.com/education/besthigh-schools/california/districts/ piedmont-city-unified-school-district/piedmont-high-school-3029 Parents recognized that funding is a part of the equation but felt that the school district needs to focus more strongly on the strengths and needs of its students who are having a more difficult time getting into the universities of their first choice. The April 28 meeting was the first of several forums hosted by ALPS, which has been Piedmont’s leading advocate for curricular excellence and the provider of resources and events that foster academic attainment for more than a decade. For more information visit PiedmontALPS.org . Staff photo A large group of parents and faculty members attended the ALPS meeting on defining Academic Excellence, held in the PHS library on Thursday April 28.
articles.title: ALPS parent group wants excellence as core value of Piedmont education

articles.text: Much attention has been focused on the importance of early foreign language learning. Some research reports that younger children learn languages better than older children and adults. With so many demands already placed on children, parents ask if it is important that a child learn a second language at a young age. What program options are available? Benefits of knowing a second language In addition to developing a lifelong ability to communicate with people from other countries and backgrounds, other benefits include improved overall school performance and superior problem-solving skills. Students of foreign languages tend to score higher on standardized tests. Results from the SAT show that students who studied a foreign language for 4 or more years outscored other students on the verbal and math portions of the test. Knowledge of a second language also seems to coincide with high academic achievement. One study shows that students who were in “rigorous” programs in high school, which included 3 years of foreign language study, were likely to earn better grades in college. Learning another language can enhance knowledge of English structure and vocabulary. The benefits to society are many. Americans fluent in other languages improve global communication, enhance our economic competitiveness abroad, and maintain political and security interests. In recent years, the U.S. government has expressed a need for fluent speakers of languages other than English, particularly in less commonly taught languages such as Arabic and Chinese. Learning a language at any age is beneficial. Some studies have shown that the human brain is more open to linguistic development during the years between birth and pre-adolescence and that children who learn a language before the onset of adolescence are more likely to develop native-like pronunciation. When children have an early start to a long sequence of language instruction that continues through high school and college, they will be able to achieve levels of fluency that have not been possible in the past due to the late start of most language programs. At the same time, older children and adults can still be successful at learning a second language, although the level of attainment may be less predictable because of factors that can influence language learning. Any exposure to a second language and culture is beneficial, even if native-like proficiency is not the goal or the outcome. Options available in Piedmont The types of language programs available can be placed on a continuum. At one end of the continuum are immersion programs, which offer the greatest amount of time in language study and produce students with the highest levels of proficiency. At the other end are programs that explore language and do not have language proficiency as a goal. Piedmont Language School, through ¡Viva el Español!, provides Spanish language for children and adults in the East Bay. All classes use a full-immersion approach. Today’s children need to be prepared to live and work in a global context. It is a before- and after-school program teaching Spanish to young amigos in Piedmont’s elementary schools. The teachers are native Spanish speakers with extensive experience teaching kids. The curriculum includes singing, dancing, cooking, painting, reading stories, and playing games with kids – all in Spanish. Give your child the gift of foreign language at Piedmont Language School. For more information contact www.piedmontlanguageschool.com.
articles.title: Why and when should my child learn a second language?

Cultural Connection — Playtime in groups allows children to move beyond cultural boundaries to make discoveries, learn new things and reach a deeper understanding of others. articles.text: Readmont, a community-wide reading project in its 12th year, will culminate with an evening of guest speakers on May 19 and will be on Zoom. Hosted by Piedmont High School librarian Kathryn Levenson and English department chair Beth Black, the event will include a discussion of this year’s selection, A Thousand Splendid Suns, a novel by Afghani-American author Khaled Hosseini. A panel discussion will follow with a discussion of women’s rights and refugees by Fouzia Azizi, Director of Refugee Services for Jewish Family and Community Services of the East Bay, and Humaira Khan of Toronto, Canada, an expert on women’s rights in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The event will be held on Zoom on Thursday, May 19, from 7:00 to 8:00 p.m. A Thousand Splendid Suns chronicles the story of two women living in Kabul, Afghanistan. The book is appropriate for ages 14 and up. For younger readers, the English Department recommends the book I am Malala for ages 10 to 14, and Malala, My Story of Standing up for Girls’ Rights, appropriate for age 6 through 10. “We chose this book for its beautiful story of love in an unforgiving time and as a way for our community to discuss the recent events in Afghanistan and the increase of Afghan refugees to the Bay area,” said Black. Books may be checked out from the library at any Piedmont school. Books are funded through a grant from the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee, and are available for purchase with a 20% discount at A Good Place for Books bookstore in Montclair, 6120 La Salle Avenue. Questions may be addressed to Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us, or to Black at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us.

articles.text: Colgate University has announced that Emily Yu, Charlotte Prendergast, and Tuck Backer of Piedmont have been named to the Dean’s List and received the Dean’s Award with Distinction for the Fall semester. articles.text: Jabbar Weaver On April 23, researchers from the University of Delaware shared the results of a landmark study of Reading Recovery, a common literacy intervention for young children. Reading Recovery popularized an alternative to phonics—an approach called MSV, which teaches children to decipher words using a complex analysis of multiple cues (MSV stands for “meaning, syntax, and visual”). Kids learn to infer the word from “what makes sense,” “what sounds right,” and using clues from the story illustrations, in addition to considering the letters in the word. The study—funded by the US Department of Education, including more than 9,000 students, and led by authors who had studied Reading Recovery for more than a decade—found surprising results. Students who received Reading Recovery in 1st grade made shortterm progress, but they lost all their gains and actually did worse by 3rd and 4th grade compared to a control group. What went wrong? One explanation for the disappointing results is that MSV (also known as “three-cueing”) has been discredited by other research, including findings from the 2000 National Reading Panel and subsequent studies. MSV is commonly used in Piedmont schools and is thought to be especially problematic for students with learning differences and those from less advantaged backgrounds. Decades of evidence highlight the critical role of phonics and that MSV distracts kids away from learning phonics. This latest study sheds new light on a decades-old controversy that has recently been reignited. Literacy experts such as Professor Lucy Calkins—the author of Piedmont’s main literacy curriculum—have now revised their materials to discourage using MSV with students. “We have changed important things…. We emphasize to teachers that when a child is stuck on a tricky word, the best response is ‘look at the letters,’” wrote Dr. Calkins in an April 1 blog post to teachers. What does this mean for Piedmont? Piedmont schools, stressed by the demands of the pandemic, have made gradual shifts away from instruction grounded in MSV. PUSD leaders will present an update on literacy curriculum at the upcoming May 11 school board meeting. However, removing MSV from teaching is no easy task. MSV is embedded throughout Piedmont’s early reading instruction—from the classroom books, to our benchmark assessment, to our curriculum for struggling readers: Leveled Literacy Intervention, which is based on Reading Recovery. These long-term findings on a MSV-focused program may stir doubts for Piedmont parents whose kids appeared to benefit from Leveled Literacy Intervention in 1st grade only to see continued struggles in later grades. Many families have hired private tutors to get the strong foundational skills instruction their kids need to catch up. But, what happens to students whose families do not have the necessary knowledge or resources to get that help? It’s critical for teachers and families to have up-to-date information on evidence-based practices. A group of Piedmont parents and educators have formed a support group to share ideas on helping all kids become strong readers. Want to learn more? Drop us a line at piedmontreading@gmail.com Esti Iturralde, PhD is a licensed clinical psychologist and Piedmont parent. Jabbar Weaver is a 25-year teacher and principal, a member of the California and Oakland NAACP Education Committees, and Co-Founder of FULCRUM (Full and Complete Reading is a Universal Mandate)
articles.title: A major new study draws attention to literacy curriculum in Piedmont schools

articles.text: Students interested in neurodiversity may want to contact Eye to Eye for details on its summer fellowship program. Eye to Eye is a national organization focused on empowering students by elevating their voices, fostering empathetic teacher-to-student experiences, and creating inclusive communities, It currently is looking for people to participate in its Fellowship Program. The Fellowship Program is self-directed for students who have shown exceptional interest in learning disability and neurodiversity. It offers them an opportunity to explore a topic of their choosing and create a portfolio that demonstrates their findings. Fellows work closely with the senior team (including Piedmont resident David Flink, the CEO), build connections with neurodiverse adults, and hone their research and communication skills. Eye to Eye has a preference for topics related to Anti-ableism, educator experiences, stigma, youth organizing, and issues facing BIPOC disability communities. The Fellowship Program runs throughout the summer, and requires weekly meetings and independent research. It offers an opportunity to share your research with our community, including staff, other Fellows, and the broader Eye to Eye community. Ideal candidates are recent or anticipated high school graduates. Eye to Eye will formally announce the call for applications in early May on www. eyetoeyenational.org. To join the mailing list, e-mail marketing@ eyetoeyenational.org. For more information, visit https://eyetoeyenational.org. We emphasize to teachers that when a child is stuck on a tricky word, the best response is ‘look at the letters,’” wrote Dr. Calkins in an April 1 blog post to teachers. What does this mean for Piedmont? Piedmont schools, stressed by the demands of the pandemic, have made gradual shifts away from instruction grounded in MSV. PUSD leaders will present an update on literacy curriculum at the upcoming May 11 school board meeting. However, removing MSV from teaching is no easy task. MSV is embedded throughout Piedmont’s early reading instruction—from the classroom books, to our benchmark assessment, to our curriculum for struggling readers: Leveled Literacy Intervention, which is based on Reading Recovery. These long-term findings on a MSV-focused program may stir doubts for Piedmont parents whose kids appeared to benefit from Leveled Literacy Intervention in 1st grade only to see continued struggles in later grades. Many families have hired private tutors to get the strong foundational skills instruction their kids need to catch up. But, what happens to students whose families do not have the necessary knowledge or resources to get that help? It’s critical for teachers and families to have up-to-date information on evidence-based practices. A group of Piedmont parents and educators have formed a support group to share ideas on helping all kids become strong readers. Want to learn more? Drop us a line at piedmontreading@gmail.com Esti Iturralde, PhD is a licensed clinical psychologist and Piedmont parent. Jabbar Weaver is a 25-year teacher and principal, a member of the California and Oakland NAACP Education Committees, and Co-Founder of FULCRUM (Full and Complete Reading is a Universal Mandate) Eye to Eye Summer Fellowship offered to student mentors Students interested in neurodiversity may want to contact Eye to Eye for details on its summer fellowship program. Eye to Eye is a national organization focused on empowering students by elevating their voices, fostering empathetic teacher-to-student experiences, and creating inclusive communities, It currently is looking for people to participate in its Fellowship Program. The Fellowship Program is self-directed for students who have shown exceptional interest in learning disability and neurodiversity. It offers them an opportunity to explore a topic of their choosing and create a portfolio that demonstrates their findings. Fellows work closely with the senior team (including Piedmont resident David Flink, the CEO), build connections with neurodiverse adults, and hone their research and communication skills. Eye to Eye has a preference for topics related to Anti-ableism, educator experiences, stigma, youth organizing, and issues facing BIPOC disability communities. The Fellowship Program runs throughout the summer, and requires weekly meetings and independent research. It offers an opportunity to share your research with our community, including staff, other Fellows, and the broader Eye to Eye community. Ideal candidates are recent or anticipated high school graduates. Eye to Eye will formally announce the call for applications in early May on www. eyetoeyenational.org. articles.text: Piedmont High School science teacher John Savage invited the Post into his Period 5 Chemistry class on Friday, April 8 to observe a titration lab in action. The class of sophomores was tasked with finding the concentration of an unknown hydrochloric acid solution while discovering the functions of science instruments none of them had used prior. PHS purchased new lab equipment via grant money from the Makers Club and the Piedmont Parents Club. In the lab, a solution of acid and water sat in a beaker with a solution above it that slowly dropped a base into the acid. For the first time students used a digital pH probe which was connected to a laptop graphing the change in pH as the base dropped. “We haven’t used the pH recorder or the drop recorder, so this lab was interesting to learn how to use them,” said 10th grader Jonah Dupree. “The purpose of the lab was to measure what the concentration of the Hydrochloric acid is, so we are going to do that by finding data like the level of the pH of the solution in order to find the concentration.” The drop recorder had to be calibrated prior to use, and it digitally took record of how many drops of the basic solution were needed to turn the acid solution to a neutral 7 pH. The calibration process gave students a measurement equating the number of drops per mL. Students learned first-hand how to solve an equation with Thomas Worthington (left), Mateo DeVries, and Will Becker watch closely as Alex Aires measures a volume of base for their titration lab. Macy Puckett (left) and Isabella Wire check the pH graph on their computer while Ali Gallacher makes sure the drop counter is aligned properly. John Savage demostrates the lab for his class. two knowns, the volume of the acid and the concentration of the base, along with the discovered volume of the base to determine the concentration of the acid. Labs like this were missing from Piedmont during distance learning. “Being back in a laboratory for a science class has different challenges compared with doing it online through distance learning. In-person class is definitely challenging in some aspects, but there is a lot of knowledge to learn,” said sophomore Ray Gentemann. Savage divided students up into table groups, emphasized the importance of using goggles while using acids and let them loose to experiment. Savage, a PHS graduate of 2005 himself, frequently gathered the class around exemplary set ups to demonstrate the processes and instruments new to the whole class. “The instructions on the paper were kind of confusing but once [Mr. Savage] explained it, it really made sense,” said Siddharth Bhatia, whose group’s setup was shown to the class as an example by Savage on a number of occasions. Towards the end of the period Savage drew the class’ attention to another new tool, a volumentric flask that only measures to 1000 mL. “This container is good for one thing and one thing only, measuring exactly to 1000 mL. Why would that be? What use does this have?” he asked. The neck of this bulbous container is skinny, giving a measurement with a high level of accuracy and small room for differentiation as liquid fills up to the only line of measurement. Abstract concepts and foreign instruments are used in Savage’s class, a class that requires a challenging level of plasticity of the mind to question, contemplate and discover. In less than two hours the class acquired a new skill, titration, and received their first experience with several new instruments. Savage’s classes have long been favored by students and his commitment to achieving the honorable, the high school motto, were on display that afternoon. Spencer Barlow (left) and Jonah Dupree work as a pair setting up their experiment. John Savage shows his class what their graphs mapping pH levels should look like when the pH probe is connected to their laptops. Ali Gallacher measures the appropriate amount of base for her group using a pipette.

articles.text: Staff Photos Lenni Burchardt finished second in singles at the WACC Tennis Championships. Playing at Chabot College on Friday and Saturday, April 29-30, Piedmont’s tennis team came home with some impressive achievements. German foreign exchange student Lenni Burchardt, a junior, advanced to the singles finals and settled for 2nd place in the tournament. Ben Breber and Monte Imburg teamed up to placed third in the doubles ladder. Burchardt entered as the No. 4 seed and defeated No. 1 Elijah Cho from Berkeley in the semifinals in straight sets, 6-3, 6-3, using his powerful forehand and backhand for winning points. “It was a good game. Everything was working pretty well, My serve was landing and my form was better than usual. It feels good to hit winners because I’m not a very patient player,” said Burchardt with a laugh. Prior to Saturday’s semis and finals, Burchardt defeated Castro Valley’s Josh Kuwana in the first round, 6-0, 6-0, and Berkeley’s Michael Alaharazy in the second round, 6-2, 6-2. Burchardt lost to Berkeley’s Leighton Sproul in the finals, 6-1, 6-2. Sproul did well to return hard forehands by quickly lobbing shots back over the net. Breber and Imburg faced teammates Kai Baudendistel and Charlie Sullivan for an all-PHS 3rd place doubles match. The match had some friendly banter back-and-forth, with Breber/ Imburg winning in three sets, 4-6, 7-6, 6-3. “It was great to play friends in such a competitive match. We play each other all the time in practice, and it was different this time with so much at stake,” said Breber. “Yeah, it was really fun to play where we actually tried out hardest, as opposed to practice. I thought we played a great game, Monte and Ben played a great match,” added Sullivan. Breber and Imburg entered with the No. 3 seed and defeated Andrew Regan and Yanir Charney-Weibstraub of Berkeley in the first round, 6-1, 7-6, and No. 6 ranked Elias Cross and Felix Moon of Bishop O’Dowd, 6-2, 6-2, in the second round. Sullivan and Baudendistel, meanwhile, were the No. 5 ranked team and defeated Alex Byrd and Neo Chai of BOD in the first round 6-2, 6-1, and No. 4 Joaquin McCall and Celian De Labrouille of Berkeley in the second, 6-7, 6-3, 6-3. Breber and Imburg lost to No. 2 Mason Conlin and Julian Morris of Alameda in the semifinals, 6-4, 6-2, while Sullivan/Baudendistel fell to No. 1 Ethan Fang and Andrew Lottich of Castro Valley, 6-3, 6-0. Charlie Lambert was given the No. 3 seed in singles. He defeated Aidan Boscovich of Alameda in Ben Breber (left) and Monte Imburg earned third-place with a 4-6, 7-6, 6-3 win over Piedmont teammates Kai Baudendistel and Charlie Sullivan.

articles.text: The streak continues. The Piedmont boys’ lacrosse team got the job done at Witter Field on Friday, April 29, upsetting the favored Bishop O’Dowd Dragons 10-9 to win the Western Alameda County Conference championship. It was Piedmont’s sixth consecutive league title. “I care for a lot of O’Dowd’s seniors. I’m very happy for us, and I feel for them, but for our boys to come out and pull this off the way they did made me so proud. Quite honestly, that was the best I’ve seen our boys play,” said coach Al Yu, who formerly coach at O’Dowd. Piedmont entered as the No. 2 seed after losing to O’Dowd 13-7 earlier this season. With some defensive adjustments, the Highlanders prevailed. “Throughout the season, we’ve just been working on improving the kids’ strengths. Our emphasis now is to just not give up easy shots. As long as we do that, we’re going to do well,” added defensive coordinator Dave Haffner. The match required a huge game out of Piedmont’s freshman Photos by Ken DeCrosta Jack Nelson helped solidify Piedmont’s win with a critical defensive stop in the final seconds of action. goalie Gus Von Metzsch, and he delivered big time. He recorded 19 saves, including six in the second quarter, seven in the third, and five in the critical fourth quarter. In the biggest game of his high school career, Von Metzsch delivered like a pro. “There was a lot of motivation and pressure to play well. In the first match against them, we let them shoot more often and make cuts inside. This time, we knew what they were going to do, who their players were, and how to play against them,” said Von Metzsch. Friday’s drama came down to the final 8 seconds after O’Dowd scored a goal with 7.9 seconds left and won the faceoff. But junior midfielder Jack Nelson put a crunching check on the BOD attacker to force a turnover and ground ball recovery as time expired. “That was the last play of the game, He would have had a chance to score if he got past me. I had to give it my all,” said Nelson. It was also a big game for junior Soren Dixon, leads the team with four goals and three assists. He mentioned that the O’Dowd players were consistently badgering them on social media prior to the match. “In the first game, they were talking a lot of smack. They were confident this time they would Goalie Gus Von Meszch had a phenomenal performance against O’Dowd with 19 saves.

articles.text: Piedmont’s swim team posted six wins at the league championship meet at Chabot College on Friday, April 29, Piedmont swimmers had eight qualifying times for the North Coast Section championships, to be held this weekend, Friday and Saturday, May 6-7 at the Concord Community Pool. Girls Results Senior Kate Aubrecht won the 50 Freestyle in a field of 28 with a time of 24.39 seconds, earning an automatic North Coast Section bid. She also placed second in the 100 Free with a time of 54.23, also an automatic NCS bid. Sophomore Taylor Rolefson finished third of 29 in the 200 Free with a time of 2:01.74, and qualified for NCS. She also placed third of 20 in 100 Butterfly in 1:02.71. Sophomore Josie Oesterer won the 100 Backstroke with a time of 1:01.59 in a field of 20. Her time qualified for NCS. Maddie Payne finished second of 20 in 100 Back with a time of 1:07.26. Sonja ten Grotenhuis was third out of 25 swimmers in the 200 Individual Medley with a time of 2:21.98. She was also fifth in the 100 Free in 59.15. The girls’ relay team of Aubrecht, Rolefson, Oesterer and ten Grotenhuis won the 200 Medley with a time of 1:52.89 against seven other teams, and the same group won the 200 Freestyle relay in 1:42.39 in a field of eight. Both times qualified for NCS. Boys Results Junior Simon Lins won two individual events on Friday with automatic NCS times, including 20.49 seconds in the 50 Free and 50.91 in the 100 Back in in a field of 22. Lins, who two years ago was attempting to qualify for the 2020 Summer Olympics, is poised to reach the CIF State Championship on May 12-14 in Concord. Li ns, sophomore Tom Rolefson, junior Ryan Stokes, and junior Farris Saffouri were third of eight in the 200 Free Relay with a time of 1:31.22. articles.text: The Piedmont girls’ lacrosse team, entered as the No. 2 seed, took an early exit from the Western Alameda County Conference playoffs on Wednesday, April 27 in a barnburner, losing 13-12 to No. 3 Berkeley in double overtime. It marks the first time Piedmont has not reached the league finals since joining the WACC in 2017. It ended championship wub streak at four. “It was a great game. The girls didn’t give up and that was certainly a lesson-learned. I’m sure there were a lot of plays that the girls wanted back,” said coach Carlton Chan. The Highlanders were without their top defender Hailey Marshburn, who sustained an injury in the season-finale against Berkeley on Friday, April 22, which Piedmont won 15-11. Marshburn’s absence forced Eleanor Lavin from midfield to defense, and Holland Feinberg picking up Marshburn’s marking role. “Hailey was such a difference-maker in the last game against Berkeley. We just couldn’t get as many possessions. We usually put her on their top-player, and we switched it up to Holland, who did a really nice job. But it forced us to move Eleanor to defense, which takes away from our midfield rotation,” said Chan. Although Piedmont was without its best defensive starter, the team did well to force the game into two three-minute overtime periods. Berkeley got the game-winner with just seconds remaining by way of a shooting-space penalty, enabling Berkeley’s Maggie Fern to make a run toward the net before sending in a low shot for the Golden Goal. Fern had five goals on the night. Piedmont had to battle back from an 11-7 deficit in the second left, while Theut tied with 13 seconds left. The Yellowjackets came hot out the gates with four unanswered goals to lead 11-7 with 16 minutes left. From there, Berkeley was held scoreless for 13 minutes. Kinne got Piedmont’s attack going with 14:26 left, followed by Elizabeth Ethington three minutes later, 11-9. Katherine Kinne scored with 5:36 to go, 11-10. Berkeley made it 12-10 with 3:45 remaining, but Kinne struck again after recovering a shot attempt with 2:43 left. With 57 seconds left, Theut scored to tie the game. In the buildup prior to netting the 12-12 goal, Berkeley attempted to run out the clock with 1:15 left in the game, but Feinberg alerted the referees of the Jackets’ attack in an offside position. Realizing she was correct, the referees turned the ball over to PHS. Both teams were scoreless in the first overtime period, although each team had chances at net with penalties and shot attempts going wide. The game went down to the final 43 seconds in the second overtime period when Fern scored the golden goal for BHS. Final stats: Kinne had three goals, three assists, and five ground balls. Theut had three goals and two ground balls. Mahany also had a hat trick and a ground ball. Ashton scored twice and had one ground ball. Elizabeth Ethington one goal and four assists. Piedmont goalie Lindsay Kottle had four saves in the first half, and Sophia Ethington had four. It was very similar to the last game we played on them, they opened it up in the second half and were up 7-11, we closed the gap and we had to battle with 2 minutes left. At that point, it was all heart” said Chan. The Highlanders entered the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs on Tuesday as the No. 10 seed and traveled to Petaluma to face No. 7 Casa Grande. See next week’s Post for game results and details. Loss to Berkeley in Semifinals Piedmont opened with the first three goals, with Molly Ashton after two-and-a-half minutes, Charlotte Theut three minutes later, and Audrey Mahany with 18:37 to go. But PHS went on an 11 minute scoring drought which allowed Berkeley to take a 5-3 lead with 9:02 left in the half. Ashton got PHS back on the board with 7:33 left, followed by Mahany for two consecutive to bring the score to 6-6 with 5:40 to go before halftime. articles.text: The much-awaited next step for the Piedmont’s varsity football program finally occurred. After more than a month of searching, the high school has announced the hiring of Jordan Seiden, a former head coach at Skyline High in Oakland. He was hired on April 26 and will start planning for Spring Ball this week. Seiden grew up in Berkeley and played at St. Mary’s High School before playing collegiately for UC Davis as a receiver and running back from 1992- 1995. He was a classmate of Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame 2014 inductee Rich Watts while at Davis. He comes with pedigree of coaching, working under local legend and former San Jose State head coach Alonzo Carter as McClymond’s offensive coordinator in 2005-2006. He also worked under former 25-year Bishop O’Dowd head coach Paul Perenon in the early 2000s. “I’m born and raised in Berkeley and played for St. Mary’s. It’s funny, one of the only pictures I have left from those days are of a run I had against Piedmont. I played two years at Diablo Valley College and transferred to UC Davis. I returned to Berkeley where I got my first chance to coach, and then I had the opportunity to coach under Paul Perenon while he was at Bishop O’Dowd. It was a terrific opportunity,” said Seiden. “Alonzo and Paul were all about focus and hard work. All the things that attracted me to football were [being able to work] with coaches like that. They held themselves to high expectations,” he added. Seiden was most recently the head coach at Skyline High in 2018. Prior to Skyline, He took several years off of coaching to watch his son, Jordan Jr., play football for Moreau Catholic. Seiden was the offensive coordinator at Arroyo from 2011-2012, was Cupuchino’s head coach in 2010, offensive coordinator at Contra Costa College in 2009, and head coach at Castro Valley in 2007-2008. Earlier he was McClymonds’ offensive coordinator (2005- 2006), Berkeley’s defensive coordinator (2004), Chabot College’s defensive backs coach (2003), a Berkeley offensive assistant (2002), Bishop O’Dowd’s JV head coach (2000-2001), Berkeley’s DBs coach (1999), O’Dowd assisPiedmont High finalized its long search for a head football coach by hiring Jordan Seiden. tant (1998), Diablo Valley College’s linebackers coach (1997), and Berkeley’s DBs coach to start his coaching career in 1996. He currently works in the Oakland School District as a case manager, giving him a wealth of experience with students from a wide range of backgrounds. “It really helps with communication and understanding. I have a firm line with kids, but I know how to bring myself to their level. It helps bridge the gap. Kids are kids and they all need guidance and support in their own special way,” he said. Seiden walks into a situation where he’s tasked with building a new a culture of football in Piedmont, a school that has had football teams for more than 100 years. The team has had fewer kids signing up since Covid changed lives more than two years ago. “Building a culture comes with how you present yourself. There’s always positive energy with new coaches. If you can maintain that you can develop a culture. When I was growing up, Piedmont was a very good program and put out a lot of good players over the years. I played against Richie Watts (Piedmont’s quarterback in 1988-89( and got to know him at Davis. It starts with the foundation and how you build. If you have the right people to help build one step at a time, you have a really good opportunity.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 4, 2022 15 Piedmont falls to Berkeley 13-12 in double OT By Jonathan Comeaux The Piedmont girls’ lacrosse team, entered as the No. 2 seed, took an early exit from the Western Alameda County Conference playoffs on Wednesday, April 27 in a barnburner, losing 13-12 to No. 3 Berkeley in double overtime. It marks the first time Piedmont has not reached the league finals since joining the WACC in 2017. It ended championship wub streak at four. “It was a great game. The girls didn’t give up and that was certainly a lesson-learned. I’m sure there were a lot of plays that the girls wanted back,” said coach Carlton Chan. The Highlanders were without their top defender Hailey Marshburn, who sustained an injury in the season-finale against Berkeley on Friday, April 22, which Piedmont won 15-11. Marshburn’s absence forced Eleanor Lavin from midfield to defense, and Holland Feinberg picking up Marshburn’s marking role. “Hailey was such a difference-maker in the last game against Berkeley. We just couldn’t get as many possessions. We usually put her on their top-player, and we switched it up to Holland, who did a really nice job. But it forced us to move Eleanor to defense, which takes away from our midfield rotation,” said Chan. Although Piedmont was without its best defensive starter, the team did well to force the game into two three-minute overtime periods. Berkeley got the game-winner with just seconds remaining by way of a shooting-space penalty, enabling Berkeley’s Maggie Fern to make a run toward the net before sending in a low shot for the Golden Goal. Fern had five goals on the night. Piedmont had to battle back from an 11-7 deficit in the second left, while Theut tied with 13 seconds left. The Yellowjackets came hot out the gates with four unanswered goals to lead 11-7 with 16 minutes left. From there, Berkeley was held scoreless for 13 minutes. Kinne got Piedmont’s attack going with 14:26 left, followed by Elizabeth Ethington three minutes later, 11-9. Katherine Kinne scored with 5:36 to go, 11-10. Berkeley made it 12-10 with 3:45 remaining, but Kinne struck again after recovering a shot attempt with 2:43 left. With 57 seconds left, Theut scored to tie the game. In the buildup prior to netting the 12-12 goal, Berkeley attempted to run out the clock with 1:15 left in the game, but Feinberg alerted the referees of the Jackets’ attack in an offside position. Realizing she was correct, the referees turned the ball over to PHS. Both teams were scoreless in the first overtime period, although each team had chances at net with penalties and shot attempts going wide. The game went down to the final 43 seconds in the second overtime period when Fern scored the golden goal for BHS. Final stats: Kinne had three goals, three assists, and five ground balls. Theut had three goals and two ground balls. Mahany also had a hat trick and a ground ball. Ashton scored twice and had one ground ball. Elizabeth Ethington one goal and four assists. Piedmont goalie Lindsay Kottle had four saves in the first half, and Sophia Ethington had four. Tuesday vs. Casa Grande Piedmont traveled to No. 7 Casa Grande last night, May 3, and lost 19-8 to the favored team from Petaluma. See next week’s Post for match details. Photo by Ken DeCrosta Audrey Mahany scored three goals and a ground ball recovery. half. “They got up on us, and we had to call an early timeout. It was very similar to the last game we played on them, they opened it up in the second half and were up 7-11, we closed the gap and we had to battle with 2 minutes left. At that point, it was all heart” said Chan. The Highlanders entered the Division 2 North Coast Section playoffs on Tuesday as the No. 10 seed and traveled to Petaluma to face No. 7 Casa Grande. See next week’s Post for game results and details. Loss to Berkeley in Semifinals Piedmont opened with the first three goals, with Molly Ashton after two-and-a-half minutes, Charlotte Theut three minutes later, and Audrey Mahany with 18:37 to go. But PHS went on an 11 minute scoring drought which allowed Berkeley to take a 5-3 lead with 9:02 left in the half. Ashton got PHS back on the board with 7:33 left, followed by Mahany for two consecutive to bring the score to 6-6 with 5:40 to go before halftime. Berkeley went ahead 7-6 with five minutes Charlotte Theut (20) scored the tying goal to force the game into double overtime. After more than a month of searching, the high school has announced the hiring of Jordan Seiden, a former head coach at Skyline High in Oakland. He was hired on April 26 and will start planning for Spring Ball this week. Seiden grew up in Berkeley and played at St. Mary’s High School before playing collegiately for UC Davis as a receiver and running back from 1992- 1995. He was a classmate of Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame 2014 inductee Rich Watts while at Davis. He comes with pedigree of coaching, working under local legend and former San Jose State head coach Alonzo Carter as McClymond’s offensive coordinator in 2005-2006. He also worked under former 25-year Bishop O’Dowd head coach Paul Perenon in the early 2000s. “I’m born and raised in Berkeley and played for St. Mary’s. It’s funny, one of the only pictures I have left from those days are of a run I had against Piedmont. I played two years at Diablo Valley College and transferred to UC Davis. I returned to Berkeley where I got my first chance to coach, and then I had the opportunity to coach under Paul Perenon while he was at Bishop O’Dowd. It was a terrific opportunity,” said Seiden. “Alonzo and Paul were all about focus and hard work. All the things that attracted me to football were [being able to work] with coaches like that. They held themselves to high expectations,” he added. Seiden was most recently the head coach at Skyline High in 2018. Prior to Skyline, He took several years off of coaching to watch his son, Jordan Jr., play football for Moreau Catholic. Seiden was the offensive coordinator at Arroyo from 2011-2012, was Cupuchino’s head coach in 2010, offensive coordinator at Contra Costa College in 2009, and head coach at Castro Valley in 2007-2008. Earlier he was McClymonds’ offensive coordinator (2005- 2006), Berkeley’s defensive coordinator (2004), Chabot College’s defensive backs coach (2003), a Berkeley offensive assistant (2002), Bishop O’Dowd’s JV head coach (2000-2001), Berkeley’s DBs coach (1999), O’Dowd assisPiedmont High finalized its long search for a head football coach by hiring Jordan Seiden. tant (1998), Diablo Valley College’s linebackers coach (1997), and Berkeley’s DBs coach to start his coaching career in 1996. He currently works in the Oakland School District as a case manager, giving him a wealth of experience with students from a wide range of backgrounds. “It really helps with communication and understanding. I have a firm line with kids, but I know how to bring myself to their level. It helps bridge the gap. Kids are kids and they all need guidance and support in their own special way,” he said. Seiden walks into a situation where he’s tasked with building a new a culture of football in Piedmont, a school that has had football teams for more than 100 years. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco launched an exhibition entitled Still Lives in Contemporary Art on March 31. The exhibition will be on view through August 12. The group exhibition brings together an international group of artists who have unique takes on contemporary art and still life. The artists have created works within a framework of Black diasporic identities, histories, and collective experiences. Featured artists include Sadie Barnette, LaKela Brown, Elizabeth Colomba, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, David Antonio Cruz, Awol Erizku, Leslie Hewitt, Yashua Klos, Deana Lawson, Azikiwe Mohammed, Rashaad Newsome, Toyin Ojih Odutola, Brittney Leeanne Williams, Untitled (Birds of Paradise), 2018. Acrylic on canvas. 10 x 10 in. Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Devan Shimoyama, William Villalongo, and Brittney Leeanne Williams. The exhibit is on the third floor gallery. To make a reservation, visit https://www.moadsf. org/exhibitions/elegies-still-lifesin-contemporary-art.

The concert centers on Vilna Poems, David Garner’s song cycle on Yiddish poetry by The chord progression to I Got Rhythm by George Gershwin has become the most common four-chord progression in jazz, with the nickname “rhythm changes.” Half of the doo-wop songs from the thirties through fifties use them. Rhythm changes were used in countless jazz compositions, with a new melody. Such a composition is called a contrafact. Since chord progressions cannot by protected by copyright, contrafact songs are legal. View the list of jazz contrafacts on Wikipedia on your computer and you can click on the “original song” column header to sort by song and scroll down to find over 50 songs – all based on I Got Rhythm (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ jazz_contrafacts). The featured example in this column uses core melody on rhythm changes. Core melody was demonstrated in the “Parker’s Core Melody” column printed on October 21 in the Post. See the chapter “Core Melody with Baroque-Bebop Ornamentation” at the link below. Read the section I-VI-II-V Two-BeatPer-Chord Song Studies. https:// drive.google.com /f ile/d/1XWRcPjOOtssqO7NDdlAjuUXjUA1AY7Sk/view?usp=sharing Lisa Delan, soprano René Mandel, violin Avrom Sutskever, written for Lisa Delan. George Gershwin, composer of “I Got Rhythm.” Core melody begins with one or two duality tones per bar, common to the scale and the current chord. Fma7 contains F-A-C-E. In making a melody during an Fma7 accompaniment chord in the key of “C” with the C major scale, (C-D-E-F-G-A-B), bringing emphasis to the “E” note in the melody makes “E” a duality tone. Next, a harmonic framework is built with a melodic curve by adding passing and neighboring scale tones. Final options include ornamentation, chromatics (notes between the scale tones) and other chords melodically superimposed over existing chords. See the Guitar Improv chapter “Core Melody Built with Duality Tones” at this link: https://drive. google.com/file/d/1mcWi3YQ8ofAj-E1ckTN5bAluq5kvWEBF/ view?usp=sharing Starting at bar 35 in Rhythm Changes, there are labels above the music notation, such “1-#1- 2-#2. These refer to core melody tones in relation to the Bb major key scale tones that are the basis of the melody. “1” is “Bb”, “#1” is “B” and “2” is C, etc. In the Rhythm Changes study, all of the core melody sequences are chromatic, each sequence forming four consecutive frets on the guitar. The continuous numbers in varied orders of 1-2-3-4 are fretting hand finger numbers, where the index finger is “1”. Starting at bar 103 in Rhythm Changes, core melody sequences above the music notation, such “1-b3-4-b3-1 are pentatonic melody sequences, a popular choice in bebop and jazz blues. articles.text: Lafayette-based Gold Coast Chamber Players will present a concert in its Cultural Crossroads series on Saturday, May 14, at 7:30 p.m. The performance will be held in the Don Tatzin Community Hall at the Lafayette Library, 3491 Mt. Diablo Boulevard in Lafayette. Cultural Crossroads explores the Black and Indigenous influences on late 19th Century Czech composer Antonin Dvorak. The program will feature the Alexander String Quartet, Native American flutist R. Carlos Nakai, soprano Michele Kennedy, and Gold Coast Chamber Players founder violist Pamela Freund-Striplen. T he prog ram i ncludes Dvořák’s String Quintet, op. 97 and the Lento from his String Quartet, op. 96. Also on the program are two original works by R. Carlos Nakai, commissioned by Gold Coast Chamber Players, as well as his arrangement of Amazing Grace. Guests will hear two songs by African American composer Florence Price, as well as some African American Spirituals that influenced Dvořák. The program’s finale is an arrangement for the entire ensemble of Goin’ Home, taken from Dvořák’s New World Symphony written in 1893 when Dovrak was Director of the National Conservatory of Music of America. articles.text: A scene from The Farewell, written and directed by Lulu Wang. The Farewell is in so many ways remarkable, a nuanced and yet explicit film about what it means to leave your country of origin and come to America and be confronted by a spectrum of language, norms, attitudes and behavior that can seem overwhelming and all but insurmountable. At the outset, the process of acculturation can be an exhausting and demanding journey. Once made, it is never completely over. The Farewell focuses on one closely held norm that seems uniquely Chinese and comes into conflict with the values of a thoroughly Americanized young woman. Written and directed by Lulu Wang, she captures with insight and humor as well high stakes seriousness just how complex and multilayered culture can be. And how painful it is to live rooted in two places at the same time. For the central character Billi (Awkwafina), a twenty-something New Yorker, those two places are America and China. She came to the U.S. at the age of six with her mom, Jian (Diana Lin), and her father Haiyan (Tzi Ma). In the opening scenes Billi is told by her parents that her much loved grandmother, Nai Nai (Shuzhen Zhov), diagnosed with stagefour lung cancer, has only a few months to live. Billi learns that her family has made two decisions immediately: first, by agreement of family members in New York and China, they will not to tell Nai Nai the truth regarding her illness. Secondly, the family will leave for city of Changchun in China within the week, using the imminent wedding of a nephew as an excuse to gather, but in effect to say goodbye to Nai Nai. Billi, however, is told that she must remain behind. The reason being that the family does not trust her to keep the secret from her grandmother; she’s too emotional, her connection to Nai Nai such that she will break down when the two meet. Billi, of course, has also made clear that she feels her grandmother should be told the truth. And this is only act one. Unbeknownst to her parents, Billi takes a later flight and arrives at her grandmother’s home just as the now extended family is getting ready to sit down to the first of many meals. They all watch Billi closely, anticipating that she will reveal to Nai Nai the truth. What follows in act two is the developing tension between the family (the doctors and the hospital are also complicit) and Billi. In effect, it’s a clash of two cultures, told as the family struggles to maintain a patina of celebration during the wedding ceremony. The Farewell defines in so many subtle ways what it means to be an immigrant – the resilience and courage required to adapt and prevail, as well as the pain of separation from what is often referred to as the home country and those left behind. All of these issues are threaded through this nicely done film. The Farewell. Written and directed by Lulu Wang. Starring Awkwafina, Tzi Ma and Diana Lin. With some English subtitles. 1 hr., 38 min. Rated PG. Released in 2019. Now streaming on Prime and Apple tv. Published in the Post in 2019
