articles.text: All public events at Piedmont Center for the Arts require photo ID and valid proof of full vaccination including booster shot for entry, as well as proper masking while inside. Friday, May 6, 6-8 p.m. Opening reception Michael Friedes art exhibit Former Piedmont resident Michael Friedes, an artist and interior designer, will have an art exhibit, “A Time of Place”, celebrating Friedes’ 20th anniversary living in California. This new collection is a reflection of living in the East Bay, San Francisco, and Sonoma. The collection features an array of abstract landscape paintings. An opening reception will be held this Friday from 6-8 p.m., with gallery hours on Saturday and Sunday, May 7-8, Saturday and Sunday, May 14-15, and Saturday and Sunday, May 28-29 from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. The exhibit is part of the 3rd annual Piedmont Art Walk this Saturday, May 7, and will be open to the public that day from 12:00 to 5:00 p.m. Saturday, May 14, 7:30 p.m. Chamber Music Society of SF Join the Chamber Music Society of San Francisco for their season finale, featuring guest artist Kay Stern, concertmaster for the SF Opera Orchestra in a boisterous program of works by Ludwig van Beethoven, Jessie Montgomery, and Felix Mendelssohn. Tickets are available at: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/season-finale-with-kaystern-tickets-215185143557 Sunday, May 15, 4 p.m. Berkeley Symphony & Friends The Berkeley Symphony Chamber Music series, in its ninth year in Piedmont, continues with a concert featuring soprano Lisa Delan and Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director and audience favorite René Mandel on violin. The concert includes Mendelssohn’s iconic D minor piano trio and Reena Esmail’s transcendent Saans for violin, cello, and piano. The concert centers on Vilna Poems, David Garner’s song cycle on Yiddish poetry by Avrom Sutskever, written for Lisa Delan. Other musicians performing include Evan Kahn, cello, Roman Fukshansky, clarinet, and Kevin Korth, piano. Tickets are $35 and are available online at https://tickets.berkeleysymphony.org/TheatreManager/1/online?performance=5260. They are also available by calling the Box Office at 841-2800, ext. 1, or at the door. Sunday, May 22, 5 p.m. Festival Opera Recital Performed and curated by mezzo-soprano Lily Bogas and countertenor Matheus Coura, a recital titled They Sing will explore feelings from sublime to irreverent to comedic. The program will feature arias, songs, and duets by Monteverdi, Handel, Mozart, Bizet, Strauss, Kurt Weill, and Ricky Ian Gordon. Purchase tickets at https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/they-sing-lily-bogas-matheus-coura-zachary-gordin-in-recital-tickets-267822292687. Friday, May 27, 7 p.m. Michael Stehr Art Lecture “A Stroll in Rome: The Ponte Umberto to Saint Peter’s” will describe and review a recent trip hosted and led by local artist Michael Stehr. More details to follow soon. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events.

articles.text: A scene from Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home. The first Free Willy movie made such a splash, so to speak, that it was inevitable there would be a sequel. After all, what’s not to like? An orphaned, malcontent street kid named Jesse, age 12 (played by Jason James Richter), on the verge of becoming a teenager, is rescued by a 7,000-pound orca, and the tween manages to do the same for Willy. Literally. The enduring strength of the franchise is that Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home also has at its center a family theme. The most immediate difference is that Jesse is now a newbie 14-year-old teen, and has settled nicely in with his foster parents, Glen and Annie Greenwoods (Michael Madsen and Jane Atkinson). Sadly, Jesse discovers that his long ago missing mother has passed away; however, to his surprise he discovers that he has a younger half-brother called Elvis (Frank Capra), who comes to visit and is generously taken in by the Greenwoods. He’s a fast-talking wiseacre who would rather tell a fib, even if the truth would serve just as well. To make things even more interesting, and given that there are teen hormones all in a swirl, Jesse is introduced to Nadine (Kate Schellhardt), his age, who is the granddaughter of the theme park’s handyman, Randolph (August Schellenberg), a Native American. They have immediate chemistry, hence there will be, of course, an innocent kiss in their future. And so the adventure begins. The Greenwoods suggest that the family take a brief holiday to the ocean. Jesse is sitting in a cove, playing his harmonica, looking out at the Pacific, when, to his amazement, Willy appears. Only this time, the now massive orca is in the company of his pod family. It’s a joyous reunion for both, and Jesse rides Willy in the surf and Nadine joins them as well. To add to the developing narrative, the kids discover that there is a grounded tanker not far off shore, which is leaking oil into the ocean, a spill that threatens all the sea life in the area, most especially Willy and his pod. If the oil gets into the orcas blowholes it could prove fatal. The question now posed is: what can the kids do to prevent what will be an ecological disaster? Adding to the tension is the plan by the owners of the tanker and the greedy owners of the theme park to capture Willy and return him to the theme park in order to perform once again. There are countless narrow escapes. A marine biologist, Kate Haley (Elizabeth Pena), shows up and explains that if the whales are not able to escape the oil spill (they are now trapped in the cove) it will prove deadly to the pod. Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home will once again engage a younger audience as they root for Jesse, Nadine and Elvis Elvis, and in their common cause to save the whales. As sequels go, it’s a winner. Free Wily 2: The Adventure Home. Directed by Dwight H. Litle. Starring Jason James Richter, Mary Kate Schellenhardt, Michael Madsen, and Jane Atkinson. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released in 1995. articles.text: Recently I spotted an article in the New York Times by columnist Ross Douthat regarding the demise (he uses the word “end”) of movies as we, for generations, have come to known them. My answer would be yes, and no. However I would add to his analysis the impact the global pandemic has had on what was once a cultural phenomenon – walking into a darkened room and watching with strangers a larger than life story told on an expansive screen, one still framed, on occasion, by heavy felt curtains. My response to the word “end” is that Hollywood will, of course, continue to make movies predicated on the conviction that we love to be told a story. We can easily imagine our antecedents sitting around campfires, listening to dramatic tales told and retold, recounting the countless variations of the then human experience, each filled with embellished magic. I would suggest that this is not the end of the narrative feature; rather, it is the beginning of what I think of as our post-pandemic movie-viewing period. What has changed is the way that feature films are today created and delivered. Well before the pandemic, movies were being watched on screens of all sizes, from large, wall-mounted televisions, to computers, to hand held smart phones, The stories were enhanced when needed by CGI (computer-generated imagery). But what brought this technology truly mainstream was the government Covid019 quarantine mandate. Seemingly overnight, theaters became hothouses of the virus. The very air in enclosed spaces was and continues to be a possible threat as were the people in the seats before and behind. The alternative to going to the theater quickly became obvious: view movies in the safety of your home. And so the word “streaming” became part of the lexicon, a panoply of choices delivered by a host of subscription-driven companies, examples being Netflix, Prime, Hulu, VUDU/, HBO, and Showtime. In trying to avoid slipping into hyperbole, this change has been revolutionary and culture changing, equated with the now ubiquitous cellphone (which I generously compare to Gutenberg’s invention of type-setting print). My prediction is that even when Covid and variants are regarded with just another form of the flu (with annual vaccinations offered), we will not return to the theater, and even the term blockbuster will take on a much-diminished definition. As Douthat points out in his piece, even this year’s 10 films nominated for Academy Awards, which shared a bevy of top-tier actors, major directors, as well as classic genres such as epics or meet-cute romances, well, almost nobody went to see them (nine out of the ten made less than $40 million in box office revenue). As a result more and more recent releases are now opening simultaneously in theaters and streaming for home viewing. The question begged is: Even when this awful virus is behind us, will the movie-going audience ever return in the pre-pandemic numbers experienced in 2019 and before? Douthat, for one, suggests that 1990 was the peak. And will the annual Oscars ceremony ever again be compelling, or find am audience or generate the anticipation it once found in those halcyon days of the 20th century when movie stars were iconic celebrities, larger than life? Have they too been diminished down to what Douthat opines as ordinary size and now regarded as simply part of the viewed content? We’ll soon find out.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 4, 2022 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home is a winner A scene from Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home. By Chris Honore’ The first Free Willy movie made such a splash, so to speak, that it was inevitable there would be a sequel. After all, what’s not to like? An orphaned, malcontent street kid named Jesse, age 12 (played by Jason James Richter), on the verge of becoming a teenager, is rescued by a 7,000-pound orca, and the tween manages to do the same for Willy. Literally. The enduring strength of the franchise is that Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home also has at its center a family theme. The most immediate difference is that Jesse is now a newbie 14-year-old teen, and has settled nicely in with his foster parents, Glen and Annie Greenwoods (Michael Madsen and Jane Atkinson). Sadly, Jesse discovers that his long ago missing mother has passed away; however, to his surprise he discovers that he has a younger half-brother called Elvis (Frank Capra), who comes to visit and is generously taken in by the Greenwoods. He’s a fast-talking wiseacre who would rather tell a fib, even if the truth would serve just as well. To make things even more interesting, and given that there are teen hormones all in a swirl, Jesse is introduced to Nadine (Kate Schellhardt), his age, who is the granddaughter of the theme park’s handyman, Randolph (August Schellenberg), a Native American. They have immediate chemistry, hence there will be, of course, an innocent kiss in their future. And so the adventure begins. The Greenwoods suggest that the family take a brief holiday to the ocean. Jesse is sitting in a cove, playing his harmonica, looking out at the Pacific, when, to his amazement, Willy appears. Only this time, the now massive orca is in the company of his pod family. It’s a joyous reunion for both, and Jesse rides Willy in the surf and Nadine joins them as well. To add to the developing narrative, the kids discover that there is a grounded tanker not far off shore, which is leaking oil into the ocean, a spill that threatens all the sea life in the area, most especially Willy and his pod. If the oil gets into the orcas blowholes it could prove fatal. The question now posed is: what can the kids do to prevent what will be an ecological disaster? Adding to the tension is the plan by the owners of the tanker and the greedy owners of the theme park to capture Willy and return him to the theme park in order to perform once again. There are countless narrow escapes. A marine biologist, Kate Haley (Elizabeth Pena), shows up and explains that if the whales are not able to escape the oil spill (they are now trapped in the cove) it will prove deadly to the pod. Free Willy 2: The Adventure Home will once again engage a younger audience as they root for Jesse, Nadine and Elvis Elvis, and in their common cause to save the whales. As sequels go, it’s a winner. By Chris Honoré Recently I spotted an article in the New York Times by columnist Ross Douthat regarding the demise (he uses the word “end”) of movies as we, for generations, have come to known them. My answer would be yes, and no. However I would add to his analysis the impact the global pandemic has had on what was once a cultural phenomenon – walking into a darkened room and watching with strangers a larger than life story told on an expansive screen, one still framed, on occasion, by heavy felt curtains. My response to the word “end” is that Hollywood will, of course, continue to make movies predicated on the conviction that we love to be told a story. We can easily imagine our antecedents sitting around campfires, listening to dramatic tales told and retold, recounting the countless variations of the then human experience, each filled with embellished magic. What has changed is the way that feature films are today created and delivered. Well before the pandemic, movies were being watched on screens of all sizes, from large, wall-mounted televisions, to computers, to hand held smart phones, The stories were enhanced when needed by CGI (computer-generated imagery). But what brought this technology truly mainstream was the government Covid019 quarantine mandate. Seemingly overnight, theaters became hothouses of the virus. articles.text: Spring green is the theme for this quick salad that announces much-awaited spring vegetables. After so many months of kale, collards and broccoli, sugar snap peas at farmers markets signal a big shift in what we’ll have on our plates for the coming weeks. Sugar snap peas are a variety where the tender pod is eaten along with the pea inside. They are adorably plump and tender, a rightful star of this quick salad. (An Asian-style snow pea is similar but has a flat pod.) Just remember to remove the string that runs along the length of the pod. I make a version of this salad when sugar snap peas are prolific (read: a bit more affordable) at my favorite farmers’ stands. It’s an easy adjustment to use asparagus, sliced cucumbers, and/or radishes, if you enjoy those options, but sometimes a few exquisite ingredients are all that are needed for a perfectly satisfying salad. I leave everything raw as I love the taste of fresh, raw sweet peas. And the crunch. But feel free to do a quick blanch in boiling water, then a plunge into an ice water bath, if that’s how you prefer. Admittedly this does result in a showier, bright green snap pea. Hopefully this will be a springboard into multiple variations to enjoy in the coming months. Sugar Snap Pea and Spinach Salad with Lemony Mint Dressing.

articles.text: The Walking on Wednesdays groups has announced that Will Adams will conduct a special walking tour of historical, Albert Farr-designed, Piedmont structures on May 18. Adams is a planner, urban designer, and architect who has lived in Piedmont for thirty years, and writes a biweekly column, “Walking Piedmont”, in the Piedmont Post. The tour will start at 10:30 a.m. at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) and will be approximately 90 minutes in duration. Albert L. Farr was an American architect who designed buildings and homes in the Mediterranean, Craftsman, and Georgian styles. During the first decades of the city of Piedmont’s development, Farr was engaged to design many of Piedmont’s most prominent buildings, including City Hall, a long-gone Commercial Center, Piedmont Community Church, and the Exedra Plaza. Adam’s tour will include these structures and approximately four Piedmont houses. This special tour is a return of Adams to Walking on Wednesdays. In August 2021 he conducted a similar tour of Julia Morgan-designed homes in Piedmont, an event that attracted 60 walkers. “Albert Farr was a Bay Area master in the early 20th century, but he, like all masters, also made a few errors. We will be discussing these as well,” said Adams. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Residents queue up for Will Adams’ tour of Julia Morgan homes in August 2021.
articles.title: Will Adams to lead tour of Albert Farr buildings in Piedmont

pages.text: Wednesday, May 4, 2022 23 INGREDIENTS Snappy Pea and Spinach Salad ideal for early summer By Deborah Quok Spring green is the theme for this quick salad that announces much-awaited spring vegetables. After so many months of kale, collards and broccoli, sugar snap peas at farmers markets signal a big shift in what we’ll have on our plates for the coming weeks. Sugar snap peas are a variety where the tender pod is eaten along with the pea inside. They are adorably plump and tender, a rightful star of this quick salad. (An Asian-style snow pea is similar but has a flat pod.) Just remember to remove the string that runs along the length of the pod. I make a version of this salad when sugar snap peas are prolific (read: a bit more affordable) at my favorite farmers’ stands. It’s an easy adjustment to use asparagus, sliced cucumbers, and/or radishes, if you enjoy those options, but sometimes a few exquisite ingredients are all that are needed for a perfectly satisfying salad. I leave everything raw as I love the taste of fresh, raw sweet peas. And the crunch. But feel free to do a quick blanch in boiling water, then a plunge into an ice water bath, if that’s how you prefer. Admittedly this does result in a showier, bright green snap pea. Hopefully this will be a springboard into multiple variations to enjoy in the coming months. For the dressing: • 2 tablespoons lemon juice, freshly squeezed • 3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil • 2 tablespoons fresh mint, minced • 1/2 teaspoon Dijon mustard • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • 1/4 – 1/2 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, to taste For the salad: • 10 ounces sugar snap peas, sliced thinly on a steep diagonal • 6 ounces baby spinach, the size of a typical bag of triple-washed greens • 1/4 cup chives, cut in 1/2-inch lengths INSTRUCITONS Sugar Snap Pea and Spinach Salad with Lemony Mint Dressing. For the dressing: Combine the mustard, lemon juice, sea salt and pepper in a small bowl and mix well. Slowly drizzle in the olive oil, whisking to help emulsify the dressing. Add the minced mint. Set aside while you prepare the salad. For the salad: 1. Rinse the sugar snap peas and remove the tough string that runs down the length of the pod where the peas are attached inside. Slice on a steep diagonal, maybe 4 – 5 slices depending on the size of the pod. 2. Slice the chives in 1/ 2-inch lengths 3. Add the sliced sugar snap peas to a 3-quart bowl. Add the dressing and gently toss. Add the chives and spinach and toss again to distribute the dressing throughout. This is a very lightly dressed salad, which we prefer, so the delicate flavor of the sugar snap peas shines through. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com. articles.text: An excellent turnout of 36 walkers and one K-9 best friend was on hand for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays outing April 27, a beautiful morning in Piedmont. It was announced that former Piedmont Mayor Bob McBain will host the walkers on a tour of Tyson Lake, in two weeks, on Sunday, May 15. Last week, April 27 the walkers enjoyed the second of two walking tours of Piedmont front gardens that were part of the 18th Annual “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Features Showcase.” Hope Salzer, a Board member of Piedmont Connect, led the walkers to the first garden the previous week, Hope’s own garden on Cambrian Avenue. This week took the group to the second garden belong to Nancy McKee-Jolda and Rob Jolda on Harvard Road. To qualify for the Natives Garden Tour, gardens were requited to have at least 70% California native plants. The walkers went down Highland to Wildwood Avenue, and then Prospect Road which ends at Harvard Road. Nancy told the group that she had been inspired some years earlier during a trip to France. The “Monet gardens” made her want to create her own lovely garden. Hiking in the East Bay Regional Parks also provided a fascination about what our area looked like 150 years ago, and it motivate Nancy to “jump into nature and native gardens.” She found that she loved gardening and the lifecycle process of plants going from seed to flower and back to seed again. All the seasons provide a rich garden experience for her. Nancy shared a list of 24 succulents, shrubs & large bushes, and flowering plants in her garden, and identified many of them for the group. They included Douglas irises, different buckwheat varieties, mugworts, purple Self-Heals, huckleberry, wild roses, and a mock orange with its first buds. She noted that many of these native plants were used by indigenous people as medicines and for teas. Explaining her native plants garden, Nancy said, “My intent was to show how ‘natural’ such a garden is, how simple and attractive and important.” Nancy’s husband, Rob, said how much he appreciates the work she has done with the garden. It was announced that former Piedmont Mayor Bob McBain will host the walkers on a tour of Tyson Lake, in two weeks, on Sunday, May 15. Last week, April 27 the walkers enjoyed the second of two walking tours of Piedmont front gardens that were part of the 18th Annual “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Features Showcase.” Hope Salzer, a Board member of Piedmont Connect, led the walkers to the first garden the previous week, Hope’s own garden on Cambrian Avenue. This week took the group to the second garden belong to Nancy McKee-Jolda and Rob Jolda on Harvard Road. To qualify for the Natives Garden Tour, gardens were requited to have at least 70% California native plants. The walkers went down Highland to Wildwood Avenue, and then Prospect Road which ends at Harvard Road. Nancy told the group that she had been inspired some years earlier during a trip to France. The “Monet gardens” made her want to create her own lovely garden. Hiking in the East Bay Regional Parks also provided a fascination about what our area looked like 150 years ago, and it motivate Nancy to “jump into nature and native gardens.” She found that she loved gardening and the lifecycle process of plants going from seed to flower and back to seed again. All the seasons provide a rich garden experience for her. Nancy shared a list of 24 succulents, shrubs & large bushes, and flowering plants in her garden, and identified many of them for the group. They included Douglas irises, different buckwheat varieties, mugworts, purple Self-Heals, huckleberry, wild roses, and a mock orange with its first buds. articles.text: The 40+ Women’s 3.5 Daytime Team from Corey Reich Tennis Center in Piedmont won the USTA Northern California Sectional Championships at Broadstone Sports Club in Folsom on the weekend of April 22-24. The team, comprised mostly of Piedmont moms and captained by Midori Antebi and Cathy Papahadjopoulos, had a very successful regular season with 9 wins and 1 loss against teams from Walnut Creek, Oakland, Moraga, and Clayton, and then two playoff wins against teams from Walnut Creek. When not scheduled for hospital treatments, Elizabeth volunteers to provide hospice care for an elderly neighbor on the weekends. Elizabeth was the victim of multiple break-ins because of the disintegrating fencing that surrounds her backyard, and her garden has been raided several times. The scope of this year’s project for PCSC included rebuilding large sections of the fence and two gates, rebuilding a rear entry porch and stairs, repainting portions of the house, helping organize her belongings in her tiny house, and making various improvements to increase her safety. This year’s project had a late start but the project team was able to select a project, plan and complete it in record time, roughly half the time, covering nine work days and many planning sessions. Piedmont now enters the Division 1 North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 13 seed, and hosted No. 4 Vista del Lago of Folsom yesterday, May 3. As WACC league champion, Piedmont was allowed to host the came. The Eagles placed second in the Sacramento Valley League. See next week’s Post for match details. Beating O’Dowd for the title The Highlanders ended the first quarter with a 2-1 lead and went into halftime leading 6-4. O’Dowd tied the game at 7-7 in the third quarter, but PHS scored three straight goals in the fourth to jump ahead 10-7. BOD scored two goals in the final five minutes, including one with 8 seconds remaining to make it 10-9. Piedmont opened the game with a 2-0 lead after Dixon scored two minutes into the game, and sent in another goal with seven minutes to play. O’Dowd made it 2-1 with a goal with 34.6 seconds left in the quarter. BOD tied it 2-2 in the second with a goal in the first 50 seconds, but Nate Fredericks found Dixon for his third goal with 10:44 to go. From there, Von Metzsch made three saves before Fredericks tossed a long ball over the O’Dowd defense toward Spencer Settlemier, who retrieved the ball on a bounce and darted toward the net, unloading for a goal with 7:40 to go. BOD scored with 5:42 and 5:03 remaining to tie the game at 4-4. Piedmont closed the second quarter with Jack Nelson flicking an assist to Dixon with 2:04 left. In the closing seconds, PHS scored again with a man-advantage when Dixon found Settlemier for the goal and a 6-4 advantage at halftime. O’Dowd opened the third quarter with two straight goals at 9:27 and 9:06 to tie the game again at 6-6. With 7:10 left, Nelson had a ground ball recovery in the attacking area, weaved by a defender, and landed the go-ahead goal, 7-6. O’Dowd scored with 20.5 seconds left for another tie, 7-7. In the final quarter, Fredericks scored on a low underhand shot with a man-advantage in the first 30 seconds of play. Nelson scored again with 9:53 on the clock, while Dixon assisted Fredericks with a pass from behind the net with 9:14 left in the game as PHS jumped ahead, 10-7. From there, Von Metzsch stonewalled BOD with three critical saves at 7:14, 6:51, and 6:34 left in the game. BOD scored with 4:41 left to trail PHS 10-8, and Von Metzsch had one more save with one minute left/ O’Dowd scored its final goal with 7.9 seconds left to narrow the score to 10-9. The Dragons won the faceoff and moved into the attacking area. But instinctively, Nelson pounced on the ball carrier to force a ground ball, and recover possession as time expired. The PHS bench stormed toward Von Metzsch in goal to celebrate his outstanding performance. Final stats: Dixon had four goals, three assists, and a ground ball. Nelson had one goal, three assists, and a ground ball. Fredericks had three goals and a ground ball. Settlemier scored twice. Von Metzsch had 19 saves. PHS beats Berkeley 9-6 in WACC semifinals Piedmont led Berkeley 3-1 after the first quarter and 6-4 at halftime. Both teams scored one in the third, and PHS finished strongly with a 9-6 victory. Final stats: Fredericks scored four goals, two assists, two ground balls. Dixon and Settlemier had two goals each. Nelson had a goal, two assists, and three ground balls. Piedmont will not be in a league next season. Its Athletic Director Bradley Smet indicated to schools in the league late last year that the PHS may not field a varsity team due to small roster size. After petitioning to re-join the Shoreline Division, the majority of teams had already set their schedules and said they could not accommodate the Highlanders. She also wanted the cities where we live to be fun and not be boring and static. This quote of Jacobs from a speech she made in 2002 sums up exactly how I feel relative to my various thoughts, observations and suggestions made relative to our built environment: “The suggestions I’ve made may not be politically possible. There may be better or different means of accomplishing similar aims. My purpose is to help stir up creative thinking about how to enlist time and change as practical allies, not as enemies that must be regulated out and fended off on the one hand, or mentally surrendered to, on the other. We might as well learn how to make constructive alliances with the workings of time because time [and change] is going to continue happening”. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. New and Old Buildings Together: buildings that vary in age and condition make for economic diversity and aesthetic character. This is evident in both the new high school and the relatively new Havens Elementary School where thoughtful planning and architecture response to older existing buildings provide interest and a rich historic texture to the place. Density: a sufficient number of people is necessary for the vitality, interest and safety of any city, as shown in this wonderful 3-story area of Mexico City’s Zócalo. In the center of Piedmont the raised three story portion of the Albert Farr-designed Piedmont Community Church suggests that a limited number of additional stories for increased density is not aesthetically objectionable.

articles.text: Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel, a Russian-American author, contributor to the New York Times, and lecturer, offered insight on Putin’s war on Ukraine at a well-attended public discussion at Piedmont Center for the Arts on April 20. Edel, a native of Kransodar, Russia, moved permanently to America in 1997. She is the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, an informational text published in 2015 that details Russia’s view of the West and the country’s expansion; her contributions to New York Times provides anecdotal observations of growing up in late-era USSR. Since the onset of the invasion in late February, Edel has been interviewed by CNN, MSNBC, and NBC Bay Area to speak on the historical and cultural entanglement of the neighboring countries. Edel herself grew up in the heavily Ukraine-influenced Russian south; she offered photos of her childhood and described the centuries-long history of Russians and Ukrainians living peacefully side by side. Edel led the discussion with correspondence between herself and a friend living in Ukraine, who described the moment he first heard and witnessed Russian military forces attacking their city. An organized presentation by Edel touched on many points of the conflict, including the conPiedmont resident Anastasia Edel, a Russian-American journalist, lecturer and social historian, spoke at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on April 20 about Russia’s invasion of neighboring Ukraine.
articles.title: Anastasia Edel provides PCA audience with inside look at Putin’s war in Ukraine

articles.text: Piedmont’s inaugural Food Fest drew a crowd of an estimated 1500 people on Sunday, April 24 in Piedmont Park. The Fest, the inauguration of what is likely to become an annual event, included food vendors, local breweries and wineries, and music performed on a stage in the Main Park. The Food Fest was conceived by resident Roger Tsai in 2021 and marketed widely by Lisa Chan Carnazzo. Hours of preparation, talent scouting, logistics, and marketing and promotion transpired over the course of nearly a year, culminating into a wildly successful and well-attended festival. “Piedmont Food Fest exceeded our wildest expectations at every turn,” Tsai said. “The degree to which our community showed up to attend, and the final estimate of attendees came in at 1500. The event was spread out in Piedmont Park over the course of five hours, and included six food trucks, six food booths, eight local breweries and wineries, multicultural stage performances, and a kid-centric activity zone. Tsai and his team of volunteers partnered with the city, school district, and sponsors to bring the event to life. The goal of the event was to showcase food, music and entertainment offerings in the broader Bay Area community, aiming to enrich the experiences of the Piedmont community. “Piedmont Food Fest was attended by visitors from across the Bay, including not only immediate neighbors from Oakland and Berkeley, but also San Francisco, Fremont, Danville, Food Fest creator Roger Tsai and wife Diana Lee. in terms of fundraising, opened doors to vendors and sponsors, and showed up to support the event was unbelievable.” At least 1300 people registered
articles.title: Piedmont’s first Food Festival draws 1500 people

articles.text: The Diversity Film series continues with a screening of Power to Heal on May 5. The event is being co-hosted by the City of Piedmont, Adult Education Program, the Piedmont League of Women Voters, and the Piedmont Anti-racism Diversity Committee (PADC). A Zoom webinar will feature The Power to Heal: Medicare and the Civil Rights Revolution, a film by Charles Burnett. The documentary highlights the genesis of Medicare, when it was signed into law, as well as its relation to the Civil Rights Revolution. The hour-long documentary movie describes the history of segregated hospitals and a brief summary of civil rights activism to the internal workings of the federal government that led to integrated hospitals and African American access to health care. It narrates the early days of health inequity, powerfully demonstrating how race and poverty denied African Americans equal access to healthcare. Included are interviews that reveal personal experiences of African Americans’ struggles with illness and death without adequate healthcare. The film transitions from these individual stories to a broader review of disparities in hospital care throughout the United States. Physicians, civil rights leaders, and historians recount the dangerous tasks of documenting egregious incidents, tracking down patients, and the risks of blacks and whites working together to put desegregated structures in place. Following the screening, viewers will hear from Dr. Neil Powe, a leader in Public Health and the ongoing effort to correct healthcare disparities. Dr. Powe is a Harvard-trained physician, a professor of medicine at UCSF, and Chief of Medicine at San Francisco General Hospital. Viewers will hear from him about the history and current-day status of healthcare and will be able to ask him questions after the screening. To stream The Power to Heal, and for the conversation on zoom with Dr. Neil Powe from 6 p.m. to 7 p.m. on Thursday, May 5, click on diversityfilmseries.org. The streaming link for The Power to Heal will be active from May 2 through 5. Dr. Neil Powe is the guest speaker on May 5.
articles.title: Power to Heal to be shown May 5 in Diversity Film series

articles.text: April 19 marks first public meeting on the draft housing plan The ad-hoc Housing Advisory Committee, tasked with providing feedback on Piedmont’s 6th cycle Housing Element, received an informational report on the process thus far at its meeting on April 19. Members of the committee offered comments following a presentation by Lisa Wise Consulting, the firm hired by the city to guide the process. The Housing Advisory Committee was created by Piedmont City Council in 2021 to review and provide feedback on documents related to the housing element and programs, and meets as needed throughout the planning process. Feedback from its members will be considered by the Planning Commission and City Council when finalizing the element. The committee consists of Planning Commission Chair Rani Batra, June Catalano, Jane Lin, Justin Osler, and Claire Parisa. The Housing Element serves as an opportunity for community conversation on how to address long-standing housing challenges at the local level. It is meant to address various issues related to housing, including affordability, design, density, and site locations that could sustain more housing. “Although we are a small town, our [housing opportunity] sites are so unique, and the circumstances and opportunities for building is unique. So you need a long ‘menu’ to figure out what combination will work to make a site productive in terms of generating additional housing,” Batra said. Committee members offered comments on what goals and programs could be utilized to increase Piedmont’s housing stock. “It will be important to develop ways to make Accessory Dwelling Units (ADU) more affordable” Catalano said. “We will hopefully follow-up by including more detailed ways on how to do that in the Draft Housing Element.” She added that financial incentives for ADUs should provide for an increased number of units in Piedmont. ADUs have allowed Piedmont to meet its prior Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA). However, the city will need to identify room for 587 new units, so the lion’s share of that allocation cannot be ADUs. Locations for multifamily units are being explored to help satisfy the RHNA. “We talked about the Corp. Yard and Blair Park as [possible locations] for low-income multifamily housing, but I’d like to see more specifics on Measure A-1 funding ($2.2 million) from the county that would support building for low- income housing,” Parisa said. The city has asked for a second extension of the use of Measure A-1 funds, approved by Alameda County voters in 2016, and is currently waiting for the Board of Supervisors to consider it at a public hearing. City Council authorized City Administrator Sara Lillevand to request the second extension. The city projects that City Council will review the Housing Element this summer, and the City will then submit it to the state for review in summer 2022. Piedmont is targeting a Housing Element 2023 - 2031 adoption by May 2023. Public comment may be given at an upcoming Planning Commission meeting on Monday, May 9 or Thursday, May 12, and by emailing PiedmontisHome@ piedmont.ca.gov. Use the interactive tool “Piedmont Housing Puzzle” to drop suggestions and comments on where the city can sustain new housing units. Find the tool at https://piedmont.abalancingact. com/housingsim. will likely be priced out and have to close our business,” said Hodgkinson. pages.text: Wednesday, April 27, 2022 7 By Kevin Clark Last week more than 30,000 people from 43 countries attended the 4-day FIRST Robotics Competition World Championship in Houston, Texas. Among the 450 robotics teams competing for top honors, Piedmont High School’s Highlander Robotics earned a place among the top three percent of all competitors internationally with their robot “Selkie”. The FIRST Robotics Competition, which frames high school robotics as a full contact sport complete with mascots and cheering sections, announces a new game in January of each year to be played by two alliances of three robots in an arena about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season and competitions start in the eighth week. In this year’s game, Rapid React, remotely controlled robots up to 120 pounds score points by collecting and shooting 9.5-inchwide tennis balls into a funnel 8 feet high and 4 feet wide before climbing a set of inclined monkey bars. Teams who qualify for the World Championship at regional tournaments in seven countries are placed into six divisions of 75. After 10 qualifying rounds with randomly selected partners, the highest ranked eight teams become alliance captains and draft three others to work with throughout the double-elimination playoff brackets. Draft selections are so key to success in the playoffs that all teams at Highlander Robotics in semifinals at Worlds Selkie becomes a hometown celebrity the elite level dedicate significant time and personnel to track every robot’s performance across 125 qualifying rounds. After the first day of qualifications on Thursday, April 21, the Highlanders found themselves with a record of 1 win and 4 losses and ranked 60th of 75 in their division despite a season high shooting percentage of 95%. “It was incredible how well we were doing so we looked past the record and unlucky matchups” said team captain Charlie Lambert. On day two, the Highlanders’ shooting percentage paid off and they ended the day with a 5-5 record and had risen to 36th place. With 32 teams to enter division playoffs the next morning, some anxiety remained. “I felt like our chances to advance were decent, but if we went as a 3rd-round pick we likely wouldn’t play unless our partner robots had mechanical problems” said Lead Mentor Kevin Clark. On Saturday morning, Highlander Robotics was selected as the 2nd-round pick by the third seeded alliance captained by Team Appreciate from Austin, Texas. “It felt extraordinary,” said PHS Senior and Pit Crew member Angie Foo. The Highlanders won the first round of the quarterfinals decisively 166-105 after a wire came loose at the 30-second mark on a robot crewed by More Martians from Goodrich, Michigan. In the second round, Selkie made 19 shots with no misses for 38 points The Highlander Robotics team with Selkie, the robot, celebrating advancing to the semifinals of the World Championships. PHS senior Angie Foo repairs Selkie in the Highlander pit. Selkie shoots 9.5” tennis balls at the First Robotics Competition World Championship in Houston. and secured a 146-134 win to advance to the semifinals. In the semifinals the Highlanders found themselves matched against the No. 2 alliance captained by former World Champions Spartan Robotics from Mountain View, California. Spartan won 173-132 in the first round, but hope was kept alive when the Highlanders’ alliance was able to pull off an upset 138-119 to force a tie breaker. “In the pit I could feel the adrenaline and excitement as we made repairs,” said Foo. As the tie break round began, the Highlander alliance pulled ahead with a modest 4-point lead which expanded to 10 with one minute to go. With aggressive defense plaguing Selkie’s shooting opportunities, the gap closed until the score was tied 104-104 at the buzzer with climbing scores still to be applied. The Spartans advanced to division finals with a 140-134 final score. Selkie was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Asha Byers and supported by drive coach Charlie Lambert, technician Nate Hart, and human player Arun Brahma. Alex Ware led the pit crew of Helena Young, Beck Peterson, Peter Stokes, Reece Beck, and Angie Foo which kept the robot running smoothly through fifteen matches. Jasper Tripp ran scouting operations with Charlie Clowes, Tiago de Figueiredo, Caetano de Figueiredo, Kasper Jansson, Clio Salzer, Elizabeth Long, Matteo Scanu, Thomas Worthington and Jack McInnis. Chloe Kessinger, Lewy Seiden, and Vale Prieto Black acted as team ambassadors, answering questions, building connections with other teams, and representing the team to FIRST Judges. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and is comprised of 31 students from Piedmont High School, College Prep, Las Lomas, and Head Royce Upper School. The Highlanders will begin off-season training in the fall and accept 9th to 12th grade students of all experience levels. To learn more, come to an open house on May 16 from 7-8 p.m. in the PHS engineering lab, or contact Kevin Clark at kevin.clark@gmail.com. articles.text: The Piedmont parent group ALPS (Advanced Learners Program Support) will host a meeting tomorrow night, Thursday, April 28, titled “Defining Academic Excellence in Today’s Learning Environment.” The meeting is ay 7 p.m. and will be held in the Piedmont High School Library. Michael Malone and Ella Grossberg are the co-presidents of ALPS. All Piedmont parents are invited to attend and learn how Piedmont School District can maintain its focus on academic excellence and ensure all students have access to rigorous, relevant, and engaging curriculum. ALPS aims to identify positions of broad appeal, to be communicated back to the community at-large and help to build consensus. The ALPS goal is to foster and promote academic advancement for all students, modeled from a place of joy in learning rather than performance stress. ALPS hears Superintendent Randy Booker and Curriculum Director Cheryl Wozniak explain the district’s needs and trajectory, but they often come across as visions that overlook the existing needs of the Piedmont community This is a chance for parents to brainstorm and share feedback on their child’s academic needs, how well they are being met by the district, and what more the district could and should do to equip students with the tools they need to experience academic progress and success in Piedmont schools and beyond. Issues that may be discussed include: • Local Resources and Opportunities for Learning • LCAP Academic Goals: other specific language to define more clearly • Social Emotional Learning • STEAM • Early Reading and Literacy • Mathematics: Foundational • Differentiated Instruction • Writing, English and Language Arts • Fostering DEI in programs To register for the free event, visit: Docs.google.com/forms/d/e/ 1FAIpQLSfhOR48XRATYvllHplfWU5Fma67Qi3bgOyLlpYbv6D7B39R3g/viewform Light snacks will be served.

articles.text: Piedmont Community Service Crew, a youth-led club, operating under the auspices of the Piedmont Council of Boy Scouts of America, is well underway on their annual project collaborating with Rebuilding Together Oakland. The Crew has worked on roughly 20 different major projects to renovate homes of low-income elderly people in Oakland. The work project is the highlight of the crew’s year, and often the reason a teen joins PCSC. Since 2009, PCSC is the only youth organization that is a full sponsor of RTO. This year they are renovating a home owned by Elizabeth who previously worked as a social worker for children and domestic violence cases. She spends time with her two parrots and in her garden, which often attracts monarch butterflies. Although plagued with multiple health issues, she volunteers to care for an elderly neighbor every Saturday and Sunday. She has recently been the victim of multiple break-ins because of the disintegrating fence surrounding the backyard. Her large garden is a source of food, but it has been raided multiple times. Members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew are raising money to complete needed repairs, including building a new fence and gates, and doing home repairs and painting. If interested in joining PCSC to help with this rewarding project, contact youth leader Julia Banuelos at jbb3047@gmail. com, or Crew Advisor Ken Li at ken.i.li@sbcglobal.net. Also consider donating to help us reach the $12,000 sponsorship goal. To make a donation click on: https:// www.rtoakland.org/blog/pcsc.
articles.title: Community Service Crew welcomes volunteers for RTO project

articles.text: On March 16, Piedmont Education Foundation confirmed the appointment of Rita Fabi, Patricia Keller, Ruchi Medhekar, Chad Olcott, and Bridget Schreiber as new members of the board. We are thrilled to be able to accept this impressive group of school supporters on the PEF Board,” said Committee Chair Rebecca Thornborrow. In addition to being a dedicated Giving Campaign representative for Havens School, Rita Fabi is an online safety expert. Patricia Keller, a 45-year Piedmont resident and retired dental hygienist, is an avid Beach Revue volunteer. Ruchi Medhekar, with a Ph.D. in Microbiology, Immunology, and Molecular Genetics, was last year’s Beach Parents Organization president. Chad Olcott, once named the Education Foundation’s “Person of the Decade” for his considerable volunteerism and contributions, is owner of Mulberry’s Market. Bridget Schreiber is a finance and investment professional who moved to Piedmont because she believes community involvement is an essential part of a public education. “Since living in Piedmont, I have met many PEF Board members and have been incredibly impressed with the work they do and the passion they have for helping our schools. I share that passion,” Schreiber said. PEF Board terms are two years with a three-term limit. Terming out in June are Eileen Ruby, and Mary Lou Righellis. After three years of Giving Campaign leadership and service as Vice Chair, Amelie Kappes was unanimously elected as Chair of the board for 2022-23. Current Board Chair Nicki Gilbert will continue to serve on the Board and Executive Committee. Rick Smith will become the new board Treasurer, Cortney Allen is the new Secretary, and Tonya Antonucci and Dana Lung were named as Vice Chairs.
articles.title: Ed Foundation announces 5 new board members

articles.text: We all get stuck. You may not know how to finish a math problem, create a concluding paragraph, tabulate the earned income for the fiscal quarter or wash a white shirt with red stripes. But in school, and math and science particularly, getting stuck is not just a nuisance, it’s generally a sign that a student is approaching their subject matter inefficiently and ineffectively: relying on memory instead of logic. If students are stuck, they need to: 1) Get comfortable being stuck. 2) Know they can get past being stuck. 3) Follow the “unsticking” techniques. • You’re supposed to get stuck – a lot Too many students have a completely opposite mindset about being stuck. Here are all the things I get students to change in terms of their thinking about being stuck. • You’re supposed to get stuck. • Learn to be comfortable not being sure how to solve a problem. • You can figure this out. Trust yourself. I tell students to take a minute and become comfortable being unsure how to solve a problem. Just sit for a few seconds and don’t panic. Learn to transition from saying, “I don’t know what to do,” to saying, “I don’t know what to do, yet.” Once they are calm and comfortable with the idea that they can get themselves unstuck, we can move forward. • It’s time to start figuring things out If you can’t remember what the teacher taught you, know that it’s time to start figuring out how to solve the problem. Figuring out how to solve a problem is a completely different mindset than remembering what the teacher taught. Students need to change their mindset. • How to figure things out Here are some steps you can take to start figuring out how to solve a problem. • Don’t stop. • Re-read the question. Being stuck on a problem is a challenge to embrace. • • • • • Try anything and everything. Solve using logic. Write things down. Ask yourself whatever you would ask the teacher. Use multiple choice answers to your advantage. • Don’t stop: try anything and everything The most important rule is to never stop and never give up. It’s OK to try things even if you aren’t sure that they will get you the right answer. Just keep trying things and keep going. • Re-read the question strategically If you are stuck, it’s possible that you didn’t read the question correctly or missed some aspect of the question. So, the first thing you should do is to re-read the questions in a specific way: • Read every single word. Pretend you are reading it out loud to someone else. • Did you miss any part of the question the first time you read it? • Is there any part of the question that you haven’t used yet? • Write everything down The mind can process better when it can see what it is working with, so write everything down. • Equations: first write the equation, then re-write it with values. • Shapes and measurement: geometry is a visual process. If a shape is described, draw it yourself. If you are given measurements, write them in. • • • Graphs, lines, and points: Graphing is also visual. Don’t try to work with them without seeing their values. Values: especially for word problems, write down anything that can have a value. Write down their values too, or a question mark for those you don’t know What you are looking for?: Sometimes it helps to just see what you are looking for. • Start with what you want, nt what you are given Logical problem-solving involves thinking about what information the question is asking for and thinking about what you need in order to get that answer. Memory involves thinking about what data you are given and trying to remember what you have been taught to do with that. Focus on what they want and what you need to get that. Then look at the problem for what you need. It’s there, go find it. • Ask yourself what you would ask the teacher You know how you can ask the teacher a question, and halfway through asking you figure out what you need to solve the problem? Well, be the teacher. Ask yourself whatever you would ask the teacher and try to answer your own questions. • Use multiple-choice answers If you are taking a multiple-choice test, the answer choices can help. articles.text: Inventive and creative spirit filled the high school campus at the Piedmont School Maker Faire on the Sunday, April 24, a beautiful afternoon. Piedmont Makers hosted the 8th Annual Riveropolis, an interactive nature play experience that was recently featured at the California Academy of Sciences, provided Makers the opportunity to build and race boats made of cork, wood and rubber bands. Faire, with over 80 Makers displaying a varied array of work at an event that attracted more than 1,200 people. The Faire celebrates K-12 Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Math (STEAM) education. Hands-on opportunities abounded at the Faire. Outdoor demonstrations filled the high school Quad, and the new STEAM building’s outdoor area. Crowd favorites Rocket Zone and Nerdy Derby were continuously surrounded by dozens of Makers, designing, hammering, hot gluing, decorating, and iterating their rockets and race cars. Student and community Makers exhibited projects across the spectrum. PHS junior Max Schleuning built and programmed an impressive Golf Launch Monitor that allowed guests to test the flight path from their swings. Middle School teacher Laura Archer hosted the Earthquake Shake Table Challenge, providing young engineers the opportunity to build structures and test whether they could support weights and remain standing through an earthquake. Sixth grader Ben Fisher and grandfather Gene Switkes designed and constructed a magnetic ball-bearing controlled lemonade dispenser mounted on a custom wooden stand. At the elementary school level, Beach 4th grader Ethan Grossberg shared his knowledge on cancer-fighting Turkey Tail mushrooms, and Wildwood 5th grader Evan Yamanaka crafted an Ocean Diorama using clay and epoxy resin. Havens 1st grader Jacob Dickinson and his father Robert taught visitors how to make electric cars powered by batteries or solar panels. Makers explored chemistry through creating their own scented Bath Fizzies with Piedmont Education Foundation volunteers. Wildwood students William Bridges and Jack Shim teamed up with mom Margaret Bridges to teach people how to build Marshmallow Shooters, and then test their aim. The Faire showcased the thriving Piedmont Robotics community with representation from all four robotics leagues. The Piedmont Highlanders team qualified for the FIRST Robotics Competition World Championships in Houston and advanced to the semi-finals. They shared videos from their season. FIRST Tech Challenge teams constructed an arena in the STEAM Engineering Patio and allowed guests to test drive their Freight Frenzy robots. FIRST LEGO League Challenge teams demonstrated their Cargo Connect robots and missions, and FIRST LEGO League Explore teams shared their Expo projects. Max Seiden presents a motorized Go Cart that he built from scratch and an art bike he cut and welded at the Crucible LEGO my Sandwich! Charlie Cordani (left), Ganden Deming, Spencer Tsai, and Rory Hull present their sandwich-making robot using parts from their respective robotics FLL Challenge teams. articles.text: Nº 53 in a biweekly series Emmanuel Macron, the centrist president of the French Fifth Republic, has been elected to a second five-year term, 58% to 42%. It’s difficult to imagine how anxious the French have been about his far-right opponent Marine Le Pen. He trounced her by a 2-1 margin in the 2017 election, but his own popularity had eroded, while Le Pen’s had increased due largely to a messaging makeover that softened her delivery style and pegged her just a few ticks behind him in the polls. French politics are a multiparty system giving rise to a crowded field of presidential hopefuls that seldom yields a majority and requires a runoff. The campaign debate, Marine Le Pen versus Emmanuel Macron The candidates face off in a tense exchange during debate on April 20. In the first round on April 10, a total of 12 candidates appeared on the ballot, and none drew a majority. With Macron at 28%, Le Pen at 23%, Macron’s fivepoint margin was not particularly comforting. The other far right candidates, Eric Zemmour and Nicolas Dupont-Aignon, together garnered a surprisingly low 9% that would flow to Le Pen’s side. But the third highest tally of 22% belonged to socialist Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leftist leader that Macron had spent the last five years alternately annoying and enraging on a slew of issues. The five breakaway socialist candidates who shared a combined 13% did not throw their support to Macron, other than Paris mayor Anne Hidalgo with 1.75%. The left’s resentment was palpable. Macron was distrusted, a turncoat on the environment, cost of living, and major issues: workers might stay home in the runoff. For the once powerful Socialist party, this presidential election had proved devastating: it was disheveled and splintered into six parties. Mélenchon, a significant player in the National Assembly, was the preferred candidate to oppose Macron, not Le Pen. Disappointingly, Mélenchon trailed by just slightly more than one point. Macron’s first term, his first time in elected office, was viewed as riddled with mistakes. Voters might defect to Le Pen’s enticements for squelching inflation and protecting the borders; or they might abstain. During two frantic weeks after Round One, a chastened Macron asked the disgruntled for their votes. He frankly acknowledged that some votes would come from people more fearful of Le Pen than supportive of him. He asked for a second chance. His website AvecVous.fr (with you) and his campaign motto Nous Tous (all of us) underscored inclusion. Macron labels himself a centrist liberal and a French Socialist prior to founding La République En Marché! Valérie Pécresse of Les Républicains, the defeated conservative-centrist candidate with 5% of the vote threw her support to Macron, but the leftists pointedly did not mention Macron by name when they urged supporters to not vote for Le Pen. Last Wednesday’s debate was the only tête à tête between the opponents, and they assaulted each other verbally for nearly three hours. Macron made headway, accusing Le Pen of “being in Putin’s pocket” which she angrily denied. “Tu fou” (you’re crazy) she proclaimed, “I’m a free and independent woman,” but this is her Putin problem. She and her National Rally party are saddled with a 2014 Czech-Russian loan now ballooned to $13 million and beholden to a shadowy Russian financial contractor indubitably tied to Vladimir Putin. Macron kept pounding home the point Le Pen is obliged to Russia, which she Voters in queue in the 18e arrondissement in Paris during Sunday’s runoff election for President of France. Emmanuel Macron, showing the emotional high stakes of the election he won. Marine Le Pen conceded her loss, but did not extend congratulations to her opponent, as is the tradition. decried as French banks denying her loans. She borrowed another $10 million in 2022 from Hungary helped by Viktor Orbán, the ruling despot soundly in Putin’s orbit. Le Pen was unwavering, but Macron scored. She counterattacked on his sore point, a controversial proposal to postpone worker pensions until age 65. Macron dealt with thorny problems in his term: the pandemic, three national lockdowns; the laggard vaccine distribution; vanishing environmental pledges; over-zealous policing of Gilets Jaunes (Yellow Vests) and other protesters; the general strike over workers’ wages without resolution; budget cuts to education and childcare; tax breaks to the rich; and plenty of fodder for Le Pen and Socialists alike. Two days before the election, in an Opinion published by Le Monde and penned jointly by the Prime Ministers of Spain and Portugal and Germany’s Chancellor, they spoke out against Marine Le Pen with her longtime ties to Putin. While Le Pen disapproves of Russia’s Ukraine invasion, she declines to fault Putin. Russia’s bloody atrocities against Ukraine disrupt world peace, and they warn that a Le Pen presidency could pursue Frexit where France exits the EU in a scenario Le Pen has described since 2010.

articles.text: WACC singles, doubles tourney this week Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team clinched another league championship after being undefeated in the Western Alameda County Conference. They defeated league opponent Castro Valley 6-1 on Monday, April 25 at home, but lost to North Coast Section rival Lick Wilmerding 4-3 in San Francisco on Wednesday, April 20. The Highlanders finished their regular season with a 13-4 overall record and perfect 10-0 against league opponents. Postseason play starts with the WACC Singles and Doubles Tournament this Friday and Saturday, April 29-30 at Chabot College in Hayward. Charlie Lambert and Lenni Burchardt will play singles. The doubles teams will include Kai Baudendistel and Charlie Olcott, the team’s No. 1 doubles pair all season, along with Ben Breber and Monte Imburg. articles.text: Piedmont is finishing its track and field season with some record performances. articles.text: Staff Photos The PHS boys’ lacrosse team and coach Alex Yu look ahead to a rematch with Bishop O’Dowd in the league playoffs this week. Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team split its last two games of the regular season, defeating Acalanes in overtime on Tuesday, April 19 in Lafayette, but losing to Novato 10-6 on Friday, April 22 at Witter Field. Both are considered top-level contenders in Division 2 of the North Coast Section. Piedmont was moved up to Div.1 in 2020 after winning the championship. “Novato and Acalanes are playing all Division 1 (opponents), and they are Div.2, explained Piedmont first-year head coach Alex Yu. “I’ve known Novato’s coach, Mike Hardy, since the old school, We played against each other back in 88’-89.” The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record to 7-7 overall, second to O’Dowd in the WACC with a 4-1 record against league opponents. The Dragons won their regular season match 13-7 on March 18. The Highlanders will receive a first-round bye as the No. 2 seed, and will play No. 3 Berkeley (12- 9) today, April 27 at 5:30 p.m. Witter Field is the host site for this year’s championship game on Friday, April 29 at 5:00 p.m. Piedmont has won every WACC Championship since entering the league in 2017 but faces stiff competition from a strong O’Dowd team. “We’ll see Berkeley on Wednesday and we don’t want to look past them. It’s one game at a time and we have to take care of business first,” said Yu. The Dragons enter the playoffs with the No. 1 seed for the first time since 2017. They defeated PHS 8-7 during the regular season, but the Highlanders went onto win the 2017 championship 9-8 in overtime. Yu was an assistant coach with O’Dowd on that team. 15-14 OT win over Acalanes It was a heated contest pm April 19 against the Dons of Acalanes. Piedmont trailed 5-4 by the end of the first quarter but went ahead 8-7 by halftime. The Dons stormed ahead with five goals in the third quarter to take a 12-10 lead. In the fourth quarter, PHS scored four goals to jump ahead, 14-13 with 1:21 left in the game. Acalanes tied the match with 36 seconds left to play to force overtime. In OT, the Highlanders were able to kill a 90-second penalty, and Jack Nelson scored the game-winner in the closing minutes. Midfielder Noah Lindenbaum was awarded the game ball after recording a pivotal clearance in overtime that changed possession and helped Piedmont win the game. Final stats: Nate Fredericks led with six goals and one assist. Soren Dixon had four goals and four assists. Spencer Settlemier scored twice. Jack Nelson had two goals and an assist. Rylan Nelson scored once. 10-6 loss to Novato Novato came out the gates with a 5-1 lead in the first quarter and 7-2 by halftime. Piedmont narrowed the score to 7-4 in the third period, but a 3-goal deficit was the closest it got, ending in a 10-6 win for Novato. Final stats: Fredericks scored twice with two ground balls. Dixon had a goal, assist, and a ground ball. Jack Nelson scored once with six ground balls. NEXT UP Piedmont (7-7 overall, 4-1 league) plays in the league semifinals against Berkeley on Wednesday, April 27 at 5:30 p.m. They will likely face Bishop O’Dowd in the WACC Championship game on Friday, April 29 at 5:00 p.m. at Witter Field.

articles.text: Piedmont beats Acalanes 10-7, Berkeley 15-11 Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team finished up its regular season with a 10-7 win over Acalanes at Witter Field on Tuesday, April 19 and a 15-11 win at Berkeley in the season-finale on Friday, April 22. PHS record is now 8-8 overall and 3-1 against league opponents. They will enter the WACC Playoffs with the No. 2 seed, behind No. 1 Bishop O’Dowd for the first time since entering the league in 2017. It was the only year the Dragons won a WACC title. The Highlanders will face No. 3 Berkeley on Wednesday, April 27 at 7:00 p.m, in a playoff-double header with the boys’ team at Witter Field. The WACC Championship game will be hosted at Witter Field on Friday, April 29 at 7:00 p.m. Friday’s game against Berkeley was perhaps a sign of things to come. The game was a physical affair which included a Berkeley player being red carded (ejected from the game), and Piedmont picking up some knocks along the way. Coach Carlton Chan is hoping to temper emotions and keep referees attentive on fouls. “We’re getting the girls excited, it’s definitely a big week. Unfortunately, we lost our top defender against Berkeley. They had a lot of dangerous stick swings, and an ejection, and four or five yellow cards, We will have a discussion with the referees before the game and ask Berkeley’s coaches to watch for dangerous checks. During the game, our kids began fearing for their safety, so that put jitters into them because they were afraid to get hurt. If things start getting chippy, we’ll call a timeout and bring the refs and coaches together to make sure we’re staying safe,” said Chan, who has won every WACC banner since entering the league in 2019. After losing to BOD 7-6 on March 18, the Highlanders have extra motivation to win. But first they must get past Berkeley. “We aren’t even mentioning O’Dowd right now. Our focus is Berkeley and we’ll prep for O’Dowd when the time comes,” said Chan. 15-11 win over Berkeley The Highlanders led 10-7 by halftime but had to rally from a 5-2 deficit with 13 minutes remaining in the half. Piedmont added a goal from Ruby Guzdar and Katherine Kinne two minutes later to make it 5-4. Berkeley scored once before halftime but wouldn’t score again until 40 seconds were left. Charlotte Theut scored make it 6-5 and Photos by Todd Marshburn Elizabeth Ethington had three goals and seven assists vs. Berkeley. Kinne tied the match at 6-6, and PHS ahead 7-6 with 4:55 left in the half. Kinne scored again, and Eleanor Lavin boosted Piedmont’s lead to 9-6. Berkeley scored with 40 seconds left, but PHS added another on the very next possession by Kinne. In the second half, PHS came out with goals by Kinne and Elizabeth Ethington in the first five minutes for a 12-7 advantage. Berkeley made it 12-8 with 15 minutes to go but didn’t score again for 11 minutes. The Highlanders, meanwhile, added goals by Molly Ashton, Kinne, and Elizabeth Ethington. With Piedmont safely in control, Berkeley scored three times in the final five minutes of action. Final stats: Kinne scored seven goals and two assists. Elizabeth Ethington had three goals and seven assists. Theut scored twice. Lavin, Ashton, and Guzdar had individual goals. Goalies Sophia Ethington had six saves in the first half while Lindsay Kottle had eight saves. 10-7 win over Acalanes The Highlanders were well ahead of Acalanes by halftime, leading 7-2, but allowed the Dons to get closer before closing it out at 10-7. Final stats: Theut scored four goals with one assist. Kinne scored twice with two assists. Elizabeth Ethington had one goal and four assists. Audrey Mahany scored twice. Molly Ashton scored once. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-8 overall, 3-1 league) hosts Berkeley on Wednesday, April 27 at 7:00 p.m. at Witter Field in a double-header with the PHS boys’ team. With a victory, they would host the WACC Championship game, likely with Bishop O’Dowd, on Friday, April 29 at 7:00 p.m. Piedmont prepares for the WACC Championship semifinals tonight with a rematch against Berkeley.

articles.text: Staff Photos Michael Aikawa had a home run against Mt. Eden, and went 3-for-5 versus the Monarchs in a second game on April 20. going. Second baseman Michael Aikawa smacked a leadoff home run in Friday’s game against Mt. Eden, and nearly cracked a homer in the previous game as well. “It was a line drive over the left field fence, I thought it was going to hit the fence, but it went over,” said Aikawa. articles.text: Piedmont’s softball team suffered a 3-0 loss to Alameda on Wednesday, April 20. They also competed in the NorCal Classic at the Tracy Sports Complex on Friday and Saturday, April 22-23, losing to Vacaville 8-2 on Friday, losing 12-8 to Pacheco on Saturday, and defeating Mountain House 4-3 later on Saturday. The batch of games brings Piedmont’s record to 11-6 overall. They are still undefeated at 6-0 in the WACC Shoreline Division. The Highlanders have four games left in the regular season before the start of the WACC Playoffs on May 10; they host Mt. Eden today, Wednesday, April 27 for their final home game of the season, travel to San Lorenzo on April 29, Encinal on May 4, and Hayward on May 6. With a good end to the season, Piedmont should enter the league playoffs with a No. 1 seed and host the No. 4 seed. The championship game will be played on May 13. 4-3 win over Mountain House Piedmont won its most recent game over Mountain House, a school outside Tracy, 4-3 after trailing 2-0 in the first inning. Piedmont scored two runs in the bottom of the second and another two in the bottom of the third to leap ahead, 4-2. Mountain House scored its final run in the top of the fifth. Chiara Lundin led off the second inning with a single and stole second during Izzy Epstein’s at bat. Epstein hit a single to score Lundin, followed by Epstein scoring on a double by Gretchen Gerhardy. In the third inning, Miya Fujimoto reached first base on an error and stole second. Epstein hit another single to score Fujimoto, and Gerhardy smacked an RBI single to score Lundin. Mountain House closed the score to 4-3 in the top of the fifth and had two runners on base with no outs. No problem: Epstein methodically struck out the next three batters to end the inning. On the mound, Epstein pitched all seven innings for 10 strikeouts and six hits allowed. Final stats: Gerhardy went 2-for-3 with a double and two RBIs. Epstein was 2-for-3 with two RBIs and a run scored. Lundin was 2-for-3 with two runs scored. Leah Bell went 3-for-4. Fujimoto scored one and had a stolen base. 12-8 loss to Pacheco Piedmont scored twice in the top of the first, but allowed a run Staff Photos Izzy Epstein batted 2-for-3 against Mountain House and pitched a complete game with 10 strikeouts. articles.text: Wilson Wong had eight spikes against Encinal. The PHS volleyball team is contending for its first North Coast Section playoff berth in its first year of eligibility. The Highlanders defeated Encinal 3-1 on Thursday, April 21 at home and now have a league record of 5-6. Prior to Thursday’s match, the Highlanders honored their four seniors: Mason Kimball, Felix Broach, Atom Rognuson, and Adel Sahuc. Piedmont was able to allow some players to play different positions. “It was really fun to let Felix move to the back row, because he’s a middle and never plays there,’ said coach Mariah Cardenas. “He made our last kill to win the game, so it was really fun to watch. If we can win the next two matches, we can go to the next portion [post-season playoffs].” To qualify for the playoffs, PHS must finish with a .500 overall record, league record, or record against Div. 3 NCS teams. Given that all Piedmont’s matches have been against WACC opponents, the basis of qualifying could be their results against Div. 3 teams; PHS is now 2-2 against divisional opponents following Thursday’s win over the Jets. “If we can win the next two matches, we’ll be assured to get into the playoffs. The goal is to go into the matches strong, we want to shake off the jitters early and shake off the dust from spring break, and continue to take this season into playoffs,” said Cardenas. With a season-finale against Alameda, a D2 school which PHS beat 3-1 in the season-opener on March 8, the Highlanders are looking to officially punch their ticket to NCS. “The focus is to win. We need to win to make NCS [playoffs] so all focus in practice and games has to be there. We lost the first set against Encinal, and we can’t let something like that happen again,” said senior leader Mason Kimball. 3-1 win over Encinal The Highlanders dropped the first set 25-17 after starting the match with some reserve players on the floor. PHS powered back in the second set to win 25-21, won 25-22 in the third set, and finished with a dominant 25-14 fourth set. In the second set, Encinal opened with three of the first four points but PHS went ahead 5-4 and never relinquished the lead. The Highlanders held its largest lead at 20-10 and were able to bring in some reserves, once again. At 23-21, James MaNugyen slammed down backto-back spikes to win. In the third set, Encinal opened with three straight points, but the Highlanders reclaimed the lead at 5-4 and never conceded their advantage. Encinal began a comeback while trailing 23-16, narrowing the gap to 23-20 and 24-22, but a Jets’ offensive attempt going into the net closed it 25-22. In the fourth game, the win was never in doubt. Encinal held a 4-3 lead briefly, but Piedmont went on multiple scoring runs to extend their lead to 17-9. The Highlanders got the final five points thanks to Jets’ defense being out of rotational position to draw instant penalties. Broach got the winning kill, 25-14. Final stats: Wilson Wong Staff Photo Mason Kimball had five kills and four aces against the Jets. Staff Photo had eight kills and an ace. Kimball had five kills and four aces. Broach had three kills. MaNugyen had three kills. Shunji Higashi had two aces. Brayden Ellis had an ace and Kai Lambert had individual aces. Tuesday vs. San Leandro The Highlanders played at San Leandro yesterday, April 26. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-6 overall) plays its final match of the season at Alameda tomorrow, Thursday, April 28 at 5:15 p.m. The first round of NCS playoffs begins on Tuesday, May 3, with quarterfinals on May 5, semifinals on May 10, and finals on May 12. Photo by Midori Lambert Piedmont’s volleyball team gathers for a photo before its final home game of the season. Pictured are (front): James MaNguyen (left), Eric OlaruHagen, Shunji Higashi, John Champion, Owen Kelly; (back): Coach Mariah Cardenas, Kai Lambert, Brayden Day, Mason Kimball, Felix Broach, Atom Rognuson, and Wilson Wong. Not pictured: Adel Sahuc.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s swim team finished its regular season in strong fashion, defeating both Mt. Eden and Encinal in a 3-school meet at Mills College on Friday, April 22. The boys’ team finished with 121 points against Mt. Eden’s 43, and 108 versus Encinal’s 61. The girls, meanwhile, defeated Mt. Eden 129 to 33 and Encinal 102 to 68. Piedmont honored its 12 seniors on the roster: Frankie Broening, Georgia Gaylord, Andrew Grasman, Frank Udovch, Kate Aubrecht, Claire Dean, Cece Johnson, Lauren Quick, Josh Sachs, Holden Temple, Clayton Toste and Sophia Ware. Aubrecht announced that she will continue her swimming career next year at Amherst College in Massachusetts. The boys team finished the season with a 5-3 overall record and the girls were 6-2. The Highlanders will compete this Friday, April 29 at the Western Alameda County Conference Championship meet at Chabot College Results The girls’ 200 Medley relay team of Josie Oesterer (backstroke), Taylor Rolefson (breast), Kate Aubrecht (fly), and Tyler Dacanay (free) won with a time of 2:01. Aubrecht, Oesterer, Rolefson, and Sonja ten Grotenhuis won with in 1:44.94. The 400 freestyle relay team, including Tyler Dacanay, Odessa Dando, Emily Fitzgerald and ten Grotenhuis, won the meet’s signature event in 4:27.71. In individual events, Aubrecht won the 50 Free in 25.35 and 100 Free in 57.68. Rolefson won the 500 Freestyle in 5:51.80 and was second in the 100 Fly in 1:06.41. Oesterer won the 100 backstroke with a time of 1:01.75. The boys’ 200 medley relay team of Simon Lins (back), Evan Byun (breast), Ryan Stokes (fly), and Tom Rolefson (free) won in 1:48.03. The same team paired for the 200 Freestyle relay, winning with a time of 1:35.16. The 400 freestyle relay team of Farris Saffouri, Evan Dickason, Holden Temple and Andrew Grasman won in 3:59.99. In individual events, Lins won the 50 Freestyle in 21.33 and 100 Backstroke in 1:03.48. Rolefson won the 200 Free in 2:07.65 and the 100 Free in 56.18. Ryan Stokes won the 100 Breast with a time of 1:06.50 and was second in the 200 Individual Medley in 2:14.85. The 200 freestyle team of NEXT UP Piedmont’s swim boys’ and girls’ swim teams head to Chabot College in Hayward on Friday, April 29 for the WACC Championship, starting at 9:00 a.m. Kate Aubrecht helped win the 200 medley and 200 freestyle relays, and also won the 50 free and 100 freestyle.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Commission, which oversees the Recreation Department, is asking community members to offer their suggestions on the possibility of creating beach volleyball courts in town. A short survey, completed by May 10, is available at https:// bit.ly/piedmontvolleyball. The Commission hopes to learn what types of volleyball activities Piedmonters would like to see in the coming months. Commissioners Dick Carter, Lisa Gardner and Aamir Virani will host three discussions at the Exedra: • Monday, May 2, 8:30-9:30 a.m. • Tuesday, May 3, 1:30-2:30 p.m. • Friday, May 5, 5:30-6:30 p.m. “We hope our neighbors will share their thoughts on volleyball and Piedmont Recreation. Our city wants to prioritize what is important to our residents, Please take the survey. Share your thoughts with us to help make Piedmont better,” said sub-committee chair Aamir Virani. Comments may also be sent by email to piedmont.bvb@gmail.com. For more information, contact Lisa Gardner at Lgardner555@gmail.com.
