articles.text: Legion of Honor, of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, is showing Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy now through September 5. The fashion exhibit features the extraordinary designs of Chinese couture designer Guo Pei, who is widely considered China’s first couturier. More than 80 works over the past two decades will be on display, many of them were shown on Beijing and Paris runways. Pei is known for her craftsmanship, embroidery, and unconventional dressmaking techniques. “As a creator and artist, there is no greater honor than to share my creativity with a wider audience,” the artist said. “I hope that, through the artistry of couture and universal language of art, that it will foster cross-cultural appreciation, connections, and ideas.” To obtain tickets, visit https://legionofhonor. famsf.org/guo-pei?utm_medium=email&utm_ source=famsfmktg&utm_campaign=guopei&utm_ content=consideration_20220408&mc_cid=e- 25a62443e&mc_eid=573801a180. articles.text: The Ruth Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek will host its Golden Jubilee Gala on May 13. It is the organization’s largest fundraiser. The gala will include a silent auction, Fund a Need live auction and will present an award to an individual recognized for providing outstanding support of the garden. The event will be held outside and will include cocktails, hors d’oeuvres and dessert, live music, and other festivities. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth Bancroft when it was her private, personal garden, but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Ruth created a garden full of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. The gala begins at 5:30 p.m. Those who cannot attend the gala may watch it virtually. articles.text: Conductor Gustavo Dudamel let San Francisco Symphony in Mahler’s masterful Symphony No. 5 Guest conductor Gustavo Dudamel was back with gusto, leading “this foaming, roaring, raging sea of sound,” as Mahler once described his own raging Symphony No. 5. The Venezuelan led with fire – and no printed score – through this 71-minute masterpiece that Mahler’s compatriots in Vienna would call “gefühlsmȁssig” – surfeited with emotion. The crowd at Davies Hall stayed hushed in awe, without fidget or distraction, in hearing a master at work with the virtuoso San Francisco Symphony. Until the patrons’ jubilant ovations at the end. Often lost in all the flames and embers of this night is the clarity and articulation of strings, one result of the conductor’s early violin studies. This refinement was already evident in the Mozart Symphony No. 38 (“Prague”) that went just prior, with a far smaller orchestra (devoid of Mahler’s army, which added trombones, cymbals, clarinets, harp, tuba, bass drum). Under Dudamel, this was a virtuoso orchestra, prepped as if going on tour. If Beethoven had the definitive Fifth for the 19th century, Mahler produced his own for the 20th century. This vast Fifth from 1902 runs the gamut from keys in the funereal minor mode, on a scale like Verdi’s, to the ultra-serene Adagietto for strings (these days the most often excerpted Mahler selection). Then onto a playful and exuberant final movement where, if anything, the heavens appear to open up, suggesting perhaps that all is well after all. Quite simply, every one has feelings. But Mahler had them ever more intensely, high drama all the way, from groveling despair to unsurpassed exultation, and was able to set them to music with his vast musical forces. Working without a score, Dudamel was unafraid to let them all ring out. Today he occupies a unique position among Latin American podium figures, creating not only great music but also recognized as one of the most important music educators (via El Sistema) of recent decades. There were many highlights, from the opening growling basses simulating earthquakes up to the flutes and the shimmering trumpet solos of Mark Inouye. And in between, the softest pianissimos of which strings are ever capable. And did we mention the exquisite crescendos, the chattering woodwinds, and the versatility of Robert Ward and his horn section, at times with bells turned upward to provide a more country-village sound? The focus and intensity from the podium waned only in the finale – mobile, but less engrossing. The April 21 program had opened with the Mozart Symphony No. 38 in which the brass vied to be dominant. Consummate refinement, with the roars all held back till later. MUSIC NOTES – Dudamel, now in his 40s, led throughout from memory. He may have been the shortest man on stage, but once again, he stood tall. This was a rare Northern California appearance, as he also leads the L.A. Philharmonic on a heavy schedule. Also one year ago he was named the music director of the Paris Opera, a surprise venture given his heavy symphonic immersion over the years. SAN FRANCISCO SYMPHONY with guest Gustavo Dudamel on the podium in Mahler, Mozart, through April 24. For info: (415) 864-6000, or go online, www.sfsymphony.org. Paul Hertelendy, a Piedmont resident, has been a SF Bay Area classical-music critic for years.
articles.title: Fire and Ice: Dudamel conducts Mahler

articles.text: Piedmont alum Raphael Gold and the Diluvian String Quartet will perform a concert of chamber music inspired by the New World. Come be part of an intimate evening of music at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, April 29 at 7 p.m. The quartet includes Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. The program includes String Quartet No. 1 by Heitor Villa-Lobos, Five Pieces for String Quartet by Erwin Schulhoff, and Antonin Dvořák‘s masterful String Quartet No. 12 in F Major (“The American”). The concert will feature works inspired by the great American music of the turn of the 20th century, including pieces by composers Antonin Dvorak, Heitor Villa Lobos, and Erwin Schulhoff. You’ll hear quotes and rhythms from jazz, tango, and folksong. Proof of vaccination is required. articles.text: Summer festival begins on July 15 Music@Menlo, one of the foremost Bay Area music festivals, returns this year with a special program on its 20th anniversary. Performances begin on July 14, and tickets are now on sale. Music@Menlo is an internationally acclaimed chamber music festival founded by David Finckel and Wu Han. Begun in 2003 at Menlo School, the festival features concerts, lectures, and a training program for aspiring professional musicians. The festival’s mission is to engage and sustain an audience for chamber music that is programmed, presented, and performed at the highest level of artistic excellence. Concerts are performed by some of the finest chamber musicians around the world and held in intimate settings at Menlo School and Spieker Center for the Arts in Menlo Park. To view a list of all events and descriptions of artists, and to purchase tickets. see https://musicatmenlo.org. Music@Menlo co-founder David Finckel.

articles.text: The Revenant is an extraordinary film: intense, unrelenting, gorgeous to behold and unflinching in its realism. The year is 1823. It’s mid-winter in Montana and South Dakota. A group of men, working for the Rocky Mountain Fur Company, are just completing six months of trapping, preparing pelts and readying their riverboat for a return trip to their basecamp, a roughly constructed fort downstream. The trip will be long and arduous. The forest is quiet, wind stirs high in the trees when suddenly a man, in mid-sentence, is shot in the throat by an arrow. The group is set upon by Arikara warriors, and the trappers must fight a desperate and brutal battle as they attempt to get to the boat and escape. Among the few survivors are Hugh Glass (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his son, Hawk (Forrest Goodluck), who is part Pawnee. During one of their stops along the way Glass is attacked by a grizzly sow, protecting her cubs. It is one of the most heart-stopping scenes in the film, a mauling that leaves Glass close to death. The party makes the decision to leave behind three men, including Hawk, to bury Glass when he dies (they are certain he is near death) and then make the journey on their own to the fort. His son, killed by one of the trappers, Glass – still alive – is thrown into a shallow grave and partially buried. Through sheer will, he eventually emerges, discovers the body of his dead son, and thus begins what will be a 200-mile journey across some of the coldest and unforgiving landscape imaginable. His mission is to find the men who were responsible: John Fitzgerald (Tom Hardy), a ruthless, mercenary man, and a young, unsuspecting neophyte, Jim Bridger (Will Poulter). Simply put, this is a story of vengeance, privation and endurance. What is remarkable, truly remarkable, is the balance between the poetry of the cinematography – it will take your breath away – and the crucible Leonardo DiCaprio stars in The Revenant. of pain and exhaustion that Glass endures as he moves forward, against all odds. His suffering is palpable as he is forced to cross bone-chilling rivers, sleep in snow caves, stand in icy waters and gorge on raw fish, cauterize with gun powder a neck wound so he can swallow – all as he pushes forward with an unrelenting tenacity. At the heart of The Revenant is its cinematographer, Emmanuel Lubezki, an artist of unparalleled ability. The winter landscapes are blindingly beautiful while also lethal and silently threatening. The film was shot in Canada, the U.S., and Argentina, absent any forms of CGI. Its director, Alejandro Inarritu (“Birdman”), and Lubezki agreed that it be photographed only in natural light, no matter how short the days. And so the images are stark, the skies gray, the rising mountains white beyond white, the lichen-covered trees reaching toward the frozen heavens, swaying in a harsh, biting wind. In scene after transcendent scene, it is magical and stirring and as moving as is the journey of Hugh Glass. Having said that, the acting is also superb, for it is evident that each actor brought to this film a grinding and heartfelt commitment. Tom Hardy and Leonardo DiCaprio all but disappear into their characters. It is hard to imagine what they, like their characters, endured as they struggled to survive what proved to be a long and grueling shoot. articles.text: Honey Boy is a raw, gritty, semi-autobiographical film, released in 2019, written by Shia LaBeouf wherein he reveals a period in his life when he was living in a seedy L.A. motel with his father, who he names James Lort (LaBeouf). His two alterego characters are 12-year-old Otis (Noah Jupe), a child actor, and the twenty-something, Otis (Chris Hedges) who has become a self-destructive movie star ordered into rehab by a judge. It’s in rehab, during sessions with a therapist, that Otis tells his story in a series of long flashbacks. The year is 1995. James, as becomes quickly evident, is not so much a father as a man locked in perpetual battle with his own demons, while young Otis struggles to avoid becoming collateral damage. James – an alcoholic, ex-con, veteran, and former rodeo clown – riffs and rants and rages, his verbal abuse of Otis on occasion turns physical. Their interaction pretty much takes place in the confines of their motel room, usually before James takes Otis to the set on his motorcycle or in the evening when they have returned to their claustrophobic room. James is ostensibly managing Otis’ career as a child star acting in B-movies. And while Otis is on set, James attends AA meetings, veterans therapy groups, or plants rows of marijuana along a nearby freeway. Their dysfunctional relationship is that of father and son; however, it’s also one in which the son assumes the role of the reasonable adult and the father becomes the unreasonable child. There are times when Otis hates his father, the man who has exposed him to alcohol, weed, and cigarettes, seems to relish denigrating him while demeaning the size of his pre-adolescent penis. He meets and then tosses Otis’ Big Brother/mentor into the motel pool. He often rides off on his Harley, leaving Otis to spend long nights fending for himself. But then Otis also loves his father, craves his attention, and wants above all to be wrapped in his arms and protected. Regardless, James seems only intent on transferring to Otis – a lonely, precocious boy – the gnarled and twisted damage likely visited upon him. Honey Boy is not a vanity project by LaBeouf; rather, it’s a bleak, personal psychological dive into a complex relationship that haunts both father and son. If James is addicted to rage and chaos (now that he’s no longer drinking), Otis is addicted to his need to be loved by this tortured man. The performances of all three actors (LaBeouf, Jupe and Hedges) are astonishingly good. As is this strangely named film, Honey Boy. Honey Boy. Directed by Alma Har’el. Starring Shia LaBeouf, Lucas Hedges and Noah Jupe. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Lucas Hedges, Shia LaBeouf and Noah Jupe (front) star in Honey Boy.

The Revenant – winner of 3 Oscar Awards By Chris Honore’ The Revenant is an extraordinary film: intense, unrelenting, gorgeous to behold and unflinching in its realism. The year is 1823. It’s mid-winter in Montana and South Dakota. A group of men, working for the Rocky Mountain Fur Company, are just completing six months of trapping, preparing pelts and readying their riverboat for a return trip to their basecamp, a roughly constructed fort downstream. The trip will be long and arduous. The forest is quiet, wind stirs high in the trees when suddenly a man, in mid-sentence, is shot in the throat by an arrow. The group is set upon by Arikara warriors, and the trappers must fight a desperate and brutal battle as they attempt to get to the boat and escape. Among the few survivors are Hugh Glass (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his son, Hawk (Forrest Goodluck), who is part Pawnee. During one of their stops along the way Glass is attacked by a grizzly sow, protecting her cubs. It is one of the most heart-stopping scenes in the film, a mauling that leaves Glass close to death. The party makes the decision to leave behind three men, including Hawk, to bury Glass when he dies (they are certain he is near death) and then make the journey on their own to the fort. His son, killed by one of the trappers, Glass – still alive – is thrown into a shallow grave and partially buried. Through sheer will, he eventually emerges, discovers the body of his dead son, and thus begins what will be a 200-mile journey across some of the coldest and unforgiving landscape imaginable. His mission is to find the men who were responsible: John Fitzgerald (Tom Hardy), a ruthless, mercenary man, and a young, unsuspecting neophyte, Jim Bridger (Will Poulter). Simply put, this is a story of vengeance, privation and endurance. What is remarkable, truly remarkable, is the balance between the poetry of the cinematography – it will take your breath away – and the crucible Leonardo DiCaprio stars in The Revenant. of pain and exhaustion that Glass endures as he moves forward, against all odds. His suffering is palpable as he is forced to cross bone-chilling rivers, sleep in snow caves, stand in icy waters and gorge on raw fish, cauterize with gun powder a neck wound so he can swallow – all as he pushes forward with an unrelenting tenacity. At the heart of The Revenant is its cinematographer, Emmanuel Lubezki, an artist of unparalleled ability. The winter landscapes are blindingly beautiful while also lethal and silently threatening. The film was shot in Canada, the U.S., and Argentina, absent any forms of CGI. Its director, Alejandro Inarritu (“Birdman”), and Lubezki agreed that it be photographed only in natural light, no matter how short the days. And so the images are stark, the skies gray, the rising mountains white beyond white, the lichen-covered trees reaching toward the frozen heavens, swaying in a harsh, biting wind. In scene after transcendent scene, it is magical and stirring and as moving as is the journey of Hugh Glass. Having said that, the acting is also superb, for it is evident that each actor brought to this film a grinding and heartfelt commitment. Tom Hardy and Leonardo DiCaprio all but disappear into their characters. It is hard to imagine what they, like their characters, endured as they struggled to survive what proved to be a long and grueling shoot. Clearly they, along with Lubezki and Inarritu, will be recognized by the Oscars for what is a beautiful and difficult story to watch. Film can be art and both director and cinematographer have given us a gift, a primeval story, elegant in its simplicity yet framed by sublime moments of pain. The film won Academy awards for DiCaprio as Best Actor in a leading role, for Alejandro González Iñárritu as Best Director, and Emmanuel Lubezki for Best Cinematography. The Revenant. articles.text: Mud, released in 2013, is a remarkable coming-of-age film about two boys, Ellis (Tye Sheridan) and Neckbone (Jacob Lofland) who live on the Mississippi River, Ellis in a water’s edge wooden shack with his increasingly estranged parents (Ray McKinnon and Sarah Paulson). His mother, who has lived on the river all of her life, yearns to move to town. His father, a stern fisherman, stubbornly resists. Ellis declares that he too loves the river and never wants to be a “townie,” and increasingly feels the tension that exists between his parents. Written and directed by Jeff Nichols, Mud begins with Ellis and Neckbone, having heard of a motorboat wedged high up in a tree during a violent storm, and using Ellis’ flat-bottomed riverboat, motor out to a small island to investigate. To their surprise they find the tree and climb up to investigate the boat. As they inspect the interior, they discover that someone is living on board. That person turns out to be a man who calls himself Mud (Matthew McConaughy). Clearly he’s a drifter, and explains that he is living on the boat, but if the boys will help bring him some food, he’ll give them the boat. He later reveals that he is a fugitive wanted for murder, and is waiting to be reunited with his girlfriend, the love of his life, called Juniper (Reese Witherspoon). She’s in town, he explains, staying in a motel, waiting. Ellis, on the cusp of full-blown adolescence, his hormones swirling, is caught up in Mud’s romantic story, and despite Neckbone’s skepticism, is intent on helping Mud, first with food and later with tools and rope (to lower the motorboat) and an engine. Meanwhile Ellis crushes on a local girl, May Pearl (Bonnie Sturdivant), two grades ahead of Ellis and to his confusion flirts with him while rejecting him when her friends are nearby. As the boys soon learn, not only is Mud hiding out from the law, but from bounty hunters, hired by King, the father (Joe Don Baker) of the man that Mud killed trying to protect Juniper. Ellis is undaunted and tells Neckbone that they should do whatever they can to help Mud and Juniper. Jeff Nichols’ screenplay is part mystery, fable, and thriller, and is, in the imagination of both Ellis and Mud, a love story. Clearly, Mud can be called a Southern Gothic tale, as much about its authentic characters as about place and language. It rings true in all respects. As a story, it is in the best tradition of Tennessee Williams and Mark Twain. It is also a noir metaphor for how a newbie teen copes with the imminent divorce of his parents, who have grown disenchanted with the idea of loving one another. All of this leads to a satisfying, but violent act three that ends with a twist. Mud, Written and directed by Jeff Nichols. Starring Matthew McConaughy, Reese Witherspoon, Tye Sheridan, and Jacob Lofland. 2 hrs., 10 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2013. Now streaming on Tubi/Amazon Prime. articles.text: A place where the trees are thin and the locals are wide Howdy. How y’all? That’s how they talk here. Ain’t no Violins. They’s fiddles. No opera, neither. Grand Ole Opry ain’t no opera. I love it. Don’t worry. I wear a jacket and a tie every day. They call me dude. That’s better than Groucho. They called him schnorer. (Look up the lyrics to Hooray for Captain Spalding.) And now for the rest of the story… When you’re out of the Bay Area you gotta learn how to talk. Here’s what you need to know. Standard English don’t have a second person plural for you. In New York it’s youse. In Pittsburgh it’s yins, and throughout the South it‘s y’all. We don’t use no double negative, neither. Such has been the development of our once eloquent language. In Nashville they eat well down here. Lots of big folks. The trees are thin and the locals are wide. Look like former football players. That brings me to the food. Nice transition, huh. Barbecue is big here. So is catfish. Our first really good meal was a large basket of fried local catfish with French fries and hush puppies. Grits are a frequent side dish, and chicken with waffles is Dolly Parton is a legend in Nashville, Tennessee. popular everywhere. The large catfish platter was $12.50 and we sampled a local beer. The folks here are very proud of their local beer. It was very light and had a clean hops finish. There is a great variety of barbecue throughout the south. In Texas it is all based upon beef. The barbecue sauces can vary from sweet and mild to fiery hot and spicy. In South Carolina the barbecue sauce has a mustard base. Be sure to choose the wood carefully for the smoker. We arrived at the dock five minutes after the scheduled departure. The first words we heard from the ticket taker were, “Relax, the ship is waiting for you.” Yep, you guessed it, they held ship for us. The boat was an old-fashioned paddlewheeler and the musical show was an extravaganza. All of the entertainers were first rate musicians and singers. Many of them had impressive solos. For the pure musical value, the show was exceptional. But everything these days needs a large dose of glitz. The entertainers changed their outfits after every number. I thought it unnecessary, but the public screamed vociferously. As I watched the audience, they seemed to know the words to every song. Even the junior high school kids knew the words to the songs. Enthusiasm was everywhere. As I walked on the deck of the General Jackson paddlewheeler, I was reminded of a great story. In the 1840s the Norwegian-American violinist Ole Bull was very popular in America. He was a big, muscular and handsome man, and looked kind of like a violin-playing version of Arnold Schwarzenegger. While Bull was walking on deck, a man came up behind him demanding his money. The violinist turned around, picked up the robber, and threw him into the river. And that is a true story. This being Nashville, music is everywhere. At breakfast, I heard the people at the table next to me talking about music. The names were a veritable Who’s Who of country stars. There was Minnie Pearl, Tex Ritter, Conway Twitty, Waylon Jennings, and of course Elvis. The Nashville sound deserves its reputation. articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s annual White Elephant Sale found a way to bring people back for a live sale. With a series of several sale days with limited attendance, it raised over $1.4 million, money that will directly support the museum and its programming. The sale, touted as Northern California’s “biggest rummage sale,” is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The sole purpose of the board, a group of over 100 year-round members, has been to raise proceeds to support the museum’s art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, and capital improvements. Since its inception in 1959 it has contributed more than $23 million to the Museum. The board has many volunteers from Piedmont who help at the White Elephant Sale each year. Last year, the sale was held entirely online in response to the COVID pandemic. Shoppers were welcomed back to the warehouse this year while observing safety protocols. Over the fiveweek-period of the sale, visitors shopped a range of used goods including furniture, household items, clothing, artwork, ceramics, sporting goods, music, books, and a plethora of other items. “We were so excited to safely welcome shoppers back to the warehouse for our 63rd White Elephant Sale and continue our mission to support OMCA,” said Renata Dowdakin, President of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. “I’m so proud of our board and our dedicated volunteers for their commitment to this tradition under these extraordinary circumstances.” “We are so grateful for the Board’s extraordinary commitment to OMCA throughout the past 63 years,” said Oakland Museum CEO Lori Fogarty. “As the single largest donor to OMCA, the board and their annual White Elephant Sale are essential to the success of the museum. As we begin to navigate this new normal together, we extend our heartfelt thanks to the leadership of the Women’s board and the hard work of hundreds of volunteers who make the White Elephant Sale possible each year.” Carpet-Vinyl-Hardwood-Linoleum-Tile WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX on all materials with installation. articles.text: Lee Cliff, co-founder of the Piedmont 4th of July Parade in 1965 and its first Uncle Sam, peacefully passed away on March 20, 2022 in Cupertino surrounded by family members. Born Lee Harker Cliff on August 7, 1930, he was the son of Frank and Margaret Cliff. Lee graduated from Palo Alto High School in 1948, and Dartmouth College in 1952. He served in the U.S. Army from 1952-1955, attending the Army Language School in Monterey, and then stationed in Japan, Korea, and the Philippines. After the service Lee earned his Law degree from UC Berkeley School of Law in 1958, and practiced law in San Francisco at Hall, Henry, Oliver and Mcreavy until the mid 1980s. He then worked as a legal mediator before settling into full retirement. In the years in which he lived in Piedmont, he and a close friend Dick Johnson decided that the city needed to have its own 4th of July Parade, so they created one in 1965. Johnson was then on the Recreation Commission, and with the tall, lean Lee Cliff, he had the ideal Uncle Sam for the parade. “My dad and Lee were super close friends,” explained Kathy Kelleher, the daughter of parade co-founder Dick Johnson. The Johnsons and the Cliffs were great family friends and vacationed together. “We did a big crepe paper float of the American flag on a Piedmont 4th of July Parade founders Dick Johnson (left) and Lee Cliff. Lee Cliff leads the Piedmont 4th of July Parade as Uncle Sam. flatbed trailer. The trailer was hooked up to a pickup truck and Nell Cliff (as Betsy Ross) was hand-sewing American Flags in the back of the truck. Lee was at the front leading the parade as Uncle Sam. “All the neighborhood kids could hardly wait for our dads to come home from work, because we worked on the floats as a neighborhood in the evenings.” On August 12, 1955 Lee married Nell Sesnon, with whom he spent his life until she passed away in November 2021. They raised four children in Piedmont and then moved to Santa Cruz where they were active in the community for 30 years. Lee and Nell lived their last 11 years at The Forum at Rancho San Antonio in Santa Clara County. Lee enjoyed photography, bread making, woodworking, and making wine from chardonnay grapes that he grew. He was an avid reader, and enjoyed Dixieland and bluegrass music. Above all, Lee loved thoughtful conversation with anyone who would participate. He was intelligent, knowledgeable and had a strong sense of fairness. Lee is predeceased by his wife, Nell Sesnon Cliff, daughter Molly Cliff Hilts, and brother Frank B. Cliff. He is survived by his children Dan (Martha) Cliff, Susan Cliff, Peter (Sheila) Cliff, his son-in-law Dave Hilts, six grandchildren, and many nieces and nephews. Memorial contributions may be made to the Equal Justice Initiative (www.eji.org), a non-profit founded by social justice activist Brian Stevenson.

articles.text: Joan Beamer Metcalf, a lifelong resident of Piedmont, passed away at home on April 15, 2022, at the age of 81. She will be greatly missed. Born in Oakland, California on September 6, 1940, she was the daughter of Scott and Alpha Mae Beamer and the oldest of five children. In her youth, Joan attended Havens Elementary School and Piedmont High School before enrolling in San Francisco State University. Joan raised a family of four children in Piedmont. She was always available to her children and lavished love and attention on her grandchildren. Joan was an organizer and planner, and a renowned hostess with a reputation for entertaining and creating wonderful gatherings. Her door was always open, and her greatest joy was gathering people together. From football team banquets to birthday parties to family holiday dinners, friends and family were welcomed to her home for festive events and unforgettable meals. The table was full when friends were there. Joan was a devoted mother and a generous gourmet cook who was known for her famous toffee recipe. She loved sunshine and enjoyed traveling, reading fiction and cookbooks, and tending her garden. She loved her family above all else and took pride in her children and grandchildren, cherishing time spent with them on vacations, at their athletic events, school performances, and in the family home – an unofficial Piedmont landmark. Much of her time was spent in the service of others, and she taught her children and grandchildren selflessness as she gave her time to schools, Campfire Girls and Cub Scouts. She found fulfillment from her membership and leadership in a variety of charitable organizations Lifelong Piedmont resident Joan Metcalf died on April 15 at age 81. and developed great friendships during her years of volunteer work. She was a long-time member of Hollyhocks for Lincoln Child Center, and Hill Branch of Children’s Hospital in Oakland with time and energy contributed to The Winter Ball. The entire family had many happy years attending the Ball together. More recently, Joan was active in Home Gardeners and relished their field trips. She had a passion for the Oakland Museum of California and was a member of The Oakland Museum Women’s Board since 1978. She was an ardent supporter of the White Elephant Sale, chairing the Household Department for many years. Her organizational skills found a home in sorting merchandise, and she and her mother, Alpha Mae Beamer, were a dynamic team in the years they worked together. Joan further brought her love of planning and hosting events to these groups by opening her home to annual parties and celebrations that became traditions for her friends. Joan will be missed by her four siblings, her four children, and six grandchildren. Her life will be celebrated in a private service for family. In lieu of flowers, please make donations to the charity of your choice. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 11am-5:30pm 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org

articles.text: color. At the time Hope was developing an understanding of drought-tolerant, native plants and the importance they play in the ecosystem and in water and soil conservation. She started the transformation of her yard, planting natives that now dominate. There are over 50 species of native trees and shrubs that provide food, cover, and homes for native insects, bees, birds, butterflies and more, including several species of native Californian oaks. These trees are considered a “keystone” species because of the vast number of animals which they support, numbering in the low hundreds. In lieu of a conventional lawn, Hope has established a native wildflower meadow of deep-rooted native grasses that prevent soil erosion and feed native wildlife mixed with perennial and annual re-seeding wildflowers. When grasses go to seed, the seedhead is actually the flower of the grass plant. Some of the plants have edible flowers, and Hope provided Tami DeSellier with some samples. In 2016, Hope’s garden qualified as a Certified Monarch Waystation with areas planted in native milkweed, the sole food plant for the Monarchs in their pre-chrysalis larval form. Hope is thrilled to see Monarch caterpillars and butterflies enjoying her garden every year. Hope also told the group of her efforts to live a sustainable, carbon-neutral life with her family in their home. During the winters they wear layers inside the house, and keep the thermostat temperature in the upper fifties. The family is also conscious of minimizing the carbon associated with their travel. After the visit and tour of her garden, the walkers retraced their steps back to the Community Hall parking lot. On Wednesday, April 27, the group will go with Hope to the garden of Nancy McKee Jolda and her husband Robert as Part 2 of the “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour.” The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Late Wednesday afternoon, April 20, Piedmont police were notified by the Automatic License Plate Reader system of a stolen vehicle that had crossed into the Piedmont on Crocker Avenue. The vehicle, a 2010 silver Volkswagen Jetta occupied by three people, was reported stolen from Oakland on April 14. A Piedmont police officer spotted the vehicle on the 200 block of Hampton Road. Upon spotting the patrol vehicle, the driver took off at a high rate of speed. A second police officer and several resident bystanders witnessed the car driving recklessly through Piedmont. Minutes later, the police received a report of a vehicle crashing into a tree at a residence at Park Way and Highland Avenue. Witnesses reported seeing three suspects running from the scene of the collision. A short time later officers located all suspects. After initially resisting arrest, all three suspects were detained. The driver and one passenger were taken into custody, arrested and sent to Santa Rita jail. The driver Lashay Pierce, 43, from Oakland, was charged with possession of a stolen vehicle, possession of methamphetamine, committing a hit and run with property damage, possession of someone else’s ID and credit cards, and providing a false identify to officers. Passenger, Marchand Womack, a 44-year-old transient, was charged with delaying officers, resisting arrest, and obstructing police. A second passenger was cited for possession of methamphetamine, delaying police, but was taken to the hospital due to injuries.
articles.title: Stolen vehicle crashes on Highland Ave.; 2 arrested after running away

articles.text: Two of my neighbors were celebrating their 50th wedding anniversary. It turns out that the husband had a very famous customer. Dolly Parton bought all of her fingernail polish and cosmetics in his father’s store. The wife then chimed in reminding everybody that Dolly Parton came to their wedding and sat on the groom’s side. Other people told me some lovely stories about Dolly Parton. Not only was she a great musician and a superb performer, she was a great philanthropist and gave generously towards young peoples’ education. And that’s the way things should be, shouldn’t they?

CRIME REPORT By Jay Russell Stolen vehicle crashes on Highland Ave.; 2 arrested after running away Late Wednesday afternoon, April 20, Piedmont police were notified by the Automatic License Plate Reader system of a stolen vehicle that had crossed into the Piedmont on Crocker Avenue. The vehicle, a 2010 silver Volkswagen Jetta occupied by three people, was reported stolen from Oakland on April 14. A Piedmont police officer spotted the vehicle on the 200 block of Hampton Road. Upon spotting the patrol vehicle, the driver took off at a high rate of speed. A second police officer and several resident bystanders witnessed the car driving recklessly through Piedmont. Minutes later, the police received a report of a vehicle crashing into a tree at a residence at Park Way and Highland Avenue. Witnesses reported seeing three suspects running from the scene of the collision. A short time later officers located all suspects. After initially resisting arrest, all three suspects were detained. The driver and one passenger were taken into custody, arrested and sent to Santa Rita jail. The driver Lashay Pierce, 43, from Oakland, was charged with possession of a stolen vehicle, possession of methamphetamine, committing a hit and run with property damage, possession of someone else’s ID and credit cards, and providing a false identify to officers. Passenger, Marchand Womack, a 44-year-old transient, was charged with delaying officers, resisting arrest, and obstructing police. A second passenger was cited for possession of methamphetamine, delaying police, but was taken to the hospital due to injuries. Dolly Parton bought all of her fingernail polish and cosmetics in his father’s store. The wife then chimed in reminding everybody that Dolly Parton came to their wedding and sat on the groom’s side. Other people told me some lovely stories about Dolly Parton. Not only was she a great musician and a superb performer, she was a great philanthropist and gave generously towards young peoples’ education. And that’s the way things should be, shouldn’t they?

articles.text: Talk at Center for the Arts tonight, April 20 Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel, author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, will speak at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 7:30 p.m. on Wednesday, April 20 about Russia’s invasion of neighboring Ukraine, and its implications worldwide. Why did Vladimir Putin attack the sovereign nation of Ukraine, with which Russia shares centuries of common past? What’s behind the brutality of Putin’s war? How much popular support does he enjoy in Russia? Edel, an acclaimed writer, social historian and New York Times contributor, talks about her experience of growing up in the heavily Ukraine-influenced Russian south, the historical and cultural entwinement of the two countries’ natives, and the consequences of this war for Russia and the world. In lieu of an entrance fee, consider making a donation to Help Ukraine Center that supports refugees and distributes humanAnastasia Edel on MSNBC

articles.text: The theme of Piedmont Community Church’s Mexico trip during Spring Break was building sanctuary – creating inclusivity, safety and a refuge for those around us, and the families for which we would build a home. We came together to erect 12 beautiful homes built by hand and without any power tools, outside of Tijuana in only four days. We built both physical and spiritual sanctuaries. Artificial hierarchies of ages and cliques vanished, and the beauty of our high schoolers shined through. The strength of our young women was on display as was the vulnerability of our young men. We created a space safe enough for all of us to be ourselves. We made concrete one batch at a time, and built every wall, raised rooves and installed doors. The Yellow Team, led by seniors Cole Anderson and Sophie Nevis, built a home for a six-person family that included two special needs adults, a three-year-old named Jose Luis, and their blind grandmother Rosa. Our days began at 6:30 a.m., leaving our tents to temperatures colder than one would expect in Mexico, at 40 degrees. Later in the day it would reach a perfect 75. After breakfast each day we drove our team vans to our building sites, with music blasting to hype us up. Once on site we held hands and thanked our families as we began our work. The homes we built were 11’ x 22,’ small by our standards, but enormous in value to our families. After arriving on Sunday, April 10, day one of work began Monday and included laying the concrete foundation by hand, which had to be level and perfectly sized to install seven walls later in the week. Levelling is sometimes no small feat. The Black Team required 50 cinderblocks to create a level surface. “With many members of our team being first-time volunteers, we fell behind on the first day. But we were eventually able to catch up with the help of our committed team, parent leader Doug Biehn and our hardworking rovers,” said Black Team leader,
articles.title: Piedmont Community Church Mexico House Building trip – building sanctuary

articles.text: Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King delivered a State of the City address in City Hall on Monday, April 17. The text edited for length follows. After two long years of pandemic shutdown, after countless mind-numbing zoom meetings, I am thrilled that we are finally able to join together in Piedmont’s own City Hall. Healthy, vaccinated, a little weary – but thoroughly optimistic about what the future holds for the city of Piedmont. Right off the bat, I’d like to acknowledge the unsung heroes of my 8-year tenure on City Council. This job takes a lot. A lot of time, thought, energy, passion. My children Nicholas, Allison, and Danny are always – well generally – supportive and loving as I pursue my passion for public service. Thanks for your understanding and I love you so much. These kids were in second grade and pre-school when I was first elected to city council, so they have been on this journey with me for a long time. And I want to recognize my partner John Whitehurst and my dad Kenneth Gray – always supportive of everything I do. I want to say what a pleasure it is working with this council. Vice Mayor Jen Cavenaugh, Councilmember Betsy Smegal Anderson, Councilmember Conna McCarthy, and our newest colleague -- Councilmember Jennifer Long. Your wisdom and professional experience bring so much to our small but mighty government. When I was first elected in 2014, former Mayor Margaret Fujioka started a tradition of a state of the city address. Over time, that tradition has come and gone, but following the historic challenges of the last two years – and with all the great things that the city is doing, I wanted to take this opportunity to let you all know about the amazing transformation that Piedmont is undergoing. articles.text: The inaugural Piedmont Food Fest is coming to town on Sunday, April 24, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., and there will be something for everyone at this food, drink, and musical showcase. The Food Fest team is seeking enthusiastic volunteers to help make this community event a success. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org/volunteer for details and come join the fun. The Food Fest has taken the whole village to come to life. In partnership with the city, schools, local businesses, community partners, and the fiscal sponsor Social Good, Piedmont Food Fest welcomes visitors to the family-friendly event. Come enjoy the food, stories of the people behind the food, locally sourced beer and wine, as well as multicultural stage performances, and a kid activity zone. If all goes well, this event may even turn into another annual tradition the community can look forward to year after year. A central mission of Piedmont Food Fest is to showcase the many diverse offerings of the broader Bay Area community that help enrich the experiences of our community and our neighbors. The event will feature food from Curry Up Now, Ceviche & Co, Swahili Spot, Kiss My Boba, Piedmont’s Robert Dorsey Catering, and others. Live music will be provided by the mariachi duo Son Nuestro, the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Black Music Incubator Showcase, and the Oakland Samba Revue. To register or volunteer, please visit www.piedmontfoodfest. org. While you’re there, be sure to check out the premium wine & beer tasting package, which includes a limited edition tumbler while supplies last.
articles.title: Piedmont Food Fest comes to town this Sunday

And I want to recognize my partner John Whitehurst and my dad Kenneth Gray – always supportive of everything I do. I want to say what a pleasure it is working with this council. Vice Mayor Jen Cavenaugh, Councilmember Betsy Smegal Anderson, Councilmember Conna McCarthy, and our newest colleague -- Councilmember Jennifer Long. Your wisdom and professional experience bring so much to our small but mighty government. When I was first elected in 2014, former Mayor Margaret Fujioka started a tradition of a state of the city address. City staff will present an overview of Piedmont’s current reach codes, the 2022 Energy Code, and initial considerations for the next set of reach codes, followed by a community workshop where attendees will be asked to provide comments and recommendations about the current and future code. While not required, registration for the in-person event is strongly encouraged at: https:// docs.google.com /for ms/d /e/ 1FAIpQLSfzsKAQ32t2hhk59XZIlC8k83R8GTjocs_EvbkIQygjQmr4UQ/viewform. Additional information about building electrification, rebates, resources, and incentives available for Piedmonters can be found at: https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning _ _ _building/about_ building_/electrification. articles.text: Looking for a summer camp experience for adults? Come play in the woods with us from May 4–6, connect with other women, and experience camp like a kid again. articles.text: Friday is deadline to restore Prop 58 and Prop 193 The California Association of Realtors ran a costly, misleading campaign in November 2020 which pushed through the passage of Proposition 19 by a 51% margin. The ads touted expanding portability across all counties for seniors, the disabled, and wildfire victims by permitting relocation to new homes while retaining their tax base. But the ads failed to mention Prop 19’s “Death Tax.” April 22, 2022 – Friday this week – is the deadline for submitting 1,000,000 valid signatures to get the “Repeal the Death Tax” initiative on November’s ballot and to the voters. Many voters at the time were distracted amidst the global pandemic, endless smoky wildfires, shelter-in-place, and the struggle to run a free and fair presidential election. Prop 19 amended the state constitution by effectively removing Prop 58 and 193 protections which allowed parents the ability to transfer property of any value to their children without triggering reassessments and without increasing market-driven taxes. The same protection for grandparent to grandchildren transfers were also removed by Prop 19. The working class will suffer the most, as Prop 19 also eliminated any exemption of taxable value for other property. Restaurants, farms, small businesses, small multi-unit buildings will be reassessed at full market value; Daniel and Yee Ju Riddell gather signatures outside Lucky’s Market in Rockridge in April. children who cannot afford the crippling new tax bill will be forced to sell, effectively closing their businesses. Increased food insecurity, challenges in retaining staff, higher rents or forced evictions will result. Prop 19 is terrible for California. My husband, Daniel Riddle, and I have taken efforts to restore Prop 58 and 193 protections that Californians overwhelmingly voted for. This will allow a parent to transfer a primary residence of any value to a child without a tax reassessment to market rate, while simultaneously restoring an up to $2,400,000 exemption (adjusted for inflation) in taxable value of other property. For more information and to help provide signatures contact Yee Ju Riddell at 510-543-0991 or visit Forcalifornians.com. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Bookmark, the non-profit bookstore in Old Oakland that helps support Oakland Public Library, is have its semi-annual four-day Spring Sale from Thursday to Sunday this week, April 21-24. Bookmark, celebrating its 30th anniversary throughout the year, is located in Old Oakland at 721 Washington Street in Oakland. All proceeds from the sale of gently used, donated books will benefit the Oakland Public Library. The Bookmark features books of general interest, CDs, LPs, comics, jigsaw puzzles and a selection of collectible books. Members of the Friends of the Oakland Public Library save 50% on all purchases made on day one of the sale, April 21. Membership may be purchased on the day of the sale for $25 per year, $15 for seniors and full-time students. All book lovers receive a discount of 30% on Friday, and the discount increases each day up to 50% discounts on Sunday, April 24. The discount applies to already low prices of $3 to $6 for most of the 17,000 books in the store Friends of the Oakland Public Library is a nonprofit organization dedicated to supporting the Oakland Public Library. Through funds raised by operating a used bookstore and through its membership program of nearly 1,000 members, the Friends donated over $1 million to the Oakland Public Library over the past five years. To become a member, call 444- 0473 or click on FOPL.org.
articles.title: Huge discounts at Bookmark Book Sale this weekend

articles.text: Health services company Curative offers COVID-19 testing in Piedmont in the Community Hall parking lot five days a week. Testing is available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in the Community Hall parking lot at 711 Highland Avenue. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will celebrate Arbor Day with community-wide activities and events for all ages beginning April 25. Chalk Art contest for kids The Piedmont Park Commission is coordinating a Chalk Art contest for kids. Participants can select their favorite street tree or tree in a park next to a sidewalk, decorate the sidewalk with chalk art, and take a photo of themselves by the tree. Submissions may be sent to Piedmont Parks and Projects Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov between April 25 and 29. Gift certificates from Fentons Creamery will be awarded to the winners. Gratitude trees Trees in Piedmont Park, Dracaena Park, Crocker Park, and Linda Park will be designated as “Gratitude Trees” during the week of April 25, identified by barricades and signage. Park visitors, students, and preschool classes are invited to stop by and write messages of thanks on tags provided at each park tree. Heritage tree winners On Thursday, April 28, the day before Arbor Day, the Park Commission will announce the winner of the 2022 heritage tree program. The event will be held at Piedmont Community Hall at 8 p.m. Winning nominators will be acknowledged and “pinned” with a heritage tree lapel. The Public Works Department staff will also be there to answer questions about street trees, parks, storm and sanitary sewers, and maintenance and road questions. Movie in the Park At 8:30 p.m. on April 28, following the Heritage Tree winner announcement, a movie in the park will be shown. Intelligent Trees, a 45-minute documentary about how nature communicates with us and itself, was chosen this year by the Park Commission. Cub Scout volunteers will hand out raffle tickets and free popcorn, donated by the Piedmont Garden Club. Two raffle winners will win a 15-gallon Cercis Redbud tree to bring home, donated by Devil Mountain Nursery.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont published its draft report of the 6th Cycle Housing Element for 2023- 2031 on April 8. It considers new land uses, housing types, building types, heights, residential density, code changes, and other housing-related initiatives and policies that aim to accommodate nearly 600 new units by 2031. All Bay Area local governments have until January 2023 to update their Housing Elements. Planning Commission and Housing Advisory Committee Chair Rani Batra encouraged all Piedmont residents and other stakeholders to participate in upcoming public meetings, as well as share their thoughts on the draft Housing Element. “We can all look forward to seeing the public review draft of the Housing Element and then being able to engage together on it at three different public forums this spring,” she said. “We really appreciate hearing [community] voices.” The next Planning Commission public hearing will be held on May 12 at 5:30 p.m. Residents may also email comments to the city at PiedmontisHome@piedmont. ca.gov, or mail them to ‘Draft Housing Element, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611.’ “It is going to take all of us to make room for more housing in Piedmont,” Batra said. Piedmont declined to appeal its Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA), which requires the city to make room for 587 affordable housing units. These can be in the form of Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs), Junior Accessory Dwelling Units (JADUs), and lot-splitting; as well as finding parcels of land where more dense housing could be developed. Nearly every city in California received a higher RHNA in the next housing cycle, and many have appealed their allocations before the end of 2021. The Housing Element does not require the city to physically increase its housing stock; instead, it is meant to provide an analysis of development constraints and the immediate and long-terms housing needs in the city. The Element must also identify land and financial resources that will meet the city’s RHNA, establish policies that address those needs, and include programs that would help implement those policies. “Our Housing Element holds the key to many issues including our approaches to housing, greenhouse gas emissions reduction, transportation, educational opportunity, and others. Housing is fundamental to the health and well-being of any community, including Piedmont,” explained Mayor Teddy Gray King. The city projects that City Council will review the Housing Element this summer, and the City will then submit it to the state for review in late summer. Piedmont is targeting a Housing Element 2023 - 2031 adoption by May 2023. Comments from public Unattributed comments collected from community workshops and focus groups between July 2021 and March 2022 are included in the draft Housing Element. A key finding was that an average Piedmont household has an income more than double the Alameda County average, with a median household income of $224,659. One community workshop participant was quoted, “I work in Piedmont, but cannot afford to live in the city.” Another comment stated, “we need affordable housing for firefighters, city staff, and teachers.” Public comment reflected an interest in small (400 sq-foot) units to accommodate students and young professionals, more housing for seniors, more mixed-use housing developments (commerce and residential), and smaller homes (less than 2,000 sq. ft.). Those who attended public meetings and provided comment before the draft Element was released also stated that there is a need to include voices outside of Piedmont, and that there is a need to change negative perceptions and assumptions about affordable housing and density. The draft document also reports that a large portion of Piedmont residents, both renters and homeowners, are cost-burdened, meaning they pay more than 30% of their income on housing and bills. Additionally, the analysis, prepared by Lisa Wise Consulting, noted that Piedmont seniors have few options to “downsize” and agein-place; whereas families with young children have found it difficult to find their “starter home” in Piedmont. Read the draft in full at www. piedmontishome.org.

articles.text: The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present a Zoom webinar at 6 p.m. on Thursday, May 5, entitled Power to Heal, featuring the documentary film The Power to Heal: Medicare and the Civil Rights Revolution, a film by Charles Burnett. The event will be co-hosted by the City, the Piedmont League of Women Voters, Piedmont Anti-racism Diversity Committee, and Piedmont Adult Education. The documentary highlights the genesis of Medicare, when it was signed into law, as well as its relation to the Civil Rights Revolution. Following the screening, viewers will hear from Dr. Neil Powe, a leader in Public Health and the ongoing effort to correct healthcare disparities. Dr. Powe is a Harvard-trained physician, a professor of medicine at UCSF, and Chief of Medicine at San Francisco General Hospital. Viewers will hear from him about the history and current status of healthcare. He will have a question and answer session. Register for a link to stream the webinar at diversityfilmseries.org. The streaming link for The Power to Heal will be active from May 2 through May 5. Dr. Neil Powe
articles.title: Diversity film series to present Power to Heal on May 5

articles.text: Readmont 2022, a community-wide reading project in its 12th year, will culminate with an evening of guest speakers on Thursday, May 19. The event will be on Zoom. Readmont, hosted by Piedmont High School librarian Kathryn Levenson and English Department chair Beth Black, will include a discussion of the novel A Thousand Splendid Suns by Khaled Hosseini. It will include a panel discussion of women’s rights and refugees featuring Fouzia Azizi, Director of Refugee Services for Jewish Family and Community Services East Bay, and Humaira Khan of Toronto, Canada, an expert on women’s rights in Afghanistan and Pakistan. The event was originally scheduled for April 21 but will be held via Zoom on May 19 at 7 p.m. Student discussions began on April 19 and will continue through April 21. A Thousand Splendid Suns chronicles the story of two women living in Kabul, Afghanistan. The book is appropriate for ages 14 and up. For younger readers, the English Department recommends the book I am Malala for ages 10 to 14, and Malala, My Story of Standing up for Girls’ Rights, Fouzia Azizi, a refugee from Afghanistan and Director of Refugee Services at Jewish Family and Community Services East Bay, is a featured speaker. appropriate for ages 6 through 10. “We chose this book for its beautiful story of love in an unforgiving time and as a way for our community to discuss the recent events in Afghanistan and the increase of Afghan refugees to the Bay Area,” Black said. The books may be checked out at any school district library. Books are funded through a grant from the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee (PADC). A Good Place for Books bookstore in Montclair at 6120 La Salle Avenue is offering a 20% discount on A Thousand Splendid Suns. Questions may be addressed to Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us, or to Black at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us.
articles.title: Readmont 2022 speaker event date changed to May 19

articles.text: As spring has sprung, we see flowers and fruits pop up all around us. What about Earth makes it so special for growing so many plants? Earth is unique because it has the conditions needed to support life: air, water, and sunlight (temperature). Earth’s atmosphere has Carbon Dioxide gas; which plants rely on for photosynthesis. The water cycle provides freshwater for plants via rainfall, lakes, and groundwater. The planet’s approximate distance from the sun provides energy and comfortable temperatures for plants to thrive in as well. Plants that are adapted to survive within Earths’ conditions might not do so well in foreign environments. The Moon has no atmosphere, which means it is exposed to the extreme conditions of space. There is no air, no liquid water, and unreliable temperatures. The soil is mostly rock and dust, which provides little to no nutrients for healthy plant growth. Mars has an atmosphere that is very different from Earth’s, with 96% being Carbon Dioxide gas. The average temperature on Mars is -81°F, which is too cold for plants and there is no liquid water that we know of. Its soil is rich in iron-oxides which gives the planet its rusty, red color, but missing many of the essential minerals and nutrients required for plant growth. As astronauts plan missions to the Moon and Mars, they must think about how to provide plants with these vital resources when there are none. Both of these environments have new, unexpected, and unexperienced challenges for plant growth. In order to investigate what resources plants need to grow, try an experiment on sprouting beans. Adult supervision is recommended throughout this 7. Together, make some predictions about the beans: • How long do you think it will take for them to start growing? • Do you think they will all grow the same rate, size, etc.? 8. Each day for the next 7-10 days, check on the beans. Record observations and track their growth using the data sheet. Ask some of the following questions: • What do you notice about the beans? • What do you notice about the environment inside the bag? • Are they all growing the same? Which beans are growing more, or less, and why do you think that is? 9. Determine what plants need to survive based on the results of your experiment. Discuss some of the following ideas to expand further: • How do you think the beans grow without soil? • What are some of the differences between Earth and The Moon? Or Mars? • What resources might be missing on The Moon or Mars? Water, air, sunlight, and soil are some of the main ingredients needed to grow healthy crops. Haley Thiltgen is an Educator at Chabot Space & Science Center, is a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth. Chabot is located at 10,000 Skyline Boulevard in Oakland. Bean sprouts experiment. Bean seeds are small and easy to swallow. 1. Gather your learners and the materials needed: • Bean seeds: lima beans, pinto beans, lentil beans, or mung beans work well • Cotton Balls or Paper • Towels • Plastic Bags (small-medium) • Water • Bowl for water • Tape • Window (or place with good lighting) • Marker • Writing utensil • Ruler (optional) 2. Begin with a discussion, using some of the questions below: • What do plants need to grow? • What about Earth makes it so special for growing plants? • Do you think a plant could survive without water, air, sun, or soil? 3. Give everyone a plastic bag and label them with a permanent marker. 4. Fill a bowl with water. Dip a few cotton balls or paper towels into the water and place them into the plastic bag. 5. Next, add 2-3 beans into each bag. Be careful not to overfill the bag. 6. Tape the bag up on a window, or a place with plenty of light.
articles.title: Springtime sprouting experiment

articles.text: High drama in warmup for World Championship in Houston Charlie Lambert (left) and Vaughn Khouri place Selkie before a match. Seventeen students from Highlander Robotics, Piedmont High School’s robotics team, traveled with their robot “Selkie” to San Jose State on April 8 to compete as one of 59 teams from as far away as the Dominican Republic in the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Silicon Valley Regional Tournament. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game in January of each year to be played by two alliances of three robots, built by 9th to 12th grade students, in an arena about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season. In this year’s game, Rapid React, robots up to 120 pounds score points by collecting and shooting 9.5-inch-wide tennis balls into an 8-foot high 4-footwide funnel before climbing a set of inclined monkey bars. FRC Tournaments, which frame robotics as a sport complete with mascots and cheering sections, consist of a day of practice matches, a day and a half of qualification matches, and half a day of playoffs with alliances formed through a draft system. Teams expect to compete in 9 to 12 qualifying rounds with 30-60 minute breaks in between, leaving little time for repairs in an atmosphere akin to F1 Racing. The Highlanders were coming off success at the Sacramento Regional where they qualified for the World Championship in Houston next week. In San Jose they looked to refine their robot and skill, but ran into problems early into practice matches when a belt on their drive train broke and they found themselves without a spare. “Typically, we can borrow parts when that happens” said Lead Mentor Kevin Clark, “but this particular belt was more obscure than we’d anticipated, and I thought we might be going home that night,” he added. Thankfully a spare was eventually found by another team and Selkie was back up and running. In the fast-paced and high-scoring qualifying rounds, the Highlanders went 7-2 and finished 11th of 59 teams. In one round the two sides were so capable that the number of balls scored confused the field sensors, causing miscounts and requiring a rematch. In the playoffs, The Highlanders were selected by 4th seed RoboDores from Monterey and advanced to the best-of-three quarterfinals against an alliance captained by 5th seed Berkelium from Berkeley. In the first round, the opposition fielded only two robots due to mechanical issues and they opted to use the round to go back to their pit for repairs. The result seemed to be a foregone conclusion until Selkie’s intake, part of the robot that extends to pick up balls, got caught on Berkelium’s intake. The round devolved into a tug of war across the field in an effort to prevent one another from scoring points or forcing penalties. The Highlanders won 83 to 59 but in the process bent a piston on their intake. Twenty seconds into second round match, Selkie’s main breaker blew and it was left immobile after a solid hit by Jump Robotics. That match ended 56 to 65. With less than 20 minutes until the quarterfinal tie breaker, the Highlander pit crew flew into action: replacing the breaker, fixing the bent piston, and running pre-match checks. With less than two minutes remaining for Selkie to enter the field or be disqualified, it was discovered that a vital sensor had been damaged. With no time to return to the pit, the team duct taped the sensor casing and hoped for the best. As the round started, teammates in the stands let out a collective sigh of relief as it was clear that the damaged sensor was still working and Selkie began racking up points. With 30 seconds left and a 10-point lead, a part on Selkie’s intake failed and the robot was unable to pick up any more balls. The match ended in a 83-83 tie and Berkeley’s alliance won based on tie break rules. Selkie was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Asha Byers and supported by drive coach Charlie Lambert, technician Nate Hart, and human player Arun Brahma. Alex Ware led the pit crew which kept the robot running. Jasper Tripp and Charlie Clowes ran scouting operations which informed alliance selection for the playoffs. Chloe Kessinger and Lewy Seiden acted as team ambassadors, answering questions, building connections with other teams, and representing the team to FIRST Judges. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and is now comprised of 31 students from four schools – Piedmont High, College Prep, Las Lomas, and Head Royce. For more information contact Kevin Clark at kevin.clark@gmail.com. Highland Robotics robot Selkie (#8033), shoots nine and a half inch tennis balls at an eight-foot-high funnel.
articles.title: Highlander Robotics tests its mettle in San Jose

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department has enacted a new policy entitled “Military Equipment,” posted on the department’s Transparency Portal page at https://www.piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/police/ transparency_portal. Assembly Bill 481, authored by Assemblyman David Chiu (D-San Francisco) and approved by Gov. Gavin Newsom on September 30, 2021, requires all law enforcement agencies to provide guidelines for the approval, acquisition, and reporting requirements of military equipment. The bill is intended to increase transparency and provide oversight on the use of military weapons. Military equipment includes specialized firearms and firearms and ammunition of .50 caliber or greater, excluding standard-issue shotguns. The Piedmont Police Department has prepared a list of equipment that qualifies as “military equipment” under the bill, which includes 10 M4 rifles which cost an average of $1,000 apiece. The purpose of this equipment, the policy states, is to “enable officers when in compliance with the Department’s Use of Force Policy, to address medium to long distance threats, or those threats who are heavily armed, armored, or both.” Piedmont officers must complete a certified 24-hour patrol rifle course as required by law. Community members with questions are invited to contact the Police Department at (510) 420-3010.
articles.title: Police Dept. publishes information on military-grade equipment funding

Assembly Bill 481, authored by Assemblyman David Chiu (D-San Francisco) and approved by Gov. Gavin Newsom on September 30, 2021, requires all law enforcement agencies to provide guidelines for the approval, acquisition, and reporting requirements of military equipment. The bill is intended to increase transparency and provide oversight on the use of military weapons. Military equipment includes specialized firearms and firearms and ammunition of .50 caliber or greater, excluding standard-issue shotguns. The Piedmont Police Department has prepared a list of equipment that qualifies as “military equipment” under the bill, which includes 10 M4 rifles which cost an average of $1,000 apiece. The purpose of this equipment, the policy states, is to “enable officers when in compliance with the Department’s Use of Force Policy, to address medium to long distance threats, or those threats who are heavily armed, armored, or both.” Piedmont officers must complete a certified 24-hour patrol rifle course as required by law. Community members with questions are invited to contact the Police Department at (510) 420-3010. Rec. articles.text: PHS athlete has second-highest decathlon score in U.S. Parker Terrill won the Del Campo Decathlon in Fair Oaks near Sacramento on Saturday. Piedmont senior Parker Terrill proved he’s much more than a one-event athlete. The recent holder of a new school record in the pole vault at 15-feet, 5-inches, on Saturday he added nine more events and won the decathlon with a score that is second best in the U.S. He ran, threw, and jumped his way to a first-place finish in a field of 12 at the Del Campo Decathlon on Friday and Saturday, April 15-16, at Fair Oaks High School near Sacramento. His 5,964 total points for the 10 events was the second-highest decathlon score in the country this year behind Kaden Passey of Team Shadow Ridge in Arizona. At the Terrill eclipsed Piedmont’s all-time pole vault mark, he said that his prime focus was improving as a complete athlete for the decathlon. Last weekend he provided some proof. At Del Campo he notched personal bests in the 400 and 1500 meters, in addition to the shot put, high jump, and long jump. “I just really wanted to get all my personal records and lifetime bests, and I got five of them. It’s been really fun to see it come all together,” he said. At Del Campo, he defeated Axel Verdoorn of Pleasant Grove in Sacramento by 400 points, and Collin Friedman of El Camino in Sacramento by 600 points. The decathlon is scored by performance in 10 events instead of overall finish. Running events include the 100, 400, and 1500 meter runs, in addition to the 110- meter hurdles. Throwing events are the shot, discus, and javelin, while the jumping events include the high jump, long jump, and Terrill’s specialty, the pole vault. “What matters most is the distance you threw or time you ran. There is some strategy with priority in different events. Throws are pretty significant because they are the first events. Jumps are also significant; points and are based upon how difficult the events are,” explained Terrill.
articles.title: Parker Terrill wins Del Campo Decathlon

articles.text: Photos courtesy of San Jose Earthquakes Will Richmond has made two MLS appearances with the San Jose Earthquakes. and was a starter in Tuesday’s U.S. Open Cup match. Will Richmond, a 2018 Piedmont High grad, is receiving playing minutes with the San Jose Earthquakes in his first year as a professional soccer player after being signed on January 10. He’s in the first year of a threeyear contract after being a former Earthquakes’ Academy player. Although Richmond is churning through a reserve role, it’s impressive to see him getting time in his rookie season. The Earthquakes are currently in last place in Major League Soccer’s Western Conference with a 0-3-4 overall record, Richmond, 22, has made two appearances as a substitute but is regularly listed on the Earthquakes’ game day lineup. So far this season, he’s played in 23 minutes against Philadelphia Union on March 12. and played 22 minutes in a match with Minnesota United on March 19. Against Philadelphia, Richmond completed nine of 13 passes, created one shot opportunity, and had 17 total touches. In his 22 minutes against Minnesota, he had one shot attempt, completed five of seven passes, with a successful dribble by a defender, had one tackle, and finished with 11 touches on the ball. “Will is a player we’ve kept our eye on for several years and we’re happy with the strides he’s made in college,” Earthquakes general manager Chris Leitch said after signing Richmond. “We’re confident he would have been selected very early in the MLS SuperDraft and we’re Will Richmond (left) with Earthquakes general manager Chris Leitch. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 11am-5:30pm 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org

articles.text: The Piedmont Mountain Bike team traveled to Modesto for the NorCal Cycling League’s Modesto Flow event on Sunday, April 10. articles.text: When mentioning the athletic accomplishments of students at Piedmont High, often overlooked are the careers of those who have continued their athletic careers in college. Here’s a look at four Piedmont athletes currently competing in college. Luke Barrett St. Mary’s College, Basketball Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, just finished the winter season as a sophomore on St. Mary’s men’s basketball team. He played in five games last season, including an appearance in the Gaels’ 82-53 win over Indiana in the first round of the NCAA Tournament, where he recorded two rebounds in three minutes of action. Barrett suited up for 15 games last season, averaged 3.9 minutes per game and scored his first career point against Southern Utah in November. He scored a high of five points against Stanislaus State on December 14, where he also recorded two steals and an assist. He also finished with two points, three rebounds, and three assists in just seven minutes of action on February 10 against San Diego. Barrett finished 2022 with 59 minutes played and scored 17 points by making eight of 17 shots from the field (47 percent), converted one 3-point shot, had 14 total rebounds, six assists, and three steals. He’s a member of Piedmont’s 2020 Div. 4 North Coast Section Championship team, and was named Athlete of the Year by the Post. Photo courtesy of SMCGaels.com Luke Barrett, PHS Class of 2020, just finished his sophomore season on the St. Mary’s basketball team. Photo courtesy of Palo Alto Online Miles Fawcett, PHS Class of 2019, is a junior on the Hampton University men’s lacrosse team. Miles Fawcett Hampton University, Lacrosse Miles Fawcett, PHS Class of 2019, is currently a junior and competing on the Hampton lacrosse team this spring, He was a member of Piedmont’s Div.2 North Coast Section championship team. Fawcett has started all nine games for Hampton this season, and has scored eight goals with one assist, 16 shots on target on 34 total attempts, to go along with four ground balls. He’s scored two goals on three occasions this season, scoring twice on February 19 against Mount St. Mary’s, two goals and one assist against Vermont Military Institute on February 21, and two goals against Mercer on April 9. Zoe Torok University of Chicago, Lacrosse Zoe Torok, PHS Class of 2019, a junior at the University of Chicago, is a full-time starter on its lacrosse team, now 12-1, and its leading scorer. She was a member of Piedmont’s Div. 2 North Coast Section Championship team in 2019. Torok leads her team with 42 points, is second on the team with 26 goals, and third with 16 assists. She has six multi-goal games so far, including hat tricks against Hamline University on March 13 and Carroll University on April 7. In 2021 as a sophomore, Torok appeared in 13 games and scored 16 goals to go along with nine assists. The team has three games left in its regular season before the College Conference of Illinois and Wisconsin playoffs. Huggins was an influential starter for the squad, appearing in 24 games and made 21 starts. In 2021-2022, Huggins averaged 21.4 minutes per game and 8.5 points per game, nearly five rebounds per game and an assist per game. She finished with 514 total minutes, made 90 of 177 field goal attempts (51 percent) and was 23 of 37 from the free throw line, to go along with 117 rebounds, 26 assists, 35 steals, and nine blocks. Her best performance came against Cal Maritime on November 10 with 11 of 13 field goals for 23 points, seven rebounds, two assists, and a steal in 17 minutes of action.
