articles.text: Photo courtesy of FIFA.com The 2022 World Cup Draw is out with the United States in Group B with England and Iran, and Wales facing Ukraine or Scotland to play in. The list of teams for each group in the 2022 World Cup was announced on April 4. The United States is in Group B with England, Iran, and the European playoff winner between Wales and Ukraine or Scotland. Instead of the usual July start for the 92-year-old tournament, this year’s World Cup will be played in the winter months due to the excessive summer heat of Qatar, the host country located on the Persian Gulf. Group stage matches will be played November 21 through December 2, with the Round of 16 December 3-6, and quarterfinals on December 9-10. The World Cup semifinal games will be played December 13-14, with the third-place game on December 17 and the championship game on December 18. The U.S. men’s team currently is ranked No. 15 and is the second-highest team in the group behind England at No. 5. If Wales (No. 18) or Ukraine (No. 27) qualify, Group B will be the only group with all four teams in the world’s top-30. Scotland, meanwhile, is no cookie at No. 39 overall. The U.S. and England are set to play the day after Thanksgiving, Friday, November 25, and could be the most-watched U.S. Men’s team game of all time. Provided below is a primer for each team and its key players. England The Three Lions of England are the hands down favorite to win the Group B. Their only loss in a year and a half was on a penalty shootout with Italy in the UEFA Euro Finals on July 11. British fans will undoubtedly have high expectations that the cup will be “coming home” to the argued birthplace of European football. England has a roster of superstars led by Tottenham striker Harry Kane, who has 49 international goals in 69 appearances for England. Other star players who could make the squad include Manchester City’s Raheem Sterling, Jack Grealish, and Phil Foden, Arsenal’s Bukayo Saka, Manchester United Marcus Rashford and Jadon Sancho, and Chelsea’s Mason Mount. If England has any weakness it’s at center back and goalkeeper. Their top choice at CB is Man. United’s Harry Maguire, who is an accident waiting to happen. At keeper, Leicester’s Jordan Pickford likely remains the first choice, but hasn’t been in good form this year. Iran Iran will head into Group B as the biggest underdog. A player to keep an eye on is goalkeeper Alireza Beiranvand, who is more akin to an Olympic Discus thrower. He holds the Guinness World Record for a long-toss in an official match at an estimated 61.26 meters (67 yards). They’ll likely draw a solid crowd of supporters in Qatar. Wales, Ukraine/Scotland On June 5, Wales will face the winner of the Ukraine vs. Scotland match on June 1. Wales’ roster has talent in several top divisions of Europe. Real Madrid’s Gareth Bale, at 32, is a legendary goal scorer and plays at a more inspired level when with his national team. Leeds’ Daniel James is a pacey forward, while Tottenham’s Ben Davies provides a veteran leadership on the backline. Ukraine could become quite the story with the ongoing war with Russia. It’s still unclear if the current situation will prevent them from even competing after postponing the original March 24 play-in against Scotland. Their team has quite the roster with West Ham’s Andriy Yarmolenko, Man. City’s Oleksandr Zinchenko, and Benfica striker Roman Yaremchuk. Scotland will have a strong defense with Liverpool’s Andy Robertson and Arsenal’s Kieran Tierney, and talented midfielders Man. United’s Scott McTominay and Aston Villa’s John McGinn. My prediction would be for Wales to make it into Group B. United States So how does the United States shape up? This is perhaps the most talented U.S. team all time, with players who could represent the USA over the next eight years. There are no excuses for this team to not succeed, with a wealth of players in the top divisions of Europe, to include Chelsea’s Christian Pulisic, Juventus’ Weston McKennnie, RB Leipzig’s Tyler Adams, Dotrmund’s Gio Reyna, and RB Salzburg’s Brenden Aaronson. My early prediction is the United States finishes second to England with wins over Wales and Iran.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 20, 2022 15 HIKING WITH JON Walking among old growths at Portola Redwoods State Park By Jonathan Comeaux Nestled in La Honda of San Mateo County is Portola Redwoods State Park with groves of first- and second-generation old growth redwood trees. The park is a 2,800-acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than those found in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails, although some popular destinations such as Tiptoe Falls are closed due to COVID-19 protocols. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200-year-old giant at the end of the trail that bears its name. the Old Tree Trail. It’s an easy 1.2- mile out-and-back walk. Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within the park. Aside from the awe-striking size, the thousand Take the Summit Trail to start your loop. The path becomes narrow on the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail. You’ll walk along Peter’s Creek on your way back to the car. A look at the ferns along Pescadero Creek. Staff Photos Hikers can still spot the char marks from fires from previous decades along the first- and second-generation redwoods in Portola State Park. The Old Big Tree at the end of the Old Tree Trail is estimated to be a 1,200-year- old redwood 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter. year old tree is among the few old growths to survive the mass lumbering of the 1800s. Continuing back to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill ascent for nearly two miles with an elevation gain of 550 feet. Upon intersecting with the Slate Creek Trail, turn left to start a loop trail back to your car at Peter’s Creek. Turning right begins a 1.5 mile-hike to an historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles with 500 feet in elevation gain to the end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to less than 6-feet wide, so you’ll have to be patient when sharing the trail with other hikers. If you turn left, the trail continues another 0.8 mile until intersecting with Upper Escape Road. Turn right again to get a brief glimpse of Peter’s Creek on the trip back to the car, making it a 4-mile day. We passed 40 people on the day, so just 10 people per mile on average. But it’s worth noting that we crossed 18 hikers on the 0.6 out-and-back Old Tree Trail. Those numbers would be larger if the campgrounds were open, given its popularity with young families. Aside from towering redwoods visible in every direction, you can often spot chickadees chirping about, an occasional banana slug wriggling beneath you, and the knocking of woodpeckers in the distance. Also closed in the park are the Coyote Ridge and Pomponio trails due to wildfires. The Iverson Trail on the way to Tiptoe Falls is also closed. However, the brief walk to the Pascadero Creek is open. Originally published in the Piedmont Post in January 2021. Downed trees line your path on many of the 18 miles of hiking trails in Portola Redwoods State Park. Watch out for banana slugs, a common sight in coastal parks.

articles.text: Marin Theatre Company’s production of Hotter Than Egypt ends this Sunday, April 24, and tickets are still available. The show, written by Yussef El Guindi and directed by John Langs, was selected by MTC’s new Associate Artistic Director Nakissa Etemad. It received its world premiere in a co-production with ACT in Seattle. This play follows protagonist couple Paul and Jean as they travel to Cairo, Egypt for their 24th wedding anniversary. Long-standing troubles within their marriage start to percolate, and their two Egyptian tour guides, newly engaged Maha and Seif, become entwined in the crisis. The play, which the writer describes as a “dramedy,” is set in the aftermath of the Egyptian revolution and explores the uneven power dynamics between these Western tourists and the locals. The cast members include Paul Morgan Stetler, Wasim No’mani Seif, Naseem Etemad, Jen Taylor, and Ahmad Kamal. To purchase tickets, email boxofficer@marintheatre.org or call the box office in Mill Valley at (415) 388-5208. Playbill for Hotter Than Egypt, now playing at Marin Theatre.

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre is currently showing Fefu and her Friends, written by Maria Irene Fornes. The live production, directed by Pam MacKinnon, will be performed now through May 1 at the Strand Theatre in San Francisco. The show, written by Yussef El Guindi and directed by John Langs, was selected by MTC’s new Associate Artistic Director Nakissa Etemad. articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is currently showing exhibition of the works of artist Tauba Auerbach. Born in 1981 in San Francisco, Auerbach creates work that considers the ways that structure, pattern, and gestures function. She is a life-long student of mathematics and physics, and her work connects the microscopic to the universal scale. The artist uses a variety of media – ranging from painting and photography to book design. In her first solo exhibition, Auerbach showed a series of text-based drawings that explored various linguistic systems that included calligraphy, Morse code, semaphore signals, the Ugaritic alphabet and Alexander Melville Bell’s visible speech. The title of the exhibition, “S v Z” is a reference to the close Artist Tauba Auerbach yet indeterminate relationship between form and meaning that surfaces throughout the artist’s materials. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/tauba-auerbach-s-v-z/ to learn more and to plan your next visit to SFMOMA. articles.text: Jules Leyhe and The Family Jules Band brings some of the East Bay’s finest musicians to the Piedmont Center for the Arts for a show on Saturday, April 23. The band features saxophonist Nancy Wright, keyboardist Ian McArdle, and drummer and drummer Isaac Schwartz, who bring a funky jazz flavor to Leyhe’s fantastical vision. Leyhe’s eighth and most recent CD release, Your First Rodeo, has been featured in Premier Guitar and Vintage Guitar magazines. The band looks forward to playing an intimate East Bay show in Piedmont. A 2008 graduate of Piedmont High School and Berklee College of Music in Boston four years later, Leyhe’s career has included performances with legendary musicians Buddy Guy, Jimmie Vaughan, Huey Lewis, Chris Cain, Charlie Musselwhite, and Fantastic Negrito. Leyhe twice performed the National Anthem for the Oakland A’s at the Oakland Coliseum last year, and performs the Hendrix version of the National Anthem each year in the Piedmont 4th of July Parade. During Covid, Leyhe spent time as tour manager for blues legend Taj Mahal. The Family Jules Band stayed busy during Covid, recording three albums. Recent highlight performances include The Club Fox in Redwood City and Napa’s esteemed Blue Note. Tickets for the family-friendly concert in Piedmont are available online at https://bpt.me/5418175. Your First Rodeo CD This ain’t your granddaddy’s blues – heck it ain’t even your daddy’s blues. On this CD guitarist Jules Leyhe is on an entirely different trip, juxtaposing futuristic elements with down-home tones. He has been featured in Guitar Player, Premier Guitar, and Vintage Guitar. His album, Your First Rodeo, is a whimsical mashup of blues, hip-hop, fusion, rock and Latin music. Picture Duane Allman jamming with jazz piano great Gil Evans, or Jimi Hendrix playing in Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band. Jules Leyhe will be performing at the Center for the Arts this Saturday.

Wednesday, April 20, 7:30 PM Ukraine Insight by Anastasia Edel Why did Vladimir Putin attack the sovereign nation of Ukraine, with which Russia shares centuries of common past? What’s behind the brutality of Putin’s war? How much popular support does he enjoy in Russia? Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel, an acclaimed writer, social historian and New York Times contributor, talks about her experience of growing up in the heavily Ukraine-influenced Russian south, the historical and cultural entwinement of the two countries’ natives, and the consequences of this war for Russia and the world. Friday, April 22, 7:00 PM Piedmont School Orchestra Recital Members of the Piedmont High School and Middle School orchestras will perform a recital with solo and chamber pieces. This event is open to all, and donations will be requested at the door. A brief reception will follow the recital. Saturday, April 23, 5:00 PM The Family Jules Jules Leyhe, guitar, and The Family Jules Band bring some of the East Bay’s finest musicians to PCA. Leyhe’s 8th and most recent release, Your First Rodeo, has been featured in several guitar magazines, and the band is pleased to return to Piedmont after their outdoor appearance in early summer. A 2008 graduate of PHS and of Boston’s Berklee College of Music, Leyhe’s career has included performing with many legendary musicians, and he performed the national anthem for the Oakland A’s at the Coliseum twice last year. Advance tickets for this hip-hop, blues, rock, and Latin music show will be available soon. Sunday, April 24, 4:00 PM Victoria Hurd, piano In an effort to support Save the Children Foundation’s Ukraine Crisis Relief Fund, highly-regarded pianist and harpsichordist Victoria Hurd, a graduate of both Vassar and Stanford, will perform a fundraising recital. Whether a Barcarolle, a Sonata, or a Prelude, that literature is full of stories of dreams, sorrow, love, and joy. The program includes the music of Mozart, Beethoven, Chopin, and Fauré. The receipt for any donation to Save the Children will serve as a ticket for admission. You may donate at: https://bit.ly/Recital4UkraineCrisis. Friday, April 29, 7:00 PM. Diluvian String Quartet with Raphael Gold. Piedmont alum Raphael Gold and the Diluvian String Quartet will perform a concert of chamber music inspired by the New World in a concert on Friday, April 29 at 7 p.m. The quartet includes Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. The program includes String Quartet No. 1 by Heitor Villa-Lobos, Five Pieces for String Quartet by Erwin Schulhoff, and Antonin Dvořák‘s masterful String Quartet No. 12 in F Major (“The American”).

articles.text: Piedmont alum Raphael Gold and the Diluvian String Quartet will perform a concert of chamber music inspired by the New World. Come be part of an intimate evening of music at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, April 29 at 7 p.m. The quartet includes Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. The program includes String Quartet No. 1 by Heitor Villa-Lobos, Five Pieces for String Quartet by Erwin Schulhoff, and Antonin Dvořák‘s masterful String Quartet No. 12 in F Major (“The American”). The concert will feature works inspired by the great American music of the turn of the 20th century, including pieces by composers Antonin Dvorak, Heitor Villa Lobos, and Erwin Schulhoff. You’ll hear quotes and rhythms from jazz, tango, and folksong. Proof of vaccination is required.

articles.text: Classical music and Hollywood film composer Erich Korngold. The tawdry spectacle of the most recent Academy Awards accomplished many things. I’m glad to have missed it. Hollywood is a fantasy world onto itself. I’d liken its history to a parabola – with humble beginnings, then the brilliance of music during the Weimar Republic fructified Hollywood. In its present state, Hollywood has regressed into the Stone Age… And that’s being generous. The excellent book Exiles in Hollywood by David Wallace gives a fine overview of the events. Many musicians went to Hollywood because of the lure of the almighty dollar. Stravinsky, in particular, was attracted by the dollar sign. He didn’t have a kind word to say about Hollywood in general, but the money more than made up for it. Rachmaninoff was the exact opposite. He liked the weather in California but rejected everything that Hollywood represented. Others, like George Gershwin, sought legitimacy. And so it was with many musicians. What is so interesting about the entire scene is that all of the exiles maintained close and friendly relations. There were the philosophers, and the writers, and every kind of Hollywood big shot and musicians all over the place. My aunt was the personal secretary to the writer Thomas Mann, and my parents knew the entire Otto Klemperer family. Two of the most interesting musicians of the era were the composers Erich Wolfgang Korngold and Erich Zeisl. Both were born in Vienna around the turn-of-the-century. Korngold had a most sensational childhood and arrived in Hollywood before the catastrophe struck Europe. Zeisl and his wife escaped just in the nick of time. pages.text: Wednesday, April 20, 2022 19 The Musical Gourmet Hurd piano concert at PCA Apr. 24 a benefit for Ukraine Crisis Relief Fund The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Pianist, harpsichordist, and piano teacher Victoria Hurd, a graduate in Early Music at Vassar College and Stanford University, will perform a benefit piano concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, April 24 at 4 p.m. The recital will be grounded in traditional piano literature. Whether a Barcarolle, a Sonata, or a Prelude, the music is filled with stories of dreams, sorrow, love, and joy, all of which we hope the Ukrainian people live to experience. Come hear the stories in music by Mozart, Beethoven, Chopin, and Faure. Ukraine Crisis Relief Fund is part of Save the Children, a top national charity. The receipt for any donation to Save the Children will serve as a ticket for admission. Audience members will need to present vaccination and booster certificates as well as donation receipts, and wear masks while indoors. articles.text: Dan Flanagan is a Berkeley violinist who currently teaches violin at UC Berkeley, is Principal Second of the Berkeley Symphony, Concertmaster of the Sacramento Philharmonic and Opera, Concertmaster of West Edge Opera, and performs with the San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Ballet. He has previously performed as concertmaster with Oakland Symphony, California Symphony, Symphony San Jose, Santa Rosa Symphony, California Musical Theater, Modesto Symphony, and Opera Parallele. He has performed recitals at the Piedmont Center for the Arts multiple times. Dan has been an avid collector since he discovered baseball cards at the age of five. He lost interest in them as a teenager but with the advent of Ebay when he was in grad school, he amassed an impressive collection of historical violinist memorabilia. When he moved to Berkeley 12 years ago, he discovered art auctions and open studios; that’s when the real trouble started. Since then his focus has been French Impressionists and Bay Area abstracts. The works on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts include 45 of his favorite pieces. Many of the artists were in the original Impressionist exhibits of the 1870’s and 1880’s. Dan has a project titled “The Bow and the Brush,” where he performs new compositions inspired by paintings. Two of these pieces were performed in the Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert series on April 10. Twenty-one of these works, each inspired by paintings currently exhibited at the Piedmont Center for the Arts ere, will be premiered by Dan at his Carnegie Hall debut on October 3, followed by the West Coast premieres at Hertz Hall in Berkeley on October 16. Robert Antoine Pinchon (French, 1886-1943). Bruxelles, pluie sur la Grand-Place (Brussels, rain on the Grand-Place), Oil on canvas, 1928. Jose Gonzalez Garcia composed “Cadenza II,” inspired by this painting.

For 11 years he was a volunteer high school basketball coach with the Native American Health Center’s Tribal Athletics Program. After displaying his art at a few powwows and recording a live interview on KPFA, Patten’s art began to sell really well, leading him to acquire a studio off of Piedmont Avenue. He currently uses the space just to paint and for private viewings. “We are drawing people in. The business is taking off on its own, and people are inquiring about us. It is really strange; I didn’t have any intentions to be in art,” Patten said. He credits his wife for being the inspiration and giving him a gift that has grown into something much more. While not open to the public yet, Patten uses the window space Gabriel Patten, a Piedmont resident for over 20 years, recently discovered a secret talent – painting. Patten’s powerful artwork shines a light on Native American tribal culture. His rise to success started with a Christmas present in 2021, when his wife bought him an easel and some paints. “I have been in art all my life, but never had time to do art,” he said recently. “I haven’t been painting very long. I used to doddle, it always came out nice, but that was the extent of it. In the first week [with the easel] I must have put out 10 to 15 paintings. I just started pushing them out. I surprised myself and my wife obviously,” he explained. Patten said he had no intention to show other people his art – he was just painting. However, after sharing images on social media, he started getting requests for prints and t-shirts with his art on it. “I started sharing them with some friends on social media. I had no intention of being a mainstream artist or being out here. But my friends said, ‘You gotta print this; you gotta put this on t-shirts.’” Within three weeks he sold 128 shirts. With the sudden demand, he was taking orders for 300 and 400 shirts at a time. A plumber by trade, Patten has been able to slow down on his plumbing and find more time to paint. Much of his work revolves around Native American themes; he is a full-blood San Carlos Apache Indian, from Arizona and “Prayers Up” by Gabriel Patten pictures a blue sky behind the intersection of tipi poles. Gabriel Patten stands in front of his paintings, “Geronimo” (left) and “Apache Gaan Dancer.” The latter shows Patten’s unique design of the headgear and dress of a crown dancer, like those in Apache Indian ceremonies.
articles.title: Gabriel Patten’s sudden emergence as an artist

articles.text: Josh Brolin, Jeffrey Donovan and Benicio Del Toro star in Sicario: Day of the Soldado Granted, Sicario: Day of the Soldado is a sequel to the first Sicario, but it’s also a standalone, prescient narrative. Like the first, it is superbly written by Taylor Sheridan who has penned, as well, two remarkably good noir neo-westerns, Wind River and Hell or High Water. And it isn’t just the screenwriting talent of Sheridan that lifts Sicario into a different realm of storytelling, but the spot-on performances delivered by Benicio del Toro as Alejandro Gillick and Josh Brolin portraying Matt Garver who appear in both movies as federal agents working the U.S. Mexican border. This region, dangerous in the extreme, is the turf of traffickers who once dealt in cocaine, but have found that it’s far more lucrative to smuggle migrants, meaning those desperate and vulnerable people escaping Central America, many with children in arms, ready to pay the cartels’ coyotes whatever is necessary to get them to their final destination: America. It’s impossible to watch this film and not think of what is currently unfolding on the border. The film opens with images of border agents tracking a group of migrants from a helicopter in the dead of night when one peels off. Alone, he kneels down, takes something out of a backpack, and as a ground patrol closes in detonates a bomb. Cut to three men entering a grocery store in a U.S. border town. Suddenly there are three devastating detonations and bodies are scattered everywhere. This is followed by a photo of three prayer rugs, unfurled, sideby-side, left behind by what is assumed to be the suicidal Jihadi bombers. This gives the government a War on Terror justification to set in motion a plan aimed directly at the cartels who run unobstructed and hugely profitable human trafficking from border towns on both sides. It’s at this point that Graver and Gillick are recruited by U.S. officials to construct a black ops plan intended to start internecine warfare between two competing cartels. The idea: kidnap Isabel Reyes (Isabella Moner), the twelve-year-old daughter of a border trafficker kingpin and place the blame on a rival. And so begins a dark and nihilistic story, one that is searing and gritty, while simultaneously a sublime A-list pulp cinema. It unabashedly examines a harrowing world of consummate evil, where having a conscience or a sense of morality are viewed as character flaws. And yet this is the subtext of the last two acts as the ensuing, overt mayhem proceeds with a bluntness that is relentless. It’s all but impossible to watch a film such as Soldado and not feel sheltered and insulated from the truths that are now unfolding along our southern border. Remarkably, at the center of this narrative is Isabel, a child, really, and it is Alejandro and Matt who each arrive at a point where they are prepared to risk all to save her. One final note: if the above seems a bit vague, it is intended. Sicario: Day of the Soldado is best seen fresh, with as little foreknowledge of plot as possible. Sicario: Day of the Soldado. Directed by Stefano Sollima. Starring Benicio el Toro, Josh Brolin, and Isabel Merced. 2 hrs., 2 min. Rated R. Released 2018. Now streaming on Prime.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Sicario: Day of the Soldado a morality play at the U.S.-Mexico border

articles.text: Encanto, released in theaters in 2021, and now streaming on Disney+, was the winner of the Oscar for Best Animated Feature Film. It has surged in popularity, a musical fantasy with eight songs written by Lin-Manuel Miranda (Hamilton) and has been compared to the remarkable Frozen. Since it appeared it has become a cultural phenom. It tells the tale of an extraordinary, extended, magical Latino family, headed by a 75-year-old matriarch, abuela Alma (Maria Cecelia Botero), who was forced to flee her home with her triplets due to violence that killed her husband Pedro. Because of the suffering she endured, Alma was granted magical powers that are bestowed on her family, to include a sentient house – a casita, located on the side of a hill in the town of Encanto, where the floorboards, staircase, and shutters pulse and throb. In the first song, “The Madrigal Family,” we are introduced to the clan. Each member has passed through a coming-of-age ritual in which they discover their own magical power, also called a “gift.” Emotional Pepa (Carolina Gaitan) can control the weather; beautiful Isabella (Diane Guerrero) can make flowers bloom; sensible Julieta (Angie Cepedal) can heal with her cooking; and Luisa (Jessica Darrow) can lift things. Everyone lives happily in the casita, except for Mirabel (Stephanie Beatriz), a 15-years-old, who is the only member of the family not to receive a special gift. Mirabel is crestfallen, for she realizes that it is the magical powers of the Madrigals that is the source of the community’s continuity. But improbably, it is Mirabel who begins to notice that the foundation of the casita is cracking, and Alma sees that their magic candle is growing dimmer. However, the Madrigals disregard their concerns. As it turns out, it will be up to Mirabel to restore her family’s magic. This effort will involve her uncle Bruno (John Leguizano), the family’s black sheep (conveyed through the song “We Don’t Talk About Bruno”) who can see the future and always tells the truth, no matter how scary. Family, however dysfunctional, is the essence of Encanto, and represents the essential life force, despite each member of the Madrigals secretly feeling the weight of their gift. Luisa, for example, sings the song “Surface Pressure” that expresses the burdensome demands that are made of her. The narrative point made, in so many ways, is that people are worthy because of who they are and not what they do. The challenge is to see your family members for who they really are. The visuals of Encanto are extraordinary, lush and compelling. And there are countless, intimate close-ups of Mirabel, whose emotions consist of bespectacled expressions that convey this smiling tale of family reconciliation. Encanto. Directed by Jared Bush and Byron Howard. With voices of Stephanie Beatriz, Maria Cecilia Botero, and Diane Guerrero. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated PG. Released in theaters in 2021. Now streaming on Disney+.
articles.title: Encanto a lovely, magical Oscar winner

But improbably, it is Mirabel who begins to notice that the foundation of the casita is cracking, and Alma sees that their magic candle is growing dimmer. However, the Madrigals disregard their concerns. As it turns out, it will be up to Mirabel to restore her family’s magic. This effort will involve her uncle Bruno (John Leguizano), the family’s black sheep (conveyed through the song “We Don’t Talk About Bruno”) who can see the future and always tells the truth, no matter how scary. Family, however dysfunctional, is the essence of Encanto, and represents the essential life force, despite each member of the Madrigals secretly feeling the weight of their gift. Luisa, for example, sings the song “Surface Pressure” that expresses the burdensome demands that are made of her. The narrative point made, in so many ways, is that people are worthy because of who they are and not what they do. The challenge is to see your family members for who they really are. The visuals of Encanto are extraordinary, lush and compelling. And there are countless, intimate close-ups of Mirabel, whose emotions consist of bespectacled expressions that convey this smiling tale of family reconciliation. Encanto. Directed by Jared Bush and Byron Howard. With voices of Stephanie Beatriz, Maria Cecilia Botero, and Diane Guerrero. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated PG. Released in theaters in 2021. Now streaming on Disney+.

articles.text: One of my favorite wine tastings of the year is the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) tasting in San Francisco which was held this year at the Palace Hotel on March 27. Zinfandel is not really native to California. Most ampelographers from UC Davis now believe it came to California from Croatia in the 1800s, but it’s certainly the trademark grape of the state. There was even a bill before the state legislature to declare it the official state wine (the Cabernet and Pinot producers protested). Ninety nine percent of the world’s Zinfandel is grown in California and because there is no French equivalent, it is the closest thing we have to a native son. World class Zinfandels are still much less expensive than world class California Cabernets, but unfortunately the price is edging upward. Most of the wines listed below retail for between $25 and $45. These wines can often be found at lower prices at places like the Wine Club in SF or on Wine.com. A note about my prejudices: I like Zinfandels that are fruitladen, big bodied, intense and rich. However it is also important to me that they have acid and structure and not be overblown fruit bombs. I am no fan of the lean and mean “finesse” Zinfandels. (If I want finesse I’ll drink Pinot Noir). Also, I have chosen not to write about the two best known and masterful Zin producers Ridge, and Ravenswood, as most wine lovers already know how great their wines are. Instead, I have sought out lesser-known producers who are doing an outstanding job. The wines below are the cream of this years Zinfandel crop. • 2019 Wilson Zinfandel Reserve, $32 The Wilson Family of wineries makes many outstanding Zinfandels and in the past I have highlighted Mazzocco and St. Anne’s Crossing. This year I was delighted with the 2019 Wilson Reserve Zin. It shows powerful, sweet aromas of ripe black cherries, boysenberries and currants, w i t h s u b - tle wood and spice in the backg rou nd. L a y e r e d , f u l l- b o d ie d , d e n s e, a nd opulent, it is nicely concentrated and yet exquisitely balanced with a long, satisfying finish. • 2019 Rockpile Zinfandel Jack’s Cabin Vineyard, $50 The Rockpile AVA is coming on strong as a producer of world class Zinfandel. Jack’s Cabin Vineyard is planted at 950 feet elevation and is a premier site. The wine made by the Mauritson family reveals copious quantities of earthy, smoky, toasty new oak notes along with saddle leather, and a perfumed mushroomy, blackberry scented nose. Drink this briery, perfumed, concentrated Zinfandel over the next 6 to 7 years. • 2019 Kokomo Zinfandel, $28 This wine from Sonoma’s Dry Creek Valley opens with a nose of cherries, raspberry preserves, and plu ms with hints of baking spices, licorice and chocolate. Big, rich and full-bodied, it packs in the dark fruit flavors with a firm, chewy frame and tons of tart freshness, finishing long and savory • 2020 Castoro Zinfusion The Udsen family started Castoro in 1983 making them one of the pioneer wineries in the Paso Robles area. The Zin grapes are supplemented with Petite Sirah, Primitivo and a splash of Tannat. It offers delicious red and black fruit, violets, herb and barbeque smoke characteristics as well as a lush easygoing mouthfeel finishing with a kiss of vanilla. • 2020 Trentadue La Storia Zinfandel This wine has been a “go to Zinfandel” for many years never failing to please. It is made by the talented winemaker Miro Tcholakov who also has his own label (Miro). This shows off chocolate and cherries notes with touches of prunes, earth, baking spices and raspberry jam. Full, rich, and opulent in the mouth it has stunning harmony with lots of layers and a rich satisfying finish. • 2018 Storrs Zinfandel Rusty Ridge, $34 Storrs has sourced these grapes from a series of old vine vineyards located on the eastern edge of the Santa Cruz Mountains. This area often gets overlooked in the stampede to acquire Napa and Sonoma wines but I find Santa Cruz to be every bit their equal in producing quality wine. The wine offers up copious notes of sweet boysenberry fruit, roasted herbs and a touch of vanilla. Lovely, pure, full-bodied and complex, as well as fresh and elegant, this vibrant, exuberant Zinfandel should drink well for up to 8 years. • 2019 Peachy Canyon Zinfandel Bailey Vineyard, $50 This wine hails from the Adelaida district in Paso Robles. The nose offers, crème de cassis, cherries and dusty soil. The palate is big and rich, full and fruity with blackberry pie, and plum flavors. The finish is long and savory and cries out for some BBQ pork ribs.

The nose offers, crème de cassis, cherries and dusty soil. The palate is big and rich, full and fruity with blackberry pie, and plum flavors. The finish is long and savory and cries out for some BBQ pork ribs. • 2019 Andis Zinfandel Grandpere Vineyard, $60 The famous Grandpere Vineyard was planted in the Sierra Foothills around 1869 and is still in production today. This rubyhued Zin offers briery, cherry, pepper, earth and wildflowers in the bouquet. Lots of blueberry and plum fruit on the medium bodied palate. Good acid and structure on the finish. • 2016 Green and Red Zinfandel Tip Top Vineyard, $42 Medium garnet-purple colored, the Tip Top Zin gives aromas of new leather, spice box, strawberries, and earth. Medium bodied with lots of dried berry and spice flavors on offer in the mouth, it has velvety tannins and plenty of freshness to harmonize and lift the finish. The fresh acidity would make it a great partner to Italian pasta dishes. • 2018 Quivira Black Boar Zinfandel, $55 Quivira is one of the standout wineries in Sonoma County’s Dry Creek Valley and the Black Boar is their premium zinfandel. It shows vivid black cherry and currant fruit notes intertwined with notions of lavender and spice. With a medium to full-bodied mouthfeel, a luscious, pure style, plenty of complexity and elegance. It is delicious now but should last for 7 or 8 years. • 2017 Alexander Valley Vineyards Redemption Zinfandel, $22 The theologically named Redemption Zin from Alexander Valley Vineyards has the varietal’s peppery, raspberry, and cherry fruit, earth and spice, and nice meatiness. It has great structure to support the ample black and red fruit, and a character that begs for some grilled tri-tip or flank steak. • 2018 Baca Zinfandel Home Base, $40 Jennifer Brown shepherds this new Zinfandel label which is part of the Hall family of wines. It is medium garnet-purple colored and opens with lovely potpourri and baking spice notes over a core of blueberry and plum fruit plus touches of dried herbs and leather. Opulently fruited with lots of spicy berry preserves flavors and a chewy frame, it has a good long, refreshing finish. • 2017 Bella Grace Zinfandel Estate, $34 This wine hails from Plymouth in Amador county in the Sierra foothills and I have had the pleasure to write about them before. The nose offers scents of blueberries, cinnamon, spice with notes of cherry preserves, soil and stone fruit aromas emerging with time in the glass. The palate is medium to full-bodied, with lush fruits and plush tannins finishing long and lifted. Great effort. • 2019 Gluntz Family Zinfandel Dante Dusi Vineyard, $40 The Dusi family owns some prime old vine Zinfandel Vineyards in Paso Robles and the Gluntz winery is the beneficiary of these prime grapes. The dense, thick, juicy 2019 Gluntz Zin displays a deep color. Ripe boysenberry and blueberry fruit intertwined with pepper and balsam wood notes are found in this long glycerin-imbued Zinfandel. It is so packed with fruit and flavor, no food is required – it is a meal in itself. • 2018 Hendry Zinfandel Block 28, $38 I have lost track of how many times Hendry has appeared in my list of top Zinfandels – their consistency is inspiring. The 2018 Block 28 Zin is an attractive, juicy wine layered with plums, dark red fruit and licorice. Hightoned and floral notes and a hint of pepper ad lift to the finish. This is a totally inviting, luscious red best enjoyed in its exuberant youth. • 2020 Florence Vineyard Zinfandel This is the first release under the Florence label for Jack Florence a grower in the Rockpile AVA. The debut offering offers blackberry and cassis notes with a subtle plum laced undercurrent plus spice box, black soil and floral hints. The concentrated medium-bodied palate is densely packed with dried berry and baking spice flavors with plush tannins and a lively lift to the finish. Future looks very promising. • 2019 Once and Future Zinfandel Oakley Road, $50 Most people don’t know that one of the best old vine Zinfandel vineyards in the entire state is in, of all places, Contra Costa County. The suburban town of Oakley boasts historic Zin vineyards planted a hundred years ago. Blackberry liqueur infused with smoke jumps from the glass of this delicious Zinfandel. Explosive in the mouth, with ample extract levels, fruit, and glycerin, but no heaviness or heat, this is an opulently textured luscious offering to drink over the 5-6 years. • 2019 Seghesio Zinfandel Home Ranch, $70 Seghesio’s Home Ranch Zinfandel is a perennial top performer at the ZAP tasting. The enormous bouquet of blackberries, chocolate, cherries, herbs, and coffee is as exotic as it is multidimensional. The wine exhibits opulently rich, expansive, full-bodied flavors oozing with extraction. This is a terrific, full-bodied voluptuously textured Zin for drinking over the next decade. • 2019 St. Francis Zinfandel Reserve, $45 Sonoma County’s St. Francis winery has put forth a compelling wine graced with expressive dark red fruit, flowers, mint, and licorice. It shows gorgeous finesse, plenty of mid-palate richness and terrific overall balance. Sweet floral notes and succulent black cherries wrap around the finish. • 2019 Rombauer Zinfandel Twin Rivers, $42 The Twin Rivers Zin is medium garnet-purple colored and scented of crushed cherries blackberry pie with hints of Chinese five spice and dried herbs. Full-bodied, rich, and spicy in the mouth, it has a solid frame of soft tannins and a firm backbone, finishing long and peppery. • 2019 Trestle Glen Zinfandel This was my first introduction to Sonoma County’s Trestle Glen Winery. Their 2019 Zin reveals ripe blueberry and plum fruit with notions of spice and pepper in its fragrant, expressive bouquet. Medium-bodied, with nicely integrated wood and no hard edges, it will drink well for 5 or 6 years. Nice effort. • 2017 David Clinton Zinfandel Mounts Vineyard, $30 A beautiful nose of licorice blackberries, cherry liqueur, and underbrush emerges from this dense ruby/purple-colored wine. In the mouth, it is medium bodied, powerful as well as elegant, intense and balanced, with well-integrated acidity, alcohol and wood. This graceful yet substantial effort would be a great partner to roast pork or carnitas. • 2019 Easton Estate Zinfandel, $35 The 2019 Easton Zin offers gorgeous plum, prune, cherry and raspberry fruit notes intermixed with chocolate, smoke, pepper and earth. It has a big round mouthfeel with loads of dark berry fruit that is nicely balanced with good acid and structure. Would be an excellent partner to some grilled steak.

articles.text: Well-meaning family members and friends often give an enthusiastic “Yes!” when someone asks for a little help at home due to age, illness, or other life change that leaves them in need of support. It feels good to help someone out and make them happier, after all. However, this temporary commitment can soon expand into something that requires more than they can handle in terms of time, physical strength, or emotional stamina. Injured on the “Job” A family member may offer to help someone simply step safely out of the tub, and then find themselves with a back injury. There are proper techniques for lifting someone from a chair or bed, or assisting them in the bathroom, which professional caregivers receive training for. A possible solution is to determine which aspects of care seem the riskiest for the person who is helping out, then hire a caregiver to step in for those specific tasks instead. This might mean just an hour or two per day; giving the family member a little break and keeping them safe as well. What’s burnout? The definition of burnout is “fatigue, frustration, or apathy resulting from prolonged stress, overwork, or intense activity.” When an untrained family member or friend attempts to be a caregiver, while possibly balancing work or family responsibilities, they can burn out. It’s impossible to keep adding more and more to your plate, especially when you don’t really know what to do, or what’s coming next… Eventually the plate comes crashing down. Establishing boundaries is important for family caregivers so that they don’t experience burnout. If they’re not careful other issues can develop while caring for an elder loved one, such as stress at work or with children in the home. Consider asking other friends or family to share the responsibilities of caregiving or hire someone to be part of your care team. Feelings matter Caregivers can feel resentful, and it’s perfectly natural, especially if they give too much of themselves without much in return. Ideally, a care relationship can involve both give and take so that resentment doesn’t develop. Finding others who are having similar experiences can be helpful for negative feelings affecting a caregiver. There are all kinds of support groups, both online and in person, in which family caregivers can vent, learn, and share. Support groups might be for caregiving in general or for a specific type of caregiving such as for someone who is living with dementia or Parkinson’s disease. These groups may be an offshoot of an organization such as the Alzheimer’s Association or a local church. When a family member or friend begins to experience some of the possible challenges of caregiving, a professional caregiver can step in to ease the burden. Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com.
articles.title: Caregiver burnout and other risks

articles.text: Did you know that April is National Poetry Month? It reminds us that poets have an integral role to play in our culture and that poetry matters. Over the years, it has become the largest literary celebration in the world. Our own Oakland Public Library has a variety of programs, new books of poetry on display, and performances by Oakland’s poets to help you celebrate. My interest piqued, I asked myself ”why poetry?” Researchers at Johns Hopkins University have found that poetry can provide comfort and boost mood during periods of stress, trauma and grief. It’s a powerful combination of words, metaphor and meter that help us better express ourselves and make sense of the world and our place in it. The benefits of poetry can extend to just about anyone. Using poetry to find our own voice can open up new ways of expressing ourselves and discovering ways to heal and restore us. The residents at The Lake Merritt – Independent Senior Living have a monthly club where they share their favorite poems with each other as well as offering up some they have written. Our resident Cleo told me, “Poetry says a lot in so many ways to different individuals. It’s a way of expressing yourself to others.” Another resident, Laura, agrees and remembers her mother reading poetry to her when she was a baby. Laura recited and actually performed “Mumps,” by Elizabeth Madox Roberts. Besides winning first place, I can still recite that poem several decades later. Our community has always been engaged with the local public library. Last fall we hosted a special online reading by the award-winning young writers from the Oakland Youth Poet Laureate Program, a program of the Oakland Public Library. Designed to celebrate literacy through poetry and connect young writers to the public, we were happy to have two of the program’s finalists speak to us. Dara Kashayar and Siara Edmond read some of their poems and were asked questions by our residents and those watching our online Zoom program. You still have time to celebrate National Poetry Month. Stop by your local library and pick up a book of poetry by Walt Whitman or Maya Angelou. Boost your brain power by committing a poem to memory. You’ll be glad you did. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living. For more information about The Lake Merritt or its current Topics of Merritt series, call 510-903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com. Lake Merritt resident Gloria Frey enjoys reading poetry. then recited a poem to me that she remembered from her early childhood. Laura’s experience supports the theory that our brains are highly attuned to rhyme and rhythm in poetry. As every parent knows, infants respond to rhymes, youngsters and teenagers respond to lyrics, which are like poems combined with melody, and even football fans enjoy participating in rhythmic chants at the stadium. Studies have also shown that some poetry boosts memory and encourages self-reflection. Words can stick with you and inspire you to re-read a poem and often memorize the words. Poetic words tend to be easier to memorize than non-poetic ones. Our resident Laura reminded me of my second-grade speech competition where I memorized, Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just got a MacBook Pro, and since I am not going into work, I have time to learn how to use it. I am coming from the PC world, so everything is different. Where do I start? –Leslie G., Oakland Dear Leslie: Congrats on your new purchase, and luckily, there are many good sources that provide information on becoming comfortable on the Mac platform. You can find help with books, online print sources, and videos. Here are some of my favorite sources. Books: I am still a page turning learner, and if I am learning something new, I like to sit with a highlighter and a book, and study like the old days! There are some excellent books on switching to Mac, whether you are a tech savvy user, or more of a beginner. The “For Dummies” series is excellent, and there is a “Switching to a Mac for Dummies”. Anything by David Pogue is great, although a bit more technical. One that I would strongly recommend is “macOS Catalina for Dummies” by Bob LeVitus. Also, the “for seniors” volumes are usually well written, specifically “Mac OS Catalina for Seniors” by Scott La Counte. Be aware that if these volumes are not current (2019 or later), the info might be outdated. Websites: Apple itself has a web page devoted to folks who switched to Mac from PCs: https://support.apple.com/en-us/ HT204216 You can find lots of good info here. I also really like the “How to Geek” (https://www. howtogeek.com/437168/how-toswitch-from-a-windows-pc-to-amac/). Another good source is wired. com. If you do a Google search “switching from PC to Mac” there are countless links from established sites Videos (YouTube): This is most likely your best bet. Anson Alexander has really good video series and his Mac tutorial for beginners is excellent (https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=67keaaWOKzE). Another good video is by macmost.com, including a video on “Questions New Mac Owners Have When Switching from Windows” (https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=vau_4NpkEB8). Of course, there are plenty of videos by helpful pros, and if you just got a new mac, you can always call AppleCare with any questions: 1-800-275-2273. I think you will find that there are many similarities, and the differences are mostly for power users. Of course, the file structure is different, and the user experience is also a bit different. If you are a photographer, artist or musician, you will appreciate the amount of software for you. And these days, the current version of Microsoft Office apps like Word and Excel are almost exactly the same on the Mac as PC. I would say that within a month or so you will feel like a pro. If you need more guidance, contact me, I am doing all of my support appointments remotely these days. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com.

Our resident Cleo told me, “Poetry says a lot in so many ways to different individuals. It’s a way of expressing yourself to others.” Another resident, Laura, agrees and remembers her mother reading poetry to her when she was a baby. Laura recited and actually performed “Mumps,” by Elizabeth Madox Roberts. Besides winning first place, I can still recite that poem several decades later. Our community has always been engaged with the local public library. Last fall we hosted a special online reading by the award-winning young writers from the Oakland Youth Poet Laureate Program, a program of the Oakland Public Library. Designed to celebrate literacy through poetry and connect young writers to the public, we were happy to have two of the program’s finalists speak to us. Dara Kashayar and Siara Edmond read some of their poems and were asked questions by our residents and those watching our online Zoom program. You still have time to celebrate National Poetry Month. Stop by your local library and pick up a book of poetry by Walt Whitman or Maya Angelou. Boost your brain power by committing a poem to memory. You’ll be glad you did. Tim Johnson is Executive Director of The Lake Merritt - Independent Senior Living. For more information about The Lake Merritt or its current Topics of Merritt series, call 510-903-3600 or visit www.thelakemerritt.com. Lake Merritt resident Gloria Frey enjoys reading poetry. then recited a poem to me that she remembered from her early childhood. Laura’s experience supports the theory that our brains are highly attuned to rhyme and rhythm in poetry. As every parent knows, infants respond to rhymes, youngsters and teenagers respond to lyrics, which are like poems combined with melody, and even football fans enjoy participating in rhythmic chants at the stadium. Studies have also shown that some poetry boosts memory and encourages self-reflection. Words can stick with you and inspire you to re-read a poem and often memorize the words. Poetic words tend to be easier to memorize than non-poetic ones. It feels good to help someone out and make them happier, after all. However, this temporary commitment can soon expand into something that requires more than they can handle in terms of time, physical strength, or emotional stamina. Injured on the “Job” A family member may offer to help someone simply step safely out of the tub, and then find themselves with a back injury. There are proper techniques for lifting someone from a chair or bed, or assisting them in the bathroom, which professional caregivers receive training for. A possible solution is to determine which aspects of care seem the riskiest for the person who is helping out, then hire a caregiver to step in for those specific tasks instead. This might mean just an hour or two per day; giving the family member a little break and keeping them safe as well. What’s burnout? The definition of burnout is “fatigue, frustration, or apathy resulting from prolonged stress, overwork, or intense activity.” When an untrained family member or friend attempts to be a caregiver, while possibly balancing work or family responsibilities, they can burn out. It’s impossible to keep adding more and more to your plate, especially when you don’t really know what to do, or what’s coming next… Eventually the plate comes crashing down. Establishing boundaries is important for family caregivers so that they don’t experience burnout. If they’re not careful other issues can develop while caring for an elder loved one, such as stress at work or with children in the home. Consider asking other friends or family to share the responsibilities of caregiving or hire someone to be part of your care team. Feelings matter Caregivers can feel resentful, and it’s perfectly natural, especially if they give too much of themselves without much in return. Ideally, a care relationship can involve both give and take so that resentment doesn’t develop. Finding others who are having similar experiences can be helpful for negative feelings affecting a caregiver. There are all kinds of support groups, both online and in person, in which family caregivers can vent, learn, and share. Support groups might be for caregiving in general or for a specific type of caregiving such as for someone who is living with dementia or Parkinson’s disease. These groups may be an offshoot of an organization such as the Alzheimer’s Association or a local church. When a family member or friend begins to experience some of the possible challenges of caregiving, a professional caregiver can step in to ease the burden. By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just got a MacBook Pro, and since I am not going into work, I have time to learn how to use it. I am coming from the PC world, so everything is different. Where do I start? –Leslie G., Oakland Dear Leslie: Congrats on your new purchase, and luckily, there are many good sources that provide information on becoming comfortable on the Mac platform. You can find help with books, online print sources, and videos. Here are some of my favorite sources. Books: I am still a page turning learner, and if I am learning something new, I like to sit with a highlighter and a book, and study like the old days! There are some excellent books on switching to Mac, whether you are a tech savvy user, or more of a beginner. The “For Dummies” series is excellent, and there is a “Switching to a Mac for Dummies”. Anything by David Pogue is great, although a bit more technical. One that I would strongly recommend is “macOS Catalina for Dummies” by Bob LeVitus. Also, the “for seniors” volumes are usually well written, specifically “Mac OS Catalina for Seniors” by Scott La Counte. Be aware that if these volumes are not current (2019 or later), the info might be outdated. Websites: Apple itself has a web page devoted to folks who switched to Mac from PCs: https://support.apple.com/en-us/ HT204216 You can find lots of good info here. I also really like the “How to Geek” (https://www. howtogeek.com/437168/how-toswitch-from-a-windows-pc-to-amac/). Another good source is wired. com. If you do a Google search “switching from PC to Mac” there are countless links from established sites Videos (YouTube): This is most likely your best bet. Anson Alexander has really good video series and his Mac tutorial for beginners is excellent (https://www.youtube.com/ watch?v=67keaaWOKzE). Another good video is by macmost.com, including a video on “Questions New Mac Owners Have When Switching from Windows” (https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=vau_4NpkEB8). Of course, there are plenty of videos by helpful pros, and if you just got a new mac, you can always call AppleCare with any questions: 1-800-275-2273. I think you will find that there are many similarities, and the differences are mostly for power users. Of course, the file structure is different, and the user experience is also a bit different. If you are a photographer, artist or musician, you will appreciate the amount of software for you. And these days, the current version of Microsoft Office apps like Word and Excel are almost exactly the same on the Mac as PC. I would say that within a month or so you will feel like a pro. If you need more guidance, contact me, I am doing all of my support appointments remotely these days. Cookie Segelstein is the Macmama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com. articles.text: Tom Webster died at home in Piedmont peacefully, after a hemorrhagic stroke, surrounded by his family on February 26, 2022. He was 80 years old. Tom was born on January 13, 1942, in North Hollywood. The son of Phillip and Lilian Webster, he was the oldest of five children – brothers Calvin, John, and Bill and a sister, Barbara. Tom’s father was a mechanic and from the beginning of Tom’s life it was clear that he inherited his father’s genes. He had an insatiable desire to understand how things worked, both tangible and intangible. Tom started by getting in trouble for taking apart the family toasters and televisions when he was small, then moved on to working on cars throughout his youth and adolescence. Tom attended high school in Folsom, CA where he played football and cruised around in his 1955 Chevy. He was elected senior class president and was named Best All Around for the class of 1959. Tom graduated from UC Berkeley with a degree in Mechanical Engineering in 1964. After graduation, his best friend Ben Clawson, also a mechanical engineer, decided with Tom it was time for an adventure so they set out to build a sailboat. Six years later, Galatea, a 38-foot trimaran was finished and Tom, and Chris Weahunt – his girlfriend who became his wife of almost 50 years – and Ben started sailing adventures over a period of several years. The adventures took them down the coast of Mexico, out to Cocos Island, and onto the Galapagos where they were among the last group of private boats allowed to visit unaccompanied by a guide or organization. It was on these adventures, and especially time spent with Peace Corps volunteers in Central America where he became inspired to apply his engineering background to sustainable energy, moving onto the solar energy group at Lawrence Berkeley Lab (LBL). Tom and Chris were married for 48 years and had a loving and enduring relationship of 52 years. They went on many travels and adventures together over the years, from sailing trips, backTom Webster, a resident of Piedmont since 1993, died on February 26, 2022. He was 80. packing, travels through Central and South America, Europe, and numerous family vacations. They supported each other’s passions and interests and shared commitments of family, adventure, health, good food and wine, and sustainability. Tom was a loving, and committed father to two children, Brett (1982) and Kelsey (1986). Even through his busy and successful career of 53 years as an engineer, Tom made himself available to his children whenever they needed him – from before-school breakfasts, playing catch in the yard and attending ballet classes and performances, to lending a compassionate ear and shoulder to cry on, Tom was ever-present for his children. He and Chris made an excellent parenting team, something his children now attempt to emulate with their own children. Tom was the officiant at Kelsey and Nate’s wedding in 2014, as well as Brett and Laney’s in 2021. For the last years of his life, Tom was an exemplary grandfather (“Opa”) to Kelsey’s two children, Skylar (2017) and Hayden (2021). Laney is expecting a child this year, unfortunately one who won’t meet her Opa in person. Tom worked as an engineer initially for a few different companies before becoming a research engineer (upon return from his sailing adventures) for UC Berkeley. He worked at LBL (1976-1982) and Center for the Built Environment (CBE, 1995-2017), using a break from 1982-1995 to co-start an independent HVAC controls company, Energyline. Tom and his family moved to Piedmont in 1993 after their Oakland home was lost in the 1991 Oakland Hills fire. After his retirement from CBE, Tom became involved with Piedmont Connect, generously volunteering his engineering experience to help the City reduce greenhouse gas emissions. His meticulous energy and cost calculations and advocacy helped make plans for an all-electric city pool in Piedmont. In addition to engineering, Tom was very interested and dedicated to the study of Buddhism and spirituality. He began meditating and doing spiritual growth work in 1995, deepening and expanding his practice throughout the remainder of his life. He started following Adyashanti in 2005 and attended several silent retreats at Spirit Rock and Tassajara. Tom was a deeply kind, generous, loving person with a zest and energy for life that was unmatched. He made a lasting impact on people, whether they knew him for years or met him only briefly, with his genuine curiosity and interest in the well-being and goings-on of others. He had a rich and wonderful life, and he will be so sorely missed by all those who had the pleasure of knowing him, especially his family.

On the drive to the campground Lauren “Mai” Levy said, “I feel really excited because this will be my first campout with Troop 15.” When all the cars had arrived at Two Rocks campground, Senior Patrol Leader Nate Woodley gathered everyone into a circle so we could introduce ourselves before Nate went over the rules and discussed the agenda for the weekend. We learned about choosing a good spot for a tent and put up our tents over ground cloths, laid out our sleeping pads and sleeping bags, and stowed our gear. “My favorite thing about the campout was when I set up my tent with the friends I was sharing the tent with,” said Ganden Deming. “I learned the importance of keeping my tent door zipped shut,” added Scout Bryan Heafey. The Scouts split into groups of Ashlan Mitchell, a Havens 5th grader, with her mother Dana Mitchell. Havens fifth grader Willow Thomas with her mom, Diana Thomas. Henry Ciriacruz (left), Lucas Bekele, Alex Mikhailov, Chase Knapp and Joaquin Fierro fish using gear they cobbled together at Lake Chabot. Parent David Ragones replenishes hot water while Evan Friedman (left) washes his pre-wiped plate under the watchful eye of Diego Branneria and Alex Mikhailov. Joaquin Fierro, Lucas Bekele, and Quinton Cole look up to Nate Woodley while preparing dinner. Adelina Mbise secures a rain fly over her tent. three with helpful, older Scouts teaching the skills necessary to fulfill rank requirements. We learned about knives, an ax and saw, and practiced using different knots – the taut line hitch, square knot, and two half hitches. We fused and “whipped” the ends of ropes so they wouldn’t fray. When we broke for lunch, Nate encouraged each patrol to prepare a skit for later. We took off for a mile-long hike with our packed lunches to the shore of Lake Chabot. On the trail, we used the buddy system to ensure safety, discussed outdoor ethics, identified some poison oak, and made sure to not litter. We spotted a salamander in the creek. We hung out with our new friends eating lunch and playing cards. Some made simple fishing gear from natural poles, using worms as bait and gear discarded by fishermen. Patrol Leader Christiane Zuber put her new patrol members at ease with a conversation on various topics. At the lake we saw some beetles, and spiders. During the afternoon we formed new groups so more people could meet each other. We learned about basic first aid for rattlesnake bites, burns, cuts and scrapes, and assembled first aid kits to keep in our packs. We practiced reciting the Scout Oath and Scout Law from memory. Soon it was time for each patrol to make dinner. Some Scouts made pasta and sauce, some made hamburgers, and others made grilled cheese sandwiches. The day ended with a closing circle, in which we gave thanks to the parents, drivers, Scout leaders, and fellow Scouts who had supported us. The Scouts fell asleep to the sound of crickets and owls. Assistant Scoutmaster John Woodley noted that 5th graders not yet comfortable sleeping outside their home or away from family are welcome to bring along a parent. articles.text: Piedmont City Council voted unanimously to move forward with full electrification of the new Piedmont Community Pool at an April 4 meeting. With high costs to bear, Council members also directed city staff to seek fundraising and partnership opportunities before the pool’s completion in summer 2024 aimed to offset the costs of an all-electric aquatic facility. An Energy Use Report provided to the city by Guttman & Blaevoet Consulting Engineers found that electrifying the entire facility would be feasible, if a combination of electric heat pumps, photovoltaic/thermal (PVT) Panels, and integration with the clean electrical grid was employed. Upfront costs required to construct an all-electric pool is estimated at $500,000 - which includes 18 heat pump childless, four heat exchangers, HVAC-related items, seismic work, and other construction costs. Operational costs are more difficult to calculate, according to an accompanying staff report; however, the costs savings of electric versus gas is estimated to be more than $1,150,000 over 25 years. The report stated, “the combination of PV and PVT panels and electrified systems provides the best return on investment saving over $1.5 million over the 25-year period studied while reducing the carbon equivalent emissions to zero for the site when we consider the clean energy sources available to the City of Piedmont.” The City of Mountain View adopted a plan to electrify its community pool on February 8, 2022; Mountain View City Council awarded the construction contract for the Rengstorff Park Aquatics Center Project to Bobo Construction, which is scheduled to begin completion this month with a completion of Sumer 2023. The project features an all-electric system of solar panels that provide PV and solar thermal energy to heat the 500,000-gallon pool. Cou nci l me mbe r Con n a McCarthy acknowledged that moving forward with all-electric would be a “real opportunity for Piedmont to be a leader” in sustainable community aquatic facilities. articles.text: Piedmont Housing Puzzle open for public comment through May 1 The City of Piedmont has published its Draft Housing Element for the 6th Housing Cycle on the city website and Piedmontishome.org. The 374- page document, published April 8, details policies that aim to increase housing access and affordability in Piedmont. All community members, including city staff and school employees, are encouraged to review and provide comment on the draft that will be considered by City Council and Planning Commissioners. Comments received before May 5 will be considered by Planning Commissioners at the first public hearing regarding the draft housing element. “This document (Draft Housing Element) is foundational for us as a City, in regard to how we look forward to build our community for the next several years,” said Mayor Teddy Gray King at the March 24 community workshop, which included a report on the progress of work to prepare the Draft Housing Element. “Our Housing Element holds the key to many issues including our approaches to housing, greenhouse gas emissions reduction, transportation, educational opportunity, and others. Housing is fundamental to the health and well-being of any community, including Piedmont.” To review the document, visit https://www.piedmont.ca.gov/ government/city_news___notifications/draft_housing_element_ released. Comments may also be e-mailed to Piedmontishome@ piedmont.ca.gov, using the Piedmont Housing Puzzle (see below), or by mail to: Draft Housing Element, 120 Vista Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611. Interested parties may also attend the upcoming Housing Advisory Committee meeting on April 19, and/or the Planning Commission meeting on May 12. Both meetings start at 5:30 p.m. Piedmont Housing Puzzle The City has launched the Piedmont Housing Puzzle, an interactive digital tool that allows residents to choose appropriate locations in town for 587 new housing units. The deadline to provide comment is May 1. So far, over 200 Piedmont community members have participated in the tool, Piedmont Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald confirmed. The City will produce a draft of the next housing element by mid-April. “We have received approximately 90 housing plan submissions, as of [Friday, April 8], and we hope to reach even more community members. We are compiling all of the results and all of the comments from the red comment bubble feature in the Piedmont Puzzle for the Planning Commission review at their public hearing on May 12,” Macdonald said. To submit comments and suggestions before the May 1 deadline, visit: https://piedmont.abalancingact.com/housingsim.
articles.title: Draft Housing Element now available

articles.text: Parents for Educational Excellence in Piedmont, a 501(c) (4) Changes to Piedmont School District’s curriculum inspired by Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging (DEI-B) have happened, and more are in the planning stages. These changes go beyond the Humanities and Social Sciences and they negatively impact STEM subject areas. Parents may not be aware that curriculum decisions used to be made by the teachers in each of the subject areas they taught. The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) funded a position to centralize curriculum decisions and their speaker series promoted widely disputed educational pseudo-science. For PUSD there is no statistically significant difference in CAASPP academic performance between White and NonWhite (a.k.a. BIPOC) students. Distance learning during the pandemic caused a real decline in CAASPP performance, and many more Piedmont students are delaying going to college than ever before. Despite these facts, the administration is seeking principals for both Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School who will primarily comply with the district’s DEI-B agenda and are trying to hide their hiring rubric with a non-disclosure-agreement. Piedmont School District has gone to great lengths to encourage appreciating racial and cultural diversity. Racism will never be wiped out completely and doesn’t justify radical changes to the curriculum that will negatively impact educational excellence in Piedmont. The link to my CAASPP study with splits by Gender and White/ Non-White is https://harititan. com/CAASPP_Piedmont_Unified_School_District.pdf.
articles.title: What is Piedmont School District’s new standard for educational excellence?

articles.text: Many Christians do something very odd on Palm Sunday. We gather together and we intentionally tell only part of a story. We read the passion narrative where Jesus is arrested and murdered by the empire. And we stop there. We intentionally do not read on to the positive end of the story. Luke’s version of the passion narrative simply ends, “On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.” I always feel a bit like a child being read a bedtime story by a parent, who closes the book right when you can’t stand it to end, and says, “It’s time for bed and you need your rest”. I want to cry out, “No, don’t stop at this part of the story”. I would rather run past the deep turmoil of the passion story to the victorious end we read on Easter Morning. But Palm Sunday teaches us to close the book and rest in a place of introspection right in the middle of our turmoil, by taking the time to be mindfully present to what we are truly feeling in the present. pages.text: 2 Wednesday, April 13, 2022 Opinion What is Piedmont School District’s new standard for educational excellence? By Hari Titan Parents for Educational Excellence in Piedmont, a 501(c) (4) Changes to Piedmont School District’s curriculum inspired by Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging (DEI-B) have happened, and more are in the planning stages. These changes go beyond the Humanities and Social Sciences and they negatively impact STEM subject areas. Parents may not be aware that curriculum decisions used to be made by the teachers in each of the subject areas they taught. The Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) funded a position to centralize curriculum decisions and their speaker series promoted widely disputed educational pseudo-science. For PUSD there is no statistically significant difference in CAASPP academic performance between White and NonWhite (a.k.a. BIPOC) students. Distance learning during the pandemic caused a real decline in CAASPP performance, and many more Piedmont students are delaying going to college than ever before. Despite these facts, the administration is seeking principals for both Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School who will primarily comply with the district’s DEI-B agenda and are trying to hide their hiring rubric with a non-disclosure-agreement. Piedmont School District has gone to great lengths to encourage appreciating racial and cultural diversity. Racism will never be wiped out completely and doesn’t justify radical changes to the curriculum that will negatively impact educational excellence in Piedmont. The link to my CAASPP study with splits by Gender and White/ Non-White is https://harititan. com/CAASPP_Piedmont_Unified_School_District.pdf. There is no way to peace; peace is the way By the Rev. Scott Denman Many Christians do something very odd on Palm Sunday. We gather together and we intentionally tell only part of a story. We read the passion narrative where Jesus is arrested and murdered by the empire. And we stop there. We intentionally do not read on to the positive end of the story. Luke’s version of the passion narrative simply ends, “On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.” I always feel a bit like a child being read a bedtime story by a parent, who closes the book right when you can’t stand it to end, and says, “It’s time for bed and you need your rest”.
