articles.text: The California Building Standards Code (California Code of Regulations, Title 24) sets statewide building code standards. Title 24, Part 6, also known as the California Building Energy Efficiency Standards or “Energy Code”, contains mandatory measures for residential buildings (single family and multi-family) and non-residential buildings and sets an energy budget for each type of building. Title 24 receives updates every three years to incorporate the latest changes in construction and technology. The latest update (2019 Energy Code) went into effect on January 1, 2020. Starting January 1, 2023, the 2022 Energy Code will go into effect. When the Energy Code is updated, all cities and counties need to adopt the new Code and any local amendments to the Code. Reach codes are local amendments that go above and beyond existing California building codes to improve the energy efficiency of buildings and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Here in Piedmont, the City Council adopted Ordinance 750 N.S., establishing reach codes in Piedmont, in February 2021. The ordinance went into effect on June 1, 2021 for low-rise residential buildings. The primary goal of the reach codes is to help Piedmont meet its Climate Action Plan (CAP) 2.0 emission reduction goals by reducing natural gas use and increasing building electrification efforts. Natural gas use in residential buildings is one of the biggest obstacles to achieving the City’s CAP 2.0 goals, consistently comprising about half of Piedmont’s in-territory emissions. Since June 1, 2021, Piedmont has made it a priority to assess the implementation of reach codes for residential buildings in Piedmont. These efforts include evaluation of building permits and the effectiveness of the policy, in addition to community outreach and engagement. This process is important to the City as staff begin to prepare for adopting the new energy code and re-adopting applicable reach code amendments. To help inform residents, City staff members are launching the 2022 reach code public engagement process. The first component is asking residents to complete an online survey to provide feedback about the current reach codes and suggestions for the next round. The online survey is live and will be open until May 20. A link to the survey can be found online at the City’s Reach Code Information page at https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning _ _ _building/about_ building_/reach_code_information. All those who complete the online survey will be enrolled in a raffle to receive a bill credit from Piedmont’s local electricity service provider, East Bay Community Energy (EBCE). The second component will be a Reach Code Community Forum next Wednesday, April 20, from 6:00 to 7:30 p.m. at Piedmont Community Hall, 701 Highland Avenue. City staff will present an overview of Piedmont’s current reach codes, the 2022 Energy Code, and initial considerations for the next set of reach codes, followed by a community workshop where attendees will be asked to provide comments and recommendations about the current and future code. Registration for the in-person event is encouraged but not required. To register, see: https:// docs.google.com /for ms/d /e/ 1FA I p QL Sf z s K AQ32 t 2 h h - k59XZIlC8k83R8GTjocs_EvbkIQygjQmr4UQ/viewform. All attendees will be entered into a raffle to win a free energy savings kit and EBCE bill credit. For more information about the reach codes and upcoming events, visit the City’s Reach Code Information webpage. Additional information about building electrification, rebates, resources, and incentives available for Piedmonters can be found at https://www.piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ planning _ _ _building/about_ building_/electrification. Alyssa Dykman is the city’s Sustainability Program Manager. She can be reached at adykman@ piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Upcoming events on City’s Reach Codes

articles.text: The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present a Zoom webinar at 6 p.m. on Thursday, May 5, entitled Power to Heal, featuring the documentary film The Power to Heal: Medicare and the Civil Rights Revolution, a film by Charles Burnett. The event will be co-hosted by the City, the Piedmont League of Women Voters, Piedmont Anti-racism Diversity Committee, and Piedmont Adult Education. The documentary highlights the genesis of Medicare, when it was signed into law, as well as its relation to the Civil Rights Revolution. The hour-long film describes the history of segregated hospitals and a brief summary of civil rights activism to the internal workings of the federal government that led to integrated hospitals and African American access to health care. It narrates the early days of health inequity, powerfully demonstrating how race and poverty denied African Americans equal access to healthcare. Included are interviews that reveal personal experiences of African Americans’ struggles with illness and death without adequate healthcare. The film transitions from these individual stories to a broader review of disparities in hospital care throughout the United States. Physicians, civil rights leaders, and historians recount the dangerous tasks of documenting egregious incidents, Dr. Neil Powe will be the speaker following the screening. tracking down patients, and the risks of blacks and whites working together to put desegregated structures in place. Following the screening, viewers will hear from Dr. Neil Powe, a leader in Public Health and the ongoing effort to correct healthcare disparities. Dr. Powe is a Harvard-trained physician, a professor of medicine at UCSF, and Chief of Medicine at San Francisco General Hospital. Viewers will hear from him about the history and current status of healthcare. He will have a question and answer session. Register for a link to stream the webinar at diversityfilmseries.org. The streaming link for The Power to Heal will be active from May 2 through May 5.
articles.title: Diversity film series to present Power to Heal on May 5

articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Council held their Annual Recognition Dinner on the night of Thursday April 7th in the Piedmont Community Church’s Guild Hall. articles.text: After five years of helping grow Piedmont Language School, Blair Paige will step down as Executive Director at the end of the school year. The PLS Board, students, and parents thank her for her time, work, and dedication in promoting world languages in Piedmont. Almost 50 years ago, a group of Piedmont parents created the independent language school, independent of Piedmont School District, in an effort to expose children at a young age to foreign languages, primarily French, Mandarin, Spanish, and Japanese. The organization grew to a size where it needed a part-time staff. PLS currently offers only Mandarin and Spanish to students in grades K-6, using classrooms at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary school classrooms, in addition to the middle school and Piedmont Community Church. The Spanish curriculum and teachers are overseen by Viva el Espanol, while simplified Mandarin is taught by local teachers who have been with PLS for years. As with all schools, PLS was challenged by the COVID pandemic. This year the Spanish classes were in person, and Mandarin classes have been hybrid. Anyone interested in taking the reins to make sure the Mandarin and Spanish classes continue is asked to email piedmontlanguageschool@gmail.com.
articles.title: Blair Paige to leave Piedmont Language School

articles.text: On March 25, School Superintendent Randy Booker spoke with the Parents’ Club about the process he intended to follow for hiring a new principal for Piedmont High School. Applications for the position were closed on March 14, and Booker said he intends to make a recommendation to the school board for the new hire at a closed session of the school board meeting on April 27. Prior to the first round of interviews, video and writing Submission were due March 23. The first round of interviews started on March 30. At the March 25 meeting with the Parents Club, Booker did not give exact numbers of applicants, indicating that there were at least seven or eight, and adding a puzzling comment; “We are going to have some community engagement opportunities moving forward.” Booker focused on the need to provide anonymity for the candidates. “That process has to be really confidential until you are a finalist. A principal looking to be a principal [in Piedmont] might not want to tell their superintendent or community right away because it can harm their reputation or relationship with the district in which they are currently working,” Booker explained. A panel of around 25 individuals conducted first-round interviews. The group included certificated staff, classified staff, administration, students, parent club leaders, school site council members, and community support group leaders including PREC, PADC and Maker’s. Booker’s comments on job requirements commonly returned to one issue. “A lot of our work right now has to do with diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging. That will be a big focus for interview questions and conversations. We require someone to be focused on that work,” Booker said, “That is not a flash-in-the-pan program right now,” he added. articles.text: Allyson Aleksey Arithmetic and middle school algebra are basic, right? But even parents who use advanced math in their daily lives may have trouble now helping their kids with math . The California State Board of Education adopted the Mathematics Framework on November 6, 2013 changing the way mathematics is taught. It is known as common core. What has changed? Factor trees are gone. Fractions are taught by using the “Big One” method and the all mysterious “algebra tiles” are used to build visual representations of polynomials. As a tutor I have witnessed time and again the frustration of parents because the way they teach relatively rudimentary math principals has changed. For example, long multiplication and division are now called “standard algorithm.” A parent could be driven mad by the new term M.A.D. (Mean Absolute Deviation). Often a weird new term for something basic can be the final straw for parents to look for a tutor. However, not everyone can afford a tutor or find a good fit. So, what’s another option? One technique I use if there is a disconnect between Common Core is how I learned a math method: pass the chalk to the student and let them teach. When they can teach it to someone else, they certainly will be able to “teach it to the test.” Using a big chalk board or white board can make this process fun and give students the feeling they have an arena to teach while parents, siblings or friends can sit back and watch. Don’t underestimate the power of a white board. Students can write big and get some personal space without having someone looking over their shoulder to see a small piece of paper. Letting them teach the new method may open the door for you to teach the old, tried and true way that gets to the answer as well. In sharing multiple ways, a deeper understanding can be reached. “New” method isn’t so new Teaching fourth grade Common Core mathematics in the classroom wasn’t an obstacle. Often the roadblock came when my students’ parents and guardians insisted that the “new method” was too complicated, and very foreign from the way they were taught decades ago. As a teacher, I had to reconcile with learning a different method, too. In reality, the way your child is learning is not a “new” method; it’s simply a way to encourage children to think of numbers and the amounts they represent. Instead of encouraging memorization, Common Core mathematics aims to equip students at all levels with reasoning ability. Here’s an example: a student is asked to solve 4 x 27. Anyone over the age of 25 will likely line the numbers vertically, multiply the ‘ones’ place, carry the 2, and find the product is 108. Children are now encouraged to think of the quantity the number represents. Students now solve that same problem as 4 x 25 = 100, plus 4 x 2 = 8, with both those products added together to get 108. Although the latter may seem more complicated and probably foreign, it is aimed to have a student quantify rather than memorize. Common Core standards used in California schools encourage students to explain how they figure out their answers. When you find yourself struggling to help your child with homework, ask them to show you what they know. Find an equation to solve in your child’s textbook, homework sheet or on a previous test. Write it down and tell your child that you will try to solve it, and have them solve it their way simultaneously. When you’ve both arrived at your answers, take a look and see if you’ve arrived at the same answer. Now ask them to walk you through how they worked out the problem. Polls show that Californians by-and-large support the Common Core curriculum. In 2017, former president Donald Trump led an anti-Common Core rhetoric. His Education Secretary, Betsy DeVos, called the teaching standards “dead,” but the interference was met with opposition from education leaders throughout California. For all intents and purposes, it appears that Common Core is here to stay. If you are having trouble figuring out how to solve your child’s homework, consider taking a backseat and play the role of a student. If you see your children are still struggling to explain how they work through a problem, talk with their teacher and ask them if they notice your child struggling in the classroom. Always remember that the parent-teacher team is a powerful one, and that you are both working toward one common goal. Jay Russell has over 10 years of experience as a tutor; he specializes in essay writing and algebra. Allyson Aleksey is a former 4th grade teacher at a private, accelerated school in Metairie, Louisiana.
articles.title: The “New” Math

articles.text: There are many volunteer opportunities for high school students in Piedmont that fit around a traditional school schedule. Here are just a few that offer after-school and summer opportunities. Oakland Museum Volunteering at Oakland Museum of California gives teens the chance to get more involved with a local museum, and an opportunity to learn more about the state’s rich history. The museum is always recruiting enthusiastic volunteers to assist with school groups, events, office work, and more. Volunteer informational sessions are offered several times a year, where museum staff discuss the various types of opportunities available. Apply to volunteer by visiting https://www.shiftboard.com/museumca/. If your application is accepted for consideration, you will be notified about next steps including an orientation and training date. e-Buddies E-Buddies promotes social inclusion online for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities such as autism and Down syndrome. Like a modern version of a letter writing program, the organization pairs your child and a child with developmental disabilities as e-mail pen pals. It is a great opportunity for students who would like to volunteer remotely and helps encourage technology literacy and communication skills. Participants are matched based on age, gender, and similar interests; anyone over the age of 10 and with parents’ permission can participate in e-Buddies. To sign up, visit https://www.bestbuddies.org/whatwe-do/ebuddies/. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes well over one million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping at distribution sites, and translating written materials. Visit https://mercybrownbag.org/volunteer/ to sign up. Wardrobe for Opportunity Wardrobe for Opportunity Oakland provides access to transformational career support services for low-income individuals seeking employment. The organization was founded in 1995 to help low-income women look professional in workplace settings and has since evolved to provide a complete suite of career development services to men, women, and youth. There are various ways you can volunteer with the organization, which is seeking volunteers to conduct mock interviewers, style clients, facilitate workshops, and process donations. Wardrobe for Opportunity also accepts gently used and new clothing donations. Visit https://www.wardrobe.org/donate to learn more. articles.text: I recently was listening to a podcast featuring Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith in which she was discussing the seven different kinds of rest that we need. One really stood out to me: Creative Rest. Her definition of creativity is any time we need to solve a problem. By that definition, basically every moment of parenting is an act of creativity. How do we get the kids out of the house in the morning when they are moving as slow as turtles? How can we get the siblings to stop arguing over who gets to choose the show to watch during screen time? How do we convince an unwilling child to engage in homework that is hard? All of these problems require creativity in order to solve them, and we parents are in a constant state of creative thinking. Dr. Dalton-Smith recommends that those of us who are in creative thinking mode all day every day need a rest from that kind of work and that we can find that rest through viewing beauty. That could be through seeing art in an art gallery, going to see live theatre, listening to music or spending time in nature. I realized that, in my life, pre-pandemic, I engaged in a lot of these activities–exploring a new exhibit at a museum, watching musicals and plays, going to live concerts–but all of these activities came to an abrupt halt when the shut-own started. Parents need to take creative rest in nature. Instead, I drastically increased my time in nature. Like so many of us, taking walks, going on hikes, camping, cross country skiing. . . all of these became a lifeline for me. It wasn’t until I heard this podcast that I realized that being outdoors – in the mountains, at the beach, observing wildflowers – had taken on a critical new dimension, both physical and spiritual. Now, the arts and culture sector has opened again. I am seeing shows again and it feels amazing. But I am still in nature whenever possible, and I have a newfound appreciation for the creativity and beauty of nature. • The wind in the trees is a symphony. • The sunset is a glorious painting. • Two squirrels arguing over an acorn is theater. • The movement of the waves as they crash on the shore is modern dance. As we move into the spring and summer, I want to encourage all of us parents to take the Creative Rest we need. Find the beautiful things that inspire you! Go see the shows and enjoy the exquisite nature all around us. It might just give your depleted system the rest it needs. Nina Meehan is the CEO and founder of Bay Area Children’s Theatre, currently playing “The Imaginaries: An Immersive Musical,” and the host of the Creative Parenting Podcast.
articles.title: Finding creative rest in a busy world

articles.text: Jan Howland (left), Nathan Walden, and children’s author Lisa Riddiough. Former Piedmont resident Lisa Riddiough recently unveiled her second children’s book, Letters to Live By: an Alphabet Book with Intention. A book-signing event was hosted by Nathan Waldon at his Nathan & Co. gift shop on Piedmont Avenue on Saturday, April 2. “Lisa is a longtime friend and we’re so excited to add Letters to Live By to our selection of children’s books,” said Waldon. “The book’s message is exactly what we look for when curating our collection: It inspires by reinforcing core values that help create a better world.” The book signing event coincided with the shop’s 16th anniversary. “What better way to celebrate? A friend, an inspiring children’s book, and cookies,” said Walden. Letters to Live By is Riddiough’s second book, illustrated by Asa Gilland. The author describes it as a social-emotional concept picture book that teaches young readers the power of setting intentions and embracing mindfulness. Letters to Live By is her debut picture book and is dedicated to Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Greenbaum. “It is surreal to have two books out in the world,” Riddiough said. The author’s first published book, Elvis and the World as it Stands, references Letters to Live By. “When I was writing Elvis, my main character needed to refer to an alphabet book early in the story, so I used my own book. Little did I know both would be published around the same time, let alone published at all. It’s a little ‘Easter egg’ of sorts and makes the publication of both books all the sweeter,” she said. “I knew I wanted alliterative phrases that could be both intentions and action items that could be accessible to younger readers,” Letters to Live By is Lisa Riddiough’s latest children’s book. Riddiough said of the inspiration behind Letters to Live By. “I was reminded of a phrase that one of my kids’ teachers used to say. Mr. Greenebaum, of Piedmont Middle School, sends his students home at the end of each week with his signature line, ‘Rest up, have fun, read something, and practice peace.’ I first heard this at back-to-school night and, as a picture book writer, ‘Practice Peace’ stuck with me.” Riddiough said she was a slow reader as a child and found it difficult to concentrate on required reading. This led her to choose literature with plenty of illustrations and white space, “and always stories with animals,” she added. “It’s perfectly okay to choose a book that is short, has large font, and plenty of illustrations,” she said. Riddiough’s first published piece was in the Piedmont Post, (Volume 13. No. 32) an article entitled “Happy Birthday, You Two,” a tribute to her father and the Golden Gate Bridge on their concurrent 75th birthdays. Riddiough’s book Letters to Live By is available at Nathan & Co. on Piedmont Avenue, and online booksellers including Target and Amazon. articles.text: Ellie Black within 4 seconds of behind Sally Wood’s school record Jack Stein placed his name in the Piedmont High record books once again on Saturday, April 9 at the prestigious Arcadia Invitational near Los Angeles. His time of 9:12.62 in the 3200 meters broke Steve Brown’s record set 27 years ago in 1994 by slightly over five seconds. Brown was inducted into the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame in 2008. Stein finished 12th in a field of 82 runners. His school record comes one week after setting the school’s 11-year old record in the 1600 meters at the Stanford Invitational. Piedmont’s all-time top-five times in the 3200 is as follows: Jack Stein, 9:12.62 (2022) Steve Brown, 9:17.71 (1994) Tom Phelps, 9:35.72 (2000) Carl Moren, 9:38.60 (1998) Crosby Freeman, 9:39.8 (2001) The Arcadia Invitational is a showpiece some of the top runners from throughout the U.S. “Arcadia is a super-special event. You have competition from all over the country there. It’s a great experience, I remember going into the tent and everyone is asking each other where they are from. I think runners from 29 states were there,” said Stein. He entered the race just three seconds behind Brown’s all-time record after running a 9:20.56 at the Stanford Invitational. Stein knew that Arcadia would be the perfect setting to break it. In doing so, he ran a 4:37 in his first mile and a 4:35 to close. “Many heats were coming out really fast. I stayed in the back for the first mile and settled in. I wanted to run a negative split for that second mile; I knew I had the record in me, it’s an awesome accomplishment to have and to PR by nearly seven seconds felt amazing to do,” said Stein. His time is the third individual record broken by the boys’ team this season, two by Stein and Photo by Steve Zirkelbach Jack Stein is now Piedmont High School’s record holder in booth the 1600 meters and 3200 meters. Parker Terrill’s new pole vault record. In addition, the boys’ distance medley relay team of Christian Taylor, Parker Long, Cooper Downing and Stein also set a PHS record at Arcadia with a time of 10:28.77 to finish eighth of 21 teams. Ellie Black nears Sally Wood’s 3200 record Ellie Black had a strong run at Arcadia with a third place finish in a field of 60 runners with a time of 10:46.09 in the 3200 meters. In the biggest meet in the state, she was the best runner from California. She placed behind No. 1 Hailey Burns from Boseman, Montana, and No. 2 Shelby Jensen from Westlake in Utah. Black’s time is a major achievement, and puts her within 3.64 seconds of Sally Woods’ 37-year-old record of 10:42.45. She has been clawing away at Woods’ record after clocking 10:57.05 at the Dublin Distance Fiesta on March 19. “I had a feeling that the race would come out very quickly, which it did. I felt pretty good about my first mile. In the second mile, my mindset was to start racing and try to beat the girl in front of me,” said Black. “I’m at a place where I can push myself and my teammates are always so supportive. Just being able to enjoy [running] takes some of the pressure off,” she added. Piedmont’s all-time top-five times in the 3200 is as follows: Sally Wood, 10:42.45 (1985) Ellie Black, 10:46.09 (2022) Jamie Kent, 11:07.80 (2007) Jehan Sparks, 11:14.79 (2004) Lucy Richardson, 11:19.38 (2018) Photo by Steve Zirkelbach Ellie Black is just 3.64 seconds behind Sally Wood’s 37-year old school record in the 3200 meters.
articles.title: Jack Stein breaks school record in 3200 meters

articles.text: On April 5, Piedmont High School senior Parker Terrill was awarded a commemorative beltbuckle for setting a new school record in the pole vault. Terrill’s vault of 15 feet, 5 inches, broke Marshall Wentworth’s record set 11 years ago by 1 foot, 5 inches. The brass buckle with a raised image of a pole vaulter was given to Wentworth by the family of Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame inductee Irving Moore, whose record of 13-feet was set in 1940. According to coach Jeanine Holmlund, the buckle was given to Wentworth with the understanding that he would pass it on to the next school record holder. It is now Terrill’s duty to pass it onto the school’s next record holder when and if it occurs. Photos by Jay Russell Parker Terrill was presented with a commemorative belt buckle for breaking the Piedmont High School pole vault record. Pictured are former PHS pole vault coach Chris Smith (left), Terrill with the belt buckle, current PHS pole vault coach Steve Horvath, and head coach Jeanine Holmlund. Parker Terrill and his mother, Susan Terrill.
articles.title: History of pole vault belt buckle

articles.text: Editor: I read about the incredible performances by Ellie Black, Jack Stein, and Parker Terrill at this year’s Arcadia Invitational. Terrill’s 6th place finish in the Invitational Pole Vault and Black’s 3rd place finish in the Rated 3200 Meter Race were exceptional. But it was Stein’s performance I had my eye on. It was with mixed emotions that I read that he broke my school record for 3200 meters. I suppose records are meant to be broken and mine was no different. School records aren’t broken every day, though. The one I broke was set by Tim Tyler in 1970. My school record was set at the 1994 CIF State Track & Field Championships. I came in 12th, running 9:17.71. The winner that day was Mebrahtom Keflezighi who went on to win the Silver Medal in the 2004 Olympic Marathon. There was once a video of the race on YouTube and if you had the patience to wait for a while, you could see me crossing the finish line 20 seconds after him. It took years for it to sink in what an honor it was to compete in such an elite prep race. High school distance running is now at a completely different level than when I competed. I am blown away by the outstanding performances of this generation’s athletes. I hope Arcadia is a preview of things to come for Stein this season and beyond. I hope he takes as much pride in his new record as I did in mine. Leaving that aside, I hope he finds as much joy running as I have. Above all, I hope that the next generation of Piedmont athletes looks at that record, 9:12.62 or faster if Stein breaks the record again, and trains a little harder, dreams a little bigger, and thinks, ‘Records are meant to be broken and this one is no different. Why shouldn’t I be the one to break it?’ Steve Brown, PHS Class of ‘94 Oberlin, Ohio

articles.text: PHS tops Hayward 4-0, Tennyson 10-0 Piedmont’s softball team powered its way into Spring Break with two dominant shutout wins over league opponents. They defeated Hayward 4-0 at home on Tuesday, April 5, and bashed Tennyson 10-0 on the road two days later. The pair of wins boosted Piedmont’s record to 10-3 and a perfect 6-0 in league against Shoreline Division teams. “We’re just having fun. In the past, I have been known to be a stickler about things. We’ve just been focused on having the most fun as possible – so far so good,” said coach Gene Denard. Hayward was considered one of the biggest challengers for Piedmont High in league, meaning that the Highlanders are now in the driver’s seat for a league championship. With four of their five remaining games in league, PHS is on-track for its first title since 2018, a year they finished at 10-0. Izzy Epstein had 14 strikeouts against Hayward, and 5 strikeouts in 2 innings with Tennyson. Chiara Lundin had a triple against both Hayward and Tennyson. Staff Photos Leah Bell hit her first home run of the season against Hayward. 4-0 over Hayward Piedmont scored twice in the bottom of the third inning, once more in the bottom of the fourth, and put up its last run in the bottom of the sixth. Senior pitcher Izzy Epstein got the start, throwing a complete 7-inning game with 14 strikeouts and two hits allowed. In the bottom of the third, power hitter Leah Bell stepped to the plate with two outs, and on a 2-2 count, cracked a two-run homer over the center field fence – her first homer of the season. Piedmont scored in the bottom of the fourth on some Hayward miscues. With two outs, Gretchen Gerhardy reached base on an error, followed by Annabel Castronovo hitting a single that brought Gerhardy all the way around to score after an error by the Hayward outfielder. Piedmont’s final run in the bottom of the sixth came after a leadoff triple by Chiara Lundin that went to the right field fence. Epstein singled home Lundin for the final run. Final stats: Bell went 1-for-3 with a homer, two RBIs, and a run scored. Epstein was 1-for-3 with an RBI. Lundin was 1-for-3 with her triple and a run scored. Castronovo was 1-for-3 with a run scored. Miya Fujimoto was 1-for-2 with a walk. 10-0 over Tennyson Piedmont opened seven runs in the top of the first inning, then added two more in the top of the third and a final run in the top of the fourth. The Highlanders started with four straight walks, and Angelina Wu and Bell scoring on wild pitches. Fujimoto scored on a wild pitch followed by Lundin’s RBI single to bring in Morgan Hunt. Lundin also scored on a wild pitch with Gerhardy at bat, followed by Epstein scored on a wild pitch with Julia Banuelos.
articles.title: Highlanders win back-to-back shutouts

articles.text: The Piedmont girls’ and boys’ teams came away with victories over Arroyo High on Thursday, April 7 prior to their spring break. The final score was not provided. Piedmont High swept both the freestyle and medley relay events for each girls and boys teams, while winning 12 individual events. The girls’ varsity 200 Medley Relay team of Odessa Dando, Emily Fitzgerald, Anne Reardon and Sonja ten Grotenhuis as the last leg logged a winning time of 2:21.18. In the 200 Free Relay, the girls’ team featured Fitzgerald, Cavenaugh, ten Grotenhuis, and Dando for a winning time of 2:03.52. Cavenaugh won 50 Free and 100 Breast with respective times of 30.24 and 1:22.82. Dando, who also plays water polo, won the 100 Free with a time of 1:07.71 and the 200 Free in 2:22.07. Olivia Kaltner won the 100 Fly with a time of 1:30.35 and finished second in 50 Free in 32.55. Anne Reardon won the 500 Free with a time of 7:03.94 and placed second in 200 Free in 2:37.46. Ten Grotenhuis won the 200 IM and 100 Back with times of 2:34.38 and 1:07.18 respectively. Boys’ results The boys’ medley relay team of Simon Lins, Ryan Stokes, Evan Byun and Andrew Grasman clocked a winning time of 2:06.59. The 200 Freestyle Relay team of Lins, Stokes, Chuck White and Byun won with a time of 1:44.63. Byun won the 200 Individual Medley with a time of 2:18.61 and was second in the 100 Breaststroke in 1:08.98. Andrew Grasman won two events, the 200 Free in 2:17.24, and clocked a time of 1:03.61 in the 100 Backstroke. Stokes won the 100 Breast with a time of 1:07.31 and the 50 Free in 25.44. She’s the third leg on the Medley relay team. Ryan Stokes won the 100 Breast and the 50 Free against Arroyo.

articles.text: Editor: Jack Stein ran 9:12.62 in the 3200 meters at the prestigious Arcadia meet on Friday night. That is an incredible time, and a new school record. Breaking the mile record also in the same season is quite a double. In each case he blew away his prior PR times. High school team has had great results this season, including a 1:55 in the boy’s 800 (by Cooper Dowling) and 15’+ in the pole vault (by Parker Terrill). Jack still has some big meets where he could lower his times. No boundaries. All this is more impressive knowing the impact of Covid for the past two years. Congratulations to Jack and coach Jeanine Holmlund. Go Piedmont! –David Brown Dave Brown is the father of Stephen Brown, who set the school record in the 3200 meters in 1994. ht t ps://ca .mile split .com/ meets/455677-arcadia-invitational-2022/results

articles.text: Nico Defazio went 2-for-3 with two RBIs, a walk, and a stolen base against St. Mary’s. The Piedmont High baseball team traveled to St. Mary’s in Berkeley on Friday, April 8, losing 4-2 in a defensive battle with a former longtime rival. The Panthers are a Division 4 opponent in North Coast Section, and the two sides could certainly meet each other once again in the postseason. The pair of games brings PHS’ record to 8-6 overall heading into Spring Break. The Highlanders started strong with one run in the top of the first inning but fell behind 3-1 by the next inning. PHS narrowed the gap to 3-2 in the top of the firth, but St. Mary’s tacked on one more in the bottom half of the fifth. In the top of the first, Piedmont had two runners on base with two outs after Peter Krumins and Davis Alazraqui were hit by pitches. Nico Defazio hit a ground ball through the infield to score Krumins from third. PHS had runners in scoring position in the top of the second after Liam Campbell and Michael Aikawa recorded singles, but a double play ended the inning. St. Mary’s answered with three runs in the bottom half of the second inning, scoring two with two outs after hitting a single and triple. The Highlanders closed the deficit to 3-2 in the top of the fifth with Alazraqui drawing a walk and advancing to second on a wild pitch. Defazio cracked a single to center to score Alazraqui all the way from first. Defazio Third baseman Peter Krumins with a throw to second. advanced to second on the throw. But the Highlanders couldn’t bring him to score. St. Mary’s rallied for its fourth run in the bottom half after their leadoff hitter walked and stole second, advancing to third on a sacrifice bunt. With one out, the Panthers brought him in on a sacrifice fly to right field for the 4-2 final. St. Mary’s forced a 1-2-3 inning in the top of the sixth. In Piedmont’s final opportunity in the top of the seventh, St. Mary’s struck out the side. Final stats: Defazio went 2-for-3 with two RBIs, a walk, and a stolen base. Aikawa went 1-for-4. Krumins had a run scored. Alazraqui had a run scored and drew two walks. Campbell went 1-for-3. Alex Tafapolsky got the start on the mound, throwing five innings and striking out three with one earned run. Scott McKenzie pitched one inning in relief and struck out two. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-6 overall, 1-1 league) returns from Spring Break on Tuesday, April 19 for a game with Albany at 4:00 p.m.
articles.title: Highlanders fall 4-2 to St. Mary’s

articles.text: Legion of Honor, of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, is showing Guo Pei: Couture Fantasy now through September 5. The fashion exhibit features the extraordinary designs of Chinese couture designer Guo Pei, who is widely considered China’s first couturier. More than 80 examples from the past two decades will be on display, many of which were shown on Beijing and Paris runways. Pei is known for her craftsmanship, embroidery, and unconventional dressmaking techniques. “As a creator and artist, there is no greater honor than to share my creativity with a wider audience,” the designer said. “I hope that through the artistry of couture and universal language of art it will foster cross-cultural appreciation, connections, and ideas.” To obtain tickets to the exhibit, visit https://legionof honor. famsf.org/guo-pei?utm_medium=email&utm_source=famsfmktg&utm_campaign=guopei&utm_content=consideration_20220408&mc_cid=e- 25a62443e&mc_eid=573801a180. Guo Pei’s “Da Jin” (“Magnificent Gold”) gown is a hand-embroidered design that helped launch her fashion career. It will be one of the many items now on display at the Couture Fantasy exhibition at the San Francisco Legion of Honor.
articles.title: Legion of Honor is hosting Guo Pei’s Couture Fantasy

articles.text: Playwright Dave Malloy, a three-time Tony Award nominee, makes his debut at Berkeley Rep with Octet, beginning April 20. Directed by Annie Tippe, the show features a score for an a cappella chamber choir and an original libretto inspired by internet comment boards, scientific debates, religious texts, and Sufi poetry. Octet explores addiction and nihilism within the messy context of 21st century technology. It was commissioned, developed, and produced by Signature Theatre in New York City, and follows the lives of eight “internet-obsessed” people who meet in real life to share their stories, using nothing but a pitch pipe and a cappella voices. Or Matias is music director. The cast includes Kim Blanck, Adam Bashian, Alex Gibson, Justin Lopez, J.D Mollison, Kuhoo Verma, Margo Seibert, and Isabel Santiago. Tickets to Octet are available now at: https://www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/octet/.
articles.title: Dave Malloy’s Octet opens at Berkeley Rep April 20

articles.text: Berkeley-based Shotgun Players is presenting Passing Strange live through April 23. Passing Strange is directed by William Thomas Hodgson with music direction by Daniel Alley. The play follows the story of a young Bohemian who charts a course for “the real,” through sex, drugs and rock and roll. The play is set in middle-class America, Amsterdam, and Berlin. Passing Strange won a Tony Award for Best Book of a Musical. “Watching Passing Strange changed me, changed what my art could be. I just saw myself in this.” said Hodgson. “There’s just something about the rock nature of this where I’m just having such a good time. And I don’t always feel that in the theatre. The commune between the actors, the musicians, and the audience: it feels like centering that in a theatre experience is sometimes what I’m missing from my theatre experience. There’s something that’s so accessible in this play, in the writing.” The cast includes Angel Adedokun, Rolanda Bell, Myles Brown, Devin Cunningham, and Albert Hodge. Visit https://shotgunplayers. org to purchase tickets. Shotgun Players is located at 1901 Ashby Avenue in Berkeley. Tel.(510) 841-6500. The Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco launched an exhibition on March 31 entitled Still Lives in Contemporary Art. The exhibition will be on view through August 12. A group exhibit, it brings together an international group of artists who have unique interpretations of contemporary art and still life. The artists have created works within a framework of Black diasporic identities, histories, and collective experiences. Featured artists include Sadie Barnette, LaKela Brown, Elizabeth Colomba, Njideka Akunyili Crosby, David Antonio Cruz, Awol Erizku, Leslie Hewitt, Yashua Klos, Deana Lawson, Azikiwe Mohammed, Rashaad Newsome, Toyin Ojih Odutola, Paul Mpagi Sepuya, Devan Shimoyama, William Villalongo, and Brittney Leeanne Williams. The exhibition is on the third floor Gallery of Music. For tickets, visit https://www.moadsf.org/ exhibitions/elegies-still-lifes-incontemporary-art.
articles.title: MoAD: Still Lives in Contemporary Art exhibit now on view

articles.text: Mendocino Music Festival returns live this summer, beginning July 9 at Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg. Tickets are on sale now. The festival was established in 1986 by Allan Pollack, Susan Waterfall and former principal bassoonist of the San Francisco Symphony, Walter Green. The festival features a blend of genres; evenings include orchestral concerts, Big Band, chamber music ensembles, dance, blues, jazz, world, folk, bluegrass and more. Daytime events include lectures and recitals at the Piano Series, a performance by participants in the Emerging Artists Program, and small concerts in intimate venues throughout the historic town of Mendocino on the coast. To see a full list of all events, see: https://mendocinomusic.org/ events/2022-07/. The featured artists and bands this year include Steel Wheels, Spencer Myer, Gloria Cheng, and Kim Nalley. Proof of vaccination will be required for entry. Masks must be properly worn while on event premises, and concerts will be limited to one hour with no intermission. The festival will follow official recommendations of local and state public health agencies as July approaches. Mendocino Music Festival concerts will take place this summer in the Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg.
articles.title: Mendocino Music Festival returns July 9 - 23

articles.text: Piedmont alum Raphael Gold and the Diluvian String Quartet will perform a concert of chamber music inspired by the New World. Come be part of an intimate evening of music at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, April 29 at 7 p.m. The quartet includes Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. The program includes String Quartet No. 1 by Heitor Villa-Lobos, Five Pieces for String Quartet by Erwin Schulhoff, and Antonin Dvořák‘s masterful String Quartet No. 12 in F Major (“The American”). The concert will feature works inspired by the great American music of the turn of the 20th century, including pieces by composers Antonin Dvorak, Heitor Villa Lobos, and Erwin Schulhoff. You’ll hear quotes and rhythms from jazz, tango, and folksong. Proof of vaccination is required.
articles.title: Diluvian String Quartet to perform American Dream concert Apr. 29 at PCA

articles.text: Jules Leyhe and The Family Jules Band brings some of the East Bay’s finest musicians to the Piedmont Center for the Arts for a show on Saturday, April 23. The band features saxophonist Nancy Wright, keyboardist Ian McArdle, and drummer and drummer Isaac Schwartz, who bring a funky jazz flavor to Leyhe’s fantastical vision. Leyhe twice performed the National Anthem for the Oakland A’s at the Oakland Coliseum last year, and performs the Hendrix version of the National Anthem each year in the Piedmont 4th of July Parade. Your First Rodeo CD This ain’t your granddaddy’s blues – heck it ain’t even your daddy’s blues. On this CD guitarist Jules Leyhe is on an entirely different trip, juxtaposing futuristic elements with down-home tones. He has been featured in Guitar Player, Premier Guitar, and Vintage Guitar. His album, Your First Rodeo, is a whimsical mashup of blues, hip-hop, fusion, rock and Latin music. Picture Duane Allman jamming with jazz piano great Gil Evans, or Jimi Hendrix playing in Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band.

articles.text: Work of 40 artists to be displayed Piedmont’s 3rd annual Art Walk will take place in neighborhoods through the city on Saturday, May 7, and will feature 40 local artists representing a wide array of art. Under the leadership of founders Jon Schleuning and Larraine Seiden, the outdoor art exhibit will showcase paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, photography, jewelry, and textile art. The displays will be in front of or near the artists’ homes. All art will be on sale, and 20% of the proceeds will be donated to the Piedmont Education Foundation to support art programs in Piedmont schools. More than $17,000 was raised at last year’s Art Walk. Visit https://piedmontartsfund. org/piedmont-art-walk-2022 to view featured artists.
articles.title: Annual Art Walk Scheduled for May 7

Mendocino Music Festival returns July 9 - 23 By Allyson Aleksey Mendocino Music Festival returns live this summer, beginning July 9 at Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg. Tickets are on sale now. The festival was established in 1986 by Allan Pollack, Susan Waterfall and former principal bassoonist of the San Francisco Symphony, Walter Green. The festival features a blend of genres; evenings include orchestral concerts, Big Band, chamber music ensembles, dance, blues, jazz, world, folk, bluegrass and more. Daytime events include lectures and recitals at the Piano Series, a performance by participants in the Emerging Artists Program, and small concerts in intimate venues throughout the historic town of Mendocino on the coast. To see a full list of all events, see: https://mendocinomusic.org/ events/2022-07/. The featured artists and bands this year include Steel Wheels, Spencer Myer, Gloria Cheng, and Kim Nalley. Proof of vaccination will be required for entry. Masks must be properly worn while on event premises, and concerts will be limited to one hour with no intermission. The festival will follow official recommendations of local and state public health agencies as July approaches. Mendocino Music Festival concerts will take place this summer in the Cotton Auditorium in Fort Bragg. articles.text: Dan Flanagan is a Berkeley violinist who currently teaches violin at UC Berkeley, is Principal Second of the Berkeley Symphony, Concertmaster of the Sacramento Philharmonic and Opera, Concertmaster of West Edge Opera, and performs with the San Francisco Opera and San Francisco Ballet. He has previously performed as concertmaster with Oakland Symphony, California Symphony, Symphony San Jose, Santa Rosa Symphony, California Musical Theater, Modesto Symphony, and Opera Parallele. He has performed recitals at the Piedmont Center for the Arts multiple times. Dan has been an avid collector since he discovered baseball cards at the age of five. He lost interest in them as a teenager but with the advent of Ebay when he was in grad school, he amassed an impressive collection of historical violinist memorabilia. When he moved to Berkeley 12 years ago, he discovered art auctions and open studios; that’s when the real trouble started. Since then his focus has been French Impressionists and Bay Area abstracts. The works on view at the Piedmont Center for the Arts include 45 of his favorite pieces. Many of the artists were in the original Impressionist exhibits of the 1870’s and 1880’s. Dan has a project titled “The Bow and the Brush,” where he performs new compositions inspired by paintings. Two of these pieces were performed in the Berkeley Symphony & Friends Chamber Concert series on April 10. Twenty-one of these works, each inspired by paintings currently exhibited at the Piedmont Center for the Arts ere, will be premiered by Dan at his Carnegie Hall debut on October 3, followed by the West Coast premieres at Hertz Hall in Berkeley on October 16. Robert Antoine Pinchon (French, 1886-1943). Bruxelles, pluie sur la Grand-Place (Brussels, rain on the Grand-Place), Oil on canvas, 1928. Jose Gonzalez Garcia composed “Cadenza II,” inspired by this painting.

Wednesday, April 20, 7:30 PM Ukraine Insight by Anastasia Edel Why did Vladimir Putin attack the sovereign nation of Ukraine, with which Russia shares centuries of common past? What’s behind the brutality of Putin’s war? How much popular support does he enjoy in Russia? Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel, an acclaimed writer, social historian and New York Times contributor, talks about her experience of growing up in the heavily Ukraine-influenced Russian south, the historical and cultural entwinement of the two countries’ natives, and the consequences of this war for Russia and the world. articles.text: Piedmont High School and Middle School musicians will present a chamber music recital of solo and small ensemble pieces on Friday, April 22 at 7 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The program includes a string quartet by Czech composer Bedřich Smetana, a movement from one of Camille Saint-Saëns’ cello concertos, as well as a viola duet by Antonin Dvořák. A 6th grade violin soloist will play a piece by French composer Jean-Baptiste Lully and an oboe soloist from the high school Symphonic Band will play “Semeliami” by Alejandra Odgers. The concert is open to all, and donations will be requested at the door to cover concert costs. A brief reception will follow the recital.
articles.title: School chamber music concert at PCA April 22

articles.text: Pianist, harpsichordist, and piano teacher Victoria Hurd, a graduate n Early Music at Vassar College and Stanford University, will perform a benefit piano concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, April 24 at 4 p.m. The recital will be grounded in traditional piano literature. Whether a Barcarolle, a Sonata, or a Prelude, the music is filled with stories of dreams, sorrow, love, and joy, all of which we hope the Ukrainian people live to experience. Come hear the stories in music by Mozart, Beethoven, Chopin, and Faure. Ukraine Crisis Relief Fund is part of Save the Children, a top national charity. The receipt for any donation to Save the Children will serve as a ticket for admission. Audience members will need to present vaccination and booster certificates as well as donation receipts, and wear masks while indoors.

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Gardens and Nursery in Walnut Creek will host its Golden Jubilee Gala on May 13. It is the Gardens’ largest fundraiser of the year and will be in person this year. The gala will include a silent auction, Fund-a-Need live auction, and will present an award to an individual recognized as providing outstanding support of the garden. The event will be held outside and will include cocktails, hors d’oeuvres and dessert, live music, and other festivities. Bancroft Gardens and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth Bancroft when it was her private, personal garden, but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Bancroft created a garden filled with dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. The gala begins at 5:30 p.m. Those who cannot attend the gala will be able to watch it virtually. Visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/garden-gala-2022/ to purchase tickets. Ruth Bancroft Gardens and Nursery in Walnut Creek.
articles.title: Bancroft Gardens annual Gala set for May 13

articles.text: Violinist Dan Flanagan led a stellar afternoon concert at the PCA. My week ran something like an Abbott and Costello comedy routine. Friday is a big day throughout the world. TGIF is an expression which all of us know, but Friday this week is Good Friday. It is also the first day of Passover. Those things formed the original inspiration for this column. Every idea was in place for my column…but then there was a marvelous concert Sunday afternoon at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. TGIF can be interpreted in many ways. It has many connotations. In a recent column, we discovered why people ate fish on Fridays. Things changed in 1966 and 1985. Lamb is in the spotlight now – Spring lamb, Pascal Lamb… Whatever. My wife suggested that I join her at the PCA on Sunday afternoon after my informal music gig. The concert was yet another excellent chamber music concert by musicians with Berkeley Symphony, a series of concerts in its ninth year at the Center for the Arts. This one centered around the outstanding violinist-composer Dan Flanagan. Not content to be a violinist of superlative attributes, Flanagan is a gifted composer and an art collector as well as an art connoisseur. This presents a considerable problem to your music critic. Many examples of his art collection were on the walls of the Center, and Flanagan personally commissioned a variety of composers to write music inspired by the art. He played some of these compositions and told the audience how everything related. The vocal presentation could not have been better. There was humor in everything that he said. And when he put his bow to his violin, I said to myself: “that’s the way the violin should be played.” Flanagan told me confidentially that he is usually nervous, but one would never know it. articles.text: Children’s Fairyland is bringing back its premiere fundraising gala, Once Upon a Time in Fairyland, to the shores of Lake Merritt on May 25. Single tickets are now available. Once Upon a Time in Fairyland is a rare and coveted opportunity for adults to experience the park without their children. The 8-acre property is kid-centric in every sense of the word; but on May 25, it will transform into an elegant evening space for food, wine, and costumes. The fundraiser makes magical programming at Children’s Fairyland possible for Oakland and Bay Area families. All attendees will be required to show proof of up-to-date vaccination; due to the service of alcohol, no one under the age of 21 will be admitted. Tickets can be purchased by visiting https://fairyland.formstack.com/forms/gala_tickets_22.
articles.title: Tickets for May 25 Fairyland Gala on sale

One of Flanagan’s original compositions was a piece for solo violin and was a violinistic tour de force. I wonder why Hollywood does not engage him as a composer. I guess Hollywood prefers paint-by-number composers rather than artist-composers who have imagination. The concert centered around Flanagan, but the other five represented a veritable Who’s Who of Bay Area musicians: Roman Fukshansky, clarinet, Alex Camphouse, French horn, Chloé Mendola, cello, Michel Taddei, bass, and Elizabeth Dorman, piano. Space limitations prevent me from a complete review. Suffice it to say that the entire concert was virtuoso in the way that makes immense difficulties look like child’s play. Next, Flanagan will take his entire concert of art-related compositions to Carnegie Hall. Just a suggestion: It might be worth the trip. A recipe from the Musical Gourmet This version of Navarin of lamb will be marvelous on Friday. If you are religious, it can be for Good Friday, or the first night of Passover, or just for your enjoyment, religious or not. First you will need some lamb. One lamb shank per person is perfect, but you can substitute turkey thighs, beef shanks, or other cuts of lamb. You will need a little bit of flour or matzah flour seasoned with salt and pepper to dust the lamb. Preheat the oven to 400° and put the meat in an oven-proof casserole with some olive oil and a pinch of sugar. Add 2 cups of red wine, about 3 tablespoons of tomato paste, a minced garlic clove and the usual herbs. Cover and bake for one hour. In a skillet, sauté one chopped onion in oil and add it to the casserole. Return the casserole to the oven and bake another 30 minutes. This dish is traditionally served with turnips, but I like to cook them separately. For convenience you can bake apples or pears at the same time. Serve with couscous or kasha. These are good because they absorb the delicious sauce. Preparation for this beautiful dish takes no more than 10 to 15 minutes. Violinist Dan Flanagan led a stellar afternoon concert at the PCA. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth Bancroft when it was her private, personal garden, but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Bancroft created a garden filled with dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. articles.text: “No Strings Attached.” Right. The ending of this movie was telegraphed in the first 20 minutes. It was just a matter of waiting and enduring the following 90 minutes while two 20-somethings, Emma (Natalie Portman) and Adam (Ashton Kutcher), who’ve decided to be friends with benefits (sex buddies, no strings attached), begin what is loosely called a relationship. Their intent is disclosed via a lengthy montage of urgent groping and coupling in hospital storage rooms, an empty operating theater, her apartment, and his house. Ground rule: rinse and repeat. Adam, breaking one of the fundamental rules of their encounters, concludes he is falling in love with Emma. She, however, is opposed to any attachments that go beyond the physical. In other words, she’s commitment adverse and “no strings” is a metaphor, of sorts, for a personality disorder that is completely inexplicable. Of course, there’s not one person in the audience that believes that she will not completely reassess her position by act three, and “No Strings Attached” will suddenly have lots of strings. And while we’re on the subject of strings, sticking with this movie through the credits is like trying to push string. Meanwhile, because Emma and Adam are intent on not building a relationship, they avoid any and all conversations that might involve self-disclosure. No issues are raised. Hence, little if anything is known about them as people. In fact, they are emotional strangers to one another. There is Adam’s dad, Alvin (Kevin Kline), a pot smoking, skirt chasing (under 30), fading television star who is in denial when it comes to the fact that he is old. His character is needless and silly. For Kline, a superb actor, this role has a very short shelf life and he walks through it with a “what, me worry?” grin and little else. The dialogue, such as it is, that moves the film forward, is coarse and crude and vacuous. This may be a generational thing, but tell me that this is not the way young people interact. Nature abhors a vacuum, but not Hollywood. They’ve created the contemporary romantic comedy, a seemingly endless string of them over the last several years, all formulaic, predictable, many similar in plot (“No Strings Attached” brings to mind the recent “Love and Other Drugs”). Think of Hollywood as some kind of rom-com Pez dispenser and just when you thought it was safe to go back into the movie theater, another shallow, existential black hole of a film appears. “No Strings Attached” could have been an interesting film. There is a qualitative difference between hooking up with someone and actually wanting to know them. Just Emma’s deep-seated fear of relationships offers the prospect of a story line that might have yielded something deeper than the banal and the nonsensical. Adam and Emma have backstory, they have careers. Adam wants desperately to be a writer; however, he never so much as shares a word he’s written with Emma. Emma is working 36-hour shifts to be a doctor, and obviously cares about people; however we never hear her touch on her motivations for wanting to care for people. Of course, they’re busy not talking, not disclosing, not reflecting – to the detriment of their relationship and the film. No Strings Attached. Starring Ashton Kutcher, Natalie Portman, Olivia Thirlby and Greta Gerwig. Directed by Ivan Reitman. 2 hrs., 34 min. Rated R. Review originally published in 2011. Natalie Portman and Ashton Kutcher star in No Strings Attached.
articles.title: No Strings Attached – save your money

articles.text: If you love movies, then it’s likely you’ve heard of director Peter Weir. Now 68-years-old, his work dates back to 1975 and the chilling Australian film, Picnic at Hanging Rock, followed by The Year of Living Dangerously, Gallipoli, Witness, Dead Poets Society, The Truman Show, The Mosquito Coast, and the incomparable Master and Commander, shot in 2003 and based on the Patrick O’Brian stories. The Way Back has an epic feel, and it transcends what may, at first blush, seem a rudimentary plot: the year is 1940 and a rag tag group of men improbably escape a Russian gulag work camp. Against all odds they trek more than 4,000 miles across some of the most inhospitable country imaginable. Their destination, as it turns out, is British-controlled India. This is not a road trip. It is not simply about walking. This is a film, shot by the deeply talented cinematographer, Russell Boyd, celebrates the human spirit, and the unrelenting will of these individuals to not only endure but to prevail, and, in the end, be free. Not all will survive, we’re told at the outset; however, each character – Janusz (Jim Surgess), Mr. Smith (Ed Harris), Valka (Colin Farrell), Tamasz (Alexandru Potocean), Irena (Saoirse Ronan) – becomes three dimensional as does the landscape, which conspires to defeat them. They escape Siberia; find, against all odds, Lake Baikal; cross the plains of Mongolia; survive the heat and sandstorms of the Ghobi Desert; and face the snows and spires of the Himalayas, the gateway to Tibet. Beyond is India. How they accomplish this remarkable feat makes for an astonishing tale, not unlike, in some strange way, the survival tale, 127 Hours. Both experiences are testimony to the depth of the very human desire to survive. While 127 Hours is relatively static and claustrophobic, The Way Back is all about movement and space, filling the screen with vistas that are startling in their seemingly benign beauty, though clearly malevolent in their raw harshness and inherent deprivations. The performances by the international ensemble are outstanding, led by Harris as a stoic American engineer who came to Moscow in the 1930s with this teenage son to work on Moscow’s Metro. During a purge, his son is killed and he is sent to the gulag. Sturgess portrays Janusz, a young Polish cavalry officer, accused by his wife of spying. And there’s Farrell’s fine performance as the gangster who cannot connect Stalin’s “reign of terror” to his own incarceration. Ronan is perfect as Irena, a young girl who finds the group weeks after they have escaped and joins them on their journey. The film belies the theory that January (with the exception of late Oscar releases) is caught in the movie doldrums. This Peter Weir film, if it portends anything, is hopefully the first of other fine films to follow. The Way Back. Directed by Peter Weir. Starring Jim Sturgess, Ed Harris, Colin Farrell, Mark Strong, and Saoirse Ronan. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13. Released and originally reviewed in the Post in 2011.
articles.title: The Way Back a fine film by Peter Weir

articles.text: A scene from the 2015 Oscar nominated animated film Shaun the Sheep. Shaun the Sheep Movie, the 2015 Oscar nominated claymation animated feature film from the British Aardman Studios of Wallace and Gromit fame, is now streaming on HBO Max/Prime. It’s a winning family movie, absent any intelligible dialogue (lots of facial expressions, grunts and pointing), delivered in the spirit of Buster Keaton. The story begins when Shaun, a free-spirited sheep, who lives with his flock on the Mossy Bottom Farm owned by a local farmer (John Sparkes). Shaun decides that life on the Mossy Bottom, which includes three boorish pigs, a bull and some ducks is decidedly monotonous. And so he and his wooly compatriots make a plan to keep the farmer sound asleep in his trailer, counting his sheep. Meanwhile, they are going to spend the day in the farmer’s house eating snacks and watching TV. Of course, things don’t go exactly as planned, and the trailer rolls away with the sleeping farmer, and his faithful dog Blitzer, inside. It ends up in the big city. Along the way, the farmer gets a knock on the head, and wakes up in the city hospital with a case of amnesia. Shaun and the flock quickly learn that life on Mossy Bottom isn’t so easy without the farmer, and so they disguise themselves as humans and head to the city on two buses in search of the farmer. And thus begins their city adventure, which is far from boring. It involves a malevolent animal control guy, named Trumper (Omid Djalili)., who captures Shaun and Blitzer. With the help of a homeless dog, Slip (Tim Hands), the three manage to escape. Meanwhile, when the flock finally finds the farmer, he doesn’t recognize any of them due to his amnesia. Shaun and crew get to work in devising a new plan to get the farmer back to Mossy Bottom. Unexpectedly, Trumper is right behind them, and furious. But in the nick of time, the farmer regains his memory, outsmarts Trumper, and life on the farm returns to normal. The only difference is that Shaun and crew come to realize that they should always be careful what they wish for. Shaun the Sheep Movie is pure fun, filled with chases, narrow escapes, and lots of romps. There’s even a hilarious scene where the farmer, having had extensive shearing experience, briefly becomes a famous city hairstylist. It’s the first of many sight gags, jokes and thrills. Shaun the Sheep Movie. Directed by Mark Burton and Richard Starzk. With the voices of Justin Fletcher, John Sparkes, and Omid Djalili. 1 hr., 25 min. Rated PG. Released in theaters in 2015. Now streaming on HBO Max/Prime.
articles.title: Shaun the Sheep Movie – pure fun and very funny

articles.text: Raya and the Last Dragon, an Oscar nominated, Disney animation feature film released in 2021, is now streaming on Disney+. Its visuals are eye-popping, a gorgeous palette of vibrant colors, the feel-good story is set in the Pan-Asian/South Asian fictional land of Kumundra and is filled with memorable characters. It stars the voices of Kelly Marie Tran as Princess Raya; Awkwafina as Sisu the dragon; Gem ma Chan por t raying Namaari, Raya’s nemesis; Daniel Dae Kim in the role of Benja, chief of the kingdom Heart, and father of Raya; Izaac Wang as boy captain; and Benedict Wong as Tong, the boy warrior. The quest to reassemble the Dragon Gem is the thematic McGuffin for what is a breezy, laugh-filled, and compelling adventure undertaken by a young warrior princess, Raya, who speaks to us in the set up about a broken, dystopian world, asking how it became that way. Then comes a flashback to a time some 500 years earlier when the magical land of Kumandra prospered with humans and friendly dragons living in remarkable harmony. But a plague, in the form of purple-black tornadoes, called Druuns, descended on the land and turned every dragon to stone, save for one, Sisu, who used the magical Dragon Gem to defeat the Druuns, and then disappeared. The story moves forward in time a half-millennium, and it’s then that we meet Raya, training with her father, Benja, to become the guardian of a shard of their Dragon Gem, hidden in a deep cave in their kingdom known as Heart. There are now five Kingdoms, Heart, Fang, Talon, Tail, and Spine that no longer peacefully co-exist, each possessing a fragments of the Gem. Apparently the Druun has returned, and just before Benja is turned to stone, he tells her that it will be her mission to journey to the four other kingdoms where she must find the other Dragon Gems, reunite them, find the last dragon, Sisu, and thereby bring back harmony to Kumandra. Along the way she crosses amazing, challenging landscapes, engages in beautifully choreographed martial arts battles, and gathers around her a cohort of enchanting, interesting characters, to include the improbable, playful (even goofy), incandescent dragon, Sisu. She also learns to trust Namaari, initially her nemesis. Faith and trust are two embedded themes in this remarkably gorgeous, extraordinary animated tale. Raya and the Last Dragon. Directed by Don Hall & Carlos Lopez. Disney animation. With the voices of Awkwafina, Kelly Marie Tran, Sandra Oh, and Daniel Dae Kim. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG. Released in theaters in 2021. Now Streaming on Disney+.
articles.title: Raya and the Last Dragon a beautiful, magical film

pages.text: Wednesday, April 13, 2022 23 Retiring early? Know your health care choices Life doesn’t always go as planned. For example, you might think you’ll retire at 65 or later, when you’ll be eligible for Medicare. But if you retire before then, how will you pay for your health care? Without insurance, you risk incurring thousands of dollars of expenses if you are injured or become seriously ill. And if you must pay for these costs out of pocket, you might have to dip into your IRA, 401(k) or other retirement accounts earlier than you had planned – which could result in a less desirable retirement lifestyle than you had envisioned. What, then, are your options? It depends on your situation, but here are four possibilities: • Employer retiree health benefits If your former employer offers health coverage to retirees, it could well be your best choice, especially if the employer continues to pay a share of the premiums. However, fewer employers are offering continuing health coverage to former employees, and among those who do, they may use certain criteria – such as length of service and position within the company – to limit eligibility. • Spouse’s plan If you’re married and your spouse still has employer-provided insurance, you may be able to get coverage under this plan or continue this coverage if you have it already. If the employer subsidizes premiums for spouses, this plan could be an affordable choice – if not, though, it might be more expensive than other options. • COBRA The Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA) allows you to maintain your existing coverage with the same benefits and provider network. However, COBRA is typically only available for a specific time – usually 18 months – after you leave your employer, and coverage can be expensive. Your previous employer subsidized a portion of the premium as a benefit, but once you’ve retired, you’ll likely have to pay the entire premium, plus an additional charge. • ACA Marketplace plan Through the Affordable Care Act Marketplace, you can find a variety of plans from which to choose, possibly including ones that include your existing network. If you qualify for subsidies, the premiums for your coverage may be similar to employer-sponsored coverage; if not, though, they can be more expensive. For information on ACA Marketplace plans, visit www.healthcare.gov. If you have options for health insurance, you’ll want to take into account differences in coverage and cost. Check whether your desired health care providers are in-network and try to determine if your current medications and the benefits you rely on are covered. You may also want to consider a plan that allows you to open a health savings account (HSA), which offers potential tax benefits. To contribute to an HSA, you must be covered by a high deductible health plan (HDHP), so there’s that cost to consider, but if you’re in generally good health and you don’t expect to depend heavily on your health insurance until you’re eligible for Medicare, you might want to consider an HDHP. One final note: Even when you do enroll in Medicare, you will still incur expenses for premiums, deductibles and co-pays, so you’ll want to budget for these costs in your overall financial strategy. In the meantime, explore your health insurance options. The future is not ours to see – so you’ll want to be prepared for anything. READ IT IN THE POST Dear Abby A pet column compiled by Piedmont pets The return of Noqui, the pug By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: Good news. Noqui was reunited with her owners. They picked her up on Sunday. She was thrilled to see them. I guess she got loose in the car and wiggled out the door and they couldn’t find her. They contacted multiple Animal Services and finally saw my post. Her name is actually Luna. Nice, right? I’m so grateful for the help. –Natalia Dear Natalia: You made our Pug Day. We are so happy that Luna made it back to her owners. What a gift. I can imagine how happy her owners were, and Luna, too. That you found a lost, uncollared dog wandering in a Trader Joe’s parking lot, protected her from all the cars and carts, and found her owners is truly staggering. You saved her life. We are all grateful to you. Woof, high paws. –Abby Dear Abby: Have you heard of any dog Easter Egg Hunts happening in Piedmont? Or anywhere? I know that Tucker and Rocky would love to hunt a few eggs and I’d love them to get exhausted so that we could have a peaceful ham supper. Egg tossup? –Tucker, Rocky and their tired owner, Henry Dear Tucker, Rocky and Henry: Wags Hotel did offer an Easter Egg Hunt for Dogs in Alameda before the pandemic, but we couldn’t find any news of one in 2022. Setting up a dogfriendly egg hunt in your yard is an easy way to test your dog’s sense of smell – and wear them out, too. Here are some tips for doing it yourself: 1. Some people say use hard boiled eggs out of the freezer, 2 eggs per dog, but my vote is to put their fav treat into the same cheap, plastic Easter eggs you bought for your kids and teach them to hunt them. Remember you must help the dogs open them up—no cracking the plastic. We don’t want any plastic getting into the intestinal tract. 2. Another option is to just hide treats around the yard in small paper bowls – they’ll be happy either way. Some people tie balloons to the treats in case the dog or the human needs help finding them. It’s easier for eventual clean up, too. We always found an egg a month or so later in the yard that the kids hadn’t found. 3. The best treats for an Egg Hunt are the smelly ones – the smellier the better. Dogs with more advanced noses (retrievers & Labs) will be happy with a tiny doggy biscuit placed in an egg. But if you have a Frenchie or a Bulldog, they may not get the sniffing idea. Help them out a bit; show them an egg with a smelly treat. Xylitol-free peanut butter is always a good one. Eventually they will understand that eggs mean treats. If they don’t just keep showing them. Ideas for treats are freeze-dried liver, small squares of cheese, tiny pieces of chicken jerky, cubes of cooked chicken, or regular old kibble. 4. While most dogs are not totally color-blind, bright pink won’t help them. So don’t worry about egg colors. If your grandchild loves pink, keep the pink ones away from the doggies. 5. If you want real Martha Stewart points, put bunny ears over their ears and send us pics. 6. Fenced yards are a must. If I hear of any Hunts, I will let you know but right now, it looks like you’ll be doing the Hunt in your yard. This is all good nose work. Happy hunting. –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at melandogs@gmail.com. articles.text: A robust group of 28 individuals and one K-9 best friend showed up for a Walking on Wednesdays excursion on April 6: Stella Houston, Rob Smith, Pat Sheehan, Sherry Jacobs, Albert Chen, Priscilla Wanerus, Melba Yee, Lois Price, Dena Belinkoff, Claudia Lopez, Pat McMahon, Lynn Richmond, Bob Wong, Kat Lang, Alicia Rivera, Jo Normington with K-9 best friend Penny Lane, Adrienne Hamlin, Elizabeth Richter, Quincy Dong, Pat Keller, Mike Henn, Jim Kuo, Sarah Johnson, Elane Rehr, Harriette Louie, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Elane Rehr and Pat Keller brought their husbands, Howard Davis and Greg Keller. On Wednesday, April 6, Lois Price informed members of the Walking on Wednesdays group it was “National Walking Day,” a designation created in 2007 by the American Heart Association on the first April Wednesday of every year. The group was reminded that on April 20 and 27 Hope Salzer will lead sneak preview tours of two Piedmont gardens that are part of the 18th Annual “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Features Showcase.” And after that, on May 4, former Piedmont mayor Bob McBain will host the walkers on a visit to Tyson Lake at the back of his Sotelo Avenue home. With the weather on the warm side last week, it was thought that it would be good to avoid a long walk with lots of climbing. Going through the center of town to Coaches Field and Kennelly Skate Park off Moraga Avenue was a level, relatively short walk. To keep the group refreshed on Piedmont history, they were reminded that Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area in 1852, had originally named this road “Vernal Avenue” because it was so lush with vegetation. When the group got to the end of Highland (Vernal) at Moraga Avenue, more of Blair’s history from Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research was shared. This included the fact that across the street on Moraga was the original entrance to Blair Park in 1884. This was Blair’s large, picnic park attraction that generated ridership for his Piedmont Railway horsecars. The group walked over the boardwalk along Moraga that spans the edge of the canyon below, and serves as a sidewalk to Coaches Field. In the parking lot in front of the field more of the area’s history was shared. This was once Piedmont’s landfill before the canyon of what is now Coaches Field was filled. The park was first dedicated in 1994; and in 2001, with the support of Piedmont native and Otis Spunkmeyer Cookies founder Ken (Bebe) Rawlings, the sports field was created. It honors the many Piedmont coaches who have worked with the city’s youth. A copy of the City Council-approved Coaches Field Expansion Concept Plan map was also shared with the walkers. The project is unfunded but is what the City would like to do with the field some day. The next destination was the Kennelly Skate Park, just beyond the left field and up a hill. With some trepidation they admired the deep bowls that much younger people fearlessly skate up and down. Most of the walkers did manage to descend some stairs that led into one of the bowls for a group photo. Though a little scary, the concrete bowls are impressive. From the skate park the walkers had a view of San Francisco and the Salesforce Tower in the distance. On the way back they admired front yards, one of which had an orchid plant that was about as big as a mid-sized Christmas tree, as well as beautiful bougainvillea and wisteria flowers. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome by registering with the Piedmont Recreation Department at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.
