articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group, sponsored by Piedmont Recreation Department, met outside the Tea House in Piedmont Park on April 4 for a discussion of its April selection, Destiny of the Republic by Candice Millard. Eighteen members of the group were on hand to enjoy the beautiful weather and the book. Carol Long and Alicia Rivera continued to spoil the group with chocolate and fruit treats that added fuel to the conversation. Destiny of the Republic is Millard’s 2011 book that tells the story of the life and assassination of James A. Garfield, the 20th President of the United States. However, it is a three-way biography of President Garfield, Charles Guiteau, the president’s assassin, and inventor Alexander Graham Bell. Most Americans know little about President Garfield. Sadly, it is a story with a tragic ending. Garfield may have been one of the most extraordinary men ever elected president. He was born into poverty, but through his hard work and outstanding abilities, he became a scholar, a Civil War hero, and an admired reformist congressman. He was nominated for president against his will and fought against the corrupt political establishment of the time. articles.text: Kathleen “Kathy” Cutter Shelly, a beloved wife, mother, grandmother, and active member of Corpus Christi and St. Joseph’s Catholic Churches, passed away on March 5, 2022 at Washington Hospital in Fremont surrounded by her loving husband and children after a valiant 7-month battle with cancer. She was 75. The daughter of Joseph (né Antonio) “Duke” Reboli and Katherine “Becky” Bannon. Kathy was born on November 16, 1946 at a premature weight of 4 pounds, 13 ounces in Oakland, California. Kathleen Anne Reboli grew up within the protective confines of her parents’ Irish-Italian household, which sat atop her grandfather C.P. Bannon’s mortuary. With a mother as an accomplished pianist and organist, Kathy often kept her company, sitting at her feet while she played for both the mortuary and local Catholic churches. The experiences greatly influenced Kathy’s love of classical, opera, and sacred music. Kathy’s mother also played music for the likes of Charlie Chaplin and other actors in silent films, including playing the pipe organ at the Grand Lake Theater in Oakland At one point she was the youngest member of the Musician’s Guild. At the time, she had broken a number of glass ceilings, having learned piano and helped to support her family from the age of 5 as a woman in the entertainment business. Kathy’s mother had a successful career into her 40s, prior to establishing a family after the birth of Kathy. She also influenced Kathy’s career-minded views and her later retirement at age 70. Kathy’s father was a professional golf instructor at the Claremont Country Club and had retired as the head golf professional at the Richmond Country Club. He volunteered during both World Wars, and was stationed on the U.S.S. Yorktown, known as “the Fighting Lady,” which was found on the Pacific Floor 56 years after it sunk. Throughout her childhood, Kathy endured multiple corrective procedures and leg braces in order help her walk. A born fighter, she eventually was able to rollerskate competitively in San Leandro and across California, with practice often beginning in the predawn hours before high school. She attended St. Bernard’s grade school and Notre Dame High School in the Bay Area. Working at Highland Hospital before becoming a collections deputy for Alameda County, Kathy subsequently worked in the telecommunications and cellular field for over 30 years, a time when pay phones were more prevalent than cell phones. Kathy was a also single mother for several years prior to meeting her beloved husband Stephen “Steve” Doyle Shelly in 1982 on a blind date. The couple was married in 1983 and would have celebrated their 39th anniversary this May. The couple began its journey in a house Kathy co-designed – a glass house on steel girders that in the 1970’s sat on a terrarium housing a cougar named “Cynthia.” Steve adopted Kathy’s children Terésa and Duke as his own, taking care of them while Kathy worked long hours and went back to school to complete a Master’s degree in Psychology at John F. Kennedy University while working full-time and commuting. Steve brought into the marriage his own son Mark, whom Kathy considered as her eldest son. In Piedmont and Fremont, where they split their time during their golden years, they were surrounded by family, neighbors, and friends who became lifelong connections. Kathy and Steve were frequent visitors at Corpus Christi Church with their granddaughter, Élodie, who remembers those Sundays fondly. The grandparents also served St. Joseph’s-Mission San Jose parish and gave back to the Catholic Church and community at large, including sponsoring the upbringing of several children around the world. Kathy was known by many for her pilgrimages to the Vatican and the churches of Croatia, Italy, and Ireland, pilgrimages that she also shared with her family and grandchildren. Kathy also became a minister of communion and RCIA teacher for several years, as well as spending time volunteering at a shelter for battered women. She later helped raise awareness for the victims of sexual trafficking. She was known for her inner strength, principles, and great faith, inspiring many to turn to prayer, even touching those who cared for her during her valiant battle with cancer. Kathleen walked in the steps of her faith throughout her life and illness, suffering and giving up her life during this Lenten season. We look forward to her resurrection during the Easter season. Kathy is survived by her husband, Steve Shelly, children Terésa Cutter Nordenfelt, Duke Cutter, and Mark Shelly, and grandchildren Killian Shelly, Keegan Shelly, Natalie Nordenfelt, Oliver Nordenfelt, Joseph Cutter, and Élodie Nordenfelt.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 13, 2022 27 Cozy corners to inspire connection By Laura Martin Bovard Much of the lifestyle we became accustomed to before we were blindsided by a pandemic has transformed. I joke with one of my beloved clients that I have learned the art of pivoting due to her sometimes quickly changing mind. My ability to pivot has also been fortified from the rapidly changing industry of building materials and furnishings brought on by the pandemic. It feels like emotional whiplash learning and subsequently delivering news about delays and discontinued items with clients. Were it not for my robust spiritual practice, I would be catatonic dealing with the stress of this industry, not to mention the heartbreak in the world today and the emotional fallout of being a mom, a wife, a friend, and a business owner. The most heart-centered way I can move forward is to focus on creating beautiful home spaces that encourage our clients’ families to gather. Gathering presents itself differently for many of our clients, so we take that into account when designing their spaces. The Bay Area is teeming with foodies and home chefs who adore a well-appointed kitchen. A sitting area keeps friends and family out of the way while creating an invitation for everyone to participate in the theater of cooking. The breakfast nook is an ideal way to accomplish that and serves even more purposes. Whether preparing and enjoying a meal, doing homework, reading a magazine, or playing Wordle, a nook is the pandemic’s answer to staying close and modernizing the dining experience. More and more, I hear stories from friends and clients about how they are beginning to see friends again. I see how humanizing that is. One underlying theme I hear most is that we are all holding our beloveds a little closer, and lingering in hugs a little longer. Witnessing the atrocities happening in Ukraine invites us to remember that nothing in life is guaranteed. The highlight of my weekend was receiving a text from a client who shared that they were enjoying their atrium with friends. “The room feels warm and wonderful and playful,” he wrote. How does it get any better than that?! (Thank you, Chris!) It can be difficult to feel gratitude instead of guilt when we are blessed with so much. However, as many wise people have reflected, feeling bad for others does not make their situation better. In fact, recognizing gratitude and meaning in our own lives is the best thing we can do to keep us out of fear and inaction. What better way to be in gratitude and feel close to your people than cozying up in a banquette? For those who might feel stifled sitting in a booth, it’s important to round out the experience with a couple of chairs. I’ve curated some inspirational nooks, along with tips for creating perfect multipurpose gathering spaces in homes. Here are five tips when considering a breakfast nook: 1. Find a corner where a built-in can be added along with a small round table and one or two chairs. 2. Curved lines and ovals make it easier to slide in and out 3. Make it a destination and a cozy container. 4. Consider putting one in your formal dining room. Laura Martin Bovard is the principal at LMB Interiors, located in downtown Oakland. Since 2002 she has helped clients create beautiful, joyful, and functional homes. The firm has garnered numerous awards and recognition as one of the Bay Area’s most sought after interior design agencies. For information see laura@lmbinteriors. com

articles.text: Nº 52 in a biweekly series France held its presidential election on Sunday and President Emmanuel Macron faces a runoff against far-right nemesis Marine Le Pen on April 24, and once again he will have to defeat her to remain President. But unlike five years ago, pundits predict a close race while they tug over voters’ struggle with inflationary costs. The race is Macron’s to lose, a critical match where a loss to Le Pen could lead to hostility toward the European Union of which France is a founding member. Le Pen sidled up to Putin for years, and she opposes the financial sanctions imposed on Russian aggression. She warns that sanctions could backfire and cost runaway inflation, though she is sympathetic to Ukrainians. This is her third and last attempt, she says, to win the presidency. At age 18 she joined the right-wing party National Front founded by her firebrand of a father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, climbing through the ranks, until she ousted him in 2011 and renamed the party National Rally. She’s a member of the National Assembly and represents Calais, a region that struggles with migrants en route to the U.K. For decades she’s railed about the failure of multiculturalism and unchecked immigration. Her father is an unapologetic anti-Semite and Holocaust denier, eager to tell any listener that Nazi gas chambers are but a footnote in history. With the election of Donald Trump, Marine encouraged the political likeness. She aligned herself with Brexit, a financial catastrophe for the U.K. Voters report that Marine appears calmer, more personable, and willing to focus on pocketbook issues to win over voters. Known for her toxicity, Marine’s team has worked to sand down rough edges to appear presidential. Where Macron trounced Le Pen in the last presidential runoff with 66% of the vote to her 34%, this race will not be a cakewalk. Macron was an energetic newcomer when he led the centrist En Marche! Party in 2017 and he scored impressively against the vastly more seasoned Le Pen. As a result of Sunday’s primary election, Macron holds first place with 27.84% of the vote versus Marine Le Pen’s 23%. France takes democracy seriously, and typically 80% of French voters head to the polls. In this round, 73.69% voted, a notable abstention of six percentage points. A more robust turnout is expected in Round Two, and political discourse is expected to be elevated over the next two weeks. Macron vigorously campaigned last election, but he did little formal campaigning for reelection. Did Macron sacrifice his reelection chances in exchange for the prestige of diplomacy? Macron is highly visible in his current role as chief spokesman for the European Union Council, a rotating duty for the 27 member nations. The world anxiously watches Europe’s interactions with Russia’s impenetrable President Vladimir Putin. Macron’s role as mediator appeared to burnish his reputation as a global statesman, and a recent poll confirmed that 88% of the French Ballot counting in the primary round on Sunday, April 10. Former President Nicolas Sarkozy says he will vote for Macron (right) in the election runoff. Far-right National Rally party candidate Marie Le Pen enters Round Two opposing President Macron. But he pushed aside the duties and protocol of a political campaign, even delaying formal entry into the race, which annoyed his opponents in a field of 12 candidates. Though few questioned his seriousness for reelection, he didn’t hold a campaign rally until the weekend before the election. Though an excellent debater, Macron declined to debate any of the candidates. By election night Macron was backpedaling on a signature issue to prop up the budget, one that Le Pen spins as his “obsession.” Macron wants to keep workers on the job until age 65, rather than starting their pensions at age 62, which enrages workers. France is the seventh largest economy in the world and has 67 million people. It’s one of the world’s nuclear powers. France is a permanent member of the five-seat Security Council of the United Nations and a founding member of the European Union. The Ukraine crisis is monumentally complex to resolve, and no one projects with confidence a leader such as Le Pen in the role. Russia’s daily Pravda ignores European news, other than approval for Hungary’s Viktor Orbán, and drones to readers that “at least two-thirds of the world’s population does not fault Russia for its actions in Ukraine.” Russia deems any evidence to the contrary to be a fraud, and agreement over evidentiary facts is elusive. Comments on the other candidates Of the three top candidates having close results, the hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon came in third receiving 21.95%. He spun a victory story on election night when the vote was close to overtaking Le Pen’s 23%. He leads France Unbowed, a breakaway Socialist party that splintered into six individual parties. Mélenchon congratulated a win of nearly two percentage points over the party’s 2017 performance. A former Senator and elder statesman, Mélenchon is calling it quits in politics. He preached to his flock, “Like Sisyphus, we must keep pushing the stone back up the hill,” and without a mention of Macron by name, he intoned, “We must not give a single vote to Le Pen.” The hard-left contender Éric Zemmour, neither a politician nor experienced in government, is a public figure and opinionated intellectual, a writer of some 20 books, and columnist for the conservative Le Figaro. Zemmour A local election voting center harshly blames immigrants for recolonizing France and blasts neoliberals for social ills that have fallen French society. His extreme pontificating served Le Pen well in making her appear almost moderate. Zemmour eked out 7.2% of the ranked vote, and he immediately turned to his supporters to vote for Marina Le Pen in the runoff. Les Republicain (LR) candidate Valérie Pécresse clawed away a very low outcome, just 4.8% of the vote. Supporters reacted to the death knell as the vote indicated a near collapse of France’s traditional center-right party that was founded in 1958. It has elected presidents Nicolas Sarkozy, Jacques Chirac, and Charles de Gaulle. In the prior election, LR suffered the defeat of candidate François Fillon caught in a graft scandal. Macron’s magical opportunity came as he swept to a 2017 win as the new center-right candidate. LR is the most solid party in all of France represented widely in municipalities, but it is without a national candidate. Pécresse immediately threw her support behind Macron, and against Le Pen. But Pécresse is in a critical financial bind, and on election night, she publicly appealed to the French to donate to help pay off the €16M campaign debt. The vote of 4.8% is insufficient for the campaign to meet the 5% voter threshold. Only a much smaller figure will be reimbursed by the state. She personally vouched for €5M, and she’s on the hook to pay by May 15. The environmental candidate Yannick Jadot of Europe-Ecologie-Les Verts received 4.63% of the vote, very close to Pécresse’s result. Jean Lassale of Résistons! party that pursues the media’s careless reporting got 3.13% and will run for the National Assembly in the June. At age 18 she joined the right-wing party National Front founded by her firebrand of a father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, climbing through the ranks, until she ousted him in 2011 and renamed the party National Rally. She’s a member of the National Assembly and represents Calais, a region that struggles with migrants en route to the U.K. For decades she’s railed about the failure of multiculturalism and unchecked immigration. Her father is an unapologetic anti-Semite and Holocaust denier, eager to tell any listener that Nazi gas chambers are but a footnote in history. With the election of Donald Trump, Marine encouraged the political likeness. She French National Election, Round One aligned herself with Brexit, a financial catastrophe for the U.K. Voters report that Marine appears calmer, more personable, and willing to focus on pocketbook issues to win over voters. Known for her toxicity, Marine’s team has worked to sand down rough edges to appear presidential. Where Macron trounced Le Pen in the last presidential runoff with 66% of the vote to her 34%, this race will not be a cakewalk. Macron was an energetic newcomer when he led the centrist En Marche! Party in 2017 and he scored impressively against the vastly more seasoned Le Pen. As a result of Sunday’s primary election, Macron holds first place with 27.84% of the vote versus Marine Le Pen’s 23%. France takes democracy seriously, and typically 80% of French voters head to the polls. In this round, 73.69% voted, a notable abstention of six percentage points. A more robust turnout is expected in Round Two, and political discourse is expected to be elevated over the next two weeks. Macron vigorously campaigned last election, but he did little formal campaigning for reelection. Did Macron sacrifice his reelection chances in exchange for the prestige of diplomacy? Macron is highly visible in his current role as chief spokesman for the European Union Council, a rotating duty for the 27 member nations. The world anxiously watches Europe’s interactions with Russia’s impenetrable President Vladimir Putin. Macron’s role as mediator appeared to burnish his reputation as a global statesman, and a recent poll confirmed that 88% of the French Ballot counting in the primary round on Sunday, April 10. Former President Nicolas Sarkozy says he will vote for Macron (right) in the election runoff. Far-right National Rally party candidate Marie Le Pen enters Round Two opposing President Macron. But he pushed aside the duties and protocol of a political campaign, even delaying formal entry into the race, which annoyed his opponents in a field of 12 candidates. Though few questioned his seriousness for reelection, he didn’t hold a campaign rally until the weekend before the election. Though an excellent debater, Macron declined to debate any of the candidates. By election night Macron was backpedaling on a signature issue to prop up the budget, one that Le Pen spins as his “obsession.” Macron wants to keep workers on the job until age 65, rather than starting their pensions at age 62, which enrages workers. France is the seventh largest economy in the world and has 67 million people. It’s one of the world’s nuclear powers. France is a permanent member of the five-seat Security Council of the United Nations and a founding member of the European Union. The Ukraine crisis is monumentally complex to resolve, and no one projects with confidence a leader such as Le Pen in the role. Russia’s daily Pravda ignores European news, other than approval for Hungary’s Viktor Orbán, and drones to readers that “at least two-thirds of the world’s population does not fault Russia for its actions in Ukraine.” Russia deems any evidence to the contrary to be a fraud, and agreement over evidentiary facts is elusive. Comments on the other candidates Of the three top candidates having close results, the hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon came in third receiving 21.95%. He spun a victory story on election night when the vote was close to overtaking Le Pen’s 23%. He leads France Unbowed, a breakaway Socialist party that splintered into six individual parties. Mélenchon congratulated a win of nearly two percentage points over the party’s 2017 performance. A former Senator and elder statesman, Mélenchon is calling it quits in politics. He preached to his flock, “Like Sisyphus, we must keep pushing the stone back up the hill,” and without a mention of Macron by name, he intoned, “We must not give a single vote to Le Pen.” The hard-left contender Éric Zemmour, neither a politician nor experienced in government, is a public figure and opinionated intellectual, a writer of some 20 books, and columnist for the conservative Le Figaro. Zemmour A local election voting center harshly blames immigrants for recolonizing France and blasts neoliberals for social ills that have fallen French society. His extreme pontificating served Le Pen well in making her appear almost moderate. Zemmour eked out 7.2% of the ranked vote, and he immediately turned to his supporters to vote for Marina Le Pen in the runoff. Les Republicain (LR) candidate Valérie Pécresse clawed away a very low outcome, just 4.8% of the vote. Supporters reacted to the death knell as the vote indicated a near collapse of France’s traditional center-right party that was founded in 1958. It has elected presidents Nicolas Sarkozy, Jacques Chirac, and Charles de Gaulle. In the prior election, LR suffered the defeat of candidate François Fillon caught in a graft scandal. Macron’s magical opportunity came as he swept to a 2017 win as the new center-right candidate. LR is the most solid party in all of France represented widely in municipalities, but it is without a national candidate. Pécresse immediately threw her support behind Macron, and against Le Pen. But Pécresse is in a critical financial bind, and on election night, she publicly appealed to the French to donate to help pay off the €16M campaign debt. The vote of 4.8% is insufficient for the campaign to meet the 5% voter threshold. Only a much smaller figure will be reimbursed by the state. She personally vouched for €5M, and she’s on the hook to pay by May 15. The environmental candidate Yannick Jadot of Europe-Ecologie-Les Verts received 4.63% of the vote, very close to Pécresse’s result. Jean Lassale of Résistons! party that pursues the media’s careless reporting got 3.13% and will run for the National Assembly in the June. French Communist party leader Fabien Roussel got 2.28% of the vote. Euroskeptique Nicolas Dupont-Aignan raked in 2.06%; and the mayor of Paris, Socialist Anne Hidalgo got an embarrassingly paltry 1.75%. Two more candidates, who may or may not surface again in a political race, had less than one percent of the vote apiece. Patricia Forsyth and Michael Mathews decamped to Paris to be tourists in The City of Light. articles.text: March arrived with a special, rare treat. For Piedmont Scouts in Troop 1 it meant a double outing – two overnight outings in one month. Usually, the Scouts go on one outing per month, however COVID surges delayed a January ski trip by two months. This meant that we would have two outings, our annual Kirby Cove trip at a campground near the Marin side of the Golden Gate Bridge, and a spring skiing trip to Bear Valley. This trip was physically a lot easier. Mentally? Not so much. I was grateful for the spacious lodge and heater; however, it definitely had its downsides. Have you ever spent three hours in a car with your best friend, her sister and parents? Oh, and let’s not forget my dad and the fact that he and my friend’s dad were endlessly talking (solar, expensive daughters, etc.). It was exhausting. Maybe we should focus on the destination instead of the journey. It’s breaking the rules of a clichè, but technically, “the journey never ends,” so it’s not a destination – it’s a stop. Upon returning to the lodge the rest of our Troop had arrived. After chaos about one of the gas burners and a movie, we found our rooms but barely slept. articles.text: French, Spanish and Mandarin classes featured in school event Throughout the day on Monday, April 4, Piedmont High School’s World Language Department held the spring iteration of its biennial singing competition outdoors in the school amphitheater. Each foreign language class performed a song in the language they were studying, with songs in French, Mandarin and Spanish. In 2017 PHS French teacher Christele David began the tradition by having her French classes serenade students in other classes with French carols. Since then, the event has expanded into an informal all-day singing competition. Now the event is cross-curricular, as the Ceramics students provide trophies for each winning class period. “It is an acapella event. The whole point is for students to showcase their talents and to sing in the target language,” said Spanish teacher Señora Jessica McMillen. articles.text: Piedmont Garden Club members cloaked the city in an array of bouquets on April Fool’s Day. Displays went up quietly before dawn, and some remained through the weekend. By Monday morning, the messages disappeared. This was the club’s third planned “Flash Flower bomb,” taking inspiration from Lewis Miller’s flash flower movement. Passersby were treated to vivid exhibits that served as messages of peace, gratitude, and ceremony. Garden Club members Agnes Kang and Cathy Glazier decided on a floral display of peace in solidarity with Ukraine. Kang said the Flash Flower caper was enthusiastically embraced by new club members Sara Kimball, Terri Ashton, Lisa Lomenzo, and Christine Wente von Metzsch. Club President Lori Adams joined the crew in adorning the Magnolia tree on the green triangle of Sheridan and Highland Avenues with eight floral wreaths in purple and gold, which were hung from the tree in bright yellow ribbon. “Expression of solidarity with the Ukrainian people was an obvious theme,” Kang explained. “Flowers used were those that Photo by Rob Yelland Sunflowers, Ukraine’s national flower, adorned the Bufano bear statues in Crocker Park. would hold up well for four days out of water: yellow chrysanthemums and carnations, green ruscus, and purple statice. Yellow ribbons, usually displayed in Photo by Rob Yelland Wreaths hung from a tree on Highland Avenue, a thoughtful decision by Agnes Kang and Cathy Glazier. support of troops abroad, not only added color but significance to the wreaths. The Alameda County Public Health Department advised recently that residents should continue to exercise preventative measures including standing six feet apart, wearing masks, and getting tested if exposed. “Even though conditions have improved, COVID is here to stay and the choices we make will affect us, our households, and the community,” said Dr. Nicholas Moss, Alameda County Health Officer. “The past two years taught us that COVID-19 vaccines, masks and other precautions work and can be tailored based on our environment, age and health condition. articles.text: The City of Piedmont will host a virtual discussion tomorrow, April 7, on equitable real estate practices that support an inclusive community. The event, entitled “Welcome to Piedmont: Real Estate Practices in Support of an Inclusive Community,” is co-sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters, Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee, and Piedmont Racial Equity Committee. The discussion will be moderated by Piedmont resident Carol Galante, founder of the Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley. Panelists include retired Piedmont real estate agent Maureen Kennedy, a member of the Clinton Administration, Farrah Wilder, Chief Diversity and Equity Officer at California Association of Realtors, and Ashley Gardner, Community Outreach Coordinator for California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). Residents and real estate professionals who tune in will learn about the current context for real estate practices and its impact on the demographics of the Piedmont community. A moderated discussion between the above professionals will focus on the benefits of an inclusive community and how Piedmont residents can help affirm the city’s commitment to be a more welcoming and diverse community. “Real estate transactions and the interplay between sellers, real estate professionals and potential buyers is one piece of a complex puzzle we are striving to solve... how to bring more diversity to Piedmont,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said. “We look forward to an engaging dialogue focused on evolving practices and new ideas to help shape the Piedmont of the future.” In September 2021 Gov. Gavin Newsom signed into law over 30 affordable housing bills that focused on cutting red tape and holding cities accountable for providing their fair share of housing. To participate in this event, use the Zoom Registration Link at https://piedmont-ca-gov. zoom.us/webinar/register/WN_ zGnJ-AWnT4KFzrNxe2mKlg.
articles.title: City discussion on equitable real estate practices tomorrow

articles.text: Talk at Center for the Arts on Wednesday, April 20 Anastasia Edel on MSNBC Piedmont resident Anastasia Edel, author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, will speak at the Piedmont Center for the Arts at 7:30 p.m. on Wednesday, April 20 about Russia’s invasion of neighboring Ukraine, and its implications worldwide. Why did Vladimir Putin attack the sovereign nation of Ukraine, with which Russia shares centuries of common past? What’s behind the brutality of Putin’s war? How much popular support does he enjoy in Russia? Edel, an acclaimed writer, social historian and New York Times contributor, talks about her experience of growing up in the heavily Ukraine-influenced Russian south, the historical and cultural entwinement of the two countries’ natives, and the consequences of this war for Russia and the world. In lieu of an entrance fee, consider making a donation to Help Ukraine Center that supports refugees and distributes humanitarian aid. https://helpukraine. center/ A question and answer session will be held following her talk. Edel’s writing has appeared in The New York Review of Books, The New York Times, Foreign Policy, Project Syndicate, World Literature Today and others. She recently has appeared on CNN, PBS, NBC and MSNBC to discuss the crisis in Ukraine. She has taught at Piedmont Language school, and taught a six-week course on Russian politics and culture at the UC Berkeley OLLI Institute. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmontpost.org Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Allyson Aleksey PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Jay Russell Ed Gilligan SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: (A reflection on Enoch and Jude) In the Bible studies I lead at Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church week by week we have been considering one passage from each book of the Bible. Over a year ago we began with Genesis. Now, we are soon to reach Revelation. Before reading from Revelation, we will read the entirety of the short. 24-verse book of Jude. Of Jude, Marcus Borg writes, “Jude is perhaps the strangest document in the New Testament. It is one of the shortest, about a page long, and is the most enigmatic.” One of the interesting things about Jude is its several references to the Book of Enoch. Enoch, a most fascinating book, is a compilation of apocalyptic writings from Second Temple Judaism. The world view expressed by Enoch played a formative role in the Maccabean revolt celebrated by Hanukah and in the stories of Jesus as told by the gospel writers. Over a century ago R.H. Charles, in an introduction to the Book of Enoch, wrote, “We study the Apocalypses to learn how our spiritual ancestors hoped against hope that God would make all right in the end.” Jude, who powerfully emphasizes God’s judgement on the ungodly, views Enoch as something of a kindred spirit. articles.text: Assembly Bill 1993, which would have mandated COVID vaccinations for all California businesses and independent contractors, was halted by its author, Assemblymember Buffy Wicks. Wicks, who represents Piedmont in the State Assembly, said she is putting the bill on pause to “allow space for conversations to continue and progress.” She introduced the bill to address concerns from employers and constituents who expressed the need for vaccine requirements in the workplace but felt unable to mandate it. “Our priority during this pandemic has been to make sure all Californians are as safe as possible by following the data and science around public health, which is why California continues to have some of the lowest COVID case rates, deaths and injuries per capita,” she said. Wicks added, though, that we are “in a new and welcome chapter in the pandemic, with the virus receding for the moment.” Her hope is to work more collaboratively with labor groups and employers to address concerns and questions raised by the bill. Strong opposition of the bill came from Wicks’ Republican colleagues, namely Assemblymember Kevin Kiley (R - Sacramento) who called the bill “radical.” “While I’m disappointed in the opposition to our bill by public safety unions, it’s my hope that they’ll ultimately come to the table to make sure all of their workers are vaccinated, and that every job sector in California has the tools necessary to keep their workers safe from COVID,” Wicks said. articles.text: Piedmont Community Church will offer special services during Holy Week, beginning on Palm Sunday, April 10 at 10 a.m. A Maundy Thursday service begins at 7:30 p.m. on April 14, preceded by a dinner in Guild Hall at 6:30 p.m. Parents with young families, as well as new members and visitors, are especially encouraged to attend. The cost for the dinner is $15 for adults with a reservation or $20 at the door, and $5 for children age 10-17. Children under 10 are free. For more information, contact Jean Leahy at Jean@Piedmont Church.org to attend. A Good Friday service begins at 7:30 p.m. on April 15. The Sanctuary will be open 30 minutes prior to the Maundy Thursday service and Good Friday service for meditation and reflection. The church will host two traditional Easter worship services on Sunday, April 17 at 8:30 a.m. and 10 a.m. Vaccination (or negative COVID-19 test within 48 hours) and masks required for all services in the Sanctuary. Masks will be available at the door. Piedmont Community Church is located at 400 Highland Avenue.

articles.text: The Clean Water Program, a consortium of agencies in Alameda County that help facilitate the Federal Clean Water Act, will host a free webinar on April 14 entitled “Growing Food the EcoFriendly Way.” Viewers will learn how to grow food in their own backyards, whether they have a “green thumb” or are beginner gardeners. Learn how to use water efficiently and conservatively, how to manage pest problems without the use of chemicals, and how to grow an abundance of food. The webinar begins at 5 p.m., and is part of a monthly series about organic gardening and non-toxic pest control. Classes are presented by Suzanne Bontempo, a certified gardening and pest management advocate, and Charlotte Canner, a certified gardening and composting educator. Visit https://www.cleanwaterprogram.org to register for this free Zoom event. Scan to book your estimate!

articles.text: Girl Scout Troop 33426, a group of nine freshmen at Piedmont High School, ventured to Lake Chabot for a backpacking trip over the 3-day weekend of March 25-27 (no school in Piedmont on Friday). The Scouts hiked with backpacks into the campground the first day, hiked around the entire lake the second day, and hiked from the campground to the exit point on the other side of the lake on the third day. On their down time the girls practiced their first aid skills, knot tying and lashing, and wilderness survival skills in preparation for the annual Girl Scout Skills Camporee on April 30 in Woodside. articles.text: Piedmont families are reading A Thousand Splendid Suns by Khaled Hosseini for this year’s community-wide Readmont project, now in its 12th year. The project culminates with an evening event featuring guest speakers on April 21. A Thousand Splendid Suns, a novel published in 2007, was written by Afghan-American author Hosseini following the success of his debut novel The Kite Runner, which enjoyed a 15-week run as the New York Times No. 1 best-seller. A Thousand Splendid Suns chronicles the story of two women living in Kabul, Afghanistan. According to the Piedmont High School’s English Department, the book was chosen “for its beautiful story of love in an unforgiving time and as a way for our community to discuss the recent events in Afghanistan and the increase of Afghan refugees to the Bay Area.” The book is appropriate for ages 14 and up. For younger readers, the English Department recommends the book I am Malala for ages 10 to 14, and Malala, My Story of Standing up for Girls’ Rights, appropriate for age 6 through 10. Check out a book now at any one of the school libraries. Books are funded through a grant from the Piedmont Appreciating DiverA Thousand Splendid Suns by Khaled Hosseini sity Committee (PADC). A Good Place for Books bookstore in Montclair at 6120 La Salle Avenue is offering a 20% discount on A Thousand Splendid Suns. Piedmont High School (PHS) English Department Chairperson Beth Black and PHS Librarian Kathryn Levenson will facilitate student discussions beginning April 19. The community read will culminate on April 21 with an evening of guest speakers who soon will be named. The evening event is open to the entire community. Questions may be addressed to Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us, or to Black at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us. I Am Malala by Nobel Peace Price winner Malala Yousafzai. articles.text: The following article appeared in the Post on March 10, 2021 when everyone was deep in COVID isolation. COVID has been the absolute worst for screen time and my kids. To say we have increased would be the understatement of the century. My boys use gaming as their only way of connecting with friends, so I say yes, because I know they are lonely and miss their friends. But if the boys are on their screens my daughter wants to be on...and the cycle continues. So, here are five totally wacky ideas to get kids off screens, even if it’s for just a few extra minutes. 1. Ipad Scavenger Hunt Hide the ipad. Yes, for real, hide it really well. Then create a series of clues directing your kids all over the house or backyard – or both – in order to find it. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department is seeking teenage volunteers for its “Summer Sidekicks” camp program. Teenaged “sidekicks” will be paired with campers in adaptive programing to help build relationships and strengthen children’s recreational skills. The Recreation Department is seeking teens age 14 or older who can commit to the summer session to be held on Thursday afternoons for six weeks. A Thousand Splendid Suns, a novel published in 2007, was written by Afghan-American author Hosseini following the success of his debut novel The Kite Runner, which enjoyed a 15-week run as the New York Times No. 1 best-seller. articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop 11 spent the weekend of March 25-27 on an overnight camping trip to Pinnacles National Park near Soledad in San Benito County. Overall, the Scouts were excited about the trip, though they were tired after am epic 12-mile hike on Saturday. Their reward was a Patrol cook-off meal that night. The hike was very hilly with a lot of switchbacks. It went down and flattened out going through two talus caves known as the Balconies cave system. They ate lunch on a ridgeline in the cool shade of a large rock formation. From there they could see both the west and east entrance of the 26,000 acre park, known for its ancient volcanic formation. They went through a large cave, going under rocks that had fallen to create the Bear Gulch caves. They came out of the first cave near a small reservoir, where they took a small snack break. During the hike, the Scouts saw condors, turkey vultures, wild turkeys, deer, and plenty of ground squirrels. They hiked Scouts explore the talus caves. Troop 11 Scouts in the talus caves. The Pinnacles are eroded rock formations from an extinct volcano. Scouts eat lunch at the Pinnacles. Kajsa Benson hikes toward some rock formations. Members of the Moldy Carrots patrol gather for breakfast. Members of the Moldy Carrots and Elder Meese patrol eat dinner at sunset. A baby rattlesnake likes the shade and is making a run for it. The Golden Spatula award winning dinner of spaghetti with a spinach and meatball sauce and salad. Playing cards by lantern light. Troop 11 Scouts at Bear Gulch reservoir.

articles.text: PHS tops San Lorenzo 22-12, Encinal 11-2 Piedmont’s softball team exploded last week with 33 runs in two games, defeating San Lorenzo 22-12 on Wednesday, March 30, and 11-2 over Encinal on Friday, April 1. Both games were at Witter Field. The dominant offensive display was highlighted by Morgan Hunt smacking a grand slam against San Lorenzo and a 3-run shot against the Jets. “I got a new bat,” said Hunt with a laugh. “I just have to believe I can do it and follow through. We’re the top team in the league right now, and if we can continue to hit this way, we’ll be able to make it far.” Staff Photos Senior Izzy Epstein hit her first career home run against Encinal. Gretchen Gerhardy had two RBIs and a run scored against San Lorenzo. Morgan Hunt was all smiles after hitting a three-run homer against Encinal. She also had a grand slam against San Lorenzo. Friday’s win also featured senior Izzy Epstein hitting the first home run of her high school career. She thinks wearing Chiara Lundin’s jersey due to a wash-machine mishap helped get the mojo going. “I was just shocked at first, and then I couldn’t stop smiling. It’s funny because I was wearing Chiara’s jersey, and she hits home runs all the time, and then I hit onel today,” said Epstein. The victories bring Piedmont’s record to 8-2 overall and 4-0 against WACC Shoreline Division teams. 11-2 over Encinal Piedmont scored once in the bottom of the second inning and twice in the bottom of the third. The Jets narrowed the deficit to 3-2 by the fifth inning, but PHS piled on six runs in the bottom of the fifth behind homers by Hunt and Epstein. They added two more runs in the sixth. Piedmont’s monster fifth inning was started by Angelina Wu’s leadoff slap single to center field. Leah Bell was hit by a pitch, putting two runners on base. With one out, Hunt smashed a shot to the left field fence. Lundin reached base on an error, setting up Epstein for her opposite-field home for two runs. In the bottom of the sixth, Lundin got an RBI double to score Miya Fujimoto, and Hunt scored on an error. Final stats: Hunt went 4-for-4 with a home run and a double, four RBIs and three runs scored. Epstein went 3-for-3 with a homer, two RBIs, and a run scored. Wu went 1-for-3 with two runs scored. Fujimoto went 1-for-3 with two runs scored and an RBI. Gretchen Gerhardy went 1-for-3 with an RBI and run scored. Epstein pitched a complete game with seven strikeouts and four hits allowed. 22-12 over San Lorenzo Piedmont led 8-1 after the first inning and 3-2 after the second, but it turned into an offensive barrage by both teams. San Lorenzo rallied to close the score to 15-12 by the fifth, but Piedmont had its own rally for seven runs in the bottom of the sixth, and won by the 10-run rule. Final stats: Hunt had a grand slam for 4 RBIs. Lundin went 3-for-3 with four runs scored. Gretchen Gerhardy went 1-for-3 with two RBIs and a run scored. Julia Banuelos went 1-for-2 with three runs scored and a walk. Bell went 1-for-3 with two runs scored and three RBIs. Wu went 2-for-2 with three runs scored, an RBI and walk. Epstein had a walk and two runs scored. Annabel Castronovo pitched four innings and Ginger Gardner entered in relief for the final two innings. Tuesday vs. Hayward The Highlanders hosted Hayward yesterday, April 5. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-2 overall, 4-0 league) travels to Tennyson in Hayward tomorrow, Thursday, April 7 at 4:00 p.m.

articles.text: Staff Photos Will Sprague (center) celebrates with teammates Peter Krumins (left) and Nico Defazio. Piedmont’s baseball team won two of three games last week, defeating league opponent Hayward 3-2 on Wednesday, March 30 at home, but losing to the same team 4-2 two days later on the road. The Highlanders followed up with a dominant 14-0 win at Oakland Tech on Saturday, April 2. Piedmont’s game-winning run March 30 came when Will Sprague stole home when Hayward tried to catch Markos Lagios stealing second base. Solid base running is a hallmark of an Eric Olson-led ball club. “We were just trying to grind one out. We had to get a guy on and get him over somehow and put some pressure on Hayward. We were able to get Will over to third; that was our ground-attack,” said Olson. Hayward’s team is the best in recent memory. Their pitchers did well with Kiefer Kiley and Nate Cordoba throwing complete games. “We saw at the beginning it would be a battle. They had a good pitcher. We came together in the last inning to grind it out,” said senior shortstop Nico Defazio. 3-2 win over Hayward The Highlanders took a quick 1-0 lead, but Hayward went ahead 2-1 by the in the top of the third inning. PHS tied it in the bottom of the fourth and didn’t score the winning run until the very end, in the bottom of the seventh inning. Pitcher Tobin Cantrill got the start and threw six innings with five strikeouts and six hits allowed. Sprague finished with a 1-2-3 top of the seventh. Piedmont’s opening run came with Lagios drawing a walk and stealing second. He advanced to third on a ground out, and with two outs, Davis Alazraqui smacked a hard ground ball through the infield to score Lagios. Down 2-1 entering the bottom of the fourth, Ryan McConathy drove in Logan Campbell from second with a single through the infield. Hayward tried to throw out Defazio at second base, resulting in Campbell making his way to home. With game tied 2-2 in the seventh inning, Sprague led off by drawing a walk. Lagios came through with a timely infield hit and beating the throw to first base. Sprague advanced to third on the botched throw. With Michael Aikawa at bat, Lagios stole second and the Farmers’ low skipped into centerfield. Sprague raced home for his second game-winning run this season. Final stats: Alazraqui went 2-for-3 with one RBI. Ryan McConathy went 1-for-3 with one RBI. Lagios went 1-for-3 with one run scored, stolen base, and walk. Defazio went 1-for-3. Sprague had a run scored and a walk. 4-2 loss to Hayward The Highlanders led 2-0 by the top of the fourth, but Hayward put up four runs in the bottom of the fourth and neither team produced any more scoring. Final stats: Aikawa went 2-forTobin Cantrill threw six innings with five strikeouts in Wednesday’s win over Hayward. Davis Alazraqui smacked a threerun homer against Oakland Tech.

articles.text: Parker Terrill awarded commemorative buckle for new school record in pole vault It’s not often a school gets to celebrate two new all-time records at the same time. On Saturday, April 2, Piedmont senior Jack Stein had an historic run at the Stanford Invitational, clocking a blazing time of 4:14.77 in the 1600 meters, edging past Tom Phelps’ record set 21 years ago by .15 of a second. In a furiously fast mole race at Stanford, Stein placed 8th in a field of 28 top runners from Photo by Jay Russell Piedmont’s new record holder, pole vaulter Parker Terrill, received an honorary belt buckle for his accomplishment. Northern California. “I didn’t come into the season thinking the mile would be in the book for me, I’m more of a 2-mile guy. I knew the race at Stanford was going to be a really fast race; I had raced some of the people in previous meets, and knew that I was only five seconds away, which was achievable but still difficult in the mile.” “It was so awesome – it was a huge-huge goal and accomplishment. I’m super proud of it,” said Stein. Piedmont’s all-time top-five times in the 1600 Jack Stein, 4:14.77 (2022) Tom Phelps, 4:14.92 (2001) Mark Ceraldi, 4:17.40 (2005) Will Sanford, 4:23.65 (2001) Reece Proctor, 4:24.70 (2017) Stein’s time was a 5-second improvement from his previous best, set March 19 at the Dublin Distance Fiesta. Stein has qualified for the prestigious Arcadia Invitational this weekend, April 8-9, considered the equivalent of the Western Regional championship. “I’m running the 3200 this weekend in Arcadia and it’ll be another fast race,” said Stein. Stanford Invitational Results Cooper Downing also qualified for the Stanford Invitational, and finished seventh of 28 runners in the 800 meters with a blazing time of 1:55.84. articles.text: The Highlander tennis team finished a successful week by beating league rival Berkeley 5-2 on Tuesday, March 29 at home but lost narrowly 4-3 to NCSfoe University on Wednesday, March 30 at Golden Gate Park in San Francisco. PHS then hosted Pleasant Valley from Chico on Saturday, April 2, and won easily 6-1. The University Red Devils won the Div. 2 North Coast Section in 2018 and 2019, so coach Jim Landes knew the match would be close. “If we had stopped this match just after halftime, we would have won handily. We were up 3 -1 with first doubles [Charlie Olcott and Kai Baudendistel] in the third set super breaker and Charlie Lambert and Lenni Burchardt in their second sets. But, we lost all three matches. It was a tough one, but we’ll get them next time,” said Jim Landes. The match at Golden Gate Park came with gusting winds and required major adjustments on the fly by Piedmont players. “The conditions at Golden Gate Park are very windy. Our opponents were very steady players and didn’t miss many shots or give us anything for free. The wind was definitely manageable, but took some getting used to,” said senior leader Kai Baudendistel. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, April 6, 2022 By Jonathan Comeaux It’s not often a school gets to celebrate two new all-time records at the same time. On Saturday, April 2, Piedmont senior Jack Stein had an historic run at the Stanford Invitational, clocking a blazing time of 4:14.77 in the 1600 meters, edging past Tom Phelps’ record set 21 years ago by .15 of a second. In a furiously fast mole race at Stanford, Stein placed 8th in a field of 28 top runners from Photo by Jay Russell Piedmont’s new record holder, pole vaulter Parker Terrill, received an honorary belt buckle for his accomplishment. Jack Stein sets PHS record in 1600 at Stanford Invitational Parker Terrill awarded commemorative buckle for new school record in pole vault Northern California. “I didn’t come into the season thinking the mile would be in the book for me, I’m more of a 2-mile guy. I knew the race at Stanford was going to be a really fast race; I had raced some of the people in previous meets, and knew that I was only five seconds away, which was achievable but still difficult in the mile.” “It was so awesome – it was a huge-huge goal and accomplishment. I’m super proud of it,” said Stein. Piedmont’s all-time top-five times in the 1600 Jack Stein, 4:14.77 (2022) Tom Phelps, 4:14.92 (2001) Mark Ceraldi, 4:17.40 (2005) Will Sanford, 4:23.65 (2001) Reece Proctor, 4:24.70 (2017) Stein’s time was a 5-second improvement from his previous best, set March 19 at the Dublin Distance Fiesta. Stein has qualified for the prestigious Arcadia Invitational this weekend, April 8-9, considered the equivalent of the Western Regional championship. “I’m running the 3200 this weekend in Arcadia and it’ll be another fast race,” said Stein. Parker Terrill placed second of 15 in the pole vault with a height of 13 feet, 9.25 inches, four inches below the winner, Owen Arreguy of Rocklin. Terrill recently set a school-record of 15 feet, 5 inches. The lower heights at Stanford were the result of a later-start in the early evening hours, causing athletes’ Photo by Steve Zirkelbach Jack Stein broke a 21-year old school record in the 1600 meters with a time of 4:14.77. poles to lose its flexibility due to the cold wind at Stanford’s Angell Field. On Tuesday, April 5, at Witter Field, Terrill was awarded a commemorative belt buckle for setting a new school record. Terrill also competed in the Shimansky Pole Vault Invitational at San Ramon Valley on Saturday, April 2 and won with a height of 14 feet, 6 inches in a field of nine vaulters. articles.text: Girls’ team wins 3-way meet with O-Dowd, San Leandro Photos by Katherine Rolfeson Tyler Dacanay (right) is congratulated after one of her two wins against Alameda. The high school swim team raced twice in successive days last week. The girls’ team defeated Bishop O’Dowd and San Leandro in a 3-school meet at San Leandro on Thursday, March 31, and the boys’ team finished second, five points behind O’Dowd. The following day, both the girls’ and boys’ teams lost to Alameda at the Encinal pool. It marks their final appearance prior to Spring Break. They will return on April 22 with a 3-way meet with league opponents Mt. Eden and Encinal. The season-ending Western Alameda County Conference Championship Meet is set for April 29 at Chabot College. Girls win meet with San Leandro, O’Dowd The PHS girls won all three relay events to propel them to victory. The relay team of Sonja ten Grotenhuis, Taylor Rolefson, Josie Oesterer, and Kate Aubrecht won the 200 freestyle, and the same foursome clocked 1:57.69 to also win the 200 Individual Medley relay. The 400 free relay team of Maddie Payne, Annika Nilsson, Shelby Cavenaugh and Odessa Dando also won with a time of 4:13.6. Taylor Rolefson won the 100 Butterfly with a time of 1:03.4 and placed second in the 200 Free Andrew Grasman in the 100 backstroke against Alameda. with a North Coast Section consideration time of 2:02.64. Josie Oesterer won two events, the 200 IM in 2:20.92 and the 100 Back in 1:02.2. Kate Aubrecht won the 50 Free in 24.8 and Maddie Payne was second in 26.2. Aubrecht also placed second in the 100 Free in 54.71 seconds. Cavenaugh won the 100 Breast with a time of 1:19.3. The boys won the 200 IM Relay in 1:45.29 with Simon Lins, Ryan Stokes, Tom Rolefson, and Evan Byun. The team of Lins, Stokes, Rolefson and Farris Saffouri won the 200 Free relay with a time of 1:32.27. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 11am-5:30pm 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org

articles.text: Piedmont’s volleyball team took a pair of losses against Western Alameda County Conference opponents last week, falling 3-0 to division power Berkeley (25-20, 25-17, 25-18) on Tuesday, March 29, and falling in a narrow 3-2 battle against Arroyo of San Lorenzo (25-11, 25-22, 17-25, 21-25, 16-14) on Thursday, March 31. “Those were tough losses,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. “That was the first game that went to five sets for us; it was amazing. The boys played so well and worked so hard.” The pair of matches brings Piedmont’s overall record to 4-4, with four league matches remaining; Castro Valley away on April 7, at home against Encinal for Senior Night on April 21, at San Leandro on April 26, and at Alameda on April 28. The Highlanders earlier defeated Encinal 3-0 on March 16 and Alameda 3-1 on March 8. To qualify for North Coast Section, PHS must finish with a .500 overall record, league record, or record against Div. 3 NCS teams. They are currently 1-1. In their match with the Dons of Arroyo, Piedmont responded well after dropping the opening two sets, powering their way to 25-17, 25-21 wins in the third and fourth to force a fifth-set 15-point tiebreaker. Piedmont held match point in the fifth set, 14-13, but Arroyo won three straight points for the 16-14 win. “We couldn’t get it together in the first set but we came out swinging in the second set and knew that the third- and fourthset were meant for us,” said team captain Wilson Wong. “In the end, there were a lot of calls that got into our heads and we let it slip, but they were a good team. I definitely think we can beat them.” 3-2 loss to Arroyo The Highlanders dropped the opening two sets but the Dons began to lose their accuracy in the third set, leading to PHS claiming the first three points and an eventual 7-2 lead. But the Dons scored eight straight points to jump ahead 10-7, PHS regained the lead at 11-10, but conceded five straight to trail 15-11. From there, Piedmont scored 10 straight points for a 21-15 advantage. Mason Kimball then got two spikes to lead 24-17, and Higashi helped get the winShunji Higashi gets ready for a serve. ner with a serve that was mishandled, 25-17. In the fourth set, PHS took five of the first six to lead 5-1 but the Dons went on to tie it 7-7. The two sides traded points until PHS inched ahead at 15-11. Arroyo narrowed the gap until the Highlanders moved in front at 20-18. Piedmont won five of the next seven points with a spike from Wilson Wong and a few errors by Arroyo. The fifth-set tiebreaker featured four lead changes until an extra point at 16-14 in favor of Arroyo. The Dons opened 2-0, but PHS went ahead 4-3 thanks to an ace by Kimball. From there, Arroyo tied the match four times until PHS held an 11-9 lead. Arroyo went ahead 12-11, and the teams traded points ahead until PHS took a 14-13 lead for match point. However, the Highlanders had a shot go into the net, 14-14, a Piedmont block attempt went out, 15-14 Arroyo, and a block deflected out of bounds, allowing the Dons to claim victory. Final stats: John Champion had three kills and three aces. Kai Lambert had two kills and one ace. Wong had 11 kills and two aces. James MaNguyen had one kill. Felix Broach had one kill. Owen Kelly had two kills. Kimball led the way with 15 kills and one ace. 3-0 loss to Berkeley The Highlanders took a threeset loss against Berkeley, 25-20, 25-17, 25-18. Final stats: Higashi had one kill and two aces. John Champion had two kills and an ace. Kai Lambert had two kills and an ace. Wong had six kills and one ace. Owen Kelly had three kills. Kimball had four kills and an ace. Tuesday vs. Bishop O’Dowd The Highlanders played at Bishop O’Dowd yesterday, April 5, but lost. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-5) travels to Castro Valley tomorrow, Thursday, April 7 at 5:15 p.m. Mason Kimball powers a spike against Arroyo.

articles.text: Shotgun Players is presenting a production of Passing Strange now through April 23. Directed by William Thomas Hodgson with music direction by Daniel Alley, the play follows the story of a young Bohemian who charts a course for “the real,” through sex, drugs and rock and roll. The play is set in Amsterdam, Berlin, and middle-class America. The show won a Tony Award for Best Book of a Musical. “Watching Passing Strange changed me and changed what my art could be. I just saw myself in this.” said director Hodgson. “There’s just something about the rock nature of this where I’m just having such a good time. The commune between the actors, the musicians, and the audience feels like centering in a theatre experience. There is something that’s so accessible in this play and in the writing.” The cast includes Angel Adedokun, Rolanda Bell, Myles Photo by Ben Krantz Devin Cunningham with Myles Brown (left), Angel Adedokun, Chanel Tilghman, and Shakur Tolliver in Shotgun Players’ current production of Passing Strange. Brown, Devin Cunningham, and Albert Hodge. For tickets, see https://shotgunplayers.org. Shotgun Players is located at 1901 Ashby Avenue in Berkeley. Tel.(510) 841-6500.

articles.text: Work of 40 artists to be displayed Piedmont’s 3rd annual Art Walk will take place in neighborhoods through the city on Saturday, May 7, and will feature 40 local artists representing a wide array of art. Under the leadership of founders Jon Schleuning and Larraine Seiden, the outdoor art exhibit will showcase paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, photography, jewelry, and textile art. The displays will be in front of or near the artists’ homes. All art will be on sale, and 20% of the proceeds will be donated to the Piedmont Education Foundation to support art programs in Piedmont schools. More than $17,000 was raised at last year’s Art Walk. Visit https://piedmontartsfund. org/piedmont-art-walk-2022 to view featured artists.
articles.title: Annual Art Walk Scheduled for May 7

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is currently showing Water by the Spoonful through April 23. Winner of the 2012 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, Quira Alegria Hude’s play is a heartfelt medPhoto by Jessica Palopoli Salim Razawi and Xander DeAngeles in the Water by the Spoonful, now playing at San Francisco Playhouse. itation on lives on the brink of redemption. Set in Philadelphia, Eliot has returned from Iraq and is working at a Subway sandwich shop while trying to jumpstart his acting career. “Quiara Alegría Hudes’s masterful Pulitzer Prize winner speaks even more profoundly to our world today,” said Bill English, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director. “Separated from friends and loved ones by the pandemic, we, like the characters in Water by the Spoonful, celebrate our human resourcefulness, which will overcome any distance to build connection and hope.” The play is directed by Denise Blasor. To obtain tickets, visit https:// w w w.sf playhouse.org /sf ph / upcoming-plays/. Proof of up-todate vaccination is required to attend. Berkeley Symphony presents LIBBY LARSEN

Under the leadership of founders Jon Schleuning and Larraine Seiden, the outdoor art exhibit will showcase paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, photography, jewelry, and textile art. The displays will be in front of or near the artists’ homes. All art will be on sale, and 20% of the proceeds will be donated to the Piedmont Education Foundation to support art programs in Piedmont schools. More than $17,000 was raised at last year’s Art Walk. Visit https://piedmontartsfund. org/piedmont-art-walk-2022 to view featured artists. By Allyson Aleksey Shotgun Players is presenting a production of Passing Strange now through April 23. Directed by William Thomas Hodgson with music direction by Daniel Alley, the play follows the story of a young Bohemian who charts a course for “the real,” through sex, drugs and rock and roll. The play is set in Amsterdam, Berlin, and middle-class America. The show won a Tony Award for Best Book of a Musical. “Watching Passing Strange changed me and changed what my art could be. I just saw myself in this.” said director Hodgson. “There’s just something about the rock nature of this where I’m just having such a good time. The commune between the actors, the musicians, and the audience feels like centering in a theatre experience. There is something that’s so accessible in this play and in the writing.” The cast includes Angel Adedokun, Rolanda Bell, Myles Photo by Ben Krantz Devin Cunningham with Myles Brown (left), Angel Adedokun, Chanel Tilghman, and Shakur Tolliver in Shotgun Players’ current production of Passing Strange. Brown, Devin Cunningham, and Albert Hodge. For tickets, see https://shotgunplayers.org. Shotgun Players is located at 1901 Ashby Avenue in Berkeley. Tel.(510) 841-6500. Water by the Spoonful at SF Playhouse through April 23 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Playhouse is currently showing Water by the Spoonful through April 23. Winner of the 2012 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, Quira Alegria Hude’s play is a heartfelt medPhoto by Jessica Palopoli Salim Razawi and Xander DeAngeles in the Water by the Spoonful, now playing at San Francisco Playhouse. itation on lives on the brink of redemption. Set in Philadelphia, Eliot has returned from Iraq and is working at a Subway sandwich shop while trying to jumpstart his acting career. “Quiara Alegría Hudes’s masterful Pulitzer Prize winner speaks even more profoundly to our world today,” said Bill English, San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director. “Separated from friends and loved ones by the pandemic, we, like the characters in Water by the Spoonful, celebrate our human resourcefulness, which will overcome any distance to build connection and hope.” The play is directed by Denise Blasor. To obtain tickets, visit https:// w w w.sf playhouse.org /sf ph / upcoming-plays/. Proof of up-todate vaccination is required to attend. articles.text: Grammy-nominated musician Art Lande will perform at Piedmont Piano Company at 5 p.m. on Saturday, April 9. He will be joined by guitarist Tim Wendel and saxophonist Carl Schultz. Lande is known internationally for his innovative approaches to teaching piano, improvisation, and ear training. He currently resides in Boulder, Colorado, and taught music and piano in Switzerland. articles.text: Jules Leyhe and The Family Jules Band brings some of the East Bay’s finest musicians to the Piedmont Center for the Arts for a show on Saturday, April 23. The band features saxophonist Nancy Wright, keyboardist Ian McArdle, and drummer Isaac Schwartz, who bring a funky jazz flavor to Leyhe’s fantastical vision. Leyhe’s eighth and most recent CD release, Your First Rodeo, has been featured in Premier Guitar and Vintage Guitar magazines. The band looks forward to playing an intimate East Bay show in Piedmont. A 2008 graduate of Piedmont High School and Berklee College of Music in Boston four years later, Leyhe’s career has included performances with legendary musicians Buddy Guy, Jimmie Vaughan, Huey Lewis, Chris Cain, Charlie Musselwhite, and Fantastic Negrito. Leyhe twice performed the National Anthem for the Oakland A’s at the Oakland Coliseum last year, and performs the Hendrix version of the National Anthem each year in the Piedmont 4th of July Parade. During COVID, Leyhe spent time as tour manager for blues legend Taj Mahal. The Family Jules Band stayed busy during COVID, recording three albums. Recent highlight performances include The Club Fox in Redwood City and Napa’s esteemed Blue Note. Tickets for the family-friendly concert in Piedmont are available online at https://bpt.me/5418175. Your First Rodeo CD This ain’t your granddaddy’s blues – heck it ain’t even your daddy’s blues. On this CD guitarist Jules Leyhe is on an entirely different trip, juxtaposing futuristic elements with down-home tones. He has been featured in Guitar Player, Premier Guitar, and Vintage Guitar. His album, Your First Rodeo, is a whimsical mashup of blues, hip-hop, fusion, rock and Latin music. Picture Duane Allman jamming with jazz piano great Gil Evans, or Jimi Hendrix playing in Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band. Jules Leyhe will perform at the Piemdont Center for the Arts on April 23.

articles.text: World Harmony Chorus, directed by Betsy Blakeslee, invites adults to learn stunning 4-part a cappella arrangements in Spanish, Quebecois, Maori and Turkish and be part of the chorus’ next performance. articles.text: Piedmont High School and Middle School musicians will present a chamber music recital of solo and small ensemble pieces on Friday, April 22 at 7 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. articles.text: Piedmont alum Raphael Gold and the Diluvian String Quartet will perform a concert of chamber music inspired by the New World. Come be part of an intimate evening of music at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, April 29 at 7 p.m. The quartet includes Elizabeth Castro Abrams and Jessica Scrimale, violin, Raphael Gold, viola, and Sylvia Woodmansee, cello. The program includes String Quartet No. 1 by Heitor Villa-Lobos, Five Pieces for String Quartet by Erwin Schulhoff, and Antonin Dvořák’s masterful String Quartet No. 12 in F Major (“The American”). The concert will feature works inspired by the great American music of the turn of the 20th century, including pieces by composers Antonin Dvorak, Heitor Villa Lobos, and Erwin Schulhoff. You’ll hear quotes and rhythms from jazz, tango, and folksong. Proof of vaccination is required.

articles.text: The introduction to Mr. Sandman uses arpeggiated chords called turnarounds in an exercise-like manner with an “up-down” design: four arpeggio tones ascending one chord, then four arpeggio tones descending the next. Jazz improvisers began their development practicing such melodic designs but developed them into endless variations. Turnarounds became common in bebop through contemporary jazz music in the improvisations of Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Sonny Rollins, Stan Getz, Joe Pass, Barney Kessel, Wes Montgomery and George Benson. ter “Modal II-V-I Cadences and Turnarounds”. Read the first section, Overview: http://guitarimprov.com/zc-Modal_II_V_I_ Cadences_and_Turnarounds.pdf Variations of the Mr. Sandman turnaround design include six directional types of turnarounds, octave displacement, varying the order of chord tones, syncopation, pickups, pushes, substitute chord progression and chromaticized turnarounds. Turnarounds”/Building Turnarounds (link above). When a song is said to be in a key, a main note is the focal point of the piece of music. Sense of key can be defined in many ways, including the root of the chord you would expect the piece to end on. A chord “root” is the lowest imaginable note in a chord. You can play a “C” major chord with a “G” in the bass (one of its three notes), but if you imagine the lowest note played in the bass in a classic ending, the lowest imaginable note would be “C”. For common chords (triads, sevenths, ninths), organizing the notes of the chords in thirds (F-A-C-EG-B-D-F, etc.) would show the chord root as the lowest pitch. The common chord progression that establishes the I chord as a key (the “C” chord in the key of “C”) is V to I (“G” to C”). An elaboration of that idea evolved in classical music in creating a secondary progression to play the “V” of the “V” chord. In terms of the key of I (“C”), “V of V” is “II”. Dm-G-C is IIm-V-I in C. For a melodic example of II-V-I turnarounds, check out Hold Your Peace (“Post Columns” link below). Also play turnarounds in chords. Progressive Late To Pickup Cadences (“Post Columns” link below) previews the harmonic use of II-V-I cadences while also showing top voice leading, cadence rhythms and comping rhythms. The eight examples progressively start II-V-I cadences earlier in the bar, showing they can be earlier at faster tempos. articles.text: Entries due by April 15 Filoli House and Garden in Woodside is conducting a haiku contest based on its spring blooms. Interested participants may submit entries by April 15 and may submit up to three original haiku poems. The poems should be in the traditional haiku form of three short lines of five, seven, and five syllables. Submissions in languages other than English are strongly encouraged as long as they follow the haiku poem structure. Filoli is also launching the Filoli Ecopoetry Award this year, awarded to an individual whose haiku engages with the connection between humans and the environment. Haiku submissions should be inspired by Filoli’s spring garden and blooms. Judges will look for work that is eco-conscious and critical as well. By Jim Gleason The introduction to Mr. Sandman uses arpeggiated chords called turnarounds in an exercise-like manner with an “up-down” design: four arpeggio tones ascending one chord, then four arpeggio tones descending the next. Jazz improvisers began their development practicing such melodic designs but developed them into endless variations. Turnarounds became common in bebop through contemporary jazz music in the improvisations of Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis, John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Sonny Rollins, Stan Getz, Joe Pass, Barney Kessel, Wes Montgomery and George Benson. See the Guitar Improv chapter “Modal II-V-I Cadences and Turnarounds”. Read the first section, Overview: http://guitarimprov.com/zc-Modal_II_V_I_ Cadences_and_Turnarounds.pdf Variations of the Mr. Sandman turnaround design include six directional types of turnarounds, octave displacement, varying the order of chord tones, II-V-I Turnarounds syncopation, pickups, pushes, substitute chord progression and chromaticized turnarounds. See “Modal II-V-I Cadences and Turnarounds”/Building Turnarounds (link above). When a song is said to be in a key, a main note is the focal point of the piece of music. Sense of key can be defined in many ways, including the root of the chord you would expect the piece to end on. A chord “root” is the lowest imaginable note in a chord. You can play a “C” major chord with a “G” in the bass (one of its three notes), but if you imagine the lowest note played in the bass in a classic ending, the lowest imaginable note would be “C”. For common chords (triads, sevenths, ninths), organizing the notes of the chords in thirds (F-A-C-EG-B-D-F, etc.) would show the chord root as the lowest pitch. The common chord progression that establishes the I chord as a key (the “C” chord in the key of “C”) is V to I (“G” to C”). An elaboration of that idea evolved in classical music in creating a secondary progression to play the “V” of the “V” chord. In terms of the key of I (“C”), “V of V” is “II”. Dm-G-C is IIm-V-I in C. For a melodic example of II-V-I turnarounds, check out Hold Your Peace (“Post Columns” link below). Also play turnarounds in chords. Progressive Late To Pickup Cadences (“Post Columns” link below) previews the harmonic use of II-V-I cadences while also showing top voice leading, cadence rhythms and comping rhythms. The eight examples progressively start II-V-I cadences earlier in the bar, showing they can be earlier at faster tempos.
