articles.text: Matthias Schoenaerts stars in The Mustang. The Mustang is beautifully made, raw and unsparing, as well as being an example of fine writing. What might have been an obvious, shallow metaphor is instead a subtle and nuanced character study that resonates and compels. The story begins with a wide-angle shot of a large herd of wild horses roaming free on desert rangeland with a haze of blue mountains in the distance. Smash cut to these same horses being rounded up and herded by helicopter into large corrals. Some will be taken to Nevada’s Ely State Prison and become part of a Wild Horse Inmate Rehabilitation Program where prisoners are each given a horse to tame and then sold at auction to the Border Patrol, law enforcement, or private parties. That is the context. The narrative focuses on one inmate, Roman Coleman (Matthias Schoenaerts), doing 12 years for domestic violence. He has recently been released from solitary confinement and will again enter the prison’s general population, something he would rather avoid. “I’m not good with people,” he says. This opening scene shows Roman seated across from a staff psychologist-counselor (Connie Britton) who asks him a series of inane questions. Roman sits in silence, his laconic responses, when he makes them, barely audible, his emotional revetments impenetrable. Absent much discussion, she assigns Roman to an outdoor maintenance detail, cleaning stalls and corrals which means shoveling manure. This is his introduction to the horses and to the inmates who work with them. His attention is drawn to a ragged shed containing a wild mustang that is kicking and banging against the walls. Curious, he looks through an opening and then begins to open a narrow door, but is harshly admonished to stay away from the shed by the director-trainer for the wild horse program, Myles (Bruce Dern), who sends him back to his shovel and wheelbarrow. What is almost immediately evident is that the caged horse and Myles and the men who work with the horses have captured Roman’s attention. It’s not long before Myles senses the silent inmate’s interest. Pointing to the mustang now in a small corral, he explains that if he can spend just five seconds alone with the mustang, he is in the program. And thus begins what will be a difficult and painful journey for both Roman and this wild, dangerous, seemingly untamable animal that refuses to yield to its confinement. It’s evident that Roman faces not only the lethal rage of the mustang but his own. He is told by Myles that if he cannot control his anger (he confronts the mustang with his fists) he will be judged unfit for the program. He chooses to stay. This is a film of spare dialogue yet contains deep currents and a riptide of unexpressed emotions. What is revealed is a master class in acting, delivered by Schoenaerts. In one powerful scene, his estranged pregnant daughter, Martha (Gideon Adlon), barely out of her teens, comes to visit him for the first time in years. She wants only for him to sign a document allowing her to sell her grandmother’s house. He does, too quickly, and then tells her not to come back. But he fails to initial several pages and so she returns for a second and then a third time. With each visit, Roman’s wall of torment and alienation crumbles, a reality that is never conveyed by what he says but by the anguish etched in face, his attempt to look away into the distance failing him. And it’s in the final visit that Shoenaerts delivers what can only be described as a transcendent moment, the camera holding on his haunted eyes as he reveals to his daughter his remorse for the damage he has done to his family (and himself). Barely able to glance across the table, struggling for each word, he searches for a sign of redemptive forgiveness from Martha. But Roman finds his daughter protected by her own long ago constructed walls of judgment and memory. She simply stands and leaves. Roman’s journey is a given, but is not crafted from a series of clichés, nor does it find surcease in melodrama. Rather, it is created by writer/director Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre in such a direct and honest way that she finds the story’s metaphoric sweet spot and never backs away. If there is redemption to be found, it begins in the singular corral where that wild horse gives not an inch until it does. For Roman that makes all the difference. The Mustang is a wonderful movie. The Mustang. Directed by Laure de Clemont-Tonnere. Starring Matthias Schoenaerts, Gideon Adion, Bruce Dern, 1 hr., 36 min. Rated R. Now streaming on HBO Max/Prime. Originally published in the Post in 2019.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Mustang an uplifting story of redemption

articles.text: David Sheff and his son Nic, the inspirations for the movie Beautiful Boy. Beautiful Boy is an adaptation of two memoirs, written by journalist David Sheff (Beautiful Boy) and his son Nic (Tweak). The titles for Sheff’s book and the film are lifted from John Lennon’s tender lullaby Beautiful Boy, composed for his son, Sean: “Have no fear, the monster’s gone/ He’s on the run and your daddy’s here.” It’s a haunting song and threads its way throughout the narrative, sometimes so softly it’s all but a whisper. And indeed, this film is about that ever-present promise that reassures: daddy’s here regardless of what life brings, so be not afraid. The monster is on the run. Only in Beautiful Boy the monster is crystal-meth (and other drugs) which grips David’s (Steve Carell) talented, gifted teenage boy, Nic (Timothée Chalamet), sending his life out of control, a spiraling descent into the jaws of addiction, He battles all who love him – his mother, Vicki (Amy Ryan); his stepmother, Karen (Maura Tierney); and his two small siblings who are impacted by the familly chaos that is felt but not understood. Nic’s journey into addiction is framed by a harsh and unforgiving anger and denial – remorse, reflexive dissembling, recrimination – as well as a sense of profound helplessness on the part of his father in Marin County and mother in L.A.. To describe Nic as he drifts away is to attempt to find an adequate metaphor. Perhaps it’s as if he is drowning, slipping under the waves, just within reach As he is momentarily pulled into the frantic embrace of his family, he slips from their grasp and so the cycle begins again: clean, sober, home, relapse, rehab. The anguish is palpable. The impotence is heartbreaking as Nic and his family confront a drug so powerful it actually alters the physiology of the brain. It is the monster. Early in the film there is a scene when David meets Nic at a small diner and they sit in a booth across from one another. David’s sense of desperation is evident, writ large in the grim set of his fearful eyes and his clenched jaw, wanting only to reach across the table and embrace his son with his words, to rescue Nic from demons that neither understands. It’s a harrowing scene, doomed before the first word is spoken, the ravages of Nic’s addiction there, before them. When he finally does get up, his stinging words suspended in the air, David is left to sit alone with his pain and isolation. He wonders what can he do? His beautiful boy. Throughout the film, director Felix Van Groeningen threads a series of fragile flashbacks of father and son together, each vignette conveying how deeply Nic is cared for. The cycle of addiction transforms those tender reflections into a dark dream in which Nic takes a wrecking ball to all of their lives. Truth is the casualty – spoken, shouted and ultimately framed by betrayal. Reason (you can do this, we can do this, rehab can do this) – becomes the unreliable scaffolding that is never enough. Beautiful Boy is a punishing story, difficult to watch, unrelenting in its unfolding, while also engaging and compelling. Over and over it reminds the viewer that addiction doesn’t just happen to the addict but to all who want only that beautiful boy back. The cast is superb, each portrayal convincing. The performances by Carell and Chalamet are remarkable, each a tour de force. Whenever David and Nic embrace and say goodbye, they whisper to each other one word, “Everything.” If only that word had the force and power to defeat the monster. Beautiful Boy. Directed by Felix vanGroeningen. Starring Steve Carell, Timothée Chalamet, Maura Tierney. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated R. Originally pubished in the Post in 2011.
articles.title: Beautiful Boy a harrowing tale of addiction

articles.text: There’s a spoken line in the remarkable 2022 Oscar-nominated animated feature film The Mitchells vs. the Machines that is so quietly offered up, it will likely go unnoticed nu many viewers. Katie, the teen daughter of Rick and Linda Mitchell now away at college, in a zoom conversation with her parents, is asked the typical parental questions: “Are you getting enough to eat? How’s class?” But then Linda asks two unexpected questions, though not unexpected for the Mitchell family. Linda asks Katie, “Are you and Jade official?” Followed by, “Will you bring her home for Thanksgiving?” And with those questions, the film introduces a gay character (Katie wears a rainbow pin throughout). This zoom scene, which takes place during the denouement of the story, is included intentionally by co-directors Michael Rianda and Jeff Rowe. Rianda explained, “This is who she is. We wanted to say that this is a realistic family. We also did a lot of iterations to find the right balance. Ultimately, the story is about dealing with your family, and not about Katie’s sexuality. Her hair is red, she likes girls, and it’s normal. If it’s normal in real life, why isn’t it normal in animation?” We learn that before arriving at college Katie has been zooming with fellow students. One of them is Jade (Sasher Zamata), and it is made clear that the friendship has turned romantic once Katie arrived at the school. In thinking about this aspect of the film, it occurs to me that in all the animated films I’ve screened, I don’t recall ever even a nod being given toward a gay teen, or seeing a handicapped kid in a supporting role. Certainly there are countless handicapped youngsters who are enamored with animated feature films, and seeing a familiar face would be uplifting. Ditto Katie. articles.text: Hollywood writers have gotten a lot of mileage out of the dysfunctional family road trip, one that relies on a familiar trope: what can go wrong will go wrong. It usually results for the audience in headshaking chuckles to outright laughter. The Mitchells vs. The Machines is no exception. It was released in theaters and to Netflix streaming in April 2021, and received an Oscar nomination for Best Animated Feature Film at this year’s Academy Awards. At the center of this hilarious, emotive film is Katie Mitchell (Abbi Jacobson), a teen who loves movies, yearns to be a filmmaker, and dreams of moving to California, heartland of the fantasy industry. She lives with her mom, Linda (Maya Rudolph), a teacher and maker of grotesquely charming cupcakes; a pug named Monchi; her little brother Aaron (Mike Rianda), obsessed with dinosaurs; and her dad, Rick (Danny McBride), a hulking outdoors, Mr. fix-it guy with whom she doesn’t quite feel at ease. But then he’s the kind of guy who considers a non-slip screwdriver the perfect birthday gift, loves to build stuff, and worries that Katie’s dream of making movies will likely end in failure. So father and daughter are at an emotional impasse, and their relationship is often fraught with door-slamming tension and hurt feelings. Rick, confused, wonders where his little girl (who believed he could do anything) has gone, causing him to ask: who is this budding, newbie teen-stranger called Katie? Inspired, believing he has found a solution that will bring the family closer, Rick decides that what the family should do is not say goodbye to Katie at the airport as she heads off to college, but cancel her ticket and take a family road trip instead. Katie is not so sure, even a little mortified at the thought of arriving at her new college with (gasp) her parents. Nevertheless, so begins a series of really “wide-eyed”, “good grief ” misadventures from food poisoning to a visit to a seedy dinosaur theme park, all punctuated with minor family squabbles. Let’s just say that there is a lot going on, much of it hypermanic, filled with a variety of reactions that give new meaning to the term “bug-eyed.” Act three, unexpectedly, involves techie stuff, involving a hoodie-wearing IT guy named Mark Bowman (Eric André), a billionaire who has invented countless bots, and smart phones implanted with the ubiquitous voice of PAL (Olivia Colman). The bots are deemed benign and created to serve their master… oh, sure. As it turns out, the bots have a scheme to send all the humans into outer space and then create a bot-machine utopia. Naturally, it’s up to the Mitchells to save the world and undermine the bot plan and thereby avoid an impending apocalypse. The animation dazzles, the plot is a media-mix of cacophony and wonderfully stylized, audacious lunacy. But at the center of all the chaos is the Katie-Dad relationship in which they team up to save the world, and in the process affectionately realize the importance of the talents they each possess. Kids will be dazzled by the animation and the story. The Mitchells vs The Machines. Computer animation. Directed by Mike Rivanda and Jeff Rowe. With voices of Abbi Jacobson. Danny McBride, Maya Rudolph. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG. Now streaming on Netflix/Prime. Originally published in the Post in April 2021.

pages.text: Wednesday, April 6, 2022 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS The Mitchells a groundbreaking animation story By Chris Honoré There’s a spoken line in the remarkable 2022 Oscar-nominated animated feature film The Mitchells vs. the Machines that is so quietly offered up, it will likely go unnoticed nu many viewers. Katie, the teen daughter of Rick and Linda Mitchell now away at college, in a zoom conversation with her parents, is asked the typical parental questions: “Are you getting enough to eat? How’s class?” But then Linda asks two unexpected questions, though not unexpected for the Mitchell family. Linda asks Katie, “Are you and Jade official?” Followed by, “Will you bring her home for Thanksgiving?” And with those questions, the film introduces a gay character (Katie wears a rainbow pin throughout). This zoom scene, which takes place during the denouement of the story, is included intentionally by co-directors Michael Rianda and Jeff Rowe. Rianda explained, “This is who she is. We wanted to say that this is a realistic family. We also did a lot of iterations to find the right balance. Ultimately, the story is about dealing with your family, and not about Katie’s sexuality. Her hair is red, she likes girls, and it’s normal. If it’s normal in real life, why isn’t it normal in animation?” We learn that before arriving at college Katie has been zooming with fellow students. One of them is Jade (Sasher Zamata), and it is made clear that the friendship has turned romantic once Katie arrived at the school. In thinking about this aspect of the film, it occurs to me that in all the animated films I’ve screened, I don’t recall ever even a nod being given toward a gay teen, or seeing a handicapped kid in a supporting role. Certainly there are countless handicapped youngsters who are enamored with animated feature films, and seeing a familiar face would be uplifting. Ditto Katie. A scene from the Oscar nominated animation movie, The Mitchells vs. The Machines. articles.text: Napa Valley, the most famous wine-growing region in America, is divided into 16 different American Viticulture Areas (AVA). It is the government’s attempt to bring some sort of order and clarity to the labeling of wine. In addition to deciding what is and is not included under the term Napa Valley, it sets up subregions to give even more detailed information about where the grapes were grown. One of my favorite AVAs is Calistoga tucked into the northern part of Napa Valley. The town of Calistoga is only 8 miles north of St. Helena in the heart of the valley, but it seems about two decades away. St. Helena has become gentrified, tourist-filled and upified, and has gone way upscale. Calistoga on the other hand still seems to have some country roots from a simpler time. It is just a more down-home place. • 2017 Bragg Cabernet Sauvignon Mario’s Vineyard Bragg Vineyards is a boutique family winery producing only about 125 cases of wine per year. This 100% Cabernet has a wonderfully hedonistic perfume of roses, chocolate, and anise over a core of cassis, blueberries and blackberry pie plus wafts of tobacco and leather. Full-bodied and beautifully structured with ripe fine-grained tannins, it has vivacious fruit and a long, fragrant finish. • 2017 Kenefick Ranch Cabernet Franc Caitlin’s Select This family-owned winery has been a favorite in years past and this year’s Cabernet Franc is no exception. Unlike the Cab Francs from France’s Loire Valley, this wine is beautifully ripe and full of fruit with no vegetal tones. It has a black currant scented nose, sweet, rich, full-bodied blueberry flavors, and smooth tannins on the finish. The wine is nicely textured and pure and should age well for two decades. In most places in North America, the farther north you get the cooler the temperature becomes. Napa Valley is the opposite. Because of the presence of San Pablo Bay at the bottom of Napa Valley the southern region of Carneros is the coolest part of Napa Valley. Calistoga at the northern end is the warmest. It can get very toasty there and growers have no trouble getting their grapes to ripen fully. Calistoga is at least 300 feet above sea level, with vineyards up to 1,200 feet above sea level. The AVA has the most extreme diurnal swing in Napa Valley, meaning it has the highest changes in average daytime and nighttime temperatures which tend to give the grapes better balance. The Calistoga AVA is also blessed with a high percentage of volcanic soils which give good drainage and tends to concentrate the flavor within the berries. The area also has the highest rainfall in Napa Valley which keeps grapes from suffering during water shortages. Calistoga is mostly famous for their Cabernet Sauvignons and the grapes makes up 56% of the plantings in the AVA. The Calistoga Wine Growers Association held a tasting in San Francisco in February and I had the opportunity to taste from many of the area’s most outstanding wineries. The quality of the wines at the tasting was extremely high making it difficult to separate the good from the great. At the end of the day the following wines were the ones that stood out. These are the best of Calistoga. • 2017 Poggi Cabernet Sauvignon Diamond Mountain District The Poggi family’s tiny micro winery quietly turns out one of Calistoga’s finest Cabernets. This wine exhibits a beautiful nose of flowers, tobacco, crème de cassis and blueberries. Young and fresh and fabulously concentrated, the wine impresses with its intensity, complexity and youthfulness. It will probably not peak in quality for a decade and has 20 to 30 years of aging potential. Try also the lovely sister wine from the Twin Palms Vineyard. • 2015 Tom Eddy Cabernet Sauvignon Tom Eddy is a revered figure in Napa Valley wine – a true

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok A dish of Curry Codfish cakes is a nourishing and tempting meal. INSTRUCTIONS Easy enough for a weeknight dinner, these curry codfish cakes do not skimp on flavor nor appealing presentation. We have a version of codfish cakes on a nearly weekly basis. Curry flavors are near the top of the list of favorites, but I often change the flavor profile depending on what I’m craving; Spanish, Mexican, Thai, Chinese – well, you get the idea. Celery, shallots (or onion), diced tomatoes for moisture, and cilantro are staples in most versions. If you do not enjoy cilantro, flat-leaf parsley, mint or other herbs can be used as substitutes. Bonus Hint: Omit the raw egg and serve this delicious mix as a salad! I leave the crackers in larger pieces or toast up a piece of naan bread for extra crunch. Curry Codfish Cakes Makes 4 fish cakes INGREDIENTS • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • 1 pound codfish fillet, fresh or thawed 2 whole bay leaves 1 lime, divided into about 1/4 of it sliced to add to poaching liquid, the remaining lime juiced for adding to the codfish cake mixture 1 stalk celery, about 1/2 cup finely diced 1 medium shallot, about 1/2 cup finely diced 1/2 cup diced fresh tomatoes 1/2 cup fresh cilantro, coarsely chopped 1 generous tablespoon mayonnaise 1 tablespoon extra-virgin olive oil 2 teaspoons Dijon mustard 1 extra-large egg 3/4 cup coarsely crushed saltine crackers 1 tablespoon curry powder blend, to taste 1 teaspoon sea salt, to taste 5–6 whole black peppercorns, plus an additional 1/2 teaspoons freshly ground pepper, to taste Position an oven rack to the lower third position. Preheat the oven to 375°F, or on convection roast setting to 350°F. Line a baking sheet with parchment paper (optional but eases release of the fish cakes from the pan and clean-up). Poach the codfish: Place fillets, lime slice, bay leaves and a few black peppercorns into a 2-quart saucepan. Add water to just barely cover. Bring the water to a low simmer over medium heat, then continue cooking for about 6–7 minutes. Cooking time will vary depending on the thickness of the fish. Check as needed to ensure the fish just loses its transparency. Remove thinner pieces if needed. Important: Resist over-cooking. Drain and set aside to cool. If you fear you’ve overcooked the fish, cool it quickly with a bath of cold water. Combine the egg, mayonnaise, mustard, olive oil, lime juice, curry powder, sea salt and black pepper in a small bowl. Set aside. In a large bowl, mix the celery, shallot, tomatoes, cilantro, and cracker crumbs together. Flake the codfish fillets into the bowl, taking care to leave some of the pieces at least about onehalf inches in diameter. Gently mix the fish with the vegetables and crackers, then finally fold in the wet ingredients. Take care to preserve some large flakes of fish. Divide the fish cake mixture into four portions and shape into patties about 1-inch thick. Place on baking sheet and bake for 15-18 minutes until lightly browned and egg is fully cooked. If you use an instant-read thermometer, the middle of a fish cake should reach 160°F. Serve as-is, but a quick salsa of the same vegetables used in the fish cakes, with some minced jalapeno pepper or added cayenne pepper for a bit of zippy heat, is a nice upgrade.
articles.title: Curry Codfish Cakes

I’m glad that is now changing. This is a huge wine, oozing dark jammy fruit, chocolate, tar and leather. It shows considerable depth and richness in a style that delivers most of its pleasure right away. Crank up the grill, throw on the burgers and pop the cork on this beauty. Produced and bottled by Romeo Vineyards. • 2019 Solario Family Syrah This Syrah is deeply colored and boasts attractive aromas of black cherries, mocha, vanilla and hints of tobacco on the nose. It is medium bodied, silky-textured, and nicely proportioned overall with a long, savory finish. I can see this as a great partner to roast pork or carnitas. • 2018 Girard Zinfandel Old Vine This is a wonderfully energized, deep, rich, full-bodied Zinfandel with terrific levels of black raspberry, strawberry, and cherry fruit as well as lavender, ground pepper and Provencal herbs. The finish is long, smooth, and tannin-free. It should continue to offer gorgeous drinking for at least another decade. articles.text: A large group was on hand March 30 for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays excursion. Pictured are: Priscilla Wanerus, Lynn Richmond, Jo Normington with K-9 best friend Penny Lane, Alicia Rivera, Charlene Louie, Dena Belinkoff, Ken Young, Kat Lang, Judy Wang, Harriette Louie, Alan Goldhammer, Tyler Johnson, Jim Kuo, Marion Lim Yankowitz, SiowFang Tan, Mike Henn, Pat McMahon, Martin Levy, Brenda Ferrero, Pat Sheehan, Pat Keller, Sherry Jacobs, Edith Lee, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Albert Chen, Renee Goldhammer, and Dick Carter. On a cool Wednesday morning, March 30, 28 walkers and one K-9 best friend were at the Exedra for the weekly Walking on Wednesdays stroll through the city. The group wanted to complete some unfinished business. In February the Post had reported on two Public Works projects, retaining walls on San Carlos and Oakland Avenue. The destination this day was Oakland Avenue at Sunnyside Avenue, which the group had not seen since its retaining wall was completed. The walk took the group across the Oakland Avenue Bridge and on Sunnyside, Lake, Linda, and Rose Avenues to see the northwest side of Piedmont. Based upon information from Gail Lombardi, president of the Piedmont Historical Society, Oakland Avenue Bridge was the historic entrance to Piedmont. Albert Farr designed it in 1910 as a significant entrance to Piedmont. Farr used the same Spanish design that he had used in the Piedmont City Hall and the Bonita Avenue School (later named Havens School). The bridge replaced an old wood trestle that was built in 1890 for the cable cars that served the area in its early years. The bridge was designed in 1911 by John Buck Leonard of Union City, Michigan, who was a pioneering bridge designer, architect, and early advocate for reinforced concrete structures. It is a concrete arch bridge over Linda Avenue with a 160-foot arch span and retaining wall supported approaches in a closed spandrel concrete deck arch design. The largest span is 159 feet and the total length is 343 feet, which is more than a football field. The new lampposts, lights, and guardrails make the Oakland Avenue Bridge a lovely entrance to the city. At the high end of the bridge is the new retaining wall. The walkers continued up Sunnyside to Lake Avenue, then onto Linda Avenue past Beach School. One block later they came to the lovely fully landscaped Linda-Kingston Triangle built in 2016 as a project paid by the city and neighborhood residents. A handsome stone bench was built into the wall facing out to Linda Avenue at the 3-way corner of Linda, Kingston and Rose Avenue, one of the city’s boundary with the city of Oakland. The group crossed Linda and went a short distance up it to Rose Avenue. It was reported that this is one of the oldest streets in Piedmont. Actually, only the south side of the street is in Piedmont. The Oakland/Piedmont city line runs through the middle of it, and its north side homes are in Oakland. The walkers noted a beautiful, restored, gray with white trim “Cottages & Castles” Victorian built in 1894. A set of stairs leads up to its front door and there are a turret and two gables as part of its roof. The walkers crossed Grand Avenue and went down (and up) Arroyo Avenue to Monticello Avenue. They noted a hidden pathway that goes to the Lorita Avenue cul-de-sac, which they had missed on a previous walk. The group turned onto Ramona Avenue and made their way to the well named Bonita Avenue (pretty in Spanish). A right on Bonita brought the group back to Magnolia Avenue, where they passed lovely cedar shake shingle homes, draught tolerant gardens, pink dogwoods, emerging red bud blossoms, primroses, and other front yard beauty; as well as Havens School playground enthusiasts. The walkers emerged on Magnolia, one block from their starting point. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome nu registering with the Piedmont Recreation Department at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. FUTURE WALKS On April 20 and 27 Hope Salzer will take the walkers on sneak preview tours of two Piedmont gardens that will be part of the 18th Annual “Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Features Showcase.” After that former Piedmont Mayor Bob McBain will host the walkers on a visit to Tyson Lake at the back of his Sotelo Avenue home. articles.text: Nearly 60 years ago, Rachel Carson’s New York Times bestseller Silent Spring was published. Many consider the book to be a catalyst for the modern environmental movement. Throughout the following decade, many landmark moments shaped the world. From the passage of over 300 federal environmental protection regulations from 1963 to 1969, to the 1969 oil spill in Santa Barbara, and the celebration of the first Earth Day in 1970, that decade of U.S. history marked a major turning point for environmentalism. On April 22, 1970, the United States celebrated its first Earth Day, mobilizing an estimated 20 million Americans in a national teach-in and celebration, largely thanks to the work of U.S. Senator Gaylord Nelson and activists Denis Hayes and John McConnell. The first international Earth Day occurred in 1990, mobilizing 200 million people in 141 countries. Over the past 52 years, Earth Day has become an annual international event, celebrating both the history of the environmental movement and encouraging citizens of the world to invest in the planet. Today, Earth Day is considered one of the largest secular observances in the world and is celebrated throughout the month of April. Many Earth Day celebrations are returning in person after two years of virtual programs, centering on the theme of “Invest in Our Planet.” The City of Piedmont will be celebrating Earth Day with a family-friendly Earth Day Scavenger Hunt, a community forum on the City’s Reach codes, and a free compost giveaway. Details and registration information for these events can be found on Piedmont’s Earth Day website page. For more information, visit https://www.piedmont.ca.gov/ services___departments/planning___building/about_building_/earth_day. Annie Wensley is Piedmont’s Climate Action Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: In-person tour on April 30 and May 1 The 18th annual Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour will include the gardens of Piedmont residents Nancy Mckee-Jolda and Robert Jolda, and Hope and Larry Salzer on Saturday, April 30. Tours of Bayside gardens take place April 30 and Inland gardens take place May 1. A virtual tour is available April 16 and 17. The tour invites those who register to tour water-conserving native plant gardens that feature plants native to California and its varied climate. “What’s special about California native plants? They are adapted to our soil and climate, naturally water conserving, and easy to care for,” said tour media contact Kathy Kramer. “California native plants are better than non-native plants when it comes to attracting native birds, butterflies, and other forms of wildlife. And, as the gardens on the Tour show, these lovely gardens display a sense of place that is uniquely Californian.” Registrants will have an opportunity to learn how to design a native plant garden that is rich in color and is symbiotic with its surrounding environment. Many gardens on the tour attract pollinators, including butterflies, bees, and avian life. Salzer explained that attendHope and Larry Salzer’s garden will be featured in the upcoming Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour. ing past garden tours inspired her to create a native-dominant, wildlife-friendly garden. Her efforts began when she moved to Piedmont in 2010 and accelerated throughout the pandemic. This will be her first year on the tour. “During the last two years of the pandemic, we replaced our final lawn areas, transforming them into native meadows. We’ve also planted over a dozen varieties of native trees,” she explained. “It’s still a work in progress, but the transformation is lovely. We also host two beehives on our property, have installed a fullhouse greywater system, make Nancy Mckee-Jolda and Robert Jolda’s garden is featured in the upcoming in-person Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour on April 30. articles.text: There is something to recommend each of these perspectives. In that evil is undoubtedly alive and well, often seeming to driven by its own life force, I find the perspective of Enoch to be worthy of serious consideration. Equal in importance to Enoch’s understanding of evil is its articulation of hope. In its apocalyptic worldview, hope is outside human striving. It is not created by human intention. It is solely the will and work of God. Expressive of this hope are the four archangels Enoch identifies: Michael, Raphael, Gabriel and Phanuel. Michael is “merciful and long-suffering.” Raphael is “set over all the diseases and all the wounds of the children of men.” Gabriel is “set over all the powers.” Phanuel is “set over the repentance unto hope of those who inherit eternal life.” In Enoch’s vision, evil is alive and well. Yet, so is divine hope. Divine hope is not dependent on our efforts. It comes from God alone. It comes on the wings of angels who have power over those forces that hurt and harm. for aging. In fact, virtually all of the fine architectural designs we see employ a hierarchy to this end, with massing, fenestration, or detailing composition that results in these punctuation point(s). Often they depart somewhat from the main overall style or character of the building, but remain compatible enough to relate to, enhance, and enrich the overall appearance. This is all a matter of degree, and certainly can be overdone. But the opposite, the absence of punctuation or architectural feature, would be an unimaginative, stark, repetitive building, examples of which are obvious, and far too common, in our built environments.
